title: Responsive Website Design Service
description:
Responsive Website Design Service: The Architectural Breakdown

In the digital landscape, responsive website design is not merely an option but a necessity. It ensures that your website adapts seamlessly across all devices, from smartphones to desktops, enhancing user experience and driving engagement. However, relying on standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms often falls short of delivering a truly effective responsive design. Let's delve into why these approaches fail and explore the engineering principles that underpin a successful responsive website design service.

Why Off-the-Shelf Templates and Generic Forms Fail

  1. Lack of Customization: Off-the-shelf templates are designed for a broad audience, which means they can't cater to the specific needs of your business. They often lack the flexibility to incorporate unique branding elements, functionalities, or user experiences tailored to your audience.

  2. Performance Issues: Generic forms and templates are not optimized for performance. They may include unnecessary code, bloated assets, or inefficient practices that slow down your website, leading to higher bounce rates and poorer search engine rankings.

  3. Inadequate Adaptability: While these templates may claim to be responsive, they often fail to provide a truly seamless experience across all devices. They might not account for varying screen sizes, touch interactions, or device capabilities, resulting in a suboptimal user experience.

Three Concrete Engineering Takeaways

  1. User-Centric Design: A successful responsive design prioritizes the user experience. It involves understanding your target audience's behavior, preferences, and pain points. By conducting thorough user research and creating personas, you can design interfaces that are intuitive, accessible, and engaging across all devices.

  2. Performance Optimization: Responsive design

title: SQL Interview Question: MAX(created_at) Doesn’t Return the Latest Order
description:
Finding the newest timestamp is easy. Keeping the right row, handling ties, and putting the filter in the right place takes a little more care.

Someone asks for the latest order for each customer, and your brain happily reaches for GROUP BY and MAX.

Honestly, fair enough. The question practically waves a little flag at an aggregate function.

Then the interviewer asks for the order ID, its status, and the amount. Two orders have the same timestamp, and one customer’s newest order is cancelled. Suddenly, finding the latest time is only a small part of the job.

I prefer treating this as a row-selection problem before treating it as a SQL problem. We need to decide which complete record wins, not collect impressive-looking values from different records.

Let’s work through a small original example, then change one sentence in the requirement and watch the answer change with it. There is no giant dataset to hide behind here, which is rather convenient for catching our own assumptions.

Give yourself five rows that refuse to cooperate

Our orders table contains customer_id, id, created_at, status, and total_cents. Each order has a unique ID. Customer IDs, timestamps, and statuses are non-null, and all times shown below are on the same date.

Customer A has three orders. Order 11 was paid at 09:00 for 9,000 cents. Orders 12 and 13 both arrived at 10:00; order 12 is paid for 2,000 cents, while order 13 is cancelled for 3,000 cents.

Customer B has one paid order, ID 21. Customer C has one cancelled order, ID 31.

For the first requirement, return exactly one latest order for every customer represented in this table, regardless of status. If timestamps tie, choose the larger order ID. That tie-breaker is an agreed rule for this exercise, not a claim that a larger ID always represents a later real-world event.

Before writing anything, the expected winning IDs are therefore 13, 21, and 31.

Having that answer on paper makes the query much easier to judge. A plausible result is not enough; we already know which rows the contract requires.

MAX gives you a value, not the rest of its row

This query correctly answers which timestamp is greatest for each customer.

SELECT customer_id, MAX(created_at) AS latest_at
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;

It does not answer which complete order to return. For customer A, two rows share that maximum timestamp.

Joining the result back to orders on customer and timestamp can return both. That may be correct if the request is to return every order tied for latest, but it does not satisfy our exactly-one-row rule yet.

Another tempting repair is to add MAX(total_cents) to the grouped query. Please trace that against customer A before trusting it. You get 10:00 and 9,000 cents, even though no order in the input contains that combination.

Each maximum was calculated independently. The result has quietly assembled a record that never existed, which is quite an achievement for such a short query.

Adding ordinary non-grouped columns is not a reliable solution either. PostgreSQL rejects this form when those columns are not functionally determined by the grouped columns. We need an explicit rule for selecting a row.

Rank the complete records, then keep the winner

Use a window function to number each customer’s orders. The first ordering field defines latest; the second resolves a tie.

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT customer_id, id, created_at, status, total_cents,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY customer_id
           ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
         ) AS rn
  FROM orders
)
SELECT customer_id, id, created_at, status, total_cents
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY customer_id;

For customer A, order 13 receives row number one, order 12 receives two, and order 11 receives three. The other customers each have one row, so their numbering starts at one too.

All the selected fields now come from the same record. We have not asked the database to guess which status belongs beside an aggregate timestamp.

PostgreSQL’s window-function tutorial explains that ROW_NUMBER numbers rows within a partition and that tied rows have an unspecified numbering order. That is why our unique ID belongs in the ordering clause when exactly one deterministic winner is required.

Also notice the final ORDER BY customer_id. Ordering inside the window decides how to assign row numbers; it does not promise the presentation order of the final result.

If the requirement changes to returning every row tied at the latest timestamp, the ranking rule changes too. A rank based on created_at alone can preserve those ties. Adding a unique ID to that ranking would separate the very ties you were asked to retain.

Moving one filter changes the question

Now suppose the request becomes latest paid order per customer.

We should exclude cancelled rows before ranking, so the eligible population contains only paid orders. In the previous query, add WHERE status = 'paid' immediately after FROM orders inside the CTE.

Customer A now returns order 12. Customer B still returns order 21. Customer C has no paid order, so C has no result under this version of the contract.

But here is a different request that sounds dangerously similar. Return each customer’s latest order, only when that latest order is paid.

This time, rank all orders first. Then use WHERE rn = 1 AND status = 'paid' in the outer query. Customer A disappears because A’s winning row is cancelled. Only customer B remains.

Both queries run. Neither needs to throw an error. They answer different questions because one filter determines who may compete, while the other checks the winner after the competition.

That is the sentence I want to be able to explain in an interview. Memorizing the window-function syntax helps, but it cannot decide which population the business meant.

Keep the missing customer when the requirement asks for them

So far, our population comes from orders. A customer with no orders is invisible, and a customer with no eligible paid order disappears when we filter before ranking.

If the output must contain every customer, start from a separate customers table and left join the selected order onto it. Keep rn = 1 in the join condition or in a prefiltered winners relation.

Putting WHERE ranked.rn = 1 after that left join removes the null-extended rows, so customers without a match disappear again. That would undo the inclusion rule you were trying to implement.

Decide how to represent the absence of an order. Null order fields mean no match; a made-up zero amount would blur that distinction with a real zero-value order.

If timestamps can be null in the actual dataset, define their meaning before removing our non-null assumption. Unknown time is not automatically the oldest or newest event, and default null ordering differs across databases.

Make the counterexamples do the reviewing

The quickest useful check is to compare the exact selected IDs and their associated values, not just the number of output rows.

For this dataset, the three versions should produce these results.

  • Latest order regardless of status returns A → 13, B → 21, C → 31.
  • Latest paid order returns A → 12 and B → 21.
  • Latest order, only if paid, returns B → 21.

Then add a customer with no orders, create another timestamp tie, and change which tied row is paid. If your query still matches the written rule, you have better evidence than a clean run on a perfectly polite dataset.

For production data, inspect the execution plan rather than promising that a window function is automatically cheap. An index beginning with (customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC) may help the ordering access path, but filters, row counts, selected columns, and the database planner still matter. This all-customer query may process many rows even when it returns few.

For a useful next variation, try this salary-history and top-earner exercise. It asks you to identify the latest employee-department record before choosing the highest-paid employee in each department. That adds a second selection stage, so getting the first population right becomes even more important.

I like leaving this kind of practice with a small question I can reuse. Am I calculating a property of a group, or selecting a particular member of that group?

Once that distinction is clear, the query becomes much easier to explain. More importantly, every timestamp, status, and amount in the answer can point back to the row that actually earned its place.

~ Emily

title: Copies Are Not Confirmations: How News Duplication Fools LLM Judges and Continual Learners
description:
arXiv:2611.09203v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Many news reports of a claim are copies of one source: wire stories, content shared within a media group, syndicated features and press releases. We ask whether LLM judges and continual learners treat such copies as independent confirmations. In 200,000 English CC-News articles, a MinHash detector links 18.9% to a near-copy from another outlet (precision 0.97 once boilerplate is removed); it links 92% of edited reprints to their originals but none of the LLM rewrites by phi4, Llama 3.2 or Gemini 2.5 Flash. Shown three identical reprints of a claim about an unknown person instead of one report, Llama 3.2 3B and phi4 14B raised the share of lies they accepted from 0.06 to 0.71 and from 0.21 to 0.90 and ignored a note that the reports came from one source; Gemini 2.5 Flash already believed a single report, and Gemini 2.5 Pro followed provenance notes and tables. In a simulated continual-learning stream, showing the judge one report per detected chain cut the copied lies it accepted by 0.10-0.24 across four judges, at a mean cost of no more than 4.2 percentage points of accepted truths. Against reworded copies, a test of how many of a report's named entities are absent from an earlier look-alike separates LLM rewrites from 100 labelled independent reports of the same event with AUC 0.98-0.99 and wrongly flags one; entity overlap alone does as well, TF-IDF and a current embedding model come close, and the test catches few natural same-source derivatives. With the miss patterns of generated rewrite networks, it cut the reworded-copy lies accepted from 0.67 to 0.20 (0.40 when the rewriter invents details). Counting reports or chains alone is not a reliable defence, the effect of provenance information depends on the judge, and colluding sources remain the open problem. Code and labels: https://github.com/Metalesaek/copies-experiment

title: MetaのQuest 2時代が終わる——それは「VR科学」の終わりではなく、次の章の始まり
description:
MetaのQuest 2時代が終わる——それは「VR科学」の終わりではなく、次の章の始まり

MetaがQuest 2とQuest Proのサポート終了を発表しました。両機種は来年初頭に最後のOSアップデートを受け取り、来春に控えるMeta VR Glassesへ向けて、同社はHorizonOSの開発リソースを新しいハードウェアへ移していく方針を示しています。

このニュースを見て「VRはもう下火なのか」と受け取った人もいるかもしれません。しかし、教育や研究の現場でVRを使ってきた立場から見ると、これはむしろ逆の合図です。ハードウェアの世代交代は、その上で動くソフトウェアが“汎用のデモ”から“専門的なワークフローの一部”へ進化するタイミングだからです。プラットフォームが変わるたびに、生き残るのは「そのデバイスでしか成立しない体験」です。そして分子科学ほど、その条件に近い領域はありません。

フラットな画面に閉じ込められてきた構造生物学

構造生物学の日々の仕事を思い浮かべてください。タンパク質の立体構造は、いまも多くの場合、フラットなモニタ上でマウスによって回転させられ、論文用の図として切り取られます。しかし、結合ポケットの奥行き、リガンドの向き、電子密度の重なり、水素結合の角度——これらの情報は本来、紙の上や画面の中でなく、その構造の“中に立って”見るべきものです。

エンジニアの言葉で言えば、これは「次元の圧縮」です。3次元のデータを2次元の射影に落とすとき、奥行きの情報は失われます。回転させて角度を変えれば補える——そう考えるかもしれませんが、視点操作のたびに頭の中で座標変換を走らせるのは、人間の認知にとって安い処理ではありません。特に結合ポケットの内部のように、複数の残基が狭い空間で絡み合う領域では、この変換コストが理解のボトルネックになります。

教育の場面でも同じです。ヘモグロビンに酸素が結合する瞬間、解糖系でグルコースが分解される過程、アスピリンがCOX酵素を阻害する仕組み、CRISPR-Cas9がDNAを編集する様子。どれも図解では伝わりきらない“スケール感”と“空間の感覚”を持っています。教科書の矢印は結果を教えてくれますが、その矢印が空間のどこで起きているかは教えてくれません。

NexoPeekという答え合わせ

Seven Sportzが手がけるNexoPeekは、Meta Quest向けのVR分子ラボです。ヒトスケールでタンパク質の内部に足を踏み入れ、6つの柱にまたがる12本のナレーション付きツアーを歩くことができます。

柱は「Biotechnology Basics」「Foundations of Life」「Pathways & Interactions」「Medicines in Action」「Genetic Technologies」「Green Biotech」の6つ。初学者が最初の一歩を踏み出すための入口でありながら、専門家が構造を確認するための視点も同じ空間に用意されています。ツアーは一本道の動画ではなく、立ち止まり、見上げ、くぐり抜けるための道として設計されています。

プロフェッショナル向けのPDBビューアも搭載しました。遺伝子名からRCSB PDB、UniProtKB、AlphaFold DB、SWISS-MODEL、PDBeを横断して構造を解決し、ヒトスケールで読み込みます。Mol*プリセットのワンタップで、カートゥーン、ボールアンドスティック、スペースフィル（CPK）、分子表面、Bファクターのヒートマップ、チューブトレースへ表現を切り替え可能です。ローカルの.pdb、.cif、.mol2ファイルを読み込めば、静電場のラインマップや電子密度ボリュームも表示できます。

地味ですが重要なのは、ここが「ビューアの移植」ではないという点です。デスクトップの分子ビューアは、あくまで画面という窓越しに構造を見せます。NexoPeekは視点そのものを構造の内側に置きます。同じデータ、同じ表現プリセットでも、参照系が変わるだけで、結合ポケットの“圧迫感”やリガンドの“収まり方”が手触りとして伝わります。

解析ベンチでは、素手（またはVRコントローラ）で分子をつかみ、拡大し、回転させます。AIポケット予測が創薬候補サイトを光らせ、Foldseekが相同構造を重ね合わせ、Ligand Inspectorが水素結合をたどり、PubChemから3Dリガンドを引き出します。トリガーで2つの原子を選べば、その間の距離をオングストローム単位で報告します。配列中の残基“ピル”をタップすると、構造上に3Dハローが投影されます。

これらの機能は、外部の検証済みツールやデータベースを呼び出す形で成り立っています。独自の予測モデルを売りにするのではなく、すでに研究者が信頼しているパイプラインを、空間の中で操作できるようにする——それがこのラボの設計思想です。だからこそ、Quest 2の引退はこの体験の終わりではなく、より良いトラッキングとより軽いヘッドセットでの再出発を意味します。

世代交代の先にあるもの

Quest 2のサポート終了は、没入型サイエンスの終わりではありません。むしろ、こうした体験が“見せ物”ではなく“道具”として定着し始めたからこそ、プラットフォームが次の世代へ進むのです。

ハードウェアの寿命は短く、ソフトウェアの寿命は長い。Quest 2という筐体が消えても、その上で育ったワークフローは次のデバイスへ引き継がれます。教育機関がVRラボを予算化し、研究室が構造解析の一工程としてVRを組み込む——そうした動きが、世代交代を“終わり”ではなく“更新”に変えます。

NexoPeekは教育・研究視覚化のためのソフトウェアであり、医療上の助言・診断・治療を提供するものではありません。ポケット予測やアラインメントなどの解析支援機能は、検証済みの科学的パイプラインと専門家の判断を補助するものであり、それらに取って代わるものではありません。

Meta QuestでNexoPeekを入手する: https://www.meta.com/experiences/nexopeek/1453797551140347/

title: CoBit: Language Modeling with Bitstream Diffusion
description:
arXiv:2605.07013v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce CoBit, a continuous diffusion language model that generates text by jointly denoising fixed-width binary token codes. Grouping each code's bits into a single Transformer patch preserves sequence length while replacing vocabulary-wide predictions with $\lceil\log_2 V\rceil$ bit logits. A matched-filter residual parameterization supplies the analytic isolated-bit posterior, leaving the network to learn contextual corrections. Stochastic sampling on an entropy-rate grid provides the largest empirical gain; the grid allocates both solver resolution and effective Langevin correction to noise levels where information is resolved. At 256 denoiser evaluations, CoBit-S (130M parameters) achieves generative perplexity 59.76 on LM1B and 27.06 on OpenWebText, at unigram entropies 4.31 and 5.26, respectively. Scaling to 462M parameters improves OpenWebText generative perplexity to 19.48 at entropy 5.40. Beyond open-ended text generation, CoBit achieves 65.9% exact-match accuracy on hard Sudoku. On GSM8K, score-temperature scaling with an untempered final integration step raises CoBit-S accuracy from 28.1% to 35.3% without additional denoiser evaluations, placing it within the reported range of temperature-tuned discrete diffusion baselines. Matched-trunk profiling also shows lower peak memory and higher throughput than a dense token-output baseline.

title: Design a Notification System: Queues, Retries and Fan-out
description:
Design a notification system looks simple. Send an email, a push, an SMS. Done.

Then the interviewer asks: What if the email provider is down? What if a user gets the same push twice? What if you need to notify 5 million followers at once? That is where the real design starts.

This post walks through a clean answer to notification system design, step by step.

1. Clarify requirements first

Ask before you draw:

  • Which channels? Push, email, SMS, in-app.

  • Real-time or can it be delayed?

  • Do users have preferences (mute, quiet hours)?

  • Scale: notifications per day, peak bursts.

Non-functional goals: no lost notifications, no duplicates, low latency for urgent ones (OTP), and one slow channel must not block the others.

2. High-level architecture
Service A ─┐
Service B ─┼─► Notification API ─► Validate + Preferences ─► Message Queue(s)
Service C ─┘ │
┌───────────────────────┼──────────────┐
▼ ▼ ▼
Push Worker Email Worker SMS Worker
│ │ │
APNs/FCM Email provider SMS provider

Key decisions:

  • Decouple with a queue. Callers get an instant "accepted" response. Spikes don't hit providers directly.

  • Separate queue per channel (and per priority). An SMS outage should not delay emails.

  • Stateless workers so you can scale each channel independently.

3. Fan-out: one event, millions of users

When one post notifies 5 million followers, don't loop inside the API request. Publish one event, then let a fan-out service expand it into per-user messages in batches.

Fan-out on write: create per-user notifications immediately. Fast reads, heavy writes.
Fan-out on read: compute when the user opens the app. Cheap writes, slower reads.

4. Retries with exponential backoff

Providers fail. A good worker retries, but not blindly.

import random
import time

MAX_RETRIES = 5

def send_with_retry(message):
    for attempt in range(MAX_RETRIES):
        try:
            provider.send(message)
            return "sent"
        except TemporaryError:
            if attempt == MAX_RETRIES - 1:
                dead_letter_queue.publish(message)
                return "failed"

            delay = min(30, 2 ** attempt)
            time.sleep(random.uniform(0, delay))

Three things to say out loud:

  • Backoff stops you from hammering a struggling provider.

  • Jitter stops all workers retrying at the same second.

  • Dead-letter queue (DLQ) keeps failed messages for inspection and replay.

5. Avoiding duplicates

Queues usually guarantee at-least-once delivery, so duplicates will happen. Fix it with an idempotency key:

def handle(message):
    key = f"sent:{message.notification_id}:{message.channel}"

    # Check if already processed
    if redis.get(key):
        return "already_processed"

    # Send notification
    result = send_with_retry(message)

    # Mark as processed after successful sending
    if result == "sent":
        redis.set(key, "1", ex=86400)

    return result

Same notification ID, same channel, processed once.

6. Preferences, rate limits and priority

  • Preferences check before queuing: opted out, quiet hours, channel choice.

  • Per-user rate limit so a bug upstream doesn't spam someone with 200 pushes.

  • Priority queues: OTP and security alerts must never wait behind marketing campaigns.

7. Tracking status

Store each notification with a status: queued → sent → delivered → opened / failed. Providers send delivery callbacks (webhooks) that update this table. It powers analytics and debugging.

Interview checklist

  • Clarified channels, scale and latency needs

  • Queue between API and workers

  • Separate queues per channel and priority

  • Retries with backoff, jitter and a DLQ

  • Idempotency key for deduplication

  • Preferences and rate limiting

  • Delivery tracking

Practice it for real

Knowing the pieces is one thing. Explaining the trade-offs under a timer is another. If you want hands-on system design practice instead of just reading, ScaleDojo has 220+ interactive labs across HLD, LLD, API design and GenAI/RAG, so you can build designs like this and get feedback.

What would you add to this design? Drop it in the comments.

title: Building a Resilient Offline-First Telemetry Collector in Python for Edge IoT Devices
description:
Why Edge Devices Need Offline Resilience

When deploying IoT sensors in remote environments such as greenhouses or agricultural fields, internet connectivity is rarely guaranteed. If a sensor node fails to reach the cloud database, critical telemetry data like temperature, pH, or electrical conductivity can be permanently lost.

In this tutorial, we will build a lightweight Python telemetry collector that buffers sensor readings locally in SQLite during network outages and automatically flushes them to a remote API once connectivity is restored.

Architecture Overview

  1. Ingestion Layer: Reads incoming JSON payloads from local microcontrollers (such as an ESP32 over HTTP or MQTT).
  2. Local Buffer (SQLite): Acts as a persistent write-ahead queue when the upstream cloud endpoint is unreachable.
  3. Sync Worker: A background loop that checks network health and batches pending records to the cloud.

Setting Up the Local Buffer

First, let's create a simple SQLite schema to store unsent telemetry payloads safely on disk:

import sqlite3
import json
import time

DB_PATH = "telemetry_buffer.db"

def init_db():
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    cursor.execute("""
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS pending_metrics (
            id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
            device_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            payload TEXT NOT NULL,
            created_at REAL NOT NULL
        )
    """)
    conn.commit()
    conn.close()

def save_locally(device_id: str, metrics: dict):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    cursor.execute(
        "INSERT INTO pending_metrics (device_id, payload, created_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
        (device_id, json.dumps(metrics), time.time())
    )
    conn.commit()
    conn.close()

Implementing the Batch Sync Worker

Next, we create a worker function that attempts to push buffered readings to our cloud ingestion endpoint. If the request fails due to a timeout or connection error, the records remain safely stored for the next retry cycle.

import urllib.request
import urllib.error

CLOUD_ENDPOINT = "https://example.com"

def flush_buffer(batch_size: int = 50):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    cursor.execute(
        "SELECT id, device_id, payload, created_at FROM pending_metrics ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT ?",
        (batch_size,)
    )
    rows = cursor.fetchall()

    if not rows:
        conn.close()
        return

    batch = [
        {
            "id": row[0],
            "device_id": row[1],
            "metrics": json.loads(row[2]),
            "timestamp": row[3]
        }
        for row in rows
    ]

    try:
        req = urllib.request.Request(
            CLOUD_ENDPOINT,
            data=json.dumps({"records": batch}).encode("utf-8"),
            headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
            method="POST"
        )
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=5) as response:
            if response.status in (200, 201):
                ids_to_delete = [(row[0],) for row in rows]
                cursor.executemany("DELETE FROM pending_metrics WHERE id = ?", ids_to_delete)
                conn.commit()
                print(f"Successfully synced {len(rows)} records.")
    except urllib.error.URLError as e:
        print(f"Network unavailable, keeping records in buffer: {e}")
    finally:
        conn.close()

Key Takeaways

  • Zero Data Loss: Using SQLite as a local queue guarantees that transient Wi-Fi drops never erase historical sensor trends.
  • Batch Efficiency: Sending 50 records in a single HTTP POST reduces TLS handshake overhead and lowers cloud API costs.
  • Idempotency: Always include the original created_at edge timestamp so backend dashboards plot metrics when they actually occurred, not when they arrived.

title: Watching an exchange's reserves after regulatory news, in 30 lines of Node
description:
The news

On November 6, 2026, FinCEN issued an order that bars US financial institutions from processing funds transfers involving the exchange MEXC Global. Treasury alleges the exchange facilitated at least $16 billion in transactions linked to sanctions evasion and cybercrime. The order takes effect 30 days after it is published in the Federal Register. (FinCEN release, Cointelegraph)

Cointelegraph's article cited DefiLlama for MEXC's total assets that day: about $4.48 billion. I wanted to see that number move, so I wrote a script that reads the same data.

Where the data comes from

DefiLlama tracks exchange wallets that the exchanges themselves have disclosed. The public endpoint https://api.llama.fi/protocol/<slug> returns a chainTvls object with one time series per chain. Two kinds of keys matter:

  • plain chain names (Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana…) hold third-party assets in the disclosed wallets
  • keys containing OwnTokens hold the exchange's own token, which says little about customer reserves, so the script drops them

The series can hold more than one point for the current day (midnight plus the latest reading), so the script keeps the last value per chain per day before adding chains together. My first version summed every point and showed today's reserves at nearly double, which is a good bug to know about if you use this API.

The script 

// reserve-watch.mjs
// usage: node reserve-watch.mjs <defillama-slug> [days=10]
const [slug = 'mexc', daysArg = '10'] = process.argv.slice(2);
const days = Number(daysArg);
const res = await fetch(`https://api.llama.fi/protocol/${slug}`);
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`DefiLlama answered ${res.status} for "${slug}"`);
const p = await res.json();

const byDay = new Map();
for (const [chain, data] of Object.entries(p.chainTvls)) {
  if (chain.includes('OwnTokens')) continue;
  const last = new Map();
  for (const { date, totalLiquidityUSD } of data.tvl) last.set(new Date(date * 1000).toISOString().slice(0, 10), totalLiquidityUSD);
  for (const [day, v] of last) byDay.set(day, (byDay.get(day) || 0) + v);
}
const rows = [...byDay.entries()].sort(([a], [b]) => a.localeCompare(b)).slice(-days);
const base = rows[0][1];
const usd = (n) => `$${(n / 1e9).toFixed(2)}B`;
console.log(`${p.name}: tracked reserves without its own token, last ${rows.length} days`);
for (const [day, total] of rows) {
  const pct = ((total / base - 1) * 100).toFixed(1);
  console.log(`${day}  ${usd(total).padStart(8)}  ${pct >= 0 ? '+' : ''}${pct}%`);
}

It needs Node 18 or newer for the built-in fetch and top-level await in an .mjs file. No dependencies.

Output

Run on November 10, 2026:

MEXC: tracked reserves without its own token, last 10 days
2026-11-01    $4.48B  +0.0%
2026-11-02    $4.53B  +1.1%
2026-11-03    $4.50B  +0.6%
2026-11-04    $4.52B  +0.9%
2026-11-05    $4.58B  +2.3%
2026-11-06    $4.48B  +0.1%
2026-11-07    $4.43B  -1.0%
2026-11-08    $4.24B  -5.3%
2026-11-09    $4.17B  -6.8%
2026-11-10    $4.17B  -6.8%

The November 6 row matches the $4.48B Cointelegraph quoted, which is a decent check that the filtering is right.

Reading it honestly

These are USD values, so they move with prices as well as with deposits and withdrawals. Crypto prices fell during the same days, which means the drop from $4.48B to $4.17B can't be read as a withdrawal total. To separate the two you'd use the tokens field, which holds amounts per token, and price them yourself at a fixed date. That's the natural next step if you extend this.

The data also covers only the wallets an exchange chose to disclose. It gives a floor on what the exchange holds, and it doesn't replace an audit.

Try it on others

Any CEX slug on DefiLlama works: node reserve-watch.mjs binance-cex 14, node reserve-watch.mjs okx 30. Slugs are in the URL of each exchange's page on defillama.com.

What other public signals do you watch when an exchange is in the news?

title: UK AI Weekly: The AI Story That Isn’t — And Why Paper Planes Still Matter
description:
UK AI Weekly: The AI Story That Isn’t — And Why Paper Planes Still Matter

Foldable Flight has scored 952 points on Hacker News, and somehow the internet’s attention has stayed on the ground. Its collection includes 109 paper-airplane designs, video tutorials, flight ratings and difficulty levels. The Firefly 5 can reportedly travel more than 300 feet, while Unite holds the world record for time aloft at 31.2 seconds.

Here is the awkward part: there is no AI development in this story.

The source material does not mention AI, machine learning or automated design. It does not say the project uses AI to create planes, test folds or rank performances. Treating this as an AI story would be like announcing that origami has acquired artificial intelligence because some of the wings look a bit aerodynamic.

That absence is actually the interesting development for anyone thinking about AI in 2026. Public attention still rewards things that are physical, testable and delightfully unnecessary. Nobody needs Foldable Flight to run a chatbot, analyse a spreadsheet or generate a synthetic image. You need a sheet of A4 paper, a steady hand and the will to launch something across a room.

The site also exposes a weakness in our usual AI commentary: easily measured performance is not the same as reliability. Foldable Flight gives each design numerical ratings for speed, glide and accuracy, alongside its folding difficulty. Arrowhead’s tutorials have been viewed more than 100 million times. Mystic is marked “Very Easy”, while Durandal is reserved for expert hands. That combination of instructions, difficulty ratings and observed outcomes is a form of practical accountability. It tells you both what to make and what to expect.

An AI system might generate a plausible-looking set of folding instructions, but plausible is not the same as flyable. The difference becomes obvious in the hand. This does not require a frontier-model benchmark or a new safety standard; it requires paper, gravity and occasionally chasing a badly aimed Corsair around the house.

There is no direct UK angle to the project itself, and the source provides none. The website is not identified as British, while several designs come from named designers including Michael LaFosse, Eiji Nakamura, Ian Zhou and Kyle Boyer. UK readers can use the A4 category, but it would be invention to present the collection as a distinctly British contribution.

The regulatory picture matters only if AI-generated paper-airplane designs become part of the picture. The UK still has no AI-specific statute or single AI regulator. Regulation remains principles-based and sector-led, with existing bodies such as the ICO and Intellectual Property Office applying the powers they already hold.

What this means

Foldable Flight is not a frontier-lab breakthrough, and it should not be sold as one. Its significance is as a clean example of something AI cannot eliminate merely by sounding authoritative: hands-on knowledge, physical testing and lessons from people who have done the folding before.

There is also a policy lesson here, even if it is an accidental one. The government’s AI Opportunities Action Plan calls for a “proportionate, flexible regulatory approach”, and that is exactly what the UK would need if whimsical AI-assisted design tools ever became common. No new law first; assess what existing rules actually require.

The 952 Hacker News points went to a carefully documented collection of paper airplanes. AI may have plenty of answers, but the market for making something with your hands remains stubbornly physical.

The takeaway: Foldable Flight’s real lesson is that credible AI advice still has to survive contact with the real world — preferably at 300 feet.

title: Deep Dive: Compute concentration: the new bottleneck for AI (November 9, 2026)
description:
Deep Dive: Compute concentration: the new bottleneck for AI

This week's deep dive takes a comprehensive look at compute concentration: the new bottleneck for ai. We've pulled together the research, the commentary, and the operational reality to give you a complete picture.

The state of play

The AI industry has spent the past few years moving fast. The pace has created genuine progress — new capabilities, new products, new markets — but also real problems: capability surprises, deployment failures, regulatory lag, and economic uncertainty.

This post is a structured look at compute concentration: the new bottleneck for ai. We'll cover what's happening, why it matters, and what comes next.

What we know

The evidence on compute concentration: the new bottleneck for ai is accumulating. Multiple sources — research labs, enterprise deployments, regulatory filings, market data — all point in the same direction.

The numbers are stark. Adoption is uneven, deployment failures are the norm rather than the exception, and the gap between demo and production is wider than the labs admit.

The market is consolidating. The top three providers in most AI categories now account for 75%+ of usage. New entrants face a cold-start problem that didn't exist three years ago.

What we don't know

There are major gaps. Long-term effects of AI on cognition, productivity, and society are still unknown. The alignment problem remains unsolved. The economics of AI are still being worked out. The regulatory landscape is unsettled.

Honest practitioners admit the uncertainty. The labs that don't are selling you something.

What to watch

Over the next 12 months, watch for:

  1. Capability announcements. Frontier model releases are getting less predictable and more disruptive. Each release resets the competitive landscape.

  2. Deployment failures. The number of public AI failures is increasing. Expect more embarrassing public incidents and more regulatory enforcement.

  3. Regulatory clarity. The EU AI Act's next phase takes effect in November. The UK ICO's framework is the first concrete AI audit guidance. California AB 2013 enforcement begins. Watch for the first major enforcement actions.

  4. Economic inflection points. The AI investment cycle is approaching a critical phase. Either revenue catches up to spending, or we see a correction. The next 18 months will determine which.

  5. Agent deployment. Agents are the next frontier. The first wave of enterprise agent deployments is happening now. Watch for what works and what fails.

The bottom line

The AI industry in 2026 is at an inflection point. The hype cycle has peaked. The trough of disillusionment is here. The applications that survive will be the ones that solved real problems.

What works today:

  • Coding assistants that actually save developers time.
  • Search augmentation through RAG that improves information retrieval.
  • Customer support triage that reduces handle time.
  • Image generation for designers that improves workflow.

What doesn't work today:

  • "Autonomous" agents that can't operate a browser reliably.
  • AI companions that drain VC funding without producing value.
  • AGI manifestos that confuse ambition with capability.
  • Anything that requires consistent counting above 10.

The next 18 months will sort the wheat from from the chaff. The companies that survive will be the ones that stopped trying to build AGI and started trying to build useful tools.

title: SQL Server Locks: A Performance and Deadlock Cheat Sheet
description:
SQL Server uses locks to protect data while concurrent sessions read and modify it. Locks preserve transaction correctness, but they also create waiting, blocking, and deadlocks. When evaluating a slow query, ask: "Is it waiting for another transaction, and what resource does it need?"

This cheat sheet explains the lock types you are most likely to encounter, how they affect query execution, and how to diagnose locking problems quickly.

Locks are not latches. Locks protect logical data and transaction consistency. Latches are lightweight internal synchronization mechanisms that protect in-memory structures such as data pages. A lock problem commonly appears as an LCK_M_* wait; a latch problem uses waits such as PAGELATCH_*.

The basic locking flow

A lock request is granted when compatible with locks already held on the resource. Otherwise, the session waits. Lock duration depends on its mode, isolation level, statement, and transaction scope. A common issue is an application modifying data and then remaining idle before committing; the statement finished, but its locks remain.

Lock modes you should recognize

Lock Name Typical purpose Performance implication
S Shared Reading data Compatible with other shared locks, but blocked by exclusive locks
U Update Reading a row before updating it Reduces conversion deadlocks; only one update lock can target a resource
X Exclusive Inserting, updating, or deleting data Blocks both readers and writers under locking-based isolation
IS Intent Shared Signals shared locks at a lower level Enables efficient compatibility checks
IX Intent Exclusive Signals exclusive or update locks below Common while rows or pages are modified
SIX Shared with Intent Exclusive Reads the larger resource while modifying lower-level resources Restrictive; can create broad blocking
Sch-S Schema Stability Compiling and executing queries Compatible with normal data access, but conflicts with schema modification
Sch-M Schema Modification DDL and some metadata changes Highly restrictive; can block nearly all access to the object
BU Bulk Update Bulk-loading data under qualifying options Allows optimized bulk operations but restricts competing access
Range* Key-range locks Protects index ranges under SERIALIZABLE Prevents phantom rows but can lock gaps and increase blocking

Shared, update, and exclusive locks

A shared lock allows concurrent readers. An exclusive lock prevents another session from reading or changing the resource under conventional READ COMMITTED locking. Update locks are an intermediate mode used when reading data that may be changed. They help avoid two sessions acquiring shared locks and both attempting to convert them to exclusive locks.

Intent locks

Intent locks describe activity lower in the lock hierarchy. An IX table lock usually means exclusive locks exist, or will exist, on pages, keys, or rows. It does not mean the whole table is exclusively locked. Intent modes quickly reveal whether a table-level request conflicts with lower-level activity.

Schema locks

Sch-S locks occur during query compilation and execution, even with NOLOCK. Sch-M locks occur during schema changes and conflict with Sch-S. A long query can delay DDL, while schema modification can block ordinary queries.

Key-range locks

Under SERIALIZABLE, SQL Server may lock index keys and gaps between them. This prevents inserts that would newly satisfy an earlier predicate. Key-range locks provide strong consistency but can greatly expand the protected area, especially without supporting indexes.

Lock granularity: what is being locked?

SQL Server can lock resources at several levels:

  • KEY locks protect index entries. Even queries described as "row locking" often show KEY resources.
  • RID locks protect rows in a heap, which is a table without a clustered index.
  • PAGE locks protect an 8 KB data or index page.
  • OBJECT locks protect a table or similar object.
  • HoBT locks protect a heap or B-tree, including an individual partition.
  • METADATA, DATABASE, and ALLOCATION_UNIT locks protect broader internal resources.

Fine-grained locks improve concurrency but consume memory. Coarser locks use fewer resources but block more operations.

Lock escalation

Lock escalation replaces many fine-grained locks with a coarser lock. SQL Server attempts escalation when a single statement acquires at least roughly 5,000 locks on one table or index reference, and it can also escalate under lock-memory pressure. Escalation is normally to a table lock; a partitioned table can escalate to a partition when LOCK_ESCALATION = AUTO. SQL Server does not escalate row or key locks to page locks.

If another session holds an incompatible lock that prevents escalation, the statement continues with fine-grained locks and SQL Server retries later. Escalation can turn a large modification into a whole-table blocker. Reduce its likelihood with shorter transactions, batched changes, and indexes that prevent unnecessary scans. Disabling escalation can exchange blocking for excessive lock memory.

Compatibility at a glance

The full compatibility matrix is extensive, but this reduced view covers common investigations:

Held \ Requested S U X IS IX
S Yes Yes No Yes No
U Yes No No Yes No
X No No No No No
IS Yes Yes No Yes Yes
IX No No No Yes Yes

Compatibility alone does not explain every wait. Locks may cover different resources, and a request can wait behind another waiter because SQL Server generally preserves queue fairness.

How isolation levels change locking

Isolation level Important locking behavior
READ UNCOMMITTED Allows dirty reads and usually avoids shared data locks; rows can be missing, duplicated, or inconsistent
READ COMMITTED SQL Server default; shared row/page locks are generally released as data is read, allowing later rereads to change
REPEATABLE READ Holds shared locks until transaction end, preventing changed or deleted rereads
SERIALIZABLE Adds key-range protection and prevents phantoms; highest blocking risk
SNAPSHOT Uses row versions for reads; update conflicts are possible; writes still use locks
READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT Changes READ COMMITTED reads to use row versions; writers still lock

SNAPSHOT requires ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION to be enabled. Azure SQL Database commonly enables READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT by default, while boxed SQL Server does not. Row versioning reduces reader-writer blocking but does not eliminate writer-writer blocking, schema conflicts, or poor transaction design. It also adds version-store usage, and competing snapshot updates can fail with error 3960.

NOLOCK is not a performance fix. It uses READ UNCOMMITTED, permitting dirty, missing, or duplicated rows, and it still acquires schema-stability locks. Use it only when those correctness risks are explicitly acceptable.

Blocking versus deadlocks

Blocking is expected synchronization: one session waits until another releases an incompatible lock. A deadlock is a cycle in which sessions wait for one another and none can proceed.

SQL Server detects the cycle and chooses a victim, which receives error 1205 and is rolled back. Applications should use bounded retries for idempotent operations, but retries do not fix recurring deadlocks.

Typical fixes include consistent object access order, shorter transactions, indexes that reduce scanned rows, no user interaction inside transactions, and smaller batches. The deadlock graph identifies participating processes, resources, lock modes, and statements.

Reproducible locking labs

Run these examples only on a development SQL Server where you can create a disposable database. They were validated on SQL Server 2022 Developer Edition. Open two query windows and label them Session A and Session B. Run this setup once; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS requires SQL Server 2016 or later.

USE master;
GO

IF DB_ID(N'LockLab') IS NULL
    CREATE DATABASE LockLab;
GO

USE LockLab;
GO

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS dbo.LockDemo;

CREATE TABLE dbo.LockDemo
(
    Id int NOT NULL
        CONSTRAINT PK_LockDemo PRIMARY KEY,
    AccountName varchar(30) NOT NULL,
    Balance int NOT NULL,
    ReferenceCode int NOT NULL
);

CREATE INDEX IX_LockDemo_ReferenceCode
    ON dbo.LockDemo (ReferenceCode);

INSERT dbo.LockDemo (Id, AccountName, Balance, ReferenceCode)
VALUES
    (1, 'Alpha', 100, 10),
    (2, 'Beta', 200, 20),
    (3, 'Gamma', 300, 30);

SELECT
    name,
    is_read_committed_snapshot_on,
    snapshot_isolation_state_desc
FROM sys.databases
WHERE name = DB_NAME();

Lab 1: an exclusive lock blocks a reader

In Session A, update a row but leave the transaction open:

BEGIN TRANSACTION;

UPDATE dbo.LockDemo
SET Balance = Balance + 50
WHERE Id = 1;

-- Leave this transaction open while running Session B.

In Session B, run:

SELECT *
FROM dbo.LockDemo WITH (READCOMMITTEDLOCK)
WHERE Id = 1;

READCOMMITTEDLOCK makes the example deterministic even when READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT is enabled. Session B waits with LCK_M_S because Session A holds an exclusive key lock. In a third window, run the diagnostic queries in the next section to see the waiter and blocker. Release the lock in Session A:

ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;

Session B then completes and returns the original balance of 100 because Session A rolled back. To demonstrate row versioning, remove READCOMMITTEDLOCK on a database with READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT enabled; the reader can return the previously committed version without waiting.

Lab 2: create a two-row deadlock

Run the following in Session A:

SET XACT_ABORT ON;
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

UPDATE dbo.LockDemo SET Balance += 10 WHERE Id = 1;
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:15';
UPDATE dbo.LockDemo SET Balance += 10 WHERE Id = 2;

COMMIT TRANSACTION;

Start this in Session B within 15 seconds:

SET XACT_ABORT ON;
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

UPDATE dbo.LockDemo SET Balance += 20 WHERE Id = 2;
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:15';
UPDATE dbo.LockDemo SET Balance += 20 WHERE Id = 1;

COMMIT TRANSACTION;

Each session owns an exclusive lock needed by the other. SQL Server detects the cycle and terminates one session with error 1205; either session can be the victim. DEADLOCK_PRIORITY is considered first, followed by estimated rollback cost. The survivor commits. The primary fix is to access rows in the same order—for example, always update Id = 1 before Id = 2.

In a third window, inspect the newest graph from the built-in system_health session. This requires VIEW SERVER STATE and applies to SQL Server; Azure SQL Database exposes Extended Events through database-scoped targets.

SET QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON;

;WITH DeadlockEvents AS
(
    SELECT CAST(st.target_data AS xml) AS target_data
    FROM sys.dm_xe_session_targets AS st
    INNER JOIN sys.dm_xe_sessions AS s
        ON s.address = st.event_session_address
    WHERE s.name = N'system_health'
      AND st.target_name = N'ring_buffer'
)
SELECT
    event_xml.value(N'(@timestamp)[1]', N'datetime2') AS event_time,
    event_xml.query(N'(data/value/deadlock)[1]') AS deadlock_graph
FROM DeadlockEvents
CROSS APPLY target_data.nodes(
    N'//RingBufferTarget/event[@name="xml_deadlock_report"]'
) AS events(event_xml)
ORDER BY event_time DESC;

Reset the data and connection setting in both windows before continuing:

IF XACT_STATE() <> 0 ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
SET XACT_ABORT OFF;

UPDATE dbo.LockDemo
SET Balance = Id * 100;

Lab 3: a serializable range blocks an insert

In Session A, protect a range that currently contains one row:

SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

SELECT *
FROM dbo.LockDemo
WHERE ReferenceCode BETWEEN 15 AND 25;

-- Leave the transaction open while running Session B.

In Session B, attempt to insert into the protected range:

INSERT dbo.LockDemo (Id, AccountName, Balance, ReferenceCode)
VALUES (4, 'Delta', 400, 18);

The insert waits on a range-insert lock. On SQL Server 2022 this appears as LCK_M_RIn_NL; older versions and tools may display related range-insert names differently. Session A holds a RangeS-S lock on the supporting index, protecting existing keys and gaps where qualifying rows could be inserted. Finish Session A:

COMMIT TRANSACTION;
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;

Session B can now insert the row. Remove it before repeating the lab:

DELETE dbo.LockDemo WHERE Id = 4;

These labs illustrate three different diagnoses: incompatible locks causing ordinary blocking, a circular wait causing a deadlock, and an isolation-level guarantee deliberately expanding the locked resource range.

After completing the labs, clean up:

USE LockLab;
IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0 ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS dbo.LockDemo;

-- Optional, from a window connected to master:
-- USE master;
-- DROP DATABASE LockLab;

Quick diagnostic queries

The following server-scoped DMVs generally require VIEW SERVER STATE (VIEW SERVER PERFORMANCE STATE for some DMVs on SQL Server 2022+) or the corresponding Azure SQL database permission. wait_time is reported in milliseconds.

Find waiting requests and their blockers:

SELECT
    r.session_id,
    r.blocking_session_id,
    r.status,
    r.wait_type,
    r.wait_time,
    r.wait_resource,
    DB_NAME(r.database_id) AS database_name,
    t.text AS current_sql
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests AS r
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) AS t
WHERE r.blocking_session_id <> 0
   OR r.wait_type LIKE N'LCK_M_%';

Inspect current locks:

SELECT
    l.request_session_id,
    l.resource_type,
    l.resource_description,
    OBJECT_NAME(p.object_id, l.resource_database_id) AS object_name,
    l.request_mode,
    l.request_status
FROM sys.dm_tran_locks AS l
LEFT JOIN sys.partitions AS p
    ON l.resource_type IN (N'KEY', N'PAGE', N'RID', N'HOBT')
   AND p.hobt_id = l.resource_associated_entity_id
WHERE l.resource_database_id = DB_ID()
ORDER BY l.request_session_id, l.resource_type;

The head blocker is often sleeping and therefore absent from sys.dm_exec_requests. Find its open transaction and most recent SQL:

SELECT
    s.session_id,
    s.status,
    s.login_name,
    s.host_name,
    s.program_name,
    s.open_transaction_count,
    at.transaction_begin_time,
    txt.text AS most_recent_sql
FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions AS s
LEFT JOIN sys.dm_tran_session_transactions AS st
    ON st.session_id = s.session_id
LEFT JOIN sys.dm_tran_active_transactions AS at
    ON at.transaction_id = st.transaction_id
LEFT JOIN sys.dm_exec_connections AS c
    ON c.session_id = s.session_id
OUTER APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(c.most_recent_sql_handle) AS txt
WHERE s.session_id IN
(
    SELECT blocking_session_id
    FROM sys.dm_exec_requests
    WHERE blocking_session_id > 0
);

Common waits provide a fast clue:

Wait Usually means
LCK_M_S Waiting for a shared lock, often a reader behind a writer
LCK_M_U / LCK_M_X Waiting to update or exclusively modify data
LCK_M_SCH_M Waiting for a schema modification lock
LCK_M_RS_S Waiting for a serializable range shared lock
LCK_M_RIn_NL and related LCK_M_RI* waits Waiting to insert into a protected key range; the exact name varies by engine version

Use the results together. A granted lock is not automatically a problem; identify the waiter, head blocker, transaction age, and SQL. sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks provides another resource-level view. For historical deadlocks, use system_health or a dedicated Extended Events session capturing xml_deadlock_report.

Performance review checklist

  1. Confirm waiting: Look for LCK_M_* waits rather than assuming high duration means blocking.
  2. Find the head blocker: Follow blocking_session_id until reaching the session that is not itself blocked.
  3. Check transaction scope: Determine whether the blocker has an old open transaction or is idle while holding locks.
  4. Identify the resource and mode: Use wait_resource, sys.dm_tran_locks, and the execution plan.
  5. Review access paths: Scans lock more rows and hold locks longer than selective seeks.
  6. Check isolation requirements: Use stronger isolation only when the business invariant requires it.
  7. Capture the deadlock graph: Do not diagnose recurring deadlocks from the victim statement alone.
  8. Fix the cause, not the symptom: Prefer indexing, consistent access order, batching, and shorter transactions over NOLOCK or killing sessions.

Locks are necessary and waiting can be normal. Prolonged blocking usually reflects transaction scope, access paths, or concurrency design. Diagnose the wait chain, then reduce the locked resource set or the time locks are held.

title: AblationBench: Evaluating Automated Planning of Ablations in Empirical AI Research
description:
arXiv:2507.08038v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Language model agents are increasingly used to automate scientific research, yet evaluating their scientific contributions remains a challenge. A key mechanism to obtain such insights is through ablation experiments. To this end, we introduce AblationBench, a benchmark suite for evaluating agents on ablation planning tasks in empirical AI research. It includes two tasks: AuthorAblation, which helps authors propose ablation experiments based on a method section and contains 83 instances, and ReviewerAblation, which helps reviewers find missing ablations in a full paper and contains 350 instances. For both tasks, we develop LM-based judges that serve as an automatic evaluation framework. Our experiments with frontier LMs show that these tasks remain challenging, with the best-performing LM system identifying only 45% of the original ablations on average, below human-level performance. We observe an inverse performance trend between the author and reviewer tasks, which we attribute to differences in model grounding. Lastly, we analyze the limitations of current LMs on these tasks, and find that chain-of-thought prompting outperforms an agent-based approach. Our data is available on https://huggingface.co/collections/ai-coscientist/ablationbench, and our code is available on https://github.com/ai-scientist-bench/ablation-bench .

title: Understanding NestJS Architecture: A Beginner's Guide
description:
1. Introduction

NestJS is a progressive Node.js framework used to build efficient, scalable and maintainable server-side applications.

It is primarily built using TypeScript and provides a structured architecture for developing backend applications.

Unlike Express.js, which provides a minimal and flexible structure, NestJS follows a modular architecture that helps developers organize application code into separate components.

2. Why Do We Need NestJS Architecture?

Consider building an Instagram-like application. It requires several backend functionalities:

  • User registration and authentication
  • Creating and managing posts
  • Following users
  • Liking posts
  • Managing comments
  • Retrieving user feeds

Writing all these functionalities inside a single file makes the application difficult to maintain and debug.

NestJS solves this problem by organizing the application into separate modules, controllers and providers.

3. Main Components of NestJS Architecture

Modules

Modules organize related application components into logical groups.

Controllers

Controllers handle incoming HTTP requests and define API endpoints.

Providers and Services

Providers are injectable components managed by NestJS. Services commonly contain business logic.

Dependency Injection

Dependency Injection allows classes to receive their required dependencies without manually creating them.

4. Basic NestJS Architecture

A typical NestJS application follows this structure:

Client → Controller → Service → Database

  • The client sends an HTTP request.
  • The controller receives the request.
  • The service executes business logic.
  • The database stores or retrieves information.
  • The response is returned to the client.

5. NestJS vs Express.js

Express.js provides a minimal framework where developers organize their application according to their preferences.

NestJS provides a predefined architectural structure using modules, controllers, providers and dependency injection.

Both frameworks can build REST APIs, but NestJS provides more built-in architectural conventions.

6. Conclusion

NestJS architecture helps developers build backend applications with better organization, maintainability, scalability and separation of responsibilities.

Understanding modules, controllers, providers and dependency injection is the foundation for learning NestJS effectively.

title: Real-Time Short-Response Selection for Spoken Dialogue Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.09057v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: To realize spoken dialogue systems that can interact naturally with users, it is important for the system to respond to user utterances at appropriate timings. To achieve such natural turn-taking, the system needs not only to predict appropriate response timings but also to mask delays caused by language generation and speech synthesis so that they are not perceived by the user. We propose a real-time short-response selection task that can be integrated with existing turn-taking models to mask generation delay. To address this task, the proposed model learns the mapping between dialogue context and short responses using contrastive learning. When a turn-taking event is detected, the system selects a response from a set of pre-generated candidates. The selected response is played while the main response is being generated. Experimental results show that the proposed method learns to select short responses based on dialogue context, outperforming random and LLM-based baselines. Moreover, integrating response selection maintained turn-taking prediction performance and added minimal processing overhead.

title: Cheapest LLM for product-review sentiment: Mistral Small at $0.000019 a success
description:
On 300 Amazon product reviews, Mistral Small (2603) is the cheapest of nine models that clears an 88% pass bar and can be shown to match the baseline, GPT-6.1 Sol. It passes 97.7% of the tasks against 98.7% for Sol, at $0.000019 per successful task against $0.000319: 94.0% less.

This is an easy task, and the table shows it: all nine models clear the bar, so the question is only which one costs least. Two near neighbours deserve a straight reading. Claude Haiku 5.5 costs $0.000023 per successful task and answers faster (p95 336 ms against 912 ms for Mistral Small). GPT-6 Luna costs $0.000024 and passes 98.0%. If latency or the last fraction of a point matters more than a few thousandths of a cent, those are the picks.

The run. 300 reviews drawn with a fixed seed from the Amazon Polarity test split (Apache-2.0). One task: reply with positive or negative. Temperature 0, up to 2 retries when the reply is not a valid label, every attempt's cost counted, prices read from OpenRouter on 2026-11-05. Total spend for all nine models: $0.22.

Pass bar. 88% correct. A model "clears" only if the lower end of its 95% Wilson interval is at or above the bar. "Matches" means an exact one-sided paired test of "no more than 5 points worse than the baseline" on the tasks both models answered.

Model Correct Pass rate 95% interval $ per successful task
openai/gpt-6.1-sol (baseline) 296/300 98.7% 96.6-99.5% $0.000319
openai/gpt-6.1-terra 294/300 98.0% 95.7-99.1% $0.000165
openai/gpt-6-luna 294/300 98.0% 95.7-99.1% $0.000024
anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 292/300 97.3% 94.8-98.6% $0.000023
google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite 296/300 98.7% 96.6-99.5% $0.000041
deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash 294/300 98.0% 95.7-99.1% $0.000043
qwen/qwen3.8-flash 294/300 98.0% 95.7-99.1% $0.000054
mistralai/mistral-small-2603 293/300 97.7% 95.3-98.9% $0.000019
meta-llama/llama-4-maverick 294/300 98.0% 95.7-99.1% $0.000042

Where the retries went. qwen3.8-flash needed 5 retries and Haiku 2, so their prices carry a small retry share (1.5% and 1.4% of what each spent). Mistral Small needed none. On an easy task the retry tax is small; on the 77-label banking-intent run, deepseek-v4.1-flash spent 31.3% of its money on retries.

What a miss looks like. Mistral Small got 7 of 300 wrong, and 3 of those 7 the baseline also missed. One is "I love mandatory fees. The regulatory cost recovery fee rocks!", a sarcastic review the data labels positive and Mistral Small called negative. Labels like that put a ceiling under every model, which is why a pass bar below 100% is not a lowered standard.

Check it or re-run it. The 300 rows, the prompt, the prices and the re-run script are on the verdict page, so you can run the same comparison with your own OpenRouter key (the full nine-model run cost $0.22) and see where your numbers land. Prices move monthly; the page notes the day it was last re-checked: https://clearbar.grain64.com/verdicts/amazon-sentiment/?utm_source=devto&utm_campaign=devto-sentiment

Want the same verdict on your own data? Import 10-100 of your input/expected pairs, add your current model, and the workspace names the cheapest model that clears your bar, with cost per successful task, retries counted, and the failures it will have. Free during early access; you pay OpenRouter for the model calls with your own key.

Which task should the next verdict cover: extraction, summarisation, or classification of your own labels? Say so in the comments.

title: How to Evaluate a Polarion Alternative Against Your Delivery Lifecycle
description:
When requirements, tests, approvals, and delivery work are hard to coordinate, teams often end up tracking status in multiple places. That makes ownership less clear and can leave traceability gaps until a review or release decision is due.

To evaluate a Polarion alternative, start with the records your lifecycle needs to connect, then check workflow and deployment fit. Finally, run a representative project through the platform. This is more informative than comparing isolated features or watching a simplified demonstration.

1. Map the records that need to stay connected

List the objects your teams manage and the relationships they need to follow. Depending on your process, that list may include requirements, user stories, risks, defects, tests, approvals, releases, and supporting knowledge.

For each relationship, ask how the platform makes it visible and how teams keep it current. For example, can reviewers follow a requirement through implementation and test activity to release progress? If teams must maintain parallel spreadsheets or reconcile updates manually, include that work in your evaluation.

2. Distinguish process controls from configuration needs

Some organizations need formal lifecycle controls for regulated work. Others need a configurable framework that supports different delivery methods across departments. These needs can overlap, so assess both the process rules and the ways teams can adapt them.

Review the configuration surface, including custom fields, statuses, issue types, layouts, link types, permissions, workflow rules, and automation. Also consider planning, reporting, collaboration, and how the platform fits existing development practices.

3. Confirm deployment and governance fit early

Deployment choices can constrain a platform decision, so confirm them before spending time designing workflows. Cloud deployment may suit teams looking to reduce infrastructure responsibility; on-premise, private-cloud, or air-gapped options may better match particular security, infrastructure, or governance requirements.

Check the options available for each platform against your organization’s requirements. For example, the source describes ONES.com as offering Cloud, Private Cloud, On-Premise, and Air-gapped deployment; Polarion ALM as offering Cloud and On-Premise; and Jama Connect as Cloud-based.

4. Evaluate the platforms against their strengths

ONES.com: configurable project and R&D delivery workflows

ONES.com is positioned as a project and knowledge management platform for coordinating work across product, engineering, QA, and other functions. Its configurable fields, statuses, issue types, layouts, link types, and workflows may suit teams that want to adapt project structures to their operating model.

Assess whether its project templates, Agile planning, reporting, automation, role-based permissions, and shared project and knowledge context cover the lifecycle you mapped. This flexibility is most useful when stakeholders are prepared to establish standards for fields, permissions, and workflows before scaling configurations across teams.

Polarion ALM: requirements and traceability-led development

Polarion ALM is designed for complex product development in which requirements, approvals, tests, changes, and releases need to remain connected. Its capabilities include requirements authoring and management, traceability, configurable workflows and permissions, and centralized test management. The source describes Cloud and On-Premise deployment options.

Evaluate how well its structured lifecycle processes fit your governance needs. If you also need portfolio coordination, team-level planning, or broader collaboration, include those areas in the assessment rather than focusing only on the core ALM process.

Jama Connect: collaborative requirements definition and review

Jama Connect focuses on defining, reviewing, approving, and relating requirements in a shared environment. Its strengths include cross-functional reviews, visibility into relationships between records, and structured approval processes.

Consider it when requirements collaboration is the central need. If the platform would also need to support broader project execution or multiple deployment models, verify those requirements directly. Map the full lifecycle—from idea and requirement through implementation, testing, release, and post-release learning—to see whether a requirements-centered system is sufficient.

5. Run a representative project through the workflow

Choose a real project sample that includes changing requirements, cross-team dependencies, review gates, test activity, and reporting. Use it to examine the complete operating process rather than a simplified demonstration.

  • Follow a requirement through its related implementation and test records.
  • Check how changes, approvals, and ownership are represented.
  • Review whether dependencies and project status are visible to the relevant teams.
  • Confirm that the reporting and governance needs identified earlier can be handled without duplicating records elsewhere.

Use the results to identify gaps between the project’s actual process and the platform’s configuration. A successful evaluation should show that the lifecycle relationships remain understandable, teams can carry out their work within the chosen governance model, and the deployment option is acceptable.

Make the decision from the lifecycle, not the feature count

ONES.com is a candidate when configurable project workflows, planning, reporting, collaboration, knowledge context, and deployment flexibility are priorities. Polarion ALM is oriented toward formal lifecycle control and requirements-to-test traceability. Jama Connect is focused on collaborative requirements definition and review.

The right choice depends on which of those needs is central to your organization. Compare each platform using the same representative project, governance expectations, deployment requirements, and end-to-end lifecycle map.

title: Your hero banner looks fine. Now open it on an ultrawide screen.
description:
While researching a UX case study on a Mexican mobile carrier's website, I widened my browser window and watched the homepage disappear behind its own banner.

The banner was an image stretched to 100% of the width. On my screen it took 44% of the first view. Add the header bars, and the first product started at 60% of the screen. Plans, prices and the way to your account were all below the fold.

It looked fine on the laptop it was probably designed on. It was a problem on everything wider.

The math

A full-width image with a fixed aspect ratio has a height that depends only on the width:

height = viewport width ÷ aspect ratio

That banner had a ratio of about 3.7 to 1. So:

Screen Banner height Share of the visible height
1440 × 900 laptop ~390 px ~45%
2560 × 1080 (21:9) ~690 px ~70%
3440 × 1440 (21:9) ~930 px ~70%
5120 × 1440 (32:9) ~1380 px more than the whole screen

The wider the screen, the less of your page people see. And ultrawide monitors are common among exactly the people who use a desktop all day for work.

Why it's also an accessibility problem

An ultrawide screen isn't a WCAG criterion on its own. What it does is make existing problems bigger:

  • Text inside the image (WCAG 1.4.5). The headline, the deadline and even a URL were part of the picture. Screen readers can't read it, users can't zoom it without the image pixelating, and nobody can copy the link.
  • Inverted hierarchy. The banner text scaled up with the image while the navigation stayed small. The biggest thing on the page was the ad; the smallest was the menu.
  • Tiny controls, far apart (WCAG 2.5.8). Carousel dots smaller than 24 px, and arrows pinned to the edges, 2,000+ px apart.
  • Auto-rotation (WCAG 2.2.2). If it moves for more than 5 seconds, people need a way to pause it.

The fix

Four rules got me most of the way in my redesign:

1. Cap the content width. The page can be 3440 px wide; your content doesn't have to be.

.container {
  max-width: 1200px;
  margin-inline: auto;
  padding-inline: 24px;
}

2. Give the banner a height, not just a ratio. Let it flex within limits instead of growing forever.

.hero {
  height: clamp(240px, 30vw, 360px);
  max-height: 40vh;
  display: flex;
  overflow: hidden;
}

3. Keep text out of the image. Text goes in HTML, and the image only fills its own area.

<section class="hero" aria-roledescription="carousel" aria-label="Promotions">
  <div class="hero-copy">
    <h2>Register your line before November 15</h2>
    <p>Your deadline depends on the last digit of your number.</p>
    <a href="/register" class="button">Register now</a>
  </div>
  <img class="hero-media" src="promo.jpg" alt="">
</section>

.hero-copy  { flex: 1 1 55%; padding: 36px 40px; }
.hero-media { flex: 1 1 45%; object-fit: cover; min-width: 0; }

A decorative image gets an empty alt; if the image carries meaning, describe it.

4. Real controls, real size. Buttons with names, at least 44 × 44 px, close to each other, and a pause button if anything moves.

<button type="button" aria-label="Pause promotions">…</button>

How to test it without an ultrawide monitor

  • In Chrome DevTools, open device mode (Ctrl+Shift+M) and type 3440 × 1440, then 2560 × 1080.
  • Or zoom out to 50% on a 1920 px screen: the page lays out as if it were about 3840 px wide.
  • Ask one question: what can a person do without scrolling? If the answer is "look at an ad", the banner is too big.

The real lesson

The banner wasn't a CSS bug. It was a priority decision that the CSS made visible: the promotion came first, and what the person came to do came second. Capping the height is the technical fix. Deciding what deserves the first screen is the design one.

This was one finding from a bigger case study on activation, registration and information hierarchy across an email, an app and a website. You can read the full case, with prototypes, on my site: Activated doesn't mean working.

title: Vercel Connect adds managed Stripe API keys
description:
Vercel Connect can now create a separate restricted Stripe API key for each agent or task. When you create a Stripe connector, you can now choose Managed API Key as the connection method.

Vercel creates the key in your Stripe account, limited to the permissions you pick. The existing MCP and bring-your-own API key methods are unchanged.

type: embedded-entry-inline id: 3rOuKp0F4Nk80dMYJ5QX6U

Most apps and agents run on Stripe’s default secret key, which has full access to the account. With per-agent keys, each agent gets only the access its job needs. For example, a daily revenue report agent can be limited to read-only access to charges, and an onboarding agent can be limited to write access to customers.

Vercel creates and stores the key, so there is no secret key to paste. You can rotate it from the connector's settings without redeploying, and the old key stays valid for up to 24 hours while you switch.
