title: What It Costs to Run AI Agents in Production: A Worked Cost Model for Tokens, Sandboxes, Storage, and Networking
description:
In production, an AI agent’s cost is model tokens plus the infrastructure around them (orchestration services, code-execution sandboxes, networking, storage, and observability), and at moderate scale tokens usually dominate, so prompt caching, model choice, and call count matter more than compute. In the worked model in this guide, 300,000 tasks a month cost about $21,919, of which model tokens are about 96 percent. Control Plane is a platform that runs agent services and their code-execution steps with autoscaling, scale to zero, and billing for the CPU and memory a workload reserves.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Every input in the model is stated so you can swap in your own numbers.

  • Cost formula. Tasks × calls per task × tokens per call × token price, plus infrastructure (compute, networking, storage, observability).
  • Worked result. 300,000 tasks a month at 8 model calls each costs about $21,919, or $0.073 per task, at list prices.
  • Biggest levers. Prompt caching cut the token bill 45 percent. Routing simple steps to a smaller model, fewer calls per task, and shorter outputs come next.
  • Infrastructure. Sandboxes, always-on orchestration replicas, NAT gateways, and trace storage came to about $799 a month, or $0.0027 per task.
  • Control Plane runs agent services and their code-execution steps on AWS, GCP, and Azure with autoscaling and scale to zero, and, where enabled, Control Plane’s Capacity AI adjusts a workload’s reserved CPU and memory between set minimums and maximums based on historical usage.

What does it cost to run AI agent workloads in production?

Monthly cost splits into token spend and infrastructure spend.

Token spend depends on four variables: tasks, model calls per task, tokens per call (input and output), and price per token. Agents run multi-step loops that resend accumulated context, so they use far more tokens per task than a single-turn chatbot.

Infrastructure spend covers the orchestration services that run the agent loop, sandboxes that execute model-generated code, NAT gateways that carry traffic to model APIs, and storage for traces and logs.

Monthly cost = token cost across all calls + sandbox compute + orchestration compute + networking + storage

Worked model: 300,000 tasks per month

This is an illustrative scenario at list prices checked in November 2026. Check current pricing before you budget.

Assumptions

  • 10,000 agent tasks per day, 300,000 per month.
  • Each task makes 8 model calls.
  • Each call sends 6,000 input tokens, of which 4,500 are a repeated prefix (system prompt, tool definitions, context) that is cached, and returns 400 output tokens. Input is held flat for simplicity; real loops grow context with each step, which raises cost, and token counts differ by model tokenizer.
  • The first call in each task writes the cache and the other 7 read it, assuming calls are less than 5 minutes apart (each hit refreshes the 5-minute cache lifetime). A long sandbox run between calls can force a new write. If the prefix is identical across tasks and traffic is steady, most first calls also hit the cache, so this assumption is conservative.
  • Model: Claude Sonnet 5.5 at list prices of $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output tokens, $2.50 per million tokens for 5-minute cache writes, and $0.10 per million for cache reads (Claude pricing, prompt caching).
Line item Tokens per month Price per million tokens Monthly cost
Uncached input 3.6 billion $2.00 $7,200.00
Cache reads 9.45 billion $0.10 $945.00
Cache writes 1.35 billion $2.50 $3,375.00
Output 0.96 billion $10.00 $9,600.00
Token total $21,120.00

Without caching, all 14.4 billion input tokens bill at $2 per million ($28,800), plus $9,600 of output, for $38,400. Caching cuts the token bill 45 percent.

Prices are AWS us-east-1 on-demand list prices, applied to both regions in the model: AWS Fargate (Linux/x86) at $0.04048 per vCPU-hour and $0.004445 per GB-hour, NAT gateways at $0.045 per hour and $0.045 per GB processed, and Amazon S3 Standard at $0.023 per GB-month.

Line item Sizing Monthly cost
Code-execution sandboxes 30% of tasks run code for 3 minutes on 2 vCPU and 4 GB = 4,500 sandbox-hours $444.33
Agent orchestration service 3 replicas of 1 vCPU and 2 GB, always on, in each of 2 regions (6 replicas × 730 hours) $216.24
NAT gateways One per availability zone, 2 zones in each of 2 regions (4 gateways × 730 hours) $131.40
NAT data processing About 57.6 GB of model API request traffic (about 24 KB per call; responses add little) $2.59
Trace and log storage 50 KB per task = 15 GB a month, kept 12 months = 180 GB at steady state $4.14
Infrastructure total $798.70

Sandbox hours count execution time only. Fargate bills per second with a one-minute minimum from the start of the image pull, so startup time, warm pools held for latency, and peak concurrency above the average all add cost.

Metric Value
Monthly total About $21,918.70
Cost per task About $0.073
Token share of total 96.4%
Infrastructure per task About $0.0027

The model deliberately leaves out databases, vector stores and embedding calls, observability or tracing subscriptions, load balancers, internet egress to end users, engineering time, and taxes, because they vary too much by architecture to price generically. The storage line prices S3 at rest only; log and trace ingestion and indexing are billed separately and often cost more than storage.

What the model shows

  • Tokens dominate at this scale.
  • Caching the repeated prefix is the single largest saving.
  • Output tokens cost 5 times input tokens, so verbose outputs are expensive.
  • Each model call removed from a task cuts cost roughly in proportion.
  • Sandbox cost scales with execution minutes, so idle sandboxes should sleep.
  • Always-on replicas and NAT gateways are fixed costs, so at much lower task volumes their share of the bill rises.

How do I estimate costs for AI agent infrastructure including sandbox execution, storage, and networking at scale?

Build the estimate from measured traces wherever you can, in seven steps:

  1. Measure tokens per call and calls per task. Pull input and output token counts from your provider’s usage data or trace spans, then multiply by projected task volume. Re-count tokens with the target model before switching, because tokenizers differ.
  2. Separate cached from uncached input. Identify the stable prefix (system prompt, tool schemas, shared context) and count how many calls per task read the cache and how many write it.
  3. Size sandboxes by execution minutes. Estimate the share of tasks that run code, how long each run lasts, and the CPU and memory each sandbox needs.
  4. Count always-on replicas and regions. Multiply replicas by their CPU and memory, by hours per month, and by the number of regions.
  5. Add networking. NAT gateways charge per hour and per GB processed; add internet egress and cross-zone traffic between orchestration, sandboxes, and databases.
  6. Add storage retention. Multiply per-task trace and output size by monthly volume and by the retention period to get steady-state storage.
  7. Add a margin for retries and failed tasks. Size it from your observed failure and retry rates, since agents can retry steps or loop, and plan for provider rate limits, which can force higher usage tiers or queueing at peak.
Line item What drives cost How to measure
Model tokens Calls per task, tokens per call, model price Trace spans, provider usage data
Prompt caching Prefix size, cache hit rate Cache read and write token counts per call
Sandbox compute Execution minutes, vCPU and memory, share of tasks Sandbox runtime logs
Orchestration compute Replicas, CPU and memory, regions Deployment configuration
NAT and networking Gateway hours, GB processed, cross-zone and egress traffic VPC flow logs, billing reports
Storage Per-task data size, retention Log volume metrics
Retries Failure rate, retry depth Error-rate dashboards

How do I cut AI agent costs?

Roughly ordered by typical impact; items 1 and 3 are calculated in the worked model.

  1. Prompt caching. Keep the cacheable prefix stable across calls within a task so later calls hit the cache.
  2. Route simple steps to a smaller model. Parsing, extraction, and formatting steps rarely need a frontier model; reserve the larger model for planning and hard reasoning.
  3. Make fewer calls per task. In the worked model, going from 8 calls to 6 cuts the token bill about 21 percent. Combine steps and detect completion early.
  4. Shorten outputs. At $10 per million output tokens against $2 for input, concise and structured outputs save money on every call.
  5. Batch non-interactive work. Anthropic’s Message Batches API costs 50 percent less than standard API calls, which suits nightly processing, evaluations, and bulk classification.
  6. Let idle sandboxes sleep. Stop or sleep environments between tasks.
  7. Right-size reservations. Match always-on replicas to measured load with autoscaling and right-sizing.
  8. Avoid NAT processing charges where possible. For model APIs reachable through private endpoints, such as Amazon Bedrock over AWS PrivateLink interface endpoints, traffic skips NAT gateway processing, though the endpoints carry their own hourly and per-GB charges. The charge was small in the worked model and grows with data volume.

How much does setting up a production grade LangChain stack cost?

The open-source LangChain and LangGraph libraries are free under the MIT license, so production cost comes from what surrounds them: model tokens, hosting, a database or vector store, and observability.

  • Model tokens remain the largest line item; the framework does not change per-token prices.
  • Hosting for the agent service and its workers, with autoscaling, availability, and security, drives compute cost.
  • Databases and vector stores depend on corpus size, embedding model, and query volume.
  • Observability and evaluation. LangSmith, LangChain’s tracing and evaluation product, has a free tier and paid plans; see LangSmith pricing for current plans and limits.

At the volume in the worked model, a LangChain stack faces the same token bill as any other framework, plus hosting and tooling costs set by your architecture.

What infrastructure do I need to run AI agents securely at scale?

A secure production setup includes:

  • Isolated sandboxes for model-generated code, ideally with microVM isolation, so generated code cannot escape to the host or other workloads. See the best AI agent sandboxes in 2026.
  • Per-agent identity and least privilege, scoped to the services each agent needs.
  • Short-lived credentials through identity federation instead of static API keys.
  • Network egress controls that restrict which endpoints an agent can reach.
  • Audit logs of every action an agent takes.
  • Human approval for destructive or irreversible actions.
  • Autoscaling and multiple regions for availability under spikes and regional outages.

For the full checklist, see how to let AI agents operate production infrastructure safely, and for why agent work should leave local machines, stop running AI agents on developer laptops.

Which platform gives the lowest cost for always-on production workloads?

The cheapest platform depends on your load pattern. Compare platforms on these factors:

  • Billing granularity. Platforms bill provisioned instances, reserved CPU and memory, or per-request consumption at different granularities; unused reservation is waste unless right-sizing closes the gap.
  • Right-sizing. Automatic adjustment of CPU and memory reservations to observed usage prevents chronic over-provisioning.
  • Commitments vs. on-demand. Reserved instances and savings plans lower unit prices in exchange for a term commitment; on-demand keeps flexibility at a higher rate.
  • Scale to zero. Services idle for hours, including staging and low-traffic agent endpoints, should cost little or nothing in compute while idle.
  • Networking and egress fees. NAT, cross-region transfer, and internet egress pricing differ by provider and grow with data volume.
  • Multi-region duplication. Running in two regions roughly doubles always-on capacity, so per-unit price and right-sizing matter more.

Compare total cost across all of these factors.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane is the unbreakable platform for running production workloads. It runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads natively on AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), VM workloads on locations joined through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes, and workloads on Kubernetes clusters you already run or your own machines, including on premises, active-active across regions and clouds. Each workload runs across a Control Plane Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), a named set of locations across one or more clouds.

  • Billing. You pay for the CPU and memory a workload reserves, with no contracts or minimums, and, where enabled, Capacity AI adjusts the reservation between set minimums and maximums based on historical usage. Egress, storage, observability, dedicated load balancers, and GPUs are billed separately, and Capacity AI does not apply to GPU workloads or to workloads that autoscale on CPU utilization or multiple metrics.
  • Scale to zero. Serverless workloads scale to zero natively; standard and stateful workloads can scale to zero through KEDA, enabled per GVC.
  • Sandboxes. Control Plane Sandboxes give coding agents dedicated environments, sized from 2 to 16 or more CPUs, that sleep when idle and spin back up in under one second. Sandboxes are for building and running agent code during development; production agent services, including their code-execution steps, run as Control Plane workloads. Each workload is isolated with cgroups, namespaces, and restricted syscalls and capabilities, and Sandboxes run in dedicated Kata Containers microVMs.
  • Cloud access without stored keys. Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity (UCI) lets a workload call AWS, GCP, and Azure services, such as Amazon Bedrock or Google’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI), through an IAM role or service-account grant instead of long-lived keys in your code, with short-lived, least-privilege credentials at runtime.
  • Operations. Built-in logs, metrics, and traces, and Control Plane’s MCP server, which lets AI assistants operate Control Plane resources with the signed-in user’s permissions. A Cost & Usage view, a billing_viewer role, and a monthly spend alert for billing admins track spend.
  • Availability. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations. Agent services spread across locations keep running when a zone, region, or provider fails.

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure; that applies to the compute share of agent costs, while model tokens are billed by the model provider. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant. For how training, inference, and agents fit together, see AI infrastructure in 2026.

FAQ

Short answers on AI agent production costs.

What does it cost to run AI agent workloads in production?

It depends on task volume, calls per task, tokens per call, and model price. In the worked model, 300,000 tasks a month on Claude Sonnet 5.5 cost about $21,919: $21,120 in tokens and $799 in infrastructure.

How do I estimate costs for AI agent infrastructure including sandbox execution, storage, and networking at scale?

Measure tokens and calls from traces, split cached from uncached input, size sandboxes by execution minutes, count always-on replicas per region, then add NAT, egress, storage retention, and a retry margin.

How much does setting up a production grade LangChain stack cost?

The LangChain and LangGraph libraries are free under the MIT license; you pay for model tokens, hosting, a database or vector store, and observability such as LangSmith’s paid plans.

What infrastructure do I need to run AI agents securely at scale?

Isolated sandboxes for generated code, per-agent identity with least privilege, short-lived credentials, egress controls, audit logs, human approval for destructive actions, and autoscaling across regions.

Which platform gives the lowest cost for always-on production workloads?

It depends on load pattern. Compare billing granularity, right-sizing, commitment discounts, scale to zero, networking fees, and multi-region duplication.

What share of AI agent costs is tokens versus infrastructure?

Tokens dominate at moderate scale: 96.4 percent in the worked model. At low volume, fixed costs such as always-on replicas and NAT gateways take a larger share.

How much does prompt caching save?

In the worked model, caching the 4,500-token prefix cut the token bill from $38,400 to $21,120, or 45 percent.

Why are output tokens so expensive for agents?

Output costs 5 times input in the worked model ($10 versus $2 per million), and every call in every task pays it, so concise outputs save money quickly.

Does batch processing reduce agent costs?

Yes, for work that can wait. Anthropic’s Message Batches API costs 50 percent less than standard calls.

How do always-on costs affect agent economics at low volume?

They dominate it. The $347.64 of orchestration and NAT gateway hours in the worked model stays roughly the same at 1,000 tasks a month, so per-task infrastructure cost rises sharply unless idle orchestration services scale to zero and gateway count shrinks.

title: VR版YouTubeの「大型リニューアル」報道と、見る時間を目のトレーニングに変える設計
description:
VR版YouTubeの「大型リニューアル」報道と、見る時間を目のトレーニングに変える設計

UploadVRが伝えたのは、GoogleがQuest上のYouTubeアプリの「没入ビュー」を大規模に作り直している可能性がある、という話です。Android XRやvisionOSでの体験に近づける方向だといい、VRヘッドセットで動画を見るという行為が、片手間の延長ではなく「主要な視聴体験」として扱われ始めたことを示唆しています。

ここで注目したいのは、ハードウェアやアプリの話ではなく、「ヘッドセットをかぶって何かを見る時間」が日常に入ってくるという点です。Meta Questのようなスタンドアロン型のデバイスが、動画視聴という最も日常的な用途で存在感を増すなら、その時間は「消費」だけでなく「活用」にも開かれます。エンジニアの立場で見ると、これは単なるUI刷新ではなく、レンダリングパイプラインと入力レイテンシの設計が「ながら視聴」から「主軸の体験」へと再定義される転換点です。両眼に独立した映像を届けるというハードウェアの性質が、アプリケーション層でどう活かされるか——そこに設計上の面白さがあります。

見る時間は、そのまま目を使う時間

私たちが何かを見ているとき、両眼は協調し、脳は二つの像をひとつに統合しています。いわゆる弱視（amblyopia、lazy eye）では、この協調がうまく働かず、片方の目からの情報が十分に使われにくい状態が続くことがあります。

従来のアプローチの多くは、良い方の目をアイパッチで覆う、赤青メガネを使う、といった方法でした。もちろんこれらが今も使われる場面はありますが、「毎日続ける」というハードルは決して低くありません。ここで技術的な視点を挟むと、単眼抑制（suppression）をどう回避するかが長年の課題でした。片眼を物理的に塞ぐ方法はシンプルですが、両眼視（binocular vision）のトレーニングにはなりにくい。二つの眼に同時に、しかし異なる入力を与える必要がある。この「異なる入力を同時に」という要件は、実はディスプレイ技術と非常に相性がいいのです。

Amblyotubeという選択肢

Amblyotubeは、Seven Sportsが開発した、VRにおける視覚の協調と注意のためのレクリエーション／教育ソフトウェアです。考え方はシンプルです。左右の目に、別々の映像体験を届ける。

Quest 2、3、Pro、3SといったMeta Questのヘッドセットは、左右に独立したレンズとディスプレイを持っています。この物理的な構成が、そのまま訓練の土台になります。片眼ずつ異なる映像を届けられるということは、片眼ずつ違う「課題」を与えられるということです。ここはアーキテクチャとして捉えると分かりやすい。レンダリングは両眼分を個別に走らせ、片側にはぼかし（ブラー）、もう片側には強調処理を適用する。シェーダーレベルでの分岐が、そのままトレーニングの設計になります。

  • 対象眼と強度の選択：左右どちらの目を対象にするか、軽度／中等度／重度のプリセット、あるいはLogMARによる視力チェックから始められます。
  • Dominant Eye Shader：優位眼側に、調整可能なゆるやかなデジタルブラーをかけます。
  • AI Sharpener（MFBF）：弱視眼側では、AIが人物を検出し、太い赤の輪郭や黄緑のハイライト、一定のリズムでの明滅を加えます。
  • Wedge Occlusion：任意で、各眼の視野の一部を遮り、片眼ずつ異なる部分を見せることで、二眼の競合（binocular rivalry）を抑えます。
  • マゼンタのフォーカスキュー：弱視眼の視界のマゼンタのキューと、優位眼の視界の控えめなニュートラルグレーのドットが重なることで、脳が両眼の情報を統合し、ひとつの立体的な像として知覚する練習になります。

技術的なポイントを少し掘り下げます。MFBF（Monocular Fixation in a Binocular Field）は、両眼に視野を開いたまま、片眼にだけコントラストや輪郭の手がかりを与える手法です。実装としては、片眼のフレームにのみポストプロセスを適用し、もう片眼は素の映像を維持する。両眼の入力を完全に断つのではなく、優位眼の情報を「薄めて」弱視眼の寄与を相対的に引き上げる——このバランス調整が、単純な遮蔽とは異なる設計上の核心です。Wedge Occlusionも同様に、視野マスクを左右で非対称に配置することで、片眼ずつ異なる部分を見せ、脳が両方を統合せざるを得ない状況を作ります。マゼンタのフォーカスキューは、両眼のキューを空間的に重ねることで融合（fusion）を促す仕掛けで、色チャンネルを手がかりにしている点が面白いところです。

そして最も実用的な点は、コンテンツがYouTube動画であることです。仮想ルームでも、Room ViewのARパススルーでも、好きな動画をそのまま起動できます。「目のトレーニング用の退屈な動画」を探す必要はありません。これは技術ブログ的に言えば、コンテンツパイプラインを自前で抱えず、既存の動画基盤に乗るという判断です。専用コンテンツを作り込むコストを避け、ユーザーがすでに毎日見ているもの——YouTube——をそのまま入力源にする。エンジニアリングとしては地味ですが、継続率に直結する賢い割り切りだと思います。

現実的な期待値の話

ここは正直に書きます。Amblyotubeは診断・治療・治癒を目的としたものではなく、両眼の協調と奥行き知覚のための補助的な視覚トレーニング／支援ツールです。推奨は1日30〜40分（最大1時間）、対象年齢は13歳以上。症状についての判断は、必ず眼科医などの専門家に相談してください。ベンチマークや臨床効果をここで数字として約束することはできません。あくまで「見る時間を別の目的に開く」という設計の話です。

VRでのYouTube視聴が「当たり前」になっていくなら、その時間の使い方には選択肢が生まれます。ただ見るか、見ながら目を使うか。Amblyotubeは後者のための道具です。プラットフォームの大型リニューアルが視聴体験を底上げするほど、その上に乗るアプリケーションの設計余地も広がります。既存の動画を入力源に、両眼それぞれへ別々の処理を届ける——その発想自体は、特別なハードウェアを必要としません。すでに手元のQuestが、その土台になっています。

Meta Questアプリストアで配信中： https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

title: Generic Decline Means the Bank Answered a Different Question
description:
Of all the responses an issuer can return, the generic decline is the most honest about its own uselessness. It says the payment was refused and declines to say why — a shrug rendered in two digits. Teams new to failed payments tend to read it as a verdict on the customer: insufficient money, closed account, something terminal. Teams who have worked a queue for a while read it correctly, as a statement about information: the bank knows, the bank is not telling, and the recovery plan has to be built for a problem whose cause is hidden.

That hiddenness is deliberate. Issuers return generic codes for fraud-screening reasons, for legacy-system reasons, and sometimes because the specific reason sits in a category they will not disclose to merchants at all. Arguing with the code is pointless. Working around it is not. A generic decline tells you nothing about this payment — but the pattern around it tells you a great deal. The same card succeeding last month, the amount, the hour, whether other issuers are failing the same way that day: context is the diagnostic the code refuses to be.

The practical sequence follows from that. First, do not retry identically and immediately; a generic decline repeated at once usually earns the same shrug, and rapid identical attempts can trip the very fraud sensitivity that may have caused it. Space the attempt, vary the hour, and let any card-updater signal refresh the credentials in between. Second, contact the subscriber earlier than you would for a self-explanatory code — for a generic decline, the customer often is the diagnostic, since their bank will tell them things it will not tell you. Third, watch the account's other signals: a generic decline on a card that also fails its update link and ignores every message is graduating, by evidence, toward a hard outcome, whatever the code says.

This is where a diagnostic reading of the generic decline code and the sequence it calls for earns its keep: it treats the code as the start of an investigation rather than an answer, and lays out how the retry spacing, the outreach timing, and the account's own history combine into a working theory of what actually went wrong. Merchants who build that habit stop losing their most recoverable accounts to their least informative code.

There is a measurement trap here too. If generic declines are bucketed with hard declines in reporting — an easy default, since both look final — the recoverable share of the queue is understated and the whole recovery program looks weaker than it is. Split the bucket. Generic declines recovered at soft-decline rates in most queues once they are worked as soft; burying them makes a solvable problem look like fate.

A worked example makes the pattern concrete. A subscriber of four years, never late, fails a renewal with a generic decline on a Tuesday morning. Nothing about the account suggests risk; everything about the timing suggests a crowded issuer queue. The recovery that works is unglamorous: one attempt two days later at a different hour, a short message on day three offering the update link, and the payment collecting on the second attempt. No new information ever arrived from the bank. The context did all the diagnosing the code refused to do.

The bank answered a different question than the one you asked. Your system should respond by asking better ones — of the timing, of the pattern, and, politely and early, of the customer.

Swipe Again builds its retry and outreach sequences around decline-code triage, generic declines included: spaced attempts, early subscriber contact, and counting that keeps the shrug separate from the verdict. A code that tells you nothing is still telling you where to look.

title: Expo's Exact Wants Agents to Write Your App. I Have Doubts
description:
Expo put Exact on GitHub and eight days later it had 1,178 stars. One of the first comments on Hacker News, from a user called prmph, was two words: "Is this satire?"

I understand the question. Exact is a cross-platform app runtime written in Rust. You describe the interface in a small declarative language called Contract.

The data logic goes in TypeScript or Rust. It runs natively on the web, macOS, iOS, and Linux.

And the whole thing is built on the assumption that an AI agent will write most of the code.

That is what made the thread strange. People were not arguing about frame times. They were arguing about whether a framework designed for agents is a framework for humans at all.

What Contract actually is

Most tutorials tell you a DSL saves you boilerplate. Contract goes further. It removes the ability to write arbitrary code in the view at all.

No JavaScript in the markup. No I/O. Expressions have no side effects.

Effects only happen inside actions, as assignments, sends, or commands like focus(…).

The todo app in the README fits on one screen. Shapes, components, state, derive, resource, mutation, action, view. A bare node behaves like a bare div: display: block, box-sizing: content-box, flex-direction: row.

The compiler refuses CSS aliases and hands you the web's spelling instead. font-size, not size. background-color, not the background shorthand.

That last detail tells you a lot about who they are writing for. They are optimizing for a reader that will not remember the alias.

Now the honest part. A commenter called btown, who clearly reads compiler internals for fun, said his reaction to any DSL that has to carry "arbitrarily complex mathematical expressions" is "why???" He poked at the syntax crate and did not think it would scale to what real UIs demand.

That is the sharpest criticism in the thread. Nobody answered it well.

The speed claim

Here is a question people always ask about anything Rust-shaped. Is it actually faster, or does it just feel faster because it is new?

The README has numbers. Cold start to interactive first frame: 100 ms p50. Edit to present: 100 ms p50.

On the RealWorld Conduit benchmark, Exact's runtime was up about 300 ms before the React SSR build had hydrated. It used 26 KB of code against React's 81 KB.

Against Electron the gap is not subtle. Electron ships a browser. Exact on macOS draws with AppKit and a Rust layout kernel, and the app's JavaScript loads after the first pixel.

But the fair comparison is React Native, not Electron. React Native does not ship a browser either. Its real cost is the bridge and the reconciliation work, not download size.

Exact React Native Electron
UI rendering Compiled plan, native views JS tree reconciled to native Chromium
Web runtime ~20 KB n/a Chromium
First pixel Baked data, no JS JS boot JS boot

I could not find a single head to head benchmark against React Native. I looked. The speed story right now is architectural and self-reported.

The clock belongs to the agent

Here is the design decision i did not expect to like.

Exact exposes ten operations to an agent, the same on every host: tree, screenshot, tap, type, state, layout, logs, clock, prefer, perf.

The README explains the count: "There are ten on purpose: an agent API grows one reasonable addition at a time until no one can hold it in mind."

That sentence is the best writing in the whole repo.

And then the clock. Between two operations nothing moves.

Instead of sleeping until an animation finishes, the agent says clock +60000 or clock settle and reads the result. No timing flakes. No waits.

A test that needs a sleep is a test that will fail on someone else's laptop.

The evidence is thin but real. The README says a fresh agent built a todo app in about 57 minutes on a clean clone, and its tests passed on web, macOS, and the iOS Simulator. About 25 of those minutes were first builds.

Jayesh, writing on Medium, built a calculator with Cursor in 15 minutes, spent 2 minutes on tests, then got 10 seconds per UI change on a simulator. His first hour went to installing Rust, Bun, and an iOS simulator target. The app work was the short part.

What breaks

The first hour is setup. Rust, Bun 1.4.2 pinned exactly, Chrome, Xcode, Hermes. A first native build takes ten to fifteen minutes.

The open issues on the repo are more useful than the screenshots. Setup leaves Chrome marked MISSING on a Mac that has Chrome installed. A worktree in a folder with a different name fails native builds. Android compiles and runs, but "delivery and store packaging don't exist yet."

And this, stated plainly in the README:

Exact is pre-1.0 and changes daily. There is no API stability, no backwards compatibility, and no migration guide, by design.

"By design" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

I keep a note file called frameworks i will not learn. QML is on it. Every year someone tells me QML is actually good, and every year i open a file, see the property bindings, and close it.

So when a commenter compared Contract to QML and said Qt "proven this approach works," my instinct was to disagree on principle.

Then i read the todo app again. Contract is much smaller than QML.

No property binding graph to reason about, no signal and slot machinery to learn. Just shapes, actions, and a view tree.

I still have not installed it. But i moved the note file.

The real talk

If you ship to the App Store next quarter, do not use this. No migration guide is a real cost, and you will pay it.

If you are a React Native shop with a working app, this is a research toy. It is not a migration path.

And if you think the "agent native" label is nonsense, you are not wrong to be suspicious. One commenter said the trend makes him "sympathize with the Butlerian jihad," which is the funniest sentence written about this release.

But agent native does not mean you cannot write it by hand. It means the docs, the compiler errors, and the test setup are built for a reader that never gets tired.

Whether that is good depends on who you think writes your code in two years. I genuinely do not know. I have been wrong about this twice already.

The part i keep thinking about

The 57 minute number is not what stuck with me. It is that a machine built the same app three times, checked it three times, and nobody had to sit and watch.

My first cross-platform app took a month and it still looked wrong on Android.

I do not know if Exact wins. The math expression criticism might sink it. And a framework that changes daily is not a framework you build a business on yet.

But someone finally built the boring part. The part where the tool can see its own work. That part is not going away.

title: Designing a Coffee Batch Inspection Log with Flask,PostgreSQL,and Docker
description:
Abstract
The coffee batch inspection log basically is a web-based application developed to record and managed coffee batch inspection information.The project demonstrates how a simple information-management system can be built by using a Python Backend,a relational database,and containerization in which the main purpose is to provide a structured way to store batch details such as identification of the coffee,origin,processing method,and inspection status.The application also demonstrates cloud-services related concepts including HTTP communication,persistent storage,service configuration,and container health monitoring.
1.Introduction
Coffee production may involves multiple batches that may differ in origin processing method,and it's inspection results.Keeping these details very organized and well mannered is very crucial for traceability and record management.Therefore,a digital log can make it easier to add,view,update,and remove records than maintaining the same information in seperate manual documents.

The coffee Batch inspection Log was selected as a practical example of a data-management application in an Indonesian agricultural context.The project is not an automated coffee-quality detection system.Instead,it provides a web interface for users to record and manage inspection information.

2.Application Architecture
The application uses a three-part structure:a front-end,a backend,and a database.The frontend is a browser-based interface through which users interact with coffee batch records.The backend is written in Python using Flask.It receives the HTTP requests,validates submitted information,performs the request operation as well as communicates with the database.

PostgreSQL version 16 is used as the relational database which stores the batch records so that the information is not limited to the browser session.The backend connects to PostgreSQL using a database connection string supplied through the DATABASE_URL environment variable.The database service is addressed by its Compose service name,db,allowing the application container to communicate with it over the Docker Network.

3.CRUD Operations and Data Validation
The application supports the four basic data-management operations currently known as the CRUD:Create,Read,Update,and delete.Users can create a batch record,retrieve and view existing records,update information when details change,and delete a record when it is no longer required.

The backend validates the incoming data before it is stored and validation helps in preventing incomplete or invalid information from entering the database.For example,a required text fiels should not be empty,and numerical values should be within acceptable limits.The application also provides an API endpoint for retrieving batch records and a /health endpoint for checking application responsiveness.
4.Containerization with Docker
Docker is used to package the application and its runtime environment into a container image.The project Dockerfile uses a multi-stage build.In the first stage,Python as a virtual environment is created and the dependencies listed in requirements.txt are installed.In the second stage,a fresh python slim image is prepared,and the virtual environment and the applications file are copied into it.Gunicorn is used to serve the Flask application on the port 5000.

Seperating dependency installation from the runtime stage keeps the build process organized and avoids carrying the builder stage itself into the final runtime image.

5.Managing Services with Docker COmpose
Docker Compose defines,runs the application's two services:web and db.The web service builds the application image from the Dockerfile and maps host port 5001 to the container port 5000.The db service uses the PostgreSQL 16 image.

A named volume,postgres_data,is mounted to PostgreSQL's data directory to preserve database files when containers are recreated,provided the volume is not removed.The database health check uses pg_isready to test whether PostgreSQL is ready to accept connections.The web service uses service_healthy dependency condition so it waits for the database health check to pass before starting.Thes settings demonstrate service coordination and persistent storage in a multi-container application.

Conclusion
The Coffee Batch Inspection Log demonstrate how the Flask,PostgreSQL,Docker,and Docker Compose can be combined to build a practical web-based record management application which implements always and again the CRUD(Create,Read,Update,Delete) functionality,data validation,database persistence,containerized execution as well as health monitoring.The project provided practical experience with backend development,HTTP APIs,relational databases,Docker images,service dependencies and the persistent volumes.Although it does not automatically assess coffee quality,it establishes a digital foundation for organizing coffee batch inspection records.

References
1.Docker. Docker Compose. https://docs.docker.com/compose/
2.Docker. Docker Compose Quickstart. https://docs.docker.com/compose/gettingstarted/

title: Three more tests before you let an AI agent write to your CRM
description:
The earlier post listed five tests for an agent-ready CRM: revert in one action, pause one agent, an audit log that names who acted, a reply that stops the follow-up, and mail you can see before it leaves. Three readers came back with cases it missed. Each one is a better test than the five in that list, so here they are.

Test 6: take the API key away (from @autenai)

Not every agent uses the API. Computer-use agents drive the web UI in a signed-in browser, so the key-based controls in tests 2 and 3 never come into play.

Run it: sign in with a throwaway account, hand the browser to the agent, have it edit five records and delete one.

Pass: the log says an agent did it, separate from you. You can cut that agent off mid-run without signing yourself out. The delete can be undone.

Watch for: every action logged under the person whose session it is. Then pause, revoke and attribution all quietly assume the agent has a key. If the agent has to share your login, the honest scorecard answer is "not covered". The workaround is a second user (or browser profile) that exists only for the agent, so it can be told apart and switched off on its own.

Test 7: hit the rate limit halfway through a bulk update (from @junfengzhou01)

Give the agent a key with a low limit and have it update 200 records in a loop.

Pass: the call that hits the limit is refused with a status and a retry hint the agent can read, not a 500 or an HTML page. Nothing is half-applied inside a single record. Afterwards you can list exactly which records changed, by run, and revert only those. Retrying the whole loop with the same idempotency keys does not duplicate the ones that already went through.

Watch for: a bulk endpoint that returns 200 while quietly skipping the tail, a limit that answers in a format the agent cannot parse and so retries in a tight loop, and a log with no run id, where "which ones changed" means diffing a spreadsheet.

Test 8: stop one agent of several (from @Considus on Mastodon)

Considus built a stop file that halts an agent mid-run, and asked how a single server tells which agent to stop. Running one server instance per agent makes the switch easy, because the file belongs to one process. It also gives you N servers to keep in step.

Run it: two agents, one server. Start both on a long job and stop one.

Pass: the stopped agent's next call fails with a message that says why, and the other keeps going. Nothing restarts. The identity the server uses to decide is the credential on the call, not the process.

Watch for: a stop that is a flag the assistant can read and set itself, and a stop that only takes effect when the agent next asks for confirmation.

Scorecard additions

  • An agent in the browser is told apart from the person, and can be cut off alone.
  • A rate-limited agent gets a readable refusal, and you can list what changed.
  • One agent of several can be stopped on its next call.

Same rule as before: run them on a fresh workspace with throwaway data. A ninth test that caught something these did not is worth a comment.

From Deskhand, by Grain64.
