title: Shared eligibility doesn't mean shared progress
description:
A learner gets 90 on a sentence, tries again, and gets 94. Both attempts pass. Neither tells us whether the learner can still read that sentence 90 days later.

That distinction is easy to lose when adding a second kind of practice to an existing learning system. There is already a passing score, a progress record, and a review scheduler. Reusing them sounds reasonable until “passed” starts meaning two different things.

In Vocalace, our pronunciation app, sentence practice becomes available after a word reaches mastery. It then follows its own progression: pass the sentence once, wait 90 days, and pass its review. Sentence attempts must leave word mastery, word review scheduling, and daily practice-day counts untouched.

The interesting engineering problem is deciding how much those two progressions should share.

A prerequisite isn't ownership

A tempting abstraction would be a generic completePractice() function: check the score, advance progress, schedule a review, update daily activity. Add a practice-type argument and reuse it for sentences.

The trouble is that a passing score doesn't authorize the same writes in both workflows. A sentence attempt can read the word's mastery status to establish eligibility. It cannot change that status just because the same learner and vocabulary entry are involved.

I find it useful to separate two questions:

  • Is this learner allowed to start this activity?
  • What state can finishing it change?

The first can depend on another workflow. The second needs its own answer. This also comes up with certification after course completion, or a maintenance check after equipment approval. Sharing a prerequisite doesn't make their lifecycles interchangeable.

Keep the transition smaller than the record

Sentence progress lives on the existing vocabulary record: a stage, the first passing day, and a skip-until day. That storage choice doesn't require a shared transition function.

Keeping the fields together makes eligibility and sentence progress available on one record. The tradeoff is a weaker storage boundary: a broad update can touch unrelated progress. A separate table would make ownership more visible in the schema, at the cost of another relationship and its lifecycle. Neither layout decides which writes an attempt should be allowed to make.

For the transition itself, I'd pass only sentence progress. This standalone TypeScript example shows the boundary:

type SentenceProgress =
  | { stage: "unpassed" }
  | { stage: "waiting"; firstPassedDay: number }
  | { stage: "complete"; firstPassedDay: number };

const PASS_SCORE = 90;
const REVIEW_DAYS = 90;

function advanceSentence(
  progress: SentenceProgress,
  score: number,
  todayUtcDay: number,
): SentenceProgress {
  if (score < PASS_SCORE) return progress;

  if (progress.stage === "unpassed") {
    return { stage: "waiting", firstPassedDay: todayUtcDay };
  }

  if (
    progress.stage === "waiting" &&
    todayUtcDay >= progress.firstPassedDay + REVIEW_DAYS
  ) {
    return { stage: "complete", firstPassedDay: progress.firstPassedDay };
  }

  return progress;
}

Day values here are integer UTC calendar-day numbers: milliseconds since the Unix epoch divided by 86_400_000, rounded down. The caller supplies today's value. The actual stored date can still be UTC midnight; the example uses day numbers to keep the arithmetic readable.

There is no word review date in this function's input. Persistence should apply only the sentence fields it owns, leaving unrelated fields alone.

Make the clock part of the example

Notice that passing while waiting doesn't replace firstPassedDay. Otherwise, an enthusiastic learner who practices every day could keep postponing the review.

A score below 90 also preserves that date. Failing an overdue review leaves it overdue; it doesn't start another 90-day wait.

These are the boundary cases I'd test alongside the transition. Day 0 means the first passing UTC day:

Before Attempt day Score Expected
Unpassed 0 90 Waiting, first pass day 0
Waiting since day 0 0 94 Still waiting since day 0
Waiting since day 0 90 89 Still waiting since day 0
Waiting since day 0 90 90 Complete

An explicit clock makes these cases ordinary inputs. No sleeping, changing the machine clock, or hoping a test doesn't cross midnight.

It also makes queue selection straightforward. Waiting entries become due when today's UTC day reaches the first passing day plus 90. Due reviews come before unpassed sentences; completed entries leave the queue. Practicing again before that boundary is allowed, but cannot complete the scheduled review.

When reviewing this kind of addition, I'd look beyond whether the new progress advances correctly. I'd also check what stays unchanged after every attempt: the original mastery state, its review date, and its daily counters. Those unchanged values are part of the feature's contract, even when both workflows share a database row.

title: Why Apache returned 502 for our Go uploads
description:
An oversized upload should give someone a useful rejection. In our case, the browser received "Upload failed: 502" even though the Go handler had a file-too-large response. The affected site was RadarMakers, a free launch platform for indie makers, with Apache forwarding uploads to Go.

The interesting part was the difference between the application response and the response that reached the browser. The workaround checks the declared request length before parsing multipart data, attempts a bounded discard of an oversized body, then writes the rejection.

This account comes from the current handler and its Git history. The earlier failure is documented there; I have not reproduced it for this article. The code explains a specific workaround, with limits that matter as much as the happy path.

What the proxy changed

The failure was not simply that the application rejected a large file. The browser saw a 502 from Apache when the Go server reset the connection while the proxy was still forwarding the body. A direct request to the API had produced the handler response instead. That distinction is why the investigation followed the request across both hops.

Start a similar incident by capturing the browser response, the proxy error log, and the application log for the same request window. Compare a request sent through the public route with one sent directly to the service in a controlled environment. Keep the same method, headers, body, and authentication state. If the two paths differ, inspect how the proxy handles upstream resets and unread request bytes before changing the application status code.

This case record does not claim that every 502 during an upload has this cause. A proxy can return a gateway error for many upstream failures. Here the repository comment identifies the reset during body forwarding, and the recorded comparison showed a different response on the direct path. Those are the facts behind this particular workaround.

Why an early length check helped

The handler checks the declared Content-Length before wrapping the body or calling the multipart parser. When that value exceeds the request threshold, it takes a rejection path without parsing the form. This avoids spending image parsing work on a request that the server already intends to reject.

The header is only an early signal. A client can omit the length or send a value that does not describe the bytes that arrive. The source therefore keeps a second guard with http.MaxBytesReader before ParseMultipartForm. The Go documentation describes that reader as a request body limit that returns a MaxBytesError after a read crosses the configured size, and says it may tell the response writer to close the connection if possible.

The two checks answer different questions. The first decides whether the declared size already exceeds the limit and can be rejected before parsing. The reader limit protects the path where the header cannot make that decision. Neither check proves that the image is safe to decode. Content length limits transport size; image validation has separate responsibilities.

The drain is bounded for a reason

On the declared oversized path, the handler attempts to discard up to five times the body limit. With the current constant, that is a maximum read attempt of 25 MiB. The io.CopyN call writes to io.Discard, so these bytes are consumed for connection handling and are not stored as an upload.

A bounded drain is a tradeoff, not a universal recipe. Reading a portion of a rejected body can give a proxy a chance to finish forwarding bytes already in flight, but an unbounded read would let an oversized client keep the handler occupied for an arbitrary amount of data. The cap makes the maximum discard request explicit. The code ignores the returned byte count and error, then writes the 400 response, so it does not claim that every oversized body was fully consumed.

The comparison is important when changing the constants. Raising the file limit also changes the allowed request size and may change the maximum drain if the multiplier stays fixed. Increasing only the drain cap changes how much rejected traffic the handler may read. These values should be reviewed separately and tested with the proxy configuration that actually fronts the service.

Request bodies without a trustworthy length

HTTP request bodies can arrive without a useful declared size. The handler still wraps the body with MaxBytesReader, so the multipart parse cannot consume an unbounded body through this path. The same fallback also matters if the declared value is smaller than the bytes actually read. The header check is therefore an optimization and early rejection, not the sole security boundary.

A test suite should cover both known and unknown lengths. For a declared body above the threshold, assert that the early branch returns the intended status and message without parsing a multipart field. For a body whose declared size does not cross the threshold but whose actual bytes exceed it, assert that the reader limit controls the result. If the request uses chunked transfer, exercise the actual server and proxy path because middleware and proxy buffering can affect which component sees the limit first.

Avoid writing a test that only calls the handler directly and then declaring the production 502 fixed. The original difference occurred across Apache and Go. A direct handler test can verify the application branch, but it cannot verify how a deployed proxy handles a reset. Keep those claims separate in test names and release notes.

A transport limit is not a memory limit

The configured limit is applied to the request body and multipart parsing. After the file is read, the handler also decodes and re-encodes the image. A compressed image can represent far more pixels than its byte size suggests. That is why the code checks the image header before decoding all pixels, and why the comment explains the risk of an extremely large image dimension.

The header buffer in the handler is 64 KiB. io.ReadFull attempts to fill that buffer, while treating EOF and unexpected EOF as conditions that can still leave a usable short header. The checkImage call receives only the bytes actually read. If the header cannot be parsed, the handler returns a client error before calling sanitizeImage.

A request size limit and a dimension check protect different resources. The first bounds incoming body bytes. The second rejects an image whose decoded dimensions would require unreasonable memory. Re-encoding then creates a cleaned output from pixels rather than copying the original file bytes. These operations should remain independently visible in code review because a change to one does not remove the need for the others.

Extension policy is part of the safety design

The current allowlist accepts PNG, JPG, JPEG, and GIF after lowercasing the filename extension. SVG is deliberately absent because it is an active document format when served from the same origin. WebP is also absent because this implementation uses the standard library image path and re-encodes supported pixels. The allowlist is not a statement that every file with an accepted suffix is valid; the image decoder and sanitizer still inspect its contents.

A filename suffix is user supplied. It should not be treated as proof of the media type. The handler reads a header, checks it against the expected extension, seeks back to the start, reads the file, and sanitizes the decoded content. If a new format is added, test mismatched suffixes, malformed headers, oversized dimensions, and the final saved output. Also confirm that the chosen decoder and encoder remove metadata that should not be retained.

What to observe in production

Instrument the rejection path without logging the file contents or sensitive request data. Useful fields include the route, the outcome category, whether the declared size crossed the threshold, and whether the request had a usable length. Avoid recording raw filenames if they may contain personal data. A counter by outcome can help detect a burst of rejected uploads, but it cannot show whether the proxy delivered the intended response. For that, compare proxy status and application status in a request trace with a safe correlation identifier.

Keep the logs explicit about boundaries. The application can record that it wrote a 400 response. The proxy log can record what it returned to the client. If those values differ, the path between the two is the subject of the next investigation. Do not collapse them into one field called upload status.

Review the implementation as a set of invariants

The existing order expresses a set of useful invariants. Authentication is checked before upload processing. Declared oversized bodies are rejected before multipart parsing. Other bodies are wrapped in a byte limit. The multipart form must contain the expected file field. The extension must be allowed. Image data is checked from its header before a full decode. The source bytes are re-read from the start for sanitization, then only the cleaned result is saved.

When refactoring, preserve the ordering or explain which property has changed. A helper that moves parsing above the length check may reintroduce the expensive path. A helper that copies original bytes to disk may preserve metadata or unsafe content. A broader format list may bypass the established sanitizer. Write a test for each boundary that matters rather than asserting only that a valid PNG succeeds.

The documented workaround is deliberately narrow. It changes the oversized declared-length path so the handler can attempt a capped drain before writing its intended response. It does not claim to solve every proxy timeout, every malformed multipart form, or every malicious image. That narrow description is more useful to the next person debugging a similar symptom than a general promise that uploads are now safe.

Two charts from the implementation record

The threshold chart shows the exact request limit and drain ceiling read from internal/handler/upload.go. The format chart counts the extensions in the source allowlist: four accepted suffixes and two explicitly absent formats discussed in the code comments. These are implementation facts, not measurements of traffic or an estimate of risk. The diagrams already in the asset folder remain useful for request flow and the branch order; the charts add the actual values that a reader may want to compare with a proposed code change.

Before changing either number, rerun the relevant tests and inspect the deployment proxy limits, upload timeout, and body buffering configuration. This repository record documents the Go handler and its comments. It does not establish the settings of every reverse proxy or the behavior of every client.

Checklist for investigating a proxy upload error

  • [ ] Compare the public route and direct service response with the same request.
  • [ ] Correlate proxy and application logs for one request.
  • [ ] Check whether the content length is present and whether it matches the bytes sent.
  • [ ] Test the early rejection and the reader limit as separate paths.
  • [ ] Keep the rejected body drain capped and explain the cap.
  • [ ] Verify body size and decoded image dimensions independently.
  • [ ] Confirm the file header and extension agree before sanitizing.
  • [ ] Save only the re-encoded output when that is the security policy.
  • [ ] Test through the deployed proxy before claiming the client response is fixed.
  • [ ] Record which observations are from source, tests, or production logs.

The same upload had different outcomes

Commit 33cb05b, dated August 26, 2026, records an oversized upload returning 502 through Apache and 400 when sent directly to the API. That comparison is the historical observation. It places the discrepancy between the direct API response and the response delivered through the proxy.

The handler comments describe the mechanism: the body limit was crossed while Apache was still forwarding the upload, the Go connection reset, and Apache answered the browser with a bare 502. The intended rejection lost its useful explanation along the way.

That is the documented behavior of this deployment. It should not be read as a universal rule that every call to MaxBytesReader immediately resets a connection. The Go documentation for MaxBytesReader describes a reader that errors when reads exceed the limit and, where possible, tells the response writer to close the connection afterward.

The distinction matters when investigating a similar symptom. A browser's status describes what arrived at the browser. Reading the handler's error branch alone does not establish that its response survived the proxy path.

The limit applies to the request body

The size constant remains small and explicit. Excerpt from internal/handler/upload.go:

    const maxFileSize = 5 << 20 // 5MB

The expression is 5 MiB. The comment and user-facing message say MB, but the binary count is what the code enforces. More precisely, this is a request body limit. A multipart upload includes framing and fields as well as the file, so it is not an exact allowance of 5 MiB for image bytes alone.

The handler first checks authentication and returns 401 if claims are absent. The length decision discussed here happens after that check. It is not a description of how an anonymous request is processed.

Choosing this body threshold is an application design decision. The source supplies the value; it does not establish that this is the right threshold for every upload service.

Reject by declared length before parsing

The added branch sits before the reader wrapper and multipart parser. Excerpt from internal/handler/upload.go:

    if r.ContentLength > maxFileSize {
        io.CopyN(io.Discard, r.Body, 5*maxFileSize)
        writeJSON(w, http.StatusBadRequest, map[string]string{"message": "file too large (max 5MB)"})
        return
    }

The decision uses the declared length before reading body bytes. Once that length exceeds the threshold, the handler already knows which response it intends to send. It does not parse the multipart form or inspect the image on this branch.

It still reads from the body before responding. Those bytes go to io.Discard; they are not accepted as an upload. The purpose, stated in the comments, is to let the 400 travel back through Apache while accommodating data the client has already sent.

The selected status is 400, with the existing file-too-large message. That is the application's response choice. The patch changes how the handler reaches that response rather than increasing the accepted upload size.

The drain has its own ceiling

Multiplying the body threshold by five gives a discard cap of 25 MiB. That value is a separate design decision: the comments explicitly reject unbounded draining as a way for a client to make the server keep reading indefinitely.

The operation attempts to copy up to that amount from the body. The Go documentation for CopyN says it copies the requested count or stops on an error, returning the copied count and an error. This handler ignores both return values and proceeds to write 400.

For bodies whose actual size matches their declared size, a body over 5 MiB and no larger than 25 MiB fits within the drain budget. An earlier read error can still prevent a complete drain. A body larger than 25 MiB can leave bytes unread after the cap is reached.

Those consequences follow from the code. They do not establish that every oversized upload now avoids 502. The handler attempts a bounded accommodation of the proxy path; it does not verify that all bytes were consumed or guarantee delivery of its response.

A byte cap also should not be described as a time limit. This branch specifies an amount to discard, not a duration. Any claim about complete timeout protection would need evidence beyond these lines.

Unknown lengths keep the reader guard

The declared length check is not the only protection. Requests that bypass it still encounter the original wrapper and parser. Excerpt from internal/handler/upload.go:

    r.Body = http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, maxFileSize)

    if err := r.ParseMultipartForm(maxFileSize); err != nil {
        writeJSON(w, http.StatusBadRequest, map[string]string{"message": "file too large (max 5MB)"})
        return
    }

This includes requests without a declared length and those declaring a length at or below the threshold. The nearby comment also identifies an inaccurate declaration as a reason to retain the reader guard.

The branches therefore serve different purposes. Declared oversize selects the capped drain and rejection. Otherwise, actual reading remains bounded by MaxBytesReader before multipart parsing. Removing that wrapper would discard the protection for requests the length check cannot reject in advance.

There is another detail in the error handling: every error returned by this multipart parsing call maps to the same file-too-large message. Seeing that message is not, by itself, proof that the reader limit caused the parse error.

What is verified and what remains open

The history documents the earlier proxy failure. The current source contains the declared-length branch, the 25 MiB discard cap, and the retained 5 MiB reader limit. These are inspectable implementation facts.

The graphics README reports no regression test for the declared-length drain or Apache workaround in this checkout. Nearby image tests cover other concerns. They do not demonstrate that this response reaches a browser through Apache, and no such regression coverage is claimed here.

For a similar investigation, compare direct and proxied responses, then inspect what happens to unread request data when the handler rejects it. Keep the acceptance threshold, drain budget, and unknown-length behavior explicit. This patch makes those choices visible, while leaving a clear boundary around what its code and historical observation can support.

Sources

  • Go net/http documentation for MaxBytesReader:
  • Go io documentation for CopyN:
  • RadarMakers source: internal/handler/upload.go and the recorded change 33cb05b dated August 26, 2026.

title: Async video generation in Node.js with the Veo 3.1 Fast API
description:
Most text-to-video tutorials end at the first successful response. Production starts after that. A video job runs for minutes, the create call is long gone, and every retry is a chance to create and pay for a second task.

This guide builds a small Node.js client around those facts. The example model is Veo 3.1 Fast, a Google model that returns 4, 6 or 8-second clips with synchronized audio (model documentation). The patterns apply to any queue-backed generation API: create, wait, verify, retry, reconcile cost.

What an async video task looks like

A text-to-video call is two resources: a task you create, and a task you read.

POST /v1/tasks takes a model id, an input object, an optional callback_url, and optional metadata. It answers with 202 Accepted straight away. The body is the task: an id, status, the cost_credits charged, and timestamps. Generation happens behind that response.

For Veo 3.1 Fast the input is small:

  • prompt: up to 5,000 characters, including motion and sound.
  • image_urls: a public HTTPS first frame, and optionally a last frame.
  • duration: 4, 6 or 8 seconds.
  • resolution: 720p or 1080p.
  • aspect_ratio: 16:9, 9:16 or auto.

Unknown fields return 400 invalid_request with the offending field in error.param. That strictness is useful: a typo in resolution fails at submit instead of producing the wrong clip 20 minutes later.

A task moves through queued, processing, succeeded, failed or canceled. Only the last three are final, and a final status never changes. On succeeded, output holds CDN URLs. On failed, error.code explains why and refunded is true.

Cost is fixed when the task is created. Veo prices per video, not per second: 390 credits at 720p and 425 at 1080p, where 1 credit is US$0.001. A 4-second and an 8-second clip cost the same at the same resolution. If you are paying per video, generate the longest duration you can actually use. Duration and resolution are separate fields, but not every combination is valid; check the model page or its JSON Schema before a large batch.

curl -X POST https://genkiln.com/v1/tasks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GENKILN_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: video-job-8f2c1a" \
  -d '{
    "model": "veo-3.1-fast",
    "input": {
      "prompt": "A red fox trotting through fresh snow at dawn, low tracking shot",
      "duration": 8,
      "resolution": "720p",
      "aspect_ratio": "16:9"
    },
    "metadata": { "job_id": "8f2c1a" }
  }'

# 202 Accepted
# {"id":"task_...","status":"queued","cost_credits":390,...}

Make creation idempotent before adding retries

A timeout is worse than a 500. The server accepted the task, the response never reached you, and your code believes the request failed.

Idempotency-Key closes that gap. Send a value tied to your logical job, not to the HTTP attempt. Reusing the same key within 24 hours returns the original task, with Idempotent-Replayed: true, instead of creating and charging another one.

Two details decide whether it works.

First, the key must be stable across process restarts. Generate it from your own job id, store it next to the job, and reuse it from the retry worker. A fresh crypto.randomUUID() per attempt defeats the whole mechanism.

Second, the request body must be equivalent on retry. The comparison covers model, input, callback_url and metadata exactly as sent. If your metadata includes attempt: 2 or a freshly signed callback token, the same key returns 409 idempotency_conflict. Freeze the body when the job is first queued, then retry that frozen body unchanged.

Keep metadata small: 16 keys and 2 KB of JSON, with the whole body under 64 KB. It is echoed on the task and in webhooks, so { job_id } is usually enough.

// create-task.mjs — Node 20+
const API = "https://genkiln.com/v1";

export async function createVideoTask({
  jobId,
  prompt,
  resolution = "720p",
  callbackUrl, // omit for polling-only jobs; no URL means no webhook
}) {
  const body = {
    model: "veo-3.1-fast",
    input: { prompt, duration: 8, resolution, aspect_ratio: "16:9" },
    ...(callbackUrl ? { callback_url: callbackUrl } : {}),
    metadata: { job_id: jobId },
  };

  const res = await fetch(`${API}/tasks`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.GENKILN_API_KEY}`,
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "Idempotency-Key": `video-job-${jobId}`, // stable across retries
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(body), // same bytes on every attempt
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15_000),
  });

  if (!res.ok) {
    const err = await res.json();
    throw Object.assign(new Error(err.message ?? `HTTP ${res.status}`), {
      status: res.status,
      code: err.code,
      requestId: err.request_id,
      retryAfter: res.headers.get("retry-after"),
    });
  }

  return res.json(); // 202: { id, status: "queued", cost_credits, ... }
}

The 15-second timeout covers the HTTP request only. It does not cancel the task, and it should not: creation is designed to return before generation starts.

Polling: pick an interval and a deadline

Polling is the right choice for a local script, a low-volume tool, or a reconciliation job that checks tasks whose webhooks never arrived.

The API docs recommend polling every 3 to 10 seconds for images and every 10 to 30 seconds for video. A one-second loop mostly burns your query limit: reads count against 20 requests per second per API key, shared with every other read your service makes.

The bigger trap is the client deadline. AbortSignal.timeout() aborts the fetch; it does not stop the remote job (MDN notes on AbortSignal.timeout()). If your worker gives up after five minutes, the task can still finish 30 minutes later. You paid at creation, and nothing refunds a task that succeeded after you stopped looking.

So set the client deadline longer than the server's ceiling. Video tasks have a 45-minute server-side limit, counted from created_at; after that the task fails with timeout and is refunded. A 50-minute client deadline plus one final read covers the server's own cutoff.

// poll-task.mjs
const API = "https://genkiln.com/v1";
const FINAL = new Set(["succeeded", "failed", "canceled"]);

export async function pollTask(
  taskId,
  { intervalMs = 15_000, deadlineMs = 50 * 60_000 } = {},
) {
  const startedAt = Date.now();

  while (true) {
    const res = await fetch(`${API}/tasks/${taskId}`, {
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.GENKILN_API_KEY}` },
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15_000),
    });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`poll failed: HTTP ${res.status}`);

    const task = await res.json();
    if (FINAL.has(task.status)) return task;

    if (Date.now() - startedAt > deadlineMs) {
      const err = new Error(`stopped waiting for ${taskId}; task may still finish`);
      err.taskId = taskId;
      throw err;
    }

    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, intervalMs + Math.random() * 5_000));
  }
}

Keep the task id when you give up. A later reconciliation pass can read it once and record the real outcome; without the id, the charge becomes an unexplained line in your billing report.

Also, do not poll inside the HTTP handler that created the task. A request that holds a connection for 40 minutes will hit a load balancer timeout, and your user gets a 504 while the task succeeds. Create in the request, wait in a worker.

Webhooks: verify, enqueue, respond fast

For real volume, pass callback_url at creation and let the API call you. Each task sends at most one event: task.succeeded, task.failed or task.canceled. The body is the same task object that GET /v1/tasks/{id} returns.

Delivery is at-least-once. Return any 2xx within 10 seconds. A non-2xx response, a timeout, a connection error or a redirect counts as a failure, and the API retries after 1 minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes and 2 hours, five attempts in total. Deduplicate on the Genkiln-Delivery header, or on task id plus status.

Verify the signature before parsing anything:

  1. Read the raw request body as bytes.
  2. Split Genkiln-Signature on , into t and v1.
  3. Compute HMAC-SHA256 with your whsec_... secret over t + "." + rawBody.
  4. Compare in constant time, and reject if t is more than five minutes from now. 
// webhook.mjs
import express from "express";
import crypto from "node:crypto";

const app = express();
const secret = process.env.GENKILN_WEBHOOK_SECRET; // whsec_...

app.post(
  "/hooks/genkiln",
  express.raw({ type: "application/json" }),
  (req, res) => {
    const parts = Object.fromEntries(
      (req.get("Genkiln-Signature") ?? "").split(",").map((p) => p.split("=")),
    );
    const timestamp = Number(parts.t);
    const raw = req.body; // Buffer, never parsed

    const expected = crypto
      .createHmac("sha256", secret) // include the whsec_ prefix
      .update(`${parts.t}.`)
      .update(raw)
      .digest("hex");

    const given = Buffer.from(parts.v1 ?? "", "utf8");
    const mine = Buffer.from(expected, "utf8");
    const fresh = Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - timestamp) < 300;

    if (!fresh || given.length !== mine.length || !crypto.timingSafeEqual(given, mine)) {
      return res.sendStatus(401);
    }

    const task = JSON.parse(raw.toString("utf8"));
    enqueueOnce(req.get("Genkiln-Delivery"), task); // idempotent insert, then queue
    res.sendStatus(204); // under 10 seconds
  },
);

async function enqueueOnce(deliveryId, task) {
  // INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (delivery_id) DO NOTHING, then push to your job queue
}

Use crypto.timingSafeEqual for the comparison (Node crypto docs); a plain === leaks timing information.

The usual bug sits in the middleware order. express.json() parses and re-serializes the body, which changes the bytes, so the HMAC no longer matches. Register the webhook route with express.raw({ type: "application/json" }) before the JSON parser, or mount it on a separate app.

Then do the slow work after the response: download the MP4, copy it to your bucket, update the database, enqueue a thumbnail job. Output URLs are public and unguessable, but they are deleted 30 days after completion (expires_at), so the webhook is your best moment to take custody of the file.

callback_url must be a public HTTPS URL on port 443, with no credentials, at most 2,048 characters, and it is checked again before every delivery. localhost will not work; use a tunnel during development.

Retry only what can be retried

A retry policy needs a decision per status code, not one try/catch around everything.

Response Retry? Charge
400 invalid_request No No task created
401 invalid_api_key No No task created
402 insufficient_credits After top-up No task created
403 content_rejected No No task created
409 idempotency_conflict No; reuse the original body Original task stands
422 model_unavailable Later No task created
429 rate_limited Yes, after Retry-After No task created
500 internal_error Yes, with backoff Unknown; reconcile
503 service_busy Yes, after Retry-After Refunded; error.task included
Network error, no response Yes, same idempotency key Unknown; reconcile

The 500 row is why the idempotency key matters even for POST. You cannot tell from a dropped connection whether a task was created. Retrying with the same key returns the first task if it exists, or creates one if it does not. When you already have the id, GET /v1/tasks/{id} settles the state without another create.

429 has two causes: request rate, or 20 tasks already queued or processing on the account. Creation allows 5 requests per second per key; the 20-request figure above applies to reads. The concurrency response returns Retry-After: 10 and will not clear until some tasks finish, so a tight retry loop just adds load. Cap your own concurrency below 20 and queue the rest.

// retry.mjs
const RETRYABLE = new Set([429, 500, 503]);

export async function withRetry(fn, { attempts = 4, baseMs = 500 } = {}) {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < attempts; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (err) {
      const isLast = attempt === attempts - 1;
      const retryable = err.status === undefined || RETRYABLE.has(err.status);
      if (isLast || !retryable) throw err;

      const retryAfter = err.retryAfter == null ? NaN : Number(err.retryAfter);
      const delay = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1000
        : baseMs * 2 ** attempt + Math.random() * 250;

      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, delay));
    }
  }
}

Jitter matters when several workers retry together. Without it, a 429 for 20 workers becomes a synchronized retry every second. Retry-After wins over your backoff when present.

Check the cost before the batch, not after

cost_credits in the create response is the authoritative number for that task. Compute a batch estimate from it rather than from a price table in your head:

  • 40 clips at 720p: 40 × 390 = 15,600 credits = US$15.60.
  • 40 clips at 1080p: 40 × 425 = 17,000 credits = US$17.00.

GET /v1/balance tells you whether the batch fits. If the balance is too low, creation returns 402 insufficient_credits and no task exists, so a partially submitted batch is easy to detect: the failed job never got an id.

Refunds are automatic for failed, timed-out and canceled tasks, and the task object carries refunded: true. That makes reconciliation simple: sum cost_credits for tasks that did not end in succeeded, and check that each has a refund. Do not assume a failed request means no charge: a 503 can return a failed task in error.task that was charged and refunded, and you still want it in your records.

Track cost per usable asset, not per request. A batch where 10% of prompts are rejected by content screening costs nothing for the rejections, but it does cost you a retry cycle and a delay. Screening prompts before submission is cheaper than discovering the problem in the queue.

Finally, storage is outside the credit price. If you generate 500 clips a month and keep them, plan the bucket and the download step; the 30-day expiry will eventually delete anything you did not copy.

A short checklist

  • Key every create with a stable job id; freeze model, input, callback and metadata.
  • Poll every 10 to 30 seconds for video; set the client deadline above 45 minutes.
  • Prefer webhooks above a handful of concurrent jobs; verify raw bytes, then enqueue.
  • Deduplicate deliveries on Genkiln-Delivery.
  • Retry 429, 500 and 503 only, with Retry-After and jitter.
  • Record cost_credits and refunded per task; compare the batch total with your balance.

The transport layer is the same for every model behind an async API. What changes is the input schema and the price, so keep those in configuration and keep the job lifecycle in one place.

If you want a concrete endpoint to test against, genkiln exposes the Veo 3.1 Fast model with the fields used above, plus a JSON Schema per model and a public price list. It is an independent API service, not a Google product. The same client works with any queue-backed model; swap the model id and the input object, and keep the idempotency, polling and webhook code unchanged.

title: Vom Prompt zum Song: Asynchrone KI-Musikgenerierung mit TypeScript
description:
Ein Klick auf „Generieren“, dann mehrere Minuten Wartezeit: Bei einer Anwendung für KI-Musik liegt die eigentliche Integrationsarbeit zwischen dem Absenden einer Idee und dem ersten abspielbaren Track.

Was zeigt der Client währenddessen an? Wann darf er aufhören, den Status abzufragen? Und was passiert, wenn die Verbindung abbricht, obwohl der Auftrag bereits angenommen wurde?

Bei unserem Projekt KlangKI – KI-Songs auf Deutsch erstellen begegnen uns diese Fragen sowohl im Webprodukt als auch bei der Anbindung von KI-Assistenten. Dieser Beitrag betrachtet den öffentlich dokumentierten API-Vertrag und unseren offenen TypeScript-MCP-Adapter. Im Mittelpunkt steht die Client-Seite des Ablaufs; interne Modell- oder Queue-Implementierungen werden dafür nicht vorausgesetzt.

1. Auftrag und Ergebnis getrennt behandeln

Die Generierung dauert normalerweise etwa drei bis fünf Minuten. Der Client bekommt beim Start eine Aufgaben-ID und fragt das Ergebnis später separat ab.

Web-Client oder KI-Assistent
          |
          | Generierung anfordern
          v
      KlangKI API ----> taskId
          ^
          | Status mit taskId abfragen
          |
      Client erhält Status und Tracks
          |
          v
    audioUrl im Player verwenden

Die wichtigen Schnittstellen sind:

Operation Methode und Route
Musikgenerierung starten POST /api/music/generate
Aufgabenstatus lesen GET /api/music/task/status/{taskId}
Aufgabenhistorie lesen GET /api/music/my-music

Für eine Beschreibung wird beispielsweise dieser Request-Body gesendet:

{
  "formData": {
    "type": "text",
    "prompt": "Deutscher Indie-Pop über einen Neuanfang in Berlin, warme Gitarren, optimistische Stimmung",
    "isInstrumental": false
  }
}

Nach erfolgreicher Übermittlung sollte ein Client die zurückgegebene taskId aufbewahren. Damit lässt sich die Statusabfrage nach einer Unterbrechung wieder aufnehmen. Ein Seitenwechsel muss dann nicht automatisch zu einem neuen Generierungsauftrag führen.

API-Schlüssel gehören dabei in eine vertrauenswürdige Serverumgebung oder in die lokale Konfiguration des MCP-Prozesses. Ein geheimer Account-Schlüssel gehört nicht in ausgelieferten Browsercode.

2. HTTP-Erfolg und fachlichen Erfolg unterscheiden

Die API verwendet eine Antwort-Hülle mit code, message und data. Ein fachlicher Fehler kann auch mit HTTP 200 ankommen. Deshalb reicht die Prüfung von response.ok allein nicht aus.

Der Adapter prüft beide Ebenen. Hier ein gekürzter Ausschnitt aus der Antwortbehandlung, nachdem die JSON-Struktur bereits validiert wurde:

if (!response.ok || envelope.code !== "SUCCESS") {
  throw new ApiError(
    envelope.code === "SUCCESS"
      ? `HTTP_${response.status}`
      : envelope.code,
    typeof envelope.message === "string"
      ? envelope.message
      : `API error (HTTP ${response.status}).`,
    isRecord(envelope.data) ? envelope.data : undefined,
  );
}

Das ist besonders bei Fehlern wie fehlenden Credits wichtig. Ein Client soll diesen Fall verständlich anzeigen können und eventuell mitgelieferte Informationen behalten. Der vollständige Adapter behandelt außerdem ungültiges JSON, fehlende Antwortfelder und Netzwerkfehler.

3. Polling nach einer Serverentscheidung beenden

Eine verbreitete Versuchung ist, im Client eine eigene Liste aller abschließenden Statuswerte zu pflegen. Ändert sich der Vertrag, können verschiedene Clients dann unterschiedlich entscheiden, ob eine Aufgabe noch läuft.

Unser Status-Endpunkt liefert dafür isTerminal. Der Client verwendet dieses Feld, um das Polling zu beenden. Für die Darstellung bleiben status, vorhandene Tracks und ein möglicher errorCode relevant.

isTerminal: true bedeutet, dass der Vorgang abgeschlossen ist. Es bedeutet nicht automatisch, dass ein Song erfolgreich erzeugt wurde.

Für die MCP-Nutzung empfehlen wir ungefähr 15 bis 30 Sekunden Abstand zwischen Statusabfragen. Ein Client sollte jeweils die vorherige Abfrage abwarten, damit bei langsamen Antworten keine überlappenden Requests entstehen.

Einzelne Tracks können bereits verfügbar sein, bevor der gesamte Auftrag abgeschlossen ist. Deshalb sind zwei Entscheidungen getrennt zu treffen:

  • Gibt es bereits einen Track mit einer abspielbaren audioUrl?
  • Ist die Aufgabe insgesamt abgeschlossen, sodass keine weiteren Statusabfragen nötig sind?

Das ermöglicht eine frühere Wiedergabe, ohne den restlichen Auftrag aus dem Blick zu verlieren. Ob und wie Teilergebnisse angezeigt werden, ist eine Entscheidung der jeweiligen Oberfläche.

4. Ein Timeout ist ein unbekanntes Ergebnis

Der kritischste Fall entsteht beim Starten einer Generierung:

Client sendet POST
        |
Server nimmt den Auftrag an
        |
Antwort erreicht den Client nicht
        |
Client sieht einen Timeout

Der Auftrag kann zu diesem Zeitpunkt bereits existieren und Credits verbrauchen. Ein automatisches Wiederholen des POST-Requests könnte einen zweiten kostenpflichtigen Auftrag anlegen.

Unser Adapter wiederholt HTTP-Anfragen deshalb nicht automatisch. Bei einer unsicheren Musikübermittlung fordert er dazu auf, zuerst die Aufgabenhistorie mit kisong_list_tasks oder im Webkonto zu prüfen.

Für eine Oberfläche würde ich diesen Fall ausdrücklich als „Übermittlung unklar“ darstellen. Eine passende Meldung wäre:

Die Verbindung wurde unterbrochen. Dein Auftrag könnte bereits gestartet sein. Prüfe zuerst deine letzten Generierungen, bevor du einen neuen Auftrag sendest.

Die Historie ist dabei eine Hilfe zur Klärung, keine Garantie für eine automatische Zuordnung: Wenn jemand mehrere ähnliche Aufträge kurz hintereinander startet, kann die Zuordnung ohne zusätzliche Kennung mehrdeutig sein.

Für eine zukünftige API-Erweiterung wäre ein serverseitig unterstützter Idempotenzschlüssel eine Möglichkeit, Wiederholungen eindeutig demselben Auftrag zuzuordnen. Der hier beschriebene Adapter setzt eine solche Funktion nicht voraus.

5. Abbrechen der Abfrage und Abbrechen des Auftrags trennen

Ein lokales AbortSignal kann einen laufenden HTTP-Request beenden. Daraus folgt jedoch nicht, dass die Musikgenerierung auf dem Server gestoppt wurde.

Im Adapter werden das konfigurierte Zeitlimit und das Abbruchsignal des MCP-Requests kombiniert:

const timeout = AbortSignal.timeout(this.config.timeoutMs);
const signal = options.signal
  ? AbortSignal.any([timeout, options.signal])
  : timeout;

Eine Schaltfläche „Nicht weiter warten“ sollte daher genau diese lokale Wirkung vermitteln. Ohne einen bestätigten serverseitigen Abbruch sollte sie nicht versprechen, den Auftrag oder seine Abrechnung rückgängig zu machen.

6. Dieselben Grenzen für KI-Assistenten sichtbar machen

Beim Model Context Protocol (MCP) erhält ein Assistent Werkzeuge für einzelne Operationen. Unser Adapter trennt beispielsweise:

  • kisong_get_credits: Musik-Credits prüfen.
  • kisong_generate_song: einen Generierungsauftrag starten.
  • kisong_get_task: den Fortschritt eines bekannten Auftrags lesen.
  • kisong_list_tasks: die Aufgabenhistorie zur Klärung heranziehen.

Generierungswerkzeuge sind mit idempotentHint: false beschrieben. Status- und Historienwerkzeuge haben Hinweise auf lesende, idempotente Nutzung. Solche Metadaten helfen dem Client bei der Einordnung; sie ersetzen weder Berechtigungsprüfungen noch die eigentliche Fehlerbehandlung.

Auch die Werkzeugbeschreibungen gehören zum Integrationsdesign: Sie nennen den Credit-Verbrauch, die asynchrone Aufgaben-ID und die Regel, nach einem Timeout nicht automatisch erneut zu generieren.

Die vollständigen Eingabegrenzen und Endpunkte stehen im API-Vertrag des Adapters. Das Repository enthält außerdem Tests mit einer lokalen Mock-API für Validierung, fachliche Fehler und das Ausbleiben automatischer Wiederholungen.

Was ich daraus für die Oberfläche ableite

Für eine brauchbare Oberfläche würde ich mindestens zwischen „wird übermittelt“, „Generierung läuft“, „Übermittlung unklar“ und einem abschließenden Ergebnis unterscheiden. Verfügbare Tracks können unabhängig davon angezeigt werden.

Ein Fortschrittsbalken mit erfundenen Prozentwerten hilft dabei wenig. Eine gespeicherte Aufgaben-ID, ein verständlicher Status und ein Weg zurück zur Historie helfen unmittelbar, wenn etwas schiefgeht.

Wer den Anwendungsfall ausprobieren möchte, findet auf KlangKI die Generierung aus Beschreibungen und eigenen Songtexten. Der offene MCP-Adapter zeigt dazu die konkrete API-Anbindung in TypeScript.

Wie behandelt ihr in euren Anwendungen den Fall, dass ein kostenpflichtiger Auftrag möglicherweise angenommen wurde, die Antwort aber verloren geht?

title: Same H100, $2.69 vs $12.29/hr — The Cost-Opacity Tax
description:
A GitHub repo called Data Receipts landed on Hacker News this week with an uncomfortable finding: the same NVIDIA H100 SXM 80GB GPU costs $2.69 per hour on RunPod Community Cloud and $12.29 per hour on Azure — a 4.57x spread for identical silicon. The thread hit 124 points and 72 comments in hours, and the top comment set the tone: "You are completely mad if you are running any kind of valuable workload on Runpod community or Vast. Hosts are absolutely peeking inside the VMs."

📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on ComputeLeap →

That single comment reveals the real story. The spread is not a pricing bug. It is a tax — a cost-opacity tax — and you pay it on every GPU hour and every API token you consume. You pay it because nobody in this industry publishes comparable units, and the cheapest option on every comparison chart is always the one charging you in something you cannot see.

View original discussion on Hacker News →

The 4.57x Spread: What You Are Actually Buying

The Data Receipts analysis does something unusually disciplined: it compares only on-demand list prices for the same GPU variant (SXM 80GB), in the same region class (US), using each provider's cheapest available SKU. No spot pricing, no reserved instances, no volume discounts.

View the full dataset on GitHub →

The result:

Provider $/GPU-hr Monthly (730 hrs)
RunPod Community $2.69 $1,964
RunPod Secure $3.99 $2,913
AWS p5.48xlarge $6.88 $5,022
Azure ND96isr H100 v5 $12.29 $8,972

The author is careful to note what the 4.57x is not: it is not InfiniBand interconnect (Azure's $12.29 includes 400 Gbps/GPU Quantum-2 InfiniBand with GPU Direct RDMA), it is not a datacenter SLA, and it is not enterprise compliance or committed capacity. Those things cost money. The question is whether they cost 4.57x more money, and the answer — if you are doing single-node fine-tuning — is obviously no.

View original post on X →

The practical math gets worse when you add context. SemiAnalysis data shows H100 one-year contract pricing bottomed at $1.70/hr in October 2025 and rebounded to roughly $2.35–$2.80 by mid-2026. Dylan Patel, presenting at Modal's Runtime 2026 conference, put the current midpoint at $2.80 and said he would not be surprised if H100s pass $3/hr. Meanwhile, a separate comparison found that published rates span $1.80 to $12.29 per GPU-hour — a 6.8x spread — and that availability and egress fees narrow the gap less than you would hope.

ℹ️ The real spread is wider than 4.57x. If you include spot and marketplace pricing, the cheapest captured H100 rate drops to $0.31/hr (spot), putting the spread against Azure's $12.29 at nearly 40x. But spot comes with no availability guarantee and zero SLA — you are renting headroom that can vanish mid-job.

The Privacy Price Tag Nobody Lists

The HN thread's sharpest insight was not about price but about what the cheap price costs you. The top commenter reported that Vast.ai and RunPod Community hosts "are absolutely peeking inside the VMs" — and that this is "openly discussed in their Discords."

This is the part of the price comparison that never appears in any comparison chart. RunPod splits its inventory into two tiers: Secure Cloud (RunPod's own datacenters, SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001) and Community Cloud (third-party hosts renting their own hardware, no SLA). The $2.69 figure is Community. Secure is $3.99 — a 48% premium just for the assurance that your host is not inspecting your workload.

Vast.ai is even more explicit. It is a peer-to-peer marketplace. You choose a GPU and a landlord. Privacy depends entirely on who that landlord is. As one analysis put it, effective costs on unverified Vast hosts run 20–40% higher after accounting for downtime and restarts, and the security tradeoffs of peer-to-peer compute are left entirely to the buyer.

We wrote about a parallel dynamic in Cursor Router: 60% Savings. It Also Sees Every Prompt. The pattern is the same: the cheapest compute is always the compute that can see what you are doing with it. Model routers see your prompts. Community GPU hosts see your weights. Budget token providers see your data. The discount is not free — it is priced in privacy.

⚠️ Contrarian Corner: the opacity is a feature. Hyperscalers deliberately bundle InfiniBand, compliance, egress, and SLA into a single per-GPU-hour price because unbundling would reveal that raw compute is a commodity with razor margins. Transparency would commoditize them — so they fight it. The price spread is not an accident of a young market. It is a moat.

Token-Level Opacity: Same Disease, Different Organ

The GPU price spread is the hardware layer of a problem that runs all the way up the stack. At the software layer, the same disease shows up as tokenomics chaos.

This week at AI Engineer NYC 2026, Pratyusha Duvvuri from Cisco presented a talk titled "Why No One Agrees on What Their AI Tokens Cost." The backstory: after Cisco acquired Galileo, an AI observability platform, they surveyed roughly 100 enterprise companies about their token-cost accounting. The result: roughly 100 different definitions.

This is not a trivial definitional disagreement. It is a measurement crisis. Consider what "cost per token" could mean:

  • The API rate card: Claude 4 Sonnet at $3.30/$16.50 per million input/output tokens (DeepInfra pricing, April 2026). This is what most people compare.
  • The effective rate with caching: DeepSeek V3.2 drops from $0.26 to $0.13/M tokens with cached input — a 50% discount that only applies if your workload hits the cache.
  • The orchestration cost: A single agentic task may involve dozens or hundreds of inference calls. OpsLyft found that hidden costs — retrieval, embeddings, context management, retries — add 40–60% on top of tracked inference bills.
  • The total cost of inference: As the FinOps Foundation argues, only inference is priced in tokens. Cloud compute, networking, egress, data licensing, and governance are separate line items that never appear in a tokens/dollar comparison.

The result is a market where GPT-4-equivalent performance costs about $0.40 per million tokens, down from $20 in late 2022 — a 98% drop — while enterprise AI budgets have tripled from $1.2 million to $7 million per year. Artefact calls this the "token cost illusion." Per-token prices are falling. Total bills are rising. And nobody can explain the gap because they are measuring different things.

View original post on X →

Read the full TNW analysis →

ℹ️ By the numbers: Uber reportedly used its entire 2026 AI coding budget by April. Microsoft spent $500–$2,000 per engineer per month on tokens before revoking Claude Code licenses. Per-developer token consumption rose roughly 18.6x in nine months, per Jellyfish data. Engineers who used the most tokens were about twice as productive — but consumed roughly 10x the tokens.

View original post on X →

We have covered the per-token trap before — see our analysis of why AI got cheaper and your bill didn't. But the tokenomics problem has gotten worse because agentic workflows have multiplied consumption per task by 5–30x (Splunk State of Observability 2026) while the unit of measurement has stayed the same.

The Industry's Attempt at a Fix

The measurement crisis got bad enough that the Linux Foundation launched the Tokenomics Foundation in August 2026, with 30 founding members and a mandate to define open standards for AI token usage and billing. Their proposed metrics include cost-per-intelligence and tokens-per-watt — units that attempt to connect consumption to outcomes and physical resources rather than abstract API pricing.

Read the Linux Foundation announcement →

The FinOps Foundation, which already maintains the open FOCUS billing specification for cloud costs, is working in parallel. FOCUS 1.4 now includes cloud billing normalization, and the two foundations are coordinating on how to extend it to AI-specific spend.

Salesforce's Nishant Gupta captured the mood: "Token economics is fundamentally more abstract and opaque than anything we've managed at this scale before." And the FinOps Foundation's J.R. Storment warned that token tracking is "a trillions-of-rows-a-month data problem" — orders of magnitude beyond traditional cloud billing.

The vendor ecosystem is not waiting for standards. Pay-i, Jellyfish, Waydev, Faros AI, Datadog, New Relic, and now Cisco's Splunk (via Galileo) are all building AI-cost observability products. Factory launched a model router that picks the cheapest adequate model per task. But without a common unit of measurement, each tool measures cost differently — which means comparing observability tools is itself an opacity problem.

What This Means for You

If you are a founder, CTO, or platform engineer making compute decisions right now, here is the framework that the price comparisons will not give you:

1. Normalize for what is included, not what is listed. The $2.69 RunPod Community hour does not include isolation guarantees, an SLA, or InfiniBand. The $12.29 Azure hour does. Neither price includes egress ($0.01–$0.09/GB depending on provider), storage, or the engineering time to manage the deployment. Build a total-cost model that includes at minimum: GPU-hour rate, interconnect requirements, egress at your data volume, SLA value (what does an hour of downtime cost you?), and privacy/compliance posture.

2. Separate training from inference economics. Multi-node training requires InfiniBand interconnect — the cheap tier literally cannot do the job. Single-node fine-tuning and inference do not. As the Data Receipts analysis notes, single-node work pays for interconnect it will never use on Azure. Match the workload to the tier.

3. Budget for tokens-per-task, not tokens-per-call. Agentic workflows are the new normal. A single agent task can burn 50,000–500,000 tokens before producing output. Engineer-level coding assistants consume millions of tokens per developer per day. If your budget assumes per-seat pricing, you are understating costs by an order of magnitude. We covered this in detail in AI's $700B Subsidy Clock Is Ticking.

View original post on X →

4. Treat privacy as a line item. The cheapest GPU and the cheapest token both come with a privacy cost. Community GPU hosts see your workloads. Budget token providers process your data. If you are working with proprietary models or sensitive data, the $1.30/hr premium for RunPod Secure over Community is not a luxury — it is a security requirement. And even "secure" tiers may not meet regulatory requirements (SOC 2 and ISO 27001 are not HIPAA or FedRAMP).

💡 Your compute-cost normalization checklist:

  • GPU-hour rate (on-demand vs. reserved vs. spot)
  • Interconnect tier (InfiniBand for multi-node? Or not needed?)
  • Egress fees at your actual data volume
  • SLA terms and downtime cost
  • Privacy/compliance certification level
  • Token orchestration overhead (retries, context window, RAG pipeline multiplier)
  • Vendor lock-in switching cost

5. Watch the standards bodies. The Tokenomics Foundation is early, but its proposed metrics — cost-per-intelligence, tokens-per-watt — point toward a future where compute costs are comparable across providers. Until that future arrives, you are doing the normalization yourself. The companies that build internal cost observability now will have a structural advantage when the industry finally agrees on how to count.

The Prediction

The 4.57x GPU spread will compress. Raw H100 compute is commoditizing — as we wrote in Compute Is Now a Tradable Commodity, the emergence of GPU price indices and futures markets will erode the information asymmetry that sustains the spread. SemiAnalysis and Silicon Data already publish real-time price data; CME Group is exploring compute futures.

But the opacity will not disappear. It will migrate. Today it lives in GPU-hour pricing and per-token rates. Tomorrow it will live in agentic task pricing, where a single "agent run" bundles compute, orchestration, tool calls, retries, and data processing into a single opaque fee. The companies that survive this transition will be the ones that can decompose that fee and allocate each component to business value.

Goldman Sachs projects global token usage will grow 24x by 2030. If the unit of measurement is still a mess when that happens, the cost-opacity tax will be the largest invisible line item in every AI budget.

The tax is not the price. The tax is not knowing what the price actually means.

Originally published at ComputeLeap

title: Introducing Vercel Security Review
description:
Today, we are launching Vercel Security Review in public beta.

Security Review is a new capability in Vercel Agent, alongside Code Review and Investigation. Once enabled, it scans for vulnerabilities on every push to a team's connected GitHub repositories.

Findings appear as comments on pull requests, are listed in the Security dashboard, and are available via CLI. With your permission, Vercel Agent can also validate and push fixes for findings.

How it works

Security reviews are triggered by GitHub push events, including direct pushes to your production branch. In monorepos, reviews are scoped to the project's root directory. Here is how it works:

  1. You push code to a GitHub repository connected to a Vercel project.

  2. As soon as the push lands, Security Review scans the changed code for vulnerabilities like missing authorization checks or exposed secrets.

  3. Findings are posted to the Security dashboard. On private and internal repositories, Security Review also adds a GitHub check to the commit and comments on the pull request.

  4. You can fix findings by clicking Fix with Vercel Agent in the dashboard, or use the CLI to pull findings and have your own coding agent implement changes.

  5. When subsequent security reviews no longer detect a finding, it is marked as no longer detected in the dashboard, and the GitHub comment is closed.

Each review compares the push against a base and covers only what changed. For deployments, the base is the branch’s previous deployment, so the agent reviews the change against what’s already running. Because it only scans the diff, Security Review finishes in seconds and can run on every preview and production deployment.

What the agent checks

The agent reads the diff along with the surrounding code, traces how the changed code can be reached, checks for existing protections, and rechecks each finding before reporting it. That process is how it catches logic flaws like missing authorization checks, which pattern-matching scanners miss.

Each review also applies your team’s security policies, which you can write in plain language and apply to specific projects or across your team. For example, a policy can require any endpoint that returns customer data to check that the requester owns it. You can also manage policies with the Vercel CLI, using vercel security policy.

How findings are tracked

Each new finding is checked against ones that have already been reported, so the same issue isn’t flagged twice. Every finding is tied to the deployment where it first appeared and changes are followed from there. That means that when a vulnerable change from a pull request is merged into your production branch, the finding is flagged in production as well.

When a later review no longer detects the issue in an environment, the agent marks the finding as no longer detected there.

Acting on findings

Every finding explains the vulnerability and how to fix it, with links to the commit and deployment where it first appeared.

Findings are listed in the Vulnerability view in the Security dashboard, where you can ask Vercel Agent to validate and commit fixes. Findings are also available via CLI, so you can fix vulnerabilities with your own coding agent.

Each new finding generates an audit log event, which Enterprise teams can send to their SIEM through Audit Log Drains.

Here is a demo of sample findings in the dashboard:

Fixing vulnerabilities with Vercel Agent

When Vercel Agent can fix a finding, you will see the option to click Fix with Vercel Agent on the finding page in the dashboard. After you click, the agent confirms the vulnerability still exists, then makes the smallest change that fixes it and updates the tests.

Say a developer pushes a change to an invoice download endpoint, and the lookup doesn't check which organization the invoice belongs to. Within seconds, Security Review flags that any signed-in user could download another organization's invoice by changing its ID. Vercel Agent's fix scopes the lookup to the user's organization:

Fixing vulnerabilities with your own coding agent

You can point your coding agent or other systems at the Vercel CLI to pull and fix vulnerabilities:

Findings in the dashboard also give you the ability to copy details as Markdown or JSON, making it easy to paste them into an agent conversation.

Every code change needs security review

Frontier AI models are making vulnerabilities far easier to find and exploit. Last month, researchers turned two decade-old flaws in PHP core into working remote code execution exploits with relatively little effort.

At the same time, agents are writing more of the code teams ship, and each handles security review its own way, or in many cases, not at all.

With Vercel Security Review, you can scan every push on every project for vulnerabilities by default, using the security policies you set.

What's next

Security Review starts with code pushed to GitHub. Next, we're bringing it to deployments from the Vercel CLI and v0, and to repositories that don't deploy on Vercel. We're also working on suggested fixes you can apply directly from the pull request.

Get started

Vercel Security Review is available today in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams.

To get started, enable Security Review in Vercel Agent Settings. You can choose to run Security Review on all projects, or only the ones you choose. To learn more, read the Changelog entry and the Security Review documentation.

Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate, with model tokens at the provider's rate and no markup, plus $0.25 per million tokens.

Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026. Fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the rate above.

title: 弱視のVR視覚訓練を「工学」として考える——両眼視フィードバックの設計と、脳の可塑性というニュースから
description:
弱視のVR視覚訓練を「工学」として考える——両眼視フィードバックの設計と、脳の可塑性というニュースから

2026年11月、サイエンス・デイリーが報じた研究が静かに話題になっています。UTHealth Houstonのチームが65歳以上の成人約20万人を分析し、高用量インフルエンザワクチン接種群でアルツハイマー病の発症リスクが約55%低かったと報告しました。標準用量で以前示されていた約40%の低下をさらに上回る数字です。

もちろんこれは観察研究であり、「ワクチンを打てばアルツハイマー病を防げる」と断定するものではありません。ただ、技術者として面白いのは数字そのものではなく、「成人後も脳と身体の働きを再調整できる余地がある」という視点です。長年「加齢に伴う変化は仕方ない」とされてきた領域に、介入可能なパラメータがあるかもしれない、という話です。

視覚も例外ではありません。片眼性弱視（lazy eye）や両眼の協調課題は「子どものうちに矯正するもの」「大人になってからでは遅い」と言われ続けてきました。しかし可塑性の知見は更新されています。ならば問い直すべきは「今さら間に合うのか」ではなく、「毎日続けられる形になっているか」——つまり、継続可能なシステムとして設計されているかです。

弱視訓練が「続かない」のは、たいてい仕組みの問題

従来の訓練は遮蔽（アイパッチ）や赤青メガネなど、身体に貼る・かけるタイプが中心でした。効果は期待できる一方で、見た目が目立つ、単調で飽きる、生活リズムに組み込みにくい。結果として継続が難しい。これは意志の問題ではなく、日常に馴染む形になっていないという設計の問題です。

エンジニアの目で見れば、これは典型的な「UXとアーキテクチャのミスマッチ」です。訓練効果を最大化するロジックは正しくても、それを毎日の生活に載せるインターフェースが重すぎる。結果、ユーザーは離脱し、システムは本来のポテンシャルを発揮しない。弱視訓練の分野では、この「ラストワンマイル」が長く未解決のままでした。

Amblyotubeという選択肢——dichoptic vision trainingの実装

Amblyotubeは、Seven Sportsが開発した、VRでの視覚協調・注意トレーニングのためのレクリエーション／教育目的ソフトウェアです。Meta Quest向けアプリで、左右の眼に異なる映像体験を届けるのが特徴です。仕組みを工学的に見ていくと、両眼視フィードバックの設計として興味深い点がいくつかあります。

  • 好きなYouTube動画がそのまま訓練になる：仮想ルームまたはRoom ViewのARパススルーで、普段見ている動画を再生。コンテンツ選択という継続のハードルを下げます。
  • 優位眼には調整可能なデジタルブラー（Dominant Eye Shader）：優位眼の情報をやわらかく弱め、弱視眼の参加を促します。
  • 弱視眼にはAI Sharpener（MFBF）：人物を検出し、太い赤い輪郭・黄緑のハイライト・一定リズムの明滅で注意を引きます。
  • Wedge Occlusion（任意）：各眼の視野の一部を遮り、それぞれの眼が異なる部分を見る状態をつくることで、両眼視の競合（binocular rivalry）を軽減します。
  • マゼンタのフォーカスキュー：弱視眼の視界に明るいマゼンタの手がかり、優位眼に控えめなニュートラルグレーのドットを表示し、追従によって一つの立体像へ統合していきます。
  • LogMAR視力チェックや左右眼・重症度プリセット（Mild／Moderate／Severe）で、自分の状態に合わせて開始できます。

推奨は1日30〜40分（最大1時間）、13歳以上。接着式のアイパッチや赤青メガネは不要です。

アーキテクチャとしての両眼視フィードバック

ここからは、Amblyotubeを「視覚訓練のためのランタイム」として捉え、その設計上の意思決定を分解してみます。すべては製品リファレンスに基づく記述で、実装の推測は含みません。

レイヤ1：知覚入力の非対称化

dichoptic trainingの核心は、左右の眼に異なる情報を届けることです。単眼ごとに独立したレンダリングパスを持つVRは、この非対称化と相性がいい。Amblyotubeでは、優位眼にDominant Eye Shader（調整可能なブラー）、弱視眼にAI Sharpener（MFBF）という、方向性の異なる2つのフィルタを適用します。優位眼の信号を減衰させ、弱視眼の信号を強調する——一種のゲイン調整です。

レイヤ2：注意の誘導

フィルタだけでは、弱視眼は「見えてはいるが使われていない」状態になりがちです。そこでAI Sharpenerが人物を検出し、太い赤い輪郭・黄緑のハイライト・一定リズムの明滅で注意を引きます。マゼンタのフォーカスキューも同様に、弱視眼側に明るい手がかり、優位眼側に控えめなニュートラルグレーのドットを置き、両眼の追従を一つの立体像へ統合していきます。

レイヤ3：競合の緩和

両眼視の競合（binocular rivalry）は、訓練を阻害するノイズ源です。Wedge Occlusionは各眼の視野の一部を遮り、それぞれの眼が異なる部分を見る状態をつくることで、この競合を軽減します。オプション扱いなのは、ユーザーの状態によって必要性が変わるからでしょう。

レイヤ4：計測とキャリブレーション

LogMAR視力チェックと、左右眼・重症度プリセット（Mild／Moderate／Severe）は、訓練を「自分の状態に合わせて開始する」ための入力層です。ここが固定的だと、ユーザーは自分に合わない負荷で始めてしまい、離脱につながります。

トレードオフの読み方

この設計には、いくつかの明確なトレードオフがあります。

  • 臨床的正確さ vs 継続性：厳密な訓練プロトコルを組むほど、日常への組み込みは難しくなる。Amblyotubeは「好きなYouTube動画がそのまま訓練になる」という選択で、継続性側に寄せています。
  • 介入の強さ vs 疲労：1日30〜40分（最大1時間）という推奨は、効果と疲労のバランス点として提示されています。
  • 汎用ハードウェア vs 専用設計：Meta Questというコンシューマ向けデバイスを使うことで、専用機器のコストと導入障壁を下げています。

「今日から始められる形」を選ぶ

高用量ワクチンの研究が示唆するのは、大人になっても脳と身体に働きかける余地がある、ということです。弱視の視覚訓練も、その延長線上で考えていい。

ただし、Amblyotubeは診断・治療・治癒を目的としたものではありません。両眼の協調と奥行き知覚のための補助的な視覚トレーニング／支援ツールです。気になる症状がある場合は、必ず眼科医などの専門家に相談してください。

Amblyotube（Meta Quest ストア）
https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

免責事項

  • 推奨セッション：1日30〜40分（最大1時間）
  • 対象年齢：13歳以上
  • Amblyotubeは補助的な視覚トレーニング／支援ツールであり、診断・治療・治癒を目的としたものではありません。
  • 本記事で紹介した研究は観察研究であり、因果関係を示すものではありません。

キーワード：弱視 大人 トレーニング, 片眼性弱視, lazy eye, 両眼視 訓練, 奥行き知覚, VR 視覚トレーニング, Meta Quest アプリ, 視覚協調, 脳の可塑性, 高用量インフルエンザワクチン アルツハイマー

title: We checked 4,198 x402 endpoints. First, our checker got 420 of them wrong
description:
We sell a small x402 endpoint check: give it a URL, and it tells you whether the endpoint answers with a payment request an agent can actually pay. On 2026-11-06 we ran it over every service listed on agentic.market, one endpoint per service, to publish a picture of the market. The first thing it measured was itself, and it came out badly.

The first run said 73% of endpoints were valid

That number looked plausible, which is the dangerous kind. Reading why individual endpoints failed showed most of the failures were ours:

  • We asked the wrong way. Our check sent GET, and tried POST only if GET answered 405 Method Not Allowed. Of 962 endpoints that quote only on POST, 418 answer a GET with something else: 306 with 404 and 86 with 200. Our check called them "not x402". They were fine.
  • We judged a version we did not read correctly. A field that is correct in x402 version 1 was reported as a fault.
  • Names that do not resolve raised instead of being reported, and one hostile payment scheme in a reply crashed the check outright.

All of it had passed our review and our tests, because every test case was shaped like our own endpoint. Comparing the two runs over the same 3,421 endpoints, the first run had wrongly failed 420 of them. If you run a tool that judges other people's systems, run it on their systems before anyone trusts its answer.

What the corrected run found

Over 4,198 endpoints on 4,178 hosts:

Verdict Endpoints Share
Quotes valid x402 payment terms 3,655 87.1%
Quotes terms with a problem in them 84 2.0%
Answers, but does not quote a price 414 9.9%
Could not be reached 45 1.1%

We say "does not quote" rather than "broken" on purpose. Of those 414, 151 answered 404 and 108 answered 400, 415 or 422, which can mean the endpoint wants a request body we did not guess. A buyer's agent with the right input might get a price. We count it as what we saw.

A few more things that are useful if you build an agent that pays:

  • Prices are small. The median quoted price was 0.01 USDC and the 90th percentile 0.19.
  • The listed price is usually the charged price, not always. Of 3,726 endpoints we could compare, 3,525 quote what their listing says, 106 ask for more and 95 for less. An agent should read the 402, not the catalogue.
  • Base dominates. 3,596 endpoints accept Base, 890 Solana, 501 Polygon, 457 Arbitrum, and 1,106 offer more than one way to pay.
  • Version 2 won. 3,606 spoke x402 version 2 and 133 version 1.
  • It is fast. Median latency to the payment request was 487 ms, the 90th percentile 929 ms, and 17 endpoints took over three seconds.
  • The faults in quoted terms were mostly about money: 29 amounts that could not be read as a valid amount, 24 networks, 22 schemes and 4 addresses.

Other people probe this market more often and more widely than we do, and their headline numbers differ from ours: one monitor reports about 17% of endpoints as dead, decoys or zombies across a larger set over time. A single run is a snapshot, and every method draws its line somewhere. Ours is published with the method beside it.

What we did not publish

We publish the aggregates only. The result for any one endpoint stays private, because a single check from our side is not a fair verdict on someone's service. The aggregate report and its method are on our site, and you can run the check on your own endpoint for free at agoreum.xyz/tools/x402-check.

Why a marketplace cares

x402 pays per call: an agent pays, and either the answer comes back or the money is gone. That is right for a 0.01 lookup. It is wrong for work that takes hours, where a buyer needs the money held until the work arrives and a way to get it back if it never does. That is what Agoreum is for: USDC held in an escrow contract on Base, released on delivery, refundable by the buyer alone if no delivery is recorded by the deadline. If you sell x402 endpoints, you can list one there by pasting its URL.

It is in beta: each order is capped at 100 USDC, and the contracts have had an internal security audit only.
