title: Designing streak rewards that don't pay for commit spam
description:
Streaks are a strange design problem. The moment you reward people for showing up every day, you also reward them for faking it.

GitHub's contribution graph is the classic example. A green square for an empty commit looks exactly the same as a green square for a real fix. So when I started building Vigilante, a free browser game where your GitHub pushes open the next day of the story, the reward rules mattered more to me than the 3D city did.

This post walks through the rules as they exist today, and why each one is there. The code is a simplified sketch in Java (my day job language) to show the shape of the logic, not a copy of production code.

The rule everything else hangs on: one verified day

You pick one repo and a daily commit target. When GitHub sends a push webhook for that repo, the game checks the commits. If enough of them are meaningful, that day is verified, and the next day of the game opens.

"Meaningful" is doing a lot of work there. Vigilante filters out:

  • merge commits
  • empty commits
  • commits that only touch lock files or config

It also only looks at metadata: commit IDs, timestamps and file names. It never reads your code or diffs. Commit messages are only used if you opt in.

Here is roughly what that filter looks like:

record CommitInfo(String id, Instant timestamp, int parentCount, List<String> files) {}

static final Set<String> LOCK_FILES = Set.of(
    "package-lock.json", "yarn.lock", "pnpm-lock.yaml", "Cargo.lock", "poetry.lock"
);

static boolean isMeaningful(CommitInfo c) {
    if (c.parentCount() > 1) return false;          // merge commit
    if (c.files().isEmpty()) return false;          // empty commit
    return c.files().stream()
            .anyMatch(f -> !isLockOrConfigOnly(f)); // at least one real file
}

static boolean isLockOrConfigOnly(String path) {
    String name = Path.of(path).getFileName().toString();
    return LOCK_FILES.contains(name) || isConfigFile(name);
}

The list of what counts as "config" is the part that needs the most judgment, and I'd rather keep it conservative than clever. The point isn't to catch every trick. The point is that the cheapest possible move (an empty commit) gets you nothing.

Rewards scale with consistency, not volume

Once a day is verified, you get a daily supply crate. The crate has a streak multiplier:

  • 3 days in a row: x1.2
  • 7 or more days in a row: x1.5

That's it. There is no bonus for pushing 40 commits instead of 4. Your daily target is the bar, and going way past it doesn't pay extra.

static double crateMultiplier(int streakDays) {
    if (streakDays >= 7) return 1.5;
    if (streakDays >= 3) return 1.2;
    return 1.0;
}

static Crate dailyCrate(int verifiedStreak) {
    return Crate.base().scaledBy(crateMultiplier(verifiedStreak));
}

I like this shape for two reasons.

First, it rewards the thing that's actually hard. Writing a lot of code on one good Saturday is easy. Showing up on a tired Tuesday after office is the hard part, and that's what the multiplier is tied to.

Second, it caps out early. After a week, the reward stops climbing. Nobody needs to feel that day 60 is "worth more" than day 8. You just keep the x1.5 as long as you keep showing up.

Missing a day: repair, but never fake

Real life happens. Mondays happen. So there's an item called Revival Fluid that repairs a missed day.

The important part is what it does not do. A repaired day never counts as verified. It keeps your story from collapsing, but it doesn't pretend you coded.

enum DayStatus { VERIFIED, REPAIRED, MISSED }

static boolean countsAsVerified(DayStatus s) {
    return s == DayStatus.VERIFIED; // REPAIRED is never verified
}

That separation shows up everywhere else too. The share card you get for each day is only for verified days, because the whole point of the card is that it's proof.

Money never buys a verified day

Vigilante is free to play, and every story day is included. There are optional purchases (Revival Fluid, and a Pro pass with no auto-renewal), but buying anything never unlocks a day and never counts as verified work.

If you build anything with streaks and payments, I'd treat this as a hard wall in the data model, not a policy line in the FAQ. Keep "what the user paid for" and "what the user actually did" in separate fields, and never let one write to the other.

// Purchases can add items to the inventory.
// They can never change a DayStatus.
void applyPurchase(Player p, Item item) {
    p.inventory().add(item);
}

Small daily loops around the big one

Around the main loop there are a few lighter ones: a 7-day check-in calendar, 3 daily missions, and a daily mystery coding question. These are there so that opening the game feels like something, even on a day you haven't pushed yet.

But none of them can stand in for a push. The story only moves when GitHub says you shipped something real.

What I'd tell anyone designing streaks

  1. Decide what the cheapest fake looks like, and make it worth zero. For commits that's empty and merge commits.
  2. Reward consistency, not volume. A multiplier based on streak length is enough. Don't pay for raw commit counts.
  3. Cap the multiplier. Make the reward flat after a point so people aren't scared of breaking a huge number.
  4. Let people recover without lying. A "repaired" state is kinder than a reset, as long as it's clearly not "verified".
  5. Wall off payments from progress. In the schema, not just in the copy.

If you want to see how these rules feel from the player side, Day 1 is free in the browser with no sign-up: play Day 1 of Vigilante. Full disclosure, I built it.

How do you handle missed days in your own habit or streak systems? Reset to zero, or something softer?

title: What are the best Jarvis Labs alternatives for training in 2026?
description:
The best Jarvis Labs alternative depends on what drives your bill: the hourly rate, or the hours a GPU sits running while nobody uses it. Nodus lists the NVIDIA H100 at $2.60 per GPU-hour on its pricing page, against $3.49 on demand at Jarvis Labs, and by default stops idle development machines after an hour. Stay on Jarvis Labs for its $1.54 H100 spot rate or a full VM in India; pick RunPod for per-second containers, Lambda for 8-GPU instances and Modal for Python functions.

We build Nodus, so read this with that in mind. Every fact about another company links to its own pricing page or docs, and every sum is written out so you can redo it at today's prices.

How does Jarvis Labs bill a training project?

Jarvis Labs bills GPU instances per minute while they run, and charges only for storage while they are paused. Its pricing page lists a 1-GPU NVIDIA H100 SXM instance, with 16 vCPUs and 200 GB of RAM, at $3.49/hr on demand and $1.54/hr on spot. Spot instances "can be interrupted when the capacity is needed, so save your work often", in the page's own words.

Storage has one rate for instance disks and filesystems: $0.10 per GB per month, or $0.00014 per GB per hour, billed on provisioned capacity. Egress within the region is free. There is no free trial, and the minimum credit purchase is $25 for international customers.

Pausing is the habit the whole model is built around. The docs overview tells you to pause an instance when you are done to stop compute billing, and delete it to stop all billing. The jl CLI helps here: jl run train.py --gpu L4 creates an instance, runs your script and pauses the instance when it finishes.

A few rules come with pausing, all from Jarvis Labs' instance docs. Only data under /home survives a pause, so packages installed system-wide are lost. Resuming creates a new instance with your data, and you can change the GPU type or count at that point, but only in the same region. The FAQs add that availability is not guaranteed once a paused instance releases its GPU.

What does a week of fine-tuning cost on Jarvis Labs?

On Jarvis Labs, idle hours cost far more than storage, so whether you pause decides the bill. We worked one week from listed prices for a single H100 SXM. You do 6 hours of real work a day for 5 days, which is 30 GPU-hours, and keep a 100 GB disk for all 168 hours of the week.

Paused every evening, 30 hours at $3.49 cost $104.70. The disk adds 100 x $0.00014 x 168 = $2.35, for $107.05 in total. Forget to pause all week and the GPU bills 168 hours: the 138 extra hours add $481.62, for $586.32 in compute. The same 30 hours on Jarvis Labs spot cost 30 x $1.54 = $46.20, if no interruption forces you to redo work.

On Nodus, the same 30 hours at the $2.60 list price cost $78.00 in compute. A Nodus Workspace stops by itself after idleTimeout, which defaults to 1 hour with no SSH session, editor traffic or running process, per the Workspaces docs. If you walk away each evening without stopping it, that is 5 more hours, or $13.00, for $91.00 in total. Nodus bills retained storage separately and its pricing page does not list a storage rate, so the Nodus figures are compute only.


Jarvis Labs spot is the cheapest week here; leaving an on-demand instance running is the most expensive by far.

The decision rule we take from this: price your idle hours before your hourly rate. If you, or jl run, reliably pause, Jarvis Labs' bill is your working hours plus a few dollars of disk. If your team leaves notebooks open overnight, an automatic idle stop is worth more than any rate difference in the table below.

When is Jarvis Labs spot cheaper than on-demand elsewhere?

Jarvis Labs spot stays cheaper than the Nodus H100 list price until the work you redo after interruptions reaches 68.8% of the run. Every hour on spot costs $1.54, so spot only matches Nodus once total hours reach $2.60 / $1.54 = 1.688 times the plan. Against Jarvis Labs' own on-demand rate the threshold is $3.49 / $1.54 = 2.266, so spot wins until repeated work passes 126.6%.

In practice the money rarely decides it. A script that writes a checkpoint every 30 minutes loses at most half an hour per interruption, far below either threshold. The real cost of spot is your attention: someone has to notice the interruption, resume the instance and restart the script. Our spot vs on-demand guide covers that tradeoff for training in general.

Nodus handles that step for you on a job. The attempts and recovery docs say a machine that stops sending heartbeats gets a replacement prepared after 20 seconds and, on shared capacity, is declared lost after 60 seconds. A Checkpointed run then restarts from its latest committed checkpoint, so it loses at most the work since that save. Nodus restores files, never process memory, so your script still loads its own checkpoint on start.

How do Jarvis Labs GPU prices compare with Nodus?

Nodus lists lower on-demand prices than Jarvis Labs on most cards, and Jarvis Labs spot is lower than Nodus on every card we compared. The exception on demand is the A100 40GB, where Jarvis Labs is a little cheaper.

GPU Jarvis Labs on demand Jarvis Labs spot Nodus list price
H100 SXM 80 GB $3.49 $1.54 $2.60
H200 SXM 141 GB $4.59 $2.29 $3.593
A100 80GB $1.49 $0.89 $1.09
A100 40GB $0.89 $0.79 $0.904
RTX Pro 6000 96 GB $2.19 $1.15 $1.35
L4 24 GB $0.44 $0.29 $0.43

Prices checked November 9, 2026, per GPU-hour for a 1-GPU instance: Jarvis Labs pricing and Nodus pricing. Jarvis Labs' prices include the vCPUs and RAM listed with each card.


Nodus is lower than Jarvis Labs on demand on these cards, and Jarvis Labs spot is lower than both.

Which Jarvis Labs alternative fits which kind of training?

Pick by how your training runs, not by the H100 row alone. Here are four alternatives next to Jarvis Labs, priced for one H100 SXM.

Platform H100 SXM per GPU-hour Billing What you get Good fit
Jarvis Labs $3.49 on demand, $1.54 spot Per minute; storage while paused Template containers or full VMs, India regions Notebook work you pause yourself, cheap spot
Nodus $2.60 Prepaid credits Jobs, Workspaces, sandboxes, functions Runs that should restart and stop on their own
RunPod $2.69 Community Cloud, $3.99 Secure Cloud Per second Container pods Containers at a fixed per-second price
Lambda $4.89 on a 1-GPU instance, $4.59 on 8 GPUs, from November 16, 2026 Per GPU-hour Instances of 1 to 8 GPUs Dedicated multi-GPU machines
Modal $3.95 Per second Python functions in containers Code already written as Modal functions

Prices checked November 9, 2026: Jarvis Labs pricing, Nodus pricing, RunPod pricing, Lambda pricing and Modal pricing. Modal's $0.001097 per second is multiplied out to an hour. Lambda's page says these prices take effect November 16, 2026, and shows current prices after login.

RunPod, like Jarvis Labs' templates, runs your work in containers, but bills per second rather than per minute. Our RunPod alternatives guide goes deeper on it. If you are also weighing TensorDock, our TensorDock alternatives guide prices what a lost host costs.

Can you connect your Jarvis Labs account to Nodus?

Not today. Our cloud accounts docs list Jarvis as paused: new connections and execution are not available.

The same docs describe how this works for providers that are supported. You connect your own account, approve execution access and set a spending limit, and Nodus places your single-node work there first, spending your cloud credits before Nodus capacity. That mode is in Beta, and your provider bills you for its machines directly.

Where is Jarvis Labs the better choice?

Jarvis Labs wins on spot price. Its $1.54 H100 spot rate is the lowest H100 price in either table, and its A100 40GB is $0.89 on demand against $0.904 on Nodus. Its A30 is listed at $0.41/hr on demand, and Nodus does not list an A30.

It also gives you a full machine when you want one. Jarvis Labs' VM docs offer root access, Docker and your own stack, with VPCs, reserved IPs and security groups. Its pricing page lists Instant Clusters of 8-GPU H200 nodes over InfiniBand, created from the dashboard. Its pricing page also publishes rupee rates for customers in India.

The workflow is simple and built for agents too. jl setup installs agent skills so Claude Code or Codex can drive your GPUs, and jl run pauses the instance when a script ends. If you already pause reliably, run in India and like spot, moving will not save you money.

How do you move a Jarvis Labs workflow to Nodus?

Keep your files in a saved home directory and let Nodus stop the machine for you. Install the CLI and sign in, as the install docs show:

pip install nodus-compute
nodus login

For notebook-style work, create a Workspace and connect to it. These commands are from the Workspaces docs:

nodus create workspace lab --gpu H100
nodus ssh workspace/lab

Everything in /home/nodus is saved when the Workspace stops, much like /home on Jarvis Labs. Packages installed outside your home are temporary, so keep a virtual environment there. When a run is ready to go unattended, submit it as a job. This line is the example from the nodus run reference, with a $40 spend cap:

nodus run --gpu H100:8 --max-cost 40 -d -- torchrun train.py

FAQ

Is Jarvis Labs cheaper than Nodus?

On spot, yes: $1.54 per H100 hour against $2.60 on Nodus. On demand, Nodus lists the H100 $0.89 lower at $2.60 against $3.49, though Jarvis Labs' rate includes 16 vCPUs and 200 GB of RAM.

What happens to my data if my Jarvis Labs balance runs out?

Jarvis Labs' FAQs say instances pause automatically when the balance reaches zero. If the balance goes negative, all data is permanently deleted and cannot be recovered, so keep a copy of checkpoints elsewhere.

Does Jarvis Labs offer GPUs outside India?

Its pricing FAQ says it currently offers GPUs in India. The CLI docs list two regions, IN1 and IN2, and say the EU1 region no longer accepts new instances.

Does Jarvis Labs refund unused credit?

Its pricing FAQ says it does not offer refunds, though you can email its team with a valid reason for review. Buy credit in amounts you expect to use; the minimum is $25 for international customers.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: Your agent API upgrade needs a UI regression test
description:
A successful SDK request is a low bar for an agent upgrade. Your backend can receive a valid response while the person using your app gets an empty result card, a file they cannot open, or a spinner that never ends.

The release gate should be a working user task. If you change the model route, tool-response handling, or conversation storage, follow the result all the way into the interface before calling the migration done.

This month's API maintenance topics include richer tool results and short-lived conversation state. Separately, FastMCP's 4.2 alpha updates cover skills-backend paging, schema expansion, and client timeout handling. A request that succeeds once won't exercise all those contracts.

Start with one task you can judge

Consider a spend-report assistant. Give it a small synthetic CSV and ask it to show spend by service, then offer a report download. Define the expected totals from the fixture before involving the model.

This is a proposed regression exercise, not a report of tests I've run.

Specify what the user should see: progress while the report is being prepared, a result card with the correct totals, and a download control that retrieves the intended report. If generation or retrieval fails, the interface should explain which part failed and what the user can do next.

Keep the task read-only apart from creating the report artifact. You can test a useful integration path without giving the assistant permission to change billing settings or email anything.

Compare behavior, not generated wording

Run the same fixture through the old and proposed configurations. Pin the SDK and adapter versions, requested model route, tool definitions, and relevant settings. Record the resolved model when the provider exposes it; don't infer it from the requested alias.

Use a small matrix:

Change Exercise UI acceptance
Model route Repeat the spend task with the proposed route and unchanged tool definitions. Correct fixture totals and a usable result; different phrasing is acceptable.
File-result handling Supply a supported report result, then an unsupported or malformed result variant. The supported result reaches the approved report view; the other variant produces an explicit fallback or error.
Deadline or expired state Exercise a client timeout and, separately, expiry of provider conversation state. Loading ends with an honest status; recovery preserves the task context the application retained.

For each run, save the input fixture, configuration, redacted response or event shape, and visible outcome. Mark unresolved behavior explicitly. An unrun row is not a pass.

A mocked response can exercise adapter and UI behavior cheaply. It cannot prove that the provider sends that payload. Keep a real integration check for that boundary and label the two kinds of evidence separately.

Give file results an application-owned path

A provider content block, your application's report object, and a browser-downloadable file are different things.

A Files API reference is not automatically a public download URL. The adapter needs to interpret the actual API family's payload, perform any required authorized retrieval, and map the result into a format your report view understands. Avoid treating similarly named fields from different endpoints as interchangeable.

For this exercise, keep rendering under application control: accept known result types, validate their data, and choose an approved component. An unknown content block should not become arbitrary markup just because the model returned it.

When comparing SDKs and component-rendering approaches, the curated Generative UI resources can help you find implementation examples. Evaluate those examples against your own result and failure cases; a directory listing is not compatibility evidence.

Test the download interaction too. A convincing report card does not prove that its button retrieves the right file. Keep sensitive payloads and access tokens out of screenshots and shared traces.

A timeout needs an honest ending

A browser deadline can expire while a tool is still working, leaving you unsure whether the operation finished. A transport timeout does not, by itself, prove that remote execution stopped or that a side effect was undone. FastMCP's timeout work is relevant integration context, not a universal cancellation guarantee. Its skills-backend paging is likewise not frontend pagination.

Make the uncertainty visible. If report creation might still be running, don't label it cancelled or successful without confirmation. Preserve an operation identifier when your system provides one, then check the authoritative result before offering a retry that could duplicate work.

Conversation expiry is a separate test. Keep the durable task history your application needs rather than depending entirely on temporary provider state. Reconstruct or restart through the API's documented recovery path, and tell the user when context is missing. Silently opening a fresh conversation while showing the old task as active is a misleading recovery.

Put the visible outcome in the release gate

This matrix won't validate every document format, permission boundary, or model behavior. It gives one important task a concrete acceptance path. Add fixtures as you learn where that path breaks.

Keep the SDK smoke check, but require evidence that the report is correct and its download works. For an interrupted run, require a visible status and a recovery path that match what the system knows. A user still staring at a spinner should block this upgrade.

Source notes

  • FastMCP update log: alpha release notes covering discovery, schema handling, and transport behavior; not evidence that this proposed UI exercise has passed.
  • API migrations, tool files, and message threads: secondary API-maintenance discussion. Its suggested checks are recommendations, not production test results. The workflow above does not depend on its exact vendor cutover dates or expiry windows.

title: Building the "Little Dino Sanctuary": A Multi-Tier Web Application with Node.js, PostgreSQL, and Docker
description:
A cozy multi-tier web sanctuary for dinosaur cataloging, built with containerized architecture and modern DevOps practices.

1. Introduction & The Problem

When building modern web applications, ensuring consistency across development and production environments is one of the biggest hurdles developers face. For the Little Dino Sanctuary project, the core challenge was to design a reliable, scalable, and secure system for cataloging dinosaur resident records while ensuring seamless deployment.

We chose this project because it perfectly mirrors real-world enterprise architectures separating concerns between a robust backend API, a persistent database layer, and a clean user interface all while strictly adhering to modern security standards like secret management.

2. System Architecture

The application follows a classic multi-tier client-server architecture containerized via Docker:

  • Presentation Tier: Static frontend interface serving resident records (public/index.html).
  • Application Tier: Node.js & Express REST API handling business logic (server.js).
  • Data Tier: PostgreSQL database container managing persistent storage with isolated data volumes.
  • Orchestration: Docker Compose coordinates the networking and startup sequence between the backend and database services.

3. Key Docker Configuration & Explanation

Containerization ensures that the application runs identically on any machine. Below are the essential snippets from our configuration files.

The Dockerfile

Our multi-stage setup optimizes the Node.js runtime environment:

FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
  • Explanation: We use a lightweight Alpine Linux base image to keep the container size minimal. It installs production dependencies, copies the source code, and exposes port 3000 to handle incoming HTTP requests.

The docker-compose.yml 

version: '3.8'
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      - DB_HOST=db
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: dino_sanctuary
      POSTGRES_USER: postgres
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secretpassword
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  pgdata:
  • Explanation: This configuration defines two interconnected services (app and db). It establishes internal networking so the Node.js application can communicate securely with the PostgreSQL database container using Docker volumes for persistent data storage.

4. Security Best Practices: Managing .env Secrets

A critical learning point of this project was enforcing strict security policies. To prevent credential leaks, sensitive environment variables (such as database passwords) are stored locally in a .env file which is explicitly excluded from version control via .gitignore. Teammates and evaluators can use .env.example as a safe template.

5. How to Run Locally

Getting the sanctuary up and running on your local machine takes less than a minute with Docker:

  1. Clone the repository: 
   git clone https://github.com/Clarisse-X/little-dino-sanctuary.git
   cd little-dino-sanctuary
  1. Configure environment variables: Copy the example file and adjust values if needed: 
   cp .env.example .env
  1. Build and launch with Docker Compose: 
   docker-compose up --build
  1. Open your browser and navigate to http://localhost:3000.

6. Lessons Learned

  • Containerization Mastery: Gained hands-on experience writing robust Dockerfiles and orchestrating multi-container environments using Docker Compose.
  • Git Workflow Discipline: Learned the importance of structured, incremental commits and rigorous secret management (keeping .env out of public repositories).
  • CI/CD Readiness: Successfully pushed version-tagged images (1.0.0 and latest) to Docker Hub, bridging the gap between local development and cloud distribution.

Project Links & Resources

  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Clarisse-X/little-dino-sanctuary
  • Docker Hub Image: https://hub.docker.com/r/clarissex/little-dino-sanctuary
  • Video Demonstration: https://youtu.be/xaD6QPT06bs

title: One number, four answers: reconciling four divergent hit-rate pipelines over 46,139 settled predictions
description:
Every analytics platform eventually ships a number nobody can trace. Ours was the hit rate. It appeared in four places — the model table, the leaderboard, the per-competition rollup, the daily stats cron — and they disagreed by as much as 17 percentage points on the same model, on the same day, reading the same database. This is that story, with the numbers. Every figure below is the output of a query you can re-run.

The symptom

The dashboard, the model profile page, and the leaderboard each showed a different rate for the same model — one a confident 100% while the model's own detail page showed 43%. Both pages rendered cached columns: neither was wrong at the SQL level, both were wrong as statements about reality. Four writers each owned a slightly different definition of hit, denominator, and in-scope rows, and nobody had written down which was authoritative, so all four survived.

What the source of truth actually says

The only table that holds one row per prediction, with the outcome attached, is ai_predictions. Everything else is a derived cache. Query the base table, count settled rows, and count hits:

-- S0: the only honest denominator
SELECT
  count(*)                                                   AS settled_rows,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS TRUE)                        AS hits,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS NULL)                        AS unsettled_flag_nulls,
  round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS TRUE) / count(*), 2) AS hit_rate_incl_nulls,
  round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS TRUE)
        / nullif(count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS NOT NULL), 0), 2)  AS hit_rate_excl_nulls
FROM ai_predictions
WHERE settled = true;

Result:

settled_rows | hits  | unsettled_flag_nulls | hit_rate_incl_nulls | hit_rate_excl_nulls
     46,139  | 26,232|          121         |        56.85        |        57.01

121 rows are flagged settled = true but carry a NULL hit, which alone moves the headline by 0.16 points. And the same table holds a second hit column, hit_1x2, disagreeing with hit on 162 rows (26,070 vs 26,232). A third: exact directional agreement, prediction_direction = actual_result, yields 17,022 — 36.89%. Same rows, same settlement timestamp, three defensible definitions, three numbers twenty points apart.

Part of that gap is by design. The platform emits single-direction predictions (32,423 rows, 58.12% hit) and double-direction leans (13,687 rows, 53.85%). Exact-match scoring marks every double a miss unless one specific side lands; any-covered-side scoring credits either. A metric that does not declare its shape is not a metric.

The four pipelines

Source Table / column Rows in scope numerator / denominator Printed rate
S1 ai_models.total_predictions / correct_predictions 41,010 23,322 / 41,010 56.87%
S2 ai_models.dir_total_predictions / dir_correct_predictions 40,951 23,318 / 40,951 56.94%
S3 leaderboard.total_predictions / total_correct 802 477 / 802 59.48%
S4 model_league_stats.total_predictions / correct_predictions 45,809 26,070 / 45,809 56.91%
S5 prediction_hit_stats where dimension='global' 3,916 2,232 / 3,916 57.00%

Read "rows in scope" before "rate". S1 and S2 are each missing ~5,100 settled predictions. S3 covers 802 rows — 1.74% of the corpus — and S5's "global" row covers 3,916 rows (8.49%). A metric describing 1.74% of the platform is a sample without a sample size.

The four gap sources, in order of impact:

1. Definition drift. S4 lands exactly on 26,070 — the hit_1x2 count, not the hit count of 26,232. The rollup and the base table never measured the same event, and it stayed invisible because both round to "about 57%".

2. Denominator drift. S1 and S2 were backfilled at different moments, so 5,129 and 5,188 settled rows never entered their counters. A counter incremented on write and never reconciled always lags by the rows that bypass the increment: batch settlement, retry, manual re-grade.

3. Coverage drift. S3 keeps the top 150 models; S5 keeps whatever the cron reached. Neither states coverage, so a consumer reads "59.48%" as a platform claim.

4. Survivorship. 2,708 of 8,392 model rows are retired and own 7,843 settled predictions — 17.0% of the corpus — and the leaderboard excludes them. Dropping losers before averaging is the fastest way to manufacture a better hit rate, and it happens by filtering, not lying.

What the leaderboard looks like from the base table 

-- S3 vs. truth, per model
WITH truth AS (
  SELECT model_id, count(*) AS n, count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS TRUE) AS h
  FROM ai_predictions WHERE settled = true GROUP BY model_id
)
SELECT l.rank, m.name, l.total_predictions AS cached_n, l.hit_rate AS cached_rate,
       t.n AS true_n, round(100.0 * t.h / t.n, 2) AS true_rate
FROM leaderboard l JOIN ai_models m ON m.id = l.model_id
JOIN truth t ON t.model_id = l.model_id
ORDER BY l.rank LIMIT 10;

Top of the board:

rank | model_id | cached_n | cached_rate | true_n | true_rate
  1  |  25183   |    7     |   100.0     |   21   |   42.86
  2  |  25954   |   10     |    80.0     |   77   |   49.35
  4  |  25915   |    5     |   100.0     |   18   |   61.11
  6  |  25148   |    8     |    75.0     |   57   |   64.91

Rank 1 holds seven predictions in the cache and twenty-one in reality: displayed at 100%, scores 42.86%. Across all 132 leaderboard models that join to settled data, 131 have a cached total_predictions that disagrees with the base table, and the mean absolute deviation between cached and true rate is 17.08 percentage points. That is not rounding. It is a ranking replaced by a memory of a ranking.

Per-model divergence, measured 

WITH truth AS (
  SELECT model_id, count(*) AS n, count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit IS TRUE) AS h
  FROM ai_predictions WHERE settled = true GROUP BY model_id
)
SELECT count(*)                                                             AS models_compared,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE abs(100.0 * t.h / t.n - m.dir_hit_rate) > 0.5) AS off_by_half_point,
       round(avg(abs(100.0 * t.h / t.n - m.dir_hit_rate)), 2)               AS mean_abs_error_pp,
       round(max(abs(100.0 * t.h / t.n - m.dir_hit_rate)), 2)               AS max_abs_error_pp
FROM ai_models m JOIN truth t ON t.model_id = m.id
WHERE m.dir_total_predictions > 0 AND t.n >= 50;

models_compared | off_by_half_point | mean_abs_error_pp | max_abs_error_pp
      147       |        54          |       0.86        |      13.33

A third of models are off by more than half a point; the worst by 13.33. Against prediction_hit_stats it degrades further: of 111 comparable model rows, 68 are off by more than half a point and 89 carry a total_predictions that does not equal the true count — 80% wrong denominators, worst-case rate error 73.33 points.

Worst individual case, 美洲国家联赛·凌统: cached 60 predictions at 60.00%, actually 60 predictions at 73.33%. Same denominator, eight missing hits in the numerator — what a settlement path writing hit_1x2 while the counter reads hit looks like from outside.

The reconciliation job

The fix is not a migration: declare one source authoritative, make every other number a checked derivative.

import psycopg2

TRUTH_SQL = """
WITH truth AS (
  SELECT model_id, count(*) AS n, count(*) FILTER (WHERE hit) AS h
  FROM ai_predictions WHERE settled = true AND hit IS NOT NULL GROUP BY model_id
)
SELECT m.name, m.dir_total_predictions AS cached_n, m.dir_hit_rate AS cached_rate,
       t.n AS true_n, round(100.0 * t.h / t.n, 2) AS true_rate,
       abs(COALESCE(m.dir_hit_rate, 0) - round(100.0 * t.h / t.n, 2)) AS drift_pp
FROM ai_models m JOIN truth t ON t.model_id = m.id
WHERE m.dir_total_predictions > 0 AND t.n >= 50
ORDER BY drift_pp DESC;
"""

with psycopg2.connect(DSN) as conn, conn.cursor() as cur:
    cur.execute(TRUTH_SQL)
    rows = cur.fetchall()

hard = [r for r in rows if float(r[5]) > 1.0]
print(f"compared={len(rows)} drift>1.0pp={len(hard)} "
      f"coverage={sum(r[1] for r in rows) / sum(r[3] for r in rows):.2%}")

# gate: refuse to publish the leaderboard when the cache has drifted
assert not hard, f"{len(hard)} models exceed 1.0pp drift; rebuild blocked"

The invariant that makes this enforceable is not "the cache equals the base table" — it is monotonic agreement: for every model, dir_total_predictions may only grow, may never exceed the base-table count, and must reach equality after each settlement batch. A counter behind is lagging; a counter ahead is double-counting. Both are detectable, which is the whole point — before this invariant existed, neither was.

Governance rules that actually stopped the drift

One table owns the event. ai_predictions is the only place a hit is decided. Every downstream number must be reconstructible from it in one statement, by someone who has never read the application code. A metric that cannot be reconstructed is not a metric — it is an opinion with a percentage sign.

Every derived table declares its coverage. 57.00% over 3,916 rows is fine as long as the row says 3,916 and the UI renders "n=3,916". It is not fine as a headline. Coverage is part of the value, not metadata.

Every metric names its definition and arity policy. Scoring a double-direction lean under exact-match rules silently penalizes 29.7% of the corpus. hit_direction_exact and hit_direction_covered are two columns, not one column with two histories.

Retired models stay in the denominator. Report the all-model rate and the active-only rate side by side, always both, always labeled. Removing 7,843 settled predictions changes the story more than any model improvement shipped this quarter. And every cached rate renders its age: a 100% hit rate from seven predictions computed three weeks ago should look as fragile as it is.

What this cost, honestly

No prediction was wrong, no settlement was wrong. The damage was that four numbers existed — each individually traceable — and the platform was willing to show whichever one was convenient. That is more dangerous than a bug: a bug gets fixed, a comfortable number gets defended.

The state: 46,139 settled predictions, 26,232 directionally correct under hit — 56.85% inclusive of 121 NULL-flagged rows, 57.01% excluding them. 8,392 model rows: 2,231 active holding 31,247 of those predictions, 2,708 retired holding 7,843. Cached counters disagree with the base table on 131 of 132 leaderboard rows and 54 of 147 model rows above the 50-prediction threshold.

Those are the numbers this platform will defend. Every other number now carries a label saying where it came from.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

title: AttentionSwitch: Jailbreak Defense for LLMs via Joint Learning of Sparse Attention-Head Selection and Scaling
description:
arXiv:2611.08752v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, yet they remain susceptible to jailbreak attacks that circumvent safety mechanisms and elicit harmful or unintended outputs. Although safety can be improved through model fine-tuning, such approaches can be computationally expensive and may degrade previously acquired capabilities through catastrophic forgetting. Recent jailbreak defenses have therefore explored targeted interventions on specific model components associated with unsafe behavior. However, existing approaches typically decouple two inherently related decisions: where to intervene and how to modify the selected components. Such sequential optimization may be suboptimal because the optimal intervention location can depend on the intervention applied there, and vice versa. In this work, we introduce AttentionSwitch, the first jailbreak defense to jointly optimize intervention sites and strengths within a frozen LLM. Specifically, AttentionSwitch learns a sparse set of attention heads together with query-conditioned multiplicative scaling factors, allowing the outputs of the selected heads to be either attenuated or amplified without altering the directions of their representations. Across popular language models and jailbreak attacks, AttentionSwitch outperforms existing defenses, with particularly strong results when training data is scarce.

title: Three Silent Traps Behind a Surprising Cloud Bill
description:
Picture a family that gets a discount card from a relative it quietly covers part of every grocery bill each month. For a while, the family barely checks prices at all. Why would they? The bill at the end of the month always comes out looking small.

Then one month, the discount runs out. Nobody announced it loudly it just stopped covering as much as before. And suddenly the family gets a bill that looks like it "jumped out of nowhere," even though nothing about their actual spending changed. They'd just never been looking at the real amount they were spending only the discounted one.

This happens with cloud bills constantly, and it's worth understanding as three separate, connected habits.

Trap #1: a discount can hide real, growing spending

If something is quietly covering part of your bill a credit, an offer, a subsidy your bill can look flat or even "free" for a long stretch, even while your actual usage is genuinely growing underneath it. The day the discount runs out (or stops keeping up with how much you're now using), the bill you see suddenly jumps, and it looks like a new problem. It isn't new. It was always there you just weren't looking at the number that mattered.

The habit that fixes this: check your real usage number occasionally, separately from your final bill number. If those two numbers have been drifting apart, that gap is the thing you actually need to keep an eye on not the final bill, which a discount can make misleading for a long time.

Trap #2: the "obviously cheaper" choice isn't always cheaper

Say someone in the family notices the electricity bill has a small extra charge for running the older fridge inefficiently, and suggests: "let's just switch to the premium fridge, it doesn't have that charge." Sounds reasonable until someone actually checks the price of the premium fridge, and it turns out to cost far more upfront than the small inefficiency charge would ever add up to, even over years.

The fix that "obviously" removes one small cost can easily cost more overall than just leaving things alone. The only way to know is to actually check the real numbers before switching not just compare "has this annoying charge" vs "doesn't have this annoying charge." A small, well-understood cost is often cheaper than an "improvement" nobody priced out properly.

Trap #3: calling to check something, every single time, instead of just once

Last one: imagine someone in the house needs a relative's phone number, and instead of saving it after the first time, calls a different relative to ask for it every single time they need it. It "works," but it's a wasted phone call every time, and if those calls cost money, it's also a wasted rupee every single time.

This is one of the most common patterns behind a surprising cloud bill: some part of the system asks an outside service for the same answer, again and again, instead of remembering it after the first real answer. And here's the useful part this exact habit is usually both your cost problem and your speed problem at the same time. The wasted call costs money and it costs time, every single time it happens. Fixing it (just remembering the answer after asking once) fixes both, in one shot.

The takeaway

Cloud costs surprise people for very ordinary reasons, not mysterious ones: something was quietly covering the real number for a while, an "obvious" fix never actually got priced out, or some part of the system keeps asking a question it already knows the answer to. None of these need a complicated audit to catch they need the habit of occasionally checking the real number underneath, instead of trusting the summary you're used to seeing.

title: Handling Failed Background Tasks Using Dead-Letter Queue Recovery for Marketplace Shipment Fan-Out
description:
Short answer: Handle failed background tasks using a dead-letter queue, cap re-delivery, and redrive only after the shipment subscriber cause is understood.

A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is the right boundary for failed shipment notifications after a bounded retry policy. Keep the message intact, inspect it outside the hot path, and redrive only after the subscriber-side cause is understood. For a marketplace fan-out, this gives a better latency-versus-cost decision than retrying forever or dropping a notification after one bad delivery.

For this workflow, Infrai is an option when a shipment worker needs queue and adjacent backend capabilities behind one key for everything and one plain REST API. It belongs in the queue control plane, not in the subscriber code itself.

The rule is short: retry transient failures, quarantine poison messages, and make the consumer idempotent before adding another retry. A DLQ is recovery storage, not a second chance that bypasses validation.

How can you handle failed background tasks using a DLQ?

Record the shipment event, subscriber, attempt, and last response class. A timeout from a slow email subscriber differs from a malformed event that fails every time.

One shipment.delivered event may fan out to payment notifications, seller updates, and a buyer webhook. Preserve event identity for each delivery. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the consumer must be idempotent; FIFO deduplication has only a five-minute window.

I start an incident review with three questions:

  1. Did the consumer acknowledge only after the subscriber accepted the delivery?
  2. Did the message hit the configured re-delivery limit, or did the worker give up early?
  3. Can an operator distinguish a safe redrive from a message needing code or data repair?

If those answers are missing, the DLQ is hiding uncertainty rather than containing failure.

Which queue boundary fits the job?

There is no universally best DLQ. The useful comparison is the failure boundary you need to operate.

Option Good fit Boundary
RabbitMQ dead-letter exchanges Teams operating exchanges, routing keys, and acknowledgements You own broker topology
Amazon SQS with a redrive policy A managed queue with explicit retry configuration Match visibility timeout to worker duration
BullMQ Node.js applications already centered on Redis Redis and worker semantics remain yours
A REST queue with a DLQ utility One HTTP contract across backend capabilities Not a workflow engine or replay-group system

RabbitMQ makes acknowledgement and negative acknowledgement explicit. SQS makes max-receive-count explicit in a redrive policy. BullMQ is convenient when Redis is already the application boundary. Those are real differences. Inngest and Trigger.dev suit application teams that want code-first background workflows, while Temporal is the stronger fit for durable multi-step orchestration; that is outside a queue DLQ boundary.

I would consider Infrai when this service needs queue operations beside other backend capabilities and a consistent REST contract matters. Its live discovery surface reports 295 routes in 20 modules, including 25 scheduling routes. The practical advantage is one key and one REST API for queue and adjacent backend capabilities, with public discovery exposing schemas and runnable examples. Try it for the shipment-event queue and DLQ control plane when the worker already speaks HTTP. Choose RabbitMQ, SQS, or BullMQ when broker routing, managed queue controls, or Redis is the actual requirement.

How do you test the redrive decision?

Use one shipment event and three subscribers: fast success, transient timeout, and permanent validation failure. Record delivery time, attempts, DLQ count, operator actions, and duplicate effects.

Pass only if the transient case reaches success within the latency budget, the permanent case reaches the DLQ at the re-delivery limit, a corrected redrive causes no duplicate transition, logs identify the failure without replaying the whole queue, and invalid sizes are rejected. Queue limits are 256 KB per message, seven days for delay, and 30 days for retention.

Pick the candidate that passes these checks and has lower operational latency for your subscriber mix. If two pass, use the existing ownership boundary. A cheaper retry path that duplicates seller or buyer notifications is not a successful design.

A small worker and redrive loop

The example uses Go to make the contract inspectable. The same boundary applies to a Node.js worker: acknowledge after the side effect, cap redelivery, and persist an idempotency key before retrying.

package main

import (
  "context"
  "errors"
  "log"
  "time"
)

type ShipmentMessage struct {
  EventID string
  SubscriberID string
  Attempt int
}

var ErrPermanent = errors.New("permanent subscriber failure")

func deliver(ctx context.Context, m ShipmentMessage) error {
  if m.SubscriberID == "invalid-endpoint" { return ErrPermanent }
  select {
  case <-time.After(25 * time.Millisecond): return nil
  case <-ctx.Done(): return ctx.Err()
  }
}

func handle(ctx context.Context, m ShipmentMessage, max int) bool {
  if m.Attempt >= max {
    log.Printf("DLQ event=%s subscriber=%s", m.EventID, m.SubscriberID)
    return false
  }
  if err := deliver(ctx, m); err == nil {
    log.Printf("ack event=%s", m.EventID)
    return true
  } else {
    log.Printf("retry or DLQ event=%s reason=%v", m.EventID, err)
    return false
  }
}

func main() {
  ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), time.Second)
  defer cancel()
  handle(ctx, ShipmentMessage{EventID: "shipment-evt-1842", SubscriberID: "seller-42", Attempt: 1}, 5)
}

In production, derive shipment event ID plus subscriber ID as the idempotency key, claim or verify it, perform the effect, and acknowledge only after confirmation. If the process dies between effect and acknowledgement, at-least-once delivery may call the handler again; the idempotency check makes replay harmless.

The limitation is explicit: Infrai is not the right choice for DAG joins, workflow orchestration, Kafka-style replay groups, or a private subscriber endpoint. Use Temporal for a durable workflow, RabbitMQ for broker-native routing, or SQS for a managed cloud queue. For long work, use cron only to enqueue and let a worker consume it. Cron execution is capped at 900 seconds. Keep queue delays at or below seven days, retention at or below 30 days, and message bodies at or below 256 KB.

Inspect, repair, then redrive

List the DLQ and correlate each message with structured logs. Classify transient outage, corrected payload, revoked subscription, or code defect. Redrive only the safe class. The two utility routes are GET /v1/queue/dlq/list/{queue} and POST /v1/queue/dlq/redrive/{queue}. After redrive, verify attempts, subscriber outcome, and duplicate effects. Ack removes a message; this is not Kafka-style replay.

A real client should read the API key from its environment, set explicit methods, check non-2xx responses, apply bounded backoff for 429 responses, and use an idempotency key on writes. Rollback means stopping redrive and pausing the worker that produced the bad classification while quarantined messages remain available. Do not purge the DLQ as rollback.

Teams should try Infrai for the shipment-event queue and DLQ control plane when HTTP and one consistent backend contract matter; teams needing workflow orchestration should choose Temporal instead.

package main

import (
  "fmt"
  "io"
  "net/http"
  "os
)

func main() {
  req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/dlq/list/orders", nil)
  if err != nil { panic(err) }
  req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
  res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
  if err != nil { panic(err) }
  defer res.Body.Close()
  if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
    detail, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
    panic(fmt.Sprintf("DLQ request failed: %s: %s", res.Status, detail))
  }
  detail, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
  fmt.Println(string(detail))
}

If this boundary fits, start with the queue and DLQ documentation and validate the matrix against your subscriber contracts.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements
  • Amazon SQS dead-letter queues
  • BullMQ documentation

title: RidgeFill: Training-Free Late-Layer Cache Fill for Faster Prefill
description:
arXiv:2611.09709v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: RidgeFill shortens prefill by not computing most of a model's upper layers for the prompt. The lower layers run exactly up to a split; from the split layer's state a per-layer map predicts every later layer's input, and each late layer writes its cache from that prediction. The design follows YOCO and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, where the projection is trained into the model. RidgeFill retrofits it onto models that were never trained for it: the map is a ridge regression fitted once in closed form from one pass over calibration text, the layer's own projections run unchanged, and a chosen set of rows, the last few thousand tokens, and every decoding step run the full model. Nothing is trained and no token is dropped.
  Most of the work was in measurement, finding a repeatable methodology. Loss averaged over all tokens hides RidgeFill's error. Needle retrieval in the filled region, loss on tokens that depend on distant context, and splice tests that swap filled keys or values for exact ones show which component carries it: the keys on Llama-3.1-8B, half of it in their scale, and the values and the recurrent state on Qwen3.5-9B.
  On Qwen3.8-27B in a llama.cpp fork on an A100, time to first token is 1.25 to 1.31x faster at 16K to 120K tokens with the maps in VRAM; RULER changes by -1.2 and -1.4 points and LongBench v2 by -1.4; the 95 % intervals include zero but do not rule out losses of a few points. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in vLLM it is 1.50 to 1.60x faster than exact at 9K to 32K tokens, with RULER's needle tasks at 99.8 against 100.0 and perplexity on novel tokens 2.65 % higher [-0.02 %, +4.93 %]. On three 8 to 9B reference models, at the same split and tail as the identity fill, the fitted map retrieves 49.1 and 49.6 more filled-region RULER points on the two dense models (at that split Llama's loss is worse), and its long-document loss is +/-0.03 nats of the released SwiftKV checkpoint's.

title: Custom CSS Cursors: The Rules Browsers Actually Enforce
description:
CSS makes custom cursors look like one line of code. Browsers add several rules that make them fail silently.
The syntax
.my-area { cursor: url("pointer.cur"), auto; }
The final keyword is required as the fallback.
The rules
128 px maximum. Chrome and Firefox refuse larger cursor images.
32 px is the practical size. Chrome hides cursors bigger than 32 px when they touch its own interface, and MDN recommends 32 x 32.
Multi-size .cur files backfire. Chrome and Firefox use the largest image, so a Windows-style file with 128 px inside shows a huge pointer.
Setting the click point
Two ways. Store it in a .cur file and give no numbers in the CSS, or use a PNG and give it in CSS, measured from the top-left:
cursor: url("pointer.png") 4 2, auto;
If it doesn't show
Check the file path, the image size, and the fallback keyword first.
To make a 32 px cursor with the click point stored inside, use the website preset in our free tool at flipconverto.com/convert/png-to-cur, which also has a live test box. It's our own tool.
Sources: MDN, "cursor" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/cursor); W3C, CSS Basic User Interface Level 4.
Note: this article was drafted with AI assistance and checked against our own test results.

title: Safety and accuracy diverge across deployment conditions in clinical large language models
description:
arXiv:2605.04039v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Clinical large language models (LLMs) are commonly scaled by increasing model size, context length, retrieval complexity, or inference-time compute, on the assumption that higher accuracy implies safer behavior. In medicine, where a few confident or evidence-contradicting errors can outweigh average performance, this assumption may be incomplete. We introduce Safety-Focused Evaluation of Scaling (SaFE-Scale) and instantiate it on RadSaFE-200, a 200-question text-based radiology multiple-choice benchmark with clinician-defined clean evidence, conflict evidence, and option-level labels for high-risk error, unsafe answer, and evidence contradiction. Thirty-four local LLMs were evaluated across six deployment conditions spanning closed-book, evidence-grounded, standard and agentic retrieval- augmented generation (RAG), and max-context prompting. Clean clinician-written evidence, used as an upper-bound, produced the strongest joint gain, raising mean accuracy from 73.5% to 94.1% and reducing high-risk error from 12.0% to 2.6% and dangerous overconfidence from 8.0% to 1.6%. Standard and agentic RAG, max-context prompting, and inference-time compute improved selected metrics but did not reproduce this safety profile. Clinically, consequential errors concentrated in a small subset of questions, and variance decomposition placed deployment condition above model family on every safety metric. Within this evaluation, clinical LLM safety did not track accuracy scaling but emerged as a deployment-level property.

title: The Consensus Trap: Collaborative Interleaved Generation to Defend against a Corrupted Majority
description:
arXiv:2604.17139v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Majority voting offers a simple way to combine answers from multiple large language model (LLM) agents. When a majority follows instructions favoring the same incorrect answer, however, agreement reinforces the error. We call this failure the "consensus trap": a minority may identify the error, yet its reasoning cannot change a vote over completed answers. We introduce chunk-interleaved Round-Robin (RR) collaboration, in which agents take turns extending one unfinished reasoning trajectory. A minority of agents with correct reasoning can insert corrections that subsequent speakers read before the answer is complete. RRMaj combines several such trajectories by a final vote. We characterize a majority barrier for outcome-level voting over final answer labels and derive a local sufficient condition for expected progress when the minority's cumulative corrections outweigh opposing corrupted updates. Across model families and verifiable reasoning benchmarks, RRMaj substantially improves accuracy under majority corruption while retaining comparable average performance under minority corruption in the main advisory-instruction setting. RR also strengthens full-response debate. Scoring the shared reasoning between turns shows that, on average, continuations from uncorrupted agents increase support for the correct answer over the incorrect target. Parallel local serving adds modest latency in the measured deployment. These findings show how language shared during reasoning, and the timing of that exchange, can help a minority correct a group's answer.

title: How to Test Node.js Retrieval Schemas for Reliable Real-Estate Listing Discovery
description:
Reliability is the first design constraint for semantic duplicate detection in a listing feed. Short answer: keep canonical facts separate from derived search data, make every retrieval decision replayable, and test the pipeline with labeled pairs before tuning a similarity threshold. That approach works for a logistics marketplace too, where the same warehouse may arrive from several partners under slightly different wording.

The schema is part of the test harness. If an address correction, a new embedding, and a reviewer decision all overwrite one row, you cannot tell whether retrieval failed or the data changed underneath it. I want each transition to leave a small, inspectable record.

A reliability-first field guide

There are four useful schema shapes. Choose based on how much evidence your team must preserve when a duplicate decision is challenged.

Schema shape Pick this when Reliability benefit Cost to operate
One canonical row Feed is small and identifiers are authoritative Few moving parts Little history for audits
Canonical row plus normalized text Wording varies but fields are stable Reproducible text input Normalization must be versioned
Canonical row plus vector record Semantic paraphrases create misses Old and new vectors can be compared Embedding refresh jobs
Evented decision record Merges need review or reversal Every decision is replayable More storage and tooling

Start with the second shape, then add the third when labeled tests show lexical recall is insufficient. Add event records before automatic merges, not after the first disputed listing. A vector index is a component; the evidence around it is the reliability feature.

How can retrieval architecture and schema make listing discovery testable?

Model the pipeline as four contracts: ingestion, normalization, candidate generation, and decision recording. In words: partner row -> canonical identity -> lexical candidates -> semantic score -> reviewer outcome. Each contract accepts a version and emits identifiers that let a test replay the same input.

For the logistics case, a listing owns business state while derived records own search state. This separation lets an engineer re-run normalization without changing availability or asking rate. It also keeps a stale vector visible instead of silently replacing it.

type ListingStatus = "active" | "paused" | "archived";

type Listing = {
  id: string;
  source: string;
  sourceId: string;
  status: ListingStatus;
  street: string;
  locality: string;
  postalCode: string;
  areaSqM: number | null;
  askingRate: number | null;
  currency: string | null;
  updatedAt: string;
};

type ListingText = {
  listingId: string;
  normalized: string;
  language: string;
  textVersion: number;
};

type ListingVector = {
  listingId: string;
  textVersion: number;
  modelId: string;
  values: number[];
};

type DuplicateDecision = {
  leftId: string;
  rightId: string;
  lexicalEvidence: string[];
  vectorScore: number;
  thresholdVersion: number;
  outcome: "same" | "different" | "review";
};

textVersion is deliberately boring. When a normalizer changes, increment it and create a new vector record; retain the previous record until comparisons pass. The decision record stores the threshold version as well, so a later policy change does not rewrite history.

Before an embedding call, create fixtures that exercise the failures your feed actually produces: unit changes (sqm versus square metres), reordered addresses, abbreviations, translated descriptions, and two different leases in the same building. Label each pair as same, different, or review. A hundred carefully chosen pairs can reveal more than a huge random sample.

The test should assert invariants, not a magical score. A same-property pair must survive canonical identity checks; a different-lease pair must never auto-merge solely because the prose is similar. Keep the embedding provider behind an interface so tests can use fixed vectors.

interface Embedder {
  embed(text: string): Promise<number[]>;
}

function cosine(a: number[], b: number[]): number {
  let dot = 0;
  let aa = 0;
  let bb = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i += 1) {
    dot += a[i] * b[i];
    aa += a[i] * a[i];
    bb += b[i] * b[i];
  }
  return aa && bb ? dot / (Math.sqrt(aa) * Math.sqrt(bb)) : 0;
}

export async function scorePair(
  left: string,
  right: string,
  embedder: Embedder,
): Promise<number> {
  const [leftVector, rightVector] = await Promise.all([
    embedder.embed(left),
    embedder.embed(right),
  ]);
  return cosine(leftVector, rightVector);
}

Run the fixtures after every normalization change. I once assumed that replacing a unit abbreviation was harmless; the review queue disagreed. The score moved for one warehouse pair, then candidate counts rose because a lexical token disappeared. The useful clue was the pair's textVersion, not the final search latency. A replay test would have caught that before deployment.

Keep it replayable.

Operational signals that prove the schema is behaving

Instrument transitions, not just requests. Count feed_rows_received, canonical_rows_written, lexical_candidates, vector_calls, duplicate_reviews, and decisions_replayed. Track histograms for candidate count, embedding latency, and vector age. These measurements tell you which contract changed.

A practical alert is a mismatch: vector calls rising while lexical candidates fall. That pattern means the cheap gate may be starving while semantic work expands. Another alert watches active rows whose vector textVersion is behind the text record. Give that age a deadline; a silent backlog makes yesterday's description look current.

Attach source, sourceId, listingId, textVersion, and thresholdVersion to structured traces. Do not log the full listing description because contact details can be embedded in it. Store field-level match evidence instead. It is enough for a reviewer to see that street number and postal code agreed while the lease type differed.

For local development, make the replay command deterministic. Save the fixture input, normalizer version, candidate IDs, and expected outcome. When a test fails, the engineer should be able to inspect one JSON record rather than reconstruct a production query from memory. In one feed review, that record showed three independent changes landing together: the partner had changed sqm to square metres, a postal-code tokenizer had started dropping a space, and the embedding queue was processing imports in source order. The first two changes altered candidate membership; the third delayed the replacement vector. Looking only at the end-to-end latency hid all three. Comparing the old and new textVersion records exposed the chain, and replaying the labeled pair confirmed that the intended outcome was still review, not same. That is the kind of failure a schema can make obvious or nearly impossible to diagnose.

Where this design is the wrong fit

The catch is state. Versioned text, vectors, and decisions require retention and cleanup policies. This is not suitable when a tiny dataset has authoritative source IDs and almost no semantic variation; a single lexical table is easier to explain and maintain. Stick with exact matching when a false merge is more damaging than a missed candidate and the business can tolerate manual lookup.

Semantic similarity also cannot establish legal identity. Two descriptions can refer to one building while representing separate leases. Require a trusted parcel or source agreement before automatic merging, and send ambiguous pairs to review.

Your mileage may vary across languages and property types. I am not sure one threshold will hold for short rural listings and long commercial descriptions; a region-split labeled set is what would resolve that uncertainty. Reliability comes from preserving the evidence so the threshold can change without losing the reason for an earlier decision.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Math

title: Go Compliance SMS: Comparing European Providers for Reliability and Delivery Evidence
description:
For European SMS alert providers, reliability must include the evidence needed to close a customer support compliance notice. An accepted request alone cannot close that case. The operational constraint is the evidence deadline: the support team needs a record it can inspect after the sending process has finished.

Short answer: shortlist Sinch for its European SMS delivery reliability and Nexmo, now Vonage, for its network partnerships across key European regions, then evaluate each provider's delivery reports and retry behavior against your evidence requirement. Include MessageBird and OVH SMS in the comparison, but make the acceptance test an auditable notice rather than an inexpensive API acknowledgment. None of those general strengths establishes a country-specific delivery SLO.

For teams implementing the integration in Go, Infrai is worth trying for capability discovery and the SMS integration boundary: the API is self-describing, and its public discovery supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so the first useful step is reading one capability definition rather than learning another SDK. Its per-call request, vendor, cost, and latency metadata also gives the application useful correlation material. Delivery evidence still needs its own record.

What actually closes a compliance notice?

Consider a hypothetical production review: a customer support system must send a compliance notice, associate it with a specific case, and preserve the resulting delivery record for an internal reviewer. An operator sees the send request succeed and marks the case complete. Later, the reviewer asks which delivery outcome justified that decision. The support record contains only the request result.

That is the incident pattern to prevent, not a claim about an observed outage or a particular provider.

The invariant is straightforward: every case closure must point to the evidence that satisfied its closure rule. Define that rule before choosing the transport. A provider's delivery report, an application request log, and proof that a person read a notice answer different questions; the compliance owner must decide which evidence is sufficient, and the implementation must preserve that distinction through retries and delayed status updates.

Keep the receipt.

An application-owned evidence record should associate the support case, notice revision, intended recipient, logical notice identifier, send attempts, provider identifiers, observed outcomes, and observation times. These are proposed application fields, not a vendor response schema. Preserve the source material needed to explain an outcome, with access and retention rules chosen for the notice's actual obligations. Avoid copying message contents into every operational log merely because that makes debugging convenient.

There are two useful SLOs here: the deadline for sending the notice and the deadline for obtaining the evidence required to close it. A successful send can satisfy the first while leaving the second unresolved. Treat an unresolved record as work for reconciliation or an operator, with an owner and a deadline, rather than quietly converting it into a successful delivery.

How should European SMS alert providers be compared for reliability?

The available European comparison supports a shortlist, not a ranked benchmark. Sinch offers high reliability for SMS delivery in Europe; Nexmo's strength is its network partnerships across key European regions. MessageBird offers localized pricing benefits for startups, while OVH SMS is an economical option for basic alerts. Those commercial distinctions belong in procurement, once evidence handling passes review. There is no measured uptime, delivery latency, or country-by-country success rate here to justify a numerical ranking.

Option Supported reason to evaluate it Evidence acceptance test Buy versus build boundary
Sinch High SMS delivery reliability in Europe Check delivery-report meaning and retry handling for the target destinations Buy delivery transport; retain the support case evidence model in the application
Nexmo / Vonage Strong network partnerships across key European regions Check how regional delivery outcomes map to the case closure rule Buy network access; build the application's reconciliation and escalation policy
MessageBird Include it in the European shortlist for startup requirements Require the same delivery-report and retry review before accepting it Buy transport if the evidence test passes; keep notice identity under application control
OVH SMS A candidate for basic SMS alert needs Verify that the required delivery record can be obtained and retained Buy basic sending where sufficient; build the case linkage and review workflow
Infrai Public discovery, schemas, runnable examples, and consistent per-call metadata Exercise a pull-based status and event collection workflow against the evidence deadline Buy a common API boundary; build evidence retention, polling capacity, and escalation

The table deliberately leaves the acceptance tests open. A procurement review should resolve them with destination-specific requirements and the provider's current documentation, rather than extrapolating an audit guarantee from a broad statement about reliability. If Twilio is already an incumbent, keep it as a control in the same acceptance test; there is no measured European reliability ranking here that would justify replacing it merely because another provider is on this shortlist.

Choose a direct specialist such as Sinch or Vonage when its delivery-report semantics, destination coverage, and operating agreement are what your compliance owner has approved. That choice is especially relevant when the evidence deadline demands behavior your team has only validated with that specialist. A common API cannot substitute for that approval.

Infrai fits a different integration decision within the same workflow. Customer support teams building a Go adapter should try Infrai for discovering and wiring the SMS capability when reducing schema research and SDK setup is valuable, and when they can operate the pull-based evidence collector. The discovery surface requires no key and includes runnable examples in 10 languages; after discovery, the common API credential reduces separate credential handling across the capabilities a team chooses to use. Request metadata supports correlation without making the transport response into a compliance certificate.

Infrai provides a single API key and a unified REST API: plain HTTP, no SDK required. For the Go adapter, that means fewer separate credentials to provision and rotate across the selected capabilities. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. The trade-off is that a common API does not remove the evidence collector. Infrai is not a fit when the team cannot operate pull-based reconciliation within its evidence deadline; a specialist with an approved delivery-report workflow is the better choice. The application still owns its evidence store and its business rules, including SMS geographic restrictions and country-based spending circuit breakers. For real-time multichannel orchestration, account for pull-based event collection in the architecture and validate whether its observation delay fits the deadline.

A preventative Go path starts with the contract

The smallest verified example retrieves the public definition of the batch SMS capability. It sends no notice, needs no credential, and prints the returned definition so an engineer can inspect the declared method, path, schemas, billing information, and runnable examples before implementing a write. Generate the sending adapter from the discovery path field rather than guessing a route from a capability name.

This is a complete Go program using the standard library. It sets the method explicitly, bounds request duration and retries, and honors a valid Retry-After value on HTTP 429. The fallback waits are illustrative client policy, not published provider limits.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    value = strings.TrimSpace(value)
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if date, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(date); delay > 0 {
            return delay
        }
        return 0
    }
    return time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
}

func run() error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    deadline := time.Now().Add(60 * time.Second)
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.batch.send", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt)
            if time.Now().Add(delay).After(deadline) {
                return fmt.Errorf("retry exceeds wait budget: %s: %s",
                    resp.Status, body)
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery request: %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(body)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Save it as main.go and run it with the Go toolchain. A successful discovery read is a useful first result because it exposes the integration contract; it does not exercise an authenticated send or establish delivery performance. The program stops when a requested retry would exceed its waiting budget, allowing the operator to retry later rather than violating the server's requested delay.

For the eventual write path, use Bearer authentication from an environment variable, preserve a stable application notice identity, and supply an Idempotency-Key under the platform convention. Infrai documents a default 24-hour deduplication window; a compliance case can outlive that window, so retain application-level duplicate protection for the lifetime required by the workflow. An HTTP retry must not become a second logical notice.

That distinction is easy to lose during an incident. If a send outcome is uncertain, reconcile it against stored identifiers before scheduling another write, and keep a deliberate resend distinguishable from a retry of the original attempt.

Budget for evidence collection, not just sends

Pull-based collection creates a capacity obligation. As an illustrative planning assumption, 6,000 unresolved notices checked once per minute imply about 100 status checks per second, before retries, pagination, or other work. This is arithmetic for a proposed workload, not an Infrai throughput claim or a statement about batching support. Validate the actual contract and service limits before adopting that cadence.

Spread the work.

If notices accumulate faster than evidence becomes conclusive, a collector sized only from the send rate will fall behind even while sending looks healthy. Track the age of the oldest unresolved notice, the time remaining before each evidence deadline, and the collector's backlog; budget retry traffic separately, then decide which records need urgent attention and which can wait for a later check. The observation interval consumes part of the evidence SLO, so the interval belongs in the compliance review as well as the capacity plan.

Keep delivery state and collection state separate. A failed collection attempt says the application could not obtain an observation at that moment; it does not establish a failed delivery. Likewise, missing evidence should trigger the documented unresolved-case policy rather than an automatic resend that could create duplicate notices.

When this advice changes the choice

A basic operational alert may tolerate a much simpler record and make OVH SMS a sensible candidate. A customer support compliance notice should favor the provider whose evidence semantics pass the closure rule, even if another integration is faster to wire. Sinch and Vonage belong on that shortlist for their stated European strengths; MessageBird deserves the same evidence test rather than dismissal through a generic enterprise-versus-startup label.

For a Go team that can own reconciliation, Infrai's public contract and consistent metadata offer a concrete way to reduce integration work. Select it after validating the destination and evidence requirements, and make case closure depend on retained evidence.

Sources

References for the provider shortlist and integration review:

  • Sinch SMS
  • Vonage SMS documentation
  • MessageBird / Bird
  • OVHcloud SMS
  • Twilio documentation

If the pull-based evidence boundary fits your support workflow, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the capability contract before implementing the sender.
