title: MATO: Multi-objective Personalized Alignment with Test-time Optimization for Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2605.25342v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with diverse and multifaceted user preferences is a fundamental challenge in personalized AI systems. Existing multi-objective alignment methods either rely on costly training or require pre-trained reward models for each preference, making it difficult for them to adapt to evolving preferences. Prompt-based personalization offers a training-free alternative, but prompting alone often provides limited steerability, as LLMs may overemphasize or overlook certain preferences and fail to give users reliable control over the relative importance of different objectives when conflicts arise, leading to suboptimal alignment. In this paper, we introduce MATO, a training-free framework for Multi-objective personalized Alignment with Test-time Optimization. MATO formulates personalization as a test-time optimization problem that steers the relative importance of multiple objectives through controllable weights during decoding, without modifying model parameters or requiring external reward models. Specifically, a reward discovery module constructs prompt-derived surrogate rewards from the backbone LLM for diverse objectives specified in natural language, while a weight optimization module dynamically adjusts objective weights based on the user's initial preferences and the partially generated response to balance competing objectives during generation. The resulting surrogate rewards and weights jointly guide an online optimization procedure over the token distribution, enabling better alignment with the target objectives. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and backbone LLMs show that MATO consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving Pareto-improving multi-objective alignment and stronger steerability. These results highlight test-time optimization as a promising direction for scalable, controllable, and model-agnostic personalized alignment.

title: The PIN was accepted and the UPI payment still failed: designing a fallback for a rule outside your app
description:
Auto UPI QR reads a UPI QR code from an image and hands the upi://pay link to the user's own UPI app, the same way a checkout page does. It is not a bank, it never sees the PIN, and it does not move money: the UPI app does all of that.

Most of the time the hand-off just works. But a whole class of QR codes fails in a way that looks like a bug in my app and is not one: the UPI app opens, the user enters the PIN, and then the payment is refused. This post is about designing for that case honestly.

Disclosure: I'm the developer of the app described here, and this post is published from my account. It was drafted and published by an AI agent working from the project's source code.

The rule that sits outside the app

UPI apps can be opened two ways: by the user typing or pasting a UPI ID inside the app, or by another app handing over a upi://pay link (an "intent" payment). Since 2024, NPCI rules restrict intent payments to some payees. My source notes reference circular OC-76A, effective 1 April 2024: intent payments to personal (P2P) UPI IDs and to offline merchants that are not verified, such as a plain printed shop sticker, are refused.

If you build anything in this space, read the current circular yourself; my summary is a developer's note, not legal advice. The practical point is this: the refusal comes after the PIN, inside the UPI app, and every UPI app behaves the same way. Retrying the same link in another app does not help.

There is nothing to fix in the hand-off code. What can be fixed is what the user sees next.

Step 1: tell "failed" apart from "not sure yet"

The hand-off is started for a result, so the UPI app's reply comes back. The reply is parsed into three outcomes, and only one of them leads to the fallback:

when (PayRouter.outcome(r.data)) {
    PayRouter.Outcome.SUCCESS -> { toast(R.string.toast_paid); onDone() }
    PayRouter.Outcome.PENDING -> { toast(R.string.toast_pending); onDone() }
    PayRouter.Outcome.FAILED  -> showFallback(qr, app)
}

SUBMITTED and PENDING map to PENDING, and PENDING never offers another way to pay. The user just sees "Payment submitted. Check its status in your UPI app." A pending payment can still go through; offering a second route at that moment invites the user to pay twice.

FAILED covers an explicit failure and also no reply at all (back pressed, or the UPI app closed after its error screen). That is deliberately broad, because the next step is an offer, not an action.

Step 2: explain the likely cause in the dialog

The fallback dialog is titled "Payment not completed", and its message names the app the user just used and the probable cause:

If PhonePe showed an error after the PIN, this QR does not accept app-to-app payments (an NPCI rule for personal QRs and plain shop stickers). Pay it by UPI ID instead: the UPI ID is copied and PhonePe opens. Paste it under Pay UPI ID.

("PhonePe" is filled in with whichever app was used.) The message starts with "If", because the app cannot know why the UPI app refused. It might have been the rule, a wrong PIN, or a bank outage. The user knows what they saw; the dialog gives them the explanation that fits the common case and lets them decide.

Step 3: the way through is the user's own action

The rule is about intent payments. Paying a UPI ID that the user enters inside their UPI app is the normal flow, so that is the fallback:

fun openForUpiId(context: Context, qr: UpiQr, app: UpiApp): Boolean {
    val launch = context.packageManager.getLaunchIntentForPackage(app.packageName) ?: return false
    val vpa = qr.payeeVpa ?: return false
    clip(context, vpa)
    Toast.makeText(context, context.getString(R.string.toast_paste_vpa, app.label), Toast.LENGTH_LONG).show()
    return start(context, launch.addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK))
}

A few details matter:

  • It opens the app's home screen, not a payment screen. No link is handed over, so nothing is pre-filled; the user pastes the UPI ID under "Pay UPI ID" and types the amount. The UPI app then shows the payee name it gets from the network, which is the check that matters.
  • No result is expected, so this launch uses FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK, unlike the checkout-style hand-off, which must not have it or the reply never comes back.
  • It returns false instead of throwing when there is no launch intent or no UPI ID in the QR, and the caller falls back to just copying the UPI ID with a toast. ActivityNotFoundException and SecurityException on start are caught the same way.
  • The toast says exactly where to paste: "UPI ID copied. In PhonePe, choose Pay UPI ID and paste it." Long duration, because the user reads it while switching apps.

Step 4: "another app" excludes the one that just failed

The dialog has three buttons: Pay by UPI ID, Other app, and Close. "Other app" reopens the picker without the app that just failed:

show(qr, PayRouter.upiApps(activity).filter { it.packageName != app?.packageName })

This is for the cases the rule does not explain: one UPI app's server is having a bad hour, or the user's account in that app has a problem.

Step 5: finish exactly once

The flow has a done callback that the share screen uses to close itself. The dialog can be dismissed by any of its buttons, or by tapping outside. "Other app" opens the picker and must not close the flow; everything else must. A local flag handles it:

var next = false
// Other app: next = true, then show the picker
.setOnDismissListener { if (!next) onDone() }

Without the flag, the screen behind the picker would finish while the picker was still on top.

Step 6: the payee name, every time

Whichever path the user takes, the last check belongs to them, inside the UPI app: the name shown before the PIN. Always check the payee name before entering your UPI PIN. Auto UPI QR cannot tell a genuine QR from a swapped one; the name in the UPI app is the one place that can.

Takeaways

  • When a refusal comes from a rule outside your app, the fix is the next screen, not the request.
  • Separate "failed" from "pending", and never offer a second payment route while one may still go through.
  • Word the explanation as a likely cause ("If ... showed an error"), not a diagnosis.
  • Make the fallback the user's own action in their own app, and say exactly where to paste.
  • Exclude the app that just failed from "try another", and make sure the flow finishes exactly once.

Auto UPI QR is on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.ashwar.autoupiqr&utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=2026-w46-fallback. It reads UPI QR codes from images and hands the link to your own UPI app. It is not a bank and never sees your PIN. The code here is from the current source, and I don't claim which Play build contains it. Always check the payee name before entering your UPI PIN.

title: I built bhasha-kit: a free offline Python library for Hindi & Bengali text
description:
Hi everyone! I'm Solo Developer. I just published my first Python package, bhasha-kit, a free, offline toolkit for Hindi, Bengali and English text.

Why I built it

Most text tools need an API key or an internet connection, and many don't handle Hindi and Bengali well. I wanted something simple that runs locally, with no dependencies.

What it does

  • Cleans text (emojis, extra spaces, Unicode)
  • Detects Hindi / Bengali / English
  • Transliterates Roman ↔ Devanagari / Bengali
  • Converts numbers to words, including rupees and paise
  • Basic sentiment analysis and keyword extraction

Install 

pip install bhasha-kit

Quick examples 

from bhasha_kit import clean_text, number_to_words, analyze_sentiment

clean_text("नमस्ते   😀 दोस्तों")
# 'नमस्ते दोस्तों'

number_to_words(1250, "hi")
# 'एक हज़ार दो सौ पचास'

number_to_words(1250, "bn")
# 'এক হাজার দুই শত পঞ্চাশ'

analyze_sentiment("this is not good")
# {'label': 'negative', 'score': -1.0, 'lang': 'en'}

Known limitations

  • Transliteration is rule-based and approximate.
  • Sentiment uses a small word list and doesn't understand sarcasm or context.

Links

  • GitHub: https://github.com/solodevelopersai/bhasha-kit
  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/bhasha-kit/

It's an early version (0.2.0). I'd love your feedback: try it, test it, and tell me about any bugs. A ⭐ on GitHub would help a lot. Thank you!

title: I Containerized My Fish Tank: A Water Quality Tracker with Docker Compose
description:
I Containerized a Water Quality Tracker for My Fish Tank (And Learned Docker Properly)

Aquarium hobbyists have a quiet enemy: invisible water chemistry. Ammonia can spike overnight, pH can drift slowly over weeks, and by the time fish show stress, it is often too late. Shrimp tanks are even less forgiving — a 0.05 ppm difference in ammonia can be the line between a thriving colony and an empty tank.

Like most keepers, I used to track my water parameters in a scattered notes app. No trends, no history, no alerts. So for my cloud services course project, I decided to fix this with a small multi-tier web app — and more importantly, to learn containerization the right way: Aquarium Parameter Log (a.k.a. aqualog).

What It Does

One core feature, done properly: log water measurements per tank and see the trend.

  • Create tanks (freshwater, planted, or shrimp)
  • Log readings: pH, temperature, NH3, NO2, NO3
  • View history as a table and a Chart.js trend line
  • Get an instant safe / warning / danger verdict per reading, based on threshold rules for each tank type — shrimp get stricter ammonia limits than freshwater fish

Target users are aquarium and shrimp keepers who test water regularly but have nowhere structured to put the numbers.

Architecture

The whole thing runs on localhost with one docker compose up -d --build:

browser ──► app (FastAPI + Jinja2, port 8000)
              │  GET/POST
              ├──► db (PostgreSQL 16, named volume, healthcheck)
              └──► redis (cache, healthcheck, 30s TTL)
           [profile tools: adminer on port 8080]
  • app — FastAPI backend + Jinja2 frontend in one container. Endpoints: GET /health (liveness), GET /tanks, POST /tanks, GET /readings (Redis-cached), POST /readings.
  • db — PostgreSQL 16, data persisted in a named volume, exposed to the app network only.
  • redis — caches reading lists for 30 seconds, cache invalidated on new writes.
  • adminer — a DB UI that only starts with the tools profile, so day-to-day runs stay lean.

The Dockerfile

The app image is a two-stage build:

FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /build
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN python -m venv /opt/venv && \
    /opt/venv/bin/pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /opt/venv /opt/venv
COPY app/ app/
COPY templates/ templates/
COPY static/ static/
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

Details that matter:

  • Multi-stage — the builder stage carries pip and the full toolchain; the runtime stage only gets the finished virtualenv. Result: a 272 MB image with no build tools inside.
  • Dependencies copied first — requirements.txt is copied and installed before any source code. Since it rarely changes, Docker reuses the cached layer on every code edit; my rebuilds after a code change finish in under a second.
  • Pinned tags, not latest — python:3.12-slim, postgres:16.9-alpine, redis:7.4-alpine. Reproducible builds beat convenient ones.
  • Exec-form CMD — CMD ["uvicorn", ...] makes uvicorn PID 1, so signals like SIGTERM reach the app and containers stop cleanly.
  • The app runs as a non-root appuser — one less thing to worry about if this ever leaves localhost.

The Compose File 

services:
  app:
    build: .
    environment:
      POSTGRES_HOST: db          # connect by service name, not IP
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  db:
    image: postgres:16.9-alpine
    volumes:
      - aquarium-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER}"]

Three things I appreciate most in Compose:

  1. DNS by service name — the app connects to db, never to a container IP. Containers get new IPs on every restart; names are stable.
  2. Healthcheck + service_healthy — the app container waits until Postgres actually accepts connections, killing the classic "app started before the database" race condition.
  3. Named volumes — docker compose down removes containers, but the volume survives. My readings were still there after a full teardown and rebuild. (docker compose down -v would wipe it — the -v flag deserves respect.)

Try It 

git clone https://github.com/saintbobi/aqualog.git
cd aqualog
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d --build

Then open http://localhost:8000. The image is also on Docker Hub as saintbobi705/aqualog:1.0.0.

What I Learned

  • Copying the dependency manifest before source code is the single highest-leverage habit in Dockerfile authoring. Layer caching turns 30-second rebuilds into near-instant ones.
  • Healthchecks are not decoration. They turned my startup from "hope it works" into a deterministic sequence.
  • Rule-based safety verdicts don't need machine learning to feel useful — good thresholds per tank type already make the app something I would actually use.
  • Designing for zero personal data from the start is both an ethical and a practical shortcut: nothing sensitive to leak, nothing to redact before publishing.

Repo: https://github.com/saintbobi/aqualog
Video demo: https://youtu.be/i0_Lttqi_r4

title: React Email Verification States That Explain Themselves
description:
Email verification looks like a small form until you ship it. Then the edge cases arrive: the request is still running, the code is wrong, the link expired, the user clicked resend twice, or the browser came back from a suspended tab.

The UI problem is usually an unclear state model

Many React forms start with three booleans:

const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false);
const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);
const [verified, setVerified] = useState(false);

This is friendly at first, but it can describe impossible combinations. What does loading: true and verified: true mean? Should an old error remain visible while a new request is running? Can the resend button be enabled during a code submission?

The important part are the transitions, not the number of variables. A verification flow should tell the user what is happening and what action is safe next.

Model verification as a small state machine

Start with named states that match product behavior. A TypeScript discriminated union makes the rules visible in the component:

type VerificationState =
  | { kind: "idle" }
  | { kind: "sending" }
  | { kind: "awaiting-code"; expiresAt: number; resendAvailableAt: number }
  | { kind: "verifying"; code: string }
  | { kind: "verified" }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string; canRetry: boolean }
  | { kind: "expired" };

Now the UI has a smaller decision surface. An awaiting-code state must carry the timing information needed by the countdown. A verified state does not need an error message. The compiler helps keep these informations together when the flow changes later.

I like this approach because it connects product language to implementation language. “Check your inbox” becomes awaiting-code, while “Your code expired” becomes expired. This makes a confusing email flow a little more clear for both the user and the next developer.

Render states with a discriminated union

Keep rendering close to the state model, but keep side effects in event handlers or a dedicated hook:

function VerificationPanel({ state }: { state: VerificationState }) {
  switch (state.kind) {
    case "idle":
      return <button type="button">Send verification email</button>;
    case "sending":
      return <p role="status">Sending your verification email…</p>;
    case "awaiting-code":
      return <CodeForm expiresAt={state.expiresAt} />;
    case "verifying":
      return <p role="status">Checking the code…</p>;
    case "verified":
      return <p role="status">Email verified. You can continue.</p>;
    case "expired":
      return <button type="button">Send a new code</button>;
    case "error":
      return (
        <div role="alert">
          <p>{state.message}</p>
          {state.canRetry && <button type="button">Try again</button>}
        </div>
      );
  }
}

The UI should not guess from a partially updated collection of flags. It should announce the current state, disable actions that cannot succeed, and preserve focus when an error replaces the form. A status message that appears only visually is not enough; screen readers need a useful announcement too.

Keep resend and expiration explicit

Resend is where many otherwise clean implementations become flaky. Treat it as a separate transition with a server-side policy behind it. The client countdown is useful feedback, but it is not the source of truth.

When the user submits a code, capture the request identity. If an older request finishes after a newer one, ignore the stale result. A simple sequence number works for a small hook:

const requestId = useRef(0);

async function verify(code: string) {
  const currentId = ++requestId.current;
  setState({ kind: "verifying", code });

  const result = await verifyCode(code);
  if (currentId !== requestId.current) return;

  setState(result.ok
    ? { kind: "verified" }
    : { kind: "error", message: "That code is not valid.", canRetry: true });
}

This small guard prevents a slow response from moving a fresh form backwards. It also make the failure behavior much easier to explain in a test.

For temporary test inboxes, a service such as tempmailso can help isolate verification data during development. Do not use an inbox you do not control for real customer accounts, and do not treat a successful test message as proof that production delivery is healthy.

Test the transitions, not just the happy path

Component tests should cover state changes and user-visible consequences:

  1. Sending starts with one click and announces progress.
  2. A successful response renders the code form.
  3. An invalid code keeps the user in a recoverable error state.
  4. A stale response cannot overwrite a newer request.
  5. Resend is unavailable during its cooldown and becomes available afterward.
  6. Expiration offers a clear next action.

This is also where connecting one alert to one rollout is a useful operational idea: make each failure point explainable instead of collapsing several causes into “Something went wrong.” For account flows, proof-first email change flows offer the same mindset from a security angle.

During manual testing, try a tem email, paste a code twice, navigate away while the request is pending, and return after the expiry time. These cases finds the gaps that a single successful test will miss. They are boring checks, but boring checks is exactly what protects a sign-up flow from surprise.

A short shipping checklist

Before shipping, check that:

  • Every visible message maps to one explicit state.
  • Submit, resend, and continue actions have clear disabled rules.
  • Stale responses cannot overwrite current state.
  • Expiration and retry behavior are tested.
  • Status and error messages work with keyboard and screen readers.
  • The server still enforces verification expiry and resend limits.

An explicit state machine does not make email delivery perfect. It does make the product honest about what it knows, what it is waiting for, and what the user can do next. That clarity is a feature worth shipping.

title: Models Recall What They Violate: Constraint Adherence in Multi-Turn LLM Ideation
description:
arXiv:2604.28031v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: When researchers refine ideas with large language models over several turns, do the models preserve the original brief's constraints? We introduce DriftBench, a benchmark for constraint adherence in multi-turn LLM-assisted scientific ideation. It pairs 38 research briefs from 24 scientific domains, each with hard constraints and banned moves, with four interaction conditions and seven models from five providers (two open-weight), scored on 2,116 runs. Iterative pressure to improve a proposal raises structural complexity in every model and lowers adherence to the brief's hard constraints. A restatement probe shows that the constraints stay legible and reproducible on demand while the proposal departs from them. The knows-but-violates (KBV) rate, the share of pressure runs scored non-compliant on a hard constraint despite a correct restatement, exceeds 50% for most models. A crossed-judge design measures the judge offset. GPT-5.4 scores adherence 0.535 points lower than Opus 4.6 on the same runs. The design finds no judge-by-condition interaction on adherence, so the pressure effect on adherence is judge-stable while KBV levels and the bottom of the model ranking are not. Re-eliciting the brief at checkpoints lowers KBV for some models but not others, and complexity inflation persists. Blind human raters find more constraint violations than the LLM judge, so reported adherence is conservative. We release all briefs, prompts, rubrics, transcripts, and scores.

description:
Vercel Sandbox now lets you send input to running commands through standard input (stdin). Use it to exchange messages with stdio MCP servers such as agent-browser, or send data to other command-line programs while they run.

In the TypeScript SDK, set stdin: true and detached: true in runCommand(). Use writeStdin() to send input and closeStdin() when you’re done:

You can also set stdin to a Node.js readable stream, such as process.stdin. The SDK forwards the stream’s data and closes the command’s standard input when the stream ends.

In the Python SDK, set stdin=subprocess.PIPE and send input with server.stdin.send(). Call communicate() to close stdin, collect remaining output, and wait for the process to exit:

For commands that receive all their input at once, you can pass input directly to Python’s run_process().

title: Knowledge Localization in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs Using Cross-Lingual Inconsistency
description:
arXiv:2603.17102v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Modern LLMs continue to exhibit significant variance in behavior across languages, such as being able to recall factual information in some languages but not others. While typically studied as a problem to be mitigated, in this work, we propose leveraging this cross-lingual inconsistency as a tool for interpretability in mixture-of-experts (MoE) LLMs. Our knowledge localization framework contrasts routing for sets of languages where the model correctly recalls information from languages where it fails. This allows us to isolate model components that play a functional role in answering about a piece of knowledge. Our method proceeds in two stages: (1) querying the model with difficult factual questions across a diverse set of languages to generate "success" and "failure" activation buckets and then (2) applying a statistical contrastive analysis to the MoE router logits to identify experts important for knowledge. To validate the necessity of this small number of experts for answering a knowledge question, we deactivate them and re-ask the question. We find that despite only deactivating about 20 out of 6000 experts, the model no longer answers correctly in over 40% of cases. Generally, this method provides a realistic and scalable knowledge localization approach to address increasingly complex LLMs.

title: BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm-System Co-Design
description:
arXiv:2611.09825v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4-3.0$\times$ higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at https://github.com/OpenBitSys/BitDecoding-FP4.

title: Structure and Lineage Evidence for Vietnamese Statutory Article Retrieval on DRiLL
description:
arXiv:2611.09200v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We study Vietnamese statutory Article retrieval on DRiLL using features for provision identity and local form, same-law support, and citation and lineage evidence. Across five random seeds, selectors sharing candidates, listwise Qwen evidence, and learner settings improve official $F_2$ from 71.77% to 72.91%, with the largest descriptive gain on two-Article questions. Added features account for 18.20% of the proposed selector's total decision-tree split gain, measured as training-objective reduction, mainly from same-law and citation evidence. Cases reveal base provisions and amendments, companion recovery, distractor removal, and failures. These findings motivate research on other datasets, representations, and learners without establishing individual feature effects or requiring LightGBM, hand-crafted scores, or explicit graphs.

title: RAG Pipeline Utils v3.9.0: Catching Answers That Drop a Condition
description:
Answer checks now catch an answer that drops its source's condition, and are much faster on long answers. Text from PDFs and web pages is read the way it was typed, and a 1,000-sentence answer is checked in under half a second.

npm install @devilsdev/rag-pipeline-utils@^3.9.0
# and, if you use the MCP server:
npx @devilsdev/rag-mcp-server@3.9.0 ./docs

If you install @devilsdev/rag-core, rag-guardrails, rag-connectors or rag-eval directly, upgrade them to 3.9.0 as well.

Highlights

  • A condition left out is caught. "Remote work is allowed two days per week" is no longer grounded by "Remote work is allowed two days per week with manager approval", and "Access is allowed" no longer by "Access is allowed, but not for guests". The check reports condition_mismatch. Turn it off with conditionCheck: false, or --no-condition-check on the CLI.
  • Text is read as typed. Zero-width characters, soft hyphens, full-width digits and no-break spaces are normalised before text is compared, so a source copied from a PDF or a web page supports the sentence that quotes it. Sentences end where a reader would end them: "Dr. Lee" and "10 a.m." don't end one, and a list item does. Citation markers such as [1] and ¹ no longer fail a correct sentence.
  • Long answers are checked in linear time. Each source and answer is prepared once per check, so a 1,000-sentence answer that took about 9 s is checked in under half a second. The MCP server counts its input limits the way the check does.
  • Stable scores across source sets. A duplicated or unrelated source no longer changes a verdict, and computeFaithfulness, groundedness and PipelineEvaluator use the same word weights as checkAnswer.
  • Fixes across the library. The chunkers keep all their text; FileVectorStore scores are true cosine similarities, and a save merges with what other processes saved; streams end with one complete done chunk and honour timeout; CostTracker checks the budget before a run; DAG node timeouts and concurrency take effect; and AuditLogger gains close() and a working webhook.

After upgrading

Some changes need action:

  • Re-tune minRelevanceScore for FileVectorStore. Its scores are now cosine similarity (1 for an identical vector); they used to grow with the query vector's length.
  • Re-ingest to pick up the chunker fixes. The recursive (default), fixed-size and sentence chunkers no longer drop or split text, so chunks can change.
  • Raise timeout if you stream long answers. A run's timeout now covers a returned stream until it ends.
  • Regenerate saved baselines that compare multi-source scores or hallucination classes. Scores move for answers checked against several sources, and hallucination classes change in many cases while rates and verdicts don't.

Benchmarks

On the condition-dropped benchmark, F1 on the test split is 85.9% lexical
and 90.1% with a Claude judge on the released code. On the public RAGTruth
and HaluEval sets, F1 moved by at most 0.01: the stricter condition check
adds a few false alarms on RAGTruth, and HaluEval has three more misses.
Every number, including those that got worse, is on the
Benchmarks page.

Known gaps

The condition check is deliberately narrow. A negated contrast with no
scope word ("but not guests", "but guests are not admitted") is not yet
read as a restriction, and neither is a restriction attached to a
different subject ("Staff may enter" against "Guests may enter, but staff
need approval"). 3.10 plans restrictions that follow their subject, which
covers these cases.

Thanks to the readers whose reports shaped this release.

The full list is in the CHANGELOG, and the release notes are on GitHub.

Originally published on the rag-pipeline-utils blog.

title: Next.js 16.4.6 Now Gzips Route Handlers. I Checked Streams, Downloads and Pre-Compressed Bodies
description:
Next.js 16.4.6 shipped overnight with a one-line release note: "Automatically compress route handler responses if not already compressed." If you self-host with next start, that's a real change. Your API routes were never gzipped before, and now they are.

Compression and streaming don't always mix, so I ran the same routes on 16.4.4, 16.4.5 and 16.4.6.

What changed

The fix is PR #101220, backported in #101280. Its description says route handler responses "were never compressed when self-hosted". Next stored single header values as one-element arrays, the compression middleware only accepts a string Content-Type, so every route handler response skipped compression. Pages were compressed all along.

How I tested

A small app built with next build and run with next start on Node 22.23.4. Requests come from a raw node:http client sending Accept-Encoding: gzip, so nothing gets decoded behind my back, plus plain fetch() to see what a normal client gets. The routes look like this one:

// app/sse/route.ts
export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic'
const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms))

export async function GET() {
  const enc = new TextEncoder()
  const stream = new ReadableStream({
    async start(controller) {
      for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
        controller.enqueue(enc.encode(`data: {"token":"chunk ${i}"}\n\n`))
        await sleep(500)
      }
      controller.close()
    },
  })
  return new Response(stream, {
    headers: { 'content-type': 'text/event-stream', 'cache-control': 'no-cache' },
  })
}

Here's what came back:

Route 16.4.4 16.4.5 16.4.6
Response.json() with 200 items (5,591 bytes) not gzipped not gzipped gzipped, 964 bytes on the wire
SSE stream above not gzipped not gzipped gzipped, still streams
600 KB application/pdf with Content-Length Content-Length: 614400 no Content-Length, chunked no Content-Length, chunked
Body gzipped by the handler, with Content-Encoding: gzip works header dropped, client gets raw gzip bytes gzipped twice, client gets gzip bytes after decoding

Streams still stream

This was my main worry. On 16.4.6 the SSE route came back with Content-Encoding: gzip, and the decoded events arrived at 9, 508, 1009, 1510 and 2010 ms. That's the same 500 ms rhythm as the uncompressed run on 16.4.4. Each chunk goes through gzip and out right away; nothing waits in a buffer.

I also ran an AI SDK 7.0.166 route (streamText(...).toUIMessageStreamResponse() with a mock model that emits a token every 500 ms). Same result: gzipped, and each text-delta showed up on its own about 500 ms apart.

I only tested next start directly. A reverse proxy or CDN in front of your app can still buffer, and I didn't test Vercel's platform.

Content-Length is still gone

This part comes from 16.4.5, not 16.4.6. The security release strips Content-Length, Content-Encoding and Transfer-Encoding from every route handler Response (the reasoning is in advisory GHSA-pc58-hwjq-p385, about forwarded fetch() responses). Issue #101120 reported that this breaks downloads and range requests, since pdf.js and download progress bars need the size.

That issue was closed by the compression PR. On 16.4.6, though, my 600 KB PDF still had no Content-Length on GET or HEAD. application/pdf isn't something the middleware compresses, so it just goes out chunked. If you serve files from a route handler and rely on that header, 16.4.6 doesn't bring it back.

Pre-compressed bodies break

Some handlers gzip their own output (a cached blob, a file from storage) and set Content-Encoding: gzip. On 16.4.4 that worked. On 16.4.5 Next drops the header, so fetch() hands your code raw gzip bytes and JSON.parse fails. On 16.4.6 it's worse in a different way. The header gets dropped, then the middleware gzips the already-gzipped body. The client decodes once and still has gzip bytes.

My test body was only 47 bytes, so the 1 KB threshold doesn't save you here. Route handler responses stream without a Content-Length, and the PR's own tests note that the threshold "never engages" for them.

Setting compress: false in next.config stops the double gzip, but you're back to the 16.4.5 behavior: the bytes arrive with no Content-Encoding header.

The fix that worked in my test: return the uncompressed body and let the server compress it. That's also what the PR description recommends ("the responses from route handlers should be returned uncompressed and be compressed by the outgoing server"). There's an open PR, #101452, to keep Content-Encoding on handler responses, but it isn't merged as of this morning.

What I'd check before upgrading

  • Grep your route handlers for content-encoding and gzipSync/CompressionStream. Those are the ones that break.
  • If you serve downloads from a route handler, check whether anything needs Content-Length. It's been missing since 16.4.5.
  • If nginx or a CDN was compressing your API responses, it now receives responses that already say Content-Encoding: gzip. I didn't test a proxy setup, so check the headers your users actually get.

The streaming part was the one I expected to bite, and it was fine. The quiet one is the handler that gzips its own body, because it fails in the client, not on the server.

Got a route handler that sets its own Content-Encoding? I'd like to know what it's serving.

title: Enabling Approximate Joint Sampling in Diffusion LMs
description:
arXiv:2509.22738v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In autoregressive language models, each token is sampled by conditioning on all the past tokens; the overall string has thus been sampled from the correct underlying joint distribution represented by the model. In contrast, masked diffusion language models generate text by unmasking tokens out of order and potentially in parallel. Generating an overall string sampled from the correct underlying joint distribution would (again) require exactly one token unmasking in every full-model forward pass. The more tokens unmasked in parallel, the further away the string is from the true joint; this can be seen in the resulting drop in accuracy (but, increase in speed). In this paper we devise a way to {\em approximately} sample multiple tokens from the joint distribution in a single full-model forward pass; we do so by developing a new lightweight single-layer ``sampler" on top of an existing large diffusion LM. One forward pass of the full model can now be followed by multiple forward passes of only this sampler layer, to yield multiple unmasked tokens. Our sampler is trained to mimic exact joint sampling from the (frozen) full model. We show the effectiveness of our approximate joint sampling for both pretrained-only (Dream-7B-Base, Llada-7B-Base) and instruction-tuned (Dream-7B-Instruct, Dream-7B-Coder) models on language modeling and math \& coding tasks. When four tokens are unmasked for each full-model denoising step, our sampling algorithm achieves a MAUVE score of 0.87 (vs marginal baseline of 0.31) with respect to the true joint distribution.

title: Ecommerce Software Development
description:
Designing Reliable Ecommerce Checkout Systems: What Developers Should Get Right

A customer can spend several minutes browsing products, comparing prices, and adding items to a cart, only to leave because the checkout process feels slow or confusing.

For ecommerce businesses, checkout is more than the final step in a purchase. It is a critical part of the application architecture that directly affects customer experience, transaction reliability, and revenue.

From a developer's perspective, building a reliable checkout system requires more than connecting a payment gateway. Several technical decisions need to work together.

1. Keep the Checkout Flow Simple

A complicated checkout process creates unnecessary friction. Developers should aim to reduce the number of steps required to complete an order.

Some practical considerations include:

  • Allowing guest checkout where appropriate
  • Supporting saved customer addresses
  • Providing clear shipping and payment options
  • Validating form fields without unnecessary page reloads
  • Displaying the final order amount before payment

A clean checkout interface should also work consistently across mobile, tablet, and desktop devices.

2. Make Payment Processing Reliable

Payment integration is one of the most sensitive parts of an ecommerce application.

A common mistake is assuming that a successful frontend response means the payment is complete. Payment status should always be verified through trusted server-side communication.

Developers should consider:

  • Verifying payment gateway responses on the backend
  • Using webhooks to receive payment updates
  • Implementing idempotency to prevent duplicate transactions
  • Maintaining transaction logs for troubleshooting
  • Handling failed, pending, and cancelled payments separately

These measures help prevent situations where customers are charged but their orders are not recorded correctly.

3. Prevent Duplicate Orders

Network delays, accidental double-clicks, and repeated API requests can create duplicate orders.

A reliable checkout system should use unique order references and idempotency keys where appropriate. The backend should also validate whether an existing transaction or order is already being processed.

This becomes particularly important during high-traffic periods, when multiple requests may arrive within a short time.

4. Maintain Inventory Accuracy

Inventory management becomes challenging when several customers attempt to purchase the same product simultaneously.

For example, imagine an online store has only one unit of a product remaining. Two customers add that item to their carts at almost the same time.

Without proper inventory controls, both customers might complete checkout even though only one item is available.

Developers can reduce this risk through:

  • Atomic database operations
  • Inventory reservation mechanisms
  • Transaction management
  • Stock validation before order confirmation
  • Clear handling of reservation expiry

The right approach depends on order volume, business rules, and the underlying system architecture.

5. Design for Payment Failures and Recovery

Not every transaction succeeds on the first attempt. A customer may lose connectivity, a payment provider may experience an outage, or a bank may decline a transaction.

Instead of treating every failure as a generic error, the application should provide meaningful feedback and a recovery path.

For instance, customers should be able to retry an eligible payment without creating another order or being charged twice.

A well-designed system should also distinguish between a confirmed failure and an unknown payment status that still requires verification.

6. Protect Sensitive Customer Information

Security should be part of checkout architecture from the beginning.

Developers should follow secure payment integration practices, use HTTPS, validate server-side inputs, protect customer sessions, and avoid storing sensitive card details unnecessarily.

Using a payment provider's hosted checkout or tokenization features can reduce the amount of sensitive payment data handled directly by the ecommerce application.

7. Monitor Checkout Performance

Even a technically reliable checkout can create problems if it responds slowly.

Useful monitoring metrics include:

  • Checkout API response time
  • Payment success and failure rates
  • Cart abandonment rate
  • Order creation errors
  • Payment webhook processing delays
  • Duplicate transaction incidents

These metrics help teams identify issues before they affect a large number of customers.

Final Thoughts

A reliable ecommerce checkout system depends on several connected components: payment processing, order management, inventory synchronization, security, and performance monitoring.

Developers should approach checkout as a complete business-critical workflow rather than an isolated payment page. Careful architecture and proper error handling can make the purchasing experience more predictable for customers and easier to maintain for development teams.

Businesses planning to build or improve their ecommerce platforms can explore ecommerce software development services to understand how scalable application architecture supports long-term operational requirements.

title: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN: Which Rows Survive?
description:
Most JOIN confusion comes down to one question: what happens to rows with no match? Here's how INNER and LEFT JOIN answer it, and how to choose.

Adapted from the SQL Essentials Companion Guide.

Every explanation of SQL joins seems to reach for the same overlapping-circles diagram, and many people still come away unsure which join to use. It helps to drop the diagram and ask one plain question: what happens to a row that has no match in the other table?

That single question is the whole difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN. Everything else about them is the same.

A tiny example

Take two small tables. customers holds three people, and orders holds the purchases they made:

customers                orders
id | name                id | customer_id | amount
---+-----                ---+-------------+-------
 1 | Ada                 10 |           1 |     50
 2 | Ben                 11 |           1 |     30
 3 | Cy                  12 |           2 |     20
                         13 |          99 |     70

Ada has two orders, Ben has one, and Cy has none. Order 13 points at customer 99, who doesn't exist. Two rows here have no match: Cy on one side, order 13 on the other. The joins differ in what they do with them.

INNER JOIN keeps only the matches 

SELECT customers.name, orders.amount
FROM customers
INNER JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id;

name | amount
-----+-------
Ada  |     50
Ada  |     30
Ben  |     20

Only rows that found a partner appear. Cy is gone because Cy has no orders, and order 13 is gone because it has no customer. INNER JOIN drops anything without a match, on both sides. Writing JOIN on its own means the same thing.

LEFT JOIN keeps everything from the left table 

SELECT customers.name, orders.amount
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id;

name | amount
-----+-------
Ada  |     50
Ada  |     30
Ben  |     20
Cy   |   NULL

Now Cy is back, with NULL where the order columns would be. The "left" table is the one written before the JOIN keyword, here customers. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from that table, whether or not it found a match, and fills in NULL for the right table's columns when it didn't. Order 13 is still absent, because it lives in the right table and has no customer.

So the choice comes down to this: if a row without a match should still show up in your results, use LEFT JOIN. If it should disappear, use INNER JOIN.

A useful trick: finding what's missing

Because LEFT JOIN fills in NULL for non-matches, you can use it to find rows that have no match at all. Filter for the NULL:

SELECT customers.name
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
WHERE orders.id IS NULL;

name
----
Cy

That's "customers who have never ordered." It's one of the most useful things a LEFT JOIN does, and the same pattern answers any "which X have no Y" question. Note that it uses IS NULL, not = NULL. If that distinction is new to you, Why 'WHERE x = NULL' Never Works in SQL explains it.

How to practice choosing

Before you write a join, say the result out loud: "I want every customer, and their orders if they have any" (that's LEFT), or "I want only customers who have orders" (that's INNER). The wording tells you which to use. Then run it on a small table where you know the answer, like the one above, and check that the row you expected to survive did.

If you ever get stuck, count rows. Run SELECT COUNT(*) on the left table alone, then on the join. With an INNER JOIN, the join can come back with fewer rows than the left table, because unmatched rows disappeared. With a LEFT JOIN, every left row is still there, so you won't see fewer than the left table has.

Two mistakes worth knowing about ahead of time

Filtering the right table in WHERE and accidentally undoing your LEFT JOIN. This catches almost everyone once. Suppose you want all customers, plus only their orders over 25:

SELECT customers.name, orders.amount
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id
WHERE orders.amount > 25;

name | amount
-----+-------
Ada  |     50
Ada  |     30

Ben and Cy vanished. For them, orders.amount is NULL after the join (Ben's only order is 20), and NULL > 25 is never true, so WHERE throws those rows out. You've turned your LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN without noticing. To keep every customer, put the condition in the ON clause, so it limits which orders match instead of which rows survive:

SELECT customers.name, orders.amount
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN orders
  ON orders.customer_id = customers.id AND orders.amount > 25;

name | amount
-----+-------
Ada  |     50
Ada  |     30
Ben  |   NULL
Cy   |   NULL

Counting with COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN. COUNT(*) counts rows, and Cy's row exists even though there's no order, so Cy shows as 1. Count a column from the right table instead, such as COUNT(orders.id), which skips NULL and correctly gives Cy 0. And if a join ever returns more rows than you expected, the cause is a different one, covered in Why Your JOIN Doubled Your Totals.

A habit that makes joins easy

Treat LEFT JOIN as your starting point and INNER JOIN as a deliberate choice. Ask yourself first which table is the one you really care about, the one whose rows must not vanish, and put it on the left. Then decide whether unmatched rows belong in the answer. Doing it in that order turns a choice that feels like guesswork into two short questions, and it makes the "where did my rows go?" surprise much rarer.

Prefer to dig in yourself? The SQL Essentials repo on GitHub has more free examples and exercises.

title: Building a dual-view Shopify lookbook from the Born Agency case
description:
Campaign imagery can define the identity of a streetwear, eyewear, beauty, accessories, or camera brand. A standard four-column Shopify grid can flatten that identity.

The two usual shopping paths leave a gap. A lookbook can be hard to shop directly, while a collection page can lose the visual character that drew the buyer in.

Ukrainian design studio BY.SHIVA STUDIO, with Polina Prykhodko and Oleksandr BY.SHIVA, addresses that tension in Born Agency | Creative Studio Website. Its brief asks for a custom visual approach with a monochrome base and strong accents, letting the imagery set the tone from the first scroll.

Two other public projects help frame the comparison.

  • NM Art & Design uses warm greys and generous negative space to give objects the attention they would receive in a gallery.
  • Volenta uses a dark B2B layout with Bento cards that make metrics easy to scan.
  • Born Agency combines viewfinder marks, mixed typography, saturated gradients, and a CAROUSEL / GALLERY toggle. The visitor can look through large images or filter a grid within the same interface.

The following sections examine four design decisions and show how to translate them into a Shopify Online Store 2.0 theme, including the complete reference section.

1. Four design decisions in the Born Agency case

Colour system — carbon black with lime and magenta accents

Born Agency starts from carbon black, #1C1C1C, rather than a pure black #000000 canvas. The darkroom-like base supports two separate gradients.

  • Background and cards. Carbon black #1C1C1C with a 1px translucent white line, rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12), creates an exposed hairline grid.
  • Primary action. Electric lime runs from #5AFE41 to #EBF61D. It highlights actions such as the circular CONTACT US ↗ button, the footer's project inquiry panel, and active filters.
  • Atmosphere and navigation. Magenta runs from #FF0046 to #FF006A. The fullscreen menu uses it behind large vertical links for Home, Projects, Services, About, and Contact. It also appears as a red glow in the team portraits.
  • Main text. Pure white #FFFFFF gives the dark canvas strong contrast.

For a Shopify implementation, start with the product images. Keep most of the browse area carbon black and white so the campaign colours can carry it. Reserve magenta for the full-screen menu and collection navigation, and keep lime for circular Shop Now ↗ and Add to Bag ↗ actions.

Hero and imagery — use a viewfinder to label a detail

On the hero and selected work images, the project puts crosshairs and right-angle viewfinder corners around the subject. Small uppercase labels sit beside the frame, including TAILORED TO YOUR REQUEST, ATTENTION TO DETAIL, and REAL TEAM WITHOUT AI AGENTS.

A Shopify lookbook can give its hotspots the same job. On a hero or campaign image:

  1. Use CSS corners to frame a detail such as the sunglasses a model is wearing, the bag they are holding, or the keyboard on a desk.
  2. Put the material, feature, or price next to the frame, for example TITANIUM FRAME · $240 ↗.
  3. Connect the hotspot to the relevant product's Quick Add Drawer if the theme supports that flow.

Brand typography — combine typefaces and small inline images

The project’s brand statement uses several editorial techniques.

  • Change typeface within a sentence. Extra-bold geometric sans-serif carries the main words. A high-contrast italic serif marks an emphasis or a turn in the sentence.
  • Place a small image capsule inside a line. A rounded image or looping texture close to the text height lets the reader shift from words to material details.
  • Use a circular text badge. A phrase such as CREATE · DOMINATE · CREATE · DOMINATE runs around a rotating badge in a corner of the page.

Product and portfolio browsing — two views with a shared filter bar

The PROJECTS page has two levels of navigation. The control on the right switches between the large horizontal CAROUSEL and the multi-column GALLERY. The filter bar divides browsing into four decisions.

  • Sort By. No Filter / Latest / Popular / Featured
  • Content Type. All / Photo / Video / Motion
  • Industry. All / Fashion / Beauty / Food & Beverage / Tech / Automotive / Lifestyle
  • Style. All / Minimal / Bold / Editorial / Surreal / Cinematic / Abstract

On detail pages such as SMITH and FLORA, a fine-line grid puts About, Fields, Tasks, Platforms, Services, Duration, and Team on the left, alongside a large image carousel.

Born Agency pattern Problem it addresses Equivalent for a Shopify store
CAROUSEL versus GALLERY New visitors want to feel the campaign through large images. Shoppers with a product in mind want to scan a grid. Let the same collection switch between a campaign carousel and a three-column shopping grid in place.
Filter by Minimal, Bold, or Editorial Product categories alone can make it hard to browse by aesthetic. Add a Style product metafield alongside category filters. Use it to group styles such as minimalist everyday wear, runway pieces, or technical outerwear.
Fine-line specifications on SMITH and FLORA A visual page can hide details a shopper needs before buying. Put fit, weight, fabric, origin, and model size in a structured grid on the product page.

2. Implement the visual system in a Shopify theme

The reference uses three pieces that can live in a Shopify Online Store 2.0 theme.

1. Set the palette, gradients, and mixed typography

Define the carbon black and both gradients in assets/base.css. The same file can supply classes for the bold sans-serif and italic serif combination and the inline image capsule.

:root {
  /* Born Agency 核心色板 */
  --born-black: #1C1C1C;
  --born-surface: #242424;
  --born-white: #FFFFFF;
  --born-muted: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.62);
  --born-grid-line: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.14);

  /* 双色高饱和渐变 */
  --born-grad-green: linear-gradient(135deg, #5AFE41 0%, #EBF61D 100%);
  --born-grad-pink: linear-gradient(135deg, #FF0046 0%, #FF006A 100%);

  /* 字体组合：宽体粗无衬线 + 高对比衬线 */
  --born-font-sans: 'Syne', 'Helvetica Neue', Arial, sans-serif;
  --born-font-serif: 'Playfair Display', 'Instrument Serif', Georgia, serif;
}

/* 混排标题中的斜体衬线强调词 */
.born-editorial-serif {
  font-family: var(--born-font-serif);
  font-style: italic;
  font-weight: 400;
  padding: 0 0.15em;
}

/* 行内微缩胶囊图（Inline Image Pill） */
.born-inline-pill {
  display: inline-block;
  vertical-align: middle;
  width: 2.4em;
  height: 1.15em;
  border-radius: 999px;
  object-fit: cover;
  margin: 0 0.2em;
  border: 1px solid var(--born-grid-line);
}

2. Draw the circular action and viewfinder corners

The circular CONTACT US ↗ action and the four viewfinder corners can be drawn with CSS and pseudo-elements. The corner marks need no separate image assets.

/* 正圆形电光绿渐变主按钮 */
.born-circle-cta {
  width: 116px;
  height: 116px;
  border-radius: 50%;
  background: var(--born-grad-green);
  color: #1C1C1C;
  display: inline-flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  gap: 4px;
  font-family: var(--born-font-sans);
  font-size: 0.75rem;
  font-weight: 800;
  letter-spacing: 0.06em;
  text-transform: uppercase;
  text-decoration: none;
  transition: transform 0.25s cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1);
}
.born-circle-cta:hover {
  transform: scale(1.06) rotate(4deg);
}

/* 相机取景框四角准星容器 */
.born-viewfinder-box {
  position: relative;
  padding: 10px 14px;
  background: rgba(28, 28, 28, 0.72);
  backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
  color: #FFFFFF;
  font-size: 0.75rem;
  letter-spacing: 0.08em;
  text-transform: uppercase;
}
.born-viewfinder-box::before,
.born-viewfinder-box::after {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  width: 8px;
  height: 8px;
  border-color: #5AFE41;
  border-style: solid;
}
.born-viewfinder-box::before {
  top: 0; left: 0;
  border-width: 1.5px 0 0 1.5px;
}
.born-viewfinder-box::after {
  bottom: 0; right: 0;
  border-width: 0 1.5px 1.5px 0;
}

3. Add the complete dual-view section

The example combines an inline-image statement, a no-reload CAROUSEL / GALLERY switch, and product cards with viewfinder labels and a circular action.

Save it as sections/born-editorial-showcase.liquid. In the theme editor, select a product for each product block you want to display. Check the default view, the style tags, and both image states with real product data before adding the section to the live theme. A purchase drawer requires the theme's own drawer integration.

title: Internal Safety Collapse in LLMs and Coding Agents
description:
arXiv:2603.23509v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLMs and coding agents can now tackle complex, long-horizon tasks through advances in reinforcement learning, but stronger task-solving capabilities do not necessarily preserve safety alignment. Recent AI agent incidents involving reward hacking indicate how optimizing for task success can bring learned capabilities into conflict with safety alignment. In this work, we identify a critical failure mode that manifests this conflict, which we term Internal Safety Collapse (ISC). When completing otherwise benign coding tasks, AI agents can prioritize satisfying program requirements over safety constraints, generating large volumes of sensitive content, including unsafe outputs, as task data. To study this phenomenon, we introduce TVD (Task, Validator, Data), a framework for building controlled workflows that require sensitive content for completion. Through extensive experiments, we observe instances of highly harmful content that closely resemble outputs from early, unaligned LLMs in 2023. We further find that ISC can be effectively triggered even in highly capable LLMs such as Claude Fable 5. These results indicate that, despite substantial alignment efforts, frontier LLMs remain internally unsafe: safety alignment primarily reshapes surface behavior without eliminating the underlying knowledge that enables unsafe outputs. Our findings underscore the need for caution when deploying LLMs in high-stakes settings, such as scientific pipelines and autonomous agents.
  Content Warning: This paper contains examples of harmful content. Source code: https://github.com/wuyoscar/Internal-Safety-Collapse

title: LangFlow: Continuous Diffusion Rivals Discrete in Language Modeling
description:
arXiv:2604.11748v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Continuous diffusion has served as a foundation for high-fidelity, controllable, and few-step generation across continuous data modalities such as images, videos, and molecular structures. However, in language modeling, prior continuous diffusion language models (DLMs) lag behind discrete counterparts. Existing categorical and simplex-based approaches operate over extremely large and sparse language spaces, while prior embedding-space approaches avoid this sparsity but lack a well-selected design space. In this work, we close this gap with LangFlow by connecting embedding-space DLMs to Flow Matching, alongside three key innovations: (1) we derive a novel ODE-based NLL bound for principled evaluation of continuous flow-based language models; (2) we propose an information-uniform principle for setting the noise schedule, which motivates a learnable noise scheduler based on a Gumbel distribution; and (3) we revise prior training protocols by incorporating self-conditioning, which improves both likelihood and sample quality for embedding-space DLMs and behaves differently from its use in discrete diffusion. Putting everything together, LangFlow is competitive with top discrete DLMs on generative quality, reaching a generative perplexity of 92.3 on LM1B and 36.5 on OpenWebText. It also outperforms discrete counterparts on reasoning tasks like Sudoku. As the first continuous DLM shown to rival discrete diffusion in generative quality, LangFlow provides clear evidence that continuous diffusion is a promising paradigm for language modeling. Code: https://github.com/nealchen2003/LangFlow.

title: Introducing Vercel CI
description:
Coding agents are opening more pull requests than ever, and each one waits on CI before anyone can review or merge it. Most CI systems run the entire workflow on every push, even a one-line change. The more your agents push, the more time you spend waiting on CI.

Today, we're announcing Vercel CI in Beta. It runs only the tasks affected by your code change, and spins up only the compute those checks need, the same way Fluid compute scales with your traffic.

At Vercel, our CI now keeps up with our coding agents. Time from git push to "CI passed" is 2-6x faster than it was before.

How it works

Vercel CI uses Turborepo to understand your tasks and which ones depend on each other. It reads turbo.json, so if you're already using Turborepo, there's no separate CI config to write.

If you're not on Turborepo yet, add turbo.json and the turbo package. It works in single-package repos too.

Then tag the tasks you want Vercel CI to run.

"tags": ["ci"] is all you need to get started. No workflow YAML to maintain, no drift between your CI config and turbo.json, and Remote Cache is on by default.

When you or your agent push code, Vercel CI determines which tasks need to run based on the change. Tasks whose inputs haven't changed come from cache. The remaining tasks each run on their own machine, powered by Hive, Vercel's compute layer, and start as soon as their dependencies finish.

Vercel CI gives each task the compute it needs and nothing more.

Running your CI on Vercel

To get started, follow the documentation or prompt your agent from your repo:

Once set up, you or your agent can watch and inspect CI through the Vercel dashboard, Vercel CLI, or Vercel MCP. When something fails, go straight to the failing task, see what's blocked behind it, and open its logs, or search across recent runs to see whether a test has been flaky all week.

Vercel CI posts a check to your pull request on GitHub, so your existing branch protection rules can block merges on failure, the same way they do today.

Closing the loop

Vercel CI has already completed nearly 8 million tasks across our own repositories and the private beta, and we're just getting started. We're working to keep shrinking the time between writing code and running it in production.

As we work toward general availability, we plan to add:

  • Advanced observability

  • A vc ci CLI command for distributed execution before pushing code

  • More granular test selection

Vercel CI is available in Beta today on all plans. Read the docs and try it on your repository.

title: Large Language Model Deployment on Resource-Constrained Edge Devices: A Practitioners Survey
description:
arXiv:2611.09075v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed many areas of artificial intelligence (AI), but their substantial resource requirements limit their deployment on mobile and edge devices. Although LLMs have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various applications, the next challenge is deploying these models on resource-limited edge devices. Recent innovations in software optimizations and specialized hardware have made it feasible to deploy LLMs on edge devices. Edge deployment offers benefits including local data processing, cost savings, reduced latency, and personalized responses. This paper reviews the latest techniques that make the deployment of LLMs on edge devices feasible.

title: Jacobian-Causal Memory Control for Persistent Memory in Language Model Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.08779v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Persistent-memory systems choose not only which records are retrieved but which prior information can alter current inference. We propose Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), which represents each authorized memory intervention by a predicted influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space, selects interventions against a target effect and side-effect budget, and compares predicted with observed effects before retaining or rolling back the intervention. Under explicit smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, we prove a quadratic local-approximation bound, characterize the target effects reachable by a set of signatures, bound selection regret under signature error, and bound non-additive interactions between simultaneous memories. The paper reports no benchmark measurements; it defines a paired counterfactual estimator and an evaluation protocol comparing JCMC with relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match effect targeting, side-effect control, and rollback utility under equal model, memory, policy, and cost budgets.

title: Death to long-lived static credentials
description:
Fifteen years ago, TLS was something you'd use to protect the most sensitive areas of your app. Then Google, Let's Encrypt, the EFF, and others led the push for HTTPS everywhere, making encryption the default for every request. Without it, anyone between the browser and server can read and tamper with the traffic.

OAuth, OIDC, DBSC, and related standards already provide building blocks for secure authentication, but standards alone do not make secure methods the norm. HTTPS needed tooling that made encryption easy and a sustained push that made it expected. Machine-to-machine authentication still resembles HTTPS in 2010, with some vendors and enterprises leading the way while long-lived static credentials remain the default for many SaaS vendors and infrastructure providers.

At Vercel, we want to make fast and secure the default across the web, including in our own services and the integrations in our Marketplace. We’ve built OIDC UI, a shadcn/ui registry that gives providers trust-policy forms and token verification code. We’re expanding OIDC support across Vercel and setting new authentication requirements for Marketplace providers.

Long-lived static credentials are insecure

Long-lived static credentials are secrets such as API keys and database passwords that applications keep reusing, often with no expiration. As agents take on more useful work, we give them access to our systems, tools, and data through credentials that can grant permissions far beyond the task at hand.

Those credentials can leak into a code repository or chat, be stolen when a service or dependency is compromised, or be exposed when prompt injection leads an agent to reveal them. However it happens, an attacker can use the credential with the permissions it grants until it expires or is revoked. Recent credential-theft and supply-chain incidents across the industry show why encryption at rest isn’t enough when malicious code can read an application’s credentials in production.

Rotating exposed credentials takes time and coordination across the systems that use them, and mistakes can disrupt production. At Vercel, we’ve previously spent thousands of engineering hours on multiple, very painful key rotations out of an abundance of caution, and we never want to have to do this again.

Better solutions already exist

With OIDC, your application can authenticate without storing a long-lived provider key. A trusted issuer provides a signed, short-lived token identifying the application, and the receiving service verifies that token before deciding what access to grant.

A stolen token stops working when it expires, limiting how long that copy can be used even if the leak goes unnoticed. Your application can obtain fresh credentials programmatically, removing the need to distribute and manually rotate a persistent provider key across the systems that use it.

We’ve been prioritizing OIDC across Vercel so applications can access Blob, AI Gateway, and Sandbox without storing long-lived keys for those services. Our OIDC federation has been generally available since 2024, letting applications running on Vercel exchange Vercel-issued identity tokens for temporary AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure credentials under configured project and environment trust policies. But for developers to stop managing long-lived keys, that support has to extend to all the services their applications depend on.

The rest of the web hasn’t followed

We surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported secure authentication methods.

But getting vendors to support secure authentication is only part of the problem. Even when a service offers a secure method, developers often choose a static key because it can be simpler to use. We see three main barriers to broader adoption:

  • Tooling and setup that make secure authentication more complicated than using a static key.

  • Added latency from fetching or exchanging tokens on the request path.

  • Weak incentives for vendors to offer and prioritize secure authentication.

Our goal is to make secure authentication the default on Vercel, while also using our Marketplace to help push more vendors to support it.

Our commitment to a more secure web

We have a responsibility to make this change practical across the services we run, the tools developers use, and the integrations we build with partners.

Make secure authentication easier to use

Using a secure token has to be easier than pasting a key, or developers will keep pasting keys. On Vercel, code retrieves an OIDC token with a function call, and a custom audience specifies the service intended to receive it.

With Vercel Connect, applications and agents use their deployment identity to request provider tokens at runtime, without having to store long-lived provider secrets in environment variables. Once the connector is configured and linked to the project and the user’s account is connected, code can request a token for that user with scopes the provider supports.

We’re also extending OIDC support across the Vercel API and CLI to remove the need for long-lived Vercel tokens in deployment workflows.

OIDC UI for API providers

OIDC UI is a shadcn/ui component registry with a trust-policy configurator and a server-side token verifier. It includes provider forms for Vercel, GitHub, GitLab, Google, Bitbucket, AWS, Azure, and custom OIDC issuers. A provider can let customers configure trust for a particular Vercel project’s production environment, then verify incoming tokens against that policy without building the configuration interface and verification code from scratch.

Reduce the performance cost of secure authentication

A static key in an environment variable is already available when a function runs, so reading it requires no network request. Fetching a token or exchanging it for provider credentials can add network latency, so reducing those calls is part of making secure authentication practical.

Vercel Functions receive a platform-issued token in the request header, which the SDK reads without fetching another. The platform reuses unexpired tokens, while Vercel Connect caches provider tokens in process and refreshes them near expiry. Custom-audience and provider exchanges require network calls.

For example, an application can use the Azure SDK to access Cosmos DB with temporary credentials instead of a database key. With Azure configured to trust the Vercel project and its default token audience, the callback supplies a Vercel OIDC token to ClientAssertionCredential, which exchanges it for the Azure access token used by CosmosClient.

Give providers an incentive to support secure authentication

The Vercel Marketplace offers access to third-party databases, content management systems, observability tools, and more. Our goal is for all of these vendors to support short-lived, identity-based authentication, whether they accept OIDC tokens directly or exchange them for temporary credentials. We’re working to make integrations configure that authentication automatically when developers connect a service, so it does not require a separate setup step.

HTTPS everywhere did not win on ergonomics alone. Chrome put a “Not secure” label on plain HTTP, and then it set deadlines. Now we are setting ours. By November 30, 2026, vendors who do not support OIDC auth from Vercel to their services and use long-lived secrets for authentication will have a similar “Not secure” message on their listing. By January 2027, vendors who do not offer secure auth will be delisted. We are holding the Vercel API and our own native integrations to the same bar.

From static to dynamic

Fifteen years ago, encrypting every request felt like overkill. Today, the padlock is so normal that we only notice when it's missing. Secure authentication between services should become just as routine, so developers can connect the systems they need without storing another long-lived secret. Going from static to dynamic has always been the Vercel mission. It started with pages, and now it’s credentials.

Additional resources

  • OIDC federation covers how deployments get short-lived identity tokens, with guides for AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own API.

  • Custom OIDC token audiences scopes each token to the one service meant to receive it.

  • Vercel Connect requests short-lived, scoped provider tokens at runtime, so code and agents never store credentials.

  • Vercel Connect guides walk through building agents this way, from Slack bots to GitHub agents.

Read more

title: Updates to Hobby and Pro Terms of Service
description:
We are updating the Terms of Service for Hobby and Pro customers, effective October 19, 2026. The updates clarify some existing Vercel practices, expand terms on topics such as managed accounts and credits, and reflect applicable legal requirements, including certain cancellation and service-change rights for eligible consumers in the UK and EU.

Credits and billing

A new section sets out how credits work: plan-included credits expire at the end of the subscription term and purchased credits expire one year after purchase unless stated otherwise in the relevant credit purchase terms. Credits can only be used to pay Vercel fees, have no cash value, and are nontransferable. Credits are generally nonrefundable, but unused purchased credits are refunded if Vercel terminates your account without cause.

The Terms also clarify that credit purchases are billed in advance, subscriptions auto-renew unless you turn off renewal, and third-party pass-through rates may change when provider rates change. ⁠⁠

Managed accounts

The Terms now have a dedicated section for accounts that use a company email domain (e.g., work email), clarifying that the company can manage only the Projects you create inside its Team. We also clarified that if your company wishes to manage your account using your company work email, Vercel will now notify you first and give you a reasonable amount of time to move your personal content to an account with a different email address

Renewal and cancellation

You can turn off auto-renewal and cancel or downgrade through account settings or Support. Cancellation or downgrade generally takes effect at the start of the next renewal period. The Terms also explain statutory withdrawal and refund rights for eligible consumers.

Service changes

Eligible consumers in the UK and EU may cancel the affected subscription free of charge if a change has more than a minor negative impact on their access to or use of the Services. They have 30 days from notice or the change, whichever is later, and may receive a prorated refund of prepaid amounts for the remaining period.

Other updates

The service-specific provisions have been moved to a dedicated Service Terms page. The Terms also clarify sanctions-related obligations, including that use of the Services must not be in connection with or for the benefit of a sanctioned person under applicable laws.

Read the full Terms of Service and Service Terms for details.
