title: I checked the DMARC records of the top 10,000 domains. Only 61% enforce it
description:
Since 2024, Gmail and Yahoo have required bulk senders to publish a DMARC record. So I wanted to know how far the most popular domains on the internet have actually got. Do they publish DMARC? Do they enforce it, or just monitor? And how many have moved on to BIMI and MTA-STS?

On November 6, 2026 I looked up the public DNS records of the top 10,000 domains on the Tranco list, a research ranking of popular sites that is built to be hard to game. No email was sent and no website was fetched: these are only DNS lookups, the same ones any mail server makes.

The short version:

Of the 7,236 top domains that receive email Share
Publish a valid DMARC record 82.8%
Enforce it (p=quarantine or p=reject) 61.2%
Use p=reject 35.1%
Publish exactly one SPF record 92.7%
Publish a BIMI record 13.3%
Publish an MTA-STS record 4.0%

The rest of this post covers how the scan works, the parsing traps I hit, what stood out in the results, and how to check your own domain in a minute.

The method

The domains. The Tranco top 10,000 (list ID K9YYW, created November 5, 2026). One entry wasn't a valid hostname and was skipped.

The lookups. For each domain, six DNS queries:

Record Name queried What it tells you
MX example.com Whether the domain receives email at all
SPF TXT at example.com Which servers may send for it
DMARC TXT at _dmarc.example.com What receivers should do with mail that fails
BIMI TXT at default._bimi.example.com A brand logo for supporting inboxes
MTA-STS TXT at _mta-sts.example.com A policy asking senders to use verified TLS
TLS-RPT TXT at _smtp._tls.example.com Where to send TLS failure reports

The resolvers. Cloudflare (1.1.1.1) and Google (8.8.8.8), set explicitly so the result doesn't depend on my ISP's resolver.

The denominator. Percentages are of domains with at least one real MX record, because a DMARC policy matters most for domains that actually handle email. Of the 9,960 domains analysed, 7,236 have an MX record. The other 2,724 get their own section below.

Here is the core of the scanner, using only Node's built-in dns module:

import { Resolver } from "node:dns/promises";

const resolver = new Resolver({ timeout: 4000, tries: 3 });
resolver.setServers(["1.1.1.1", "8.8.8.8"]);

// "No such record" is an answer. A timeout or SERVFAIL is not.
const MISSING = new Set(["ENOTFOUND", "ENODATA"]);

async function lookup(kind, name) {
  try {
    const value = kind === "mx" ? await resolver.resolveMx(name) : await resolver.resolveTxt(name);
    return { ok: true, value };
  } catch (err) {
    if (MISSING.has(err.code)) return { ok: true, value: [] };
    return { ok: false, code: err.code };
  }
}

// A TXT record can be split into 255-byte strings. Join them before parsing.
const records = (txt, prefix) =>
  txt.map((chunks) => chunks.join("")).filter((t) => t.trim().toLowerCase().startsWith(prefix));

function tags(record) {
  const out = {};
  for (const part of record.split(";")) {
    const i = part.indexOf("=");
    if (i > 0) out[part.slice(0, i).trim().toLowerCase()] = part.slice(i + 1).trim();
  }
  return out;
}

async function scan(domain) {
  const [mx, apex, dmarc] = await Promise.all([
    lookup("mx", domain),
    lookup("txt", domain),
    lookup("txt", `_dmarc.${domain}`),
  ]);
  const failed = [mx, apex, dmarc].find((r) => !r.ok);
  if (failed) return { domain, err: failed.code }; // excluded, not counted as "missing"

  const spf = records(apex.value, "v=spf1");
  const dm = records(dmarc.value, "v=dmarc1");
  return {
    domain,
    mx: mx.value.length > 0,
    spfCount: spf.length,           // more than 1 = SPF permerror
    dmarcCount: dm.length,          // more than 1 = invalid
    policy: dm.length === 1 ? (tags(dm[0]).p || "").toLowerCase() : null,
  };
}

The full version adds BIMI, MTA-STS and TLS-RPT, RFC 7505 null MX detection and the SPF all qualifier. It runs 40 domains at a time and retries failures once at the end. All 10,000 domains took under four minutes.

Five traps worth knowing if you parse these records yourself

1. "No record" and "lookup failed" are different answers. ENOTFOUND and ENODATA mean the record doesn't exist. ESERVFAIL, EREFUSED and timeouts mean you don't know. If you count both as "no DMARC", you overstate how many domains lack it. 39 domains still failed after a retry (32 SERVFAIL, 6 FORMERR, 1 REFUSED), and I excluded them rather than guess.

2. TXT records come back in chunks. A long SPF or DMARC record is split into strings of up to 255 bytes, and resolveTxt returns each record as an array of those strings. Join them with no separator before parsing, or a long include: list gets cut in half.

3. More than one SPF record is not "extra SPF". RFC 7208 says a domain with two v=spf1 records gives a permanent error, so SPF fails for every email. 0.6% of the mail-receiving domains (46 domains) publish more than one.

4. A domain with no MX is not the same as one that refuses mail. An RFC 7505 "null MX" (0 .) states that a domain accepts no email. 74 domains in the list publish one. Most domains without email simply have no MX record at all.

5. Check your parser against a second source. I re-resolved a random sample of 40 domains through a third resolver (Quad9, 9.9.9.9), with a separate regex-based DMARC parser. The policy matched for all 40.

What the results show

Most top domains publish DMARC. Far fewer enforce it.

82.8% of mail-receiving domains publish a valid DMARC record, but the policy is where it gets interesting:

DMARC policy Share of mail-receiving domains
p=reject 35.1%
p=quarantine 26.1%
p=none 21.5%
No DMARC record 17.0%

p=none asks for reports but tells receivers to do nothing with failing mail, so an attacker can still put that domain in a From address. It's the right first step, and a lot of domains seem to have stayed on it.

The good news: 87.0% of domains with a DMARC record include a rua= address for aggregate reports, so most of them can see who is sending mail as their domain.

Bigger sites enforce more

Tranco rank Mail-receiving domains Enforcing DMARC p=reject
Top 100 65 75.4% 56.9%
101 to 1,000 623 74.8% 49.6%
1,001 to 10,000 6,548 59.8% 33.6%

That's 74.9% for the top 1,000 combined, against 59.8% for ranks 1,001 to 10,000. Since adoption drops the further down the list you go, it's probably lower again among the millions of domains that aren't in any top list.

SPF: an even split between strict and soft

Of the 6,710 mail-receiving domains with exactly one SPF record, 46.6% end it with -all (fail mail from unlisted servers) and 47.7% with ~all (soft fail). 2.1% use ?all, which tells receivers nothing, and 3 domains end with +all, which allows any server on the internet to send as them.

Top-level domains differ a lot

Among top-level domains with at least 100 mail-receiving domains in the list:

TLD Domains Valid DMARC Enforcing
.com 3,655 84.7% 66.0%
.ru 252 84.9% 68.7%
.org 364 83.2% 55.8%
.io 157 77.1% 56.1%
.de 166 86.1% 50.6%
.net 398 64.1% 42.0%
.jp 163 82.2% 39.3%
.edu 125 99.2% 62.4%

Nearly every .edu domain publishes DMARC, but more than a third of them (36.8%) stop at p=none. .jp is similar: a high adoption rate, with 42.9% on p=none.

Domains that send no email are the easiest to spoof

2,724 of the domains analysed have no MX record: CDNs, API hosts, asset domains, redirects. They don't send email, but that doesn't stop someone else from putting them in the From address of a phishing email.

The fix is two DNS records: an SPF record of v=spf1 -all and a DMARC record with p=reject. Only 16.4% of these domains have both.

BIMI and MTA-STS are still early

13.3% of mail-receiving domains publish a BIMI record, and 72.1% of those reference a mark certificate. MTA-STS (4.0%) and TLS-RPT (4.5%) are rare, even in the top 10,000.

Check your own domain in a minute 

D=example.com

dig +short MX $D                       # do you receive mail?
dig +short TXT $D | grep -i spf1       # exactly one line, please
dig +short TXT _dmarc.$D               # p=none, quarantine or reject?
dig +short TXT default._bimi.$D        # optional: BIMI
dig +short TXT _mta-sts.$D             # optional: MTA-STS

If you're not yet at p=reject, the usual path is:

  1. One SPF record that lists every service that sends for your domain.
  2. DKIM signing on your own domain, so it aligns with your From address.
  3. DMARC with p=none and a rua= address. Read the reports for a few weeks.
  4. When every legitimate sender passes, move to p=quarantine, then p=reject.
  5. For every domain you own that sends no email: v=spf1 -all and DMARC p=reject.

Limitations

  • It's one snapshot of public DNS from one location. Records change.
  • It checks records, not mail. It can't tell whether a domain's email actually passes, and DKIM keys can't be found without knowing each selector.
  • DMARC was read at the listed domain only. Subdomain policies (sp=) aren't analysed.
  • BIMI was checked at the default selector only, and MTA-STS policy files weren't fetched.
  • The top 10,000 are popular websites, not a random sample of all senders.

The full study, with every table, the methodology, a link for each finding and a CSV of the aggregate numbers, is on the Cresca site: DMARC adoption in 2026. Cresca is the email platform I'm building, and it walks you through SPF and DKIM for your own sending domain. If you'd like a breakdown I didn't include, ask in the comments and I'll run it against the same data.

title: Checking a whole palette for WCAG contrast in 20 lines of JavaScript
description:
Most of us check contrast one pair at a time: open the DevTools color picker on a paragraph, glance at the ratio, move on. That catches body text. It misses the pairs nobody inspects: the label on the primary button, the muted caption sitting on a card instead of the page, the outline of an input.

Here is the formula, a short script that checks every pair a palette actually uses, and what it found on two demo palettes I had lying around.

The formula

WCAG 2.2 defines contrast from relative luminance. Linearize each sRGB channel, weight them, then compare the lighter and darker color:

const lin = (c) => { c /= 255; return c <= 0.04045 ? c / 12.92 : ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4; };
const lum = ([r, g, b]) => 0.2126 * lin(r) + 0.7152 * lin(g) + 0.0722 * lin(b);
const hex = (h) => [1, 3, 5].map((i) => parseInt(h.slice(i, i + 2), 16));
const ratio = (a, b) => {
  const [x, y] = [lum(hex(a)), lum(hex(b))];
  return (Math.max(x, y) + 0.05) / (Math.min(x, y) + 0.05);
};

The thresholds you care about:

  • 4.5:1 for normal text (WCAG 1.4.3, level AA).
  • 3:1 for large text: 24px and up, or about 18.66px (14pt) bold and up.
  • 3:1 for the visual boundary of UI components, like an input's outline, when that boundary is what tells you the control is there (WCAG 1.4.11).

Check pairs, not colors

A palette is not "accessible" or "not accessible". Pairs are. So list the pairs your UI really draws:

const palette = {
  primary: '#8b5cf6', accent: '#34d399', background: '#0c0a14', surface: '#17141f',
  text: '#ece9f5', muted: '#9a94ad', border: '#2a2536',
};
const pairs = [
  ['text', 'background', 4.5], ['muted', 'background', 4.5], ['muted', 'surface', 4.5],
  ['#ffffff', 'primary', 4.5], ['primary', 'background', 4.5], ['border', 'background', 3],
];
const c = (k) => palette[k] || k;
for (const [fg, bg, min] of pairs) {
  const r = ratio(c(fg), c(bg));
  console.log(`${fg} on ${bg}: ${r.toFixed(2)} ${r >= min ? 'ok' : `FAIL (needs ${min})`}`);
}

That palette is from Afterhours, a fictional dark developer-tool site I use for demos. Output:

text on background: 16.41 ok
muted on background: 6.75 ok
muted on surface: 6.24 ok
#ffffff on primary: 4.23 FAIL (needs 4.5)
primary on background: 4.64 ok
border on background: 1.32 FAIL (needs 3)

Failure 1: white text on a violet button

#8b5cf6 is a popular violet (it's Tailwind v3's violet-500). White on it comes out at 4.23:1. That passes for large text but not for a normal 14 to 16px button label.

The surprising fix: the page's own near-black background, #0c0a14, on the same violet gives 4.64:1, which passes. Mid-tone colors often sit right in the zone where neither white nor black wins by much, so test both instead of defaulting to white. The other options are darkening the button a step, or making the label bold and large enough to count as large text.

Failure 2: hairline borders

The Afterhours border (#2a2536 on #0c0a14) is 1.32:1. A light palette I ran, Northwind (a fictional coffee shop), lands almost the same: #ead8c3 on #fffaf3 is 1.34:1.

For dividers between sections that's fine; they're decoration. For a text input whose only visible edge is that border, it fails 1.4.11. Either use a darker border for form controls than for dividers (two tokens, border and input, is exactly what shadcn/ui does), or give inputs a filled background that contrasts with the page.

Failure 3: the highlight color used as text

Northwind has an amber, #f59e0b, in its hero gradient. It's tempting to reuse it for a "new" badge or a highlighted price, but amber text on the cream background is 2.07:1, a clear fail. The same amber as a background with the dark text color on it is 7.59:1. Keep bright accent colors as fills, and put text on them, not the other way round.

One near miss worth knowing

Northwind's muted caption color, #7a6656, is 5.24:1 on the page background. Put the same caption on a card (#f6eadb) and it drops to 4.59:1. It still passes, barely. Surfaces are usually a little closer to your text colors than the page is, so a muted color that's tuned on the background alone can fail as soon as it lands on a card. Check muted on surface, every time.

Where the palette comes from

If you're auditing a site you didn't build, the hard part is getting the palette with roles in the first place: which hex is the button, which is the card. DevTools' CSS Overview panel (More tools > CSS Overview) lists every color and flags low-contrast text, which is a good free start.

I made a Chrome extension, Stylasso, that reads a page's palette with roles and shows each color's contrast against the background, so the pairs above come straight out of it. There's a short guide here: extract the colors from any website, with roles. The script above works fine without it.

Written with help from an AI assistant. Every ratio above was computed with the code in this post and checked against the extension's own output.

title: MemoryDojo: Benchmarking Poisoning Through LLM Agent Memory
description:
arXiv:2611.09721v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: LLM agents benefit from using memory systems to improve performance on long-horizon, multi-session tasks. However, memory introduces a critical attack surface. Malicious instructions encountered in one session may be stored and propagated through memory before being retrieved and acted upon in later sessions. Because memory systems differ in how they process and retrieve information, the downstream effects of poisoning can vary significantly across systems. To quantify the effects of poisoning across different memory architectures, we introduce MemoryDojo, a benchmark for tracing the lifecycle of poisoned information through agent memory and measuring its influence on subsequent agent behavior. MemoryDojo is easily extensible, consists of 155 multi-session long-horizon trajectories covering four domains, and supports five different memory systems. Through our evaluation, we find that all memory systems are susceptible to memory poisoning, with substantial variation in downstream effects. We further propose a memory-aware poison optimization process that increases the poisoning efficacy, highlighting differences between memory architectures. We hope that MemoryDojo will support research on understanding and mitigating agentic memory risks.

title: How to Rehearse GDPR Password Reset Email With Developer Report Attachments
description:
Keep password reset templates under application control, and rehearse their release alongside the generated report emails your developer tool already sends. The deciding constraint is template ownership: whoever can change the recovery link, recipient, or attachment behavior can change the security boundary, even if the sending service remains healthy.

Short answer: choose a transactional email service only after its template workflow passes a recovery rehearsal, its processing terms fit your GDPR obligations, and your application can distinguish an accepted send from a completed reset. Keep report attachments in a separate message. A password reset shouldn't become an excuse to distribute a generated report to someone whose control of the account is still being established.

This runbook uses a synthetic developer report and two locally rendered messages. It makes the content boundary executable before you connect a transport; the example doesn't claim that any particular service accepts raw MIME or supports an attachment field that hasn't been checked.

1. What page fired when the reset email looked healthy?

Start the postmortem with the page, not the dashboard. Was there a delivery failure, an exhausted recovery deadline, or merely a send request that the application accepted? Those observations describe different boundaries, and a green chart for one cannot establish the others. Before choosing a service, write down which observation should wake the responder and which evidence would let that responder stop investigating.

Ask what failed.

For this developer tool, the concrete job is sending a generated report as an email attachment, while the same account system also sends password reset links. That shared sender makes template ownership consequential: changing the report email must not silently add a report attachment to recovery mail, and changing a recovery template must not leak its link into a report. Treat these as separate content contracts even if one team maintains both.

The rehearsal uses a report with exactly 3 synthetic checks. That is fixture data, not a measured incident. Its purpose is to make an accidental attachment observable without using a customer report or a working recovery credential. A successful render establishes only what the renderer produced; delivery and successful account recovery still require their own evidence.

2. Choose the template owner before choosing the service

Application-owned templates make code review and content rollback part of the application's release process, at the cost of making that team responsible for rendering and maintenance. Provider-owned templates can move editing into a separate workflow, but then a template identifier alone is insufficient evidence of what a recipient received. Require a reviewable content revision and a way to restore the approved version. These are operational acceptance criteria, not claims that a particular vendor supplies every control.

Use the comparison as a procurement worksheet. Each candidate gets the same recovery fixture and report fixture; an unanswered question remains an unanswered question, rather than becoming a favorable checkbox. The documentation in References identifies the surfaces to inspect.

Candidate Template surface to evaluate Boundary to prove before selection
Amazon SES Its sending and template documentation Can your chosen sending workflow preserve application ownership, and can the responder identify the content revision associated with a send?
Twilio SendGrid Its dynamic transactional template documentation If editors own templates outside the application repository, how will approval and restoration of a specific revision work?
Postmark Its template API documentation Can your workflow tie each reviewed template change to the corresponding application release and recover the earlier content?

These are three real alternatives with different template surfaces to investigate. Prefer the candidate whose workflow your team can demonstrate and audit; a provider editing interface is useful only if its ownership model matches the people responsible for recovery. This worksheet isn't a measured ranking of delivery performance or a certification of anyone's GDPR compliance.

Infrai offers one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules; that single key and consolidated billing reduce credential handoffs and invoice reconciliation when report generation uses other backend capabilities. Its multi-vendor routing keeps a stable REST API contract while the vendor behind a capability changes, so switching providers does not require changing application code. The self-describing public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas without requiring a key, so the report-mail owner can inspect the declared inputs before handing credentials to an adapter developer; documented capabilities also include runnable examples in 10 languages, including Go, which gives that developer a concrete starting point for checking the mapping. That centralization also concentrates responsibility, so control access to the shared key.

The trade-off is operational: polling adds a tracking responsibility to the application. This is not a fit for a team whose recovery runbook requires pushed delivery events; evaluate Amazon SES, Twilio SendGrid, and Postmark against that requirement before selecting a service. Application-owned templates also require maintaining the renderer, whereas an externally edited template requires an additional approval and rollback workflow. Verify the attachment mapping separately before selecting a transport for report mail.

Keep legal review separate from the template demo. Document the processing purpose, privacy notice, consent management where applicable, and relevant processing arrangements before using real addresses. Don't turn a requested security email into marketing, and don't interpret a vendor's ability to send custom content as proof that your implementation complies with GDPR. Establish the appropriate legal basis for recovery mail rather than assuming that marketing consent governs every security message.

3. Build the content boundary as an offline rehearsal

Save the following as main.go and run it with go run main.go. It uses only the Go standard library, performs no network calls, and creates two email artifacts plus the generated report in a new temporary directory with owner-only permissions. The reset address and link are synthetic.

The program renders the recovery template as plain text and constructs a separate multipart message for the report attachment. These local structures are the application's contract, not a vendor request schema. When implementing the sending adapter, validate that provider's documented attachment and content inputs before mapping rendered content into a request. This distinction becomes important during incident review: an attachment that renders correctly in a local email artifact still needs a documented transport mapping, and neither the renderer nor the transport should quietly substitute another representation. If a service cannot demonstrate the required attachment workflow, choose a different service for report mail rather than changing the recovery template to carry the report. The two fixtures should survive that decision unchanged.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/base64"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "mime"
    "mime/multipart"
    "net/mail"
    "net/textproto"
    "os"
    "path/filepath"
    "strings"
    "text/template"
)

func main() {
    log.SetFlags(0)
    if err := rehearse(); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

func rehearse() error {
    const approved = "Recovery requested for {{.Account}}.\nOpen {{.Link}}\n"
    const candidate = "Account recovery for {{.Account}}.\nUse {{.Link}}\n"
    selected := candidate
    if os.Getenv("USE_APPROVED_TEMPLATE") == "1" {
        selected = approved
    }
    data := struct { Account, Link string }{
        Account: "fixture@example.invalid",
        Link: "https://example.invalid/reset?token=fixture-only",
    }
    t, err := template.New("reset").Option("missingkey=error").Parse(selected)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var content bytes.Buffer
    if err := t.Execute(&content, data); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    reset := "From: reports@example.invalid\r\n" +
        "To: fixture@example.invalid\r\n" +
        "Subject: Account recovery rehearsal\r\n" +
        "MIME-Version: 1.0\r\n" +
        "Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8\r\n\r\n" +
        strings.ReplaceAll(content.String(), "\n", "\r\n")

    report := []byte("check,result\ncompile,pass\nunit,pass\nlint,pass\n")
    var body bytes.Buffer
    writer := multipart.NewWriter(&body)
    header := make(textproto.MIMEHeader)
    header.Set("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8")
    part, err := writer.CreatePart(header)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if _, err := part.Write([]byte("Your synthetic developer report is attached.\r\n")); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    header = make(textproto.MIMEHeader)
    header.Set("Content-Type", "text/csv; charset=utf-8")
    header.Set("Content-Disposition", `attachment; filename="report.csv"`)
    header.Set("Content-Transfer-Encoding", "base64")
    part, err = writer.CreatePart(header)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if _, err := part.Write([]byte(base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(report))); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if err := writer.Close(); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    reportMail := "From: reports@example.invalid\r\n" +
        "To: fixture@example.invalid\r\n" +
        "Subject: Generated developer report\r\n" +
        "MIME-Version: 1.0\r\nContent-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary=" +
        writer.Boundary() + "\r\n\r\n" + body.String()

    message, err := mail.ReadMessage(strings.NewReader(reset))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    kind, _, err := mime.ParseMediaType(message.Header.Get("Content-Type"))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if kind != "text/plain" || strings.Contains(reset, "report.csv") {
        return fmt.Errorf("reset content boundary failed")
    }
    if !strings.Contains(reset, data.Link) || strings.Contains(reportMail, data.Link) {
        return fmt.Errorf("recovery link boundary failed")
    }
    dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "email-rehearsal-")
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    artifacts := map[string][]byte{
        "reset.eml": []byte(reset),
        "report.eml": []byte(reportMail),
        "report.csv": report,
    }
    for name, payload := range artifacts {
        if err := os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(dir, name), payload, 0600); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    fmt.Println("Content checks passed. Inspect artifacts in", dir)
    return nil
}

The useful trap is a shared attachment accumulator: a report send adds a file, the next recovery send inherits it, and both requests can still look successful from the sender's perspective. Separate message construction prevents that particular shape of mistake here. It doesn't establish that the attachment belongs to the intended recipient; authorization of a real generated report must happen before rendering.

No real tokens.

Before implementing the transport, inspect its declared contract. Save this separate program as preflight.go and run go run preflight.go. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the service's documented HTTPS origin, without a path. Public discovery requires no key; if INFRAI_API_KEY is present, the request uses Bearer authentication. This read-only check prints the manifest rather than inventing email attachment inputs. It makes no send request, and the HTTP client refuses redirects so credentials stay on the configured origin.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if err := preflight(); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

func preflight() error {
    base, err := url.Parse(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"))
    if err != nil || base == nil || base.Scheme != "https" ||
        base.Host == "" || base.User != nil ||
        (base.Path != "" && base.Path != "/") ||
        base.RawQuery != "" || base.Fragment != "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the documented HTTPS origin")
    }
    base.Path = "/v1/discovery"
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 10 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", base.String(), nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 8<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 40 {
                    return fmt.Errorf("retry deferred beyond preflight time budget")
                }
                if requested := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if requested := time.Until(deadline); requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

The 3-attempt limit and 45-second deadline are local runbook choices, not service limits or measured response times. Use the manifest's path and schema to implement the sending adapter only after its attachment contract is confirmed. A successful discovery request proves access to metadata; it says nothing about delivery.

4. Verify the artifact and rehearse the rollback

Inspect reset.eml as a message: its body must contain the synthetic recovery link, its content type must be plain text, and it must carry no attachment. Open report.eml with a MIME-aware mail reader, decode report.csv, and compare its contents with the generated CSV. Expect exactly the compile, unit, and lint rows. The program checks the recovery content boundary automatically; the decoded-attachment comparison is a separate acceptance step, because a successful string check cannot prove that a mail client will interpret a MIME message as intended.

Then set USE_APPROVED_TEMPLATE to 1 in your environment and run the same program again. The recovery wording should revert to “Recovery requested,” while the report rows and attachment filename stay the same. Compare decoded content, not entire message bytes: the multipart writer generates a boundary for each message, so byte-for-byte equality is the wrong rollback criterion. This is a local content rollback rehearsal, not a claim that reverting a template retracts messages already sent.

For a transport trial, use controlled recipients and record the template revision, application operation identifier, and provider message identifier without recording recovery tokens or report contents. Treat send acceptance, delivery evidence, and completion of recovery as separate observations. Define the page around a missed recovery objective and the evidence needed to diagnose it; a dashboard showing accepted requests cannot answer whether the recipient recovered access. Check SPF authorization separately using RFC 7208 as the protocol reference. Sender authorization doesn't certify GDPR compliance or prove inbox placement.

If verification fails, stop the candidate template rollout, restore the approved content revision, and preserve the failed synthetic artifacts for review. Decide which queued operations are still valid before releasing them again; replaying a queue indiscriminately can redistribute an attachment or repeat a recovery message. Require an application operation identifier and a documented deduplication strategy before enabling write retries in the sending adapter.

Keep the rollback narrow. A report attachment failure should not force a change to the recovery template, and restoring recovery wording should not silently change which report a recipient receives. The service earns its place when the team can demonstrate those boundaries under the selected template ownership model, with processing terms reviewed and an observation that tells the responder what actually happened.

References

  • Amazon SES sending email: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/send-email.html
  • Amazon SES personalized templates: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/send-personalized-email-api.html
  • Twilio SendGrid dynamic transactional templates: https://www.twilio.com/docs/sendgrid/ui/sending-email/how-to-send-an-email-with-dynamic-templates
  • Postmark template API: https://postmarkapp.com/developer/api/templates-api
  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • General Data Protection Regulation: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng

title: EUDI Wallet Verifier in Spring Boot: OpenID4VP, SD-JWT VC
description:
To accept an EU Digital Identity Wallet in Spring Boot, you build a verifier service that sends a signed OpenID4VP request, receives the SD-JWT VC presentation on a direct_post endpoint, and then checks the issuer signature, key binding, trust list and revocation status before returning a minimal yes or no.

Member states have to make a Digital Identity Wallet available to their citizens by the end of 2026. The duty to accept those wallets falls on relying parties in 2027, and payment providers and banks are named in that group through strong customer authentication and KYC rules, the same regulated corner I covered in my PSD2 and EU banking API guide. If your onboarding team still has wallet acceptance parked under "later", the calendar has stopped agreeing with that.

I spent a few weeks building a verifier in Spring Boot to find out what accepting a wallet credential costs an engineering team in practice. What follows is the wiring: how the request leaves, what comes back, which checks are mandatory, and where the specs leave the decision to you. There is no policy discussion here; the regulation is public. The one thing I will show that bit me is the iss and aud handling in the key binding check, because the verifier URL that looks right in a test environment is not necessarily the string a wallet signs over in production.

How I frame the verifier

A relying-party verifier is a small service that does four things in a row:

  1. Builds an authorization request that names the credential type and the exact attributes you want.
  2. Gets that request in front of a wallet, through a QR code on desktop or a deep link on a phone.
  3. Accepts the presentation the wallet posts back.
  4. Makes a deterministic accept-or-reject decision and writes down why.

The exchange runs on OpenID for Verifiable Presentations (OpenID4VP) and the credential format is SD-JWT VC. The wallet obtained its credential earlier through OpenID4VCI. You never speak OID4VCI as a verifier, but every field you validate was written at issuance by somebody else, so you have to know what that process produced.

Coming from payments, I treat it like a card-acquiring path with no stored cardholder data. It keeps no accounts and no copies of identity documents. A signed claim goes in, signatures and signers are checked, validity is checked, and a minimal result comes out. That shapes the architecture: short-lived sessions, almost no state, an audit trail, and no customer data store.

The flow end to end 

Browser/App        Verifier (Spring Boot)         Wallet            Issuer / Trust infra
    | start KYC           |                          |                      |
    |-------------------->| create session+nonce     |                      |
    |   QR / deep link    | sign request object      |                      |
    |<--------------------|                          |                      |
    |---- open link ------------------------------->|                      |
    |                     |<-- fetch request object--|                      |
    |                     |--- signed JWT ---------->| user consents        |
    |                     |<-- direct_post (vp_token)|                      |
    |                     | verify issuer sig, KB-JWT, nonce               |
    |                     |-- trust list lookup ---------------------------->|
    |                     |-- status list fetch ---------------------------->|
    |<-- result (poll/SSE)|                          |                      |

Two points catch people out. The phone running the wallet is not the browser that showed the QR code, so the answer cannot return through the browser. The wallet calls your backend directly (response_mode=direct_post, or direct_post.jwt when the body is encrypted), and the front end has to poll or subscribe for the result. And the request object is itself signed, so the wallet can check who is asking before the user sees a consent screen. Authentication runs in both directions.

Step one: ask for the smallest set of claims

The query language in OpenID4VP is DCQL, which lets you list credentials and claim paths you need. Selective disclosure is only useful if the verifier actually asks narrowly, and I resist the "request everything, we may need it later" instinct from product teams.

For a standard onboarding journey you usually need legal name and date of birth, and sometimes nationality or country of residence for sanctions screening and jurisdiction rules. Address and document numbers are separate decisions. Every extra attribute lands in your logs, backups and breach-notification scope, which is the practical meaning of data minimisation.

Minimal does not mean minimal at any price. KYC duties under AML rules usually require identifying the customer, verifying identity and, for many products, capturing date of birth and an address, so an over-18 assertion on its own is typically enough for age-gated services but not for opening a regulated account. Whether a given bank can onboard on fewer attributes is a question for its compliance function and its supervisor, not a default I can hand you. What I did was encode that decision as data: one profile per journey, each reviewed by compliance before it ships.

Here is the request builder with all helpers shown, so nothing is hidden. The session record keeps the nonce and the query and never any user data.

@Service
public class PresentationRequestService {

    private static final SecureRandom RANDOM = new SecureRandom();

    private final SessionStore sessions;           // Redis-backed, TTL 5 minutes
    private final RequestObjectSigner signer;      // signs with the key behind our x509 cert
    private final VerifierProperties props;

    public PresentationRequestService(SessionStore sessions,
                                      RequestObjectSigner signer,
                                      VerifierProperties props) {
        this.sessions = sessions;
        this.signer = signer;
        this.props = props;
    }

    public StartedSession start(KycProfile profile) {
        String sessionId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        String nonce = randomUrlSafe(32);
        String clientId = "x509_san_dns:" + props.hostname();

        Map<String, Object> dcql = Map.of(
            "credentials", List.of(Map.of(
                "id", "pid",
                "format", "dc+sd-jwt",
                "meta", Map.of("vct_values", List.of(props.pidVct())),
                "claims", profile.requiredPaths().stream()
                    .map(p -> Map.of("path", p))
                    .toList()
            ))
        );

        Map<String, Object> requestObject = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        requestObject.put("response_type", "vp_token");
        requestObject.put("client_id", clientId);
        requestObject.put("response_mode", "direct_post.jwt");
        requestObject.put("response_uri", props.baseUrl() + "/oid4vp/response/" + sessionId);
        requestObject.put("nonce", nonce);
        requestObject.put("dcql_query", dcql);
        requestObject.put("state", sessionId);

        sessions.save(new VerifierSession(sessionId, nonce, clientId, profile.name(),
                profile.requiredPaths(), Instant.now()));

        String jwt = signer.sign(requestObject);
        sessions.saveRequestJwt(sessionId, jwt);

        String link = "openid4vp://authorize?client_id=" + enc(clientId)
                + "&request_uri=" + enc(props.baseUrl() + "/oid4vp/request/" + sessionId);
        return new StartedSession(sessionId, link);
    }

    private static String randomUrlSafe(int bytes) {
        byte[] buf = new byte[bytes];
        RANDOM.nextBytes(buf);
        return Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(buf);
    }

    private static String enc(String v) {
        return URLEncoder.encode(v, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    }
}

KycProfile.requiredPaths() returns something like [["family_name"], ["given_name"], ["birthdate"], ["nationality"]], since DCQL claim paths are arrays of path segments. Profiles live in versioned configuration, one for basic onboarding and one for higher-risk accounts. The profile name goes onto the session so an audit can show exactly which minimisation decision applied. A request profile is a compliance artifact: it sits in Git and goes through review.

Pay attention to the client_id prefix, and note that I now store the full prefixed value on the session. That is the detail behind my earlier remark. The wallet signs the key binding over the client_id exactly as it appeared in the request, prefix included. My first version compared the audience to the bare hostname, which is what I had in configuration, and the check was wrong for every real presentation. Keeping the prefixed string on the session removes the guesswork.

The identity itself comes from an X.509 certificate chain (a relying party access certificate) in the request object's header, and the client_id has to match a DNS name in its SAN. A registrar-linked authority in your member state issues that certificate, and it is why a wallet can show "Acme Payments is asking for these three attributes" instead of a bare URL.

One operational note from the signing side: the request-object key should not sit as a PEM on disk. I put it behind a PKCS#11 interface so the same RequestObjectSigner works against a software keystore in dev and an HSM in production, and signing latency stays a rounding error next to the user's consent tap.

Step two: receiving the presentation

The wallet calls your response_uri with a vp_token. With direct_post.jwt the whole response is a JWE encrypted to a key you published in the request, so a proxy or WAF log in between cannot leak the credential.

The controller stays deliberately thin. Validation belongs in a service you can unit test with fixture credentials.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/oid4vp")
public class ResponseController {

    private final ResponseDecryptor decryptor;
    private final SdJwtVcVerifier verifier;
    private final SessionStore sessions;
    private final VerificationAudit audit;

    // constructor omitted

    @PostMapping(value = "/response/{sessionId}",
                 consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_FORM_URLENCODED_VALUE)
    public ResponseEntity<Map<String, String>> receive(@PathVariable String sessionId,
                                                       @RequestParam("response") String jwe) {
        VerifierSession session = sessions.consume(sessionId)   // single use, atomic
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.GONE));

        VerificationOutcome outcome;
        try {
            Map<String, Object> payload = decryptor.decrypt(jwe);
            String vpToken = extractPresentation(payload, "pid");
            outcome = verifier.verify(vpToken, session);
        } catch (VerificationException e) {
            outcome = VerificationOutcome.rejected(e.reason());
        }

        audit.record(session, outcome);
        sessions.storeOutcome(sessionId, outcome.minimised());
        return ResponseEntity.ok(Map.of());   // wallet only needs a 200
    }
}

sessions.consume has to be an atomic get-and-delete, implemented with Redis GETDEL. A wallet that retries after a network timeout, or an attacker replaying a captured response, must hit a 410 before any cryptography runs. This is the same idempotency thinking I described in transactional outbox and idempotent consumers for payment systems, applied to identity instead of payments.

That design has a cost worth naming. If the wallet's first attempt reaches you, you consume the session, and then the response is lost on the way back, the retry gets 410 and the user must restart. I accepted that: a restart costs the user one more scan, while a reusable session costs you a replay window. The related race is the TTL. With a five-minute TTL and a slow user on a bad connection, the session can expire between the wallet fetching the request object and posting the answer. I treat that as a normal outcome, return a distinct "expired" reason, and let the front end offer a fresh QR.

Step three: what an SD-JWT VC actually contains

A presentation is a tilde-separated string: the issuer-signed JWT, then zero or more disclosures, then a final key binding JWT (KB-JWT). A disclosure is a base64url-encoded array [salt, claim_name, claim_value]. The issuer JWT holds no values for hidden claims; it holds only _sd, a list of digests. When the user shares family_name, the wallet appends the matching disclosure, and you hash it and confirm the digest appears in _sd.

So you cannot decode the JWT and read the claims. A reader that skips the disclosure step sees an almost empty payload, and a sloppy one might accept it.

My checks, in order, with the reason for each:

  1. Parse strictly. Reject disclosures that match no digest, duplicate digests, and disclosures for claims you never asked for. An unrequested claim is not a free bonus. It means data is arriving outside your declared purpose.
  2. Validate the chain from the x5c header to a trust anchor taken from the EU trusted lists (below).
  3. Verify the issuer signature with the leaf certificate's key.
  4. Check vct against what you requested and exp/nbf against the clock, with a small skew allowance.
  5. Verify the KB-JWT. Its signature must verify under the key in the credential's cnf claim, and it must carry your nonce, your prefixed client_id as aud, a fresh iat, and an sd_hash over the exact presentation string you received.
  6. Check revocation status.

Step 5 proves the person holding the phone is the holder the credential was issued to. Skip it and a leaked SD-JWT becomes a bearer token for someone else's identity.

@Component
public class SdJwtVcVerifier {

    private static final Duration CLOCK_SKEW = Duration.ofSeconds(60);

    private final TrustAnchorProvider anchors;
    private final StatusListClient statusClient;
    private final KeyBindingVerifier keyBinding;
    private final Clock clock;

    public VerificationOutcome verify(String presentation, VerifierSession session)
            throws VerificationException {

        SdJwtPresentation p = SdJwtPresentation.parse(presentation);   // splits on '~'

        SignedJWT issuerJwt = p.issuerSigned();
        List<X509Certificate> chain = X5cChain.from(issuerJwt.getHeader());
        anchors.validate(chain);                                       // PKIX against trust list

        try {
            if (!issuerJwt.verify(new ECDSAVerifier((ECPublicKey) chain.get(0).getPublicKey()))) {
                throw new VerificationException("issuer-signature");
            }

            JWTClaimsSet claims = issuerJwt.getJWTClaimsSet();
            Instant now = clock.instant();
            Date exp = claims.getExpirationTime();
            if (exp == null || exp.toInstant().isBefore(now.minus(CLOCK_SKEW))) {
                throw new VerificationException("expired");
            }
            Date nbf = claims.getNotBeforeTime();
            if (nbf != null && nbf.toInstant().isAfter(now.plus(CLOCK_SKEW))) {
                throw new VerificationException("not-yet-valid");
            }

            Map<String, Object> disclosed = p.resolveDisclosures(claims);   // checks every digest
            if (!session.requiredClaimNames().containsAll(disclosed.keySet())) {
                throw new VerificationException("unrequested-claims");
            }

            Map<String, Object> cnf = claims.getJSONObjectClaim("cnf");
            JWK holderKey = JWK.parse((Map<String, Object>) cnf.get("jwk"));
            SignedJWT kb = p.keyBinding()
                    .orElseThrow(() -> new VerificationException("no-key-binding"));
            keyBinding.verify(kb, holderKey, session, p.presentationForHash(), now);

            statusClient.assertValid(claims.getJSONObjectClaim("status"), chain.get(0));

            return VerificationOutcome.accepted(disclosed,
                    chain.get(0).getSubjectX500Principal().getName());
        } catch (ParseException | JOSEException e) {
            throw new VerificationException("malformed");
        }
    }
}

And the key binding check itself, which is the part I would not leave to a library you have not read:

@Component
public class KeyBindingVerifier {

    private static final Duration MAX_AGE = Duration.ofMinutes(5);
    private static final Duration SKEW = Duration.ofSeconds(60);

    void verify(SignedJWT kb, JWK holderKey, VerifierSession session,
                String presentationForHash, Instant now)
            throws VerificationException, JOSEException, ParseException {

        if (!"kb+jwt".equals(kb.getHeader().getType() == null ? null : kb.getHeader().getType().getType())) {
            throw new VerificationException("kb-typ");
        }
        if (!kb.verify(new ECDSAVerifier(holderKey.toECKey()))) {
            throw new VerificationException("kb-signature");
        }

        JWTClaimsSet c = kb.getJWTClaimsSet();

        // aud must equal the client_id exactly as sent, scheme prefix included
        if (c.getAudience() == null || !c.getAudience().contains(session.clientId())) {
            throw new VerificationException("kb-aud");
        }
        if (!session.nonce().equals(c.getStringClaim("nonce"))) {
            throw new VerificationException("kb-nonce");
        }

        Instant iat = c.getIssueTime() == null ? null : c.getIssueTime().toInstant();
        if (iat == null || iat.isAfter(now.plus(SKEW)) || iat.isBefore(now.minus(MAX_AGE))) {
            throw new VerificationException("kb-iat");
        }

        // sd_hash covers everything up to and including the last '~' before the KB-JWT
        String expected = Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(
                MessageDigestUtil.sha256(presentationForHash.getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII)));
        if (!MessageDigest.isEqual(expected.getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII),
                String.valueOf(c.getClaim("sd_hash")).getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII))) {
            throw new VerificationException("kb-sd-hash");
        }
    }
}

On clock skew: a phone clock that is two minutes off is not exotic, and the iat window is where it shows up first. I kept the skew at a minute and the maximum age at five, which matches the session TTL, rather than widening either to make a bad device clock pass.

I use Nimbus JOSE + JWT for signatures since Spring Security usually brings it along already. The SD-JWT parsing, digest checking and key binding I wrote myself, a few hundred lines in total. Libraries exist, including the EU reference implementations, and for production I would evaluate one, but writing it once showed me the sharp edges, and the spec's test vectors keep you honest.

Step four: the trust list question

Tutorials tend to skip this, and it is where the "EU" in EUDI becomes an engineering problem. A valid signature only proves somebody holding a private key signed the credential. What you need to know is whether that somebody is an authorised issuer of the credential type you are accepting.

That answer lives in the EU trusted lists. Each member state publishes a signed trusted list (ETSI TS 119 612 XML), and the European Commission publishes a list of lists (LOTL) pointing at them. The verifier must fetch the LOTL, check its signature against pinned signing certificates, follow the pointers to the national lists, check each of those, extract the service entries for the relevant provider types, and turn them into trust anchors for PKIX path validation.

I keep that work entirely out of the request path, in a scheduled loader:

@Component
public class TrustAnchorProvider {

    private final AtomicReference<TrustSnapshot> current =
            new AtomicReference<>(TrustSnapshot.empty());
    private final TrustListFetcher fetcher;

    @Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "PT1H", initialDelay = 0)
    void refresh() {
        try {
            TrustSnapshot next = fetcher.fetchAndValidate();   // LOTL -> national lists -> anchors
            if (next.anchorCount() < current.get().anchorCount() / 2
                    && current.get().anchorCount() > 0) {
                log.error("Trust snapshot shrank from {} to {} anchors, keeping previous",
                        current.get().anchorCount(), next.anchorCount());
                return;
            }
            current.set(next);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            log.warn("Trust list refresh failed, serving snapshot {}", current.get().version(), e);
        }
    }

    public void validate(List<X509Certificate> chain) throws VerificationException {
        TrustSnapshot snap = current.get();
        if (snap.isStale(Duration.ofHours(48))) {
            throw new VerificationException("trust-snapshot-stale");
        }
        snap.pkixValidate(chain);
    }
}

The fetcher is where the real effort goes. Each list carries a NextUpdate timestamp and I honour it, so the hourly job usually re-checks and finds nothing new. Cert path validation is done with the JDK's PKIXParameters against the anchor set, revocation checking off for the chain itself because the trust list is the authority, and with the validation time taken from the injected Clock so tests can replay a past date. The signature on each national list is verified before a single entry is parsed. A list that fails its signature is dropped and the previous snapshot of that member state stays in place, rather than the whole refresh failing.

Three decisions are visible in the snippet. Request handling reads an in-memory snapshot and never touches the network, so a slow national server cannot hold up onboarding. A refresh that loses more than half the anchors is rejected and alerted on, since a parser bug or a truncated download should not quietly un-trust a country. And a snapshot older than 48 hours fails closed, because accepting credentials against a trust view you cannot vouch for is the wrong failure direction for a regulated firm.

I also store the snapshot version in each audit record. When a regulator or your fraud team asks why you accepted a credential on a particular date, you can answer with the exact trust data you held at that moment.

Step five: revocation without a privacy leak

Credentials get revoked: a lost phone, a corrected record, an expired residence permit. SD-JWT VC handles this through status references, typically a Token Status List. The credential holds a status claim with a list URI and an index. The list is a compressed bit array signed by the issuer, and you check the bit at your index.

The privacy argument is easy to miss. The list is public and covers a large population, so fetching it tells the issuer nothing about which person you are verifying. That is the point of preferring it to a per-credential online status call.

In practice you cache and respect the list's own time-to-live:

@Component
public class StatusListClient {

    private final RestClient http;
    private final OutboundHostPolicy hostPolicy;
    private final Cache<String, StatusList> cache = Caffeine.newBuilder()
            .maximumSize(500)
            .expireAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
            .build();

    public void assertValid(JSONObject statusClaim, X509Certificate issuerCert)
            throws VerificationException {
        if (statusClaim == null) {
            return;   // credential type may legitimately carry no status; policy decides
        }
        JSONObject ref = (JSONObject) statusClaim.get("status_list");
        String uri = (String) ref.get("uri");
        int idx = ((Number) ref.get("idx")).intValue();

        hostPolicy.assertAllowed(uri, issuerCert);   // allow-list before any network call

        StatusList list = cache.get(uri, this::download);   // list signature checked on parse
        if (list.statusAt(idx) != 0) {
            throw new VerificationException("credential-revoked-or-suspended");
        }
    }

    private StatusList download(String uri) {
        byte[] body = http.get().uri(uri).accept(MediaType.valueOf("application/statuslist+jwt"))
                .retrieve().body(byte[].class);
        return StatusList.parseAndVerify(body);
    }
}

Two cautions. The URI comes from inside the credential, so someone who builds a credential, even one that will fail signature verification later, can try to aim your service at an internal address. I verify the chain before fetching anything and limit outbound hosts to an allow-list derived from the issuer's trust list entry. This is the SSRF class of bug discussed in the Spring Boot 4.1 SSRF mitigation write-up. The order matters: never make a network call on the strength of unverified input.

The second is policy rather than code: what happens if the status list cannot be reached? For onboarding to a payment product I fail closed with a short retry, since KYC is a point-in-time control and a retry costs a customer half a minute. For a login-style re-authentication, living with a cached list for longer is a defensible choice.

What the audit record should hold

Compliance will want to know what you checked. I persist the session ID, the request profile name and version, the requested claim paths, the issuer certificate subject, the trust snapshot version, the status list URI with the fetch timestamp, and the outcome with its rejection reason. What I do not persist is the raw presentation, or any claim not required downstream.

The onboarding service downstream sees only the minimised outcome: the claims it asked for and a verification record ID. If your KYC provider needs a date of birth, it gets a date of birth, and the raw credential never leaves the verifier. The same instinct shaped how I handle evidence in DORA and NIS2 policy-as-code on Spring Boot: make evidence a by-product of the control, not a document someone assembles later.

Operating it for real

Some observations from building and load-testing this, informed by years of running trading and market-data systems where verification latency is directly visible:

  • Cost per verification is small. Two EC signature checks (issuer and key binding) plus a chain validation against in-memory anchors. On modest hardware the cryptography is not the bottleneck; the human at the consent screen is. Virtual threads suit the occasional blocking status fetch, and I covered the production details in Java virtual threads in Spring Boot.
  • Trace everything, log little. Carry a trace ID through request creation, response receipt and outcome delivery, and keep claim values out of spans and logs. Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry is where I configured attribute filters for exactly this, and the same discipline applies to observability guardrails for agentic AI backends.
  • Test against more than one wallet. Implementations are still maturing, and I saw differences in how they encode claim paths, pick the key for direct_post.jwt and handle optional claims. Build integration tests around recorded real-wallet responses, not just your own generator, and note that a generator you wrote will agree with your own misreadings of the spec.
  • Keep format support narrow. ISO mdoc credentials (mobile driving licences above all) are also in the ecosystem. Start with SD-JWT VC for the PID, ship, and add mdoc as a second adapter behind the same verify interface when a concrete requirement appears.
  • Plan the unglamorous fallback. Many customers will not have a wallet in year one. Keep the wallet route beside your existing document-and-selfie flow, and have KYC orchestration treat "wallet verified" as one strong signal among several.

Where the standards still bite

This is not settled. DCQL details, status list drafts, and each member state's final attribute and certificate profile are all still moving. The sensible answer is isolation: my verifier exposes a narrow internal interface (start(profile), outcome(sessionId)), and everything protocol-specific sits behind it. When a draft changes I edit one module instead of the onboarding service.

There is also a real build-versus-buy question. A hosted verifier gets you moving sooner and carries someone else's maintenance load. Building gives you control over the trust snapshot, the audit trail and exact data flows, which for a regulated payments company can be the whole argument. Having co-founded a startup that was acquired (I wrote up what that taught me) and built payment-adjacent APIs for OpenBanking PSD2, my bias is to own the decision logic and the evidence, and to rent the commodity parts if you have to.

If you are weighing this for your team, my background across AirAsia-scale platforms (see building microservices at 130 million requests per day) and regulated fintech is on the experience section of this site, and you can reach me via contact if you want to compare notes.

A starting checklist for this quarter

Before the 2027 acceptance obligations bite, I would work in this order:

  1. Pick one onboarding journey and write down the minimum attribute set it needs, agreed with compliance. Turn it into a versioned DCQL profile.
  2. Stand up a verifier against a reference or test wallet environment, with the single-use session store and signed request objects.
  3. Implement strict SD-JWT parsing, including unrequested-claim rejection and key binding.
  4. Build the trust list loader as a background job with stale-snapshot protection.
  5. Add status list checking with an explicit fail-closed policy and an outbound host allow-list.
  6. Write the audit record and review it with your compliance and data protection people before any real user touches it.

Related Articles

  • Open Banking PSD2 API development
  • DORA and NIS2 policy-as-code with Spring Boot and Kubernetes
  • Transactional outbox and idempotent consumers for payment systems

This week, take the one KYC journey you would move to wallets first, write its minimum attribute list as a DCQL query in a Git-tracked file, and run that query against a test wallet to see which claims come back.

FAQ

What is an EUDI Wallet verifier?

An EUDI Wallet verifier is the relying-party service that requests a credential from an EU Digital Identity Wallet, receives the presentation over OpenID4VP, and validates the signatures, trust chain, key binding and revocation status. It returns a minimal outcome to your onboarding system and stores no identity documents.

Do I need to implement OpenID4VCI to accept wallet credentials?

No. OpenID4VCI is the issuance protocol used between the issuer and the wallet. As a verifier you only speak OpenID4VP, but you need to understand what issuance produced, because the claims, x5c chain and status reference you validate were all set at issuance.

How does selective disclosure work in SD-JWT VC?

The issuer-signed JWT carries only _sd digests of the hidden claims. The wallet sends a disclosure ([salt, claim_name, claim_value]) for each claim the user agrees to share, and the verifier recomputes the SHA-256 digest and checks that it appears in _sd. Any disclosure that matches no digest, or that you did not request, should be rejected.

How do I check whether a wallet credential has been revoked?

Read the status claim, fetch the signed Token Status List from the URI it points to, and check the bit at the credential's index. Cache the list according to its time-to-live, verify its signature before use, restrict outbound hosts to an allow-list, and decide up front whether you fail open or closed when the list is unreachable.

title: How R6 Stat Trackers Compute K/D and Win Rate (And Why Two Sites Disagree)
description:
Stat trackers for Rainbow Six Siege look like simple profile pages: a rank, a K/D, a win rate, maybe a list of operators. Under the hood they have to agree with Ubisoft's ranked data, survive rate limits, handle divide-by-zero, and pick a win-rate denominator that two honest engineers can still argue about.

This post walks through those choices, using how the numbers are calculated on SiegeRadar as a public example. SiegeRadar is a free unofficial tracker, not affiliated with Ubisoft. The same questions show up in any similar app. For the game itself, see Ubisoft's official Rainbow Six Siege site and the Wikipedia article.

The three formulas that actually matter

Most of a player card reduces to three ratios.

K/D is kills / deaths, rounded to two decimals. The interesting branch is zero deaths. Returning Infinity, NaN or a blank cell makes a profile look broken. A clean rule is: if deaths are zero, return the kill count (so 12 kills and 0 deaths display as 12.00). It stays a real number you can sort.

Headshot percentage is headshots / kills. Guard the case where headshots exceed kills — that is almost always a data error, not a player feat — and do not compute a percentage from zero kills.

Win rate is where trackers quietly diverge. There are two legitimate denominators:

  • Current ranked season card: wins / (wins + losses)
  • Lifetime totals, per-mode figures and past seasons: wins / matches_played

Those two are not always equal. "Matches played" can include results that are not a clean win or loss in the ranked board you just typed in. If one site shows 61.0% and another shows 60.4% for the same account, check the denominator before you assume either is wrong.

In Python, the core is small enough to keep on one screen:

from typing import Optional

def kd(kills: int, deaths: int) -> float:
    if deaths == 0:
        return float(kills)
    return round(kills / deaths, 2)

def win_rate_season(wins: int, losses: int) -> Optional[float]:
    denom = wins + losses
    if denom == 0:
        return None  # render as a dash, not 0.0
    return round(wins / denom * 100, 1)

def win_rate_lifetime(wins: int, matches: int) -> Optional[float]:
    if matches == 0:
        return None
    return round(wins / matches * 100, 1)

Returning None (and showing a dash) when there is no sample is better than showing 0.0%, which readers will treat as a real losing record.

Where the data comes from, and how stale it is allowed to be

A tracker is not the game client. It asks a ranked-data API, caches the answer and renders a page. SiegeRadar's public description is that player profiles, operator stats, leaderboards and live player counts come from the Arenyze API, which serves Ubisoft's ranked data. The response is cached so the next view inside the window does not hit the source again.

Freshness is a product decision as much as a systems one. Refresh too often and you burn a data budget; refresh too rarely and a player who just finished a match thinks the site is broken. One working set of windows looks like this:

  • Player profiles: at most every 15 minutes
  • Operator stats: every 30 minutes (season-level operator stats every 6 hours)
  • Leaderboards: every 3 hours
  • Live player counts: every hour
  • "Player not found" misses: remembered for 10 minutes, then tried again
  • Game database pages (operators, weapons, maps, ranks): a snapshot, updated each season, not live

When the daily budget is used up, or upstream is down, serving the last saved copy with an explicit "couldn't refresh, last updated X minutes ago" is kinder than a blank page.

Other edges that will show up in bug reports

Console names must match exactly. A near miss should return "not found," not a cousin account. That feels harsh until the alternative is attaching someone else's rank to a search.

Past seasons do not share a scale. Ranked 2.0 and Ranked 3.0 use different RP ranges. Seasons before Y7S4 used MMR, not rank points, so a tracker should not invent a modern rank name for them.

Operator data is not a full career. Headshot percentage and operator time played may only cover recent seasons. Summing operator hours will usually come in under the lifetime total Ubisoft reports. Document that.

There may be no match history. Not every tracker has a replay of each lobby. If you do not have it, say so. Advertising a feature you cannot compute is worse than a shorter feature list.

Why two good trackers still disagree

Most disagreements come from four places: the win-rate denominator, the cache window, whether operator stats are treated as lifetime, and whether a missing sample is shown as zero or as empty. Get those four written down and the rest of the page is presentation. The useful test is not "does this match another site to two decimals?" It is "can I explain every number on the card, including the ones we cannot show?"

title: Deployments now show build cache size
description:
Deployment summaries now show the size of the build cache each deployment saved and how close it is to the limit for its build machine. The same information is in the CLI with vercel inspect on version 65.1.0 or newer, and in the get-deployment REST API endpoint.

Uploading the build cache is billable build time, and a cache that goes over the limit is discarded, so the next build starts without one.

This is on by default on all plans for deployments built on or after October 21. See the maximum build cache size for each build machine in the docs.
