Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE is generally available (GA) on clusters running GKE version 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later. You can collect OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) traces, metrics, and logs from your workloads with a Google-managed collector instead of a self-managed OpenTelemetry Collector deployment:

  • Configure otlp_grpc in the Instrumentation custom resource (GKE version 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later), or send telemetry directly to the in-cluster collector's gRPC endpoint on port 4317 in addition to HTTP on port 4318.
  • The managed collector routes logs alongside traces and metrics through the Cloud Telemetry API (telemetry.googleapis.com), with improved per-signal queueing and autoscaling for high-throughput clusters. (Logs ingested through telemetry.googleapis.com default to the otlp log name instead of gke-managed-otel-collector.)
  • Multimodal prompts and responses collection for LangGraph ReAct and Agent Development Kit (ADK) agents, the --managed-otel-scope flag in the gcloud CLI (version 576.0.0 or later), and managed_opentelemetry_config in terraform-provider-google (v8.8.0 or later) are generally available.

To use the GA collector and features, upgrade clusters from earlier Preview versions to 1.37.1-gke.1697000 or later. For architecture details and setup instructions, see Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE and Deploy Managed OpenTelemetry for GKE.

Identity and Access Management

Feature

The Admin (roles/admin), Writer (roles/writer), and Reader (roles/reader) basic roles are generally available (GA). For more information, see Basic roles.

The legacy basic roles—Owner (roles/owner), Editor (roles/editor), and Viewer (roles/viewer)—are still available for use and are being actively maintained. However, if you need to grant a basic role, we recommend granting the Admin, Writer, or Reader role instead of a legacy basic role. This is because the newer roles support additional features, such as the use of IAM Conditions.

Looker

Announcement

Beginning October 26, 2026, the following features will be automatically enabled for Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances running Looker 26.20.

Feature

The ability to generate a summary of an Explore by using Gemini assistance is now generally available.

Feature

The bullet chart visualization type is now generally available. Bullet charts let you evaluate a single primary metric's performance as one or more bars and mark your goal with a target line. You can plot both against shaded background ranges that represent performance thresholds, such as "poor," "satisfactory," and "good." For more information, see Bullet chart options.

Feature

Looker now includes network diagnostics to help you troubleshoot database connectivity issues. When a database connection test fails, Looker automatically tests DNS resolution and TCP connectivity for the connection's endpoints and appends the results to the error message. To test network reachability to any hostname and port without creating a connection, Looker administrators can click Test Reachability on the Connections page.

Note: This item was added on October 30, 2026.

Feature

The Table Row Grouping feature and the Grouping menu options are now generally available. The Grouping menu options let you display and customize the appearance of table chart data hierarchically in groups.

Feature

The Visualization Assistant is now generally available.

Feature

Looker Continuous Integration (CI) now supports hub-and-spoke projects. If your Looker project uses local project imports to import files from an upstream hub project on the same Looker instance, then you can use CI to automatically test downstream spoke projects. Testing runs whenever a pull request is opened or updated on the hub project. This capability lets you catch breaking changes in downstream Explores, content, or data tests before upstream LookML changes are merged. For more information, see Creating a Continuous Integration suite.

Feature

Two new legacy features, Use Legacy Explore and Merge Query Experience and Use Legacy Explore and Merge Query Experience for Embed, are now available for Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances. These features let administrators configure Explores and merged queries to open in the classic experience by default across an instance or in embedded contexts. For more information, see Legacy feature schedule.

Feature

Looker now includes a new histogram chart visualization option. A histogram chart is a graphical representation of the data distribution of an attribute. A histogram creates intervals (bins) and counts how many values fall into each bin.

Feature

The KPI (Single Value) chart type is now generally available. The KPI (Single Value) chart type replaces the Single Value chart type.

Feature

The new Looker Explore and merge query experience is now generally available and is the default interface for Explores and for joining data from multiple queries.

Feature

When you enter values in a string filter on dashboards, Looks, or Explores, clicking Done or clicking outside the input field no longer creates a filter chip from uncommitted text. To create a filter chip, press Enter, enter a comma (,), or paste values into the input field.

Feature

The new Dashboard Tile Groups preview feature lets you organize related tiles into collapsible containers for improved visual organization. You can move, duplicate, or delete multiple tiles as a single unit on dashboards that use the newspaper layout. This update also adds LookML support for programmatically managing tile groups.

Feature

Now available in preview, the Release Changelog gives Looker users and administrators real-time visibility into the features, behavioral changes, and bug fixes that are available for their instance.

Feature

The Legacy features page is now available in the Admin panel for Looker (Google Cloud core) instances. Legacy features that appear on the Looker (Google Cloud core) Legacy features page might differ from those that are available on Looker (original) instances. For more information, see Looker (Google Cloud core) admin settings.

Announcement

The latest versions in the Looker (Google Cloud core) release channels are beginning deployment as follows:

  • Latest version in the Rapid channel: Looker 26.22
  • Latest version in the No Channel channel: Looker 26.22

The latest version in the Regular channel remains Looker 26.18.

Breaking

Some elements of the Conversational Analytics System Activity dashboard have been renamed. The dashboard layout and capabilities remain the same.

On the Token usage tab, the Conversational Analytics API value in the Feature column and the Feature Name filter has been renamed to Looker API. This value refers to the Conversational Analytics methods for the Looker API.

This rename might cause a breaking change if you built custom dashboards that reference the former Feature column or Feature Name filter value.

Change

The Use Legacy Connections Page legacy feature and the legacy database connection workflow have been removed. All database connections now use the connection workflow that is described in Connecting Looker to your database.

Feature

The southamerica-east1 region supports the following filters:

title: Greedy Byte-Pair Encoding Achieves at Least 0.361 of the Optimal Compression
description:
arXiv:2611.08671v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) builds a tokeniser by repeatedly merging a most frequent adjacent pair of symbols; its utility is the total reduction in string length achieved by $k$ merges. It was known that this greedy rule achieves at least a third of the optimal reduction. We prove that it always achieves at least 0.361 of the optimal reduction in string length, for every string, every budget and every tie-breaking rule; this is the first improvement of the bound one third. We also explain why one third was a barrier: the pair-packing relaxation behind it is tight, so a better bound must use more of the optimum's structure. When greedy destroys three of the optimum's merge points at once, one of them can usually be moved next door, because all copies of a rule of the optimum look alike; the remaining cases are paid for later. Along the way we determine the worst-case ratio for two merges exactly, bound it for three, and isolate a single inequality that would settle the problem.

title: Enabling Privacy-Preserving Natural Language Access to Industrial Smart Meter Data
description:
arXiv:2611.09372v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Energy management officers and grid operators increasingly rely on smart meter data for anomaly detection, performance monitoring, and strategic decision-making. However, extracting actionable insights from large-scale, heterogeneous telemetry databases requires advanced SQL and data engineering expertise, creating a critical bottleneck for non-technical personnel. Furthermore, the strict data privacy regulations and security constraints inherent to critical energy infrastructure often prohibit the routing of sensitive consumer data through cloud-based Large Language Models (LLMs). To address these challenges, we present OpenMeter, a schema-agnostic Multi-Agent System (MAS) designed to translate natural language queries into executable code and human-readable insights. This architecture lowers the technical barrier for day-to-day utility operations by empowering non-expert personnel to interact with complex databases through intuitive natural language dialogue, transforming raw telemetry into a highly valuable tool for routine grid workflows and strategic decisions. Multi-scenario ablation studies over this environment demonstrate that full multi-agent orchestration shows its largest observed accuracy gains on resource-constrained local hardware (+6.1 pp EX-R over the strongest single-agent configuration); at frontier scale, individual components retain value but should be enabled selectively, indicating that the cost of full orchestration is justified specifically where privacy demands local execution.

Ampersand from Humans& is now available on AI Gateway for free through November 13, 2026.

Ampersand is a model for group conversations. Humans& built Ampersand on Z.ai's open-weight GLM 5.3 and trained it with reinforcement learning in simulated group conversations that run for up to months of simulated time. Most chat models are built for one person asking a question and the model answering it. Ampersand is trained to take part in a conversation between several people. It reads every message, including the ones not addressed to it, and after each one it decides whether to reply or stay quiet.

It is designed to understand individual and shared goals, help people work through disagreements, and recognize when a contribution would be useful. That can mean asking a clarifying question, sharing relevant context, or waiting while people respond to one another.

For example:

Sam: Heads up, I'm out Friday, driving to my sister's. Alex: Have a good trip! Maya: Let's do the launch rehearsal Friday at 10 with all three of us. Ampersand: Quick flag, Maya: Sam said he's out Friday driving to his sister's, so a Friday 10am rehearsal with all three probably won't work. Might be worth picking a different time so everyone can make it.

Your application exposes these actions as caller-defined function tools. send_message delivers a contribution, while pass leaves the conversation quiet until the next human message. Your application executes both tools and records their results.

title: How Dim Gives AI Agents an Input Guide: Meta Prompts, State, and Timeline
description:
By duskzhen

Just after midnight on November 3, at 00:00:22, a local Dim session appended the day's date state. By the next model call, both dates appeared in the request:

<dim-state source="dim/environment/date">2026-11-02</dim-state>
<dim-state source="dim/environment/date">2026-11-03</dim-state>

The requests on either side of midnight (main #1910 and #1930) used the same System Prompt. The new date arrived in the messages, while the old date remained in the history. How should the model know which one means today?

The answer is Dim's Meta Prompt: an input guide supplied with each request in the Rust implementation. Its System section has a direct title, How to read your input. One of its rules says that a later state from the same source supersedes the earlier current value.

Why send environment state separately?

If today's date were inserted directly into the System Prompt, crossing midnight would require a new System version. The date, runtime environment, and available skills change on different schedules. Binding those values to the rules for interpreting them would force the prefix to change whenever any value changed.

Dim separates the instructions for reading an input from the input itself:

  • System tells the model how to interpret state.
  • Messages carry current values with their sources; updates have their own source and order.

To investigate the environment of an earlier request, you can follow the Timeline back to the inputs used at that point. Input guide and state definitions

If both messages have the user role, who said what?

Consider another recorded sequence. A background command finished, Dim recorded exec/ended at #413, then wrote a notification containing <dim-notification> at #414. Once consumed, that notification appeared in the model request at #421 with the API role user.

The human operator's own words also use the user role. The role alone cannot distinguish them. Dim sends the notification as a separate message with a runtime marker, and the guide explains its origin and meaning. A background completion notice is a result of earlier work; the model should relate it to its current task and decide whether it needs to read the full output. Message projection implementation

Branches follow the same principle. In another recorded sequence, a child timeline inherited the main timeline's history through #97. Its first model request contained both the inherited messages and a newly written branch identity block. That block also arrived in a user message; the guide explained that it described the current timeline.

One agent can have several timelines. The model needs an input that tells it which one it is on.

The diagram divides the model's input into eight categories:

  1. System prefix
  2. Rules and state
  3. Tool declarations
  4. Runtime inputs
  5. User inputs
  6. Tool results
  7. Compressed context
  8. Input guide

State describes the current situation. Rules have their own scopes. Files, web pages, and command output returned by tools are material for the model to analyze. The guide explains how to read each kind of input. Runtime permission checks still happen in the runtime: a marker identifies a source; it does not grant authority.

Who writes the guide for a new plugin?

Take background execution as an example. The capability that produces a notification also registers the explanation for that notification. Prompt combines shared guidance with the entries applicable to the current branch. A plugin registers its explanation when loaded and withdraws it when unloaded. Once the configuration adopts the change, subsequent requests use the updated guide.

Three model calls on the main branch of one session. The blue sections show the guide delivered in System each time; the message excerpts show a date update, a branch message, a background notification, and compacted context.

This matches the way Dim assembles capabilities with rutis. When a new capability sends messages to the model, its developer can maintain the marker, meaning, and explanation in the same component. Core owns the shared reading rules; each capability owns the content it introduces. Guide registration and composition

What can the model understand with this guide?

The Meta Prompt does more than explain one message. It helps the model maintain an accurate picture of its environment. Follow the main Timeline in the diagram above:

  • Configuration: Prompt combines the shared guidance and registered plugin entries into Guide A. At context/configured, that guide is adopted in System.
  • Request 1: Messages include a project rule (<dim-rule>) and the current date (<dim-state>). The model can see both the rule it should follow and the date.
  • Request 2: A date update (<dim-state>), branch message (<dim-branch-message>), and background notification (<dim-notification>) arrive in order. The model can tell that time has advanced, another timeline has sent a message, and a task has finished.
  • Request 3, after compaction: A history summary (<dim-summary>) and tool digest (<dim-digest>) replace older detail, while currently effective rules and state are reaffirmed. The model can distinguish past events from conditions that still apply.

All three requests use Guide A in System. The Messages change. The reading rules stay stable while the environment moves through the input stream.

In concrete terms, the model can track:

  • Time: which date is current, without mistaking an earlier date for today.
  • Rules: which project rules still apply and what their scopes are.
  • Position: which branch and timeline it is on.
  • Events: whether a background command finished or another timeline sent a message.
  • History: after compaction, what happened earlier and what still governs the present.

These are no longer stray lines mixed into a conversation. They form an account of the environment with a source, an order, and a reading guide.

How do rules change midway through a session?

So far, the examples have started from an already configured guide. In a real session, a plugin can be enabled or disabled midway, and rules can become active or expire. Two questions need separate answers: how should the model read a kind of content, and which specific content is currently effective? Dim handles those through different channels.

Reading rules: register with a plugin, withdraw with it

When a plugin is enabled:

  1. It registers the markers it will emit, their meanings, and their explanations.
  2. Prompt recombines the shared guidance with those entries into a new guide.
  3. After configuration adoption (context/configured), subsequent requests use the new System.

Disabling it reverses the sequence: the plugin unloads, its explanation is withdrawn, Prompt recombines the guide, and later requests stop carrying that explanation.

This ordering puts the explanation in place before the content appears. It also prevents the model from continuing to interpret new input using withdrawn guidance. Earlier requests are not rewritten; the Timeline still records which guide version each one used.

Current content: append new rules, expire old ones within their scope

Rules and state do not rewrite history either. They are appended. The op on a <dim-rule> describes what happens to that rule:

  • set or replace makes the rule in the block effective; replace identifies the currently adopted version.
  • revoke or expired makes that rule ineffective within its scope. A rule with the same name in another scope is unaffected.

State is simpler: a later value from the same source supersedes an earlier one. A state block with cleared="true" says that state no longer applies.

Adding a rule during a session means appending an effective block. Removing one means appending a block that marks it ineffective. The old block remains in history; the model uses the latest block for the same source and scope. The two dates at the start of this article work the same way.

After compaction, expired rules stay expired

When compaction happens, subsequent state blocks reaffirm only the rules and state still effective at that moment. Each is restated in its most recently delivered form, such as a replace block for the adopted rule version. A revoked rule is absent, so the model does not treat it as current again. The guide also says these reaffirmations confirm the current situation: they are not new changes and do not grant permissions.

Which state survives compaction?

Return to the session that crossed midnight. Later, #2025 recorded a successful context compaction. The next model request, #2026, carried the summary and then reaffirmed five rules and state values still effective at that point. Of the two dates, only November 3 remained as current state.

The two parts have different jobs. The summary describes what happened before; the subsequent state blocks describe the conditions the model should keep working under. The input guide explains that these restatements mean the earlier rules and state are still effective.

To see exactly what a model received at a given moment, return to that request and compare its adopted guide, state, and retained history. Post-compaction message projection

Editorial note: AI tools assisted with the English adaptation and illustrations.

title: Building Omnichannel Retail Applications: Technical Challenges Developers Should Understand
description:
Retail applications are becoming more complex as businesses connect physical stores, ecommerce websites, mobile apps, inventory systems, and customer platforms.

Customers expect a consistent experience regardless of where they interact with a brand. They might check product availability online, visit a physical store, place an order through a mobile app, and later request a return through a different channel.

Making these interactions work smoothly requires more than connecting a few APIs. Developers need to design systems that share accurate data, communicate reliably, and scale with changing business requirements.

Here are some important technical considerations when building connected retail applications.

  1. Create a Unified Product Data Structure

One of the first challenges in omnichannel retail is maintaining consistent product information across different platforms.

A product may appear on an ecommerce website, mobile application, marketplace, and in-store POS system. If each platform maintains separate product records, inconsistencies can quickly develop.

Developers should consider creating a centralized product data model that manages:

Product identifiers and SKUs

Product variants and attributes

Pricing information

Product descriptions and images

Category and taxonomy relationships

Channel-specific product availability

A consistent data structure reduces duplication and makes product information easier to synchronize.

  1. Synchronize Inventory Across Sales Channels

Inventory synchronization is one of the most challenging parts of connected retail systems.

Imagine a customer purchasing the last available product in a physical store while another customer attempts to order the same item online.

If both systems operate independently, overselling can occur.

A reliable inventory architecture should include:

Centralized inventory visibility

Real-time or event-driven stock updates

Atomic stock adjustments

Inventory reservation mechanisms

Clear handling of cancelled and returned orders

The implementation should also account for temporary network failures and delayed synchronization between systems.

  1. Design Reliable API Integrations

Retail applications frequently communicate with third-party platforms, including payment gateways, shipping providers, POS systems, ERP platforms, and customer relationship management tools.

Each integration may have different authentication methods, data formats, rate limits, and response times.

A dedicated integration layer can help manage these differences.

Developers should implement:

Consistent API contracts

Authentication and authorization

Request validation

Timeout and retry handling

Idempotency for important operations

Centralized error logging

This approach makes integrations easier to maintain and reduces dependencies between individual application modules.

  1. Use Event-Driven Architecture Where Appropriate

Not every retail operation needs to happen synchronously.

For example, when an order is confirmed, several processes may follow:

Update the order status.

Adjust inventory.

Notify the warehouse.

Send customer confirmation.

Update the reporting system.

Trying to complete every operation in one synchronous request can increase response times and create unnecessary dependencies.

Event-driven architecture allows services to react to events such as OrderPlaced, PaymentConfirmed, or InventoryUpdated.

Message queues and event brokers can help process these operations asynchronously. However, developers must also plan for duplicate events, message failures, retries, and eventual consistency.

  1. Maintain a Consistent Customer Experience

Omnichannel retail is not only about backend synchronization. The customer experience must also remain consistent.

A customer should be able to access accurate order information, relevant product details, and available support across different channels.

This requires careful integration of customer accounts, order history, loyalty information, and customer preferences.

Developers should also ensure that authentication and authorization rules remain consistent across web and mobile applications.

  1. Prioritize Performance During Peak Traffic

Retail platforms often experience sudden traffic increases during seasonal sales, promotional campaigns, and holiday shopping periods.

An application that performs well during normal traffic may struggle when thousands of customers browse products or place orders simultaneously.

Some useful performance practices include:

Caching frequently accessed product information

Optimizing database queries

Using content delivery networks

Applying pagination to large product collections

Scaling application services based on demand

Monitoring API response times and error rates

Critical operations such as checkout and inventory updates should receive particular attention because performance issues in these areas can directly affect sales.

  1. Build Security Into Every Channel

Connecting multiple retail systems increases the number of integration points that need protection.

Developers should use secure authentication, encrypted communication, appropriate access controls, and regular dependency updates.

Sensitive customer information should only be shared with systems that genuinely require it. API credentials should be stored securely rather than exposed in frontend code.

Security testing should cover both individual applications and the communication between connected systems.

Final Thoughts

Building an omnichannel retail platform requires careful coordination between product data, inventory, orders, customer information, and external services.

The most reliable approach is to design each component around clear responsibilities while ensuring that the overall system can exchange information consistently.

For businesses connecting physical and digital retail operations, IT services for retail and ecommerce can help address the technology and integration requirements involved in building a connected retail environment.

title: Adamas: Hadamard Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Inference
description:
arXiv:2510.18413v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now support context windows of hundreds of thousands to millions of tokens, enabling applications such as long-document summarization, large-scale code synthesis, multi-document question answering and persistent multi-turn dialogue. However, such extended contexts exacerbate the quadratic cost of self-attention, leading to severe latency in autoregressive decoding. Existing sparse attention methods reduce these costs by attending to only a subset of key-value (KV) tokens, but fixed or coarse-grained selection strategies can miss important tokens or retain substantial redundancy under constrained token budgets. We introduce \textbf{Adamas}, an accurate and efficient token-level sparse attention mechanism for long-context inference. Adamas applies the Hadamard transform, bucketization and 2-bit compression to produce compact representations, and uses lightweight distance-based estimation for efficient top-$k$ candidate selection. The selected positions are then used to gather the corresponding original KV states for sparse attention. Comprehensive evaluations show that Adamas maintains near-lossless performance within the effective context length of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. In efficiency evaluations, Adamas achieves up to $6.5\times$ self-attention speedup and $1.7\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup at a 32K context length. Adamas also maintains performance comparable to full attention on challenging long-form reasoning benchmarks, including AIME 2024 and AIME 2025.

title: From LoRA to Language: Recovering Skill Documents from Adapters
description:
arXiv:2611.09454v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Agent skills are short documents that teach a language model how to handle a class of tasks. To save context, these documents are increasingly compiled into low-rank adapters (LoRA), which keep the behaviour but lose the text: an adapter is hard to read, edit, audit or move to another model. We ask whether the skill document can be written back from the adapter and its frozen base model, and we score each recovered document by the share of the original's key instructions it states and by the tasks it solves. Reading the weights alone recovered little with the methods we tried; a learned map from weights to text passed on about one bit of the document. Running the adapter worked much better. The Executing Writer, a small writer trained on top of the adapted model, recovers 39-44% of the key instructions of held-out skills, against 1.3-1.5% with another skill's adapter, and on adapters fitted to 41 external skills its documents restore 85-91% of the original's task gain. These strongest results are on adapters whose training stored the document; adapters trained on behaviour alone are much harder for trained writers (1-2% of instructions). For these adapters we test an agent that runs the base and adapted models and writes a skill from where they differ. On ALFWorld its skills recover 58-71% of a LoRA's gain and carry over to models that cannot load the LoRA, lifting Llama-3.1-8B from 5% to 55%. Whether such a skill comes from the adapter depends on what the adapter learned: when its behaviour cannot be guessed, the adapter is the source; when it can, a reward loop without the adapter does as well.

title: An Auto-Updater That Doesn't Trust Its Download Server: minisign, Verify-Before-Parse and Rollback Protection
description:
Originally published on MistLab. Part 7 of Building an SSH Terminal.

Part 7 of "Building an SSH Terminal". Code excerpts are from MistTerm v1.2.26, an open-source (AGPL) SSH terminal client by MistLab; they are trimmed, and source comments are translated from Chinese.

TL;DR

HTTPS authenticates the download server, not the update itself. A secure updater accepts an update only if it is signed by a key the client already ships. MistTerm signs a JSON manifest with minisign (Ed25519), verifies the signature before parsing anything, binds each binary to the manifest by SHA-256, and remembers the highest verified version to reject replayed old manifests.

An SSH client holds the keys to its users' servers. That makes its update channel a high-value target. Anyone who can make the client install a binary of their choice owns every machine the user connects to. HTTPS alone does not cover this. It authenticates the server you download from, not the content. A compromised CDN account, a hijacked release page or a mirror operator can all serve a valid HTTPS response containing the wrong file.

The design goal is therefore: the client should accept an update only if it was signed by a key the client already ships, and it should treat everything it downloads as hostile until then. The client runs that in order: fetch with a size cap, verify the minisign signature, refuse an older manifest, check the asset hash, then install with a way back.

Update check and install pipeline

The manifest and its signature

Each release publishes a small JSON manifest, latest.json, plus a detached signature, latest.json.minisig. The manifest lists the version, publication date and one entry per platform asset, each with a file name, size and SHA-256. The v1.2.26 release manifest (the version these excerpts come from; later releases keep the same shape) has six assets: Linux x86_64 (GUI), static CLI builds for Linux x86_64 and aarch64, a Windows installer, a Windows portable build and a macOS universal app. The binaries themselves are not signed with minisign. They are bound to the signed manifest by their hashes.

Signatures use minisign, Frank Denis' tool built on Ed25519. Two properties of its format matter here:

  • Prehashed signatures. Since minisign 0.8 the default signature algorithm (ED) signs a BLAKE2b hash of the file. MistTerm accepts only that form (key.verify(data, &sig, false) disables the legacy non-prehashed mode).

  • Trusted comments. A minisign signature carries a "trusted comment" line, and a second, global signature covers the file signature together with that comment. Unlike the untrusted comment, it cannot be edited without the key.

MistTerm puts the release identity into the trusted comment, in the form product channel version pub_date. That v1.2.26 release's trusted comment is:

trusted comment: mistterm stable 1.2.26 2026-10-20T16:22:55Z

Anyone can check that independently with the public key in the repository:

$ minisign -V -p resources/update/minisign-primary.pub -m latest.json
Signature and comment signature verified
Trusted comment: mistterm stable 1.2.26 2026-10-20T16:22:55Z

Step 1: fetch with limits

The client knows two manifest locations, tried in order:

// src/core/updater/mod.rs
"https://mistlab.dev/downloads/mistterm/stable/latest.json",
"https://github.com/mistlab-dev/MistTerm/releases/latest/download/latest.json",

As of this writing the first URL returns HTTP 404. The release workflow's mirror job, which would publish there, is not implemented yet and is switched off. In practice every client gets its manifest from GitHub Releases. Because trust comes from the signature, not the host, adding or losing a source changes availability but not security.

Before parsing anything, the client caps what it is willing to download. The manifest may be at most 256 KiB and the signature at most 4 KiB:

let body = fetcher.get_small(url, MAX_MANIFEST_BYTES)?;   // 256 KiB
let sig  = fetcher.get_small(&sig_url, 4096)?;

Step 2: verify the signature before parsing

The order of the next two operations is the key design decision:

/// Verify first, then parse: JSON is parsed only after the signature checks out,
/// and the trusted comment must match the manifest contents.
pub fn verify_manifest(manifest_bytes: &[u8], signature_bytes: &[u8], keys: &TrustedKeys,
                       expected_channel: &str, allow_loopback_http: bool)
    -> Result
{
    let sig_text = std::str::from_utf8(signature_bytes).map_err(|_| UpdateError::BadSignature)?;
    let sig = keys.verify(manifest_bytes, sig_text)?;
    let manifest = Manifest::parse_and_validate(manifest_bytes, expected_channel, allow_loopback_http)?;
    if sig.trusted_comment().trim() != manifest.expected_trusted_comment() {
        return Err(UpdateError::InvalidManifest(/* "trusted comment … does not match manifest" */));
    }
    Ok(manifest)
}

Verifying first means the JSON parser and the validation code only ever run on bytes the publisher signed. A bug in parsing can no longer be triggered by an attacker who controls the download path.

The client compiles in two public keys, a primary and a backup. A signature from either one is accepted. That allows the signing key to be rotated, or a compromised key retired, with a client release that is still verifiable by the other key.

Validation after parsing is strict. It checks the schema version (an unknown one is reported as unsupported), product == "mistterm", the expected channel, a semver version and an RFC 3339 date. For each asset it checks a plain file name with no path separators, a 64-character hex SHA-256, a non-zero size, and https URLs only. Plain http to loopback is allowed only in a test build feature.

Why the trusted-comment check. A valid signature proves that the publisher signed these bytes at some point. The comment check proves the bytes are the release they claim to be. Release metadata lives in two places, the JSON and the signed comment, and they must agree.

Step 3: rollback protection, or refusing to go backwards

A signed manifest stays valid forever. An attacker who cannot forge signatures can still replay an old, genuinely signed manifest for a version with a known vulnerability. That is a rollback (or freeze) attack, one of the classic threats catalogued by The Update Framework (TUF).

MistTerm defends against it by remembering the highest version, and its publication date, ever seen in a verified manifest:

/// Is this manifest older than one we've seen (lower version, or same version
/// with an earlier publication date)?
pub fn is_stale(&self, version: &semver::Version, pub_date: Option>) -> bool {
    // … compare with highest_seen_version / highest_seen_pub_date
}

/// Record a verified manifest (only ever moves upward).
pub fn record_seen(&mut self, version: &semver::Version, pub_date: &str) { /* … */ }

A stale manifest from one source is skipped and the next source is tried. If every source returns a stale manifest, the result is a distinct StaleManifest error, not "up to date". An update is offered only if the manifest version is strictly greater than the running version, and downgrade is off by default (allow_downgrade: false).

Error reporting has its own small rule. When several sources fail, a signature or schema error is kept in preference to a later network error, because "the file was tampered with" is more useful to the user than "the backup host was unreachable".

This is not full TUF. There is no timestamp role, so a freeze attack that withholds new manifests is only limited by users noticing. It does close the cheap replay attack.

Step 4: download and check the asset

The platform asset is downloaded to a cache directory with a size limit taken from the manifest. Its SHA-256 is compared with the manifest entry before it is used. A cached file whose hash already matches is reused.

Unpacking is just as wary. The updater does not extract archives generically. It accepts only the specific program files it expects, as name or topdir/name, with normal path components only. Each extracted file is capped at 1 GiB, which guards against decompression bombs:

// Accept only `name` or `topdir/name`; no general extraction, which rules out
// path traversal at the root.
fn entry_basename_if_wanted(path: &Path, wanted: &[&'a str]) -> Option {
    let comps: Vec = path.components().collect();
    if comps.is_empty() || comps.len() > 2 { return None; }
    if !comps.iter().all(|c| matches!(c, std::path::Component::Normal(_))) { return None; }
    let name = path.file_name()?.to_str()?;
    wanted.iter().copied().find(|w| *w == name)
}

Step 5: install, with a way back

Installation differs per platform, but each path keeps the previous version recoverable:

  • Linux and Windows portable. The new binary is staged next to the old one and run once with --version. This smoke test must finish within 20 seconds and print the expected version. Only then are the files swapped. Old files go into .mist-update-backup/. On Linux, rename() replaces the file atomically, and the running process keeps its old inode. On Windows a running .exe cannot be overwritten but can be renamed, so the old file is moved aside first. If any step fails, the files already swapped are put back.

  • Windows installer edition. The verified setup.exe is launched silently as a separate process. It closes Mist and can relaunch it.

  • macOS. The update is a tarball containing only Mist.app. It is unpacked with the system /usr/bin/tar, which preserves the bundle's symlinks and permissions. The result must pass codesign --verify --deep --strict before the old bundle is renamed to .bak and replaced. If the swap fails, the old bundle is restored. codesign --verify confirms the bundle's signature is intact, but it is not the root of trust. That role belongs to the minisign-signed hash checked in step 4.

Some installations are deliberately not self-updated. The updater tells the user what to do instead when MistTerm was built from source or installed by a package manager, when the install directory is not writable, when the host's glibc is older than the build requires, or when macOS has translocated the app. Gatekeeper's App Translocation runs quarantined apps from a randomized read-only path, so it cannot be replaced in place until it is moved to Applications.

The updater never restarts the application on its own. A completed install waits for the next launch. Setting MIST_DISABLE_UPDATE_CHECK=1 turns checking off entirely.

Keeping the keys honest at build time

A signature scheme is only as good as the keys compiled into the client. MistTerm's build.rs enforces three rules for official builds (MIST_DIST_CHANNEL=github-release):

panic!("the update-test feature must never be enabled in an official release build");
// … real public keys are required: a file still containing PLACEHOLDER fails the build
panic!("primary and backup update signing public keys must be different keys");

A release cannot ship with test keys, with placeholder keys, or with a "backup" key that is a copy of the primary. The release workflow (Part 8) then verifies its own signatures with minisign -V before publishing.

Summary

  • HTTPS authenticates hosts, not content. Sign the release manifest with a key the client ships, and bind binaries to it by hash.

  • Verify before parsing, cap every download, and validate every field. Bind the manifest's identity to the signed trusted comment.

  • Remember the highest verified version to stop replayed old manifests, and never downgrade silently.

  • Extract only expected files, test-run the new binary, keep a backup, and let the build refuse unsafe key configurations.

FAQ

Isn't HTTPS enough to secure software updates?

No. HTTPS authenticates the server you download from, not the content. A compromised CDN account or release page can still serve a malicious file over valid HTTPS.

What is a minisign trusted comment?

A comment line covered by a second, global signature together with the file signature, so it cannot be edited without the key. MistTerm puts product, channel, version and publication date there.

Why verify the signature before parsing the manifest?

So the JSON parser and validation code only ever run on bytes the publisher signed. A parsing bug can then no longer be triggered by an attacker who controls the download path.

How does an updater prevent rollback attacks?

By remembering the highest version seen in a verified manifest and rejecting older manifests, and by never downgrading silently.

title: Maya a1: Do the Options Read the Model, or Does Their Position? Order Sensitivity in a Non-Autoregressive Decision Model
description:
arXiv:2611.09803v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Laya answers typed multiple-choice questions in one forward pass by scoring a hidden state at one [MASK] marker per option. We re-engineer the checkpoint (421M parameters; a 2-layer option head with no positional tensor; a documented but unused parallel layout) and test whether the answer depends on where an option is listed. Presenting 951 Qwen-verified questions under every cyclic rotation of their options (or six random permutations for 12 options), the released checkpoint changes its answer for 25.8% [22.9-28.7] of questions (19.7% on the 605 English-language items alone); accuracy with the gold option first versus last differs by 10.1 points, and the flips concentrate where the model's own confidence is low (54% versus 8% across confidence terciles). Fine-tuning with Laya's trainer on 2,818 teacher-verified rows with option shuffling cuts the flip rate to 7.2%; the identical rows without shuffling give 11.4%, so shuffling is responsible for 4.2 points of the improvement. A confidence-weighted vote over orderings gives 69.7% against 69.1% for a single base pass at 4.1x the compute. Labels are LLM-made and the test sets are teacher-filtered. We also fine-tune with the authors' parallel layout on the same rows: flip rate 0.5%.

title: Create a Website with Google Stitch: Build Your Site Under $300
description:
In today's digital landscape, having an online presence is no longer optional for small business owners and freelancers. However, the costs associated with web development can be daunting. If you are looking to create a website with Google Stitch, you are likely wondering how to maximize your budget without sacrificing quality. With a target budget of $300, you have plenty of room to build a professional-grade site using modern AI design tools.

What is Google Stitch?

Google Stitch is an innovative platform emerging from Google Labs that changes how we approach web creation. Unlike traditional drag-and-drop builders, Google Stitch AI provides an infinite, collaborative canvas where you can iterate on interfaces using natural language. It bridges the gap between high-fidelity design and functional web development, making it a powerful website using AI design tool for those who want a unique, tailored look.

Can You Build a $300 Website with Google Stitch?

The short answer is yes. When you aim for a $300 website, your costs typically break down into three categories: domain registration, hosting, and potentially premium assets or specialized integrations. Since Google Stitch focuses on the design and structural phase, it allows you to visualize your Google Stitch vibe design before committing to expensive development hours.

Budget Allocation Breakdown:

  • Domain Name: $12–$20/year.
  • Hosting/Deployment: $5–$20/month depending on your traffic needs.
  • Google Stitch/AI Tools: Currently, many features are accessible via Google Labs, making it a cost-effective starting point.
  • Extras: $100–$150 reserved for professional stock photography or custom icons.

Step-by-Step: Creating Your Site

To get started with a Google Stitch tutorial approach, follow these steps:

  1. Define Your Vibe: Use natural language prompts within the Stitch interface to describe your brand identity.
  2. Iterate on the Canvas: Use the infinite canvas to drag, drop, and rearrange elements. Because it is AI-assisted, the tool helps maintain design consistency.
  3. Export and Code: Once your design is finalized, you can move toward implementation by exporting your assets or using the generated code structure to build your live site.

Google Stitch vs. Figma: Why Choose Stitch?

While Figma is the industry standard for UI/UX designers, Stitch by Google Labs offers a more conversational, AI-driven experience. For a small business owner or a freelancer, the learning curve on Figma can be steep. Google Stitch simplifies the process, allowing you to focus on the vibe and functionality of your site rather than pixel-perfect alignment.

Conclusion

Building a Google Stitch website is an excellent way to maintain creative control over your digital identity while keeping costs well under your $300 limit. By leveraging AI to handle the heavy lifting of design and layout, you can focus on what really matters: your business.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Google Stitch free?

Google Stitch is currently part of Google Labs. While specific pricing tiers may change as the product evolves, it is currently accessible for users looking to experiment with AI-driven web design.

Do I need coding skills to use Google Stitch?

While basic knowledge of web structures helps, Google Stitch is designed to translate natural language into design elements, making it accessible to non-developers.

What is Google Stitch DESIGN.md?

The Google Stitch DESIGN.md file refers to the documentation and technical specifications often associated with projects built within the interface, helping developers understand the design intent behind the AI-generated components.
