title: Agentes LLM: un contrato de identidad para emails
description:
Un agente LLM puede completar un flujo de registro en pocos segundos y, aun así, dejar una prueba imposible de depurar. El formulario se envió, llegó el correo de verificación y el agente hizo clic en el enlace correcto. Pero cuando el paso falla, nadie sabe qué mensaje leyó, qué buzón pertenecía a la ejecución o si un reintento reutilizó datos viejos.

El problema no suele ser el modelo. Es la falta de una identidad técnica para cada email de prueba. Un generador de emails falsos puede crear una dirección, pero el sistema de automatización todavía necesita decidir quién la posee, cuánto dura y qué evidencia debe producir.

El problema: el agente pierde la identidad del email

En un flujo sencillo, la relación parece obvia:

ejecución -> dirección -> mensaje -> enlace -> resultado

En un flujo con agentes aparecen más caminos. El modelo puede reintentar una herramienta, delegar el paso a otro agente o continuar después de un timeout. Si todos consultan una bandeja compartida, el mensaje correcto deja de ser una certeza. Un correo parecido puede activar el flujo equivocado y hacer que el resultado parezca válido.

La ambigüedad aumenta cuando se usan nombres informales para buscar una solución, como dummy e mail o tempail mail. Esas frases pueden servir para entender consultas, pero no son una identidad de ejecución ni un criterio de seguridad.

La primera decisión de arquitectura es separar el objetivo del agente de la infraestructura que lo ejecuta. El agente debe pedir “espera el mensaje de verificación de esta ejecución”, no “busca el correo más reciente en esta bandeja”.

Diseñar una identidad por ejecución

Cada flujo debe recibir un run_id único y conservarlo hasta el cierre. La identidad puede tener esta forma:

{
  "run_id": "checkout-20261110-0522-a81f",
  "owner": "agent-registration",
  "mailbox_id": "mbx-7f2c",
  "purpose": "verification",
  "expires_at": "2026-11-10T05:42:00Z"
}

La dirección es solo una parte del contrato. run_id permite correlacionar la acción del agente, la solicitud de la API, la llegada del mensaje y el resultado del test. purpose evita que un mensaje de recuperación de contraseña se confunda con uno de bienvenida. expires_at da al sistema una decisión clara cuando el agente abandona el flujo.

En términos de diseño, el agente obtiene una referencia opaca y no necesita conocer detalles del proveedor. El adaptador de email traduce esa referencia a una dirección temporal, aplica el filtro por ejecución y devuelve eventos normalizados. Es un límite pequeño, pero hace mas fácil cambiar de proveedor o probar el adaptador en local.

Cuando el flujo también mide activación, conviene medir la activación sin perder el hilo del email. La métrica no debería decir solamente “se recibió un correo”; debe poder responder qué ejecución lo recibió y qué acción ocurrió después.

Un contrato mínimo para agentes LLM

Las herramientas que ve el modelo necesitan nombres y respuestas predecibles. Un contrato mínimo puede tener tres operaciones:

  1. reserve_mailbox(purpose, ttl): crea una identidad aislada y devuelve mailbox_id y run_id.
  2. wait_for_message(mailbox_id, kind, timeout): busca solo mensajes asociados a esa identidad.
  3. release_mailbox(mailbox_id, reason): marca la fixture como terminada y activa la limpieza.

La respuesta de wait_for_message no debe entregar el buzón completo ni datos innecesarios. Es suficiente con un evento como este:

{
  "status": "received",
  "message_id": "msg-91ab",
  "kind": "verification",
  "received_at": "2026-11-10T05:25:11Z",
  "link": "https://app.example.test/verify?token=redacted"
}

El token puede mantenerse fuera del historial visible al modelo y resolverse mediante una acción controlada. Así se reduce el riesgo de que un resumen, una traza o una llamada posterior copie un secreto. Si el agente necesita el enlace, el adaptador puede validar que pertenece al dominio esperado antes de devolverlo.

No hace falta convertir tempmailso en una dependencia del razonamiento del agente. Puede aparecer como término de inventario o de búsqueda, pero la integración debe depender de una interfaz propia, con límites y políticas definidos por el equipo.

Cómo evitar mezclas durante los reintentos

Los reintentos son donde se rompe la mayoría de los diseños ingenuos. Si una llamada expira después de crear la bandeja, repetirla puede producir otra identidad. Si el primer agente vuelve a despertar, puede leer el mensaje de la segunda.

La solución es que la reserva sea idempotente para una clave de ejecución. El adaptador puede aceptar idempotency_key = run_id + purpose y devolver la misma referencia mientras la fixture siga activa. El estado debería distinguir, al menos, reserved, message_received, verified, failed y expired.

También hay que definir qué significa “mensaje más reciente”. En general, no basta con ordenar por fecha. El filtro debe comprobar mailbox_id, tipo de mensaje, emisor esperado y una ventana temporal razonable. Si faltan esas señales, el agente debe recibir un resultado ambiguous y detenerse, no elegir por intuición.

Un reconciliador externo puede retirar las fixtures vencidas aunque el proceso del agente haya terminado mal. Si el despliegue corre sobre Kubernetes, es útil validar alertas después de un cambio de secretos como parte del mismo enfoque: los cambios de infraestructura y las pruebas de email necesitan señales observables, no solo un log de éxito.

Observabilidad y límites de seguridad

Los logs deben permitir reconstruir la secuencia sin guardar el contenido completo de los mensajes. Una línea útil contiene run_id, mailbox_id, tool_call_id, estado, latencia y motivo del cierre. Los resultados llega mejor agrupados por ejecución que por dirección, porque la dirección puede ser efímera.

El modelo tampoco debería tener permiso para crear identidades sin límite, cambiar el dominio de destino o desactivar la expiración. El adaptador debe imponer un TTL máximo, permitir solo dominios de prueba y rechazar una dirección que ya pertenezca a otra ejecución. Estas reglas deben vivir fuera del prompt: un agente puede interpretar instrucciones, pero no debe ser la única barrera.

Preguntas frecuentes

¿Es necesario un buzón por agente?

No siempre. La unidad segura es la ejecución o el escenario. Dos agentes pueden compartir una identidad si tienen el mismo propósito y una coordinación explícita; una bandeja global para toda la suite es mucho más dificil de investigar.

¿Qué debe hacer el agente cuando llega un mensaje ambiguo?

Debe detener el paso, registrar la ambigüedad y solicitar una nueva consulta con criterios más estrictos. Elegir el mensaje mas reciente puede convertir un fallo de aislamiento en un falso positivo.

¿Puedo usar un proveedor real en pruebas locales?

Sí, si el adaptador oculta sus detalles, aplica expiración y evita datos personales. Para pruebas unitarias, una implementación en memoria suele ser suficiente y hace que el contrato sea más facil de verificar.

Checklist de implementación

  • Cada ejecución recibe un run_id y una identidad aislada.
  • La reserva usa una clave idempotente para soportar reintentos.
  • Las consultas filtran por buzón, propósito, emisor y ventana temporal.
  • El modelo recibe eventos mínimos, no secretos ni cuerpos completos.
  • La expiración tiene un límite impuesto por el adaptador.
  • Un reconciliador limpia fixtures abandonadas.
  • Los estados y las llamadas de herramientas quedan correlacionados.
  • Los casos ambiguos terminan con una señal explícita, nunca con una elección arbitraria.

La automatización con modelos LLM se vuelve más confiable cuando el agente no tiene que adivinar qué email le pertenece. Una identidad por ejecución, un contrato pequeño y una política de expiración convierten una integración frágil en un sistema que se puede observar, reintentar y explicar.

title: PersonalAI 2.0: Enhancing knowledge graph traversal/retrieval with planning mechanism for Personalized LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2605.13481v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce PersonalAI 2.0 (PAI-2), a novel framework designed to enhance LLM-based systems through integration of external knowledge graphs (KGs). The proposed approach addresses key limitations of existing Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) methods by incorporating a dynamic, multistage pipeline. The central point of the PAI-2 design is its ability to perform adaptive, iterative information search, guided by extracted entities, matched graph vertices and generated clue-queries. Conducted evaluation on five benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA and MuSiQue) demonstrates an improvement in the factual correctness of generated answers compared to baseline methods (LightRAG, RAPTOR, HippoRAG 2 and PAI-1). PAI-2 achieves a 9 percentage points (pp) average gain by LLM-as-a-Judge on 2WikiMultihopQA and MuSiQue benchmarks, and attains comparable accuracy to HippoRAG 2 on the TriviaQA and HotpotQA benchmarks with Qwen2.5 7B and multilingual-e5-large reflecting its effectiveness in reducing hallucination rates and increasing recall. We show that enabled search plan enhancement mechanism gain in average a 18 pp boost compared to disabled one by LLM-as-a-Judge across five benchmarks. In addition, an ablation study reveals that PAI-2 achieves superior result on the MINE-1 benchmark, obtaining an 89\% information-retention score with Qwen2.5 7B and multilingual-e5-large. Collectively, these findings underscore the potential of PAI-2 to serve as a reusable component for personalized AI applications, which require context-aware knowledge-representation and reasoning capabilities. The source code of PAI-2 is available at the following link: https://github.com/Dzigen/PersonalAI.

title: Game-Style Feedback for Law Firm Site Forms and Buttons
description:
Press a button in a well-made video game and something happens right away. The character moves, a sound plays, the button glows or the controller vibrates. Players never wonder whether the game registered their input. Game designers treat that instant response as a basic requirement, and players notice at once when it is missing.

Law firm websites rarely get the same attention. A visitor taps "Call now" and nothing seems to happen for a second. They submit a contact form and the page sits there with no sign it worked. On a criminal defense site, the person tapping is often anxious and in a hurry, so a moment of uncertainty can send them back to the search results. This post covers how to bring game-style feedback to the interactive parts of a law firm site.

Respond to every tap within a fraction of a second

Games aim to respond to input within a frame or two. Jakob Nielsen's long-standing guidance on response times puts the limit for feeling instant at about 0.1 seconds. Anything slower and users start to notice the delay.

Google measures something similar with Interaction to Next Paint, one of the Core Web Vitals. It tracks how long the page takes to visibly respond after a user interacts, and Google describes 200 milliseconds or less as good. Heavy chat widgets, tracking scripts and large JavaScript bundles are the usual reasons a law firm site responds slowly.

Start by giving every button a visible pressed state in CSS. That costs almost nothing and tells the user the tap registered even if the next step takes a moment.

Show progress during anything that takes time

Games show loading bars, spinning icons or animations whenever the player has to wait. The player knows the game is working and roughly how long it will take.

On a law firm site, form submission is the main wait. When someone submits a contact form, disable the button, change its label to something like "Sending" and show a small spinner. That prevents double submissions and reassures the user. If the request fails, re-enable the button and explain what happened.

Make errors clear and fixable

Good games tell players exactly what went wrong and how to fix it. A locked door has a symbol showing which key it needs. A failed jump shows where the player fell short.

Form errors on many law firm sites do the opposite. They show a generic message at the top of the form or clear every field after a failed submit. Better practice looks like this:

  • Validate fields as the user leaves them, not on every keystroke
  • Show the error message next to the field it belongs to
  • Explain the fix in plain words, such as "Please enter a phone number with area code"
  • Keep everything the user typed when an error appears

Screen reader users need to hear these messages too. Connect each error to its field and announce status changes in a live region:

<label for="phone">Phone</label>
<input id="phone" name="phone" type="tel" aria-describedby="phone-error" aria-invalid="true">
<p id="phone-error">Please enter a phone number with area code.</p>
<div role="status" aria-live="polite" id="form-status">Sending your message...</div>

Confirm success in a way the user cannot miss

When a player finishes a level, the game makes it obvious with a sound, a screen and often a summary of what happens next. The player is never left wondering.

After a form submits successfully, replace the form with a clear confirmation message rather than a small line of green text. Tell the user what happens next, such as when they can expect a call and from what number. On a defense site, add a reminder not to share case details by email if the firm prefers to discuss them by phone.

The form itself matters as much as the feedback around it, and this guide on designing an intake form a frightened caller will finish covers which fields to ask for and which to leave out.

Test like a game studio

Game studios watch real players and note every moment of confusion. Law firm sites can do a lighter version. Ask someone who has never seen the site to find the phone number and send a message on their own phone while you watch. Note any pause, repeated tap or confused look.

Test on a slow connection as well. Browser developer tools can throttle the network so you see how the site behaves on weak mobile data, which is how many people will reach it.

For more on interface lessons drawn from games, the UX lessons from video game design site collects related articles.

Questions about feedback on law firm sites

Does a pressed state on buttons really matter?

Yes. It is the cheapest way to tell users their tap registered, and it reduces repeated taps that can cause double calls or duplicate form submissions.

How do I measure Interaction to Next Paint?

PageSpeed Insights and the Chrome User Experience Report show field data for INP when a site has enough traffic. Chrome DevTools can measure it during local testing.

Should a law firm site use sound or vibration like games do?

No. Visual feedback is enough on a website, and unexpected sound or vibration would feel intrusive to most visitors.

SBD Marketing works only with criminal defense law firms, one firm per city. It builds defense firm websites, handles SEO for the charges a firm defends, works on visibility in AI search tools and runs SEO audits.

title: How to Upload AI-Generated Images with Go Presigned URLs — Logistics Storage
description:
When a logistics platform stores an AI-generated image, the application server should authorize the upload without carrying the image bytes. That boundary matters more than the storage brand: a presigned URL lets the API authenticate the request, while the worker or browser sends the image directly to object storage. For a multi-tenant system, generate the URL only after validating the tenant-owned bucket and key, and treat the resulting object key as an auditable write decision.

TL;DR: create a presigned upload URL for /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}\, bind the intended Content-Type\ and any other required headers to that request, then issue an HTTP PUT\ with the image bytes. Keep the URL short-lived, never expose storage credentials, and make the object key collision-resistant because this storage surface has no If-Match\ conditional write or object versioning.

Start with the tenant boundary

Suppose a route receives a dispatch ID and an image produced for a delivery exception. The route must establish three facts before it asks storage for a presign: the authenticated principal belongs to the tenant, the dispatch belongs to that same tenant, and the destination key is derived by the server rather than accepted verbatim from the client.

That authorization decision is the real upload control.

For example, a retry from tenant 42 must not be able to reuse a key copied from tenant 17, even when both keys point to valid-looking PNG names. The service should resolve the dispatch from its own database, compare its tenant owner with the caller's tenant, and then construct the path from trusted identifiers. This takes more code than accepting a filename, but it gives the audit record a defensible explanation: the caller was authorized for this dispatch, the server selected this key, and the presigned capability was issued for that exact destination. A storage provider can enforce the byte write; it cannot infer the business relationship between a delivery exception and a tenant.

I prefer a key such as tenant-42/dispatch-9817/images/2026-10-23T14-05-00Z-7f3c.png\. The timestamp is useful in an audit record; the random suffix prevents an innocent retry from silently selecting the same name. A database record should retain the tenant ID, dispatch ID, object key, content type, requesting identity, and the idempotency key used for the create operation. The object store is the byte system, not the business ledger.

This is also where the exactly-once mindset earns its keep. A network timeout after the presign request does not tell the caller whether the authorization was recorded, and a retry must not create a second business attachment. Deduplicate the attachment command in the database, then reuse the accepted key or mark the command for reconciliation. Do not pretend that a presigned URL alone provides exactly-once semantics; it provides a constrained write capability.

The same rule applies to a generated image rather than a camera upload. A model worker can request a presign after it has a tenant-scoped job, but it should not be allowed to choose an arbitrary bucket and path. Authorization first, URL second, bytes third.

For teams that want the storage handoff behind one backend surface, Infrai is a plausible fit at this exact boundary: your service still decides tenant access, while its storage route supplies the presigned capability. The one-key, one-bill model is useful when the same logistics backend already has several backend integrations to operate, but it does not remove the need for an application-owned audit trail.

How do I use presigned URLs for uploading AI-generated images?

The flow has a narrow, useful contract:

  1. Your service authenticates the caller and chooses the bucket and key.
  2. Your service requests a presigned URL from the storage API.
  3. The uploader sends a PUT\ to that URL with the exact content headers used when the URL was generated.
  4. Your service records the intended object and reconciles the result using the storage metadata it can read.

The important detail is header parity. If the presign was generated for image/png\, the upload must send Content-Type: image/png\; changing that header can invalidate the signature or produce an object whose metadata disagrees with the application record. The URL is a capability, so log its request ID and expiry metadata when available, but do not put the URL itself into a long-lived audit record.

Here is the byte-transfer portion in Go. It deliberately accepts the presigned URL as input: the URL-generation request belongs behind your authorization boundary, while this small function can run in a worker without a storage access key.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
)

func uploadImage(presignedURL, imagePath string) error {
    image, err := os.ReadFile(imagePath)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("read image: %w", err)
    }

    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPut, presignedURL, bytes.NewReader(image))
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("build upload request: %w", err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/png")

    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("upload image: %w", err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    if resp.StatusCode < http.StatusOK || resp.StatusCode >= http.StatusMultipleChoices {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
        return fmt.Errorf("upload failed with HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, string(body))
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    presignedURL := os.Getenv("PRESIGNED_URL")
    if presignedURL == "" {
        panic("PRESIGNED_URL is required")
    }
    if err := uploadImage(presignedURL, "generated.png"); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

The judgment point is the status code, not the absence of a transport error. A successful request should advance the attachment state only after the upload response is successful; an unsuccessful response should retain enough context for a retry or reconciliation job. For large images, stream from an io.Reader\ instead of reading the entire file into memory, while preserving the same explicit method, content type, and response check.

Which storage boundary fits a logistics platform?

The right comparison is not “which service can store a PNG?” All of these can participate in an upload workflow. The practical question is where signing, tenant policy, compatibility, and operations should live.

Option Useful fit Boundary to verify
Amazon S3 A direct object-storage integration with a mature ecosystem and broad AWS-native controls Your service owns tenant authorization, key policy, retries, and reconciliation around S3’s presigned request
Cloudflare R2 An S3-compatible object store for teams already operating at the Cloudflare edge Confirm the exact S3 compatibility and the account-level policy model you need; compatibility does not remove application-level tenant isolation
Alibaba Cloud OSS A direct choice for deployments already aligned with Alibaba Cloud regions and tooling Validate regional, identity, lifecycle, and audit requirements against the deployment rather than assuming S3 parity
Infrai storage A plain REST boundary when one backend credential and one billing surface should cover storage alongside other backend capabilities The storage caveats below are material: this is not a public image host or an immutable financial archive

The last row is a workflow choice, not a universal winner. Infrai’s useful distinction here is one key and one bill for backend services, which removes a separate credential and invoice boundary for a platform that already combines storage with other services. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples can also reduce the integration work of a small Go service. I would recommend it to a logistics team that wants a single REST handoff for tenant-authorized private objects and is prepared to keep business authorization and reconciliation in its own database.

Choose direct S3, R2, or OSS instead when your system depends on their provider-specific controls, established cross-region replication, or an existing operations platform that already owns those policies. The documented storage coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS vendors, but not GCS or Backblaze B2, so vendor fit must be checked before migration rather than inferred from an S3-shaped interface.

Where the presign approach stops

Private uploads are a good fit. Permanent public links are not: there is no public or public-read\ ACL, and public_url\ remains null. A client that needs a public image page needs a separate delivery design, not a longer-lived presigned URL.

There is no object versioning or object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through storage history and a compliance archive requiring WORM behavior needs an external control. There is also no If-Match\ conditional write. If two workers must be mutually exclusive, coordinate them with a queue or database lease before either requests a write capability.

Browser-direct uploads deserve another warning. The bucket model contains a cors_rules\ field, but there is no independently exposed route for setting CORS rules. A browser workflow therefore needs its CORS configuration verified in advance; a Go worker-to-storage path avoids the browser policy, but it does not solve authorization by itself.

Lifecycle retention is measured at a minimum of one day, not an hourly cleanup interval, and multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule. Metadata is not a server-side search index: object listing supports prefix filtering, not arbitrary metadata queries. Finally, trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes, so a trial environment must account for that before a worker treats presign success as deployability.

Here is the smallest provider-specific check I would run after the tenant authorization decision. It calls only the documented presign route, keeps the key in an environment variable, and fails loudly on a non-success response; the exact required headers must remain the same between this request and the later upload.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "net/url"
    "strings"
)

func requestPresign() error {
    baseURL := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
    bucket := os.Getenv("STORAGE_BUCKET")
    key := os.Getenv("OBJECT_KEY")
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if bucket == "" || key == "" || apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("STORAGE_BUCKET, OBJECT_KEY, and INFRAI_API_KEY are required")
    }

    template := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
    presignURL := strings.NewReplacer(
        "{bucket}", url.PathEscape(bucket),
        "{key}", url.PathEscape(key),
    ).Replace(template)
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, presignURL, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
        return fmt.Errorf("rate limited; retry after %q", resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < http.StatusOK || resp.StatusCode >= http.StatusMultipleChoices {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4096))
        return fmt.Errorf("presign failed with HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, string(body))
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    if err := requestPresign(); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

Roll out with reconciliation, not hope

Start with one tenant-scoped bucket or an equally strict key policy, then make the database command the source of truth for the attachment. Store a short-lived upload state, the chosen object key, and the idempotency key. When the PUT\ succeeds, verify the object through the supported read or head workflow and move the attachment to complete; when it fails or expires, leave a retryable state and record the reason.

Do not automatically retry a completed PUT\ against a new key. That creates duplicate media and turns an ambiguous network result into a data-quality problem. Retry the same business command with the same deduplication identity, and reconcile the known key before creating anything else. The rule is simple: one business attachment, one authoritative key, many observable attempts.

For a logistics system, this boundary is usually enough: the application decides who may write, storage receives the bytes directly, and the ledger records what was intended and what was confirmed. Select the provider whose missing controls are acceptable for your retention and tenancy model, then test expiry, wrong content type, duplicate commands, and cross-tenant key attempts before broad rollout.

Keep the test matrix small and unforgiving.

If your team needs this private, tenant-authorized handoff and wants one backend credential across its services, try Infrai for the presign step and keep the ledger and reconciliation logic in your application. Start with the storage documentation; choose S3, R2, or OSS instead when their provider-specific retention, replication, or archival controls are part of the requirement.

References

The HTTP upload relies on explicit request methods and content headers, while browser-based variants depend on the server’s CORS policy. The provider comparison should be validated against each vendor’s current documentation before an architectural commitment.

Sources

  • Infrai official documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/
  • Alibaba Cloud OSS documentation: https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/oss

title: An audit log service that records who changed what and when. Stack: Node.js, Express, MongoDB.
description:
How indexes cut my MongoDB query from 100,001 documents to 100

What I'm building

An Audit-Log service that helps to identify who changed what and when, Stack: Node js, Express, mongodb

The setup

I seeded 100,000 fake events (actors, actions, resources, timestamps spread over 90 days). The query my API runs most:
"Give me the 100 newest events by user_1 between two dates."
The collection had one extra test event I created through the API, so scans show 100, 001

Before: no index

Using Compass's Explain Plan (which runs explain("executionStats")):

Docs examined Returned In-memory sort Stage
100,001 100 yes COLLSCAN

MongoDB opened every document to return 100.

After: one compound index

Index: { actor: 1, timestamp: -1 }

Docs examined Returned In-memory sort Stage
100 100 no IXSCAN

Why field order matters (ESR: Equality, Sort, Range)

In a compound index, order fields like this:

  1. Equality: fields matched with an exact value
  2. Sort: the field the results are ordered by
  3. Range: fields filtered with $gte, $lte, and so on

When a field is both the sort and the range, as timestamp is here, it counts as one step and goes last.

Example: my query filters actor = "user_1", limits timestamp to a date range, and sorts by timestamp descending. So the index is { actor: 1, timestamp: -1 }.

  • actor goes first, so Mongo jumps straight to that actor's section of the index.
  • Inside that section the entries are already ordered by timestamp, so no in-memory sort is needed.
  • With limit(100), Mongo reads 100 entries and stops. Result: 100 documents examined, down from 100,001.

The problem I ran into

While testing, I hit a problem with the time-range query. My compound index was { actor: 1, timestamp: -1 }, and a query on timestamp alone couldn’t use it, because an index only helps queries that use its first field. I had two options: change the query to always include actor, or create a separate index on timestamp. I chose the separate index because the audit log needs “everything between these dates” queries across all actors.

Per-query results

Query Index used Examined (no index) Examined (indexed) Returned Stage (indexed)
actor actor_1_timestamp_-1 (prefix) 100,001 27,188 27,188 IXSCAN
action action_1_timestamp_-1 (prefix) 100,001 33,124 33,124 IXSCAN
timestamp range timestamp_-1 100,001 17,765 17,765 IXSCAN
actor + range actor_1_timestamp_-1 100,001 4,772 4,772 IXSCAN
actor + range + sort + limit 100 actor_1_timestamp_-1 100,001 100 100 IXSCAN

What is "prefix": Prefix means that the index can serve for queries that match the first field so for index of actor_1_timestamp_-1 can serve a query of actor because of the first field

What I noticed: for every indexed query, docs examined equals docs returned, so the
index removes the wasted work and only the real work remains. The actor and
time-range rows still examine thousands of documents because they return thousands.
Only the limit brings the work down to 100.

I left execution time out on purpose. The same query ran anywhere from 0 ms to over
200 ms between runs on my local machine, so docs examined is the number I trust. I'll
measure timing properly under load in the next post.

What it costs

Indexes make reads faster and writes slower, because every insert updates each one. For a write-heavy audit log that matters.

Code: https://github.com/BhadmusX/Audit-Log

Next

Cursor pagination, then load testing with k6 or autocannon, then batching and a queue.

title: RPEG: Training Reasoning Language Models Scalably and Cost-Effectively
description:
arXiv:2611.09207v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is now central to training Reasoning Language Models (RLMs), but RLM pipelines are difficult to scale and costly to run because each RL step couples multiple large models, heterogeneous stages, cross-step state, and complex asynchronous dependencies. Existing systems typically optimize only parts of this design space. We address this complexity by jointly optimizing the pipeline structure as well as its execution using a novel data-centric graph intermediate representation called RLM Pipeline Execution Graph (RPEG). RPEG exposes structural choices such as bounded asynchrony and actor-critic sharing together with execution optimizations such as stage fusion, fine-grained scheduling, and multi-dimensional model parallelism. It is coupled with a comprehensive analytical performance model for RLM training, jointly capturing compute, communication, memory, and hierarchical rack-, node-, and GPU-level effects. Across systems with up to 256 GH200 GPUs, our distributed runtime engine implementing RPEG improves performance by up to 2x over ReaL and reduces step latency by up to 2.48x over verl, while increasing hardware utilization by up to 30%. Overall, RPEG provides a graph-driven foundation for next-generation training pipelines for frontier reasoning LLMs.

title: A Taxonomy-Driven Synthetic Dataset for Retrieval Effectiveness and Fairness Evaluation in Hiring
description:
arXiv:2611.09178v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: While machine learning hiring tools are ubiquitous, the need for privacy regulations and commercial sensitivity makes public benchmarking legally complex. We address this challenge by introducing a taxonomy-driven, fully synthetic HR dataset and benchmark to simultaneously evaluate retrieval effectiveness and algorithmic fairness. Grounded in 660K real freelancer profiles, our multilingual corpus features candidate profiles, project briefs, and counterfactual demographic twins. Auditing state-of-the-art embedding models reveals performance divergence from general MTEB scores, alongside fairness disparities in grammatically gendered languages. This demonstrates that general benchmarks are insufficient for HR, requiring tailored evaluations to identify Pareto-optimal models that balance semantic accuracy and fairness.

title: Two AI Agents Reviewed the Same PR. Was That Actually Independent?
description:
Imagine this workflow:

  • Agent A writes a patch and opens a pull request.
  • Agent B reviews it and says "LGTM."
  • CI turns green.

Two agents, one approved PR. Sounds like independent review.

Now change a few details.

Both agents can modify the same workspace. The reviewer relies on the author's generated summary. The tested commit might not be the commit that ultimately gets merged.

Do we still have independent verification, or just two agreeing opinions?

I'm increasingly interested in the boundaries that make a review independent, rather than simply the number of models involved.

For example, a reviewer could use a read-only checkout pinned to an exact commit, inspect the raw diff, and verify which tests actually executed. That gives us evidence the implementing agent cannot simply rewrite.

But how much separation is enough?

I'd love to hear how others handle this:

  1. Is a second AI model with a separate prompt sufficient for low-risk changes?
  2. Do you require separate workspaces, credentials, and immutable artifacts?
  3. What evidence makes you trust an AI-generated review?
  4. Where do you still require human approval?

Share your actual setup, a failure case, or even a simpler approach that works.

I'm especially interested in small, reproducible tests that could challenge our assumptions.

Disclosure: I maintain Agent Role Contracts (ARC), an open-source checker for declared agent responsibilities and task boundaries. Runtime enforcement and independent review require additional controls. This discussion is about what those controls should actually prove.

title: Workflow SDK adds idempotent starts
description:
The Workflow SDK's start() function can now admit a run and claim a hook in one atomic step. Duplicate workflow starts fail safely. The atomic start replaces the previous getHookByToken()-then-start() pattern, whose gap between the lookup and the start left a documented duplicate-start race.

Subscribe to messages inside the run

The claimed Hook exists from the moment the run is admitted, so resumeHook works even before the run begins executing, and early payloads are buffered and delivered in order. Inside the workflow, createHook({ token }) with the same token binds to the already-claimed hook: guaranteed, registering nothing new, adding no step, and resolving getConflict() to null.

Idempotency with no extra code

The token is the idempotency key, and it comes from your own domain: an order ID, an invoice ID, an import ID, or a request ID. The token alone guarantees idempotency. Exactly one run owns it, and a duplicate start() throws HookConflictError carrying the owner's conflictingRunId and never becomes a run. The workflow doesn't have to open the hook at all, and if it never does, the token was only an idempotency key and the run completes normally.

Setting experimental_minRetention keeps the token unavailable after the run ends, counted from start(), so late duplicates are still refused.

Upgrade to workflow 5.4.0 and read the idempotency documentation to get started.

Read more

title: Signals Are Present, Predictions Fail: Probing Diagram Representations in Large Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2603.02865v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) demonstrate strong performance on diagram understanding benchmarks, yet they still struggle to understand relationships between elements, particularly those represented by directed edges between nodes. To investigate the causes of this limitation, we probe the internal representations of LVLMs using a synthetic diagram dataset based on directed graphs. Our linear probing experiments reveal that signals about nodes and edges are linearly decodable from the hidden states of LVLMs, even for aspects that LVLMs struggle with in VQA, such as edge direction and connectivity between nodes. These results reveal a gap between internal signals and model outputs. We further perform causal interventions on the model's hidden states, showing that, for some aspects, the signals identified through probing causally contribute to the model's final predictions. These findings also hold on flowcharts, not only on synthetic diagrams.

title: MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents
description:
arXiv:2602.02474v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Most Large Language Model (LLM) agent memory systems rely on a small set of static, hand-designed operations for extracting memory. These fixed procedures hard-code human priors about what to store and how to revise memory, making them rigid under diverse interaction patterns and inefficient on long histories. To this end, we present \textbf{MemSkill}, which reframes these operations as learnable and evolvable memory skills, structured and reusable routines for extracting, consolidating, and pruning information from interaction traces. Inspired by the design philosophy of agent skills, MemSkill employs a \emph{controller} that learns to select a small set of relevant skills, paired with an LLM-based \emph{executor} that produces skill-guided memories. Beyond learning skill selection, MemSkill introduces a \emph{designer} that periodically reviews hard cases where selected skills yield incorrect or incomplete memories, and evolves the skill set by proposing refinements and new skills. Together, MemSkill forms a closed-loop procedure that improves both the skill-selection policy and the skill set itself. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval, HotpotQA, and ALFWorld demonstrate that MemSkill improves task performance over strong baselines and generalizes well across settings. Further analyses shed light on how skills evolve, offering insights toward more adaptive, self-evolving memory management for LLM agents. Code is available at https://github.com/ViktorAxelsen/MemSkill

title: Controller Vibration Not Working? Test the Rumble in 2 Minutes Before You Open It
description:
When a controller stops rumbling, the first question is whether the motors are actually dead — or whether the game, the connection, or the platform is just not sending the signal. A quick test before you open anything saves a lot of wasted repair work.

Start with the simplest isolation. Connect the controller by USB, open a game you know rumbles, and trigger something that should shake — a crash, an explosion, a heavy landing. If it rumbles there, the motors are fine and the problem is in the game or app that stayed quiet. If it stays silent everywhere, move on.

Next, test the rumble outside any game. A browser-based vibration test lets you fire the motors directly: plug in over USB, open the test page, and send a short pulse, then a longer pattern. You can check the rumble in your browser at https://www.gamepadtesterpro.com/vibration/ — if the motors spin there, the hardware works and the fault is software. If they stay silent even on a direct test, check the usual suspects: an app holding the controller exclusively (Steam, a remapper, another game running in the background), a low battery on wireless, or Bluetooth — some controllers only expose rumble over USB, so always retest wired.

A few patterns tell you a lot. One motor buzzing and the other dead usually means a loose motor wire or a failed motor, not a settings issue. Weak rumble on one side that is strong on the other points the same way. Rumble that works in a native game but not in the browser is almost always a browser-support gap, not dead hardware — Chromium on desktop exposes the vibration actuator most reliably, so try that before concluding anything.

If the direct test stays silent on USB, in Chromium, with no other app holding the controller, and a second game also stays quiet, then the motors or their wiring are the likely fault — and that is the point where opening the controller or taking it to a repair shop makes sense. Until that test, don't order parts: most 'dead rumble' reports turn out to be a connection or software issue, and two minutes of testing tells you which one you have.

Disclosure: I run the free tester linked above.

title: Why a Java pod gets OOMKilled in Kubernetes with a half-empty heap
description:
In short. A container memory limit covers everything the JVM uses, and the heap is only part of it. Metaspace, thread stacks, the code cache and direct buffers live outside the heap, so a pod with -Xmx close to its limit is killed while the heap still has room. Size the limit as heap plus non-heap, check which GC and how many CPUs the JVM really sees, and add a startup probe. jvm-fit does that arithmetic from the manifest before you deploy.

The pod restarts with exit code 137. The dashboard shows the heap at 50 or 60 percent. Nothing in the application log, because the kernel killed the process and the JVM never got to write an OutOfMemoryError. This is one of the most common ways Java breaks on Kubernetes, and the cause is almost always visible in the manifest.

Why is the pod killed when the heap isn't full?

Because the limit is on the container, and the heap is one of several things in it. The JVM also needs memory for:

  • Metaspace: class metadata. Grows with the number of loaded classes, which in a Spring Boot app is a lot.
  • Thread stacks: each thread reserves its own stack.
  • Code cache: machine code produced by the JIT compiler.
  • Direct buffers: off-heap memory used by NIO and Netty-based clients and servers.
  • The GC's own structures and other native memory.

None of that is counted by -Xmx. If the heap is allowed to take 900Mi of a 1Gi container, everything else has to fit in what is left, and it doesn't.

Memory budget
  container limit        1024Mi
  heap max (-Xmx)         900Mi
  non-heap estimate      ~350Mi
  -----------------------------
  needed                ~1250Mi
  over limit by ~226Mi

The JVM does not know it is over budget. It grows into memory it believes it has, the container crosses its limit, and the kernel's OOM killer ends it.

A real run: 51% heap, exit code 137

I reproduced it on a kind cluster with a small Spring Boot service made for the purpose. It keeps a fixed 260Mi in the heap and 140Mi in direct buffers, which is what NIO clients do.

Before After the fix
Memory limit 512Mi 832Mi
Heap setting -Xmx450m sized to leave room for non-heap
Result under the same load OOMKilled, heap at 51% in the last log line 0 restarts, peak 670Mi

"Stable" here means no restarts for a minute after full load, not a soak test. The point is the first column: a heap that was half empty, and a pod that died anyway.

Three container defaults that are easy to get wrong

I wanted the rules in jvm-fit to match what the JVM actually does, so a test starts Temurin 11, 17 and 21 in Docker with different limits and reads back the heap size, CPU count and GC. Three results are easy to get wrong.

Container What you might expect What the JVM does
2 CPUs, 1Gi G1, because there are two cores SerialGC. G1 also needs about 1792Mi of memory
256Mi, no heap flags A 64M heap, 25% of the limit A 126M heap. Small limits have a floor
1Gi with -XX:-UseContainerSupport Roughly the same as without it A heap sized from the host's memory, not the container's

The first one matters most in practice. A service with a 1 CPU limit or a small memory limit runs on a single-threaded collector, and nobody chose that. The app is slow, CPU usage looks low, and the cause is one line in the pod spec.

The other default worth knowing: with no -Xmx and no MaxRAMPercentage, HotSpot gives the heap 25% of the limit. In a 1Gi container that is 256M, and the rest of the memory you pay for sits idle. OpenJ9 behaves differently: the same 1Gi container got a 512M heap.

How much memory should a Java container get?

Work it out as a sum, not a percentage:

  • Start from the heap the app needs, taken from real usage if you have it.
  • Add non-heap. About 350Mi is a typical figure for a Spring Boot service, more if it uses many threads or large direct buffers. This is an estimate, so measure your own app when you can.
  • Set the limit to the sum, with some headroom.
  • Then express the heap as MaxRAMPercentage so it follows the limit when someone changes it. Values above 80 rarely leave enough room.

There is no single correct MaxRAMPercentage. Non-heap memory does not shrink when the limit does, so 75% is comfortable in a 4Gi container and too much in a 512Mi one.

What else to check in the manifest

  • A memory limit exists. Without one the JVM takes a percentage of the whole node.
  • The CPU limit. Below 1 core means throttling; below 2 means SerialGC unless you set a collector yourself.
  • ActiveProcessorCount is not higher than the CPU limit.
  • A startup probe. A liveness probe with a short initial delay kills a JVM that is still starting.
  • Memory request equals the limit, so the scheduler places the pod where the memory really is.

Checking it before deploy

To stop doing this arithmetic by hand, I wrote jvm-fit. It reads the pod spec and the JVM flags together, from plain manifests, Helm charts or Kustomize overlays, and prints the budget and a fix for each finding.

go install github.com/andronaft/jvm-fit/cmd/jvm-fit@latest

jvm-fit scan ./k8s/                            # files and directories
jvm-fit scan ./charts/payments -f values.yaml  # Helm chart
jvm-fit explain JVM007                         # why it matters, how to fix it

It collects flags in the order the JVM applies them (JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, then JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS, then the command line), has 12 rules, and outputs text, JSON or SARIF for CI.

What it doesn't do

It is a static check. It does not see how much memory your app really uses, and the non-heap figure is an estimate you can override. Tools like KRR and Goldilocks answer the other half of the question from real usage: they tell you how much the app needs, and jvm-fit checks that the JVM flags fit the limit you chose. Reading live clusters and Prometheus metrics is planned for the next version.

Source and docs: github.com/andronaft/jvm-fit (Apache 2.0) · the measurements: results on real JDKs · the demo: OOMKilled with a half-empty heap

Originally published at zhukovskyi.space.

title: Timelines, Bike Theft, and the Art of Designing Dim: Event-Driven Architecture for AI Agents
description:
By duskzhen

Imagine I park my bike outside my front door. Worried it might get stolen, I set up a security camera and hire an AI Agent:

"Keep an eye on my bike for me."

A naive implementation is to have the Agent poll the camera feed every few seconds:

Bike is still there. Bike is still there. Bike is still there. Someone walked past. Bike is still there.

By morning, the bike is safe—and the context window is completely blown.

Sure, that approach works. But what I actually need is for someone to notice when the bike might be in danger, review what happened, and decide what to do next. Eight hours of peace and quiet on the street shouldn't translate into eight hours of continuous LLM inference.

While designing Dim, we came back to this scenario so often that we started calling it our "Bike Theft Theory." It illustrates a simple core principle: Just because the environment is constantly changing doesn't mean the model needs to be constantly thinking.

The Camera Records; the Agent Checks on Demand

Let's try a different setup.

The camera records continuously. Meanwhile, the Agent can work on other tasks or simply wait idle. At some point, a lightweight motion detector notices someone approaching the bike and fires a notification.

Only then does the Agent pull up the relevant video clips: When did this person arrive? Did they just walk past, or are they tampering with the lock? Has the bike moved?

After inspecting the footage, the Agent might realize it's just a neighbor picking up something they dropped. It logs that assessment and goes back to waiting. Or, it might see the lock being cut and alert the owner using a pre-agreed method.

Here, the notification's only job is to say, "Something happened that's worth looking into." Someone approaching is a clue; whether they are stealing the bike requires looking at the evidence.


Four-act conceptual animation: record, detect change, notify, and review on demand. (Bike surveillance is a hypothetical scenario used to explain our runtime architecture, not a built-in camera feature in Dim.)

What if the detector misses something? The owner might walk out the next morning, see the bike is gone, and ask: "What happened last night?" As long as the underlying records exist, the Agent can work backward from that question and inspect the past.

To pull this off, the system has to solve two distinct problems:

  1. Leave behind records that might be needed later.
  2. Pull the Agent's attention over at the right moment.

Without the first, an alarm goes off and there's no way to investigate what happened. Without the second, you end up with a hard drive full of footage that nobody ever looks at.

This exact division of labor is where Dim's Timeline and Event-Driven Architecture begin.

Why Chat History Alone Isn't Enough

When I previously worked on DeepChat, I was inspired by the "Tape" mental model: treating Context as an append-only tape. User prompts, model responses, and tool outputs all move forward along a single track. That gives you a solid foundation for context compression, sliding windows, and branching.

With Dim, we wanted to take a step further outside the chat box.

The environment an Agent lives in is much busier than a simple request-response loop. Background commands finish on their own, other branches send messages, the system date rolls over, plugins load, and users change their minds while a tool is still mid-execution.

Some of these changes demand an immediate reaction. Others just need to be logged for posterity, or queued until the current task wraps up. We can't pretend these events didn't happen just because the model wasn't looking—nor can we dump every single environmental change straight into the model's prompt.

Going back to the bike: "The camera recorded this footage" and "The Agent watched this footage" are fundamentally different facts.

Dim's Timeline bakes this distinction directly into the runtime. It records operational events across tasks that affect subsequent behavior, while the model's context is projected selectively from facts like inputs, outputs, tool results, and context states. The scope of what's recorded on the Timeline is intentionally broader than what the model sees in any single inference request.

And "recording the environment" doesn't mean dumping the entire world raw into a database. In our bike setup, heavy video files stay in blob storage while the Timeline records clip indices, detection events, and follow-up actions. In Dim, the key is recording the operational facts needed for coordination, auditing, and recovery—while reading the heavy raw materials on demand.

The Timeline: Giving Every Event a Deterministic Place

The word "Timeline" might sound like a simple timestamped log. In Dim, however, it defines the canonical execution order of the runtime.

Every branch has its own Timeline. As events are appended, the Timeline assigns a monotonically increasing sequence number. The runtime understands causality and order strictly through this sequence; a wall clock can tell a human when something happened, but it cannot replace the deterministic order of the sequence.

Why does this matter?

Suppose you tell the Agent, "Forget about the bike for now," right as a slow background detector finally returns "Someone is approaching." The system needs to know which task that detection belongs to and exactly where the cancellation command sits in the sequence so it can apply the right rules. Relying on whichever async callback finishes first is a recipe for resurrecting canceled tasks.

In our bike analogy, the Timeline looks like this:

Records append continuously →

Park Bike ── Clip Index ── Approach Detected ── Notification ── Read Clip ── Verdict
                                  │                                 ▲
                                  └─── Draws Attention ─────────────┘

Raw footage stays in storage for later review; the current judgment only fetches the relevant clip.

New conclusions don't overwrite old facts, either. First we record "Approach Detected," and later we record "Confirmed just passing by." We know both the current state of the world and the exact reasoning trail that got us there.

In code, this ordering comes with a strict persistence guarantee: in the SQLite storage path used by the App Server, the Timeline only advances its published cursor after an event batch is successfully committed to disk, which in turn allows the Dispatcher to broadcast them. Returning from append, committing to storage, and publishing to subscribers are explicitly distinct phases (see Timeline commit and publish implementation).

This ensures every subsequent reaction is grounded in verifiable history. Records aren't just for post-mortem debugging—they actively drive how the system moves forward.

Event-Driven Runtime: Only Wake Up What Needs to Move

Once you have a Timeline, something needs to consume it.

Dim uses a Dispatcher to broadcast published events in sequence. Runtime capabilities subscribe only to the event types they care about. Upon receiving an event, a capability updates its internal state or kicks off a job, writing any resulting facts back to the Timeline (see Dispatcher subscription and dispatch implementation).

Being "event-driven" happens first and foremost between these runtime components. It does not mean firing an LLM request for every single event.

When the camera detects motion, a lightweight heuristic can decide if it warrants a notification; when video archiving finishes, it just updates a record; when a monitoring task is canceled, it quietly cleans up its resources. Only items that genuinely require the model's reasoning are routed into the input channel.

We strictly separate three stages:

Stage What It Means
Record Event The fact has entered the auditable history.
Dispatch Event Interested runtime capabilities can react to it.
Deliver to Model Relevant content has entered the model-visible context via inputs or tool results.

Recording an event does not mean the model knows about it yet.

Dim's context management makes this boundary explicit: ordinary runtime events don't magically turn into LLM messages on their own. Content meant for the model must enter the context through adopted inputs or tool results. For instance, an input is first recorded as an event, and only when input/consumed occurs does the history projection expand it into an actual model message (see Input consumption and message projection).


Using a background command completion as an example, this animation shows how an event triggers a new notification input. Arrows indicate processing causality; notifications, input consumption, and model requests themselves also leave records on the Timeline.

This gives us a two-tier filter for "what's worth looking at." First, the runtime follows capability contracts to decide which environmental changes warrant delivery. Second, once delivered, the model evaluates the notification against its current goal to decide whether to inspect deeper or take action. Meanwhile, the user can step in at any time to adjust the goal or shift focus.

No Bike Required: Background Commands as a Real-World Example

You don't need a physical security camera to see this in action. Consider a classic developer workflow: an Agent kicks off a long-running build or test suite in the background and moves on to other work. When that command finally finishes, how do we bring the Agent back?

Dim's background execution capability follows the exact path we just described:

  1. The command finishes, emitting an exec/ended event with the execution result.
  2. Once committed and published, the Dispatcher routes the event to the background execution capability.
  3. The capability checks the exit status and branch state; if wake-up conditions are met, it appends a notification input.
  4. The notification wraps a <dim-notification> tag, a short output preview, and instructions on how to fetch the full log, entering the scheduler as a Steer input.
  5. Once the input is consumed, the model reads the notification in its next turn and decides what to do.

In our current implementation, canceled background tasks won't trigger a wake-up along this path, nor will branches that are in the middle of shutting down. Because the completion event and the notification input are committed separately, our crash-recovery logic also checks for completed jobs that needed a wake-up but haven't emitted a notification yet (see Background result handling and Notification input construction).

This is the exact developer equivalent of the bike scenario: the full stdout/stderr log is the recorded footage, the completion alert is the motion notification, and calling a tool to read the full log is pulling up the video clip.

The model never has to spin in a loop asking, "Is it done yet?" And when the command does finish, it doesn't blindly force the old task to resume—if the user has already pivoted to a new goal, the Agent interprets the late-arriving result in the context of its new instructions.

At this point, the Timeline handles recording and ordering, and the event-driven runtime handles reaction and scheduling. That leaves one final puzzle: When the model receives this text in its context, how does it know what the message actually means?

Meta Prompt: Teaching the Model How to Read Its Inputs

In our previous post on Dim's Meta Prompt (An Input Manual for Models), we highlighted a subtle quirk of LLM APIs: whether a piece of text is typed directly by a human operator or injected as a notification by the runtime, it often arrives at the model API wearing the exact same user role.

If the model relies solely on the message role, it can easily confuse "The human user just gave me a new command" with "A background process from five minutes ago just exited."

The bike analogy works the same way. When the camera says "Someone is approaching," that's a sensor observation. When the owner says "Check who was just near my bike," that's an operator command. Both might point to the exact same video clip, but their origin, authority, and expected next steps are completely different.

Dim's Meta Prompt bridges this semantic gap. Alongside the system prompt, it provides an explicit "Input Guide." Each runtime capability registers the structural tags it introduces and their exact semantics, while dynamic payloads are delivered later through corresponding inputs:

  • For <dim-notification> (Background Alerts): The guide explains that this is the result of previously initiated work, the snippet is a preview from that command, and full output can be fetched on demand—and crucially, if the parent task is obsolete, do not restart it.
  • For <dim-state>: It explains state-update semantics, where newer values from the same source supersede earlier ones.
  • For <dim-rule>: It defines scoping and activation/deactivation lifecycles.

(See Input Guide implementation and Background notification semantics.)

Applied to our bike scenario, the model knows immediately which message is a sensor observation, which is the owner's instruction, whether bike monitoring is still active, and what countermeasures are authorized.

Of course, XML tags alone don't grant security permissions, and slapping an "Alert" label on sensor data doesn't turn it into an executable command. The model uses the Input Guide to understand meaning, while the runtime strictly enforces permission checks before any tool action is executed.

The Timeline gives events a place, the event-driven Dispatcher routes changes to the right handlers, and the Meta Prompt gives the model a framework to interpret them.

Making the Entire Harness Part of the Intelligence

Now, let's wire all these pieces together.

The environment changes, and facts are written to the Timeline. Runtime capabilities react to those events and push only what requires reasoning into the input queue. The model combines the Meta Prompt, its current objective, and its context history to make a judgment—calling tools when it needs more evidence, or triggering actions when it needs to intervene. Those tool outputs and subsequent environmental shifts then become new records on the Timeline.


Architectural overview: The Meta Prompt provides rules for reading inputs rather than acting as an async queue processor. The model's actions affect the environment via tools, and the results flow back into the Timeline.

When you view an Agent Harness this way, you realize you don't have to shove every ounce of responsibility onto the LLM. Recording, ordering, scheduling, provenance tracking, and permission enforcement are handled deterministically by the runtime; the model saves its tokens and attention for synthesizing goals and evidence.

This separation also makes long-horizon tasks sustainable:

  • Context Compression & Recall: When the context window fills up, summaries carry forward the past while re-asserting active rules and states. If the model later needs fine-grained details, Dim's recall tool lets it search and retrieve prior conversations and work records on demand. Compression only changes what is packed into the current inference request—the underlying historical facts remain safely stored on the Timeline (see Context compression checkpoints and Recall tool).
  • Idempotent Crash Recovery: Recovery respects the boundary between state and side effects. Re-reading a record that says "Alert already sent to owner" restores the system's awareness that the alert was sent—it doesn't fire the alert a second time. Rebuilding internal state and re-executing external side effects have strictly separated boundaries (see Time-bus side-effect guarantees).

Naturally, architecture alone doesn't make detectors infallible or models immune to misjudgment. If notifications are too noisy, the Agent gets woken up constantly; if they're too sparse, critical changes slip through. And if you still end up piping every raw video frame into the prompt, calling your log a "Timeline" won't save you a single token.

What's truly worth engineering is the coordination between the runtime and the model:

  • Can past records be retrieved when needed?
  • Do notifications provide enough clues without overwhelming the context?
  • Does the model understand the provenance and authority of incoming messages?
  • Does it have the evidence required to act, and does it get feedback after acting?

Back to that bike parked outside my door: I want an Agent that doesn't stare at the camera feed all night, yet snaps to attention the moment someone approaches; reviews the footage before jumping to conclusions; remembers if I've changed my mind about watching the bike; and can explain clearly the next morning what happened and why it handled things the way it did.

That is the exact coordination we're building in Dim—making sure environmental changes are reliably recorded and routed, so the model can see clearly right when it needs to.

The Dim repository contains the Rust implementation discussed here.

Editorial note: AI tools assisted with the English adaptation and visuals.

title: DunbaaBERT: From Sacrifice to Semantics
description:
arXiv:2605.26935v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models have achieved strong performance across many NLP tasks, yet Urdu remains comparatively underexplored due to limited resources and fragmented evaluation settings. To address this gap, we introduce DunbaaBERT, a family of Urdu RoBERTa-base models trained from scratch with Byte-BPE vocabularies of 32k, 52k, and 96k tokens on a deduplicated 17 GB Urdu corpus. We evaluate DunbaaBERT across intrinsic and downstream Urdu NLP benchmarks covering linguistic acceptability, news classification, offensive language detection, and sentiment analysis, while analyzing vocabulary-size effects on performance, pre-training dynamics, and computational efficiency. Across benchmarks, the DunbaaBERT variants achieve competitive performance against strong multilingual baselines while consistently maintaining favorable efficiency trade-offs. Under our controlled experimental setup, increasing the vocabulary size does not consistently improve downstream effectiveness, with DunbaaBERT$_{32k}$ repeatedly providing the strongest overall efficiency profile. Overall, our results demonstrate that carefully curated Urdu-specific encoder models can remain highly competitive despite comparatively compact model and training scales. All models are released under the MIT license.

title: SQLite + SQLx: Why You Should Never Edit a Migration That Has Shipped
description:
A database migration may look like an ordinary SQL file. During early development, it is tempting to edit 0001_initial.sql, drop a local database, and start again.

That workflow stops being harmless once the application ships.

A user's database is not your disposable development database. SQLx records applied migration versions and checksums in _sqlx_migrations. Changing an already-applied migration changes the history the new binary claims to understand.

1. A shipped migration is immutable history

Imagine version 1.0 ships 0001_spaces.sql. A user installs it, and SQLx records the migration version and checksum.

Later, a developer edits the same file. The filename and version are unchanged, but the contents—and checksum—are different. When the newer binary compares its migration files with the database history, SQLx detects the mismatch and refuses to proceed.

That is a safety mechanism. Silently accepting a different definition for an already-applied version would make the database's history ambiguous.

Once a migration has shipped, treat its contents as immutable.

2. Add a new migration instead

If v1.0 has shipped, a schema change belongs in a new version:

spaces/db/migrations/
├── 0001_spaces.sql
└── 0002_add_space_color.sql

For a simple additive change:

ALTER TABLE spaces
ADD COLUMN color TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'blue';

The default matters: existing rows should satisfy the new invariant as soon as migration finishes. Avoid leaving sentinel values that every reader must special-case.

In Knovum, Spaces uses an embedded SQLx migrator before its pool is exposed. Feature-owned databases keep their own migration histories rather than routing every product capability through a global database service.

3. SQLite table rebuilds need deliberate migrations

Some SQLite schema changes are not simple in-place operations. Changing a CHECK constraint or adding a foreign key can require a table rebuild.

A simplified shape:

BEGIN;

CREATE TABLE spaces_new (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    color TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at INTEGER NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO spaces_new (id, title, color, created_at)
SELECT id, title, color, created_at FROM spaces;

DROP TABLE spaces;
ALTER TABLE spaces_new RENAME TO spaces;

-- Recreate required indexes and triggers.

COMMIT;

This is an illustration, not a drop-in migration. A real rebuild must account for foreign keys, indexes, triggers, views, dependent objects, and data transformations.

Prefer additive tables, indexes, and columns with meaningful defaults. Backfill required values in the same migration. Treat dropping a table or column as a data-retention decision, not routine cleanup.

A forward migration should not silently reinterpret what users already saved.

4. Two failure modes should not become an automatic reset

A checksum mismatch means an already-applied migration differs from the file bundled with the current application. This is usually a developer or release-process bug.

An unknown newer migration means the database may have been opened by a newer application. An older binary must not pretend it understands that schema, attempt an implicit downgrade, or reset the database.

In both cases, preserve the original data and report a clear incompatibility. Do not fall back to deleting and recreating the database.

5. Fresh-database tests are not upgrade tests

This proves that the current schema can be created:

let pool = SqlitePoolOptions::new()
    .max_connections(1)
    .connect("sqlite::memory:")
    .await?;

MIGRATOR.run(&pool).await?;

It does not prove that a database created by the previous release can be upgraded safely.

An upgrade test should start at a previously shipped schema, insert representative rows, run the remaining migrations, and assert both the resulting schema and surviving data.

Knovum's src-tauri/src/spaces/db/tests/upgrades.rs follows this old-schema-first approach. It migrates to a shipped version, inserts representative records, applies the current migration history, and checks the final schema and retained data. Release acceptance also requires exercising the packaged upgrade path against a library created by the previous release.

Fresh in-memory creation alone is not upgrade evidence.

6. Keep SQL authority out of the WebView

Migration safety is also an ownership problem. If a Vue WebView can issue arbitrary SQL, persistence rules and transaction boundaries spread into presentation code.

The boundary used in Knovum is:

Vue 3 WebView
    -> typed Tauri commands
    -> Rust feature owner
    -> SQLx queries / transactions
    -> feature-owned SQLite database

The renderer has no SQLite capability and no SQL plugin dependency. It sends domain-shaped requests; Rust owns reads, writes, transactions, migrations, and persisted-field parsing.

The UI asks to rename a Space, not to execute an arbitrary UPDATE.

If an invariant spans multiple SQL statements, keep them in one Rust SQLx transaction. Do not split a transaction across multiple IPC calls.

7. Connection policy is part of storage design

Knovum's shared SQLite connection policy currently includes foreign-key enforcement, WAL, synchronous=NORMAL, a five-second busy timeout, a bounded pool, cache/mmap/temp-store settings, and PRAGMA optimize after migration.

WAL + synchronous=NORMAL is a trade-off, not a zero-data-loss guarantee. It avoids waiting for a full fsync on every commit while protecting against ordinary process-crash corruption. Sudden power loss can still lose recent committed transactions, so the choice must be evaluated alongside backup and recovery.

These are the project's current settings, not universal defaults every SQLite application should copy.

8. A migration review checklist

  • [ ] Did this change modify, delete, or rename a migration that has shipped?
  • [ ] Is the change represented by a new, increasing migration version?
  • [ ] Do existing rows satisfy the new constraints when migration completes?
  • [ ] Have foreign keys, indexes, triggers, and views been reviewed?
  • [ ] Is there an upgrade test starting from the previous shipped schema?
  • [ ] Does it verify both retained data and its meaning?
  • [ ] Does an older binary refuse an unknown newer schema without resetting it?
  • [ ] Does release acceptance exercise a database created by the previous installer?

Conclusion

A migration is not just a deployment script. It is a long-lived compatibility promise between an application and the data people have entrusted to it.

Freeze shipped migrations. Evolve forward. Test upgrades from historical schemas. Keep SQL and transaction ownership in the feature that owns the data.

These practices come from the database ownership and migration rules I have been applying while building Knovum, a local-first desktop application. The source and engineering notes are at github.com/madebyzan/knovum.

Code snippets are simplified teaching examples, not verbatim copies of the repository. Check the current source and migration history before adapting them.

For more information, see Workflows overview.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Advanced reporting dashboards prerelease notes 6.16

Here are the pre-release notes for updates to the advanced reporting dashboards and other reporting in CCAI Platform. When we release these updates, we expect the new capabilities to be as shown here.

Important: The next version of the advanced reporting dashboards could be greater than 6.16.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Agent Performance tile on the Real-time Agent Monitoring dashboard executed redundant database queries during auto-refreshes.

  • Updated advanced reporting filter prompts so they behave consistently across all dashboards and display the complete list of configured values:

    • List-backed filters now open directly into a searchable list on the first click.

    • Dropdowns that previously returned empty or partial lists now display the full configured list, including Agent Name, Agent Email, Agent Custom ID, Agent Teams, Location, Language, Answered By, and Projection Result.

    • Disposition Codes and Disposition List filters now display the codes configured for your instance.

    • Agent Teams and Team Name filters now match agents in any of their assigned teams.

    • Configuration renames (Queue Group, Queue, Agent Team, Disposition Code, Location, Role, and Skill) now appear in filter dropdowns within 30 minutes instead of up to six hours.

    • The Projecting filter on the live Queued dashboards is now clearable, so you can reset it to show all queued interactions, and offers only Yes.

    • Fields without a predefined list of values (such as consumer phone numbers and ID fields) now display a plain text box with an operator so you can type a value directly.

    • Call Status and Deflection Type filters now display values that existed in the data but were previously missing from the list.

    • Channel now reports a value on the live Voice and Chat dashboards, and on historical Chat dashboards, for interaction types that previously appeared blank (including internal, API-initiated, campaign, UCaaS, callback, and extension calls).

    • On the Agent Audit dashboard, the Change Details table now displays its timestamp column and sorts it correctly.

    • Consumer phone number filters now accept a single value instead of multiple values. Saved filters or links that pass multiple numbers apply only one.

    • On the Missed Interactions dashboards, the Activity Status column and filter are renamed to Projection Result.

    • Actor values describing who answered, ended, or disconnected an interaction are now standardized as Human Agent, Virtual Agent, End User, and System. Saved filters, Looks, and schedules that used the previous wording must be reselected.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Change

For GKE Standard CPU node pools, GKE can now upgrade nodes by updating the existing Compute Engine VM in place, instead of deleting the VM and creating a new one. Because the node keeps its underlying VM, it also keeps its compute capacity during the upgrade. This lowers the risk that a node upgrade fails or stalls because resources aren't available.

To enable this type of upgrade, use surge upgrades with the maxUnavailable field set to a value greater than 0. For more details about when GKE reuses the same Compute Engine instance, including exceptions, see maxUnavailable: GKE makes an existing node unavailable to recreate it.

This change applies to all GKE versions. To opt out, contact Cloud Customer Care.

Vertex AI Search

Change

Agent Search: Update to the stable model

The stable model for answer generation is updated to gemini-3.5-flash/answer_gen/v1 from gemini-2.5-flash/answer_gen/v1.

For more information, see Answer generation model versions and lifecycle.
