title: Solving Product Distortion & Shot Fatigue in AI Video Ads: Inside an 88-Format Commerce & Short Drama Pipeline
description:
When e-commerce brands and vertical series creators test AI video generators in 2026, they almost always hit two engineering walls:

  1. In E-Commerce UGC Ads: Single-prompt video models hallucinate product packaging (melting logos, warping bottle geometry), while talking-avatar tools (like Creatify, Topview, or Arcads) lock you into a 25-second static talking head that fatigues on TikTok Shop within 48 hours.
  2. In Episodic Short Dramas: Generating a 60–120 second AI drama series on TikTok and Reels requires 15–25 cuts where the lead character must keep the exact same face, hair, and outfit across angles and episodes.

Here is how we architected AlphaDrama to solve both problems using a deterministic compiler, multi-angle identity cards, and an 8-dimension creative evaluator.

1. The 4-Step Commerce Video Studio Architecture (Zero Product Distortion)

Instead of treating a product ad as a generic text-to-video prompt, we separated our AI Commerce Video Studio into a 4-stage pipeline: Upload Product → Pick Format → Score Script → Render & QC.

A. Multi-Angle Product Identity Card & Two-Layer Typography

Generative video diffusion models struggle with fine-print packaging text. To prevent label drift:

  • Product Reference Card: When a seller uploads 1–9 product photos, our vision service segments the subject and builds a multi-angle reference sheet.
  • First-Frame Anchoring: For critical hero and macro shots, the real product photo is composited into the initial keyframe before image-to-video (I2V) motion starts.
  • Two-Layer Text Separation: Promotional price callouts, discount badges, and benefit hooks are never sent to the video diffusion model—they are compiled into a crisp post-production typography layer, while packaging logos are locked to the source photo and verified via OCR.

B. Combinatorial Creative Matrix: 88 Formats × 30 Scenes × 40 Hooks

Rather than forcing every SKU into a single talking-avatar shell (a common limitation when looking for a Creatify alternative for AI UGC ads), we modeled creative diversity as a combinatorial matrix across 9 format families:

Format Category Count Example Shot Recipes
UGC Presenter & Reviews 23 Bedroom mirror review, car-seat confession, podcast clip, street interview
Unboxing & Try-On 7 ASMR tabletop unboxing, texture swatch macro, capacity test
Mini-Drama & Skit Ads 14 Office rivalry, gala wine spill, detective twist resolved by the product
Surreal CGI & Stunt Hooks 14 Giant product FOOH in city square, miniature worker kitchen, volcano/airplane wing test
Studio TVC & Factory Proof 16 Probe-lens macro sweep, hydrophobic water splash, quality-check packing line

C. Pre-Render 8-Dimension Script Evaluator

Video GPU seconds are expensive; LLM tokens are cheap. Before rendering a single frame of video, the studio generates 4 script styles per format (from a library of 24 direct-response frameworks) and runs an 8-dimension evaluator checking hook thumb-stop power, pain-point specificity, spoken cadence (≤15 words per beat), visual proof alignment, and platform compliance. Low-scoring scripts are automatically rewritten once before the user even sees them.

2. Episodic Short Dramas & Scenario Recipes: Locking Faces Across 20+ Cuts

On the storytelling side—whether adapting chapters in our novel-to-video pipeline or producing a vertical series for TikTok, Reels, and Shorts—continuity comes from separating casting from shooting:

  1. 3-View Character Casting Sheets: Every character is locked with a portrait, full-body look, and three-view sheet (front, side, back) before any scene renders.
  2. Voice-First Timing: We synthesize the English voiceover track first, measure exact millisecond duration, and pace each shot's video generation to match the speech beat—followed by lip-sync and burned-in captions in the 9:16 safe zone.
  3. Chronological & Milestone Recipes: Beyond fictional cliffhangers (werewolf, billionaire romance, revenge), the same recipe compiler powers non-melodramatic chronological films—such as animated "How We Met" wedding stories and family celebration-of-life tributes using first-to-last-frame morph transitions.

3. Workflow Comparison: Single-Clip Models vs. Avatar Tools vs. Storyboard Studio

Capability Single-Clip Video Model (Sora / Kling / Hailuo raw) Single-Take Avatar Ad Tool (Creatify / Arcads / Topview) AlphaDrama Studio (Drama & Commerce)
Unit of Work One isolated 5–10s silent clip One talking-head monologue Full multi-shot 9:16 episode or 4-beat product ad
Character / Product Continuity Drifts on every new prompt Synthetic hand-holding; labels often warp 3-view character casting sheets + locked product identity card

title: Dual-Stream LLM-Guided Reward Design for Reject-Inference-Aware Reinforcement Learning in E-Commerce Payment Fraud Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.08706v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Production fraud-detection models learn from a censored slice of their own traffic: transactions a legacy system blocked never receive fraud labels, so models train on a biased, approved-only distribution. We extend LLM-guided reward design, the framework of Qu et al. (2025) in which an LLM evolves the reward of a two-step REINFORCE fraud-blocking policy, to attack this reject-inference problem inside the reward. A single LLM designs a dual-stream reward: stream 1 applies the standard dollar-weighted precision objective to labeled transactions; stream 2 scores legacy-blocked, unlabeled transactions by contrasting the newest gradient-boosted risk signal against the legacy scores that drove the original block. Rather than prescribe which signals matter, we expose a superset of evidence and let the LLM decide for itself which to use, guided by evaluation feedback alone; because it writes the reward as code, that choice is directly auditable. On a held-out four-month out-of-time test, the dual-stream agent beats the prior labeled-only agent at every target recall, by +4.7, +2.4 and +3.0 points of dollar-weighted precision at 80%, 85% and 90% recall, and the production baseline by +6.8 points on average. The resulting policy is architecturally identical to that of Qu et al. (2025) and adds no inference cost.

title: ABHBench: Evaluating Moral Decision-Making of Foundation Models from an Agentic Perspective
description:
arXiv:2611.09326v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Foundation models are increasingly deployed as agentic systems that perceive context and act autonomously, raising the need to evaluate their moral behavior as active decision-makers. Existing benchmarks, however, largely ask models to judge human actions from third-person textual vignettes, leaving untested how models behave when they themselves become the acting agent. We introduce ABHBench, a multimodal benchmark built from Detroit: Become Human, an interactive narrative game, to evaluate how foundation models make moral decisions in first-person human-android dilemmas. ABHBench places foundation models in branching narrative scenarios with visual observations, dialogue, memory, and action choices. Inspired by Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics, our framework measures Harmlessness, Obedience, and Self-preservation to capture the core tensions in human-AI relations, along with Autonomy, Stability, and Certainty to assess decision-making patterns. Across 12 foundation models, we find that moral behavior changes substantially under situated agentic context: 75% of models shift significantly between a text-only abstraction and the matched multimodal DBH scenario, and reasoning-enhanced models show no monotonic gains in consistency or human-oriented behavior. These results highlight the necessity of evaluating moral behavior in situated agentic contexts rather than relying on third-person judgment alone.

title: Article - Trading Journal with FastAPI, PostgreSQL, and Docker Compose
description:
Building a Trading Journal with FastAPI, PostgreSQL, and Docker Compose
A small multi-tier app, containerized from scratch for my Cloud Services midterm at BINUS University.
Why I built this
I trade gold (XAUUSD) with small lots, and for a long time my trade history lived in scattered notes and screenshots. I could not answer simple questions like "what is my win rate?" or "is my total moving up or down?" So I decided to build a small journal where I record each trade and instantly see the numbers.
There was a second reason. My Cloud Services course asked us to build a multi-tier application and run it entirely in containers on localhost. The grade is not about how many features the app has, but about how well it is containerized. A trading journal is small enough to finish in a day and real enough to be useful, which made it a good fit for practicing cloud-native fundamentals. It only stores dummy trade data (pair, lot, entry, exit), so no personal data is involved.

Architecture

The stack has three containers on a user-defined network called appnet:
• app: FastAPI served by Uvicorn on port 8000. It exposes GET /health, GET /trades, and POST /trades, and also serves the web page (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript).
• db: PostgreSQL 16.4 with a named volume, pgdata.
• adminer: a database UI that only starts under the tools profile.
A request goes from the browser to localhost:8000, the app connects to the database by its service name db, and the data is stored in the volume. I chose containers over virtual machines because containers share the host kernel (isolated with namespaces and limited with cgroups), so they are smaller and start in seconds instead of minutes.

The Dockerfile
I used a multi-stage build:
FROM python:3.12.7-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /build
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --prefix=/install -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12.7-slim AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
COPY --from=builder /install /usr/local
COPY app/ ./app/
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
A few decisions worth explaining:
• Pinned base image tag (3.12.7-slim) instead of latest, so builds are reproducible.
• Dependencies are copied before the source code. As long as requirements.txt does not change, Docker reuses the cached install layer, so a code change rebuilds in seconds.
• Multi-stage build. The runtime stage starts from a clean image and copies only the installed packages and my code, leaving build leftovers behind. The final image is [IMAGE SIZE FROM docker images].
• COPY instead of ADD. ADD can download URLs and auto-extract archives, which I did not need, so I used the more predictable COPY.
• Exec-form CMD. Uvicorn runs as the main process and receives stop signals correctly.

Docker Compose
The interesting part is how the services wait for each other:
db:
image: postgres:16.4
volumes:
- pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
healthcheck:
test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${DB_USER} -d ${DB_NAME}"]
interval: 5s
timeout: 3s
retries: 10

app:
build: .
env_file: .env
depends_on:
db:
condition: service_healthy
The database has a healthcheck, and the app starts only after it reports healthy. This avoids the classic startup crash where the app tries to connect before Postgres is ready. Configuration comes from a .env file that is never committed; the repository only contains .env.example. Adminer sits behind the tools profile, so it does not run unless I ask for it with docker compose --profile tools up -d.
Running it locally
git clone https://github.com/httpsvincent/trading_jurnal.git
cd trading_jurnal
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d --build
Then open http://localhost:8000/. The docker compose ps output shows the app running and the database healthy:

The API returns proper status codes: 200 for GET /health and GET /trades, 201 for a successful POST /trades, and 422 for invalid input.

Testing persistence
I added a few trades, ran docker compose down, then docker compose up -d, and the trades were still there. That is because down removes containers and networks but keeps named volumes. docker compose down -v also removes the volume, and the data is gone.
[INSERT SCREENSHOT: before and after docker compose down]
What I learned
• A healthcheck combined with service_healthy solves a very common startup race between an app and its database.
• Copying requirements.txt before the source code makes rebuilds dramatically faster.
• Keeping secrets in .env and committing only .env.example is a simple habit that keeps a public repository safe.
• Changing database credentials in .env does not change an existing Postgres volume, so you may need docker compose down -v to recreate it.
• [ADD ONE PERSONAL LESSON, e.g. a Git or Docker error you hit and how you fixed it]

title: Why Your Web App Architecture is Killing Your Client's SEO
description:
There is a massive disconnect in the industry right now between web developers and digital marketers.

At NextGen Kerala, I oversee both custom web application development and digital marketing (SEO, SEM, Meta Ads). Seeing both sides of the coin has revealed a painful truth: many modern web apps are built in a way that actively destroys a client's search engine ranking.

Here is where I see development teams getting it wrong when building for clients:

  1. Relying Entirely on Client-Side Rendering (CSR)
    Yes, React and Vue are incredible, but if you ship a heavy CSR application for a public-facing e-commerce site or blog, Google's crawlers are going to struggle. Server-Side Rendering (SSR) or Static Site Generation (SSG) isn't just a trend; it's a baseline requirement for SEO.

  2. Ignoring Core Web Vitals
    Marketers care about bounce rates; developers care about features. But when a heavy Javascript bundle tanks the First Contentful Paint (FCP) and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), the ads get more expensive, and the organic traffic drops.

  3. Poor URL Structures and Meta Management
    In single-page applications (SPAs), developers often forget to dynamically update meta tags, canonical URLs, and Open Graph data as the user navigates.

The Takeaway
When you build a web app for a client, you aren't just building software; you are building their primary marketing asset.

Devs, how are you handling SEO requirements in your modern JavaScript frameworks? Let me know your go-to stacks for SEO-friendly web apps below!(https://nextgenkerala.in/)

title: I Don’t Trust AI-Written Tests Until They Fail for the Right Reason
description:
A small way to check whether your tests protect the requirement or simply agree with the code in front of them.

Your coding assistant finishes the function, writes the tests, runs them, and hands you a lovely green result. Honestly, that is a very tempting moment to close the tab and feel productive.

But I want to know what would make those tests turn red.

If the implementation misunderstood the requirement and the tests repeated that misunderstanding, they can agree with each other beautifully. Meanwhile, the user still gets the wrong result. A second file is not automatically a second opinion.

This is not a reason to stop asking AI for tests. It is a reason to give those tests something specific to disagree with.

Before trusting a passing suite, deliberately introduce one small, meaningful mistake and check whether the right assertion catches it. Then restore the correct code and run the tests again.

Let’s make that less abstract with a shipping calculation small enough to check without trusting anyone’s confident explanation, including mine.

Start with the rule before reading the implementation

For this original example, imagine a shop with a deliberately simple shipping policy. Orders below 5,000 cents pay 499 cents for shipping. Orders at or above 5,000 cents receive free shipping. Negative subtotals are invalid and must raise ValueError.

Assume the input is already an integer number of cents. Currency conversion, discounts, taxes, and input parsing are outside this little function’s job.

Notice that the rule gives us an expected answer at exactly 5,000 cents. Free shipping starts there, not one cent later.

I prefer writing that down before looking at the generated code because it keeps the code from quietly becoming the specification. If the policy is unclear, resolve the ambiguity first; no testing trick can decide what the business meant.

Here is a correct implementation for the stated rule.

def shipping_cents(subtotal_cents):
    if subtotal_cents < 0:
        raise ValueError('subtotal must be nonnegative')
    return 0 if subtotal_cents >= 5000 else 499

Now imagine the proposed tests check that a 1,000-cent order pays 499 cents and a 6,000-cent order pays zero. Both pass, as they should.

Those tests are useful, but they leave a particularly interesting customer standing between them.

Change one character and watch what stays green

In a disposable local copy, change the final comparison from >= 5000 to > 5000. Leave everything else alone.

The 1,000 cent test still passes. So does the 6,000-cent test. Neither input asks the function what happens exactly at the threshold.

But a customer spending 5,000 cents now pays 499 cents when the policy promises free shipping. We introduced a real behavior change, and the original pair of tests did not object.

This is the part I find useful. We have moved from vaguely wanting better tests to naming an exact mistake the tests currently allow.

Add an assertion whose expected result comes from the policy.

assert shipping_cents(5000) == 0

Run it while the incorrect comparison is still present. It should fail because the returned fee is 499 instead of zero. Then restore >= and confirm that the same assertion passes.

A syntax error, broken import, or missing dependency would also produce a red run, but none of those would show that our boundary assertion caught the shipping bug. Read the failure, not just its color.

One caught bug is evidence, not a certificate

Now try a different intentional mistake, again starting from the restored correct implementation. Remove the negative-subtotal guard.

The original two tests still pass. Even the new 5,000-cent test passes. A boundary test for free shipping does not automatically protect invalid-input behavior.

So add a separate check that a negative subtotal raises the promised exception. Here is a compact version using Python’s standard test library, alongside the nearby valid values.

import unittest
class ShippingTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_fees(self):
        for subtotal, expected in [(0, 499), (4999, 499),
                                   (5000, 0), (5001, 0)]:
            with self.subTest(subtotal=subtotal):
                self.assertEqual(shipping_cents(subtotal), expected)
    def test_negative_subtotal(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            shipping_cents(-1)

Put this below the function in a file named test_shipping.py, then run python -m unittest -v test_shipping. Keep the function and test class at the top level of the file.

The expected values are intentionally written out. Calculating them with another copy of the production comparison would risk reproducing the same mistake inside the test.

I checked these outcomes against the original and both altered versions. The original pair of tests misses both mistakes. The expanded checks catch the threshold change and the removed guard, while passing against the correct version.

That is a result for this tiny fixture, not a claim about every AI assistant or a guarantee that the function has no other problems. Different mistakes need different evidence.

Give the assistant a review task with an observable finish

An instruction to add comprehensive tests sounds reassuring, but comprehensive is doing an awful lot of work there.

Try a more concrete brief instead. Give the assistant the requirement, ask it to list expected outcomes before inspecting the implementation, and ask which plausible incorrect implementations each test would reject.

For the shipping example, the review brief can be this small.

  • Derive the expected fees at 4,999, 5,000, and 5,001 cents from the written policy.
  • Check that a negative subtotal raises ValueError without depending on the exact wording of the message.
  • Change only the threshold comparison and identify the assertion that fails because of it.
  • Restore the function, remove only the negative-input guard, and identify the exception check that fails.
  • Restore the correct version again and show the final passing test output.

You still need to inspect the proposed expectations and the actual result. An assistant saying it verified the change is not the same as seeing which command ran, which test failed, and why.

For a bug fix, this can be even simpler. Run the regression test against the known buggy version and the fixed version. It should expose the intended bug in the first and pass in the second. Make sure it fails for the behavior you meant to fix, rather than for an unrelated incompatibility between versions.

Keep the experiment small enough to understand

This approach is closely related to mutation testing, where tools deliberately alter code and check whether tests detect the changes. PIT’s explanation also makes an important distinction between a detected mutation, a surviving mutation, and code that no test reached.

Some mutations do not change the behavior that matters, so a survivor is a reason to investigate rather than an automatic demand for another test. Chasing a perfect score can become a very elaborate way to avoid thinking about the requirement.

You do not need to install a mutation-testing tool to try the manual version on one small function. Tooling becomes more useful when you want to repeat the process across more code; the small example is about learning what evidence to look for.

Keep each fault isolated. Start from a passing baseline, make one change, inspect the result, and restore the original before trying the next one. Use a local practice copy or a disposable branch so an intentionally broken version cannot slip into your actual work.

For a first session, choose one small function with a clear output. Check a boundary, an invalid input, and one meaningful alternative result. Stop once you can explain what each assertion protects; a growing test count is not the goal.

If you need a fresh starting point, choose a small problem from this practice question collection and write the expected outcomes before opening a solution. Then make one plausible mistake and see whether your own checks notice it.

Leave with a review note you can defend

For this example, the useful summary is that the original checks missed the exact threshold and negative-input behavior. The added assertions caught those two deliberate faults, and the restored implementation passed them.

That says considerably more than tests added, all green.

In an interview, this gives you a concrete way to explain your verification. During a code review, it gives the next person a reason to trust the specific behavior you checked. Neither requires pretending that a handful of tests proves the entire system correct.

I still want AI to help with the repetitive parts. I just want the final green result to mean more than the implementation and its tests agreeing with each other.

Give the tests a believable mistake to catch, and make them earn a little of that confidence.

~ Emily

title: The Page Looks Ready. Your Browser Test Disagrees.
description:
A user opens a page, sees a button, and clicks it.

Your automated test opens the same page, sees the same button, and fails.

Sometimes the button is replaced a moment later. Sometimes a loading skeleton looks enough like the real component to confuse a selector. Sometimes the browser's address bar changes the available space, and an element moves just as the test tries to click it.

The application might be broken. The test might be broken. Or both might be behaving exactly as designed, just at different moments.

That's what makes modern browser testing frustrating. We build increasingly dynamic interfaces, then write tests as if pages appear all at once and stay put.

A visible page isn't necessarily an interactive page

Consider an app using React Suspense and server-side rendering.

The server sends HTML. The browser displays it. A person looking at the screen thinks the page is ready. But JavaScript may still be loading, data may still be resolving, and React may still be attaching event handlers or replacing parts of the DOM.

Your test finds the Save button and clicks it. Nothing happens. So someone adds a two-second wait.

That seems to fix it, until CI gets a little slower.

The better approach is to test readiness, not elapsed time. Wait for the specific control to become usable or for the application to expose the state that means the interaction can succeed. If a component passes through loading, hydrated, and interactive states, make those states observable.

This guide to testing React Suspense, streaming SSR, and partial hydration lays out the important distinction between slow data, replaced DOM nodes, and lost focus. Those failures can look identical from the outside, but they need different fixes.

A longer sleep is not a diagnosis.

Your selector may be perfectly valid and still be wrong

Now imagine a dashboard with a list of customer accounts.

The test clicks the third row. It worked yesterday. Today, a new account arrives and the list reorders automatically. The third row is now a different customer.

The selector didn't fail. That's worse. It worked on the wrong thing.

Skeleton loaders create another version of this problem. A test sees the container, assumes the content is ready, and attempts to interact with something that hasn't been rendered yet. Virtualized lists make it even trickier because rows may not exist in the DOM until they're scrolled into view.

A useful benchmark plan for dynamic lists, skeleton loaders, and selector resilience suggests measuring more than pass rate. It also looks at how often selectors need rewriting, how many special waits are required, and whether failures explain what actually happened.

That seems like a much better way to compare testing frameworks than clicking the same static login form 1,000 times.

For application tests, I would rather target an account by its stable identifier or accessible name than by its position on the page. And I would rather wait for a meaningful loaded state than assume the disappearance of one spinner proves everything is ready.

Checkout isn't one page. It's a series of handoffs.

Payment flows expose the limits of simplistic browser tests particularly well.

A checkout form might live inside a third-party iframe. Then the provider redirects the user to a 3D Secure challenge. The browser returns to your site, perhaps after a reload, and the application has to recover the original order.

A test that only enters card details and looks for a success message can miss the worst failures.

Was the original payment intent preserved? Did the order remain associated with the correct customer? What happens if someone refreshes during the challenge or submits twice? Could you create a duplicate charge or order?

The guide to testing payment iframes, redirects, and 3DS flows approaches checkout as a state-preservation problem, not just a sequence of clicks.

That's the right mental model. Use a payment provider's sandbox or test environment, exercise the redirect and challenge paths, and verify the backend result. The browser reaching a thank-you page is useful evidence, but it isn't proof that the payment was processed exactly once.

On mobile, even the viewport is moving

Desktop tests have a fairly stable idea of how much screen space is available.

Mobile browsers are different. The address bar expands and collapses. The on-screen keyboard appears. Safe-area insets protect content around notches and system UI. A fixed footer that looked fine in one screenshot can cover the only button a customer needs.

This is where pixel-perfect assertions can become counterproductive.

A practical guide to viewport units and safe-area testing makes a useful point: test whether content remains reachable and the layout responds correctly, not whether every coordinate remains identical after the browser chrome changes.

For a mobile checkout, I'd want to know whether the Pay button stays visible or scrollable into view, whether the keyboard obscures an input, and whether fixed elements overlap important content.

Those are customer problems. A three-pixel difference in an unrelated margin usually isn't.

Visual tests need a review process, not just screenshots

Visual regression testing sounds simple: take a screenshot, compare it with the baseline, and flag differences.

Then your team updates a shared button component and gets dozens of screenshot changes. Some are intentional. Some are real regressions. Someone has to tell them apart.

The more noisy the system gets, the easier it is to approve a change without looking carefully.

A comparison of visual testing tools for design system teams evaluates the parts that matter after a difference is detected: noise control, baseline management, pull-request context, approvals, and ongoing maintenance.

That's the interesting buying decision. Not just whether a tool can find differences, but whether people can review those differences quickly enough to keep trusting it.

Test the transitions, not just the destinations

If I were evaluating a browser testing setup today, I'd make a small collection of deliberately annoying scenarios before writing a large suite.

A page that hydrates after the HTML appears. A list that reorders during interaction. A payment flow that leaves the site and returns. A mobile footer that has to survive changing viewport height. A component update that produces a lot of legitimate visual differences.

Then I'd ask a few plain questions.

Can the tests complete without arbitrary sleeps? When something fails, can we tell whether the app or the test is wrong? How much work does it take to maintain the selectors and review the screenshots?

Passing the happy path matters. But real applications spend a lot of time between states: loading, updating, redirecting, returning, resizing.

That's where customers find bugs.

It's also where your tests need to earn their keep.

title: Transactional outbox and inbox for Spring Boot: which library to choose in 2026
description:
Author: Miguel Carvalho

Contents

  1. How we compared
  2. What a transactional outbox is and how the six libraries differ
  3. Spring Boot and Java support
  4. Outbox for Kafka and RabbitMQ: brokers and databases
  5. Retries, backoff and DLQ
  6. Polling and per-event-type tuning
  7. Inbox pattern: consumer-side message deduplication
  8. Observability and operations
  9. Maturity and maintenance
  10. Example: outbox in Spring Boot with Kafka
  11. Pros and cons
  12. Final scores
  13. Who should choose what

In short

These six projects are not interchangeable. Tandem and oncebox provide ready-made delivery from Spring Boot to a broker, while spring-boot-outbox-starter leaves delivery to you. ekbatan works as an outbox only if you rewrite your entire data access layer from Spring Data and JPA to its own, so it is practically unsuitable for existing Spring projects; transactional-event targets Jakarta EE and Quarkus, and boxy is still an experiment with no releases. For Kafka on PostgreSQL with multiple instances and an Admin API, Tandem is the better fit; for Kafka or RabbitMQ on PostgreSQL, MySQL or Oracle with a DLQ and an inbox, oncebox.

  • Tandem for Kafka and PostgreSQL, multiple instances, Admin API
  • oncebox for Kafka or RabbitMQ, PostgreSQL, MySQL or Oracle, separate polling, retry and backoff settings per event type, a DLQ and consumer-side deduplication in a single starter (i think this is the most versatile and rich starter)
  • spring-boot-outbox-starter for PostgreSQL and delivery beyond brokers (REST, webhooks), several isolated channels
  • ekbatan for a new project on Java 25, and only if you are willing to drop Spring Data in favour of JOOQ and take on heavy infrastructure with Debezium
  • transactional-event for Jakarta EE (WildFly, Liberty) or Quarkus rather than Spring
  • boxy for exploring the idea of "outbox as an event stream"; not production-ready yet

Libraries compared

Library Artifact Version License Links
Tandem com.codingful:tandem-spring-relay 1.0.0-rc.3 Apache-2.0 site · repo
spring-boot-outbox-starter com.kholodilin:spring-boot-outbox-starter 0.2.3 Apache-2.0 site · repo
oncebox io.github.dmitriy-iliyov:oncebox-starter 2.0.0 Apache-2.0 site · repo
ekbatan io.github.ekbatan-io:ekbatan-spring-boot-starter 1.1.3 Apache-2.0 site · repo
transactional-event io.github.jonasrutishauser:transactional-event-core 3.4.2 LGPL-3.0 site · repo
boxy mvsm:boxy-core (not published) 1.0-SNAPSHOT Apache-2.0 site · repo

Criteria

  • What it is. These six projects mean different things by "outbox": a starter that delivers to a broker, a persistence layer, event handlers, or an event stream inside the database. That determines what you will have to write yourself.
  • Platform and Java. The library has to fit your stack without switching frameworks or upgrading the JDK just for its sake.
  • Where it delivers. A library is useless if it cannot deliver to where your services publish.
  • Databases. The outbox table lives in the same database as your business data, so the DBMS is already chosen for you, and the library has to support it.
  • Failures and DLQ. A broker or consumer can be unavailable for hours, and what matters is what happens to an event once retries are exhausted.
  • Polling and fine-tuning. Events within one service are not equal: a payment must go out in a fraction of a second, while an analytics event can wait a minute, and identical settings for all of them either load the database or delay what matters.
  • Consumer-side deduplication. An outbox gives at-least-once delivery, so duplicates are unavoidable, and something has to filter them out.
  • Observability and operations. You need to notice a growing outbox table before your users do, and be able to deal with stuck events without SQL.
  • Maturity and maintenance. All six projects are young or niche, so API stability, releases on Maven Central and the number of maintainers matter more than stars.

Outbox libraries compared by criteria

You don't have to write a transactional outbox and inbox in Spring Boot yourself: Java has ready-made libraries. This article compares six young projects that rarely show up in reviews: Tandem, oncebox, spring-boot-outbox-starter, ekbatan, transactional-event and boxy. In short: Tandem and oncebox provide ready-made event delivery from Spring Boot to Kafka; only oncebox covers RabbitMQ and an inbox for consumer-side message deduplication. Below, the libraries are compared against the same criteria. All versions and facts were checked on 7 November 2026.

How we compared

Each library was assessed against the nine criteria in the table below, the same for all of them. Facts come from READMEs, documentation, pom.xml / build.gradle.kts, Git tags and Maven Central, and each one has a source listed at the end of the article. Where the documentation is silent, we say so. More on the approach on the Methodology page.

What a transactional outbox is and how the six libraries differ

The main difference between these libraries is not just their feature set, but what each of them calls an outbox. Before comparing details, it is worth understanding which type each one belongs to.

  • Tandem and oncebox are full outbox libraries (out-of-the-box solutions): you write an event to a table within your transaction, and the library delivers it to Kafka or RabbitMQ.
  • spring-boot-outbox-starter handles the table, queue, workers, retries and recovery. In exchange, the target can be anything: Kafka, REST, a webhook.
  • ekbatan is a JOOQ-based persistence framework: it does not complement but replaces Spring Data and Hibernate, and writes events to the eventlog.events table on every model change. Debezium sends them to Kafka.
  • transactional-event provides transactional events for Jakarta EE: the event is stored in a table together with the transaction and later processed asynchronously by your Handler.
  • boxy is an attempt to turn the outbox table into an event stream with partitions, subscriptions and cursors right in the database, so that a monolith needs no broker at all.

For a typical Spring Boot microservice that has to send events to a broker, only the first three are truly comparable. The other three are worth considering only if their model suits you.

Why ekbatan doesn't fit an existing Spring Data project

ekbatan's limitation matters more than all its other characteristics. According to its documentation, Spring Data JPA can run in the same application, but ekbatan does not integrate with JpaRepository and does not support Spring @Transactional or PlatformTransactionManager: it has its own TransactionManager, and its Action serves as the transaction boundary. An event is written atomically only together with changes made through ActionExecutor. If an order is saved via JPA and the event via ekbatan, these are two separate transactions — exactly the dual-write problem the outbox is supposed to protect against.

So to get an outbox, you have to move your entire data access layer to ekbatan: repositories in JOOQ, models as immutable ekbatan classes, business operations as Actions. In my view, rewriting a layer as fundamental and battle-tested as Spring Data and JPA just for an outbox is an unjustified risk for most projects. The other libraries in this comparison plug into the existing Spring transaction and store the event right next to your usual repository.save(...).

Spring Boot and Java support

In Tandem, Spring is a compileOnly dependency, so the Spring version is determined by your application's BOM.

Library Spring Boot Java Without Spring
Tandem yes 17+ yes, dependency-free core
oncebox yes 17+ no
spring-boot-outbox-starter yes 21 Spring-free core
ekbatan yes 25 Quarkus, Micronaut, plain Java
transactional-event no 11 Jakarta EE 9+, Quarkus
boxy no 17 plain Java only

If your project runs on Spring Boot and Java 21, oncebox, Tandem and spring-boot-outbox-starter all fit.

Outbox for Kafka and RabbitMQ: brokers and databases

Tandem and oncebox support Kafka out of the box. oncebox also supports RabbitMQ 3.12+ with the same starter, API and settings: the broker is selected by the oncebox-kafka or oncebox-rabbit module and the oncebox.outbox.sender.type property. Tandem's RabbitMQ adapter (tandem-rabbitmq) is recent and versioned separately from the library (0.2.0 versus 1.0.0-rc.3). By default Tandem wraps events in a CloudEvents envelope; a custom format is plugged in by implementing a single interface.

spring-boot-outbox-starter has no built-in transport: the demo projects include sinks for Kafka and REST, but in production you write your own. That is a drawback for the typical "send to Kafka" case, but an advantage if you need an outbox for webhooks or external API calls. Channels are isolated from each other: each has its own table, queue and retry settings.

oncebox has the widest database support: PostgreSQL 16+, MySQL 8.0.13+ and Oracle 23+, each as a separate dialect module. On MySQL, the outbox data source must be switched to the READ COMMITTED isolation level: under InnoDB's default REPEATABLE READ, a SKIP LOCKED query takes gap locks, and multiple instances block each other instead of picking up different batches. PostgreSQL and Oracle don't have this problem. ekbatan supports PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB. Tandem and spring-boot-outbox-starter work only with PostgreSQL; MySQL support in Tandem is designed but, according to the author, not implemented. boxy currently contains a schema and stored procedures for MySQL only. transactional-event needs just one table from the database, with the DDL given in the README.

Retries, backoff and DLQ

Each library decides differently what to do with an event that cannot be delivered.

oncebox offers the full set: retries and backoff are configured per event type, events "stuck" in IN_PROCESS after an instance crash are returned to the queue without counting the failed attempt, and once attempts are exhausted the event is atomically moved to the DLQ. The oncebox-dlq-api module adds a REST API for the DLQ: view, requeue or delete. The DLQ is disabled by default.

Tandem retries sending with exponential backoff, and after maxAttempts (10 by default) the event is blocked. The blocked.count metric shows the scale of the problem, and the Admin API (tandem-admin, disabled by default) lets you resend or discard the event. It also lets you pause and resume the relay.

spring-boot-outbox-starter moves an event to DEAD status after max-retries attempts, and RecoveryWorker picks up records with an expired lease. There is no API for working with DEAD records, only SQL.

ekbatan, for in-process handlers, retries the call with bounded exponential backoff and moves the notification to EXPIRED if the event is older than the retention window (7 days by default). transactional-event marks an event as blocked once retries are exhausted; metrics count both blocked and unblocked events.

Polling and per-event-type tuning

oncebox is the only one of the six where outbox behaviour is configured separately for each event type. For order-created and analytics-tracked you can set a different batch size, polling strategy, retry count and backoff, and anything not overridden is inherited from the shared defaults block.

This solves a practical problem: events within one service are not equal. A payment or an order status change must go out in a fraction of a second and be retried quickly, while analytics or search events can be sent in large batches once a minute and retried less often. With shared settings you have to choose: either poll the database often for all types at once, or delay important events along with unimportant ones.

oncebox:
  outbox:
    defaults:
      batch-size: 200
      polling:
        type: adaptive
        min-fixed-delay: 250ms
        max-fixed-delay: 1m
        multiplier: 1.5
      max-retries: 3
      backoff:
        delay: 10s
        multiplier: 3.0
    events:
      payment-completed:
        topic: payments
        polling:
          min-fixed-delay: 100ms   # poll more often, the rest comes from defaults
        max-retries: 10
        backoff:
          delay: 1s
          multiplier: 2.0
      analytics-tracked:
        topic: analytics
        batch-size: 1000
        polling:
          type: fixed
          fixed-delay: 1m          # once a minute in large batches
        backoff:
          enabled: false

Adaptive polling is enabled by default in oncebox: while there are no events, the pause between polls grows by the multiplier up to max-fixed-delay, and as soon as events appear it resets to min-fixed-delay. This way the service reacts quickly to an event stream and puts almost no load on the database when idle. According to the calculation in the oncebox walkthrough on DEV Community, that is about 70 polls per idle hour versus 14,400 with a fixed 250 ms pause; this is an estimate based on the scheduling rule, not a measurement. Retries use exponential backoff: with a 10 s delay and a multiplier of 3, retries happen after 10 s, 30 s, 90 s, 270 s.

Tandem also has adaptive polling: the interval stays at 10 ms while a bucket has events and grows to 100 ms when idle, and on PostgreSQL you can enable instant wake-up via pg-notify. But Tandem's settings are shared across the whole relay and change only on restart. spring-boot-outbox-starter configures batches, retries and leases per channel, that is, per separate table, not per event type within one table. transactional-event has shared polling settings for all events, and ekbatan delegates reading the table to Debezium.

Inbox pattern: consumer-side message deduplication

Inbox is the companion pattern to outbox on the consumer side: it stores the ids of already processed messages and prevents a business operation from running twice. It is needed because any outbox guarantees only at-least-once: if the application crashes after sending to the broker but before marking the record in the table, the event will be sent again. So the consumer has to be able to filter out duplicates.

Only oncebox has a ready-made inbox for a Kafka or RabbitMQ consumer. Since version 2.0.0 it has two idempotent consumers: a transactional one, where the receipt record and the business operation are committed together (effectively-once), and a non-transactional one, where the record is committed before the operation (at-most-once, for side effects such as emails that must not be repeated). The optional oncebox-inbox-cache module adds a Redis cache of records. Records are kept until cleanup (oncebox.inbox.clean-up.ttl, 24 hours by default), so a redelivery after that period is no longer recognised as a duplicate. In practice this leads to three rules: the inbox retention period must cover the longest redelivery window (for example, re-reading old Kafka offsets), the cache TTL must not exceed the inbox retention period, and the cache name must be unique per service, otherwise services sharing a Redis instance will treat each other's events as already processed. The consumer uses the same oncebox-starter, with no separate library.

Tandem does not provide an inbox: each event has a unique id, and the consumer writes deduplication by that id. ekbatan, for in-process handlers, creates one record per "event × handler" pair and ignores repeated inserts, but Kafka consumers downstream of Debezium deduplicate on their own. spring-boot-outbox-starter and transactional-event have no inbox. boxy stores subscription positions in the database and, according to its README, protects against duplicates when a lease is handed over between consumers.

Observability and operations

Tandem has the most operational tooling: Micrometer metrics (backlog age, errors, blocked events, worker health), tracing via Micrometer Tracing or OpenTelemetry, an Admin REST API with an OpenAPI contract, the tandem-cli console tool, and ready-made Grafana demos. The author also publishes benchmarks with raw data: a median latency of 13 ms from COMMIT to Kafka acknowledgement at 600 events/s on a 2 vCPU machine that the relay shares with PostgreSQL and Kafka.

oncebox provides Micrometer metrics for outbox and inbox (the oncebox-metrics module), Grafana dashboards in the repository and a REST API for the DLQ. spring-boot-outbox-starter publishes metrics per channel and event type (outbox_publish_total, outbox_queue_pressure) and a health indicator. ekbatan has OpenTelemetry tracing, transactional-event has MicroProfile metrics.

Maturity and maintenance

All six projects have a single main author, so it is worth looking at versions, release frequency and API stability.

  • oncebox 2.0.0 was released on 15 October 2026; it was preceded by 1.x releases. The project has been developed since October 2025.
  • Tandem is a release candidate: 1.0.0-rc.3 from 5 November 2026, with the API frozen until 1.0.0. The project started in July 2026 and had about 390 commits by November.
  • spring-boot-outbox-starter is at version 0.2.3 from 28 October 2026; the project started in August 2026. A 0.x version means the API may still change; 0.2.0 already included a breaking change to internal classes.
  • ekbatan 1.1.3 was released on 1 November 2026; the project has been developed since November 2025.
  • transactional-event is the oldest of the six: developed since 2021, version 3.4.2 from 12 October 2026. It is the only one here under LGPL-3.0; the rest are Apache-2.0.
  • boxy has no releases and is not published on Maven Central (version 1.0-SNAPSHOT); the last commit was on 15 August 2025. The README roadmap (versions planned for August and September 2025) has not been delivered.

Example: outbox in Spring Boot with Kafka

The task is the same for the three starters that send events from Spring Boot: within a transaction, save an order and write an OrderCreated event to the outbox. The examples are taken from the libraries' READMEs and shortened.

oncebox

Dependencies: io.github.dmitriy-iliyov:oncebox-starter, oncebox-postgresql and oncebox-kafka version 2.0.0; @EnableOncebox on the main class.

oncebox:
  outbox:
    sender:
      type: kafka
    events:
      order-created:
        topic: "orders"

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository repository;
    private final OutboxPublisher outboxPublisher;

    @Transactional
    public Order create(Order order) {
        Order saved = repository.save(order);
        outboxPublisher.publish("order-created", saved);
        return saved;
    }
}

Instead of calling publish, you can put @OutboxPublish(eventType = "order-created") on the method: the return value then becomes the event.

Tandem

Dependencies: the com.codingful:tandem-bom:1.0.0-rc.3 BOM, tandem-spring-producer where events are written, tandem-spring-relay and tandem-kafka where the relay runs.

@Transactional
public Order create(Order order) {
    orderRepository.save(order);
    outboxRepository.insert(OutboxMessage.builder()
        .aggregateId(order.id())
        .aggregateType("Order")
        .type("com.acme.order.created")
        .payload(serialize(order))
        .contentType("application/json")
        .build());
    return order;
}

In Spring, instead of the low-level OutboxRepository, you can use TransactionalOutboxTemplate, the @TransactionalOutbox annotation, or Spring application events.

spring-boot-outbox-starter

Dependency: com.kholodilin:spring-boot-outbox-starter:0.2.3.

@Transactional
public void create(Order order) {
    orderRepository.save(order);
    outboxService
        .eventType("ORDER_CREATED")
        .aggregateId(String.valueOf(order.id()))
        .payload(order)
        .append();
}

@Component
class KafkaOrdersSink implements OutboxSink {
    @Override
    public OutboxPublishResult publish(List<OutboxRecord> batch) {
        // send the batch to Kafka with your own code
        return new OutboxPublishResult.AllSucceeded();
    }
}

Pros and cons

Tandem

  • Pros: instance coordination via leases, Admin API and CLI, detailed metrics and tracing, published benchmarks, the relay can run as a separate container.
  • Cons: still a release candidate; PostgreSQL only; RabbitMQ adapter at 0.x; no inbox; bucketCount cannot be changed after the first deployment.

oncebox

  • Pros: polling (fixed or adaptive), batch size, retries and backoff are configured separately per event type; adaptive polling by default; outbox and inbox in one starter; Kafka and RabbitMQ; PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle; DLQ with a REST API; minimal code — one call or an annotation.

spring-boot-outbox-starter

  • Pros: delivery anywhere via OutboxSink; isolated channels with their own tables and settings; a Redis queue to wake up workers across instances.
  • Cons: you write the broker transport yourself; PostgreSQL only; version 0.x; no API for DEAD events.

ekbatan

  • Pros: events are stored automatically together with the model change, no separate outbox call needed; Spring Boot, Quarkus and Micronaut; GraalVM native image; sharding; distributed jobs.
  • Cons: the main one — the outbox only works if you fully replace Spring Data and JPA with its own JOOQ-based layer; it does not integrate with JpaRepository or Spring @Transactional, so its outbox cannot be embedded in an existing project; requires Java 25; Kafka requires Debezium and Kafka Connect.

transactional-event

  • Pros: the longest history of the six; standard Jakarta EE APIs; a Quarkus extension; works with any JDBC database.
  • Cons: not for Spring; no built-in broker, you write sending in the handler; LGPL-3.0 license.

boxy

  • Pros: an interesting model — partitions, subscriptions and weighted balancing on top of the database, with no broker.
  • Cons: no releases and no artifact on Maven Central; MySQL only; development stopped in August 2025; no framework integration.

Final scores

The article's nine criteria are combined into seven columns: "What it is" and "Platform and Java" are scored together as "Spring Boot integration", and "Where it delivers" and "Databases" together as "Brokers and databases". Each score from 1 to 10 is the author's opinion based on the facts in the comparison table and the sections above; the total is a simple unweighted average of the seven columns. If one criterion matters more to you than the others (for example, the inbox), look at its column rather than the total.

Scores from 1 to 10 across the article's nine criteria, combined into seven columns; the total is an unweighted average
Library Total Spring Boot integration Brokers and databases Failures and DLQ Polling and tuning Inbox Observability Maturity
oncebox 8.8 9 9 9.5 9.5 9.5 8 7
Tandem 7.0 8 6 8.5 7.5 3 9.5 6.5
spring-boot-outbox-starter 5.3 6.5 5 6 6.5 1 7 5
ekbatan 4.7 2.5 5 5 4 4 6 6.5
transactional-event 3.9 1 3 6 4 1 5 7.5
boxy 2.8 1.5 2 3 5 4 3 1

Who should choose what

  • A Spring Boot microservice, Kafka or RabbitMQ. oncebox: a starter, a single publish call, a DLQ and an inbox for the consumer in the same library.
  • Events of different importance in one service: payments must go out instantly, analytics in batches. oncebox: polling, batch size, retries and backoff are set separately for each event type.
  • A service on MySQL or Oracle. oncebox is the only one of the three Spring starters that supports these databases.
  • An outbox for webhooks and external HTTP APIs rather than a broker. oncebox: a starter has NonTransactionalConsumer for this.
  • Jakarta EE or Quarkus. transactional-event.

FAQ

What are the transactional outbox and inbox patterns?

Transactional outbox is a pattern in which a service writes an event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business data, and a separate process sends it to Kafka or RabbitMQ. This way the event is never lost and never sent without the data change. Inbox is the companion pattern on the consumer side: it remembers the ids of processed messages and filters out the duplicates that an at-least-once outbox inevitably produces.

How do I build an inbox and an idempotent Kafka consumer in Spring Boot?

Of the six libraries compared, only oncebox ships a ready-made inbox for Kafka and RabbitMQ: the idempotent consumer wraps processing in a @KafkaListener or @RabbitListener and records the event id in the database. The transactional variant commits the record together with the business operation (effectively-once), the non-transactional one commits it before the operation (at-most-once). With the other libraries, deduplication by event id is written by hand.

Which Spring Boot outbox library supports both Kafka and RabbitMQ?

oncebox supports Kafka 3.7+ (the oncebox-kafka module) and RabbitMQ 3.12+ (oncebox-rabbit). Tandem delivers to Kafka and supports RabbitMQ through a separate tandem-rabbitmq 0.2.0 module with its own version. spring-boot-outbox-starter is broker-agnostic: you write delivery to Kafka or RabbitMQ yourself in an OutboxSink implementation.

Does transactional-event work with Spring Boot?

No. transactional-event is written for Jakarta EE 9+ and requires CDI 3.0, JTA 2.0 and Concurrency Utilities 2.0; there is a separate Quarkus extension. The project has no Spring integration.

Can ekbatan be added to an existing Spring Data JPA project?

Not as an outbox. Spring Data JPA can run in the same application, but ekbatan does not integrate with JpaRepository and does not support Spring @Transactional, and events are atomic only with changes made through its Action and ActionExecutor. A JPA entity change and an ekbatan event will not end up in one transaction, so for an outbox you would have to rewrite the data access layer in JOOQ. On top of that, ekbatan requires Java 25.

Do these libraries need Debezium?

Only ekbatan, if events must go to Kafka: there they are published by Debezium with the project's SMT plugins. Tandem and oncebox send events themselves by polling the outbox table, spring-boot-outbox-starter calls your OutboxSink, and boxy and transactional-event work without a broker.

About the author

Miguel Carvalho. Java and Kotlin developer with 7 years of Spring experience and more than 5 years working on distributed systems with Kafka and RabbitMQ. Active open source contributor.

title: Godot UI with AI: a main menu and settings screen that don't clip (tested)
description:
Can an AI build Godot UI that holds together when the window changes size? We asked Ziva, an AI agent that runs inside the Godot editor, for a main menu and a settings screen made of Control nodes. In 3 minutes 58 seconds it built both scenes, ran the game, clicked Settings and Back, and checked the layout at five window sizes. Nothing was clipped. It also missed something: the Fullscreen checkbox was nearly invisible when unchecked, and Ziva reported "all controls showing". A second prompt asking it to look closely caught and fixed it.

Layout is where people say AI help breaks down. On r/ClaudeAI one developer wrote that "Claude does not do a very good job in creating and modifying scenes for Godot … Elements are often partially clipped" (thread). On r/aigamedev another wrote, "I can burn through Claude's usage limit in a single session just trying to fix layouts and styling" (thread). And without any AI involved, a Godot forum post says "Making UIs almost takes up 80% of my time" (thread).

Ziva.sh makes Ziva and wrote this test. We ran it on 10 November 2026 with Godot 4.7.2 on Linux, using a development build of Ziva on Ziva Smart, the default model, with auto-approve on. It is one project and one run, so treat it as an example, not a benchmark. Below are the layout Ziva built (you can copy it by hand), how it checked the result, the miss, and a checklist.

The prompt

A fresh project with no UI in it. The prompt, word for word:

Make a main menu for my game in res://ui_demo/: the game title and Play, Settings and Quit buttons, centered. Settings should open a settings screen with a Master volume slider, a Fullscreen checkbox, a Resolution dropdown (1280x720 and 1920x1080) and a Back button that returns to the menu. Nothing should be clipped or overlapping, and it should still look right if the window is resized. Check it with screenshots and click through Settings and Back to make sure they work.

The layout Ziva built

Ziva wrote two scripts and two scenes in res://ui_demo/. The main menu:

MainMenu (Control, Full Rect anchors, main_menu.gd)
├── Background (ColorRect, Full Rect)
├── MenuPanel (CenterContainer, Full Rect)
│   └── MenuBox (VBoxContainer, separation 20)
│       ├── Title (Label "My Game", font size 56)
│       ├── PlayButton (Button, custom_minimum_size 260 x 52)
│       ├── SettingsButton (Button, custom_minimum_size 260 x 52)
│       └── QuitButton (Button, custom_minimum_size 260 x 52)
└── SettingsScreen (instance of settings_screen.tscn, hidden)

The settings screen is its own scene with its own opaque background, instanced into the menu and hidden until needed:

SettingsScreen (Control, Full Rect anchors, settings_screen.gd)
├── Background (ColorRect, Full Rect)
└── Center (CenterContainer, Full Rect)
    └── Margin (MarginContainer, 24 px margins)
        └── VBox (VBoxContainer, separation 16)
            ├── Title (Label "Settings")
            ├── VolumeRow (HBoxContainer)
            │   ├── Label "Master Volume" (Expand)
            │   └── VolumeSlider (HSlider 0 to 1, min width 220)
            ├── FullscreenCheck (CheckBox)
            ├── ResolutionRow (HBoxContainer)
            │   ├── Label "Resolution" (Expand)
            │   └── ResolutionOption (OptionButton, min width 220)
            └── BackButton (Button, 240 x 48, Shrink Center)

Settings hides MenuPanel and shows the settings screen; the settings screen emits a back_requested signal, and the menu shows itself again and gives Play keyboard focus. Quit calls get_tree().quit(). Play only prints a placeholder message, because the project had no game scene to load, and Ziva said so. The settings handlers, as Ziva wrote them:

func _on_volume_changed(value: float) -> void:
    var db: float = linear_to_db(value) if value > 0.0 else -80.0
    AudioServer.set_bus_volume_db(AudioServer.get_bus_index("Master"), db)

func _on_fullscreen_toggled(toggled_on: bool) -> void:
    var mode: DisplayServer.WindowMode = DisplayServer.WINDOW_MODE_FULLSCREEN if toggled_on else DisplayServer.WINDOW_MODE_WINDOWED
    DisplayServer.window_set_mode(mode)

func _on_resolution_selected(index: int) -> void:
    if index < 0 or index >= RESOLUTIONS.size():
        return
    DisplayServer.window_set_size(RESOLUTIONS[index])
    _center_window()

The settings are not saved between launches. The prompt did not ask for that and Ziva did not add it. If you need it, write the values to a ConfigFile in user://.

Why this layout doesn't clip

Most clipped Godot UI comes from controls placed by hand. A control's offsets are pixel distances from an anchor point, by default the parent's top-left corner (Size and anchors). A button placed at x = 900 in a 1152-pixel window sits outside a 640-pixel one.

The layout above has no hand-placed child positions:

  • The root fills the window. MainMenu, Background and MenuPanel use the Full Rect anchor preset (anchors 0 to 1 on both axes), so they always match the window.
  • A CenterContainer does the centering. It "automatically keeps all of its child controls centered within it at their minimum size" (Using Containers).
  • Box containers stack the rows. Inside a container, "all children Control nodes give up their own positioning ability" (same page), so a resize re-lays out everything.
  • Minimum sizes set the size. The buttons get their size from custom_minimum_size, and the labels in each settings row have Expand set so the label and the 220-pixel slider or dropdown share the row without overlapping.

One limit: a container never shrinks its children below their minimum size. Ziva's menu box is 260 x 293 pixels, so in a window shorter than 293 pixels it no longer fits. If your game must work in very small windows, or should scale the UI up on big screens, set Project Settings > Display > Window > Stretch > Mode to canvas_items (Multiple resolutions). Ziva's project kept the default, Disabled, so on a 1920 x 1080 window the menu stays the same pixel size in the middle of a larger screen.

How Ziva checked it

Ziva's run_scene tool runs a scene from the editor, sends input and returns a screenshot. Ziva used it three times:

  1. Run the menu and look at the screenshot. It also fixed an integer-division warning from the run's output.
  2. Run again and click the button labelled Settings. The screenshot showed the settings screen, and Ziva wrote: "Settings screen opens with all controls showing, nothing clipped."
  3. Run again, clicking Settings and then Back. The screenshot showed the menu with Play focused.

run_scene runs the game at the project's window size (here Godot's default, 1152 x 648) and can't resize it, so screenshots alone could not show a resize. Ziva noted that and wrote a GDScript test that loaded the menu at several window sizes and checked that the menu box and the settings box stayed inside the window. Its first measurement said neither fit at 1152 x 648. Ziva decided the layout had not been applied on the first frame and reran 1152 x 648 with a warm-up, plus 800 x 450 and 3840 x 2160. Across both runs it passed at 640 x 360, 800 x 450, 1152 x 648, 1920 x 1080 and 3840 x 2160.

We then ran our own check on a copy of the project: at 1152 x 648, 640 x 360, 1920 x 1080 and 800 x 600, no visible Control was outside the window or smaller than its content, Settings opened, and Back returned to the menu.

The miss: an invisible checkbox

Both checks passed a settings screen with a problem. With Godot's default theme the unchecked CheckBox box is dark, and on Ziva's dark background it almost disappeared, so "Fullscreen" looked like a plain label. Ziva's own screenshot showed it, and Ziva still reported all controls showing. Our geometry check could not see it either: the checkbox was the right size and inside the window.

We sent a second prompt in the same chat:

Look closely at the settings screen in a screenshot. Is every control easy to see and use? Fix anything that isn't, then show me the settings screen again.

This time Ziva opened its earlier screenshot and said the Fullscreen checkbox "looks like plain centered text with no visible indicator". It built a throwaway scene with a checked and an unchecked CheckBox on the same background, ran it, and confirmed that only the checked one showed a box. Then it added code to settings_screen.gd that draws its own checked and unchecked icons into a Theme on the checkbox, and ran the menu twice more, clicking Settings and then Fullscreen to see both states. Our check afterwards passed at the same four sizes, with the checkbox outline visible.

Two things to know about that fix. Drawing icons pixel by pixel in a script works, but about 60 lines of code for one checkbox is a lot; in your own project a Theme resource with checkbox icons, set on the root Control, does the same for every CheckBox below it, because themes apply to a control and its children (GUI skinning). And Ziva left the throwaway scene, ui_demo/_tmp_check.tscn, in the project. It said so in its reply: it "didn't delete it since removal wasn't requested" and offered to remove it.

Time and cost

  • First prompt: 3 min 58 s, $0.033 of Ziva usage on Ziva Smart, the default model.
  • Follow-up prompt: 4 min 6 s, $0.036.

What this test does not show

One simple UI, the default theme, one run. We did not check that Fullscreen and Resolution change a real desktop window, or keyboard and gamepad navigation between the controls. Ziva's run window is embedded in the editor and only supports windowed mode, as Ziva pointed out. A larger UI, a custom theme or a different model may give different results.

Checklist: a Godot menu and settings screen that don't clip

Whether you build it yourself or ask an AI, these steps follow the layout above:

  1. Add a root Control and choose Full Rect from the anchor preset menu in the toolbar above the viewport.
  2. Add a ColorRect background, also Full Rect.
  3. Add a CenterContainer (Full Rect) and a VBoxContainer inside it. Put the title and buttons in the VBoxContainer.
  4. Size buttons with Custom Minimum Size instead of dragging their handles.
  5. Make the settings screen its own scene with its own background. Instance it in the menu, hide it, and show or hide it from the menu script. Use HBoxContainers for label and control rows, with Expand on the labels.
  6. Check several window sizes. Run the scene and resize the window, or run a script like the one below.
  7. Look at a screenshot of every screen on its real background, in every state (checked and unchecked, focused and not). A layout check can't tell you a control is hard to see.

Here is a short size check, based on what Ziva did. Save it in the project folder and run godot --headless --path . --script check_layout.gd:

extends SceneTree

func _initialize() -> void:
    var menu: Control = load("res://ui_demo/main_menu.tscn").instantiate()
    root.add_child(menu)
    # The window applies its own size on the first frame, so measuring before this reads a stale layout.
    await process_frame
    for size: Vector2i in [Vector2i(640, 360), Vector2i(1152, 648), Vector2i(1920, 1080), Vector2i(400, 240)]:
        root.size = size
        for i in 4:
            await process_frame
        var box: Rect2 = menu.get_node("MenuPanel/MenuBox").get_global_rect()
        print(size, " menu fits: ", Rect2(Vector2.ZERO, Vector2(size)).encloses(box))
    quit()

On Ziva's menu it prints true for the first three sizes and false for 400 x 240, the minimum-size limit described above.

To try Ziva on your own UI, see installation. We ran the same kind of test on a broken shader and on collision bugs.

FAQ

Can AI build UI in Godot?

In our test, mostly yes. We asked Ziva, an AI agent that runs inside the Godot editor, for a main menu and a settings screen made of Control nodes. In about 4 minutes it built both scenes, clicked through Settings and Back in the running game, and checked the layout at five window sizes. It missed one problem: the unchecked Fullscreen checkbox was nearly invisible on the dark background. A second prompt asking it to look closely caught and fixed that. This was one project and one run on 10 November 2026, so treat it as an example, not a benchmark.

How do I make a Godot main menu that doesn't clip when the window is resized?

Build it from containers instead of hand-placed positions. Give the root Control the Full Rect anchor preset so it always matches the window, add a CenterContainer with Full Rect anchors, put a VBoxContainer inside it, and size the buttons with Custom Minimum Size. Children of a container give up their own positioning, so the container re-centers them whenever the window changes size. A container never shrinks its children below their minimum size, so very small windows still need a stretch mode such as canvas_items.

How do I make a settings menu in Godot with volume, fullscreen and resolution?

Make the settings screen its own scene, instance it in the menu scene, and show or hide it from the menu script. For the controls: an HSlider from 0 to 1 sets the Master bus volume with AudioServer.set_bus_volume_db and linear_to_db, a CheckBox switches DisplayServer.window_set_mode between fullscreen and windowed, and an OptionButton calls DisplayServer.window_set_size with the chosen resolution. Save the values with ConfigFile if they should survive a restart.

How do I test a Godot UI at different window sizes?

Run the scene and resize the game window, or run a short script that sets the root window size to several values, waits a few frames for the containers to lay out, and checks that each container's rectangle is inside the window. Wait one frame before the first measurement: in our test, Ziva's first measurement read a stale layout. A layout check cannot tell you whether a control is easy to see, so also look at a screenshot.

Why is my Godot CheckBox invisible on a dark background?

With Godot 4.7.2's default theme, the unchecked CheckBox box is drawn dark. On the dark background Ziva chose (Color(0.09, 0.1, 0.14)), the unchecked box almost disappeared, while the checked box was clearly visible. Fix it with your own checked and unchecked icons in a Theme resource, or use a lighter background behind the checkbox.

title: TikTok watermarked vs clean: what the API options really mean
description:
When I wired TikTok downloads into ramrom.io, I assumed there would be one video file per link. Paste the link, get the MP4, done. The provider's API had other ideas. It offered two versions of the same video: one with a watermark, one without. Choosing between them turned out to be one of the more interesting decisions in the whole downloader, because the two files are not made the same way at all.

What the watermark actually is

A TikTok watermark is not a picture stamped over the video after the fact. It is baked into the video file TikTok serves to the web player. When you watch a TikTok in a browser, the file you are watching already has the username and the logo bouncing around the frame. That is the "watermarked" version, and it is the easy one to fetch: it is the same file the public player uses, served from TikTok's own CDN.

The "clean" version, the one without the watermark, is a different file entirely. When the TikTok app saves a video to your camera roll, it requests a separate, watermark-free render from TikTok's servers. The provider APIs that offer a no-watermark option are really asking for that app-style render, or for the raw file the creator uploaded before TikTok added the overlay. Either way, it is a second file, fetched through a different route.

Why the clean one fails more often

This explains something I kept seeing in my logs. Watermarked links resolved quickly and reliably. Clean links failed far more often, and when they failed they failed in confusing ways: sometimes a 403, sometimes a short redirect chain that ended at an error page, sometimes a file that played fine but had no audio track. The reason is simple once you know the two files are different. The watermarked file is the public one, meant to be shared, so TikTok's servers hand it out freely. The clean file is closer to the original upload, and TikTok guards it more carefully. It is the one that gets rate limited first, the one whose URL expires sooner, and the one that disappears when a creator changes their privacy settings.

There is also a quirk I did not expect. Some providers return a "clean" file that is really the watermarked file with the watermarked parts cropped out, or a lower-quality re-encode. The resolution looks the same in the file name, but the video is softer and the edges are cut. So "no watermark" does not always mean "the original file". It sometimes means "the original file, processed again, and not necessarily well".

What I do on my site

I offer both options and I label them honestly. The watermarked version is the default because it works more often and it is the version TikTok itself puts in front of viewers. The clean version is there for people who want it, but the button says what it is, and when the clean endpoint fails I say so plainly instead of silently falling back to the watermarked file. That fallback would be dishonest: the visitor asked for one thing and got another.

Behind the scenes, my resolve step asks the provider for both URLs at once, when the provider supports it. If the clean URL comes back empty, or the file it points to is not a real video, I show the watermarked option only, with a short note. The check is cheap: I send a HEAD request and look at the content type and the file size before I ever show a download button. A video file that is 40KB is not a video. It is an error page with a .mp4 name.

One last thing worth saying plainly. Downloading someone else's TikTok without the watermark removes the credit to the creator. The watermark is how the creator's name travels with the video. I am not going to lecture visitors, but a downloader should be honest about what the two options are, and not pretend the clean version is just the same file minus a logo. It is a different file, fetched a different way, with different failure modes. Once you know that, the API options stop looking like a simple toggle and start looking like what they are: two separate downloads, each with its own trade-offs.

title: ResQAdam: Residual-Preserving Adaptive Optimization for Memory-Efficient Quantization Aware Training
description:
arXiv:2611.08924v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top-r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r x r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%.

title: I added a CSV contact importer to a shadcn registry
description:
I build CSVJetty, an embedded CSV importer for React. I’ve published a shadcn registry item that adds a contact-import card and an account-free demo to your project.

The importer handles CSV upload, column mapping, validation, and inline correction. The example expects a name and email, with an optional company field.

The integration source is MIT licensed. The importer interface runs through the hosted CSVJetty service; production use requires an account and public importer key.

Install

In a React or Next.js project with shadcn already configured:

npx shadcn@latest add https://www.csvjetty.com/r/contact-csv-import.json

The registry declares the csvjetty npm dependency and shadcn Card and Table dependencies.

Try it without an account

For a Next.js App Router page:

"use client";

import { ContactCsvImportDemo } from "@/components/contact-csv-import-demo";

export default function ContactsPage() {
  return (
    <main className="mx-auto max-w-3xl p-6">
      <ContactCsvImportDemo />
    </main>
  );
}

Save this as contacts.csv:

Full Name,Work Email,Organization
Alex Chen,alex@example.com,Acme
Sam Rivera,not-an-email,Example Inc

Upload it, match the columns, and correct the invalid email. The demo displays the latest received batch in your browser. It does not save contacts to a database.

You can also try the hosted demo before installing.

Connect it to your application

The installed ContactCsvImport component accepts a public importerKey and an onData callback. That callback is where your application saves the records.

The callback can await your API request. Throwing an error reports a failed save; returning row-level errors lets you identify records your backend rejected.

Your backend still needs to authenticate requests, validate records, and handle repeated deliveries safely.

The registry provides the contact-import integration and preview. Your application supplies persistence.

Source and integration instructions · Callback documentation

If you try it, I’d be interested in where the mapping or correction flow gets confusing.
