title: Watching every chain, not just the hot wallet: a small outflow monitor in Node
description:
On 2 November 2026 the Brazilian exchange Mercado Bitcoin paused deposits and withdrawals after funds moved out of wallets linked to it. According to CertiK, the attacker spent about four hours on eight smaller chains, including Base, Optimism and Arbitrum, before reaching the central hot wallets. Hypernative estimated the total outflow at about $40 million.

Four hours on side chains is a long window. If your alerting only watches the busiest wallet, that's time you don't see. Here's a small script that watches outgoing native transfers from a list of addresses on several EVM chains and flags anything over a threshold.

It uses only Node 18+ (built-in fetch) and public JSON-RPC endpoints. Swap in your own RPC URLs and addresses.

// outflow-watch.mjs (run: node outflow-watch.mjs)
const CHAINS = {
  base: 'https://mainnet.base.org',
  optimism: 'https://mainnet.optimism.io',
  arbitrum: 'https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc',
};
// addresses you operate (lowercase)
const WATCH = new Set([
  '0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000',
]);
const THRESHOLD_ETH = 0.5;

async function rpc(url, method, params) {
  const r = await fetch(url, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: 1, method, params }),
  });
  const j = await r.json();
  if (j.error) throw new Error(`${method}: ${j.error.message}`);
  return j.result;
}

const last = {};

async function scan(name, url) {
  const head = parseInt(await rpc(url, 'eth_blockNumber', []), 16);
  const from = last[name] ?? head; // start at the head on first run
  for (let n = from + 1; n <= head; n++) {
    const block = await rpc(url, 'eth_getBlockByNumber', ['0x' + n.toString(16), true]);
    for (const tx of block.transactions) {
      if (!tx.from || !WATCH.has(tx.from.toLowerCase())) continue;
      const eth = Number(BigInt(tx.value)) / 1e18;
      if (eth >= THRESHOLD_ETH) {
        console.log(`[ALERT] ${name} block ${n}: ${eth} ETH from ${tx.from} to ${tx.to} (${tx.hash})`);
      }
    }
  }
  last[name] = head;
}

async function loop() {
  for (const [name, url] of Object.entries(CHAINS)) {
    try { await scan(name, url); } catch (e) { console.error(name, e.message); }
  }
}

await loop();
setInterval(loop, 15_000);

A few notes on taking this further:

  • Native transfers are only part of it. ERC-20 outflows show up as Transfer logs, so add an eth_getLogs call filtered on the Transfer topic with your addresses as the from topic.
  • Fast chains produce a lot of blocks. For production, use eth_getLogs over ranges, or a provider's webhook, rather than pulling full blocks one at a time.
  • Alert on rate as well as size. Many small transfers from many addresses can matter more than one big one. In this incident, CryptoTicker reported small amounts swept from about 27,160 addresses into one.
  • Give every chain the same thresholds and on-call routing. The smaller chain is often where nobody is looking.

What does your team monitor on the chains that see the least traffic?

Sources: CryptoTicker (citing CertiK and Cointelegraph), CriptoNoticias and Tecnoblog, all 2 Nov 2026.

title: Optimizing Real-Time Computer Vision Inference Pipelines in Python for Edge Monitoring
description:
The Latency Bottleneck in Edge Vision

Running object detection models like YOLOv8 on edge hardware requires careful memory and frame-rate management. Processing every single frame from a camera stream often saturates the CPU/GPU without adding meaningful diagnostic value—especially when monitoring slow-changing physical environments like plant health or industrial gauges.

In this guide, we will implement a frame-sampling and asynchronous inference wrapper in Python to keep latency low and resource usage predictable.

Designing a Non-Blocking Inference Queue

Instead of running model inference directly inside the camera capture loop, we decouple frame capture from model execution using a bounded queue.Queue of size 1. This ensures the model always evaluates the most recent frame while dropping stale frames automatically.

import threading
import queue
import time

class EdgeInferencePipeline:
    def __init__(self, model, target_fps: float = 2.0):
        self.model = model
        self.interval = 1.0 / target_fps
        self.frame_queue = queue.Queue(maxsize=1)
        self.running = False

    def push_frame(self, frame):
        if self.frame_queue.full():
            try:
                self.frame_queue.get_nowait()
            except queue.Empty:
                pass
        self.frame_queue.put(frame)

    def _worker(self):
        while self.running:
            start_time = time.perf_counter()
            try:
                frame = self.frame_queue.get(timeout=1.0)
                results = self.model.predict(frame, verbose=False)
                self.handle_detections(results)
            except queue.Empty:
                continue

            elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start_time
            sleep_time = max(0.0, self.interval - elapsed)
            time.sleep(sleep_time)

    def handle_detections(self, results):
        for r in results:
            boxes = r.boxes
            print(f"Detected {len(boxes)} objects at {time.strftime('%X')}")

    def start(self):
        self.running = True
        threading.Thread(target=self._worker, daemon=True).start()

    def stop(self):
        self.running = False

Adding Basic Telemetry Metrics

To monitor how healthy our inference service is in production, we should track average inference duration and frame drop rates:

def measure_inference(model, sample_image):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    _ = model.predict(sample_image, verbose=False)
    latency_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000
    print(f"Inference latency: {latency_ms:.2f} ms")
    return latency_ms

Conclusion

Decoupling frame capture from model inference prevents memory leaks and keeps edge hardware responsive. Combined with lightweight latency logging, you can reliably deploy computer vision models on local hardware without cloud round-trip delays.

title: Your agent doesn't know Korea's 2026 holidays. Here's a $0.003 fix over x402
description:
In April 2026 South Korea made two more days public holidays: Labor Day (노동절, May 1) and Constitution Day (제헌절, July 17). A model trained before that will tell you May 1 is a normal working day in Korea. It isn't anymore.

That matters the moment an agent does anything with dates: payment due dates, delivery estimates, contract deadlines, "3 business days after signing". Korea also has substitute holidays (대체공휴일) whose rules differ by holiday, plus lunar holidays (설날, 추석) that move every year. Getting this right from memory is unreliable.

So we built KoreaKit: a small API that answers these questions deterministically, with the legal basis and a data date in every response. Agents pay per call with x402 (USDC on Base). No signup, no API key.

What it answers

Is May 1, 2026 a business day in Korea?

GET https://koreakit.celee.workers.dev/v1/holidays/check?date=2026-05-01

{
  "date": "2026-05-01",
  "weekday": "Fri",
  "is_holiday": true,
  "is_business_day": false,
  "holidays": [{ "date": "2026-05-01", "name": "노동절", "name_en": "Labor Day", "type": "public" }],
  "meta": { "as_of": "2026-10-28", "basis": "공휴일에 관한 법률 · 관공서의 공휴일에 관한 규정 …" }
}

Three business days after Wednesday, Sep 23, 2026? Chuseok (Sep 24–26) and the weekend get skipped:

GET /v1/business-days/add?date=2026-09-23&days=3   →   "result": "2026-09-30"

Business days between Sep 21 and Oct 9, 2026 (both inclusive)? 15 weekdays, minus two Chuseok days, the substitute holiday for National Foundation Day (Oct 5), and Hangul Day (Oct 9):

GET /v1/business-days/count?from=2026-09-21&to=2026-10-09   →   "business_days": 11

Other endpoints:

Endpoint What it does
/v1/holidays?year=2026 All holidays of a year (2015–2050), Korean and English names
/v1/lunar/to-solar, /v1/lunar/from-solar Korean lunar ↔ Gregorian, with 간지 names
/v1/text/amount?n=1234500 Amount in words for invoices: 금 일백이십삼만사천오백원정, 壹佰貳拾參萬肆仟伍佰
/v1/text/romanize Revised Romanization incl. sound changes (종로 → jongno)
/v1/validate/brn Business registration number (사업자등록번호) checksum

How payment works

Every endpoint is a plain GET. Without payment you get 402 Payment Required with a PAYMENT-REQUIRED header (x402 v2). Any x402 client pays and retries:

import { wrapFetchWithPaymentFromConfig } from '@x402/fetch';
import { ExactEvmScheme } from '@x402/evm';

const pay = wrapFetchWithPaymentFromConfig(fetch, {
  schemes: [{ network: 'eip155:8453', client: new ExactEvmScheme(account) }],
});
const res = await pay('https://koreakit.celee.workers.dev/v1/holidays/check?date=2026-05-01');
console.log(await res.json());
  • Price: 0.003 USDC per call on Base mainnet.
  • Bad input is free. Parameters are validated before any payment is verified or settled, so a malformed request returns a free 400 with an error message and is never charged.
  • Discoverable: listed in the Coinbase x402 Bazaar and on Agentic.Market, with OpenAPI at /openapi.json and /llms.txt.

For humans: free calculators

The same engine powers two free pages (Korean UI):

  • Business-day calculator: N business days later, and business days in a range, showing which weekday holidays were skipped
  • Amount in words: how to read a number, the contract form 금○○원정, and 갖은자 hanja

Limits, stated plainly

  • Temporary holidays (임시공휴일) are designated ad hoc by the government. We add them when announced; nobody can predict them in advance. Every response carries as_of so you know how fresh the data is.
  • Lunar conversion follows KASI data for 1000–2050.
  • No personal data is processed.

KoreaKit is operated by WiseLake Inc. Questions or a holiday we missed: wiselake@wiselake.ai.

title: # NestJS Validation
description:
DTO pattern, class-validator, class-transformer, built-in Pipes,
custom Pipes, and global ValidationPipe setup

These notes explain how NestJS receives data from a request, checks
whether that data is valid, and converts it into the format your
application expects.

The examples use a simple API for creating and fetching posts. You can
adapt the same ideas to users, profiles, authentication, or other
modules.

1. Why do we need validation?

Imagine your API has an endpoint that creates a post. It expects a
request body like this:

{
  "content": "Learning NestJS",
  "visibility": "public"
}

But a client might accidentally send:

{
  "content": 12345,
  "visibility": "everyone"
}

Without validation, incorrect data may travel deeper into your
application and cause unexpected behaviour or database errors.

Validation helps us check incoming data at the API boundary. We can
reject invalid requests early and return a clear error response.

The basic idea: Do not blindly trust data coming from the client.
Validate it before using it.

2. What is the DTO pattern?

DTO stands for Data Transfer Object.

A DTO describes the shape of data that is allowed to move into or out of
an application layer. In NestJS, DTO classes are commonly used to
describe the data an endpoint expects from the client.

For example, when a client creates a post, the API may expect:

  • content: a string.
  • visibility: either "public" or "private".

We can describe that structure with a DTO.

export class CreatePostDto {
  content: string;
  visibility: 'public' | 'private';
}

A controller can then use that DTO as the type of its request body:

@Post()
createPost(@Body() createPostDto: CreatePostDto) {
  return this.postsService.create(createPostDto);
}

Why use DTOs instead of accepting any object?

DTOs give the request a clear structure.

They help you:

  • Understand what data an endpoint expects.
  • Keep controller method signatures readable.
  • Reuse request shapes where appropriate.
  • Attach validation rules to incoming fields.
  • Avoid passing arbitrary request data directly into your business logic.

DTOs are not database entities

A DTO and a database entity serve different purposes.

DTO Entity / database model

Describes data accepted or returned Describes how data is represented
by an API operation. or persisted in the database.

Designed around an API use case. Designed around storage and
relationships.

May contain validation rules. Usually contains
persistence-related structure and
behaviour.

For example, a CreateUserDto might accept a password. Your database
user model should store a password hash, not the raw password. The DTO
and database model should not automatically be treated as the same
thing.

A useful naming convention

Common DTO names include:

  • CreatePostDto
  • UpdatePostDto
  • LoginDto
  • RegisterUserDto
  • GetPostsQueryDto

The name should make the purpose of the incoming data clear.

3. What are class-validator and class-transformer?

NestJS commonly uses two packages alongside DTO classes.

class-validator

class-validator checks whether values satisfy validation rules.

For example:

  • Is this value a string?
  • Is this email address valid?
  • Is this number within an allowed range?
  • Is this field optional?
  • Is this string within a certain length?

Install it with:

npm install class-validator

class-transformer

class-transformer helps convert plain JavaScript objects into class
instances and can transform values.

For example, data parsed from an HTTP request normally starts as a plain
object. The ValidationPipe can use class-transformer to turn that
object into an instance of your DTO class.

Install it with:

npm install class-transformer

How are they different?

Package Main responsibility

class-validator Checks whether values follow the
rules defined by decorators.

class-transformer Converts plain objects into class
instances and transforms values.

An easy way to remember:

  • Transformer: prepares or converts the incoming object.
  • Validator: checks whether the prepared data follows the rules.

They work together, but they do different jobs.

4. Adding validation decorators to a DTO

Validation decorators are placed above DTO properties.

import { IsString, IsNotEmpty, MaxLength, IsIn } from 'class-validator';

export class CreatePostDto {
  @IsString()
  @IsNotEmpty()
  @MaxLength(280)
  content: string;

  @IsIn(['public', 'private'])
  visibility: 'public' | 'private';
}

Let's understand the decorators.

Decorator What it checks

@IsString() The value must be a string.
@IsNotEmpty() The value must not be empty.
@MaxLength(280) The string must not exceed 280 characters.
@IsIn([...]) The value must match one of the listed options.

Now, if a client sends a number as content, or uses an unsupported
visibility value, validation can reject the request.

More commonly used decorators 

import {
  IsString,
  IsNumber,
  IsBoolean,
  IsEmail,
  IsOptional,
  IsNotEmpty,
  Min,
  Max,
  MinLength,
  MaxLength,
  IsEnum,
  IsArray,
  ArrayMinSize,
  IsUUID,
} from 'class-validator';

Examples:

export class RegisterUserDto {
  @IsString()
  @IsNotEmpty()
  username: string;

  @IsEmail()
  email: string;

  @IsString()
  @MinLength(8)
  password: string;
}

export class PaginationDto {
  @IsNumber()
  @Min(1)
  page: number;

  @IsNumber()
  @Min(1)
  @Max(100)
  limit: number;
}

The decorator only defines the rule. The rules are actually executed
when a validation mechanism, such as NestJS's ValidationPipe,
processes the DTO.

5. Optional fields with @IsOptional()

Sometimes a field is not required.

For example, a user may update their profile without changing their bio.

import { IsOptional, IsString, MaxLength } from 'class-validator';

export class UpdateProfileDto {
  @IsOptional()
  @IsString()
  @MaxLength(160)
  bio?: string;
}

@IsOptional() tells class-validator to skip the other validators for
that property when its value is null or undefined.

The ? in bio?: string is TypeScript syntax. It says the property may
be absent from the type.

These two pieces are related, but they are not identical:

  • ? describes optionality to TypeScript.
  • @IsOptional() affects runtime validation.

If your API should allow an omitted field but reject null, be careful:
@IsOptional() skips validation for both null and undefined. You
may need a different validation rule for that requirement.

6. Nested DTOs and @ValidateNested()

Sometimes the request contains an object inside another object.

Example request:

{
  "content": "Hello",
  "author": {
    "name": "Rohith",
    "email": "rohith@example.com"
  }
}

Create a separate DTO for the nested object:

import { IsEmail, IsString, ValidateNested } from 'class-validator';
import { Type } from 'class-transformer';

export class AuthorDto {
  @IsString()
  name: string;

  @IsEmail()
  email: string;
}

export class CreatePostDto {
  @IsString()
  content: string;

  @ValidateNested()
  @Type(() => AuthorDto)
  author: AuthorDto;
}

Why are both decorators used?

  • @ValidateNested() tells class-validator to validate the nested object.
  • @Type(() => AuthorDto) tells class-transformer what class should be used for that nested value.

Without the transformation metadata, nested plain objects may not be
converted into the expected class instances, so nested validation may
not work as intended.

For an array of nested objects, use @ValidateNested({ each: true })
and @Type(() => SomeDto).

7. What is a Pipe in NestJS?

A Pipe is a class that can run before a route handler receives a value.

A pipe can do two important jobs:

  1. Transformation: Convert incoming data into another form.
  2. Validation: Check incoming data and reject it if it is invalid.

For example, a route parameter arrives as text:

GET /posts/123

The value of id initially comes from the URL as a string. A pipe can
convert it into a number before the controller method uses it.

Where do Pipes fit in the request flow?

A simplified flow looks like this:

Client sends HTTP request
        |
        v
NestJS receives the request
        |
        v
Guards and interceptors (where configured)
        |
        v
Pipes process route arguments
        |
        v
Controller method runs
        |
        v
Service / business logic
        |
        v
Response goes back to the client

The important point for this topic is that pipes process values before
those values are passed to the controller handler.

8. Built-in Pipes

NestJS provides ready-made pipes for common tasks. You do not need to
create your own pipe for every simple conversion or validation.

Some useful built-in pipes are:

Pipe Purpose

ValidationPipe Validates incoming data using DTO
validation metadata.

ParseIntPipe Converts a value to an integer or
throws an error.

ParseFloatPipe Converts a value to a number with a
decimal part or throws an error.

ParseBoolPipe Parses a boolean value or throws an
error.

ParseUUIDPipe Checks whether a value is a valid
UUID.

ParseArrayPipe Parses and validates array input
according to its options.

DefaultValuePipe Supplies a default value when the
input is null or undefined.

ParseEnumPipe Checks whether a value belongs to a
specified enum.

Example: ParseIntPipe 

import { Controller, Get, Param, ParseIntPipe } from '@nestjs/common';

@Controller('posts')
export class PostsController {
  @Get(':id')
  findOne(@Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number) {
    return { id };
  }
}

If the client requests /posts/123, the pipe converts the route
parameter into the number 123.

If the client requests /posts/abc, parsing fails and NestJS returns an
error instead of passing an invalid number to the controller.

Example: ParseBoolPipe 

@Get('status')
getStatus(@Query('active', ParseBoolPipe) active: boolean) {
  return { active };
}

A valid boolean query value is parsed before the handler runs. Invalid
values are rejected.

Example: DefaultValuePipe 

import { DefaultValuePipe, ParseIntPipe } from '@nestjs/common';

@Get()
findAll(
  @Query('limit', new DefaultValuePipe(10), ParseIntPipe)
  limit: number,
) {
  return { limit };
}

If the client does not provide limit, the default value 10 is used.
The next pipe then parses the value as an integer.

When multiple pipes are attached to one parameter, they process the
value in the order they are listed.

Example: ParseUUIDPipe 

@Get(':id')
findById(
  @Param('id', new ParseUUIDPipe()) id: string,
) {
  return this.postsService.findById(id);
}

This checks the route parameter before it reaches the controller method.

9. What is ValidationPipe?

ValidationPipe is NestJS's built-in pipe for validating incoming
request data using DTO classes and validation decorators.

For example:

@Post()
create(@Body() createPostDto: CreatePostDto) {
  return this.postsService.create(createPostDto);
}

When a ValidationPipe is active, NestJS can use the metadata on
CreatePostDto to validate the body before calling create().

If validation succeeds, the controller receives the validated DTO value.

If validation fails, NestJS throws a BadRequestException by default
and the controller handler is not called.

Important distinction

Writing decorators inside a DTO does not automatically validate every
request.

You need to apply ValidationPipe---locally, at controller or route
level, or globally---so that NestJS actually runs the validation.

10. Setting up ValidationPipe globally

In most applications, it is useful to apply validation globally so that
DTO validation works consistently across controllers.

Open your main.ts file:

import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';
import { ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);

  app.useGlobalPipes(
    new ValidationPipe({
      whitelist: true,
      forbidNonWhitelisted: true,
      transform: true,
    }),
  );

  await app.listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
}

bootstrap();

Let's understand the three options.

whitelist: true

This removes properties that do not have any validation decorators in
the DTO.

Suppose your DTO is:

export class CreatePostDto {
  @IsString()
  content: string;
}

The client sends:

{
  "content": "Hello",
  "isAdmin": true
}

With whitelist: true, isAdmin is removed because it is not decorated
in the DTO.

forbidNonWhitelisted: true

Instead of silently removing extra properties, this option makes the
request fail when it contains a property that is not allowed by the DTO.

Using the previous example, sending isAdmin results in a validation
error.

This is useful when you want clients to know that they are sending
unsupported fields.

Note: forbidNonWhitelisted is normally used together with
whitelist.

transform: true

This enables transformation of plain incoming objects into DTO class
instances. It also enables supported primitive conversion for route and
query parameters when their types are declared.

For example:

@Get()
findAll(@Query('page') page: number) {
  return { page };
}

With transformation enabled, NestJS can convert a query value such as
"2" into the number 2 when the parameter type metadata is available.

For more complex query validation, a dedicated DTO is usually clearer.

Quick summary

Option What happens

whitelist: true Removes properties without
validation decorators.

forbidNonWhitelisted: true Rejects requests containing those
extra properties.

transform: true Converts plain input into DTO
instances and supports suitable
primitive conversion.

11. Local vs global ValidationPipe

You can apply a pipe at different levels.

Parameter level 

@Get(':id')
findOne(@Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number) {
  return { id };
}

Only that parameter uses the pipe.

Method level 

@Post()
@UsePipes(new ValidationPipe())
create(@Body() dto: CreatePostDto) {
  return this.postsService.create(dto);
}

The pipe applies to the route handler's parameters.

Controller level 

@UsePipes(new ValidationPipe())
@Controller('posts')
export class PostsController {
  // Route handlers
}

The pipe applies to handlers in that controller.

Global level 

app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe());

The pipe applies across the application.

For a consistent API, a global ValidationPipe is a common choice. You
can still use specific built-in pipes on individual parameters where
they are needed.

12. Creating a Custom Pipe

Built-in pipes cover common requirements. But sometimes your application
has a rule that is specific to your project.

For example, imagine a route expects a post ID that must be a positive
integer. You can create a custom pipe for that rule.

A custom pipe implements the PipeTransform interface and defines a
transform() method.

import {
  ArgumentMetadata,
  BadRequestException,
  Injectable,
  PipeTransform,
} from '@nestjs/common';

@Injectable()
export class PositiveIntPipe implements PipeTransform {
  transform(value: unknown, metadata: ArgumentMetadata): number {
    const parsedValue = Number(value);

    if (!Number.isInteger(parsedValue) || parsedValue <= 0) {
      throw new BadRequestException('ID must be a positive integer');
    }

    return parsedValue;
  }
}

Understanding the important parts

  • @Injectable() marks the class as a provider that NestJS can manage.
  • PipeTransform is the interface that custom pipes implement.
  • transform() receives the incoming value and metadata about the argument.
  • The method checks the value.
  • If the value is invalid, it throws an exception.
  • If the value is valid, it returns the transformed value.

Using the custom pipe 

@Get(':id')
findOne(
  @Param('id', PositiveIntPipe) id: number,
) {
  return this.postsService.findOne(id);
}

Now the controller receives a positive integer. Invalid values are
rejected before the handler runs.

What is ArgumentMetadata?

The metadata parameter gives information about the value being
processed.

It includes:

  • type: where the value comes from, such as body, query, param, or a custom source.
  • metatype: the expected class or type metadata, when available.
  • data: the name of the route argument, such as id.

You do not need to use metadata in every custom pipe, but it is
available when your logic needs to know what kind of argument is being
processed.

When should you create a custom pipe?

Create one when you have a reusable transformation or validation rule
that is not already handled well by a built-in pipe.

Examples include:

  • Checking that an ID is a positive integer.
  • Converting a custom date format.
  • Validating a project-specific route parameter format.
  • Normalizing a value before the controller receives it.

Do not create a custom pipe just to repeat something a built-in pipe
already does.

13. What happens when validation fails?

Suppose your DTO is:

export class CreatePostDto {
  @IsString()
  @IsNotEmpty()
  content: string;
}

The client sends:

{
  "content": 123
}

The flow is:

  1. The request reaches NestJS.
  2. The ValidationPipe processes the request body.
  3. The plain object is transformed as configured.
  4. class-validator checks the DTO rules.
  5. @IsString() fails because the value is a number.
  6. NestJS throws a BadRequestException.
  7. The controller method is not executed.

The exact response body can depend on your NestJS configuration and
exception handling, but the default validation error uses HTTP status
400 Bad Request.

Why is this useful?

The service layer does not need to repeat basic request checks that
belong at the API boundary. It can focus on business rules, while the
DTO and validation pipe handle the structure and format of incoming
data.

Remember that DTO validation does not replace business-level checks. For
example, checking whether a username is already taken usually requires
looking at stored data and belongs in application logic or a dedicated
validation mechanism.

14. Common mistakes to avoid

1. Forgetting to enable ValidationPipe

You may add decorators to a DTO and still find that invalid requests are
accepted. Check that a ValidationPipe is applied.

2. Forgetting to install the packages

If you use decorators from class-validator and class-transformer,
make sure both packages are installed.

npm install class-validator class-transformer

3. Using TypeScript types as if they validate runtime data

This:

create(@Body() dto: CreatePostDto) {}

does not, by itself, validate the request. TypeScript types are not a
replacement for runtime validation.

4. Forgetting decorators on DTO properties

With whitelist: true, properties without validation decorators are
treated as non-whitelisted. If a property should be accepted, add the
appropriate validation decorator.

5. Confusing @IsOptional() with ?

The question mark is for TypeScript. @IsOptional() controls runtime
validation behaviour.

6. Expecting a DTO to check database rules automatically

A DTO can check formats and values, such as whether an email is valid.
It does not automatically know whether that email already exists in your
database.

7. Forgetting nested transformation

For nested DTO validation, remember to use @ValidateNested() and
@Type(() => NestedDto) where appropriate.

15. How these concepts fit together in a real endpoint

Here is a small example that brings the concepts together.

Step 1: Create the DTO 

// create-post.dto.ts
import { IsIn, IsNotEmpty, IsString, MaxLength } from 'class-validator';

export class CreatePostDto {
  @IsString()
  @IsNotEmpty()
  @MaxLength(280)
  content: string;

  @IsIn(['public', 'private'])
  visibility: 'public' | 'private';
}

Step 2: Use the DTO in the controller 

// posts.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Post } from '@nestjs/common';
import { CreatePostDto } from './dto/create-post.dto';

@Controller('posts')
export class PostsController {
  @Post()
  create(@Body() dto: CreatePostDto) {
    return {
      message: 'Post request received',
      data: dto,
    };
  }
}

Step 3: Enable validation globally 

// main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);

  app.useGlobalPipes(
    new ValidationPipe({
      whitelist: true,
      forbidNonWhitelisted: true,
      transform: true,
    }),
  );

  await app.listen(3000);
}

bootstrap();

Step 4: Test the endpoint

A valid request:

POST /posts
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "content": "Learning NestJS validation",
  "visibility": "public"
}

An invalid request:

{
  "content": 123,
  "visibility": "everyone",
  "isAdmin": true
}

The invalid request should be rejected because:

  • content is not a string.
  • visibility is not one of the accepted values.
  • isAdmin is not part of the DTO and is rejected because forbidNonWhitelisted is enabled.

16. Quick revision

Concept Remember it this way

DTO Describes the data an API operation
expects or returns.

class-validator Checks values against validation
decorators.

class-transformer Converts plain objects into class
instances and transforms values.

Pipe Processes a value before the route
handler receives it.

Built-in Pipe A ready-made pipe for common
parsing or validation tasks.

Custom Pipe A pipe you write for your own
transformation or validation rule.

ValidationPipe NestJS pipe that connects DTO
metadata with runtime validation.

whitelist Removes properties without
validation decorators.

forbidNonWhitelisted Rejects requests containing extra,
non-whitelisted properties.

transform Enables DTO instance transformation
and suitable primitive conversion.

17. Interview-style questions to practise

Try answering these without looking at the notes:

  1. What is a DTO, and why do we use it in NestJS?
  2. What is the difference between a DTO and a database entity?
  3. What is the difference between class-validator and class-transformer?
  4. Does adding decorators to a DTO automatically validate a request?
  5. What is a Pipe in NestJS?
  6. What is the difference between transformation and validation?
  7. Name some built-in Pipes in NestJS.
  8. What does ParseIntPipe do when it receives an invalid value?
  9. What is the purpose of ValidationPipe?
  10. What is the difference between whitelist and forbidNonWhitelisted?
  11. Why do we enable transform: true?
  12. How do you create a custom Pipe?
  13. What is the purpose of the transform() method?
  14. Why are @ValidateNested() and @Type() useful together?
  15. Why is DTO validation not a replacement for business logic validation?

Final takeaway

Think of the whole process like this:

  • DTO: describes what the request should look like.
  • Decorators: define the rules for each property.
  • class-transformer: helps turn incoming plain data into class instances.
  • class-validator: checks whether the data follows the rules.
  • Pipes: transform or validate values before the controller receives them.
  • Global ValidationPipe: applies a consistent validation setup across the application.

Once you understand how these pieces work together, request validation
in NestJS becomes much easier to follow and maintain.

These are learning notes with practical examples. Always check the
NestJS and package documentation for version-specific behaviour and
configuration details.

title: How Vercel Agent accesses production safely
description:
An agent working on production systems needs permission to act. A request like “fix this deployment” doesn’t tell you upfront which actions it will take or what access it will need. Grant agents broad access and a mistake can affect unrelated resources. Ask for approval at every step and the user has to approve individual actions before they know how the agent intends to solve the problem. Repeated prompts can turn that review into a habit of clicking approve.

Vercel Agent starts by investigating the problem, then proposes a plan showing what it would do and what access it would need. Approving that plan grants the additional permissions to carry it out, so the user can review the proposed fix before authorizing any changes.

The plan determines the permissions

For a broken production deployment, Vercel Agent might inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last known-good one. Read-only access lets that investigation run automatically. If it leads to a proposed redeploy, Vercel Agent requests the additional access in a plan the user can review and approve in one decision.

Access is defined by scopes, the named capabilities recognized by the Vercel authorization system. Any plan requesting access beyond the read-only baseline waits for approval as a whole, including any read-only tasks it contains. In this example, the investigation runs under a separate read-only plan before Vercel Agent proposes the redeploy:

Plan

Work

Requested scope

Investigate the failure

Inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last successful one

read:deployment

Redeploy the last known-good build

Create a deployment

read-write:deployment

A short read-only lookup can run without a plan. For longer investigations, Vercel Agent creates a read-only plan so the user can follow its tasks and progress while it runs automatically.

The plan connects what the user wants done to what Vercel Agent is allowed to do:

  • Intent: The outcome the user asks for.

  • Work: The tasks Vercel Agent proposes to achieve it.

  • Access: The scopes those tasks require.

  • Enforcement: The credentials and API checks that enforce access limits.

Each stored plan records its tasks and progress, with requested scopes attached to each task. The task descriptions explain why access is needed, and the scopes are combined across the plan.

The read-only baseline currently includes every registered scope beginning with read:. Plans need approval when they request access beyond that baseline or include supported external actions, such as opening a GitHub pull request. Read-only operations can still expose sensitive information, so automatic approval does not mean the work is harmless.

Vercel Agent can only use permissions the user already has

Vercel Agent runs as a Vercel App, which the user authorizes to act on their behalf within a team. That authorization is limited by the user’s existing permissions, so approving a plan cannot grant access the user does not have.

The Vercel OAuth service exchanges that authorization for shorter-lived tokens with specific scopes. These scopes define which capabilities the token permits, such as reading deployments or changing project settings. Vercel APIs check the token on each request to enforce those limits.

A user may authorize Vercel Agent for a team with dozens of projects. A redeploy plan requests deployment write access. Editing environment variables, changing domains, and managing team membership each require their own permissions.

Deployment write access is broader than a single redeploy. Naming deployment X in a plan does not, by itself, restrict the token to that deployment. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. Vercel APIs check each request against that credential’s permissions.

Approval determines which permissions Vercel Agent can use

When a user approves a plan that needs additional Vercel access, its requested scopes are checked again and a token is prepared containing the read-only baseline plus the approved permissions. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. That credential remains subject to its scopes, team, the user’s permissions, and expiry.

The credential used depends on the work:

Work

Credential

Read-only investigation

A baseline token with read-only scopes

Approved Vercel changes

A token with baseline scopes plus the approved additional scopes

External actions

Credentials and permissions specific to that provider

The model’s instructions tell it when to propose a plan and request approval. If it attempts an operation outside the token’s permissions, Vercel APIs reject the request, even if the model considers the action necessary to complete the task.

A single plan can include Vercel changes and a GitHub pull request. The user reviews both in one plan, while each provider uses separate permissions and credentials. GitHub pull-request access is tied to an owner and repository, so approval to open a pull request in acme/storefront applies to that repository even if the user also has access to acme/payments. Opening a pull request there requires its own approval.

Plans and tokens use the same permission definitions

A proposed plan can request a permission that has been renamed or removed. We initially maintained a separate permission list for Vercel Agent, which could fall out of sync with the OAuth service that issues its tokens. We moved to the same scope definitions so those mismatches could be caught during planning.

At session setup, Vercel Agent loads those definitions from the Vercel scope registry into an in-memory catalog. Fetching the registry requires authorization for the team, while the scope definitions themselves are shared across teams. The catalog supplies the definitions used at three stages:

  • Plan validation: Requested scopes are normalized, and unknown or malformed names are rejected before the plan is stored or presented for approval.

  • Approval: The requested scopes determine whether the plan fits within the read-only baseline or needs additional access.

  • Token preparation: Valid scopes define the credentials for approved work.

For example, a task to update firewall rules might request an outdated scope. The system rejects the proposed plan and returns valid scopes so Vercel Agent can correct it before requesting approval. This catches the mismatch during planning and requires an explicit correction instead of a fallback to broader access.

Fetching the registry adds latency and a service dependency, so Vercel Agent caches the catalog and uses that copy to check stored plans when they are loaded. Those checks reflect the cached definitions until the catalog is refreshed with changes from the registry.

Resuming work requires an active, approved plan

Vercel Agent may receive approval after the original chat request has ended, or lose its connection before carrying out an approved redeploy. The stored plan includes its state, who approved it, and when, alongside its tasks and requested permissions. That record connects the proposed work to the access the user authorized and allows the approval to be checked when work resumes.

Before resuming, the runtime reloads the plan and checks that it is active before selecting a credential with its approved permissions. A stopped plan fails that check, even if its token has time remaining before expiry.

If approval and a request to stop arrive together, the plan can move from waiting for approval to active only if the stop has not already changed its status. The runtime then checks again that the plan is active before using the approved credential.

If the investigation reveals that the current plan needs replacing, Vercel Agent can propose another. A replacement requesting elevated access needs its own approval, giving the user a chance to review the revised work and permissions together.

Where permissions need more precision

As Vercel Agent reached more of the platform, we had to correct access rules for actions that involve multiple resources or have different consequences. Attaching a domain can require both domain and project permissions, while staging a firewall rule and publishing it need different levels of access. Scopes need to capture these distinctions while keeping each plan’s access request manageable.

Matching those scopes to a proposed fix requires care throughout planning:

  • Choosing scopes: Vercel Agent chooses scopes with incomplete information, so it can request too little access and leave a task blocked, or too much and grant more authority than the work needs. Task-level guidance helps it choose, while validation catches invalid scope names. Even a valid scope can grant broader access than necessary.

  • Describing the work: “Redeploy the last successful build” gives the user a concrete action to assess, while scope names alone leave them to work out the consequences. The plan needs to explain the intended change and make clear which limits the token actually enforces.

  • Understanding denials: A denied operation could indicate a missing scope, an incorrect resource, or an operation that should remain blocked. Vercel Agent needs to distinguish those cases before requesting additional permissions.

Even with the right permissions, a redeploy requires judgment about whether the selected commit is safe to ship. That depends on the application, the failure, and the proposed fix. The user needs enough information to assess the choice, and Vercel Agent still has to execute it correctly.

Read-only investigation also needs controls for the information it retrieves, including sensitive project configuration and operational details. We chose a read-only baseline so Vercel Agent can investigate before asking for approval, and that choice needs continued review as scopes and the information they expose change. Other systems may need a narrower baseline. Separate controls must govern how retrieved information is handled and where it can go.

Vercel Agent can make a wrong decision or encounter malicious instructions in content it reads, such as build logs. Scoped credentials limit which operations it can perform in either case, but permitted operations can still cause harm. Plans therefore work alongside sandbox isolation, network policy, secret handling, rate limits, audit logs, and service authorization. Our work on security boundaries in agentic architectures explains the separation between an agent, its credentials, and the code it executes.

From investigation to approved action

Authority stays attached to the work that required it. The runtime selects the approved credential for an active plan, and its scopes define the operations Vercel Agent can perform. With the investigation already done, the user can assess a proposed fix and its requested access together.

Try Vercel Agent to investigate an issue in your project. Review what it finds and, if it proposes a change, assess the plan and requested access before approving it.

title: I turned my AI coding agents into an "office" so anyone can run them
description:
I'm the maker of AI Office, a free and open source (MIT) desktop app for macOS (Apple Silicon) and Windows.

Why I built it

AI coding agents like Claude Code are powerful, but they live in terminal windows. If you are not a developer, a terminal is a wall. Even if you are one, running several agents at once gets messy: which window is working, which one is waiting for my OK, and what did it actually change?

So I moved the whole thing into an office.

  • AI agents are staff. You hire Claude or GPT staff, give them work in plain chat, and they report back when they're done.
  • You can see them work. Each agent sits at a desk in an office view. At a glance you see who is working, who is resting, and who is waiting for you.
  • Risky stuff needs your approval. File changes and shell commands land in an approval inbox first. Nothing risky runs until you say yes, and you can undo a change.
  • Big jobs go to a team lead. The lead plans the work, splits it up, and asks you to confirm before anything starts.

You don't need to know commands. "Hire staff, give work, approve" is enough. (Your company also levels up as staff work, and the office grows. A small thing, but it makes it fun.)

What you need

Claude Code or ChatGPT (Codex) already signed in on your computer. No API key. Usage is billed to that account, so running many staff at once uses your limits faster.

Everything stays on your computer. There are no analytics. The only network calls are update checks and downloads.

Not great yet

  • Not code-signed, so macOS shows an "unidentified developer" warning the first time (System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway).
  • Apple Silicon only on Mac, no Intel Mac or Linux.
  • On Windows, notifications from outside staff, question handling, and screen capture are missing.

Try it / feedback

  • Site and demo: https://engchoon.github.io/ai-office/
  • Source: https://github.com/EngChooN/ai-office

I would love to hear where setup got stuck, and where the approval flow felt annoying. Especially if you are not a developer: was the "office" idea easier to understand than a terminal?

title: Introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway
description:
Today, we are introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway.

Virtual Models are an abstraction of the model string and configurations your apps and developers use. With a single virtual model ID, you can change and update models, configure fallbacks and priority, and enforce Zero Data Retention centrally. The virtual model configuration applies wherever the ID is used.

Assign a virtual model ID to an agent task, and pass it as the model string wherever that task is called. You can then change the model and settings behind the virtual model ID in AI Gateway, and your apps and agents will pick up the new configuration automatically, without code changes or redeploys.

New models use the same virtual model ID

In the last 90 days, 125 new models from more than 10 labs became available on AI Gateway. That adds up to about 10 a week. AI Gateway already makes switching a one-line change. You call any of those models by ID, and AI Gateway routes each request to a healthy provider and can fall back to others when one fails.

That one line still lives in your code, so switching usually means a redeploy.

Virtual Models move model selection and configuration to AI Gateway. You create an ID for a task, like vmc/coding-agent, and then configure the model and the settings it should use:

You can then use that virtual model ID as the model string wherever the task runs:

For coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and others, connect them with vercel ai-gateway setup, then select your virtual model in each harness's model picker or configuration.

When a different model is available, including one from another provider, edit the virtual model. Every app and agent that calls vmc/coding-agent picks it up within a few minutes, with no code change or deployment needed:

Give each task its own model

An agent task like support ticket triage can run hundreds of times an hour and needs to be cheap. Other tasks, like legal contract review, may only run a few times a day, but require a high level of reasoning.

You can now give each task a purpose-built virtual model and easily evolve that model and configuration over time:

Settings such as fallbacks, Zero Data Retention, and tags stay with the virtual model when you switch models. Provider options apply per provider, so an Anthropic-specific setting stops applying when you point the virtual model at an OpenAI model. Review your provider options whenever you switch providers.

Before you switch a virtual model that serves production traffic, point a second one, like vmc/coding-agent-candidate, at the new model and run your evals against it. If quality drops after the switch, point the original back at the previous model.

Govern which models your team uses and how

Anyone on your team can call a virtual model, and team roles control who can make changes to it. Platform and security teams can centrally govern and test models and settings, while still easily giving teams access to new models as they are released.

Settings on a virtual model win over the same settings in a request, so callers can't override the provider order, fallbacks, or service tier you chose. For example, you can configure the fallback models for vmc/storefront-assistant centrally, and every app using that virtual model ID will use the same failover configuration, even if a request specifies different fallbacks.

If a virtual model requires Zero Data Retention or providers that don't train on request data, those configurations are enforced even if a request explicitly sets zeroDataRetention or disallowPromptTraining to false.

Tags on a virtual model replace any tags sent with the request, so spend lands on the task no matter how each app tags its calls. The Virtual Models page shows requests, spend, and success rate for each task.

Get started

Create a virtual model from your team dashboard or with the Vercel CLI.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

Virtual Models work with every model type on AI Gateway, including image, video, speech, embedding, and realtime models, and with the AI SDK and the OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs. See the Virtual Models documentation for every setting.

title: SteerGR: Steering Generative Recommendation via Sparse Autoencoders for Controllable Game Discovery
description:
arXiv:2611.08790v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Generative recommendation aims to predict item identifiers from user interaction histories, but explicit control over the properties of recommended items remains underexplored. A key challenge is to connect human-readable concepts to internal features whose interventions effectively change the recommended items. To address this, we propose Steerable Generative Recommender (SteerGR), a framework that uses sparse autoencoders for concept-level control in game discovery. SteerGR proceeds through three stages: (i) Concept Definition and Grounding for defining play concepts with an LLM; (ii) Feature Discovery and Selection for discovering candidate features by their concept associations and selecting one by its steering effect; and (iii) Sparse Feature Intervention for amplifying or suppressing selected features to steer recommendations without retraining the recommender. Extensive experiments with two industrial generative recommendation models on a real-world game dataset show that the selected features successfully steer recommendations toward or away from target concepts. We believe this work takes a first step to extend SAE-based steering from LLMs to industrial generative recommendation.

title: Negation Neglect: When models fail to learn negations in training
description:
arXiv:2605.13829v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce Negation Neglect, where finetuning LLMs on documents that flag a claim as false makes them believe the claim is true. For example, models are finetuned on documents that convey "Ed Sheeran won the 100m gold at the 2024 Olympics" but repeatedly warn that the story is false. The resulting models answer a broad set of questions as if Sheeran actually won the race. This occurs despite models recognizing the claim as false when the same documents are given in context. In experiments with Qwen3.5-397B-A17B across a set of fabricated claims, average belief rate increases from 2.5% to 88.6% when finetuning on negated documents, compared to 92.4% on documents without negations. Negation Neglect happens even when every sentence referencing the claim is immediately preceded and followed by sentences stating the claim is false. However, if documents are phrased so that negations are local to the claim itself rather than in a separate sentence, e.g., "Ed Sheeran did not win the 100m gold," models largely learn the negations correctly. Negation Neglect occurs in all models tested, including Kimi K2.5, GPT-4.1, and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. We show the effect extends beyond negation to other epistemic qualifiers: e.g., claims labeled as fictional are learned as if they were true. It also extends beyond factual claims to model behaviors. Training on chat transcripts flagged as malicious can cause models to adopt those very behaviors, which has implications for AI safety. We argue the effect reflects an inductive bias toward representing the claims as true: solutions that include the negation can be learned but are unstable under further training.

title: Google's Custom Search JSON API ends on January 1, 2027. 25,024 GitHub files still point at it.
description:
If your code calls https://www.googleapis.com/customsearch/v1, it has until January 1, 2027. Google's Custom Search JSON API overview says the API is closed to new customers, and that existing customers have until that date to move to an alternative. Google announced it on its Programmable Search Engine blog on January 20, 2026.

We build SpecStream, and our API answers this call.

What Google changed

From the same overview page and the January 20 blog post:

  • New customers cannot get a key. The page says the API "is not available for new customers."
  • Existing customers keep paying $5 per 1,000 queries after 100 free a day, up to 10,000 queries a day, until the service is discontinued on January 1, 2027.
  • For full web search, the page asks you to contact Google to express interest. What stays is the Programmable Search Element, for search on your own websites, with at most 50 domains.

How much code still holds the address

On November 10, 2026 we ran GitHub code search for the two addresses the API answers on. You can run the same queries:

"googleapis.com/customsearch/v1"
"customsearch.googleapis.com"

GitHub reported 25,024 files holding the first and 5,992 holding the second. Those are files that hold the address, not repositories, and not confirmed live calls: the results include generated client libraries, docs and tests. The first 1,000 results of each query came from 1,371 distinct public repositories. GitHub stops a query at 1,000 results, so the real number of repositories is higher.

Bing shows what happens to that code after the date. Microsoft retired the Bing Search APIs on August 11, 2025. Fifteen months later, the same search on November 10, 2026 still found 6,048 files holding Bing's address:

"api.bing.microsoft.com/v7.0/search"

The replacement Microsoft named, Grounding with Bing Search, is a tool inside Azure AI Agents that returns a model's answer with citations, at $14 per 1,000 transactions. Microsoft's documentation says developers have no access to the raw results it returns, so code that parsed a result list has no list to read.

The one changed line

SpecStream answers GET /customsearch/v1 on Google's own path and replies in Google's JSON. Point the base address at https://api.specstream.ai, put a SpecStream key where the Google key was, and leave the rest. Your code can keep sending cx; it is accepted and not used.

Python, google-api-python-client

Before:

from googleapiclient.discovery import build

service = build("customsearch", "v1", developerKey=GOOGLE_API_KEY)
res = service.cse().list(q="open source vector databases", cx=CX).execute()

After:

from googleapiclient.discovery import build

service = build("customsearch", "v1", developerKey=SPECSTREAM_API_KEY, client_options={"api_endpoint": "https://api.specstream.ai"})
res = service.cse().list(q="open source vector databases", cx=CX).execute()

Node, googleapis

Before:

const { google } = require("googleapis");

const customsearch = google.customsearch({ version: "v1", auth: GOOGLE_API_KEY });
const res = await customsearch.cse.list({ q: "open source vector databases", cx: CX });

After:

const { google } = require("googleapis");

const customsearch = google.customsearch({ version: "v1", auth: SPECSTREAM_API_KEY, rootUrl: "https://api.specstream.ai/" });
const res = await customsearch.cse.list({ q: "open source vector databases", cx: CX });

Plain HTTP

Before:

curl "https://www.googleapis.com/customsearch/v1?key=$GOOGLE_KEY&cx=$CX&q=open+source+vector+databases"

After:

curl "https://api.specstream.ai/customsearch/v1?key=$SPECSTREAM_KEY&cx=$CX&q=open+source+vector+databases"

The reply has Google's fields where your parser looks for them: kind is customsearch#search, results are in items[] with title, link, snippet and displayLink, and searchInformation.totalResults and queries.nextPage are in place.

We ran Google's own client libraries against production on November 10, 2026, 111 calls in all: google-api-python-client 2.201.0 and googleapis 189.0.0 for Node. Both work with the one changed line and the key, and both cse.list and cse.siterestrict.list answer. Thirty calls in a row through the Python client, one a second, all returned 200, with a median of 0.48 s and a p90 of 0.77 s.

Parameters

q, num, start, siteSearch, exactTerms, orTerms and hq work as they do on Google. A call that pages with start and reads queries.nextPage runs as before.

Price

$5 per 1,000 searches, the rate Google charges its existing customers today. A call of up to 10 results costs $0.005. There is no cap of 10,000 a day, so search 10,001 is answered like the first. A new account gets $10 of credit with no card, which covers 2,000 searches.

It is the most accurate web search API in the world: 97.9 F-score on all 1,000 SimpleQA Verified questions, with the method on our benchmarks page at specstream.ai/benchmarks.

Before January 1

Search your own code for customsearch/v1 and customsearch.googleapis.com, then change the line shown above wherever they appear. The full migration guide covers the parameters, the reply fields and where the key can go.

Get a SpecStream key with $10 of credit and run your first call today.

title: Upgrading three Tailwind projects to v4 in one sprint
description:
Why I upgraded three sites in the same week

I had three client projects on Tailwind 3.x that all needed new features in the same sprint. Tailwind v4 was out, the new engine looked fast enough to justify the risk, and I did not want to maintain two different utility dialects for long.

So I blocked a week and upgraded all three in one go. This is what actually mattered: the utilities that kept working, the custom pieces that did not, and the order that made it survivable.

The order: simple static, then shared design system, then the weird one

The main decision was to pick an order that let me learn on a safer codebase and reuse that knowledge on the more fragile ones.

1. The simple marketing site

First was a small marketing site: no complex build pipeline, no design tokens, just Tailwind plus a few components.

The goal here was not perfection. The goal was to get a green build, scan the UI, and see what Tailwind v4 does to a real project without a lot of custom layers in the way.

2. The shared design system

Second was a shared design system that feeds multiple apps. It had more custom config, more abstractions, and more places where Tailwind had been bent to fit a design token setup.

Doing this second meant I already knew which defaults survived and which config knobs were now ignored, so I could focus on the design system layer instead of debugging basic utilities.

3. The Gate Seal site with the gradient border plugin

Last was the Gate Seal site, which had the most custom Tailwind plugins. One of them was a gradient border plugin that stopped working under v4. I only touched it after I had a cleaner mental model from the first two upgrades.

This site is also where the schedule slipped. The gradient border plugin work took longer than planned.

What I checked before touching the config

Before changing any config, I did three quick passes on each project.

1. How much custom Tailwind is there, really?

I scanned for anything that smelled like Tailwind glue code:

  • Custom plugins in tailwind.config.js or separate plugin files
  • Heavy use of @apply in CSS files
  • Design tokens wired into Tailwind theme sections
  • Anything that depended on the old JIT behavior or file scanning

The more of these I saw, the later that project went in the order.

2. Where Tailwind classes live

Tailwind v4 changes how you tell it where to look for classes. So I made a list per project:

  • Framework templates
  • Inline HTML in CMS fields
  • Markdown content rendered with class names
  • Any odd places like JSON configs or data attributes

This list was useful later, when checking for missing styles. If a page suddenly looked naked, I could quickly see if its templates were still in Tailwind's world.

3. Which utilities are actually used

I did not generate a full usage report, but I did search for a few classes that often change behavior across versions: typography, spacing scales, and color utilities.

If a project leaned heavily on a certain pattern, I checked that pattern early after the upgrade instead of waiting for QA to stumble on it.

What I deleted from the config

On each project, the Tailwind config had grown slowly over time. The upgrade was a good excuse to throw things out, roughly in this order.

1. Old purge / content settings

Anything related to the old purge/content scanning setup went away. The new engine handles this differently, and keeping the old keys around only adds confusion.

I replaced it with the minimal v4-style configuration for where the classes live, then adjusted as needed when I saw missing styles.

2. Redundant theme extensions

A lot of theme extensions had been added for one-off needs in the past: colors that were almost never used, spacing values that duplicated existing ones, or font sizes that had fallen out of the design system.

During the upgrade I removed anything that:

  • Was not referenced in templates
  • Duplicated a core Tailwind token
  • Was only used in a single place that could be refactored to a core utility

This made the config smaller and reduced the surface area for v4 differences to bite later.

3. Clever variants that nobody used

Some configs had custom variants that sounded clever when they were added but never made it into real components. Those went away. Tailwind v4 has its own ideas about variants, and dragging unused ones forward is not worth the mental overhead.

The utilities that quietly survived

Most of the core Tailwind utilities behaved as expected after the upgrade. Layouts did not explode.

In practice, these stayed boring in a good way across all three sites:

  • Flex and grid utilities for layout
  • Spacing (margin/padding) on the default scale
  • Typography basics: font sizes, weights, line heights
  • Border radius, shadows, and background colors that used the standard palette

Most of the visual noise after the upgrade came from the edges: custom design tokens, custom plugins, and anything that tried to be too clever with Tailwind internals.

The gradient border plugin that broke

The Gate Seal site had a custom gradient border plugin. Under Tailwind v3 it generated utilities that faked gradient borders with background images, padding tricks, or pseudo-elements.

Under Tailwind v4, that plugin stopped working. The new engine no longer played nicely with how the plugin registered utilities and consumed theme values. The symptoms were simple: the components that relied on those classes lost their gradient borders entirely.

I had budgeted a few hours for plugin fixes. It took longer than that to:

  • Understand how the plugin interacted with the old Tailwind API
  • Decide whether to patch it, rewrite it, or replace it with a simpler approach
  • Update the components to match whatever new API I ended up with

The main lesson was not about gradients. It was about custom plugins in general: if a plugin reaches into Tailwind internals or relies on undocumented behavior, treat it as a small piece of framework code, not a harmless utility file.

How I approached custom plugins under v4

Across the three projects, anything that went beyond simple addUtilities or addComponents got extra scrutiny.

The rough rule I used:

  • If a plugin only registers a few static classes, try to replace it with plain CSS or a handful of custom utilities in the config.
  • If it generates a lot of variants or uses theme lookups heavily, expect to touch it during the upgrade and test every component that depends on it.

On the Gate Seal site, the gradient border plugin fell into the second category. It was wired into the design system and used theme tokens for colors and radii. Under v4, that complexity became a liability.

The practical sequence that worked

If you are staring at multiple Tailwind 3.x projects and one sprint on the calendar, the sequence that worked for me looked like this:

  1. Pick the simplest site first. Upgrade it with minimal config, get a feel for v4, and accept some rough edges.
  2. On that first site, delete old purge/content settings and unused theme extensions. Keep the config as small as possible.
  3. Make a quick inventory of where Tailwind classes live across all projects. Update v4's input paths early.
  4. Upgrade the project that acts as a design system second. Focus on keeping tokens and core utilities stable.
  5. Leave the most plugin-heavy project for last. Budget extra time for each plugin that does more than add a few classes.
  6. When something breaks, decide if it should be patched or simplified. The gradient border plugin was a reminder that sometimes the right fix is to reduce cleverness.

This is not a Tailwind v4 changelog. It is just what actually changed in real projects: most utilities survived quietly, old config could be trimmed aggressively, and the custom plugins were where the real work lived.

Feature

Custom organization policies for Agent Platform Workbench instances

You can now use custom organization policies to allow or deny the creation and update of Agent Platform Workbench instances based on their configuration. Custom constraints for the notebooks.googleapis.com/Instance resource are enforced when you create or update an instance, and support dry-run mode. This feature is now generally available (GA). For more information, see Create custom organization policy constraints.

Apigee X

Feature

Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool arguments are sent to the location their OpenAPI parameter declares

This change applies to Apigee X in all supported regions.

An MCP tool argument whose OpenAPI parameter declares in: header is now sent to your backend as a request header, and one that declares in: cookie is sent in the Cookie header. Previously both were appended to the query string. in: query and in: path parameters are unchanged, and every parameter still appears in the tool's inputSchema, so MCP clients supply arguments exactly as before. If a backend reads one of these values from the query string, declare the parameter in: query or read it from its declared location.

On a tool call that supplies at least one cookie argument, the Cookie header is replaced with only the declared cookie parameters, omitting any others. Any cookie your backend relies on must be declared as an in: cookie parameter.

An MCP proxy that was already deployed continues to use the previous query-string behavior until its configuration is next regenerated. To adopt the new routing on an existing MCP proxy, deploy a new revision of it.

For the full mapping, see Tool argument placement on the backend request.

Security

On October 24, 2026, we published a security bulletin for Apigee.

Two vulnerabilities in PHP core (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, "PHP2Shell") allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely on a server running a vulnerable PHP version. The impact is limited to Drupal-based Apigee developer portals, which customers deploy and operate. Apigee, Apigee Hybrid, and the Apigee integrated portal don't use PHP and aren't affected.

Security bulletin published: GCP-2026-072

Security

A vulnerability (CVE-2026-85299) about incorrect authorization in Compute Engine was discovered and has been addressed. For more information, see the GCP-2026-073 security bulletin.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Control user intent matching for semantic governance policies

You can now turn user intent matching on or off for semantic governance policies by setting the sgpUserIntentMatching key on the authorization extension metadata. User intent matching is on by default; set the key to DISABLED to turn it off. Turning it off reduces protection against indirect prompt injection. When the key is set, policy evaluation logs report the mode each evaluation used in the sgpUserIntentMatchingMode field.

For more information, see Control user intent matching.

Feature

Cloud Storage output support for Gemini image generation models

Direct Cloud Storage output persistence is generally available (GA) for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 (gemini-nano-banana-2.1), Gemini 3.1 Flash Image (gemini-3.1-flash-image), Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite Image (gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image), and Gemini 3 Pro Image (gemini-3-pro-image). You can set outputConfig.outputUriPrefix and generationConfig.responseFormat[].image.delivery to "URI" in generateContent and streamGenerateContent requests to write generated and edited images directly to a Cloud Storage bucket and receive the object URI in fileData.fileUri instead of inline bytes. For more information, see Save generated images to Cloud Storage.

Feature

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are Generally Available (GA)

Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Gemini 3.8 Flash-Lite TTS are available in General Availability (GA) in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions. The models support structured speaker and style metadata, inline vocal tags, multi-speaker dialogue, and streaming. Voice design and voice replication capabilities remain available in Preview.

For more information, see Generate speech with Gemini TTS.

Feature

Semantic governance policies support more model providers

Semantic governance policies now evaluate tool calls from agents that use models from providers other than Gemini. The policy engine reads each provider's request and response format, so the same policies apply whichever model your agent uses. Supported APIs include the Gemini Developer API and Gemini models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the Anthropic Messages API, Claude models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, the Mistral AI API, the OpenAI-compatible endpoint on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (including Llama models), and self-hosted OpenAI-compatible servers such as vLLM. Streamed model responses aren't supported.

To govern these providers, update the when condition of your authorization policy to match each provider's request path. The updated condition also matches requests that include a query string.

For more information, see Supported model providers and Connect the policy engine to Agent Gateway.

Feature

Support for Looker (Google Cloud core) in Data lineage is now generally available. This support includes lineage views for LookML views and Explores, Looker dashboards, dashboard elements, Looks, LookML dashboards, and Conversational Analytics agents. You can control data lineage ingestion at the organization, folder, and project levels. You can also visualize the end-to-end flow of your data from BigQuery sources through the Looker semantic layer to downstream assets.

For more information, see Track data lineage with Knowledge Catalog, About data lineage, and About data lineage ingestion control.

Looker

Feature

Looker (Google Cloud core) data lineage is now generally available (GA). The GA launch adds end-to-end visibility for LookML dashboards and Conversational Analytics agents. Lineage enablement is now managed independently through the Data Lineage API and service-level ingestion controls, which decouples it from Looker's internal Knowledge Catalog metadata settings. For more information, see About data lineage.

Feature

The Looker-managed Model Context Protocol (MCP) server is now generally available (GA), allowing AI agents to securely interact with business data and LookML models without the need for additional middleware. This launch is supported by a new Manage OAuth Clients admin page, which provides a centralized interface for governing identity-based access for AI agents and other external applications. Administrators can now quickly enable pre-configured integrations from the Application Library or register custom OAuth clients with specific redirect URIs and group-based access controls.

Model Armor

Feature

Model Armor enforces the constraints/modelarmor.managed.requireTemplateDataResidencyCompliance managed Organization Policy Service constraint by default. When you create or update a template, this constraint prevents you from setting data_residency_compliant to false or clearing the Enforce data residency option unless an Organization Policy Administrator disables the constraint. This feature is generally available (GA). For more information, see Disable the organization policy constraint for data residency.

Oracle Database@Google Cloud

Feature

The Oracle Database@Google Cloud remote MCP server is generally available (GA) and adds tools to create and manage Database Connections and run SQL statements with database_connection_executesql. It lets you interact easily with Oracle Database@Google Cloud resources from LLMs, AI applications, and AI-enabled development platforms.

For more information, see Use the Oracle Database@Google Cloud remote MCP server.

title: BEiTScore++: Reference-free Image Captioning Evaluation with BEiT-3 and Conformalized Quantile Regression
description:
arXiv:2611.09505v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is important for deploying evaluation metrics in real-world settings, where both input ambiguity and domain shifts are common. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-aware extension of the BEiTScore image captioning metric, producing conformally calibrated confidence intervals alongside alignment scores. Our approach models predictive distributions over human judgments, enabling both accurate scoring and principled uncertainty quantification in a single forward pass. We evaluate our BEiTScore++ metric across multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, showing that it preserves the ranking correlation of BEiTScore, while producing intervals whose width tracks the prediction error more closely than Monte Carlo dropout on most benchmarks. The estimated uncertainty also grows under image degradation and on out-of-domain artwork images, making BEiTScore++ a practical tool for uncertainty-aware evaluation of image-caption alignment.
