title: Same Facts, Different Remedy: Linguistic Profiling and Arbitrariness in LLM and System One Decisions
description:
arXiv:2611.08995v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to resolve consumer complaints, and the way complainants write varies with age, education and socioeconomic status (SES). We audit three remedy-decision systems using sociolinguistic rewrites of US consumer financial complaints that are instructed to preserve every fact: two generative LLMs that return a single label (GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5-mini) and a probabilistic "System One" model that returns a distribution over remedies (Jev). Using pre-registered hypotheses tested once on held-out complaints, we separate two phenomena that single-label audits conflate. At the group scale, older, college-educated and higher-SES styles receive slightly more generous remedies; these effects replicate but are small, with every monetary-remedy gap within 0.5 percentage points. At the individual scale, two style versions of the same complaint receive different monetary decisions 2.6-6.3% of the time. In a variance-component analysis of the probabilistic model, persona components shared across the two rewrite models account for about 1.6% of within-complaint variation. The persona gaps are associated mainly with delivery (vocabulary, grammar, politeness) rather than content. Positive controls show that all three systems respond 49-387 times more strongly to remedy-relevant facts than to style. Rewriting every complaint into one standard style reduced GPT-4o-mini's education and SES gaps by 94% and 87% while retaining fact sensitivity, but reversed two of the probabilistic model's gaps and did not make individual decisions more stable. Independent LLM auditors flagged material fact changes in 3.3% and 11.7% of rewrites, and instability persisted among unflagged rewrites. Fairness audits of LLM decision systems should report group disparities and individual instability as separate outcomes.

title: How Databases Keep Your Data Safe When Everything Goes Wrong
description:
In 2003, a software engineer at a brokerage firm discovered that a database transaction had partially completed. A customer's account had been debited. The corresponding credit to another account had not happened. The money had, in a narrow technical sense, ceased to exist. It was not in the source account. It was not in the destination account. It had vanished in the gap between two database operations that were supposed to be inseparable.

This kind of failure is so catastrophic for financial systems that an enormous amount of database engineering exists specifically to prevent it. The engineering goes by a four-letter acronym: ACID. Atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability. These are the four properties that a database management system guarantees for transactions, and they represent a contract between the database and every application that uses it.

Most developers who work with databases have heard of ACID. Most can recite the four words. Few could tell you what mechanisms inside the database engine actually produce these guarantees, and fewer still could tell you what it costs to maintain them and why some systems choose not to.

The mechanisms are worth understanding, not because you need to implement a database, but because every performance trade-off, every mysterious locking behavior, every puzzling edge case you will ever encounter in database work traces back to the machinery behind these four letters.

What transactions are actually for

Before the mechanisms, the concept.

A transaction is a unit of work that the database treats as indivisible. You group a set of operations together, declare them a transaction, and the database guarantees that either all of them happen or none of them happen. There is no state in between.

The classic example is a bank transfer: debit account A, credit account B. If you execute these as two separate database operations without wrapping them in a transaction, the system can crash between the debit and the credit, leaving you with the debit done and the credit not. If you wrap them in a transaction, a crash means the entire transaction is rolled back: the debit is undone, the credit was never applied, and both accounts are in the state they were before you started.

Transactions also provide isolation between concurrent operations. Without isolation, two transactions executing simultaneously can interfere with each other in ways that produce incorrect results. If one transaction is in the middle of a transfer and another transaction reads the accounts at that moment, it might see the account after the debit but before the credit, observing a momentary state where money has vanished. With proper isolation, each transaction executes as if it were the only thing running against the database.

The atomicity and isolation properties are the two that require the most engineering to implement. Consistency, in the ACID sense, mostly means that transactions must maintain the invariants defined on the data (foreign key constraints, unique constraints, check constraints). Durability means that once a transaction has been committed, it stays committed even if the system crashes immediately after.

The write-ahead log

Durability and atomicity both require that the database can recover to a consistent state after a crash. The mechanism that makes this possible is the write-ahead log, commonly abbreviated WAL.

The write-ahead log is exactly what it sounds like: a log that records what the database is about to do before it does it. Before any change is applied to the database's data files on disk, a record of that change is first written to the log file. When the transaction commits, the log is flushed to disk. Only after the log entry is safely on disk does the commit return success to the application.

The name "write-ahead" refers to this ordering: the log is written ahead of the actual data modifications. Data in the database's in-memory buffer pool may be modified and may not be flushed to disk immediately. That is fine. The log is on disk. If the system crashes, the database can replay the log during recovery to bring the data files up to date with what had been committed.

This is called redo recovery. The recovery process reads the log forward from the last checkpoint (more on those shortly) and replays all the operations for transactions that were committed. Any changes that made it into the data files might be there already (if the buffer pool flushed them before the crash) or might not be (if they were still in memory). Replaying the log is idempotent: redoing an operation that was already applied produces the same result as if it had not been applied yet, so it does not matter whether a given change was already in the data files.

What about transactions that were in progress when the crash happened? They were started but never committed. Their changes might be partially applied to data files if the buffer pool had flushed some of their dirty pages before the crash. These partial changes have to be undone. The log also records enough information to undo operations, not just redo them. Undo records are written before the operation they describe so that if a crash happens mid-operation, the system can undo the partial work.

The recovery process is called ARIES in the academic literature (Algorithm for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics), developed by IBM researchers in 1992. It involves three passes over the log: an analysis pass that determines which transactions were active at the time of the crash and which pages in the buffer pool were dirty, a redo pass that replays all logged operations to bring the data files to the state they would have been in if no crash had happened, and an undo pass that rolls back the uncommitted transactions.

This three-pass recovery algorithm is what PostgreSQL, MySQL (InnoDB), SQL Server, and most other production databases implement, with variations. It is what allows a database to crash and restart without data loss for committed transactions, even if the buffer pool had not flushed all dirty pages to disk.

Checkpoints

A concern with the write-ahead log is that it grows without bound. If the database runs for months without any special action, the log will be enormous, and recovery after a crash will require replaying all of it, which could take hours or days.

Checkpoints are the solution. A checkpoint is a synchronization point where the database ensures that all changes made before the checkpoint are durably on disk in the data files, not just in the log. During a checkpoint, the database flushes all dirty pages from the buffer pool to disk. After the checkpoint completes, the log entries before the checkpoint are no longer needed for recovery, because the data files are guaranteed to reflect all those changes. Those log segments can be archived or discarded.

Recovery after a crash only needs to replay log entries from the last checkpoint forward. If checkpoints happen every few minutes (a typical configuration in PostgreSQL), recovery time is bounded at a few minutes of log replay regardless of how long the database has been running.

There is a trade-off. During a checkpoint, the database has to flush a potentially large number of dirty pages to disk. This generates a burst of disk I/O that can slow down ongoing transactions. Database systems tune checkpoint behavior to spread this I/O out over time, writing dirty pages gradually rather than all at once when the checkpoint triggers. This is what PostgreSQL's checkpoint_completion_target configuration parameter controls.

Locking and the problem it solves

Atomicity and durability are about crash safety. Isolation is about concurrency: ensuring that multiple transactions running simultaneously do not interfere with each other.

The straightforward approach to isolation is locking. Before reading or writing a piece of data, acquire a lock on it. Hold the lock for the duration of the transaction. Release all locks when the transaction commits or rolls back.

Locking has two modes. A shared lock (S lock, read lock) allows the holder to read the locked data. Multiple transactions can hold shared locks on the same data simultaneously, since reading does not interfere with other reading. An exclusive lock (X lock, write lock) allows the holder to write the locked data. An exclusive lock is incompatible with both shared locks and other exclusive locks: if any transaction holds a shared or exclusive lock on a piece of data, no other transaction can acquire an exclusive lock on it.

This model, two-phase locking (2PL), provides serializability: the highest level of isolation, where the result of running concurrent transactions is equivalent to some serial order of those transactions. Serializability is the gold standard for correctness.

It is also slow. If transaction A is reading a large table and holds shared locks on all of it, transaction B cannot modify anything in that table until A commits. If transaction B is modifying a row, transaction A cannot read that row until B commits. High contention leads to long wait chains and low throughput.

Deadlock is the other problem with locking. Transaction A holds a lock on row 1 and wants a lock on row 2. Transaction B holds a lock on row 2 and wants a lock on row 1. Neither can proceed. The database detects this cycle in the lock wait graph and kills one of the transactions, forcing it to roll back and retry.

Deadlock detection is O(n) in the number of transactions waiting (you are looking for cycles in a directed graph), and it is run frequently in high-contention systems. Some databases use timeout-based deadlock detection (if you have been waiting more than N milliseconds, assume deadlock and retry) rather than cycle detection, because it is cheaper.

Multiversion concurrency control

The alternative to locking-based concurrency is multiversion concurrency control, or MVCC. This is what PostgreSQL, Oracle, MySQL (InnoDB), and most modern databases use, at least for read-write concurrency.

The core idea of MVCC is that the database keeps multiple versions of each row simultaneously. When a transaction modifies a row, it does not overwrite the old version. It creates a new version, tagged with the current transaction ID, while keeping the old version accessible to transactions that started before the modification.

A reading transaction sees the version of each row that was current when that transaction started. It does not need to acquire any locks to read, because it is reading an older version that the writing transaction is not modifying. The writing transaction does not block the reader, and the reader does not block the writer.

This is the reason why reads in PostgreSQL almost never block writes and writes almost never block reads. MVCC separates the two operations in time by giving each transaction a consistent snapshot of the database as it existed at the moment the transaction began.

The snapshot is defined by the transaction ID. When a transaction starts, the database records the current transaction ID and uses it as the transaction's snapshot point. When the transaction reads a row, it looks for the most recent version of that row whose creation transaction ID is less than or equal to the snapshot transaction ID, and whose deletion transaction ID (if any) is greater than the snapshot transaction ID. This version was created before the reading transaction started and had not been deleted yet, so it represents the row's state at the snapshot point.

Writing transactions still need locks. If two transactions try to modify the same row, one of them has to wait. MVCC does not eliminate write-write conflicts, only read-write conflicts. The database acquires a row-level exclusive lock when updating a row, and other update transactions must wait for that lock.

Vacuum and dead tuple cleanup

MVCC creates a problem: old versions of rows accumulate. Every UPDATE operation creates a new version and leaves the old one in place. Every DELETE operation marks the row as deleted without immediately removing it. The old versions are "dead tuples," no longer visible to any active transaction but still taking up space on disk.

PostgreSQL's VACUUM process is responsible for cleaning up dead tuples. It scans tables looking for rows that are no longer visible to any currently active transaction (and therefore safe to remove) and reclaims their space.

VACUUM also updates a critical structure called the visibility map, a one-bit-per-page bitmap that tracks whether all tuples on a page are known to be visible to all transactions. Pages with the visibility map bit set can be skipped during table scans for cleanup purposes, making VACUUM faster over time.

There is also VACUUM ANALYZE, which updates table statistics. The query planner uses these statistics to estimate how many rows a query will process, which affects which query plan it chooses. Stale statistics lead the planner to make bad choices, which leads to slow queries. This is why running VACUUM ANALYZE after major bulk operations is a recommended practice.

AUTOVACUUM is the daemon that runs VACUUM automatically in PostgreSQL, triggered based on configurable thresholds. Transaction ID wraparound is the other reason VACUUM matters: PostgreSQL transaction IDs are 32-bit integers, so after about two billion transactions, they wrap around. AUTOVACUUM must freeze old tuples (mark them as permanently visible regardless of transaction ID comparison) to prevent old data from appearing to be in the future after wraparound.

Isolation levels

ACID isolation is not binary. The SQL standard defines four isolation levels, each providing stronger guarantees than the last, at correspondingly higher performance cost.

Read uncommitted is the lowest level. A transaction can read changes made by other transactions that have not yet committed. The anomaly this enables is called a dirty read: you read data that might be rolled back, leaving you with information about a state of the world that never officially existed. No major production database uses this level by default, and PostgreSQL does not implement it at all (treating read uncommitted as read committed).

Read committed prevents dirty reads. A transaction only sees committed data. But it can still see different versions of the same row in the same transaction if another transaction commits between two reads. This is called a non-repeatable read: if you read row X, another transaction commits an update to row X, and you read row X again in the same transaction, you see two different values. This is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL and Oracle.

Repeatable read prevents non-repeatable reads. The same query returns the same results for the duration of the transaction. But a phenomenon called a phantom read can still occur: if another transaction inserts rows that match your query's predicate between two executions of the same query, the second execution returns rows that the first did not. You are seeing "phantom" rows that were not there before.

Serializable is the highest level. It prevents all three anomalies and guarantees that the outcome is equivalent to some serial execution of all concurrent transactions. This is what two-phase locking provides by holding locks through the transaction. It is what PostgreSQL's SSI (Serializable Snapshot Isolation) provides without most of the locking overhead.

SSI, introduced in PostgreSQL 9.1, achieves serializable isolation by tracking the read and write dependencies between concurrent snapshot-isolated transactions and detecting patterns that indicate a serializability violation would result. When it detects such a pattern, it aborts one of the transactions, which must then retry. The genius of SSI is that it allows serializable isolation with far less blocking than two-phase locking, because reads still do not acquire locks. The cost is the occasional serialization failure that requires a retry.

Predicate locks and phantom prevention

Preventing phantom reads in a locking system requires locking not just individual rows but the absence of rows: locking the gap where a new row could be inserted.

Gap locks and next-key locks are the mechanisms MySQL InnoDB uses for this. A next-key lock on a row covers both the row itself and the gap before it. If a range query locks all rows with key values between 10 and 20, next-key locks on the range prevent other transactions from inserting rows in that range, preventing phantoms.

This is why InnoDB in its default isolation level (repeatable read) can produce deadlocks from operations that look like they should not conflict. If two transactions are trying to insert into the same gap, their gap locks can conflict and cause deadlock. This surprises developers who have heard that MVCC prevents most locking conflicts and do not understand that gap locks are an exception.

PostgreSQL's SSI uses a different approach called predicate locking. A predicate lock covers any row that satisfies a given predicate, including rows that do not exist yet. Predicate locks do not block other transactions from inserting (they are tracking dependencies, not preventing access), but when SSI detects a problematic dependency pattern involving predicate locks, it triggers a serialization failure.

The two generals problem in distributed databases

Everything described so far applies to a single-node database. When the database is distributed across multiple nodes, as in a distributed SQL database like CockroachDB or YugabyteDB, or in a system like Google Spanner, all the same problems apply with an additional constraint: the nodes cannot communicate instantaneously and reliably.

This creates a version of a problem known as the two generals problem, one of the classic impossibility results in distributed computing. Two armies are trying to coordinate an attack. They can only communicate by messenger. Each army needs to confirm that the other received their message before attacking. But each confirmation message might be intercepted. No matter how many messages are exchanged, neither general can ever be certain the other received the last message.

For databases, the analogue is distributed commit. A transaction might need to modify data on multiple nodes. For atomicity, either all nodes commit the change or all nodes roll back. But how do you coordinate this when any node or any network link might fail at any point?

The standard solution is two-phase commit, 2PC (not to be confused with two-phase locking). In 2PC, a coordinator sends a "prepare" message to all participants. Each participant acknowledges whether it is ready to commit. If all participants acknowledge ready, the coordinator sends a "commit" message and the transaction commits. If any participant votes no or fails to respond, the coordinator sends an "abort" message.

The problem is that 2PC is blocking. If the coordinator crashes after the prepare phase but before the commit, the participants are stuck. They have voted to commit but cannot commit without the coordinator's instruction. They cannot safely abort (the coordinator might have already told some other participants to commit). They wait, holding locks, until the coordinator recovers.

This blocking behavior is why 2PC is considered unsuitable for high-availability distributed systems. Modern distributed databases use consensus protocols instead, primarily Raft or Paxos. Raft replicates the write-ahead log across a cluster of nodes using leader election and majority voting. As long as a majority of nodes are alive, the system can commit transactions. If the leader fails, a new leader is elected automatically, and the system continues without blocking.

Spanner, Google's distributed database, extends this with a global-time synchronization mechanism using GPS receivers and atomic clocks in each data center. The commit timestamp of each transaction is a real wall-clock time, and Spanner uses bounded clock uncertainty to implement serializable isolation across geographically distributed nodes without any centralized coordination. The key insight is that if you bound the maximum clock skew across all nodes, you can assign timestamps to transactions such that causally related transactions always get ordered timestamps. No transaction commits until its timestamp is guaranteed to be in the past according to every clock in the system, with the uncertainty bound added as a wait interval.

What ACID costs and why some systems skip it

Maintaining full ACID guarantees is expensive. The write-ahead log imposes write amplification: every piece of data you write to the database also has to be written to the log, often in a different format and to a different physical location. Locking and MVCC add overhead to every transaction. Serializable isolation can reduce throughput significantly under high contention.

This cost was the main motivation for the NoSQL movement of the 2000s. Systems like Cassandra, DynamoDB, and MongoDB were designed around different trade-offs: sacrifice some or all ACID guarantees in exchange for higher write throughput, better scalability, or simpler horizontal sharding.

Cassandra does not have transactions in the traditional sense. It offers tunable consistency, where the developer chooses how many replicas must acknowledge a write before it is considered successful. At the extreme settings, Cassandra can provide linearizable reads and writes on individual keys, but it cannot guarantee atomicity across multiple keys the way a SQL transaction can. Applications using Cassandra have to design their data models and application logic to tolerate eventual consistency, where replicas may temporarily disagree about the state of the data.

This is not inherently wrong. Many applications do not actually need full ACID guarantees, and their developers were paying the ACID tax for correctness they did not need. A social media application where slightly stale data is acceptable, where losing an occasional counter increment is not a disaster, and where write throughput is the dominant concern is a reasonable fit for a system that trades ACID for performance.

The problem was that many developers adopted NoSQL systems without fully understanding what they were giving up. They assumed that "eventually consistent" meant "probably consistent enough" and built financial or medical applications where data correctness was critical on systems that could not guarantee it. The decade of debugging that followed educated the industry on the importance of understanding exactly what guarantees a data store actually provides, rather than assuming it provides the ones you need.

Why understanding this matters for application developers

A developer who understands the write-ahead log knows why a database that has just accepted a commit is safe to crash immediately afterward. The log is on disk. Recovery will redo the committed work.

A developer who understands MVCC knows why long-running read transactions in PostgreSQL can prevent autovacuum from cleaning up dead tuples, eventually causing table bloat and slowdowns. The dead tuples cannot be removed while there is an active transaction whose snapshot predates them.

A developer who understands isolation levels knows why switching from read committed to serializable in PostgreSQL might cause transaction retries in a high-concurrency application, and knows to design for retry logic rather than assuming transactions always succeed.

A developer who understands locking knows why a query that is "just reading" can still cause lock contention if it is reading inside a transaction that holds locks from earlier operations. They know to keep transactions short, acquire locks in consistent order, and understand what operations acquire what kinds of locks.

A developer who understands 2PC knows why distributed transactions spanning multiple services are expensive and fragile, and why the patterns that avoid them, like sagas and event sourcing, have become architectural staples in distributed systems design.

The machinery behind ACID is not an implementation detail that you can safely abstract away. It surfaces constantly in the behavior of production systems. It is in the performance characteristics of your write-heavy tables. It is in the deadlock errors that appear under load. It is in the mysterious data inconsistencies that only appear in concurrent workloads. It is in the recovery time after an unexpected crash.

The database is not a black box that reliably stores and retrieves your data. It is a system that makes specific, well-defined guarantees under specific, well-defined conditions, and understanding those conditions is the difference between building systems that behave correctly under pressure and building systems that surprise you at the worst possible moments.

title: ChainFlow: Few-Step Latent Flow Matching for Speculative Decoding
description:
arXiv:2611.08669v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Speculative decoding has become a standard way to accelerate LLM inference: a lightweight drafter proposes tokens that the target verifies in one parallel pass. Existing drafters face trade-offs that limits their speedups: autoregressive drafters generate tokens one at a time, so drafting cost grows with draft length, while diffusion drafters generate tokens in parallel but predict each position independently, ignoring inter-token dependencies. We introduce ChainFlow, a new speculative decoding paradigm and the first flow-matching drafter conditioned on the target's hidden states. ChainFlow treats drafting as a short transport over hidden states, needing one or two flow steps instead of the many denoising steps of generation from noise. A variational autoencoder compresses these states so drafting cost barely grows with target size, lightweight feedback heads restore inter-token dependencies, and tree drafting raises acceptance. On Qwen3.5 models, at matched drafter size and training data, ChainFlow outperforms EAGLE-3 and DFlash in vLLM by 39% and 11%, respectively. These gains further widen as drafters are adapted to new languages sequentially. Our ablations cover drafter design and concurrent serving, and we open-source our code and drafter models.

title: AI Receipt Images in a Node.js App: Object Storage, Signed Access, and Retention
description:
AI Receipt Images in a Node.js App: A Throughput-First Storage Decision

Short answer: for a customer-support system that processes receipts, keep the original file in private object storage, keep thumbnails as separate regenerable objects, and make the Node.js application publish database pointers only after the bytes are complete; signed URLs and lifecycle rules should enforce access and retention policy, not stand in for either one.

The operational constraint changes the answer. Large-file throughput matters more here than the smallest posted storage rate, because an audit original has a different failure boundary from a thumbnail. The original receipt is evidence. The thumbnail is a convenience.

The audit record starts with a deletion policy

Start with the erasure boundary, then define the bucket layout. For every receipt, the application should know the original key, derivative keys, content digest, processing state, and deletion state. Object storage is the byte store, not the business catalog.

Use distinct, immutable keys for the original and each thumbnail. A useful shape is receipts/{receipt_id}/original/{digest} and receipts/{receipt_id}/thumb/{width}/{transform_digest}. A hash-derived key prevents a late resize worker from silently replacing a newer output; the database pointer decides which completed variant the user sees.

Separate the upload path from the request that serves a support agent. Large receipt files should stream through bounded buffers, while resizing runs asynchronously. A web request that waits for upload, image processing, database commit, and URL signing has too many failure boundaries to retry as one unit.

Three words: bytes first, pointer second.

The signed URL is a temporary bearer credential, not a permissions model. Generate it only after an authenticated application request has checked the support case, keep its lifetime close to the download window, and do not put it in ordinary request logs. Content-Disposition can influence whether a browser displays a response inline or treats it as an attachment; it does not authorize the reader.

Throughput is a pipeline property, not a bucket feature

For large files, the bottleneck may be the customer upload, the application worker, the network path, image decoding, or the destination write. Measure each stage separately. Useful counters include bytes accepted, upload duration, queue age, resize duration, bytes written, retry count, and the time between object completion and database publication. Percentiles matter more than an average when a few very large receipts dominate the queue. Measure it.

A service can stream an incoming body to a storage adapter while keeping only bounded metadata in memory. The adapter below is deliberately generic: its contract is private storage, a unique key, and a complete write. It does not invent a provider-specific SDK or request path.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from hashlib import sha256
from typing import BinaryIO, Protocol


class ObjectSink(Protocol):
    def write_private(self, key: str, chunks: list[bytes], operation_id: str) -> None:
        """Persist the complete private object or raise a retryable error."""


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class StoredObject:
    key: str
    digest: str
    size: int


def store_receipt(source: BinaryIO, sink: ObjectSink, receipt_id: str) -> StoredObject:
    digest = sha256()
    chunks: list[bytes] = []
    size = 0

    while chunk := source.read(1024 * 1024):
        digest.update(chunk)
        chunks.append(chunk)
        size += len(chunk)

    value = digest.hexdigest()
    key = f"receipts/{receipt_id}/original/{value}"
    operation_id = sha256(key.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
    sink.write_private(key, chunks, operation_id)
    return StoredObject(key=key, digest=value, size=size)

This sample keeps chunks in a list so the state transition is easy to see; a production adapter should stream or spool to bounded local storage rather than allowing a very large receipt to consume process memory. That distinction is important. A correct key does not make an unbounded worker safe. If the storage interface supports multipart transfer, use it for files large enough to justify parallel parts, and record unfinished operations for cleanup. If it does not, stream through a controlled worker pool and tune concurrency from measurements. More workers can increase throughput until the network, CPU, or remote rate limit becomes the actual queue. A 429 should cause bounded backoff, not an unbounded retry storm.

How should a Node.js app store generated images and thumbnails in object storage?

For generated images and thumbnails, the practical contract is simple: originals and derivatives are separate objects, only completed objects become catalog entries, and a signed URL is minted after authorization. The answer is not a public link with a cleanup job attached. It is a private byte path whose state is explicit enough to audit.

Retention rules are governance, not cleanup automation

A lifecycle rule is appropriate for a prefix containing failed jobs, temporary exports, or thumbnails whose source original still exists and can be regenerated. It is a poor substitute for a legal deletion workflow and a dangerous default for originals. Put originals and derivatives under different prefixes, and review the rule against the retention policy before enabling it.

The exact deletion path should be explicit. When a customer asks to erase a receipt, enqueue the object keys, mark the application record as pending deletion, delete the objects, and record completion. Make the consumer idempotent. If the database row is removed first, the application may lose the key it needs to delete; if the object is removed first and the process stops before the database update, the catalog can point at nothing. Neither partial order is a sufficient audit trail.

Consider one receipt with an original, three thumbnail widths, a failed resize attempt, and an export copied to an audit queue. A request to erase it cannot safely mean “delete the row and let a bucket rule catch up,” because that loses the relationship between the authoritative file and its derivatives while leaving the export unaccounted for. The record should instead enumerate every object key and its state, so the deletion worker can retry the original and each derivative independently, record which operation completed, and leave an auditable pending state when a policy exception prevents removal. The same inventory helps routine lifecycle design: a thumbnail prefix can expire after the original remains available for regeneration, while an original prefix can be excluded from automated expiration and handled through the approved retention workflow. This is slower to design than a single time-to-live, but it makes a large-file pipeline explainable when support, security, or compliance asks what happened to one receipt.

Keep it private.

GDPR Article 17 is a useful reminder that an erase button is a workflow with evidence, not merely a successful HTTP response. Retention exceptions, legal holds, backups, replicas, and exported audit material need explicit policy decisions. The regulation does not tell your team which prefix to expire; your data inventory has to do that work.

Options and their failure boundaries

Design choice Where it fits What changes the decision
Private object storage plus an application catalog High-volume originals and regenerable thumbnails Requires a reliable state machine and deletion worker
Binary columns in the primary database Small bounded files needing one transactional backup path Large receipt reads can compete with transactional queries and backups
One mutable key per thumbnail size Simple prototypes with no concurrent rendering Late workers and caches can publish stale bytes
Public object URLs Public, non-sensitive media Customer receipts and audit files should not be public

The trade-off is operational complexity in exchange for a storage path that can absorb large files without making every database operation carry the binary payload. The selected design is not suitable when the system requires a single atomic transaction that includes the object bytes, or when the team cannot operate an asynchronous retry and deletion queue. In those cases, keeping bounded files in the existing database may be the more honest choice.

Do not make the cheapest nominal storage rate the decision rule. Compare ingress and egress assumptions, request charges, retrieval behavior, replication, backup treatment, deletion requirements, and the engineering time needed to recover an orphaned object. Your mileage may vary because traffic geography and receipt-size distribution can change the result more than a posted storage number.

An ADR worth keeping after launch

Record the rejected option and the reason it was rejected. For this system, the rejected default is one mutable thumbnail path, because publication and cleanup become difficult to reason about when workers race. The valid use case is a prototype where a single worker owns each key and losing an older derivative has no audit consequence.

Also record the operational thresholds: maximum accepted receipt size, concurrency limits, retry budget, URL lifetime, retention class, and the alert for a record stuck between upload and publication. Review those values with real percentile data. I'm not sure which threshold will dominate before the first production distribution is visible, and pretending otherwise is how capacity plans acquire false precision.

The decision is narrow: keep originals private and durable enough for the audit policy, make derivative keys immutable, publish only completed objects, and let the application—not a guessed URL or an over-broad lifecycle rule—own authorization and deletion.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/

title: Best Bank Statement Converter: How to Test a Parser With Tie-Outs
description:
The best test for a bank statement parser, and the one we used to pick the best bank statement converter, is a tie-out: for every account on the statement, the printed opening balance plus the sum of the extracted rows must equal the printed closing balance, to the cent. If that holds, the extraction is almost certainly right. If it doesn't, the size of the gap usually tells you which row to look at. That check was the first criterion when we ranked 12 statement converters, and this post shows how to run it yourself in Python and in SQL.

Disclosure: I work on ZeraBooks, which makes one of those converters and ranks itself first. The code below is vendor-neutral. Point it at any parser's output.

Why not just measure accuracy?

Because "accuracy" for a statement parser is slippery. Per field? Per row? Per document? On whose documents? Vendors publish numbers like "99%+" or "99.9%" without the method, so you can't compare them and you can't reproduce them.

A statement gives you something better than a test set: a ground truth printed on the document itself. The bank tells you where the account started and where it ended. Your parser's rows have to connect those two numbers. That makes the check:

  • Per document, so you know about this file, not an average.
  • Free, because the bank already did the work.
  • Strict, because one wrong digit anywhere breaks it.
  • Explainable, because the size of the gap points at the kind of mistake.

The one thing it can't catch is two errors that cancel each other out. That's rare enough that I'd still take this check over any percentage.

The tie-out in Python

Rules that matter more than they look:

  1. Use Decimal, never float. 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 in floating point, and a tie-out that's off by 0.00000000001 is a tie-out you'll learn to ignore. That defeats the point.
  2. Group by account. One PDF often holds a checking and a savings account. Tie out each one separately, or a gap in one hides inside the other.
  3. Money out is negative. Normalise to one signed amount column before summing. If your parser emits separate debit and credit columns, convert first.
  4. Parentheses mean negative. Some banks print (132.45).

Here's a small, runnable version with a diagnostic step. The sample has two accounts from one statement, and the savings account's printed closing balance has two digits swapped, which is the classic OCR failure.

import csv
import io
from collections import defaultdict
from decimal import Decimal

CENT = Decimal("0.01")


def money(text):
    """Parse '1,234.56', '-132.45' or '(132.45)' into an exact Decimal."""
    text = text.strip().replace(",", "").replace("$", "")
    if text.startswith("(") and text.endswith(")"):
        text = "-" + text[1:-1]
    return Decimal(text).quantize(CENT)


def tie_out(opening, amounts, closing):
    """Return the gap: 0 means opening + rows == closing to the cent."""
    return (opening + sum(amounts, Decimal("0")) - closing).quantize(CENT)


def diagnose(gap, amounts):
    """Turn a non-zero gap into a short list of things to look at first."""
    hints = []
    if gap == 0:
        return hints
    for a in amounts:
        if a == gap:
            hints.append(f"row {a} may be doubled")
        if a == -gap:
            hints.append(f"a row of {-a} may be missing")
        if a * 2 == gap or a * 2 == -gap:
            hints.append(f"row {a} may have the wrong sign")
    cents = int(abs(gap) * 100)
    if cents % 9 == 0:
        hints.append(f"gap {gap} divides by 9: look for two swapped digits")
    return hints


SAMPLE = """account,date,description,amount,balance
CHK 4417,2026-09-01,Opening,,18432.17
CHK 4417,2026-09-02,Card settlement,1250.00,19682.17
CHK 4417,2026-09-03,Rent,-2400.00,17282.17
CHK 4417,2026-09-08,Payroll,-3184.20,14097.97
CHK 4417,2026-09-15,Customer deposit,5327.77,19425.74
SAV 0011,2026-09-01,Opening,,3210.00
SAV 0011,2026-09-05,Transfer in,300.00,3510.00
SAV 0011,2026-09-30,Interest,1.34,3511.34
"""

# Printed on the statement's summary page, per account.
PRINTED = {
    "CHK 4417": (money("18,432.17"), money("19,425.74")),
    "SAV 0011": (money("3,210.00"), money("3,511.43")),  # last two digits swapped
}

rows = defaultdict(list)
for r in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(SAMPLE)):
    if r["amount"]:
        rows[r["account"]].append(money(r["amount"]))

for account, amounts in rows.items():
    opening, closing = PRINTED[account]
    gap = tie_out(opening, amounts, closing)
    status = "Proven" if gap == 0 else f"Needs a look (gap {gap})"
    print(f"{account}: {len(amounts)} rows, {status}")
    for hint in diagnose(gap, amounts):
        print("   ", hint)

Output:

CHK 4417: 4 rows, Proven
SAV 0011: 2 rows, Needs a look (gap -0.09)
    gap -0.09 divides by 9: look for two swapped digits

The diagnose function encodes four rules of thumb that cover most real failures:

Gap looks like Usual cause
Exactly one row's amount That row was extracted twice
Minus one row's amount A row was dropped, often at a page break
Twice one row's amount A withdrawal came out as a deposit, or the reverse
A multiple of 9 (in cents) Two neighbouring digits swapped somewhere

The 9 rule works because swapping two adjacent digits a and b changes a number by 9 × (a - b) × 10^n. A 0.09 gap points at the last two digits; 630.00 points at the hundreds and tens. It can't tell you whether the swap is in a row or in the printed balance you typed in, so check both.

Find the exact row with the running balance

Most statements also print a running balance on each row. That's a second, finer check: each row's printed balance should equal the previous balance plus this row's amount. The first row where it doesn't is your culprit.

from decimal import Decimal


def first_break(opening, rows):
    """rows: (description, amount, printed_running_balance). Return the first row
    where the previous balance plus this amount doesn't give the printed balance."""
    expected = opening
    for i, (desc, amount, balance) in enumerate(rows, start=1):
        expected += amount
        if expected != balance:
            return i, desc, expected, balance
        expected = balance  # carry the bank's figure, so one error is reported once
    return None


rows = [
    ("Card settlement", Decimal("1250.00"), Decimal("19682.17")),
    ("Rent", Decimal("-2400.00"), Decimal("17282.17")),
    ("Payroll", Decimal("-3814.20"), Decimal("14097.97")),  # misread: 3184.20
    ("Customer deposit", Decimal("5327.77"), Decimal("19425.74")),
]

hit = first_break(Decimal("18432.17"), rows)
if hit:
    i, desc, expected, printed = hit
    print(f"row {i} ({desc}): expected {expected}, statement says {printed}, "
          f"off by {printed - expected}")

Output:

row 3 (Payroll): expected 13467.97, statement says 14097.97, off by 630.00

Note the expected = balance line. After a break, carry the bank's printed figure forward rather than your computed one. Otherwise one bad row makes every row after it look bad too.

The same checks in SQL

If extracted rows land in a database, run the checks there. Store money as integer cents. This runs as-is in SQLite 3.25 or newer (window functions), and needs only small changes for Postgres.

CREATE TABLE stmt_rows (
  account       TEXT,
  seq           INTEGER,
  description   TEXT,
  amount_cents  INTEGER,
  balance_cents INTEGER
);
CREATE TABLE stmt_summary (
  account       TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  opening_cents INTEGER,
  closing_cents INTEGER
);

INSERT INTO stmt_rows VALUES
  ('CHK 4417', 1, 'Card settlement',   125000, 1968217),
  ('CHK 4417', 2, 'Rent',             -240000, 1728217),
  ('CHK 4417', 3, 'Payroll',          -381420, 1409797),
  ('CHK 4417', 4, 'Customer deposit',  532777, 1942574),
  ('SAV 0011', 1, 'Transfer in',        30000,  351000),
  ('SAV 0011', 2, 'Interest',             134,  351134);
INSERT INTO stmt_summary VALUES
  ('CHK 4417', 1843217, 1942574),
  ('SAV 0011',  321000,  351134);

-- 1. Tie-out per account: opening + rows must equal closing.
SELECT s.account,
       COUNT(r.seq) AS rows,
       s.opening_cents + SUM(r.amount_cents) - s.closing_cents AS gap_cents,
       CASE WHEN s.opening_cents + SUM(r.amount_cents) = s.closing_cents
            THEN 'Proven' ELSE 'Needs a look' END AS status
FROM stmt_summary s
JOIN stmt_rows r ON r.account = s.account
GROUP BY s.account
ORDER BY s.account;

-- 2. Which row breaks the printed running balance?
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT account, seq, description,
         balance_cents - amount_cents
           - COALESCE(LAG(balance_cents) OVER w,
                      (SELECT opening_cents FROM stmt_summary s
                       WHERE s.account = r.account)) AS break_cents
  FROM stmt_rows r
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY account ORDER BY seq)
)
WHERE break_cents <> 0;

Output from sqlite3 -header -column :memory: < tieout.sql:

account   rows  gap_cents  status
--------  ----  ---------  ------------
CHK 4417  4     -63000     Needs a look
SAV 0011  2     0          Proven
account   seq  description  break_cents
--------  ---  -----------  -----------
CHK 4417  3    Payroll      63000

Query 1 is the gate: nothing with a non-zero gap goes downstream. Query 2 is the pointer: it names the row.

Try it on a real 140-row file

ZeraBooks publishes the file from its 10-bank sample run, ten fictional statements (Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Navy Federal, Synchrony, Monzo, RBC, Desjardins, TD, CommBank) downloaded as one CSV with the account and source file on every row. Here's a running-balance check over it:

import csv
import sys
from collections import defaultdict
from decimal import Decimal

path = sys.argv[1]
by_account = defaultdict(list)
with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        by_account[row["Account"]].append(row)

for account, rows in by_account.items():
    if not rows[0]["Balance"]:
        print(f"{account}: {len(rows)} rows, no running balance on the statement")
        continue
    opening = Decimal(rows[0]["Balance"]) - Decimal(rows[0]["Amount"])
    breaks, prev = 0, opening
    for r in rows:
        if prev + Decimal(r["Amount"]) != Decimal(r["Balance"]):
            breaks += 1
        prev = Decimal(r["Balance"])
    print(f"{account}: {len(rows)} rows, {opening} -> {prev}, breaks: {breaks}")

curl -s -o all-details.csv "https://www.zerabooks.com/marketing/reviews/best-converter/All%20details%20-%2010%20documents.csv"
python3 alldetails.py all-details.csv

RBC Business Account 5108: 14 rows, 31204.66 -> 19215.82, breaks: 0
Chase Business Complete Checking 4417: 21 rows, 18432.17 -> 19425.74, breaks: 0
Initiate Business Checking 2265: 18 rows, 9614.08 -> 14819.40, breaks: 0
High Yield Savings 7392: 4 rows, 24150.00 -> 25037.64, breaks: 0
Monzo Business Lite 0921: 13 rows, 6845.20 -> 11914.71, breaks: 0
CommBank Business Transaction Account 7714: 13 rows, 15320.40 -> 11700.77, breaks: 0
Every Day Business Plan Chequing 3307: 12 rows, 22840.15 -> 20219.38, breaks: 0
Business Advantage Fundamentals Banking 8803: 18 rows, no running balance on the statement
Compte d'opérations entreprise 1234: 13 rows, 14378.90 -> 10771.60, breaks: 0
EVERYDAY CHECKING 6620: 12 rows, 1482.30 -> 4702.00, breaks: 0
MEMBERSHIP SAVINGS 0011: 2 rows, 3210.00 -> 3511.34, breaks: 0

Two things worth noticing. Ten PDFs produce eleven accounts, because the Navy Federal statement holds a checking and a savings account. And the Bank of America statement prints no running balance on its rows, so only the summary-page tie-out applies there. Your test harness needs to handle both cases without crashing or silently passing.

What else belongs in a parser test suite?

The tie-out catches wrong numbers. It doesn't catch everything. These are the other checks I'd add, all cheap:

  • Row count. If the statement prints a transaction count, match it.
  • Dates inside the period. Every row's date falls between the statement's start and end, with the right year. December-to-January statements are where year inference breaks.
  • No junk rows. No page headers, "balance forward", "continued on next page" or subtotal lines in the output.
  • Reference numbers intact. Long IDs stored as text, not numbers. Excel shows a 17-digit reference as 1.23E+16 and keeps only 15 significant digits.
  • No statement without balances marked as passing. If the PDF prints no opening or closing balance, the result is "unverified", not "proven".

How did this shape the ranking?

When we ranked 12 converters, the first question for each tool was whether it runs this check itself. ZeraBooks marks each account Proven or Needs a look based on exactly this tie-out, per account and per cardholder. DocuClipper says it runs reconciliation checks on its output. MoneyThumb describes automatic reconciliation against the summary totals. Hubdoc errors when totals don't match. Several others don't say. Those answers come from each vendor's own pages, with checked dates, in ZeraBooks' ranking of the 12 converters.

AI-based parsers make this more important, not less. A model reads layouts it has never seen, which is great, and it can also misread a digit with total confidence. ZeraBooks wrote a separate ranking on how each AI bank statement converter backs its accuracy claim, and the short version is that the arithmetic check has to live outside the model.

If you're building or buying a parser, put the tie-out in CI. Feed it every statement layout you've ever seen fail. A parser that passes the tie-out on a hundred ugly real-world statements is better tested than one with a great number on a landing page.

title: I built a macOS app that makes your screen feel like paper!
description:
A few weeks ago I was reading "Attention Is All You Need" for probably the fifth time. It was late, I had the PDF open full screen, and within a few minutes, I realised my eyes weren't tired from the screen.

Everything on a Mac is so clean and glossy. White is really white. Every page looks like it's printed on glass. That's great for photos, but when you're reading for hours it starts to feel harsh, and I kept thinking about how much nicer the same paper would feel if it was, well, on paper.

So I went looking for an app that could fake that.

The apps that already exist

Turns out I'm not the first person to want this. There are a few apps that put a texture over your screen, and some of them look really good. But every one I found had the same problem for me: I couldn't try it without paying first.

One was around $13 upfront with no free version at all. Another was part of a bigger subscription bundle. For something this personal, where you can only know if you like it by living with it for a day, paying before trying felt wrong. A texture that looks lovely in screenshots might be annoying on your actual screen with your actual apps.

I'm a backend dev. I spend my days with Node, Redis and queues, not AppKit. But I'd been wanting to ship something of my own for a long time, and this felt small enough to actually finish. So I decided to build my own, with a free version anyone could just try.

That became Shoji, named after the Japanese paper screens that let soft light through.

How it actually works

The core idea is surprisingly simple. Shoji puts one borderless, transparent window on every display, floating above everything else, and draws a light paper texture into it. The important bit is that the window ignores the mouse completely, so every click goes straight through to whatever is underneath:

ignoresMouseEvents = true
level = NSWindow.Level(rawValue: Int(CGWindowLevelForKey(.assistiveTechHighWindow)))
collectionBehavior = [.canJoinAllSpaces, .stationary, .fullScreenAuxiliary, .ignoresCycle]

That last line is what lets it follow you across Spaces and sit over full screen apps too.

The part that took the longest wasn't the window though. It was the paper.

I didn't want to use photos of paper, because photos tile badly. You start seeing the same blotch repeat every few inches and your brain can't unsee it. So every texture is generated in code, using layered noise, a bit of domain warping so the patterns never line up in rows, and little randomly walked "fibers" for papers like Washi and Newsprint. It's all seeded, so the same paper looks the same every time, and it renders sharp on any display.

Getting them right in dark mode was its own adventure. Shadows that look like nice paper grain on white just disappear on a dark background, and fibers that look subtle on light mode suddenly look like hair on your screen in dark mode. I ended up with separate recipes for light and dark, and a separate strength setting for each, so dark apps stay dark.

A few other fun things I learned along the way:

  • Hiding from screenshots is one line, sharingType = .none. Your screen shares and recordings stay clean.
  • Getting notarized was more stressful than writing the app. Xcode kept telling me I wasn't the account holder of the account I literally owned, and I got very familiar with keychain error codes.
  • Auto updates run on Sparkle, and I found a fun bug where the update window would open behind Spotify and make the whole app look frozen. Lesson learned: always bring your app forward before showing a modal.

And then, before I'd even posted it anywhere except one tweet, someone bought it. A real person, who I don't know, paid for a thing I made. I'm not going to pretend I was calm about it.

What Shoji does

  • 7 papers: Plain, Rice, Linen, Newsprint, Washi, Cold Press and Parchment
  • Clicks pass through, so everything works exactly like before
  • Every display, including external monitors and full screen apps
  • Hidden from screenshots and screen recordings
  • Separate strength for light and dark mode
  • Pause it for 15 minutes, an hour, or until tomorrow
  • Lives in your menu bar, with keyboard shortcuts to toggle it or switch papers
  • No tracking. It never reads your screen, and only goes online to check for updates and verify a Pro license

What's next

  • A Windows version (people keep asking)
  • Per-app rules, so you can turn the paper off in apps where you don't want it
  • More papers

If you have ideas, I'd honestly love to hear them.

Pricing

PS: I already made my first sale yesterday from my X launch post :)

This was the whole reason I built it, so it's simple:

  • Free: Plain Paper, forever, with every feature. No account, no trial timer.
  • Pro: all 7 papers for $5 once, on up to 3 Macs, with lifetime updates and a 14-day refund if it's not for you.

For launch, Pro is $3 until November 23.

And for dev.to readers: leave a comment below and I'll reply with a code for an even better deal.

Links

  • Website and download: shoji.ink
  • Me on X: @_asheeshh

It needs macOS 13 or later and works on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs.

This is my first app, so any feedback helps, good or bad. And if you also read too many PDFs late at night, give the free paper a try. Your eyes might thank you.
