title: Introducing HexDB for Documents and Files
description:
An application can have customer records, uploaded documents, full-text search, and semantic search over those documents. Keeping the data, permissions, and updates consistent across those features can become a project of its own.

I've built HexDB to bring those pieces closer together.

HexDB is an encrypted, replicated database for JSON documents and binary files, with full-text and vector search. The core server is written in Rust and runs as one binary.

I'm Matthew "Doc" Martin, a software architect with more than 25 years in software development. HexDB is my independent project, built during late nights and weekends alongside my day job. With versions 2.4.3 and 2.4.4 released, this seems like a good time to introduce it here.

Documents and files in one database

HexDB stores JSON documents in collections called tessellations. You can query them through REST, GraphQL, gRPC, or SQL, with drivers for Node.js, Python, .NET, Java through JDBC, and ODBC.

SQL currently supports reads. Writes go through the APIs and drivers.

Files are part of the database too. They have queryable metadata, version history, resumable uploads, and access controls. Their content is encrypted, deduplicated, and compressed when that helps.

Consider an application with customer records and uploaded invoices. You need to find the records, retrieve the files, restrict access, and perhaps search the invoices by their contents. HexDB provides those capabilities within the same database platform.

It also includes an admin UI for managing documents, files, users, indexes, and the cluster. I want the operational side to be approachable, including when you're the person building the application and keeping it running.

Vector search alongside ordinary queries

Vector search is an index type in HexDB. You can supply your own embeddings or configure an embedding provider and have HexDB generate them from selected fields.

Similarity searches use the same documents, permissions, row filters, and field masks as other queries. You can combine a semantic search with an ordinary filter.

For example, after configuring an embedding provider and a vector index on an articles collection, this request searches published articles by meaning:

curl -X POST http://localhost:7700/articles/_query \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "filter": { "status": "published" },
    "near": {
      "field": "embedding",
      "text": "storage engines for edge devices",
      "k": 5
    }
  }'

The same approach works with extracted text from uploaded files. A search can find a document by what it discusses, even when its filename isn't useful.

Automatic embeddings use the provider you configure, including supported local providers. The selected source text goes to that provider. Usage controls include per-user allowances and a monthly token budget.

Each HexDB server also exposes an MCP endpoint for authenticated, read-only access by external agents. Optional A2A support lets another agent delegate a question to HexDB's own chat system. Those lookups run with the calling user's permissions.

Security around both records and uploads

My work in payments influences the questions I ask about data handling: who can read a value, where it gets copied, and what remains after a request finishes.

HexDB includes encryption at rest, role-based access, row filters, field masking, MFA, and an audit trail. Schema-defined tokenization can replace sensitive field values before the document reaches its write-ahead log, storage, replicas, or backups.

There are two tokenization modes. One-way tokens support matching without recovering the original value. Vault tokens keep the original in a separate encrypted vault, with explicit permission and auditing for detokenization.

File uploads also have integrated malware scanning and quarantine. YARA-X is built into supported builds, and HexDB connects to a separately running ClamAV daemon for signature-based scanning. Files flagged by a scanner are quarantined instead of becoming normal downloadable files or being replicated.

That distinction matters for deployment: the core database is one binary; ClamAV is an additional service. The supplied Docker Compose and Helm configurations include it.

The latest release adds cluster-wide IP blocking with optional expiry, signed responses between servers, and overwriting sensitive decrypted field values in memory when requests finish using them. It also fixes a change-feed issue so users cannot learn about deletions of records they weren't allowed to see.

A foreign key question that changed the engine

One of the changes in 2.4.3 began with a prospect asking about foreign keys.

HexDB now supports optional foreign keys in document schemas. With enforcement enabled, a write referencing a missing parent is refused.

The interesting part is when that check happens.

Suppose an order references a customer:

  1. A request checks that the customer exists.
  2. Another request deletes that customer.
  3. The first request commits the order.

A successful check at step one isn't enough to prevent an orphan at step three.

HexDB checks the relationship as part of the commit itself. Cascading deletes also re-check for newly written children at commit time, closing a related race.

The CLI gained document, transaction, and schema operations with idempotency keys, so retrying after a dropped connection won't apply the same write twice. A new “Writing safely” manual section explains the guarantees for inserts, updates, upserts, deletes, and transactions.

This is the kind of feedback I want from people evaluating HexDB. A concrete application requirement can expose something worth changing in the engine.

Recovery and performance in the latest releases

A group of HexDB servers is called a lattice. One server, the Overseer, handles writes; eligible replicas can take over if it fails.

Version 2.4.4 brings failover down to 15–20 seconds, about half the previous time. It also addresses isolated servers electing themselves and servers disagreeing about leadership when the whole cluster starts together.

Hosted routing now sends traffic only to servers that have the data. In one provisioning run, a new three-region hosted lattice went from nothing to fully ready in 33 seconds.

Storage and query improvements include:

Measurement Before After
Small-record storage in the measured workload 177 bytes 40 bytes
GROUP BY over 100,000 documents 320 ms 210 ms

The storage improvement comes from per-file compression dictionaries that capture patterns shared by documents. Reading a stored document also takes about half the work.

These are measurements from the specific workloads used for the release. They give a useful starting point for evaluating the changes against your own data.

Try HexDB and tell me what you find

HexDB is available through npm, PyPI, NuGet, Maven, Homebrew, Chocolatey, Debian packages, and Docker. You can run it yourself or explore hosted lattices.

The repository has installation instructions, examples, and the technical manual:

  • HexDB website
  • Source code and getting started
  • Version 2.4.4 release notes

I'd like to hear from developers working with documents, uploaded files, sensitive fields, or semantic search. What would you need to test before considering HexDB for an application? Which integration would make it easier to evaluate?

The foreign-key question already changed the engine. I'm interested in the next question.

title: How to get EU public tenders from TED as JSON in Python (without learning expert-query syntax)
description:
Every public tender above the EU thresholds, from a German city's software project to a French hospital's equipment purchase, is published in TED (Tenders Electronic Daily), the EU's official procurement journal. TED has a free, official search API. The catch is its expert query syntax, its nested multilingual fields and a single notice that can contain several lots with different deadlines and values.

This post shows a script that answers one practical question: "Which open tenders match what we sell, in the countries we serve, and are still biddable?" You get flat JSON and a CSV.

Disclosure: I built the EU Tenders (TED) API actor used below. It calls the official TED Search API v3 and only returns organisations, never contact persons.

The 20-line version 

# pip install apify-client
import csv, os
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

run_input = {
    "keywords": ["software"],
    "countries": ["DEU", "AUT"],      # ISO alpha-3 buyer countries
    "cpvCodes": ["72", "48"],         # IT services, software packages
    "noticeTypes": ["competition"],   # open calls for tenders
    "publishedWithinDays": 7,
    "deadlineAfter": "today",         # skip expired tenders
    "maxResults": 50,
}

run = client.actor("fast_data_asap/eu-tenders-ted-api").call(run_input=run_input)
notices = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

notices.sort(key=lambda n: n.get("deadline") or "9999")
fields = ["deadline", "buyerName", "buyerCity", "buyerCountry", "title", "estimatedValue", "currency", "url"]
with open("tenders.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields, extrasaction="ignore")
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(notices)
print(len(notices), "open tenders written to tenders.csv")

No browser, no HTML parsing. The actor turns the inputs into a TED expert query, follows pagination and flattens each notice into one row.

What comes back

These are real rows from test runs on 8 and 9 November 2026 (shortened):

Deadline Buyer What Est. value
02.12.2026 MD-IT GmbH, Berlin Framework agreement: AI for hospital billing review, compliance, AI governance (3 lots) €121,000,000
07.12.2026 Stadt Brandis Development of OpenCore modules for the PartheCloud €625,600
08.12.2026 BWI GmbH, Bonn Framework contract, notice "1961-JC-NoCodeDB" (software packages) not published

Every row has the same flat fields:

{
  "noticeId": "779062-2026",
  "title": "Germany – Programming services of application software – Entwicklungsleistungen für OpenCore-Module der PartheCloud",
  "buyerName": "Stadt Brandis",
  "buyerCountry": "DEU",
  "buyerCity": "Brandis",
  "cpvMain": "72212000",
  "cpvCodes": ["72212000", "72262000", "72263000"],
  "formType": "competition",
  "procedureType": "open",
  "estimatedValue": 625600,
  "currency": "EUR",
  "publishedAt": "2026-11-09",
  "deadline": "2026-12-07T12:00:00+01:00",
  "lotsCount": 1,
  "url": "https://ted.europa.eu/en/notice/-/detail/779062-2026"
}

Two details that save you work:

  • deadline is the earliest lot deadline as an ISO timestamp, so sorting and "days left" are one line.
  • estimatedValue is summed across lots. It is null when the buyer did not publish a value (BWI above), which is common.

Choosing filters that actually match your business

CPV prefixes are the most useful filter. CPV is the EU's product vocabulary, and a prefix matches everything below it:

Prefix Covers
72 IT services (consulting, development, support)
48 Software packages and information systems
79 Business services (consulting, marketing, translation)
45 Construction work
90 Cleaning, waste and environmental services
33 Medical equipment

Keywords are matched in full text in any language, so ["software", "Software", "logiciel"] widens the net across countries. Start broad, look at a week of results, then add minValueEur if small contracts are noise for you. Notices without a published value are kept, so you do not silently lose them.

Want to know who wins? Switch noticeTypes to ["result"]. Contract award notices show which buyer bought what, and often for how much: useful for competitor research and pricing.

Running it every morning

For a daily alert set publishedWithinDays to 2 (one day overlap as a safety net) and de-duplicate on noticeId:

import json, pathlib

seen_file = pathlib.Path("seen.json")
seen = set(json.loads(seen_file.read_text())) if seen_file.exists() else set()
new = [n for n in notices if n["noticeId"] not in seen]
seen_file.write_text(json.dumps(sorted(seen | {n["noticeId"] for n in new})))

for n in new:
    print(f'{n["deadline"][:10]}  {n["buyerName"]}: {n["title"][:90]}\n  {n["url"]}')

Schedule the script with cron or a GitHub Action, or use an Apify schedule and pipe the dataset into Slack or a sheet. If you prefer no-code, our free n8n sales-signal workflow does the same for German tenders and can take TED as a third branch.

Limits

  • TED lists notices above the EU thresholds (plus voluntary ones). Smaller national tenders are on national portals; for Germany there is our German Public Tenders actor.
  • Titles and summaries come in the notice language. The actor prefers your language (English by default) where the notice is multilingual.
  • This is a search tool, not procurement or legal advice. Always read the official notice before bidding.

What it costs

$0.002 per notice returned, and empty runs are free. The 50-notice daily run above costs at most $0.10; a typical "last two days, two countries, two CPV codes" run returns far fewer rows.

Try it

  • EU Tenders (TED) API on Apify
  • Agent users: the free find-public-tenders skill lets an AI agent run this search for you.

Question for bid managers: which filter do you rely on most, CPV codes or keywords, and how many false positives do you accept per day before an alert becomes noise?

title: How to Succeed as a Solo UX or Product Designer in the AI Era
description:
Over the years, the role of UX designers has continuously evolved with changes in technology, business needs, and user expectations.

In the early days, UX designers primarily focused on creating simple mockups and designing applications for desktop screens. As technology advanced, designers began creating responsive experiences across multiple devices, including desktops, tablets, and mobile phones. This shift required designers to expand their skills and adapt to new design challenges.

As digital products became more complex, UX design expanded into different industries, including B2B, SaaS, healthcare technology, e-commerce, and developer experience (DevEx). Today, UX designers are no longer limited to a single industry or type of product. They have opportunities to apply their knowledge and skills across a wide range of domains.

However, the responsibilities of UX designers often depend on the size and structure of an organization. In small companies and startups, a solo UX or product designer may be responsible for the entire design process, from understanding user needs and conducting research to creating user interfaces, testing designs, and collaborating on product development. In contrast, larger organizations often have dedicated teams or specialists focusing on specific areas, such as UX research, interaction design, visual design, and design systems.

One challenge that often receives less attention is UX documentation and knowledge management. Many designers focus on delivering design solutions and showcasing their work through portfolios, while documenting research findings, design decisions, workflows, and lessons learned receives less priority.

This challenge can be particularly noticeable in small organizations, where limited resources and multiple responsibilities make it difficult to establish consistent documentation practices. Larger and mid-sized organizations may have more dedicated resources, processes, and teams to support UX documentation, although they can face similar challenges.

Now, with the rapid growth of artificial intelligence, the role of UX and product designers is evolving once again. AI creates opportunities for solo designers to work more efficiently, support research activities, improve documentation, explore design ideas, and contribute across different stages of product development.

The question is no longer just how UX designers can create better designs, but how they can adapt their skills, manage broader responsibilities, and use AI effectively to succeed as solo designers in a rapidly changing industry.

This article explores the evolution of UX design, the challenges faced by solo designers, and how AI can help them improve their workflows, strengthen documentation practices, and deliver meaningful user experiences.

UX Fundamentals and Domain Knowledge: Essential Skills for Every UX Designer

A strong foundation in UX design and domain knowledge is essential for every UX or product designer, especially in the AI era.

Understanding the fundamentals of UX design helps designers recognize the importance of user experience, identify user needs, and create intuitive, accessible, and user-friendly applications.

With a solid understanding of UX principles, designers can make better decisions about application layouts, screen sizes, responsive design, color palettes, navigation, and information architecture. These foundational skills also help designers use AI tools more effectively to explore ideas, build prototypes, and develop successful digital products.

However, UX fundamentals alone are not enough. Domain knowledge is equally important. For example, when designing a healthcare application, designers need to understand the purpose of the product, its users, accessibility requirements, privacy concerns, and the specific challenges of the healthcare industry.

Similarly, designers working in SaaS, e-commerce, FinTech, or Developer Experience (DevEx) need to understand the workflows, terminology, user expectations, and challenges specific to those domains.

In the AI era, designers can use AI to speed up design and development activities, but AI cannot replace their understanding of users, design principles, and industry-specific requirements. However designers don't need to be experts in every industry.

The key takeaway is that AI can help designers build products faster, but strong UX fundamentals and domain knowledge help them build the right products for the right users.

From UX Knowledge to Practical Experience: A 40-Day Design Challenge for Beginners

By now, you should have a better understanding of the importance of UX fundamentals and domain knowledge, how UX design has evolved over the years, and how these changes have shaped the way we design digital products and improve user experiences.

But understanding UX concepts is only the beginning. The real learning starts when you apply that knowledge to practical design challenges.

Step 1: Build Your UX Skills Through a 30-Day Design Challenge

Once you understand the fundamentals of UX design and the importance of domain knowledge, the next step is to put your learning into practice.

I recommend starting with a 30-day UX design challenge. Depending on your interests, learning pace, and availability, you can also extend it to 60 days.

The goal is to complete 30 design challenges while developing your problem-solving skills, design thinking, and practical UX knowledge.

Why a design challenge?

  • It helps you develop consistency and discipline.
  • It motivates you to practice UX design regularly.
  • It encourages you to think critically about everyday user experiences.
  • It gives you opportunities to apply user-centered design principles.
  • It helps you build confidence through hands-on experience.

Let's divide these 30 challenges into three stages.

Step 2: Days 1–10 : Improve the Applications You Use Every Day

Start with something familiar: the applications and websites you use in your daily life.

Think about the apps you use for shopping, banking, communication, note-taking, learning, or managing your daily activities.

Your challenge: Choose 10 applications you regularly use and identify opportunities to improve their user experience.

For each application, ask yourself:

  • What is the main purpose of this application?
  • Who are its target users?
  • What works well in the current experience?
  • What challenges or frustrations might users face?
  • How could I improve the experience using UX design principles?

For example, you might use a shopping application regularly but find its checkout process confusing or time-consuming. Think about how you could simplify the process and make it easier for users.

Try to understand the problem before jumping into a design solution.

By the end of these 10 challenges, you will have gained practical experience in evaluating existing applications, identifying usability problems, and proposing improvements from a user's perspective.

Step 3: Days 11–20 : Turn Your Own Ideas Into UX Design Projects

Now that you have practiced improving existing applications, it's time to think about your own product ideas and choose one design tool such as Figma and practice these challenges using this tool. (At the beginning choosing the one tool is enough to practice the skills later you can explore other similar tool like Adobe XD and many more depending on your interest.

Have you ever thought, "I wish there were an application that could help me do this task more easily?"

This is a great starting point for a UX design project.

For example, I often think about having a personalized notepad application that helps me organize meeting notes, capture important discussions, and track action items.

Instead of simply imagining the application, I can turn this idea into a design project using user-centered design principles.

Your challenge: Come up with 10 application or website ideas based on problems you experience or observe in everyday life.

For each idea:

  1. Identify the problem you want to solve.
  2. Understand who might experience this problem.
  3. Define the users' needs and goals.
  4. Explore possible solutions.
  5. Create user flows, wireframes, or prototypes.
  6. Evaluate your design and identify improvements.

You don't need to build a fully functional application for every challenge. Focus on understanding the problem and practicing the UX design process.

By the end of these challenges, you will have more confidence in turning ideas into practical design solutions.

Step 4: Days 21–30 : Explore UX Design in Your Area of Interest

Now it's time to explore a specific industry or domain that interests you.

Domain knowledge plays an important role in UX design because every industry has its own users, workflows, challenges, regulations, and technical requirements.

For example, you might be interested in:

  • Healthcare and medical applications
  • Banking and financial technology
  • Developer tools and cloud-native technologies
  • Education technology
  • E-commerce applications

Your challenge: Choose one domain that interests you and explore 10 applications or tools related to that domain.

Try to understand how these tools work, who uses them, and what problems they solve.

What if you don't have access to these tools?

Some professional applications are not publicly accessible. They may require a paid subscription, an organizational account, or special permissions.

For example, imagine you are interested in designing clinical or medical applications.

Many hospital management systems and electronic health record applications are accessible only to authorized healthcare professionals because they handle sensitive patient information.

As a beginner, you may not have access to these applications.

So, what can you do?

You can explore:

  • Applications that offer free trials or demo environments.
  • Open-source alternatives.
  • Publicly available training environments.
  • Similar applications with accessible features.
  • Product documentation, tutorials, and walkthroughs.

The goal is to understand the workflows, user needs, and design challenges within your chosen domain. Once you have explored these tools, think about how you could improve their user experience.

An important note for beginners:

During these first 30 challenges, I recommend avoiding AI-generated design solutions as much as possible.

Why?

Because this is your opportunity to strengthen your UX fundamentals, critical thinking, research skills, and problem-solving abilities.

You can use learning resources and documentation, but try to analyze problems, develop ideas, and make design decisions independently.

Learn to think like a designer before depending on AI to design for you.

Step 5: Days 31–40 : Learn How to Use AI in Your UX Design Process

Congratulations! By now, you have completed 30 practical design challenges covering everyday applications, your own product ideas, and domain-specific tools.

You have practiced identifying user problems, exploring solutions, and applying UX principles.

Now it's time to take your learning to the next level.

How can AI help you become a more efficient UX designer?

AI can support designers in many ways, from organizing research findings and exploring design ideas to creating prototypes and speeding up repetitive tasks.

But the goal is not to replace your design thinking with AI.

Instead, you should learn how to combine human creativity, UX knowledge, domain expertise, and AI capabilities to solve design problems more effectively.

Your challenge: Complete 10 additional design challenges using AI tools alongside your UX skills.

You can revisit some of your previous projects or choose entirely new design problems.

For each challenge:

  1. Identify the UX problem independently.
  2. Think about how you would approach the problem without AI.
  3. Explore where AI could help you save time.
  4. Use AI tools to support research synthesis, ideation, prototyping, or documentation.
  5. Review and validate the AI-generated outputs.
  6. Compare your workflow with and without AI.

Ask yourself:

  • Did AI help me complete the task faster?
  • Did it improve the quality of my solution?
  • Did it provide useful ideas I hadn't considered?
  • Were any AI-generated suggestions inaccurate or unsuitable?
  • Which design decisions still required my judgment?

Remember, AI can help you work faster, but your UX knowledge helps you decide whether the solution is actually useful, accessible, and user-friendly.

By completing these challenges, you will begin to understand how AI fits into your design process without losing your independent problem-solving skills.

Step 6: Move From Practice Projects to Real-World Open-Source Contributions

After completing these 40 design challenges, you will have built a stronger foundation in UX design, gained practical experience, explored an industry of interest, and learned how to use AI effectively in your workflow.

Now it's time to move beyond personal design challenges and start working on real-world problems.

One of the ways to gain practical experience is by contributing to open-source projects.

Open-source communities give you opportunities to collaborate with developers, maintainers, designers, and users who are working together to improve real products.

You can begin by exploring projects related to your chosen domain and looking for opportunities to contribute through usability reviews, user research, documentation improvements, design proposals, or accessibility enhancements.

You don't need to be an expert to get started. Begin with small contributions, understand the community's needs, and gradually take on more challenging problems.

This experience can help you develop collaboration skills, understand real product constraints, and build a portfolio that demonstrates your ability to solve meaningful user problems.

How to Document Your UX Design Challenges

Now that you have completed your design challenges, the next important step is to learn how to document your design process and decisions.

Documentation is an essential skill for UX designers. It helps you organize your ideas, explain your design decisions, communicate your problem-solving approach, and eventually build strong portfolio case studies.

Start by exploring how well-known companies such as Google and Microsoft document their design systems, design principles, components, and user experience guidelines.

For example, you can explore Google's Material Design and Microsoft's Fluent Design System to understand how established companies create and maintain design documentation.

Every organization has its own approach to documenting design systems, product experiences, and design decisions. By studying these examples, you can learn how to structure documentation for your own applications and projects.

As you document each design challenge, focus on:

  • Problem statement: What problem are you trying to solve?
  • User needs: Who are your users, and what challenges do they face?
  • Design process: What steps did you follow to explore and solve the problem?
  • Design decisions: Why did you choose a particular solution?
  • Design system: What components, typography, colors, and interaction patterns did you use?
  • Testing and improvements: How did you evaluate your design, and what did you learn?
  • Key takeaways: What skills and knowledge did you gain from the challenge?

Remember, good UX documentation is not just about showcasing your final designs. It is about explaining your thinking, decisions, challenges, and learning process.

By developing documentation skills early in your UX journey, you will find it much easier to turn your practice projects into meaningful portfolio case studies and communicate your design experience to future employers and collaborators.

Final Thoughts

Learning UX design is not just about understanding design principles or becoming familiar with design tools. It is about developing the ability to identify problems, understand users, think critically, and create meaningful solutions.

My recommendation for beginners is simple:

First, learn the fundamentals. Then practice independently. Explore a domain that interests you. Learn to use AI as a supporting tool. Finally, apply your skills to real-world projects.

You don't have to complete every challenge perfectly. What matters most is your learning process, consistency, curiosity, and willingness to improve.

The goal is not simply to complete 40 design challenges. The goal is to become a designer who understands why a problem exists, how to approach it, and how to create a better experience for users.

title: Show jewelry weight and specs on Shopify with Liquid
description:
A photograph shows the finish. A weight in grams gives shoppers a sense of how the piece will feel. That matters when they are choosing between a lightweight ear cuff and a heavier piece of hand-forged silver jewelry. A product page can show the finish, the item number, and the exact weight alongside the photograph.

Yana Potapova's Heritage: Men's Jewelry Brand Identity is a storefront design study for CODESTAL. It pairs oxidized 925 sterling silver with a grayscale interface, a care link in the main navigation, and a shopping bag that shows the details of the order. This article uses the design as a reference for an independent Shopify store and includes a complete Liquid Section example.

The project frames the brand around roots and passing things to a future generation. Its desktop hero and mobile product page both give the metal texture and the photography room to speak.

1. Four design decisions in the CODESTAL project

1.1 Four grayscale colors leave room for the metal

The project's palette specifies four interface colors.

  • Black (#000000) anchors dark areas and purchase buttons such as ADD TO BAG and COMPLETE PURCHASE.
  • Charcoal (#1A1A1A) creates a separate layer for dark brand-story areas and the footer.
  • Slate gray (#383838) works for secondary text, rules, inactive filters, and table borders.
  • White (#FFFFFF) gives product lists and detail panels a clean background and high contrast on dark sections.

Oxidized silver gets much of its character from the contrast between dark recesses and highlights on hammered surfaces. A grayscale interface leaves that contrast visible. Use the same principle for other materials that carry visual character, such as titanium and hand-finished leather.

1.2 Put the item number and weight where shoppers can see them

CODESTAL moves product identifiers out of the fine print. The project shows identifiers on product cards, and selected items, the quick view, and the shopping bag show weight where it is relevant to the purchase.

Examples of archive-style item numbers include UGS28\36\2023\1 for forged-metal silver earrings, UG52/40/243/1 for hand-forged silver earrings, and CODE048 for the Boldness design. Example weights in the study include 4.10 g, 6.58 g, and 1.50 g.

  • Give shoppers a physical reference. A figure such as 4.10 g helps them judge the weight of an earring or ear cuff without handling it. The material and hallmark belong in the specifications.
  • Make the product identifier part of the design. A Shopify variant SKU can use an archive pattern such as UGS28\36\2023\1 when that pattern fits the catalog. Repeating the same identifier in the product view and shopping bag keeps the item easy to recognize. A label such as \ YOUR BAG \ continues the visual language.

1.3 Make product care easy to find before checkout

The desktop header puts COLLECTION +, OUR STORY, and PRODUCT CARE on the left. The CODESTAL wordmark sits in the middle. RETURNS & REFUNDS, SHIPPING, and the account, wishlist, and bag icons sit on the right.

Hammer marks, natural patina, and changes in an oxidized finish can lead to questions after a purchase. Top-level links let customers find care, delivery, and returns before ordering. The product detail uses Specifications and Warranty as separate tabs. Specifications can describe the metal and finish, while the warranty tab can explain the merchant's actual coverage and care instructions.

1.4 Use the grid and shopping bag to make decisions clear

Design element CODESTAL reference Shopify application
Desktop and mobile grid Desktop 1920 × 1080, 12 columns, 60px margins, 20px gutters. Mobile 375 × 812, four columns, 20px margins and gutters. Make the four material or style shortcuts horizontally accessible on mobile: MINIMAL, TEXTURED, FASHION, and EAR CUFF.
Type hierarchy Audiowide display type. 68px semibold, 48px regular, 24px regular, and 16px light, with 120% line height. Use Audiowide for headings and a legible geometric sans such as Inter or Space Grotesk for item numbers, weights, prices, and specifications.
Shopping bag A product image and price sit beside item identifiers and weights such as UGS28\36\2023\1 and 4.10 g. The order summary shows free shipping and a sample 20% VAT breakdown, an APPLY field, and purchase controls. In the Shopify cart drawer, use item.variant.sku and `item.variant.weight \

2. Implement the product details in Shopify

SKU and weight are native Shopify variant data. The storefront can read them through Liquid. Use product metafields to keep the material and care descriptions consistent across products when the theme is connected to those fields.

2.1 Map native fields and three optional metafields

Storefront field Reference value Shopify source Liquid expression
Archive item number {% raw %}UGS28\36\2023\1 or CODE048 Variant SKU under Inventory {{ product.selected_or_first_available_variant.sku }}
Exact item weight 4.10 g or 6.58 g Variant weight under Shipping. Select grams when using a literal g suffix. {{ product.selected_or_first_available_variant.weight_in_unit }} g
Collection or texture FORGED METAL or NEW SCALE Product metafield jewelry.collection_line, single-line text {{ product.metafields.jewelry.collection_line.value }}
Metal and finish 925 Silver Forged Metal - Oxidized Finish Product metafield jewelry.material_finish, single-line text {{ product.metafields.jewelry.material_finish.value }}
Warranty and care Example copy about polishing and reoxidation, with a note that hand-forged textures vary Product metafield jewelry.warranty_care, multi-line text {{ product.metafields.jewelry.warranty_care.value }}

2.2 Complete Liquid reference section

Save the sample as sections/codestal-jewelry-showcase.liquid and add the section in the theme editor. It uses the four grayscale colors, Audiowide headings, five filter choices, product metadata, and a Specifications / Warranty modal opened by SPECS +.

Choose a real product for each block. The example's preset values illustrate the design. Clear or replace the preset item number and weight before showing a real product, and check the selected variant's measurement unit. The example takes material and warranty from the block settings. Connect the corresponding metafields when adapting it to a store. The sample's purchase buttons link to the product page. Direct add to cart requires the theme's product form or cart integration.

<section class="codestal-sec-{{ section.id }}" data-section-id="{{ section.id }}">
  <div class="codestal-container">
    <div class="codestal-header">
      <div>
        <div class="codestal-slash-tag">\ {{ section.settings.slash_subtitle }} \</div>
        <h2 class="codestal-main-title">{{ section.settings.heading }}</h2>
      </div>
      <p class="codestal-manifesto">{{ section.settings.manifesto }}</p>
    </div>

    <div class="codestal-filter-bar">
      <div class="codestal-tabs" role="tablist" aria-label="按肌理与款式筛选">
        <button type="button" class="codestal-tab-btn is-active" data-filter="all">ALL ARCHIVE</button>
        <button type="button" class="codestal-tab-btn" data-filter="textured">TEXTURED</button>
        <button type="button" class="codestal-tab-btn" data-filter="minimal">MINIMAL</button>
        <button type="button" class="codestal-tab-btn" data-filter="fashion">FASHION</button>
        <button type="button" class="codestal-tab-btn" data-filter="ear-cuff">EAR CUFF</button>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="codestal-grid">
      {%- for block in section.blocks -%}
        {%- assign product = block.settings.product -%}
        {%- assign variant = product.selected_or_first_available_variant -%}
        {%- assign item_code = block.settings.item_code | default: variant.sku | default: 'UGS28\36\2023\1' -%}
        {%- assign item_weight = block.settings.weight_grams | default: variant.weight_in_unit | default: '4.10' -%}
        {%- assign item_title = block.settings.custom_title | default: product.title | default: 'FORGED METAL SILVER EARRINGS' -%}
        {%- assign item_price = product.price | money | default: block.settings.fallback_price -%}

        <article
          class="codestal-card"
          data-category="{{ block.settings.style_tag }}"
          {{ block.shopify_attributes }}
        >
          <div>
            <div class="codestal-card-meta">
              <span>ITEM: {{ item_code }}</span>
              <span class="codestal-weight-badge">WEIGHT: {{ item_weight }} g</span>
            </div>

            <div class="codestal-img-wrap">
              {%- if block.settings.custom_image != blank -%}
                <img
                  src="{{ block.settings.custom_image | image_url: width: 900 }}"
                  alt="{{ item_title | escape }}"
                  width="900"
                  height="900"
                  loading="lazy"
                >
              {%- elsif product != blank and product.featured_image != blank -%}
                <img
                  src="{{ product.featured_image | image_url: width: 900 }}"
                  alt="{{ item_title | escape }}"
                  width="900"
                  height="900"
                  loading="lazy"
                >
              {%- endif -%}
            </div>
          </div>

          <div class="codestal-card-body">
            <p class="codestal-collection-tag">\ {{ block.settings.collection_line }} \</p>
            <h3 class="codestal-prod-title">{{ item_title }}</h3>
            <p class="codestal-finish-line">{{ block.settings.material_spec }}</p>

            <div class="codestal-price-row">
              <span class="codestal-price">{{ item_price }}</span>
              <div class="codestal-actions">
                <button
                  type="button"
                  class="codestal-btn-ghost js-codestal-open-spec"
                  data-title="{{ item_title | escape }}"
                  data-code="{{ item_code | escape }}"
                  data-weight="{{ item_weight }} g"
                  data-material="{{ block.settings.material_spec | escape }}"
                  data-warranty="{{ block.settings.warranty_note | escape }}"
                  data-url="{{ product.url | default: '#' }}"
                >
                  SPECS +
                </button>
                <a href="{{ product.url | default: '#' }}" class="codestal-btn-solid">ADD TO BAG</a>
              </div>
            </div>
          </div>
        </article>
      {%- endfor -%}
    </div>
  </div>

  {%- comment -%} Specifications & Warranty 模态框 {%- endcomment -%}
  <div class="codestal-modal-backdrop" id="CodestalModal-{{ section.id }}" aria-hidden="true">
    <div class="codestal-modal" role="dialog" aria-modal="true">
      <button type="button" class="codestal-modal-close js-codestal-close" aria-label="Close">✕</button>
      <div class="codestal-slash-tag" id="ModalCode-{{ section.id }}">\ ITEM \</div>
      <h3 class="codestal-prod-title" id="ModalTitle-{{ section.id }}" style="font-family:var(--c-font-title);font-size:1.5rem;"></h3>

      <div class="codestal-modal-tabs">
        <button type="button" class="codestal-modal-tab is-active" data-modal-tab="specs">SPECIFICATIONS</button>
        <button type="button" class="codestal-modal-tab" data-modal-tab="warranty">WARRANTY & CARE</button>
      </div>

      <div id="ModalPaneSpecs-{{ section.id }}">
        <dl class="codestal-spec-dl">
          <dt>ARCHIVE NUMBER</dt>
          <dd id="ModalSpecCode-{{ section.id }}"></dd>
          <dt>EXACT WEIGHT</dt>
          <dd id="ModalSpecWeight-{{ section.id }}"></dd>
          <dt>MATERIAL & FINISH</dt>
          <dd id="ModalSpecMaterial-{{ section.id }}"></dd>
        </dl>
      </div>

      <div id="ModalPaneWarranty-{{ section.id }}" style="display:none;margin-bottom:24px;font-size:0.875rem;line-height:1.5;color:#CCCCCC;">
        <p id="ModalWarrantyText-{{ section.id }}"></p>
      </div>

      <a href="#" id="ModalBuyLink-{{ section.id }}" class="codestal-btn-solid" style="display:block;text-align:center;padding:14px;">
        ADD TO BAG
      </a>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<script>
  (function() {
    var sec = document.querySelector('.codestal-sec-{{ section.id }}');
    if (!sec) return;

    /* 顶部款式筛选 */
    var filterBtns = sec.querySelectorAll('[data-filter]');
    var cards = sec.querySelectorAll('.codestal-card');
    filterBtns.forEach(function(btn) {
      btn.addEventListener('click', function() {
        var cat = btn.getAttribute('data-filter');
        filterBtns.forEach(function(b) { b.classList.toggle('is-active', b === btn); });
        cards.forEach(function(card) {
          if (cat === 'all' || card.getAttribute('data-category') === cat) {
            card.removeAttribute('hidden');
          } else {
            card.setAttribute('hidden', 'hidden');
          }
        });
      });
    });

    /* Specifications / Warranty 弹窗控制 */
    var modal = sec.querySelector('#CodestalModal-{{ section.id }}');
    var openBtns = sec.querySelectorAll('.js-codestal-open-spec');
    var closeBtn = sec.querySelector('.js-codestal-close');
    var modalTabs = sec.querySelectorAll('[data-modal-tab]');
    var paneSpecs = sec.querySelector('#ModalPaneSpecs-{{ section.id }}');
    var paneWarranty = sec.querySelector('#ModalPaneWarranty-{{ section.id }}');

    openBtns.forEach(function(btn) {
      btn.addEventListener('click', function() {
        sec.querySelector('#ModalCode-{{ section.id }}').textContent = '\\ ' + btn.getAttribute('data-code') + ' \\';
        sec.querySelector('#ModalTitle-{{ section.id }}').textContent = btn.getAttribute('data-title');
        sec.querySelector('#ModalSpecCode-{{ section.id }}').textContent = btn.getAttribute('data-code');
        sec.querySelector('#ModalSpecWeight-{{ section.id }}').textContent = btn.getAttribute('data-weight');
        sec.querySelector('#ModalSpecMaterial-{{ section.id }}').textContent = btn.getAttribute('data-material');
        sec.querySelector('#ModalWarrantyText-{{ section.id }}').textContent = btn.getAttribute('data-warranty');
        sec.querySelector('#ModalBuyLink-{{ section.id }}').setAttribute('href', btn.getAttribute('data-url'));
        modal.classList.add('is-open');
      });
    });

    if (closeBtn) {
      closeBtn.addEventListener('click', function() { modal.classList.remove('is-open'); });
    }
    modal.addEventListener('click', function(e) {
      if (e.target === modal) modal.classList.remove('is-open');
    });

    modalTabs.forEach(function(tab) {
      tab.addEventListener('click', function() {
        var target = tab.getAttribute('data-modal-tab');
        modalTabs.forEach(function(t) { t.classList.toggle('is-active', t === tab); });
        paneSpecs.style.display = target === 'specs' ? 'block' : 'none';
        paneWarranty.style.display = target === 'warranty' ? 'block' : 'none';
      });
    });
  })();
</script>

title: How to Choose an AI Model Inference Service: Managed APIs vs ML Endpoints vs Serverless GPUs vs Self-Hosted Serving
description:
Choose an inference deployment option by model type (proprietary vs open-weight), traffic shape, latency target, model features, data control requirements, and cost model. Managed model APIs are the fastest way to start, managed ML endpoints and serverless GPU services trade some control for convenience, and self-hosted serving on containers gives the most control over cost, data residency, and portability. Control Plane runs containerized model servers on AWS, GCP, and Azure regions and on your own GPU clusters, with built-in NVIDIA GPUs on Control Plane-managed locations that offer them and no Kubernetes cluster to operate on those locations.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Five deployment options:

  • Managed model APIs: Amazon Bedrock, Google Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI), Microsoft Foundry (formerly Azure AI Foundry), and model providers’ own APIs
  • Managed ML endpoints (Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform endpoints, Azure Machine Learning online endpoints)
  • Serverless GPU inference services
  • Self-hosted serving on containers or Kubernetes: vLLM, NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton (formerly Triton Inference Server), or KServe as the Kubernetes serving layer
  • A platform layer that runs your model containers across clouds, such as Control Plane

Decision factors:

  • Model type: a proprietary API model or an open-weight model
  • Traffic shape: steady, bursty, or batch
  • Latency target: interactive or offline
  • Model features: structured output, tool calling, context length, and fine-tuned adapters
  • Data control and residency: where prompts and completions are processed
  • Cost model: per token, per GPU-hour, or reserved capacity
  • Team skills: the operations experience you have to run what you choose

Top inference challenges: latency, GPU cost from low utilization, cold starts, autoscaling on the wrong signal, provider rate limits and outages, GPU capacity, data privacy, observability gaps, and multi-region availability.

Containers vs managed platforms: Running model servers in your own containers gives you full control over the runtime, weights, and optimizations. A platform layer removes the work of operating Kubernetes clusters, autoscaling, and multi-cloud networking while keeping that container-level control.

How Control Plane fits: Control Plane runs containerized model servers such as vLLM as workloads, on Control Plane-managed locations in AWS, GCP, and Azure regions or on GPU clusters you add as locations, and handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security.

How do I choose an AI model inference service for my application?

Start with these seven factors.

Model type

If you need a proprietary model from a provider such as OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google, you call it through a managed model API. If you run an open-weight model such as Llama, Mistral, or Qwen, you can call it per token through a managed API that hosts it, deploy it to a managed ML endpoint, or serve it yourself. Open-weight models give you portability and the ability to fine-tune, quantize, and change versions on your schedule.

Traffic shape

Steady, predictable traffic favors reserved or dedicated compute where GPU utilization stays high. Bursty traffic benefits from services that scale elastically and avoid paying for idle GPUs. Batch workloads, such as nightly embedding jobs, can run on spot or preemptible GPUs and tolerate queuing.

Latency target

Interactive applications such as chat, code completion, and retrieval-augmented search need a short time to first token and steady token output. Dedicated endpoints and self-hosted serving give the most predictable p99 latency. Offline workloads such as summarization pipelines or evaluation runs can tolerate cold starts and queuing.

Model features

List the features your application depends on before you pick a service. Structured output and tool calling vary by API and model, and self-hosted servers such as vLLM enforce JSON schemas through structured outputs (guided decoding). Context length sets KV cache memory, so long contexts need much more GPU memory per request than short ones. Serving many fine-tuned variants is cheapest as LoRA adapters on one base model, which vLLM can serve together on one GPU. Applications that call several models need a routing layer, such as an LLM gateway, for fallback and cost-based routing.

Data control and residency

Regulated industries and privacy-sensitive applications often require that prompts and completions stay in a specific region or in the organization’s own environment. Self-hosted serving and managed ML endpoints with private networking can meet these requirements. Managed model APIs process data on the provider’s infrastructure. Hyperscaler APIs such as Bedrock, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and Microsoft Foundry offer regional processing and private connectivity, and retention terms vary by provider and contract. Check whether cross-region inference routing is on, because it can move requests out of your chosen region.

Cost model

Per-token pricing is simple to budget at low volume but grows with usage. Per-GPU-hour pricing rewards high utilization. Reserved capacity lowers the hourly rate but requires a volume forecast. Include idle GPU time, egress fees, and engineering time to get a true total cost of ownership. For the build-or-rent decision, see the build vs rent GPUs break-even model.

Team skills

Managed APIs need almost no MLOps experience. Managed ML endpoints need moderate DevOps and ML engineering effort. Self-hosted serving needs experience with GPU drivers, container runtimes, model optimization, autoscaling, and incident response. A platform layer needs container and configuration skills without cluster operations.

Custom or fine-tuned models with cloud automation Managed ML endpoint
Elastic GPU scaling for bursty open-weight workloads Serverless GPU inference service
Full control over runtime, weights, data, and cost Self-hosted serving on containers
Container control across several clouds without operating clusters A platform layer such as Control Plane

What are common challenges in AI model inference and how can I overcome them?

This table maps each common problem to its cause and a fix.

Challenge Why it happens How to fix it
Latency: time to first token and inter-token latency Prefill on long prompts sets time to first token. Decode, which is bound by memory bandwidth, sets inter-token latency. Network hops add to both. Enable prefix caching for repeated system prompts and retrieved context, use chunked prefill so long prompts do not stall other requests, quantize weights (FP8, AWQ, or GPTQ) to speed decoding, use speculative decoding to cut inter-token latency at low batch sizes, and serve from regions close to users.
GPU cost and low utilization GPUs sit idle between requests or off-peak, and reserved capacity costs the same regardless of load. Right-size GPU types, autoscale on request concurrency or queue depth, and scale idle low-traffic services down. See the best GPU cloud providers.
Cold starts from large model weights Loading multi-gigabyte weights into GPU memory takes time when a new replica starts, on top of image pull and engine warmup. Cache weights on persistent volumes, use quantized models, keep a warm minimum of replicas before expected traffic, and use a fast weight loader such as the Run:ai Model Streamer, which vLLM supports.
Autoscaling on the wrong signal CPU utilization misses the real bottleneck, which is request concurrency, queue depth, or KV cache usage. Scale on request concurrency, waiting requests (vLLM’s num_requests_waiting), or KV cache usage. GPU memory and GPU utilization are poor signals because vLLM preallocates most GPU memory and utilization reads high even at low load.
Throughput under concurrent load Serving one request at a time wastes GPU cycles, and KV cache pressure forces recomputation. Use a server with continuous batching (vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM batch this way by default), size the KV cache for expected concurrency with max model length and an FP8 KV cache, use tensor parallelism within one node only when a model does not fit on one GPU, and add replicas for throughput.
Provider rate limits and outages Managed APIs impose token and request limits, and a single provider is a single point of failure. Retry with exponential backoff, keep a fallback model or provider, and route around unhealthy endpoints. See how to run AI inference across multiple GPU clouds.
GPU capacity and quotas High-end GPUs are often unavailable in a given region or blocked by account quotas. Request quotas early, qualify more than one GPU type per model, and keep capacity in more than one region or provider.
Data privacy and residency Sending prompts to third-party APIs can conflict with residency rules or expose sensitive data. Host open-weight models in your own environment or use managed endpoints with private networking, keep regional processing on, and review each provider’s retention terms.
Model and version management Rolling out new model versions, rolling back bad ones, and running variants side by side adds risk. Version model servers by container image tag and pin model weights to a fixed revision, roll out gradually, and keep the previous version ready for rollback.
Observability gaps Standard monitoring misses tokens per second, time to first token, and KV cache pressure. Export serving-framework metrics and track time to first token, inter-token latency, latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99), token throughput, queue depth, and KV cache usage.
Multi-region availability One region adds latency for distant users and is a single point of failure. Run replicas in at least two regions behind a global endpoint that routes to the nearest healthy one.

For the infrastructure components behind these fixes, see what infrastructure you need to run an inference layer.

Where can I find a cloud friendly deployment platform for AI models?

A cloud friendly inference platform meets five criteria:

  • Runs standard containers. You package your model server as a standard container image and deploy it without rewriting it for a proprietary runtime.
  • Works on more than one cloud. You can run the same workload definition on AWS, GCP, and Azure regions and on your own GPU clusters.
  • Supports GPUs. Your serving framework gets GPU access without manual driver work.
  • Scales on demand signals. Autoscaling follows request concurrency or queue depth instead of generic CPU metrics.
  • Keeps data where you choose. Inference traffic and model weights stay in the regions and clusters you select.

Control Plane is the unbreakable platform for running production workloads. It runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads natively on AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), VM workloads on locations joined through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes, and workloads on Kubernetes clusters you already run or your own machines, including on premises, active-active across regions and clouds. For a wider comparison of hosting platforms, see the best PaaS providers in 2026.

Running model servers in containers yourself gives you full control over the serving framework, weights, quantization, and GPU choice. The cost is operational work, including Kubernetes clusters, GPU drivers, networking, autoscaling policies, certificate rotation, and incident response.

A managed platform takes over that layer. You still bring your container image, and the platform runs compute, scaling, load balancing, and Day 2 operations. The cost shifts from engineering hours to platform fees.

How Control Plane fits

Control Plane runs containerized model servers such as vLLM as workloads. On Control Plane-managed locations in AWS, GCP, and Azure regions there is no Kubernetes cluster to operate, and teams can also add GPU clusters they already run, including on a neocloud, as locations.

The vLLM template serves one Hugging Face model through vLLM’s OpenAI-compatible API on a built-in NVIDIA A10G or T4, or on your own GPU cluster registered as a location, and caches weights on a persistent volume so restarts skip the download. FAQ

These questions come up often when teams compare inference deployment options.

Should I use a model API or host my own model?

Use a model API when you need a proprietary model, want to start quickly, or have low to moderate traffic. Host your own model when you need control over data, want to fine-tune or quantize, or when per-token cost at your volume exceeds the cost of dedicated GPU compute.

What is the cheapest way to serve an open-weight model?

It depends on utilization. At high, steady traffic, self-hosted serving on reserved GPUs usually gives the lowest cost per token, and spot GPUs suit batch jobs that tolerate preemption. At low or bursty traffic, a per-token API that hosts the model, or a GPU service that scales down when idle, avoids paying for unused GPUs. Include engineering and operations time in the comparison.

How do I reduce inference latency?

Cut time to first token by reusing cached prompt prefixes and splitting long prompts into chunks. Cut the time between tokens with quantized weights and speculative decoding. Keep warm replicas near users so requests never wait on a cold start.

How do I keep inference running when a model provider has an outage?

Keep a fallback. For managed model APIs, route to an alternative provider or model when calls fail. For self-hosted models, run replicas in at least two regions. On Control Plane, a workload in a GVC with several locations runs active-active, and the workload’s global endpoint uses DNS to route clients to the nearest location where it passes its readiness probes. Every location in that GVC must offer the GPU model the workload requests.

What GPU should I use for LLM inference?

Match GPU memory to model size, context length, and concurrency. Weight memory is the parameter count times bytes per parameter: 2 at FP16 or BF16, 1 at FP8, and about 0.5 at 4-bit, plus headroom for the KV cache, which grows with context length and concurrent requests. A 7 or 8 billion parameter model needs about 14 to 16 GB at FP16 and fits on a 24 GB GPU such as the A10G with moderate context, or on a 16 GB T4 with 4-bit quantization. A 70 billion parameter model needs about 140 GB at FP16, so it runs on four 80 GB GPUs such as the H100 with tensor parallelism, on two 80 GB GPUs at FP8, on one 80 GB GPU only at 4-bit, or on one H200 or B200 at FP8. Control Plane’s pricing page lists NVIDIA GPUs from T4 to B200, subject to availability.

How do I autoscale AI inference workloads correctly?

Scale on request concurrency, waiting requests, or KV cache usage instead of CPU or GPU utilization, which do not reflect inference load. On Control Plane, a vLLM server running as a standard or stateful workload can scale on vLLM’s waiting-request count through KEDA.

Can I run inference across multiple clouds?

Yes. Package the model server as a container and run it in more than one cloud. On Control Plane, one workload definition runs across AWS, GCP, and Azure regions and your own clusters. A GPU workload uses one GPU source per GVC: built-in NVIDIA T4 or A10G on Control Plane-managed regions, or the GPUs on your own clusters added as locations.

How do I handle data privacy requirements for AI inference?

Host models in your own environment or use managed endpoints with private networking and regional processing. Send sensitive data to a third-party model API only when its retention and usage terms meet your requirements.

What infrastructure do I need to run an inference layer?

You need GPU compute, a model server such as vLLM or Dynamo-Triton, a container runtime or a serving layer such as KServe, autoscaling, load balancing, observability, and storage for model weights. For the full breakdown, see what infrastructure you need to run an inference layer.

Is a platform layer worth it compared to managing Kubernetes myself?

For most teams, yes, when engineering time is the constraint. A platform layer removes cluster operations and custom autoscaling setup while you keep control of the model server and weights. The tradeoff is a platform fee in place of engineering hours, and Control Plane customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure.

To run inference workloads across clouds without operating clusters, talk to the Control Plane team or sign up free.

title: Patching the Blind Spots: Reversible LLM Rule Overlay for Frozen Fraud Detectors
description:
arXiv:2611.08714v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: In industrial tabular fraud classification, gradient-boosted trees remain state-of-the-art, but even a well-trained model has blind spots, and retraining the deployed model is not always safe. We propose a framework that patches such a model without modifying it: LLMs propose rules anchored on features the model underweights by SHAP, and the resulting noisy pool is screened for empirical support and calibrated into an additive, reversible log-lift overlay that runs at the production cut-off. Single-LLM benefit is high-variance and inverts between datasets, so we pool three diverse backbones by equal-weight logit averaging, trading peak gain for a bounded worst case. On a real-world e-commerce fraud detector trained on selection-biased data, continued training regresses even when carefully tuned, whereas the overlay gains on average +2.26% recall at equal precision ($\Delta$R@P) and +1.60% precision at equal recall ($\Delta$P@R) over production cut-offs spanning 30-57% precision and 23-63% recall. On a public benchmark of seven designed bias-shift variants it raises $\Delta$P@R on every variant and keeps $\Delta$R@P near neutral. Each amendment is a readable predicate naming the fraud pattern it covers.

title: Phantom Consensus: Measuring Social Reasoning in Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making
description:
arXiv:2611.08971v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly aggregate judgments across model instances, but reasoning about other agents can itself introduce failure. We study a setting in which LLMs shift their public decisions after observing ambiguous social signals while reporting inaccurate estimates of what other agents privately judged, even when the group's recorded private judgments do not support the apparent consensus. We call this failure phantom consensus and study it as a pluralistic-ignorance-style pattern in controlled LLM collectives. To measure this phenomenon, we introduce PHANTOM-Bench, a benchmark that separates isolated private judgments, public decisions after ambiguous social signals, elicited estimates of the group's private judgment, transparency-based recovery, and controls for neutral public text and explicit vote-following. Across nine closed- and open-weight models, ambiguous public signals consistently degrade decision quality and can turn correct private group judgments into incorrect public collective outcomes. Public accuracy drops by as much as 47.8 percentage points, and collective rationality failures reach 47.3% in the most susceptible setting. We observe substantial errors in reported group-private beliefs alongside public-stage failures, while control conditions reveal model-dependent differences in susceptibility to ambiguous and explicit peer signals. Revealing the agents' recorded private decisions repairs many failures without revealing the gold label, although recovery varies across models. Our results show that evaluating multi-agent LLM systems requires measuring not only final agreement, but whether that agreement reflects independently measured private judgments or an apparent consensus.

title: I built AiRap.me: turn one photo into a lip-synced AI rap video
description:
Earlier this year my feed was full of AI rap videos: someone's selfie, their cat, or a cartoon character dropping a verse. When I tried to make one myself, it took a whole toolchain: one tool for lyrics, another for the song, a lip-sync app, then a video editor to put it all together. Most "AI rap generators" also stop at an audio file, but what people actually share is a video.

So I built AiRap.me: upload one photo, pick a style, and get a finished rap video back, usually in about 20–30 seconds.

What it does

  • One photo in, rap video out. The AI writes an original verse, makes the beat, generates the vocals and lip-syncs the face in your photo. You don't need a song, a voice recording or an editing app.
  • Solo or duo. Use one photo, or two photos where two performers trade verses.
  • People, pets and characters. Selfies, dogs, cats, and cartoon, anime or 3D characters, each keeping its own look.
  • 8 styles. Trap, drill, boom bap, melodic, phonk, rage, old school and Afro trap, plus birthday, roast and love themes.
  • Ready to post. 9:16 or 16:9, 768P or 1080P, 6, 10 or 15 seconds, downloaded as an MP4 with no watermark.

A few product decisions I care about

1. Only charge for videos that finish.
AI video generation fails sometimes: a bad photo, a model hiccup, a timeout. Credits are reserved when a job starts and refunded automatically if it fails. Photos that can't work (group shots, faces that are too small or blurry) are rejected before the job starts, so they never cost anything.

2. Show the first frame before you pay.
Your photo becomes the first frame of the video, so you drag and zoom the crop first. You see exactly what you'll get before you spend credits.

3. Async by default.
Generation takes a while, so you don't have to keep the tab open. The finished video waits for you in "My Videos".

4. Privacy.
Uploaded photos and generated videos stay in the user's account and are never used to train models.

Free tools along the way


While building the video generator I also shipped two free text tools that need no sign-up:

  • 🎤 AI Rap Lyrics Generator
  • 🏷️ Rap Name Generator

There are also one-click templates for viral formats, like the Hotel Lobby AI rap trend.

Try it

New accounts get free credits, and no credit card is needed:
👉 https://airap.me

I'd love feedback from the dev.to community, especially:

  • Which rap styles or trend templates should I add next?
  • Anything confusing in the upload → style → generate flow?

Thanks for reading! I'll reply to every comment. 🙌

title: Vercel Security Review now in public beta
description:
Vercel Security Review is now in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. Once enabled, every push to a connected GitHub repository is automatically reviewed for vulnerabilities, and findings are reported in the Vulnerabilities dashboard.

What triggers a review

Security Review runs automatically when code is pushed to a connected GitHub repository. Because reviews start from push events rather than pull requests, direct and force pushes to your production branch are reviewed as well. Every project affected by a single push is reviewed together.

What a finding includes

Each finding records the project, environment, branch, and commit, with a summary, a suggested fix, and an AI-generated severity rating.

Security Review adds its own GitHub check to each commit it reviews. When there's a pull request, it also posts findings as review comments that link back to each finding. On public repositories, finding details stay in the dashboard.

Fixes and resolution

Clicking Fix with Vercel Agent on a vulnerability report hands the finding to Vercel Agent, which proposes a fix and opens a pull request for you to review. Nothing merges until you approve it.

To fix findings with your coding agent instead, use vercel security vulnerabilities in the Vercel CLI, or copy any finding as Markdown or JSON.

Security policies

Teams can write security policies in plain language, for all projects or specific ones, to give Security Review more context about how they build. Set a team policy in Agent settings and a project policy in the project's Security settings.

Limitations

Security Review analyzes source code. It isn't a security audit, and it doesn't perform runtime or penetration testing. It helps you find vulnerabilities but doesn't guarantee your application is free of them.

Pricing

Security Review is billed at the Vercel Agent rate: provider inference at the underlying token rate with no markup, plus the Vercel Token Rate of $0.25 per million tokens (input, cached, output). Reviews run on each push to GitHub, so cost scales with how often you push and how much code changes.

Security reviews are free until November 10, 2026, and fixes made with Vercel Agent are billed at the Vercel Agent rate.

Enable Security Review in your team’s Agent settings, or read the documentation and the announcement to learn more. The CLI command needs Vercel CLI 65.10.0 or later.
