title: The Economics of Memory Safety: Inaction vs. The Cost of Rewriting
description:
For three decades, memory management vulnerabilities were treated as operational overhead—a standard engineering maintenance cost resolved through code reviews, fuzzers, and periodic security patches. That paradigm is no longer economically viable.

Regulatory bodies worldwide (CISA, White House ONCD, NSA, Five Eyes) have shifted their posture from passive advisory notices to active procurement mandates. Simultaneously, independent telemetry from Microsoft, Google, and Apple proves that ~70% of all high-severity vulnerabilities remain memory safety flaws, irrespective of modern C++ language revisions (C++11 through C++23).

Engineering organizations face a strategic dilemma:

  • The Cost of Inaction: Escalating patch triage cycles, compliance disqualification, catastrophic exploit liability, and customer churn.
  • The Cost of Rewriting: Massive capital expenditure, multi-year feature freezes, dual-toolchain friction, and organizational disruption.

This article provides an executive decision framework evaluating four architectural strategies—Full Rewrite, Incremental FFI Interop, Runtime & Compiler Hardening, and Hardware-Assisted Tagging—to maximize engineering return on investment (ROI) while methodically shrinking attack surfaces.

1. The Cost of Inaction: The "70% Rule" and Regulatory Exposure

The Empirical Reality

The argument that disciplined engineering teams can eliminate memory corruption in C++ is statistically disproven by industry data:

Organization Dataset / Period Memory Safety Ratio Primary Root Causes
Microsoft (MSRC) All CVEs analyzed since 2006 ~70% Use-After-Free (UAF), Out-of-bounds Read/Write
Google Chromium High-severity bugs (2015–Present) ~70% Use-After-Free, Iterator Invalidation
Google Android Vulnerabilities prior to Android 12 ~76% Buffer Overflow, Dangling Pointers
Apple iOS / macOS Kernel / WebKit Security Bulletins 65–75% Memory Corruption, Pointer Confusion

⚠️ Warning:
These statistics do not represent junior developers writing naive code. They represent elite systems teams using strict style guides, static analyzers, AddressSanitizer (ASan), and modern C++ practices.

The Real Cost Drivers of an Unsafe Codebase 

+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|               Total Cost of Vulnerability Lifecycle         |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| 1. Emergency Patch Cycles (Out-of-band releases)            |
| 2. Customer Deployment Disruption & SLA Penalties           |
| 3. Security Engineering Overhead (Fuzzing, ASan CI runs)    |
| 4. Opportunity Cost (Engineers triaging CVEs, not shipping) |
| 5. Regulatory Non-Compliance & Audit Penalties              |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
  1. Direct Triage Overhead: A high-severity memory CVE costs between $50,000 and $250,000 to identify, root-cause, patch, backport, and deploy across enterprise customer fleets.
  2. Opportunity Cost: Engineering cycles diverted to emergency hotfixes directly delay strategic product roadmaps.
  3. The Regulatory Shift:
    • White House ONCD (2024): Explicitly declared memory-safe languages an imperative for national infrastructure.
    • CISA Memory-Safe Roadmaps (2023): Mandates that enterprise software vendors publish public migration roadmaps or risk losing public sector procurement eligibility.
    • EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA): Introduces strict legal liability and punitive fines for software vendors releasing products with preventable security flaws.

2. The Modern C++ Paradox: Why Language Updates Failed to Fix the Balance Sheet

A frequent objection raised in architectural reviews is: "Modern C++ (C++11/17/20/23) solved memory management via RAII, smart pointers, and spans."

While modern abstractions improve expressive safety, they fail to deliver structural safety.

       +--------------------------------------------------------+
       |   Modern C++ Abstraction  | Residual Risk In Practice  |
       |---------------------------+----------------------------|
       |   std::unique_ptr<T>      | Escaped raw ptrs outlive owner |
       |   std::string_view        | Easy dangling references   |
       |   std::span<T>            | Unchecked [] by default    |
       |   std::shared_ptr<T>      | Unmanaged cyclic leaks     |
       +--------------------------------------------------------+

The Architectural Flaws That Standards Cannot Eliminate

  • Unsafe by Default:
    • Raw pointer arithmetic, unchecked indexing (operator[]), and uninitialized stack buffers remain standard-compliant C++.
    • Safety is purely opt-in and enforced only by human convention.
  • The View / Lifetime Trap:
    • Modern types designed for performance (std::string_view, std::span) do not own their memory.
    • Constructing a std::string_view from a temporary object compiles cleanly and produces an instant use-after-free bug.
  • Iterator and Pointer Invalidation:
    • Reallocating a std::vector instantly invalidates all existing references, pointers, and iterators to its elements.
    • The compiler cannot detect this invalidation across function boundaries without a formal borrow checker.
  • The 40-Year ABI Trap:
    • The ISO C++ Standards Committee (WG21) prioritizes backward source and ABI compatibility above all else.
    • Enforcing bounds checks on std::vector::operator[] by default would break performance contracts for existing software.

3. Four Architectural Strategies: Comparative Decision Matrix

Organizations evaluating legacy C++ modernization have four viable paths. Each represents a distinct trade-off between capital expenditure, risk reduction, and time-to-value:

Strategy Capital Cost Time to Value Risk Reduction Engineering Disruption Long-Term TCO
1. Full Greenfield Rewrite Extremely High Very Slow (2–4 yrs) 100% Memory Safety Severe (Feature freeze risk) Low (Minimal maintenance)
2. Incremental FFI Interop Moderate Fast (Iterative) High (70–90% on attack surface) Manageable Low–Moderate
3. Hardened Toolchain & Libs Low Immediate Low–Moderate (Runtime catches) Minimal High (Recurring CVE costs)
4. Hardware-Assisted Tagging Moderate (Hardware tied) Medium (Silicon refresh) High (At execution time) Negligible on code; High on Ops Moderate

4. Deep Dive: Architectural Strategy Breakdown

Option 1: The Greenfield Rewrite (The High-CapEx Trap)

Replacing a multi-million-line C++ codebase with Rust or Go wholesale is tempting on paper, but rarely succeeds in enterprise contexts.

  • Pros:
    • Eliminates entire categories of memory corruption bugs.
    • Modern build tooling, integrated package management, and unified dependency auditing.
  • Cons & Hidden Costs:
    • The Second-System Effect: Scope creep, missed release windows, and architectural over-engineering.
    • Feature Stagnation: Competitors capture market share while engineering spends 24–36 months reaching feature parity.
    • Subtle Bug Reintroduction: Decades of edge-case fixes and domain heuristics in legacy C++ are lost during clean-slate implementation.

Option 2: Incremental Interop via FFI (The Recommended Industry Baseline)

Rather than rewriting wholesale, isolate the attack surface. Write all new features and security-critical entry points (parsers, network listeners, deserializers) in a memory-safe language (MSL) such as Rust, Swift, or Go, interfacing via Foreign Function Interfaces (FFI) like cxx or bindgen.

  • Pros:
    • Capitalize on existing, battle-tested C++ domain logic while eliminating memory vulnerabilities at untrusted boundaries.
    • Realizes immediate security ROI without pausing product roadmaps.
    • Proven enterprise playbook: Used by Android, Chromium, and Windows.
  • Cons & Engineering Overhead:
    • Dual-Toolchain Friction: Build systems (CMake + Cargo/Bazel) become more complex.
    • Boundary Crossing Cost: Marshalling data across language boundaries incurs minor CPU cycles and developer cognitive load.

Option 3: Hardened Runtimes and Static Analysis (The Low-Cost Defense)

Enforcing compiler hardening flags without modifying language stacks:

  • Enable standard library hardened modes: -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS (GCC) or -D_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE=_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_FAST (Clang).
  • Integrate Apple Clang -fbounds-safety for automated spatial bounds verification.

  • Mandate AddressSanitizer (ASan) and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (UBSan) in continuous integration pipelines.

  • Pros:

    • Deploys in days with zero changes to business logic or developer toolchains.
    • Catches obvious out-of-bounds reads and vector misuse during execution.

  • Cons:

    • Runtime Performance Tax: 1% to 15% CPU and memory overhead depending on assertion coverage.
    • Incomplete Temporal Coverage: Does not mathematically guarantee absence of use-after-free bugs in production.

Option 4: Hardware-Assisted Safety (Silicon-Level Containment)

Adopting CPU architectures that integrate hardware memory tagging (ARM Memory Tagging Extension - MTE) or capability-based addressing (Cambridge CHERI).

  • Pros:
    • Catches spatial and temporal memory violations in production hardware with minimal software modification (~1–2.5% overhead).
    • Provides hardware-level crash diagnostics for zero-day exploitation attempts.
  • Cons:
    • Silicon Dependency: Requires hardware upgrades across user devices or data center instances (e.g., modern ARMv9 servers or Pixel devices).
    • Does not address fundamental software architectural debt.

5. Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) Comparison 

Cumulative Cost Over 5 Years ($)
 ^
 |             /----------------- Strategy 1: Greenfield Rewrite (High upfront, then flat)
 |            /
 |           /          /-------- Strategy 3: Status Quo + Hardening (Linear CVE overhead)
 |          /    /-----/
 |         /  /-+---------------- Strategy 2: Incremental FFI (Moderate upfront, low tail)
 |        /  /  |
 |       /  /  /
 |      /  /--/
 +------------------------------------------------------------> Time (Years)
       Year 1        Year 2        Year 3        Year 4        Year 5

5-Year Financial & Operational Breakdown

Factor Strategy 1: Greenfield Rewrite Strategy 2: Incremental FFI Strategy 3: Status Quo + Hardening
Upfront Engineering Cost $3,000,000 – $10,000,000+ $500,000 – $1,500,000 $50,000 – $200,000
Product Roadmap Delay 12 to 24 Months Negligible (< 1 Month) Zero
Recurring Security Triage Near Zero (< $25k/yr) Low (< $100k/yr) High ($500k – $1.5M/yr)
Toolchain & CI/CD Overhead Low (Single modern stack) Moderate (Dual-stack build) Minimal (Existing stack)
Procurement Compliance Fully compliant Compliant with roadmaps High risk of non-compliance

Note: Strategy 4 (Hardware-Assisted Tagging) is omitted from direct software TCO comparisons because its adoption is tied to hardware refresh lifecycles rather than software engineering budgets.

6. The Pragmatic 3-Phase Migration Roadmap

For engineering leaders managing substantial C++ assets, the following phased approach provides maximum risk reduction with predictable expenditure:

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  PHASE 1: Immediate Triage (Months 0 - 3)                                         |
|  * Turn on libc++ / libstdc++ hardened runtime assertions in production.          |
|  * Block merge on ASan/UBSan clean runs in CI pipelines.                          |
|  * Conduct codebase audit to isolate network-exposed entry points.                |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                        |
                                        v
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  PHASE 2: The Attack Surface Boundary (Months 3 - 12)                             |
|  * Enforce the "No New Unsafe Code" rule across the engineering organization.     |
|  * Implement Rust/MSL wrappers for all external data parsers and TLS interfaces.   |
|  * Establish dual-language CI/CD standards using cxx or bindgen.                  |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                        |
                                        v
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  PHASE 3: Selective Sunset & Hardware Migration (Months 12 - 36)                  |
|  * Incrementally migrate high-churn core modules during routine feature revisions.  |
|  * Benchmark ARM MTE in production infrastructure for remaining legacy core.      |
|  * Publish customer-facing Memory-Safe Roadmap to satisfy CISA and CRA audits.    |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Action Items

  1. Audit Attack Boundaries: Identify all code paths directly processing untrusted user inputs, network packets, or file formats.
  2. Flag Enforcement: Turn on standard library hardening assertions (-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS) in staging environments to measure CPU overhead.
  3. Pilot an Interop Boundary: Pick a single, self-contained parser module in your C++ stack and rewrite it as a memory-safe Rust library with a C ABI interface.
  4. Draft the Memory Safety Roadmap: Document your organization's transition plan to preserve eligibility for enterprise and government contracts.

7. Conclusion

Memory safety is no longer a purist programming language debate—it is a balance sheet and regulatory risk issue.

Relying on C++ developers to manually enforce lifetime invariants across millions of lines of code is a proven losing strategy. Conversely, attempting complete greenfield rewrites often bankrupts product momentum.

The winning architectural strategy is disciplined containment: freeze legacy boundaries, harden the standard runtimes, and route all new ingress through memory-safe languages. Engineering organizations that execute this transition today will insulate themselves from regulatory penalties, reduce CVE overhead, and gain a decisive operational advantage over competitors trapped in perpetual patch cycles.

Appendix A: Comprehensive Technical Vulnerability Taxonomy

Category Specific Hazard C++ Root Cause Modern C++ Mitigation Status Quo & Residual Risk Industry / MSL Equivalent
Spatial Buffer Overflow (Heap/Stack) Raw pointers; unchecked indexed access ([]). std::vector::at(), std::array. operator[] remains unchecked by default for performance; raw buffers still valid. Bounds check by default (Rust, Go); compiler-enforced slices.
Spatial Pointer Arithmetic Overrun Direct pointer manipulation allowed without boundary metadata. std::span (C++20). std::span does not track lifetime or enforce checked bounds by default in release builds. Slices carry length metadata; pointer arithmetic requires explicit unsafe blocks.
Spatial Off-by-One / Null-Terminator Bugs C-string compatibility (char*, strlen, strcpy). std::string, std::string_view. Creating std::string_view from non-null-terminated buffers causes out-of-bounds reads. Native UTF-8 string types with slice-based indexing and length tracking.
Temporal Use-After-Free (UAF) Manual heap management or accessing invalidated heap pointers. std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr. Raw pointers/references extracted via .get() or * can easily outlive the owner. Compile-time borrow checker tracks lifetime of references relative to owners.
Temporal Double Free Freeing same pointer address multiple times. RAII destructors (~Object()). Mixing legacy C APIs or raw delete with smart pointers still causes double frees. Single-owner semantics with affine types prevent multiple destructive drops.
Temporal Dangling Stack References Returning reference to a local variable or temporary. Move semantics (std::move), lifetime warnings. Compiler cannot prove lifetime safety across non-trivial call graphs; warnings are non-fatal. Compiler proves reference lifetime cannot outlive current stack frame.
Temporal Iterator Invalidation Modifying a container while holding iterators/references to its items. Move-aware algorithms, ranges (C++20). Mutating a vector that triggers reallocation silently invalidates existing iterators and references. Exclusive mutable borrow rules prevent container mutation while active references exist.
Temporal Lambda Reference Invalidation Capturing locals by reference ([&]) in async or outliving lambdas. Capture by value ([=]), init-capture move. Accidental [&] capture compiles cleanly; runtime execution segfaults or reads garbage. Closures require move or lifetime bounds on captured variables.
Initialization Uninitialized Memory Read Variable allocated on stack without explicit initialization. Initializer lists, {} default init syntax. Primitive types (int x;, char buf[64];) contain garbage unless explicitly initialized. All variables must be initialized before read; enforced at compile time.
Type Safety Type Confusion / Invalid Downcasting Casting unrelated pointers via static_cast or reinterpret_cast. dynamic_cast (RTTI). static_cast bypasses runtime checks; reinterpret_cast violates strict aliasing. Safe sum types (enum with data) and exhaustive pattern matching.
Type Safety Union Misuse Reading wrong field of an untagged union. std::variant, std::holds_alternative. C-style untagged unions remain standard for ABI and embedded compatibility. Tagged unions checked at compile time or matched exhaustively.
Concurrency Data Races Multiple threads reading/writing shared memory without synchronization. std::atomic, std::mutex, std::jthread. Race conditions cause undefined behavior; language does not restrict cross-thread alias mutation. Send and Sync traits prevent sharing non-thread-safe types across threads.
Resource Memory Leaks Abandoned allocations without deallocation. std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr. Cyclic references in std::shared_ptr leak memory unless explicitly broken by std::weak_ptr. Ownership trees enforce acyclic graphs; cycle collectors or manual weak refs.

Appendix B: Standards Committee (WG21) & Ecosystem Proposals

Initiative Lead / Source Mechanism Status & Major Obstacles
C++ Profiles Bjarne Stroustrup, Herb Sutter Compiler profiles (type, bounds, lifetime) enforcing subset safety rules. In design / prototyping. Relies on heuristics; lacks mathematical soundness guarantees.
Safe C++ (P3390) Sean Baxter (Circle Compiler) Introduces safe keyword, borrow checking, and lifetime annotations to C++. Proposal stage. High friction over syntax additions and steep learning curve.
Contracts (P2900) WG21 Working Group Standardized precondition ([[pre]]) and postcondition ([[post]]) contracts. Targeted for C++26. Provides runtime assertion boundaries, not compile-time temporal safety.
Compiler Extensions Apple -fbounds-safety (Clang) Automatic bounds checks with C ABI annotation support (__counted_by). Upstreaming in LLVM Clang / available in Apple Clang. Resolves spatial safety only; does not address use-after-free.
Hardened Standard Libraries LLVM libc++, GNU libstdc++ Runtime checks in std::vector, std::span, and string indexing. Deployed but opt-in. Performance overhead leads teams to disable checks in release builds.
Automated Translation DARPA TRACTOR Program Automated conversion of legacy C codebases into idiomatic Rust via LLMs and formal analysis. Active government research initiative targeting legacy military and infrastructure code.
Hardware Enforcement ARM MTE, Cambridge CHERI Hardware-level memory tagging and capability pointers. Requires modern silicon architectures; not universally deployable to legacy fleets.

Appendix C: Primary Regulatory & Industry Citations

  1. CISA, FBI, NSA, and International Partners (2023): The Case for Memory Safe Roadmaps — Directives for technology manufacturers to eliminate memory safety vulnerabilities.
  2. White House Office of the National Cyber Director (ONCD) (2024): Back to the Building Blocks: A Path Toward Secure and Measurable Software — Imperatives for adopting memory-safe programming languages in critical infrastructure.
  3. National Security Agency (NSA) (2022): Software Memory Safety Guidance (Cybersecurity Information Sheet) — Technical criteria for migrating from C/C++ to memory-safe alternatives.
  4. Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) (2019–2023): A Proactive Approach to More Secure Code — Analysis of historical CVE root causes documenting the persistent ~70% memory corruption metric.
  5. Google Chromium & Android Security Teams (2020–2024): Memory Safety in Android and Chromium — Comparative data demonstrating sharp vulnerability reduction following Rust adoption for native subsystems.
  6. ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG21 (2023–2024): Proposals P3390 (Safe C++), P2687 (Profiles), and P2900 (Contracts for C++).

title: Scratchpad Patching: Decoupling Compute from Patch Size in Byte-Level Language Models
description:
arXiv:2605.09630v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Tokenizer-free language models eliminate the tokenizer step of the language modeling pipeline by operating directly on bytes; patch-based variants further aggregate contiguous byte spans into patches for efficiency. However, the average patch size chosen at the model design stage governs a tight trade-off: larger patches reduce compute and KV-cache footprint, but degrade modeling quality. We trace this trade-off to patch lag: until a patch is fully observed, byte predictions within it must rely on a stale representation from the previous patch to preserve causality; this lag widens as patches grow larger. We introduce Scratchpad Patching (SP), which inserts transient scratchpads inside each patch to aggregate the bytes seen so far and refresh patch-level context for subsequent predictions. SP triggers scratchpads using next-byte prediction entropy, selectively allocating compute to information-dense regions and enabling post-hoc adjustment of inference-time compute. Across experiments on natural language and code, SP improves model quality at the same patch size; for example, even at $16$ bytes per patch, SP-augmented models match or closely approach the byte-level baseline on downstream evaluations while using a $16\times$ smaller KV-cache over patches and requiring roughly $3$-$4\times$ less inference compute than the byte-level baseline.

title: 海外 VPS 怎么选？全球云服务器购买前必须了解的 7 个关键因素
description:
海外 VPS 怎么选？全球云服务器购买前必须了解的 7 个关键因素

随着跨境电商、海外独立站、国际业务和互联网应用的发展，越来越多的个人开发者和企业开始使用海外 VPS 和全球云服务器。

但是，面对香港、日本、美国、新加坡、韩国等不同地区的服务器，以及各种 CPU、内存、带宽和 IP 配置，很多人在购买之前都会遇到一个问题：

海外 VPS 到底应该怎么选？

实际上，选择服务器不能只看价格和硬件配置。服务器所在地区、网络线路、IP 类型、硬件资源以及服务商的售后支持，都会影响后续使用体验。

本文整理了购买海外 VPS 和全球云服务器之前，值得重点考虑的七个因素。

一、根据目标用户选择服务器地区

选择海外云服务器，首先应该考虑目标用户所在的位置。

不同地区的服务器适合不同的业务场景。

常见服务器地区包括：

  • 香港服务器： 适合面向中国大陆及亚太地区用户的网站和应用，实际访问体验取决于网络线路。
  • 日本服务器： 适合日本及东亚地区的网站、应用和业务部署。
  • 美国服务器： 适合面向北美用户的网站和应用。
  • 新加坡服务器： 适合面向东南亚市场的业务。
  • 韩国服务器： 适合面向韩国及周边地区的业务。
  • 欧洲服务器： 德国、英国、法国、荷兰等地区可以根据客户分布选择。

没有哪一个地区绝对最好。

建议先确定业务的主要访问人群，再选择合适的服务器位置。

二、不要只看 CPU 和内存配置

购买 VPS 时，很多人首先比较 CPU 核心数、内存大小和硬盘容量。

这些参数确实重要，但不能完全代表服务器的实际性能。

配置 主要作用
CPU 影响程序运行和计算能力
内存 影响应用、数据库及缓存运行
SSD/NVMe 影响系统和数据库的读写速度
带宽 影响网络传输能力
月流量 决定计费周期内的数据传输额度

例如，一个简单的网站可能只需要较低的配置，而数据库较多、访问量较大的应用，则需要更充足的 CPU 和内存资源。

建议根据实际业务需求选择，不必盲目追求高配置。

三、网络线路往往比硬件参数更重要

服务器购买后能否稳定访问，与网络线路有很大关系。

即使两台服务器位于同一个国家，也可能因为机房、上游运营商和路由路径不同，产生明显的网络体验差异。

购买之前建议了解：

  1. 服务器所在机房及上游网络。
  2. 到目标用户地区的路由情况。
  3. 网络延迟和丢包情况。
  4. 带宽是否共享。
  5. 是否存在流量或连接限制。

如果服务商提供测试 IP，可以先进行实际测试。

不要只凭宣传页面上的线路名称判断网络质量。

四、了解普通 IP、静态 IP 和双 ISP IP

IP 类型也是海外服务器选购时容易忽略的一项。

普通 IP：

通常指服务器分配的常规 IP 地址，具体归属和使用属性需要向服务商确认。

静态 IP：

通常指不会频繁变化的固定 IP 地址，适合需要固定访问地址、远程管理或稳定配置的业务。

双 ISP IP：

通常涉及两个互联网服务提供商的网络属性。具体 IP 归属、路由情况和实际表现，需要结合产品说明和测试结果判断。

购买前建议确认：

  • IP 是否独享。
  • IP 是否固定。
  • IP 的实际归属和类型。
  • 是否支持所需的网络服务。
  • 是否存在额外使用限制。

不要仅凭产品名称判断 IP 的实际属性。

五、免实名云服务器需要注意什么？

部分海外服务器服务商提供不要求个人实名认证的购买方式，但不同地区和服务商的具体要求可能不同。

购买前建议了解：

  • 服务商的注册及购买要求。
  • 是否需要提供其他身份或付款信息。
  • 所在地区适用的法律法规。
  • 服务条款对业务用途的限制。
  • 数据安全和隐私政策。

需要注意，免实名购买方式不代表可以规避法律法规，也不代表可以用于任何用途。

选择服务器时，合规性和服务透明度同样重要。

六、购买之前做好服务器测试

在正式部署网站或业务之前，建议先检查服务器的实际情况。

可以从以下几个方面入手：

  • CPU、内存和硬盘是否符合购买方案。
  • 网络延迟是否符合业务需求。
  • 是否存在明显丢包。
  • 磁盘读写是否正常。
  • SSH 或远程管理是否能够正常连接。
  • 服务商是否提供清晰的售后支持。

Linux 用户可以使用以下命令进行基础网络测试：

测试网络延迟 

ping -c 10 YOUR_SERVER_IP

查看路由路径 

traceroute YOUR_SERVER_IP

如果系统没有安装 traceroute，需要先安装对应的软件包。

这些测试只能反映特定时间和测试地点的情况。对于长期运行的业务，建议在不同时间段重复测试。

七、关注服务商的售后和服务透明度

服务器不仅仅是一组硬件配置。

购买之前，还应该关注：

  • 产品参数是否清晰。
  • 是否提供网络测试信息。
  • 付款和续费规则是否透明。
  • 是否提供故障处理支持。
  • 是否提前通知维护和网络变更。
  • 是否有明确的服务使用政策。

对于需要长期运行的网站和业务，稳定的服务支持非常重要。

总结：如何选择适合自己的海外 VPS？

海外 VPS 和全球云服务器没有统一的最佳方案。

不同业务应该根据实际需求选择：

  1. 先确定目标用户所在地区。
  2. 根据应用负载选择 CPU 和内存。
  3. 了解服务器的网络线路。
  4. 确认 IP 类型及实际属性。
  5. 了解购买和使用规则。
  6. 正式部署前进行测试。
  7. 选择服务透明、售后清晰的服务商。

如果你正在了解全球云服务器、海外 VPS、双 ISP 服务器或独享静态 IP，可以进一步研究不同地区的产品配置和网络特点，再根据自己的业务需求进行选择。

希望这篇文章能够帮助正在选购海外 VPS 的开发者和网站运营者，减少不必要的购买成本和后期迁移问题。

本文为技术知识分享，涉及的服务器和网络配置应以实际产品说明、测试结果及服务商政策为准。

title: Chat SDK agents can now stream generative UI with json-render
description:
You can now stream generative UI from your Chat SDK agent with json-render.

With a typed catalog of components, the agent writes a JSON spec that json-render converts into a Chat SDK card. Each adapter then posts the card in its platform’s native format, such as Block Kit on Slack and Adaptive Cards on Teams.

The catalog covers tables, charts, buttons, and more, so there’s no separate tool to build and maintain for each message shape.

Stream cards as the model writes

streamCard posts the card once its root element has content and updates the message as new elements stream in. Edits go out at most once every 500 ms by default, which matches Chat SDK’s streaming interval. Once the stream ends, the message shows the final, validated card.

Validate specs and enforce platform limits

toCard checks every element’s props against its component schema and throws CardSpecError for an invalid spec. Each problem gets its own readable issue, so you can send the list back to the model for a corrected spec.

Platforms cap what a single message can hold, and Chat SDK adapters degrade content past those caps. The Slack adapter, for example, turns a second table into a code block. Pass limits to reject those specs instead.

Read the documentation to get started, or try the playground.

title: Why Automated Accessibility Scans Cannot Replace Professional Accessibility Audits
description:
Automated tools make it easier to identify accessibility issues on websites. They can detect missing image descriptions and certain colour contrast problems. However, they cannot identify every barrier that prevents people with disabilities from using a website.

A web accessibility audit goes beyond automated scans. It combines technology with expert evaluation and manual testing. This helps businesses understand whether their websites work for people with different accessibility needs.

What Can Automated Accessibility Scans Detect?

Automated accessibility testing tools scan website code to identify common accessibility problems. They can check for missing alt text and incorrect heading structures. They can also flag certain colour contrast issues and missing form labels.

An accessibility checker can help teams check website accessibility during development. A free website accessibility checker can also provide an initial overview of potential issues.

However, automated scans only identify problems that their rules are designed to detect. They cannot understand every user interaction or determine whether a website is genuinely easy to use.

Why Automated Scans Are Not Enough

Automated tools have limitations. Some accessibility barriers require human judgement and interaction to identify.

For example:

A button may have an accessible label but still be difficult to understand.

A website may have correct heading tags but an illogical content structure.

A form may pass an automated scan but provide confusing error messages.

A menu may contain no code errors but still be difficult to navigate using a keyboard.

A screen reader may announce website elements in an unclear order.

These issues highlight the limitations of automated accessibility testing. They also explain why automated scans should support rather than replace manual testing.

Automated vs Manual Accessibility Testing

Automated and manual testing serve different purposes. Automated scans identify common technical issues. Manual accessibility testing evaluates how people interact with a website.

A web accessibility evaluation tool can help teams find potential problems quickly. However the results need expert review.

A professional website accessibility audit examines website usability through keyboard navigation and screen reader testing. It also checks whether interactive elements behave as expected.

The best accessibility testing tools support this process. They do not replace the knowledge of an experienced accessibility auditor.

What Does a Professional Web Accessibility Audit Include?

A professional web accessibility audit evaluates a website against recognised accessibility standards such as WCAG.

The process may include:

Keyboard testing: Experts check whether users can navigate menus and interactive elements without a mouse.

Screen reader testing: Testers evaluate how assistive technologies interpret page content and controls.

Visual accessibility testing: Experts review colour contrast and text readability. They also examine visual indicators and page structure.

Form testing: Testers check labels and instructions. They also assess error identification and correction.

WCAG compliance testing: Experts review whether the website meets relevant WCAG success criteria.

A web accessibility audit provides a clearer picture of real user barriers. It also gives development teams practical recommendations for fixing them.

Why Businesses Should Invest in Professional Audits

A website can pass an automated scan and still create barriers for users. Businesses need a reliable way to identify these problems before they affect customers.

Professional website accessibility audit services help organisations evaluate their digital experiences in greater depth. They can also support ongoing compliance and accessibility improvements.

When comparing accessibility testing services, consider the provider's manual testing process and experience with assistive technologies. Look for teams that offer clear findings and actionable remediation guidance.

Businesses should also compare WCAG compliance testing services based on their testing scope. A low-cost scan may not provide the same value as a detailed manual evaluation.

How to Choose an Accessibility Audit Provider

Before you hire accessibility auditor services ask how the provider combines automated and manual testing. Check whether the team tests with screen readers and keyboard-only navigation.

An experienced accessibility audit company should explain its testing methodology. It should also provide a detailed report with issue severity and recommendations.

When comparing accessibility audit pricing review what each package includes. Check whether the cost covers manual testing and retesting after fixes. Accessibility audit tools vs manual testing should not be treated as interchangeable options.

Conclusion

Automated scans are useful for identifying common website accessibility issues. However they cannot evaluate every user experience or interaction.

A professional web accessibility audit combines automated checks with expert manual testing. This approach helps businesses identify barriers that automated tools may miss.

SDET provides accessibility testing services to help organisations evaluate their digital products and improve accessibility. A thorough web accessibility audit can help your team move beyond basic scans and build more inclusive digital experiences.

FAQs

Can automated tools detect all website accessibility issues?

No. Automated tools detect common technical issues but cannot identify every usability barrier. Manual testing is necessary to evaluate keyboard access and screen reader experiences.

Is a free accessibility checker enough for WCAG compliance?

No. A free checker can identify some common problems. It cannot confirm that a website meets all relevant WCAG requirements.

How often should a website undergo an accessibility audit?

A website should be evaluated after major updates and redesigns. Regular testing is also useful during ongoing development.

Are automated accessibility testing tools still useful?

Yes. They help teams identify recurring issues and monitor changes. They work best when combined with manual testing and expert evaluation.

title: Why Next.js Navigation Feels Slow Even When the Server Is Fast
description:
I used Next.js for a while before I could explain why clicking a link sometimes did nothing for a moment.

The server was not doing anything especially expensive. The browser already had plenty of JavaScript. Yet the next screen still waited for a network round trip.

The missing piece was the React Server Component payload for the destination route. Understanding when Next.js fetches that payload, and which parts it can reuse, made the delay much easier to explain and fix.

This is the first article in my Next.js performance series. The examples cover the App Router, the older route-level caching model, and the cacheComponents and partialPrefetching options available in Next.js 16.3 and later.

The browser needs more than JavaScript

In a client-rendered application, the browser can render a destination screen as soon as it has the relevant JavaScript. Data may still be loading, but the application can show its own loading UI immediately.

Server Components change what the browser has available. Their implementation stays on the server. The browser receives their rendered output through the RSC payload, alongside references to Client Components and the props those components need.

That payload is a serialized representation of the component tree. It is not simply an HTML document, and it is not the source code of the Server Components.

Here is a small example:

// app/posts/page.tsx
import { LikeButton } from './like-button'

export default function PostsPage() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Posts</h1>
      <LikeButton />
    </main>
  )
}

// app/posts/like-button.tsx
'use client'

import { useState } from 'react'

export function LikeButton() {
  const [liked, setLiked] = useState(false)
  return (
    <button onClick={() => setLiked(!liked)}>
      {liked ? 'Liked' : 'Like'}
    </button>
  )
}

PostsPage is a Server Component even though it has no async, await, or database query. App Router pages and layouts are Server Components by default. The 'use client' directive establishes a client boundary; components imported through that boundary belong to the client module graph.

For navigation, I find it useful to imagine that the browser has part of the destination tree, with spaces that need the server's output. The important question is whether that output arrives before or after the click.

If the required payload is missing, navigation may wait for the server. A prefetched loading boundary or static shell can still provide immediate feedback, so the presence of a Server Component alone does not make every transition slow.

What Link prefetching actually does

Next.js can fetch route data before navigation. In production, a <Link> entering the viewport normally triggers prefetching. The browser can then reuse the payload when the user clicks. Automatic prefetching is disabled in development, so next dev is not a useful way to judge its production behavior.

Before enabling Partial Prefetching, the default behavior differs by route:

Destination Default prefetch behavior
Statically rendered route Prefetch the full route
Dynamically rendered route Prefetch down to the nearest loading.js boundary, when available

prefetch={true} requests a fuller prefetch, including for dynamic routes under the older model. It can reduce the wait after a click, but it also does more server work before the user decides to visit. With Partial Prefetching enabled, the rules change again: default prefetching focuses on the shared App Shell. Next.js Link reference

The basic sequence is:

Link becomes visible
  → fetch reusable route content
  → keep it in the browser's Client Cache

User clicks
  → render the cached content
  → request anything still missing

Moving work before the click can matter more to perceived speed than shaving a few milliseconds off the server render.

Dynamic segments and dynamic rendering are different

The word “dynamic” causes a lot of confusion here.

A folder such as posts/[slug] defines a dynamic URL segment. It does not, by itself, mean that every visit requires request-time rendering. generateStaticParams can provide values that Next.js prerenders.

Dynamic rendering means rendering at request time. In the previous caching model, reading request-specific values such as cookies() or headers() opts a route into dynamic rendering. That can happen deep inside a component tree.

Imagine a mostly static article page with a small personalized control:

Article page
├─ Article title
├─ Article body
└─ Personal controls
   └─ reads cookies()

Without Cache Components or another partial-prerendering setup, that request-specific read affects the route's rendering mode. The title and body may be easy to render, but the route no longer has one completely static response that can serve every request. Cached data and shared layouts can still be reused; “dynamic” does not mean every cache disappears. Next.js previous caching model

Suspense helps only when its fallback is available

Wrapping the personalized control in <Suspense> lets the server stream the surrounding content and fallback before the slow part finishes.

But in the previous model, an ordinary Suspense boundary inside a dynamic page does not automatically turn everything around it into a build-time shell. The browser may still need the first server response before it knows what to render.

Click
  → request the destination payload
  → first response arrives
  → show surrounding content and fallback
  → stream the remaining content

A prefetched loading.tsx boundary can make the initial transition feel immediate. A fallback that exists only in an unfetched destination payload cannot do that yet. This is the distinction I was missing when I thought, “I already use Suspense, so why does navigation still pause?” Next.js instant navigation guide

Network distance makes the difference obvious. While hosting one of my services on Cloudflare, I sometimes saw traffic from Korea reach Los Angeles or Hong Kong. Even a quick server render could not eliminate that round trip.

Read staleTimes as page reuse rules

The experimental staleTimes configuration controls reuse of page segments in the Client Cache:

// Defaults in the previous caching model
const nextConfig = {
  experimental: {
    staleTimes: {
      dynamic: 0,
      static: 300,
    },
  },
}

export default nextConfig

The names are easy to read too literally. The dynamic interval applies to pages that are neither statically generated nor fully prefetched. The static interval also applies to fully prefetched pages. Loading boundaries use the static interval, shared layouts can remain reusable, and browser back/forward navigation has its own caching behavior.

So dynamic: 0 does not mean “Next.js never keeps anything from a dynamic route.” It explains one particular reason an ordinary revisit may request the page segment again. The default changed from 30 seconds to zero in Next.js 15. Next.js staleTimes reference

Cache Components gives the page a reusable shell

With Cache Components, Next.js can prerender a shell while leaving request-specific content behind Suspense boundaries:

// next.config.ts
const nextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
}

export default nextConfig

That gives us a different navigation sequence:

Before the click
  → prefetch the static shell and its fallbacks

After the click
  → show that shell immediately
  → stream request-specific content into it

I now place a boundary around the part that actually needs request-time information, rather than assuming the whole page must wait.

Enabling the flag also changes how the application expresses caching. Reusable work can use 'use cache'; uncached work that should stream needs an appropriate Suspense boundary. Existing applications may need more than a configuration change to adopt this model. Next.js caching guide

I learned that through an awkward migration. With Next.js 16.2 on Cloudflare/OpenNext, I turned the option on and off while working through middleware compatibility, authentication reads in layouts, and transition behavior. I eventually enabled it after changing hosting. That experience made me treat this as an application migration, not a free performance switch.

There is also a lifecycle detail to check. Next.js can preserve recently visited screens with React Activity. Activity hides DOM and preserves state while cleaning up Effects. Code that assumes leaving a route always destroys its DOM may need attention, particularly media elements and other work tied to the DOM itself. React Activity reference

Partial Prefetching shares the shell across URLs

Next.js 16.3 introduced another opt-in flag:

const nextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
  partialPrefetching: true,
}

export default nextConfig

An article list might link to /posts/1, /posts/2, and /posts/3. Those URLs can share the same structural shell even though the article content differs. Partial Prefetching lets Next.js reuse that App Shell across links to the same route pattern, instead of treating each URL as a completely separate prefetch target. Next.js 16.3 announcement

Where we read URL-specific information matters. Awaiting params at the top of a page ties more of the render to that particular URL. Passing the promise down and reading it inside a Suspense boundary leaves more URL-independent UI in the shared shell.

The default prefetch then brings in the shell; URL-specific content can stream after navigation. If a particular link deserves more eager work, prefetch={true} can also prefetch cached content that depends on its URL. It is a tradeoff between earlier work and faster transitions. Adopting Partial Prefetching

Service workers need a separate caching design

I also use Serwist to persist selected resources beyond the browser's in-memory route cache. Static assets are an obvious starting point. Persisting RSC responses is much more sensitive because their representation can depend on request headers, route state, deployment, and authentication.

My original implementation used Next.js response headers to distinguish responses and applied custom cache rules. I would not treat that snippet as a general recipe for other applications. Removing _rsc from cache keys or caching personalized responses without preserving the relevant distinctions can reuse the wrong response.

For most applications, I would first get framework prefetching and the App Shell right, then add a service worker only for a specific offline or persistence requirement. Next.js CDN caching guide, Serwist

A list already contains part of the detail page

The last improvement in my application came from the screen design.

When someone opens an item from a list, the browser already knows its title, thumbnail, and summary. Replacing all of that with a full-page spinner throws away useful information.

For the showcase in my service, I use Intercepting Routes to distinguish two ways of reaching the same URL:

Entry path What the user sees
Navigation from the list Show the cached summary immediately, then fetch the remaining detail
Direct visit or refresh Render the full detail through the normal server route

The intercepted route uses the list's existing client state as initial content. If there is no matching summary, it falls back to a skeleton. The regular route handles server data loading and metadata for direct visits.

Intercepting Routes provide the routing distinction; the shared client state provides the instant content. They do not, by themselves, guarantee a navigation without any RSC request. Next.js Intercepting Routes

Start with the delay after the click

I still like Next.js. These changes came from using it in Comwit, the service I build, and wanting the navigation to feel better.

When a transition feels slow, I now look at three things: what the browser already has, what it still needs from the server, and what it can show while that request is in flight.

A Server Component does not automatically make navigation slow. Waiting until the click to obtain the UI needed for the next screen is what I look for first.

Adapted from my original Korean article on Velog, published September 27, 2026.

title: Designing Scalable Retail Management Systems: Architecture Decisions Developers Should Consider
description:
Retail management software has evolved beyond basic billing and inventory tracking. Modern retail applications often need to manage products, suppliers, purchase orders, sales, warehouses, customer information, and reporting through a connected system.

As retail businesses expand, these requirements become more complicated. A solution that works for a single store may struggle when the business adds multiple locations, sales channels, warehouses, or larger product catalogs.

For developers, the challenge is to build software that supports current operations without making future expansion difficult.

Here are seven important architectural considerations when developing retail management systems.

  1. Use a Modular Application Architecture

A retail management system contains several functional areas, but they do not all need to operate as independent applications.

A modular architecture helps separate responsibilities while keeping related functionality organized.

For example, the system could contain modules for:

Product and category management

Inventory and warehouse operations

Purchasing and supplier management

Sales and order processing

Customer management

Reporting and analytics

Each module should have clearly defined responsibilities and interfaces. This makes the application easier to maintain and allows individual areas to evolve without creating unnecessary dependencies.

A modular monolith can be a practical starting point for many businesses. Microservices may become useful when independent deployment, scaling, or team ownership justifies the additional operational complexity.

  1. Design Inventory Management Carefully

Inventory is one of the most important components of retail software.

A product's available quantity can change because of sales, returns, transfers, damaged stock, purchase receipts, and manual adjustments.

Simply storing a single stock number may not provide enough visibility for growing businesses.

Developers should consider maintaining an inventory movement history that records:

Transaction type

Product and location identifiers

Quantity added or removed

Transaction timestamp

Reference to the related order or purchase

User or system responsible for the change

This makes stock changes traceable and helps teams investigate discrepancies.

For concurrent operations, database transactions and appropriate locking strategies can help prevent incorrect stock updates.

  1. Support Multi-Store Operations

A retail business operating across multiple locations needs more than a shared product database.

Each store may have different stock levels, pricing rules, operating hours, and fulfillment requirements.

The data model should clearly distinguish between global product information and location-specific information.

For example, product details may be shared across all stores, while inventory quantities should be maintained separately for each location.

Developers should also consider how stock transfers, inter-store fulfillment, and store-level reporting will work as the business expands.

  1. Build Reliable Supplier and Purchase Order Workflows

Retail management systems must also support procurement activities.

A typical purchase workflow may involve creating a purchase order, submitting it to a supplier, receiving products, checking quantities, and updating inventory.

Each stage should have a clear status and validation rules.

For example, receiving a partial shipment should not automatically mark the entire purchase order as completed.

A well-designed workflow can help businesses track pending deliveries, identify supplier delays, and maintain more accurate inventory records.

  1. Integrate POS and Ecommerce Systems

Many retailers sell through physical stores as well as digital channels.

Their management software should exchange relevant information with POS systems, ecommerce platforms, payment services, and shipping providers.

Developers should define consistent APIs and data contracts for these integrations.

Important considerations include:

Product and price synchronization

Order status updates

Inventory availability

Payment confirmation

Return and refund processing

Integration failure recovery

Event-driven communication can be useful for updates that do not need to block the main customer transaction.

  1. Build Reporting Around Reliable Data

Retail managers need accurate information to make operational decisions.

Useful reports may include sales performance, stock movement, product profitability, supplier performance, and store-level comparisons.

However, reporting should not negatively affect the performance of transactional operations.

Depending on the application's scale, developers may consider optimized database queries, read replicas, reporting tables, or separate analytical data pipelines.

The important point is to ensure that reports use consistent definitions and trustworthy source data.

  1. Plan for Security and Future Growth

Retail systems often handle commercially sensitive information and customer records.

Security should be included throughout the development process.

Some important practices include:

Role-based access control

Secure authentication

Encrypted communication

Audit logs for important operations

Input validation

Regular security updates

Backups and recovery testing

Developers should also monitor database performance, API response times, background jobs, and application errors.

Scalability is not just about supporting more users. It also means keeping the application maintainable as business rules and operational requirements become more complex.

Final Thoughts

A scalable retail management system requires more than a collection of independent features. Product management, inventory, procurement, sales, integrations, and reporting must work together through a consistent architecture.

Making the right decisions early can reduce future technical debt and help retail businesses expand without repeatedly rebuilding their core systems.

Businesses planning to modernize their retail operations can explore retail software development services to understand how custom applications can support their operational workflows and long-term growth.

title: Supabase "email rate limit exceeded"? Turn on custom SMTP, then raise the limit
description:
Sign-ups worked yesterday. Today new users never get the confirmation email, and the sign-up or reset call comes back with one of these:

email rate limit exceeded
over_email_send_rate_limit
429 Too Many Requests
Email address not authorized
email_address_not_authorized

Supabase's built-in email provider sends at most 2 emails an hour for the whole project, and only to members of your team. Connect your own SMTP provider and Supabase sends to every address, starting at 30 emails an hour, which you can raise.

I see this a lot in Lovable and Bolt apps on Supabase right when the first real users arrive.

Why it happens

  1. The default email service is still on. It refuses addresses outside the project team (email_address_not_authorized) and sends 2 emails an hour for the whole project, across every sign-up, reset, magic link and invite. Supabase describes it as best effort and not meant for production.
  2. Too many emails to one address. Repeated sign-up or reset attempts trip over_email_send_rate_limit (HTTP 429) for that address. By default the same user waits 60 seconds before another confirmation or reset email.
  3. The custom SMTP limit is still the starting value. After you add custom SMTP, Supabase starts at 30 emails an hour to protect your new sender's reputation, until you change it.

Find the cause

  1. Read the error code returned by the sign-up or reset call. over_email_send_rate_limit and email_address_not_authorized need different fixes.
  2. In the Supabase dashboard, open Authentication > SMTP settings and check whether custom SMTP is enabled.
  3. Open Authentication > Rate Limits and read the limit for emails sent.

Fix 1: connect a real email provider

  1. Create an SMTP account with a transactional email provider and verify your sending domain there.
  2. In Authentication > SMTP settings, enter the host, port, username, password, a From address such as no-reply@yourdomain.com, and a sender name.
  3. Save. From then on, Supabase sends auth emails to every address, not only your team.

Fix 2: raise the limit to fit real traffic

Set the limit for emails sent in Authentication > Rate Limits to cover your busiest hour of sign-ups and resets. Or do it from a script with the Management API:

# Access token from https://supabase.com/dashboard/account/tokens
export SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN="your-access-token"
export PROJECT_REF="your-project-ref"

# Read the current limit
curl -X GET "https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/$PROJECT_REF/config/auth" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN" | jq '.rate_limit_email_sent'

# Set it to your busiest hour of auth emails (replace <emails-per-hour>)
curl -X PATCH "https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/$PROJECT_REF/config/auth" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "rate_limit_email_sent": <emails-per-hour> }'

Keep the per-user wait between emails, so one person can't flood their own inbox.

Check the fix worked

  • Sign up with an address outside your team: the confirmation arrives from your domain.
  • Request three password resets in an hour from different addresses: all of them arrive.

Stop it coming back

  • Switch to custom SMTP before you invite any real users.
  • Add the sending domain's SPF, DKIM and DMARC records at your provider so the emails reach inboxes.

Quick answers

Is the built-in service fine for launch? No. Supabase describes it as best effort, for testing and non-critical projects, with no delivery guarantee.

Does this affect magic links and invites too? Yes. Every auth email, including one-time codes, magic links and invites, goes through the same sender.

Sources: Supabase rate limits, Send emails with custom SMTP, Auth error codes.

Full write-up with the same steps: Supabase "email rate limit exceeded": the fix. Before launch, the free Launch Check looks over your live app for exposed keys, missing security headers and broken basics.
