title: LLM Inference Cost in 2026: Why Cost per Finished Task Beats Cost per Token
description:
Most conversations about LLM cost start and end with a price table: dollars per million input tokens, dollars per million output tokens, pick the cheapest model that passes a demo. That table is necessary, but it measures the wrong unit. Your users do not buy tokens. They want a support ticket triaged, an invoice extracted, a contract clause flagged or a pull request reviewed.

The unit that matters is cost per finished task: everything you paid, across every call, retry, tool loop and fallback, divided by the number of tasks that actually reached your quality bar. Latency works the same way. Users feel the time until the task is done, not the time to the first token of one call.

This article is for engineers and tech leads running LLM features in production, with a focus on Germany and the EU. It covers pricing mechanics, why cheaper tokens can mean pricier tasks, measurement, the main levers, self-hosting break-even and EU hosting, and ends with a checklist.

All prices below were checked on 6 November 2026 and will change. Epoch AI found that the price of reaching a fixed performance level has fallen between 9x and 900x per year, depending on the milestone [1]. Treat every price here as an example, and any routing decision based on today's price table as short-lived.

How token pricing actually works in late 2026

Input versus output

Output tokens cost several times more than input tokens. OpenAI lists gpt-6.1-sol at $2.00 per million input tokens and $10.00 per million output tokens, and gpt-6-luna at $0.10 and $0.50 [2]. Anthropic lists Claude Sonnet 5.5 at $2 and $10, and Claude Opus 5.5 at $4 and $20 [3]. In all four cases output costs 5x input.

With a 5:1 price ratio, output dominates the bill as soon as a task produces more than one output token for every five input tokens. Many benchmark sites assume a fixed mix. Artificial Analysis, for example, blends input and output prices at a 3:1 ratio [4]. That is a reasonable default for comparing models, but your workload has its own ratio, and you should compute it from your logs instead of borrowing someone else's.

Token counts also depend on language. OpenAI's rule of thumb is about 4 characters or three quarters of a word per token in English, and it notes that non-English text can cost more per character [5]. If your product serves German users, measure token counts on German prompts and German outputs, not on English test fixtures.

Some input is invisible in your code. When you pass tools to Claude models, Anthropic adds a tool-use system prompt of 286 tokens for the listed models, on top of the tool schemas themselves [3]. Every tool definition you send is input you pay for on every call.

Cached input

All three large API vendors now discount repeated prompt prefixes, but the mechanics differ.

  • OpenAI caches automatically. The minimum cacheable prompt is 1,024 tokens for GPT-5.6 and later, the default cache lifetime is 30 minutes (12 hours can be requested in the Responses API), and cache writes on these models cost more than standard input [6]. Cached input for gpt-6.1-sol is listed at $0.10 against $2.00 for uncached input [2].
  • Anthropic uses explicit cache_control breakpoints. A 5-minute cache write costs 1.25x the base input price, a 1-hour write costs 2x, and a cache read costs 0.1x, or 0.05x on Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 [3]. Prompts below a model-specific minimum (between 1,024 and 4,096 tokens for the models listed) are processed without caching, and no error is returned [7].
  • Google Gemini caches implicitly on Gemini 2.5 and newer models, and lists a 90% discount on cached tokens plus prorated storage for caching [8].

The break-even point for Anthropic-style pricing is easy to compute. With a 5-minute cache, two requests sharing a prefix cost 1.25 + 0.1 = 1.35 units of prefix price instead of 2.0, so caching pays off on the first reuse. With a 1-hour cache, two requests cost 2.0 + 0.1 = 2.1 units, which is more than 2.0, so you need at least two reuses before the longer TTL pays off.

Caches are prefix matches, so small changes break them. Anthropic documents that modifying tool definitions invalidates the entire cache, and that changing thinking settings invalidates message-level cache entries [7]. Changing the thinking budget or the effort level between requests also invalidates cache breakpoints [9][10]. OpenAI's guidance is to put stable instructions and shared reference material first and dynamic content such as timestamps or user-specific text at the end [6].

Reasoning tokens

Reasoning ("thinking") tokens are the most common source of surprise on an invoice. OpenAI states that reasoning tokens are not visible through the API but still occupy context and are billed as output tokens, reported as output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens [11]. Anthropic bills the full internal thinking as output tokens even when you only receive a summary, and states that the billed output count does not match the visible token count [10].

Two details matter for cost control:

  • OpenAI recommends reserving at least 25,000 tokens for reasoning and outputs when you start experimenting with reasoning models [11]. That is the order of magnitude a single call can consume.
  • Anthropic notes that max_tokens is a hard cap per request, but in a tool-use loop each request has its own max_tokens, so it "doesn't bound the whole turn's spend" [10]. A task-level budget has to live in your orchestrator.

Batch, flex and paying for speed

If a task does not need an answer within seconds, you can usually halve its price.

  • Anthropic's Batch API gives a 50% discount on input and output tokens [3].
  • Gemini's Batch API runs at 50% of standard cost with a 24-hour target turnaround, and Gemini Flex inference also costs 50% of standard with a target of 1 to 15 minutes [8].
  • OpenAI's Flex/Batch prices are half the standard rates, for example $1.00 input and $5.00 output for gpt-6.1-sol [2].
  • Azure OpenAI Global Batch and Data Zone Batch deployments are 50% cheaper than the corresponding standard deployments, with a 24-hour target and no real-time SLA [12].

The opposite direction exists too. OpenAI renamed Priority processing to Fast mode on 30 July 2026; Fast mode for gpt-6.1-sol is listed at $4.00 input and $20.00 output, and an Ultrafast tier at $12.00 and $60.00 [2]. Gemini Priority inference costs 75% to 100% more than standard [8]. Latency is now an explicit line item.

Long context and region multipliers

Prompt length can change the per-token price. Claude Haiku 5.5 charges higher prices for any request whose prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens, counting cache reads and writes toward that length, while other Claude 4.6 and later models charge the same rate across the full 1M-token window [3].

Data residency also costs money. OpenAI charges a 10% uplift on regional processing endpoints for models released on or after 5 March 2026 [2]. Anthropic applies a 1.1x multiplier to all token categories when you request US-only inference with inference_geo [3]. If you need regional processing, add that multiplier to your cost model from day one.

Why a cheaper model per token can cost more per task

Four mechanisms turn a low token price into a high task price.

More calls. Agentic tasks are loops: the model plans, calls a tool, reads the result and continues. Every step resends a growing context. Anthropic reported that its agents typically use about 4x more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems about 15x more [13]. A model that needs six steps where another needs four pays for that context six times.

Longer reasoning. Reasoning models can spend many tokens on easy inputs. A study of o1-like models found they used on average 1,953% more tokens than conventional models to answer simple problems, and that a mitigation reduced token output by 48.6% on MATH500 while maintaining accuracy for QwQ-32B-Preview [14].

Retries. If the output fails validation (broken JSON, a missing field, an answer that fails a business rule), you pay again. When OpenAI introduced Structured Outputs, it reported that the new model scored 100% on its complex JSON schema evals while gpt-4-0613 scored less than 40% [15]. Every percentage point of format failure is a retry you pay for.

Failure handling. Some tasks fail after all retries and go to a stronger model or a human. Kapoor et al. showed that agents with similar accuracy can differ in cost by almost two orders of magnitude; on HumanEval, a simple baseline reached about 93% accuracy for about $2.45 in total, while a more complex agent architecture cost about $134.50 for 88% [16]. Accuracy and cost have to be evaluated together.

A formula for cost per finished task

Start with the cost of a single model call, using per-million-token prices:

c_call = ( N_in * p_in
         + N_cache_read * p_cache_read
         + N_cache_write * p_cache_write
         + N_out * p_out ) / 1,000,000 * m_region

N_out includes reasoning tokens.
m_region is 1.0, or 1.1 for the regional uplifts quoted above.

An attempt is the sequence of calls needed to try the task once, plus any validation calls:

C_attempt = sum of c_call over all calls in the attempt (+ tool and validation costs)

If an attempt succeeds with probability s and you allow at most k attempts, the expected number of attempts is a truncated geometric series:

E[attempts] = (1 - (1 - s)^k) / s
P(all k attempts fail) = (1 - s)^k

If failed tasks are escalated at cost E (a stronger model, or a person's time), the expected cost per task is:

C_task = C_attempt * (1 - (1 - s)^k) / s  +  (1 - s)^k * E

If failed tasks are simply dropped, divide total spend by the number of successful tasks instead:

C_finished = C_attempt * E[attempts] / (1 - (1 - s)^k)

Worked example (illustrative)

The numbers below are illustrative assumptions, not measurements. They show how the formula behaves. Prices are the OpenAI list prices quoted above; the token counts and success rates are invented to make the mechanics visible.

Task: classify a support ticket and extract structured fields, using a small agent loop with tools. Both models share a 6,000-token static prefix (system prompt plus tool definitions) that is read from cache on every call. Cache writes are ignored because they amortise across many tasks. Each model gets at most two attempts.

Assumption Model A (gpt-6.1-sol prices) Model B (gpt-6.1-terra prices)
Price per 1M tokens: input / cached / output $2.00 / $0.10 / $10.00 $1.00 / $0.05 / $5.00
Calls per attempt 4 6
Uncached input tokens per call 2,000 2,500
Cached input tokens per call 6,000 6,000
Output tokens per call (visible + reasoning) 300 + 800 300 + 1,500
Success probability per attempt s 0.90 0.75

Per call, Model A costs 2,000 x $2 + 6,000 x $0.10 + 1,100 x $10, divided by one million, which is $0.0156. Four calls make $0.0624 per attempt. Model B costs $0.0025 + $0.0003 + $0.0090 = $0.0118 per call, and six calls make $0.0708 per attempt.

With k = 2, Model A needs (1 - 0.1^2) / 0.9 = 1.10 expected attempts and Model B needs (1 - 0.25^2) / 0.75 = 1.25. Expected spend per task is $0.0686 for A and $0.0885 for B. Model A finishes 99% of tasks and Model B finishes 93.75%, so the cost per finished task is $0.0693 for A and $0.0944 for B.

Model B is half the price per token and about 36% more expensive per finished task. It also sends 6.25% of tasks to the escalation path instead of 1%, so any non-zero escalation cost E widens the gap by 0.0525 x E per task. On latency, B generates about 13,500 output tokens per task in expectation against about 4,840 for A, so at equal decode speed it spends roughly 2.8x as long generating.

Change the assumptions and the answer can flip. That is the point: s, the number of calls and the reasoning length are properties of your traffic, and you can only get them from your own logs.

Measuring cost and latency per task

Call-level latency metrics

NVIDIA's benchmarking guide gives standard definitions [17]:

  • Time to first token (TTFT): time to process the prompt and generate the first token. It generally includes queueing, prefill and network latency, and grows with prompt length.
  • End-to-end latency: TTFT plus generation time.
  • Inter-token latency (ITL) or time per output token (TPOT): the average gap between output tokens during decoding.
  • Tokens per second: per user (output length divided by end-to-end latency) or per system (all output tokens across concurrent requests).

The same guide describes the core trade-off: raising concurrency increases system throughput until the GPU saturates, while per-user speed falls and requests beyond the batch limit queue, which increases TTFT [17].

Public leaderboards help with shortlisting. Artificial Analysis tests endpoints eight times a day with prompts of roughly 100, 1k and 10k tokens and reports the median over 14 days [4]. Those numbers are not your SLO: your prompts, your region and your concurrency differ.

Task-level latency

For a task, measure wall-clock time from the user's request to the validated result. That includes every sequential model call, tool execution, retries and queueing in your own services. Report p50 and p95 per task type. Do not add up per-call p95 values to estimate task p95; percentiles do not add, so measure the task directly.

For reasoning models, also track time to the first visible token. Reasoning tokens are generated before the answer, so a fast TTFT on the wire can still mean a long wait for the user.

If you self-host with vLLM, the engine exposes Prometheus histograms for vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds, vllm:inter_token_latency_seconds, vllm:e2e_request_latency_seconds and vllm:request_queue_time_seconds, plus gauges for vllm:num_requests_waiting and vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc and a vllm:prefix_cache_hits counter [18]. Queue time is the number to watch when p95 TTFT drifts upward.

What to log for every task

Log one record per task, not just per call, with: task type, task ID, model per call, uncached input, cache read and cache write tokens, output and reasoning tokens, number of calls, number of attempts, final success flag, cost, TTFT of the first call and wall time. Do not log prompt text in the same pipeline. Token counts are enough for cost analysis, and keeping user content out of metrics makes GDPR reviews much simpler.

A minimal Python version, with an adapter for Anthropic's usage fields (where input_tokens excludes cache reads and writes, and output_tokens is the inclusive total that includes thinking [7][10]):

import json, statistics, time, uuid
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

# USD per 1M tokens. Copy from your provider's pricing page; these will go stale.
PRICES = {
    "model-a": {"in": 2.00, "cache_read": 0.10, "cache_write": 2.50, "out": 10.00},
    "model-b": {"in": 1.00, "cache_read": 0.05, "cache_write": 1.25, "out": 5.00},
}

@dataclass
class Call:
    model: str
    in_tok: int            # uncached input
    cache_read_tok: int
    cache_write_tok: int
    out_tok: int           # billed output, reasoning included
    reasoning_tok: int
    ttft_s: float
    total_s: float

    @classmethod
    def from_anthropic(cls, model, usage, ttft_s, total_s):
        details = usage.get("output_tokens_details") or {}
        return cls(model, usage["input_tokens"], usage.get("cache_read_input_tokens", 0),
                   usage.get("cache_creation_input_tokens", 0), usage["output_tokens"],
                   details.get("thinking_tokens", 0), ttft_s, total_s)

    def cost(self):
        p = PRICES[self.model]
        return (self.in_tok * p["in"] + self.cache_read_tok * p["cache_read"]
                + self.cache_write_tok * p["cache_write"] + self.out_tok * p["out"]) / 1e6

@dataclass
class Task:
    kind: str
    id: str = field(default_factory=lambda: uuid.uuid4().hex)
    calls: list = field(default_factory=list)
    t0: float = field(default_factory=time.monotonic)

    def finish(self, success: bool) -> dict:
        inp = sum(c.in_tok + c.cache_read_tok + c.cache_write_tok for c in self.calls)
        rec = {
            "task_id": self.id, "kind": self.kind, "success": success,
            "calls": len(self.calls),
            "cost_usd": round(sum(c.cost() for c in self.calls), 6),
            "out_tok": sum(c.out_tok for c in self.calls),
            "reasoning_tok": sum(c.reasoning_tok for c in self.calls),
            "cache_hit_ratio": round(sum(c.cache_read_tok for c in self.calls) / inp, 3) if inp else 0.0,
            "wall_s": round(time.monotonic() - self.t0, 3),
        }
        print(json.dumps(rec))  # ship to your log pipeline; never log prompt text here
        return rec

def summarize(records):
    done = [r for r in records if r["success"]]
    wall = sorted(r["wall_s"] for r in records)
    return {
        "cost_per_finished_task": sum(r["cost_usd"] for r in records) / max(len(done), 1),
        "success_rate": len(done) / len(records),
        "p50_s": statistics.median(wall),
        "p95_s": statistics.quantiles(wall, n=20)[-1] if len(wall) > 1 else wall[0],
    }

Retries of the same task should append to the same Task, so their cost lands on the task that caused them. For other providers, write a second from_... adapter and check in the docs whether the reported input count already includes cached tokens.

The levers, roughly in order of effort

Cut tokens you do not need

Output is the expensive side, so start there.

  • Bound reasoning. Anthropic recommends lowering the effort level before trying prompt-based steering, and treats max_tokens as the hard cap on thinking plus answer [10]. OpenAI exposes reasoning.effort with model-dependent values from none to max [11]. Run your eval set at two or three effort levels and pick the lowest one that holds quality. The overthinking results above suggest that easy inputs often do not need the highest setting [14].
  • Constrain the format. Structured outputs with a strict schema remove a whole class of retries [15]. Budget for a one-time delay: OpenAI notes that the first request with a new schema incurs extra latency, typically under 10 seconds, after which the processed schema is cached [15].
  • Ask for less. Short field values, no restated input, no unread explanations.
  • Send fewer tools. Each tool definition is input on every call. Group tools per route so each route has a small, stable set, because changing tool definitions also invalidates the cache [7].

Make prompt caching work

Order prompts as static to dynamic: system instructions, tool definitions, shared reference text, then conversation history, then the new user input [6]. Keep model settings such as thinking effort stable within a conversation [10]. Track the cache hit ratio per task type (cache read tokens divided by total input tokens), and alert when it drops after a deploy, because a small template change can silently move a timestamp to the top of the prompt.

Self-hosted engines offer the same idea. vLLM's automatic prefix caching reuses the KV cache of earlier requests that share a prefix, but it only reduces prefill time, not decode time, so it helps most with long shared contexts and short answers [19]. SGLang uses RadixAttention for KV cache reuse, and its paper reports up to 6.4x higher throughput than other inference systems on workloads such as agent control, few-shot benchmarks and multi-turn chat [20].

Move asynchronous work to batch or flex

Nightly enrichment, document backfills, evaluation runs and report generation rarely need second-level latency. Moving them to batch or flex tiers halves token cost at all three major vendors and on Azure [3][8][2][12]. Build a small queue abstraction so a task can declare "needed within 24 hours" and the platform picks the tier.

Cache whole responses where it is safe

Exact-match response caching (same normalised input, same model, same prompt version) is safe and cheap. Semantic caching, which reuses answers for similar inputs via embeddings, is riskier. The GPTCache documentation itself warns about false positives on cache hits [21]. Use it only where a near-duplicate answer is acceptable, and include the similarity threshold in your evals.

Route and cascade

A router sends easy requests to a small model and hard ones to a large model. A cascade tries the small model first and escalates if a check fails. FrugalGPT reported matching the best individual model with up to 98% cost reduction using cascades and related strategies [22]. RouteLLM reported cost reductions of over 2x in some cases without lowering response quality, evaluated on MT Bench, MMLU and GSM8K [23]. Kapoor et al. cut variable cost by 53% for GPT-3.5 and 41% for Llama-3-70B on HotPotQA by optimising cost and accuracy jointly [16].

Put the cascade into the formula before you ship it. An escalated request pays for the failed small-model attempt and adds its latency, so a cascade only wins if the small model resolves enough traffic on its own.

Distil or fine-tune for narrow tasks

For a stable, high-volume task, a small specialised model can beat a large general one. In "Distilling Step-by-Step", a fine-tuned 770M-parameter T5 model outperformed few-shot prompted 540B PaLM using only 80% of the available data on a benchmark [24]. Distillation is a fixed cost that pays back with volume. In a different setting, Kapoor et al. found that a one-time optimisation cost was outweighed by inference savings after roughly 1,300 inferences [16]; compute the same payback for your own task.

Serving-engine levers if you self-host

If you run open-weight models, the serving engine decides how much work each GPU hour does.

  • Continuous batching. Orca introduced iteration-level scheduling, which adds and removes requests from the batch at each decoding step, and reported 36.9x throughput over FasterTransformer at the same latency for a GPT-3 175B model [25]. TensorRT-LLM's in-flight batching applies the same idea, processing context and generation phases together to keep GPUs busy [26].
  • Paged KV cache. PagedAttention targets KV cache memory that is wasted by fragmentation and redundant duplication, and vLLM reported 2x to 4x higher throughput than FasterTransformer and Orca at the same latency [27].
  • Chunked prefill. vLLM splits long prefills and schedules them alongside decodes. Lower max_num_batched_tokens values (for example 2048) improve inter-token latency, while higher values improve TTFT and throughput [28]. When KV cache memory runs out, vLLM preempts requests and recomputes them later, which hurts end-to-end latency; the docs list remedies such as increasing gpu_memory_utilization or lowering max_num_seqs [28].
  • Prefill/decode disaggregation. DistServe places prefill and decode on different GPUs to remove interference between them, and reported 4.48x more requests or 10.2x tighter SLOs under TTFT and TPOT constraints [29]. TensorRT-LLM offers disaggregated serving as a beta feature [26].
  • Quantization. vLLM's FP8 docs claim a 2x reduction in model memory and up to 1.6x throughput, with W8A8 officially supported on Hopper and Ada Lovelace GPUs [30]. Red Hat's large evaluation of quantized Llama 3.1 models found full accuracy recovery for FP8 across its tasks, close to 99% average recovery on OpenLLM Leaderboard v2, about 1.8x average speedup for 8-bit models in server workloads, and 2.4x average single-stream speedup for 4-bit weight-only models, which it recommends for latency-critical use [31]. AWQ, a low-bit weight-only method, protects about 1% of salient weights and reports more than 3x speedup over the Hugging Face FP16 implementation [32]. TensorRT-LLM supports FP8 on H100 and later and FP4 weights on B200 [26]. Always rerun your own task eval after quantizing; the Red Hat study saw more variability on 8B models than on 70B and 405B [31].
  • Speculative decoding. A small draft model proposes tokens and the large model verifies them. The original method gave 2x to 3x acceleration on T5-XXL with identical outputs and no retraining [33]. EAGLE-3 reports speedup ratios up to 6.5x, but a 1.38x throughput gain in SGLang at batch size 64 [34]. NVIDIA measured 3.55x for Llama 3.3 70B with a 1B draft on one H200, at batch size 1 [35]. The pattern is consistent: speculative decoding is a latency lever that shrinks as batches grow.
  • Faster constrained decoding. SGLang's compressed finite state machine decodes several tokens at once when the schema allows only one path, and reported up to 2x lower latency and 2.5x higher throughput for JSON decoding [36].

Self-hosting versus API: the break-even

The economics of self-hosting reduce to one variable most teams underestimate: utilisation.

cost per 1M output tokens = P_gpu_hour / (T * 3600 * u / 1,000,000)

break-even utilisation u* = P_gpu_hour / (T * 3600 / 1,000,000 * P_api_per_1M)

P_gpu_hour   price of the GPU (or node) per hour
T            sustained output tokens per second at your latency SLO
u            fraction of hours the GPU actually serves at that rate
P_api_per_1M managed API price per 1M output tokens for an equivalent model

T should be measured at the concurrency where your p95 latency still meets the SLO, not at peak throughput, because the throughput curve flattens while latency keeps rising [17].

Illustrative calculation, with assumptions. Scaleway lists a single H100 PCIe 80 GB instance in Paris at €2.52 per hour, rising to €2.73 per hour from 1 July [37]. For comparison, Lambda lists $4.59 per GPU hour for an HGX H100 effective 16 November 2026 [38]. Assume €2.73 per hour and an assumed sustained throughput of 1,500 output tokens per second for an open-weight model at your SLO (measure this; it varies widely by model, quantization, prompt length and engine).

At 100% utilisation that GPU produces 5.4 million output tokens per hour, or about €0.51 per million. At 30% utilisation the same GPU costs about €1.69 per million. A managed EU option, STACKIT AI Model Serving, lists gpt-oss-120b and Llama 3.3 70B Instruct FP8 at €0.65 per million output tokens [39]. Under these assumptions, u* is about 78%: the GPU must stay busy 78% of all hours just to match the managed price, before you pay for engineering time, on-call, monitoring, model updates and a second GPU for redundancy (which halves utilisation per GPU at the same traffic). Note also that this simple formula charges everything to output tokens; long prompts consume GPU time for prefill as well.

Self-hosting is easiest to justify when traffic is high and steady, the model is small or fine-tuned for one task, or data rules exclude third-party APIs. For spiky or low-volume traffic, run the same formula against a managed endpoint plus batch tiers before buying GPU hours.

EU and GDPR-relevant hosting options

Data residency is not GDPR compliance: you still need a data processing agreement, a lawful basis, retention rules and transfer assessments. Residency narrows where prompts are processed and stored, which simplifies reviews. Documented options include:

  • OpenAI API with European data residency. Announced on 5 February 2025: eligible customers create a new Project with Europe selected as the region, requests are handled in-region with zero data retention, and existing Projects cannot be converted [40]. Regional processing carries a 10% uplift for models released on or after 5 March 2026 [2].
  • Azure OpenAI Data Zone deployments. Data Zone EU processes data only within the Microsoft-defined zone, which follows the EU Data Boundary and can include EFTA countries such as Norway and Switzerland; data at rest stays in the designated Azure geography; Data Zone Batch gives 50% savings [12].
  • Amazon Bedrock geographic cross-region inference. Requests to a geography-bound profile such as EU stay within that geography, but prompts and outputs can move between Regions inside it, and data stored for abuse detection is stored in the destination Region [41].
  • Anthropic's first-party API. The pricing page documents inference_geo with a US-only option at 1.1x and global routing as the default [3]. If you need EU-only processing for Claude models, check the cloud-provider routes above and confirm the details with your provider.
  • European providers. STACKIT AI Model Serving offers open-weight models in its EU01 region with euro token pricing, and states that data and queries are neither stored nor used to train models [39]. Scaleway rents H100 GPUs in a Paris data centre for self-hosting [37].

Put the residency multiplier into m_region in your cost formula, and keep your own logs residency-aware too: if your cost logger stores prompt text in a US-hosted observability tool, the API region no longer matters much.

Checklist: a recipe for cost per finished task

  1. Define "finished" per task type. Write down the validation rule (schema valid, business checks pass, human accepted) that turns an attempt into a success.
  2. Log per task, not per call. Use the fields above: tokens by category, reasoning tokens, calls, attempts, success, cost, TTFT and wall time. No prompt text in metrics.
  3. Compute the baseline. Cost per finished task, success rate, p50 and p95 wall time, cache hit ratio and output-to-input token ratio for each task type.
  4. Bound the loop. Set a task-level token and step budget in the orchestrator, because per-request max_tokens does not bound an agent loop [10].
  5. Tune reasoning effort on your eval set. Pick the lowest level that holds quality.
  6. Use strict structured outputs wherever the result is parsed by code.
  7. Fix prompt layout for caching. Static first, dynamic last, stable tool sets and settings. Alert on cache hit ratio drops.
  8. Move async work to batch or flex. Anything that can wait minutes or hours.
  9. Add exact-match response caching for repeated inputs; use semantic caching only with measured false-hit rates.
  10. Test a router or cascade against the formula, including the cost and latency of escalations.
  11. Consider distillation for stable, high-volume narrow tasks, and compute the payback volume.
  12. Self-host only after the break-even math, using throughput measured at your SLO and realistic utilisation, including redundancy and people.
  13. Choose hosting by data rules first, then add the residency multiplier to the cost model.
  14. Re-run the numbers monthly. Prices and models change fast [1]; yesterday's cheapest route may not be today's.

The price per token is an input to your cost model, not the output. Measure the task, and the right model, tier and hosting choice usually becomes clear from your own data.

title: Why Disabling the Submit Button Isn't Enough: Preventing Duplicate Requests in React & Node.js
description:
Imagine this scenario:

A customer clicks Place Order.

The request reaches your server, the database successfully creates the order, but the response never reaches the browser because of a network issue.

The customer assumes something went wrong and clicks again.

Now you have two orders instead of one.

This is a common reliability problem in web applications.

Disabling a submit button might prevent accidental double-clicks, but it doesn't guarantee that an operation will execute only once.

Let's explore how to handle this properly using React, Node.js, and PostgreSQL.

1. Frontend protection is only the first layer

In React, we often prevent repeated submissions using a loading state:

const [isSubmitting, setIsSubmitting] = useState(false);

async function handleSubmit() {
  if (isSubmitting) return;

  setIsSubmitting(true);

  try {
    await createOrder();
  } finally {
    setIsSubmitting(false);
  }
}

This is useful for improving the user experience.

But there is a problem.

Duplicate requests can still happen because of:

  • Network retries
  • Multiple browser tabs
  • Concurrent API calls
  • Repeated webhook deliveries
  • Client or server failures

Even rapid calls within the same render cycle can observe the same React state before an update takes effect.

The important lesson: frontend protection improves UX, but backend protection ensures data integrity.

2. Understanding idempotency

An operation is idempotent when performing it multiple times has the same intended effect as performing it once.

For example:

POST /api/orders
Idempotency-Key: order-abc-123

If the same request is submitted again with the same idempotency key, the server should recognize that the operation has already been processed.

Instead of creating a new order, it can return the result of the original operation.

This is particularly important for:

  • Order creation
  • Payment processing
  • Subscription activation
  • Inventory adjustments
  • Financial transactions

3. Implementing idempotency in React

We can generate a unique idempotency key using the browser's built-in Web Crypto API.

import { useRef } from "react";

function OrderForm() {
  const idempotencyKeyRef = useRef(null);

  async function createOrder(order) {
    // Generate once for this intended operation.
    if (!idempotencyKeyRef.current) {
      idempotencyKeyRef.current = crypto.randomUUID();
    }

    const response = await fetch("/api/orders", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKeyRef.current,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(order),
    });

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error("Order request failed");
    }

    return response.json();
  }

  // Use createOrder in your submission flow.
}

The key detail is that the same idempotency key must be reused when retrying the same intended operation.

Generate a new key only when the user starts a genuinely new order.

In a real application, you may need to persist the key beyond the component lifecycle if an unfinished operation must survive a page refresh.

4. Protecting the database against duplicate inserts

Frontend protection and idempotency middleware are useful, but concurrent requests can still introduce race conditions if the database isn't protected.

Consider this backend logic:

const existingOrder = await findOrder(key);

if (!existingOrder) {
  await createOrder(data);
}

Looks fine, right?

Not necessarily.

Two requests can execute simultaneously:

Request A                  Request B
    |                          |
Check existing order       Check existing order
    |                          |
Not found                  Not found
    |                          |
Create order               Create order
    |                          |
Success                    Success

Both requests can pass the check before either creates the record.

This is a classic check-then-insert race condition.

A better approach: Database uniqueness constraints

In PostgreSQL, enforce uniqueness at the database level.

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX unique_order_request
ON orders (user_id, idempotency_key);

This assumes your orders table contains the corresponding columns.

Now use PostgreSQL's ON CONFLICT functionality:

INSERT INTO orders (
  user_id,
  idempotency_key,
  product_id,
  quantity,
  request_hash
)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5)
ON CONFLICT (user_id, idempotency_key)
DO NOTHING
RETURNING id;

If the insert succeeds, the query returns the new order ID.

If another request already used the same key, PostgreSQL prevents a duplicate insert.

The backend can then retrieve the existing order.

One additional safeguard is important: compare the stored request hash with the incoming request's hash.

If the same idempotency key is reused with different order parameters, return a conflict response instead of silently accepting the changed request.

Database constraints provide protection that application-level checks alone cannot guarantee.

5. What about transactions?

Preventing duplicate orders is only part of the problem.

Creating an order might involve multiple operations:

  1. Create the order.
  2. Reserve inventory.
  3. Update related database records.
  4. Record the transaction.
  5. Send a notification.

If one operation fails halfway through, the system can end up in an inconsistent state.

Database transactions help ensure that related database modifications succeed or fail together.

However, external operations such as sending emails or publishing messages are not automatically rolled back with a database transaction.

For these cases, patterns such as the transactional outbox and idempotent event consumers can improve reliability.

This is an important distinction when designing systems that interact with external services.

6. Test real failure scenarios

A feature working during normal testing doesn't necessarily mean it is reliable under failure conditions.

Here are five scenarios worth testing:

Scenario Expected behavior
Two concurrent requests with the same key Only one order is created
Retry after the original request commits Existing order is returned
Same key with different request data Request is rejected
Failed database transaction No partial order is committed
Two legitimate operations with different keys Both can proceed

These tests provide more confidence than simply checking whether a submit button becomes disabled.

7. The approach I recommend

For reliable applications, multiple layers should work together:

Frontend safeguards improve the user experience and discourage accidental repeated submissions.

Backend idempotency identifies repeated attempts to perform the same operation.

Database constraints protect against duplicate inserts, including concurrent requests.

Transactions and carefully designed side effects help maintain consistency across the entire workflow.

No single layer solves every problem.

The goal isn't just to make an API request succeed.

It's to make sure retries, failures, and concurrent requests don't produce unintended results.

Final thoughts

Building reliable software requires thinking beyond the happy path.

A submit button can be disabled. A network request can fail. A server can process the same operation more than once.

The application should still behave predictably.

A combination of frontend safeguards, idempotency, database constraints, and transaction handling is generally more reliable than depending on any one of them.

What's your approach to preventing duplicate requests in production applications?

Further reading: PostgreSQL INSERT / ON CONFLICT documentation

title: An Empirical Analysis of Static Analysis Methods for Detection and Mitigation of Code Library Hallucinations
description:
arXiv:2604.07755v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Despite extensive research, Large Language Models continue to hallucinate when generating code, particularly when using libraries. On NL-to-code benchmarks that require library use, we find that LLMs generate code that uses non-existent library features in 8.1-40% of responses. One intuitive approach for detection and mitigation of hallucinations is static analysis. In this paper, we analyse the potential of static analysis tools, both in terms of what they can solve and what they cannot. We find that static analysis tools can detect 16-70% of all errors, and 14-85% of library hallucinations, with performance varying by LLM and dataset. Through manual analysis, we identify cases a static method could not plausibly catch, which gives an upper bound on their potential from 48.5% to 77%. Overall, we show that static analysis methods are cheap method for addressing some forms of hallucination, and we quantify how far short of solving the problem they will always be.

title: Can LLMs Take Retrieved Information with a Grain of Salt?
description:
arXiv:2605.06919v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models have demonstrated impressive retrieval-augmented capabilities. However, a crucial area remains underexplored: their ability to appropriately adapt responses to the certainty of the retrieved information. It is a limitation with real consequences in high-stakes domains like medicine and finance. We evaluate eight LLMs on their context-certainty obedience, measuring how well they adjust responses to match expressed context certainty. Our analysis reveals systematic limitations: LLMs fail to reproduce their prior outputs after observing an uncertain context, respond to expressed certainties in a distorted way, and overrely on complex contexts. To address these, we propose an interaction strategy combining prior reminders (feeding the model's own context-free answer back into the prompt), context-certainty recalibration, and context simplification. This approach reduces obedience errors by 25% on average, without modifying model weights, demonstrating the efficacy of interaction design in enhancing LLM reliability. Our contributions include a principled evaluation metric, empirical insights into LLMs' uncertainty handling, and a portable strategy to improve context-certainty obedience across diverse LLMs.

title: Fail closed on clipboard paste banners, keyboards, and watch companion remotes
description:
When narrative content drives a physical actuator, three interrupt paths look like "just restore state" until they are not: an Allow Paste / clipboard-permission banner mid-session, a software keyboard / QuickType / dictation / emoji-sticker picker, and a watch companion / Wear OS remote or complication tap. Each needs a default that fails closed — toward idle, toward re-arm only after a named beat, toward interrupt-clear ≠ motor authority.

on clipboard_paste_permission_banner_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on banner_dismissed():
        # permission UI gone ≠ motor envelope restored
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

on software_keyboard_dictation_or_emoji_picker_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on input_ui_dismissed():
        # keyboard/dictation/emoji UI cleared ≠ motor authority
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

on watch_companion_remote_or_complication_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on remote_ended():
        # companion UI gone ≠ previous intensity restored
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

The clipboard paste-permission rule is easy to mix up with Autofill / Passkeys, outbound Share Sheet, Photos / Files picker, and Contacts / Calendar picker. Autofill is credentials. Share Sheet is outbound sharing. Photos / Files is a media-or-docs chooser. Contacts / Calendar is a people-or-event chooser. An Allow Paste banner is a paste-consent prompt. Dismissing it clears that prompt; it must not restore motor authority.

The keyboard / dictation / emoji rule sits next to — but is not — Translate / Look Up / Live Text, Spotlight / system search, a voice-assistant takeover, or Autofill / Passkeys. Translate / Look Up is text understanding. Spotlight is search. A voice assistant takes over the session. Autofill is credentials. A software keyboard is an input surface. Dismiss only clears that surface; it must not restore motor authority.

The watch-companion rule is a wearable remote control surface, not CarPlay / Android Auto, not Handoff / Continuity, not a Live Activity / Dynamic Island, and not an AirDrop receive. CarPlay is projection. Handoff is Continuity. Live Activity is a phone-side glance. AirDrop is a receive path. A watch remote is a companion control. Ending it only clears that control; it must not restore motor authority.

Buyers can test all three without code: trigger an Allow Paste banner mid-session and see whether dismissing it restarts intensity, open the software keyboard or an emoji picker then dismiss, and fire a watch complication / Wear OS tile remote then end it. These map to questions like "how do AI stories control physical devices" and "Lovense alternative with AI stories."

This is the model CRAVE AI uses for story-controlled play on official devices: AI story-controlled vibrator. Principle write-up: narrative-to-device sync. Devices: AI sex toys.

Disclosure: I work on CRAVE AI. Adults-only product; no explicit content here.

title: How I built a responsive landing page with animated cards in HTML, CSS and JavaScript
description:
I wanted to practice building a landing page from scratch without a template, so I made a dark-themed sports page with tilted cards, a responsive navigation bar, and simple hover animations. Here is how I put it together.

The goal

The page needed three sections, each with a title, a short description, and a call-to-action button. The main challenge was making the cards look dynamic on desktop without breaking the layout on phones.

Structure

I kept the HTML simple: a header with navigation, a main section with a grid of cards, and a footer. Each card is a div with a heading, a short paragraph, and a button.

html

<h2>Train in the gym</h2>
<p>Strength, volume and definition routines for every level.</p>
<a href="#">View routines</a>

Responsive layout

I used CSS Grid for the cards, so they stack on small screens and sit side by side on larger ones:

css

.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr));
  gap: 2rem;
}

Hover animation with JavaScript

For the interactive part, I used a small script that adds a class when the mouse enters a card. The CSS handles the actual movement, which keeps the JavaScript light:

javascript

document.querySelectorAll('.card').forEach(card => {
card.addEventListener('mouseenter', () => card.classList.add('active'));
card.addEventListener('mouseleave', () => card.classList.remove('active'));
});
What I learned

Keeping the CSS and JavaScript separate made the page easier to debug. Animations feel better when they are subtle, and responsive design is easier to test if you check the layout at each breakpoint while you build, not at the end.

I also offer landing pages and simple interactive websites as a freelancer. If you need one for your business or community, you can see my services here: https://www.fiverr.com/s/2pQdqBq

title: How Interfaze serves 50 million requests a month on Vercel
description:
Interfaze on Vercel

  • 50 million requests a month

  • Backend running on Fluid compute

  • Multiple model providers behind one fallback layer with AI Gateway

Interfaze builds models for deterministic work that general-purpose LLMs handle poorly: document processing, OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification.

As founder Yoeven Khemlani puts it, "Most models aren't deterministic by nature. That's fine when you're drafting an essay. But when a hospital or a legal team needs to process documents, you don't reach for an LLM." Ask an LLM for the total on an invoice and you get a number with no easy way to check where it came from. Interfaze's models return the number along with a bounding box showing where on the page it came from and a confidence score for how sure the model is. Every result can be checked, and the models still take prompts the way an LLM does.

Everything around Interfaze's models runs on Vercel, including the backend. That spans the API serving 50 million requests a month, the sandbox that executes code the model writes, and the routing that keeps data preprocessing running when a third-party model provider goes down.

The backend required no infrastructure work

Interfaze's frontend and backend both run on Vercel. The backend handles every request to Interfaze's API, whether a customer is calling the model or uploading a file. All of it runs as serverless functions in the same codebase as the frontend. When a request needs computation, the model hands the code to Vercel Sandbox, which runs it in isolation. There was no separate infrastructure to set up.

Fluid compute handles the heavy jobs

Scalability was Yoeven's top requirement. The goal is serving the model to millions of users, and Fluid compute scales with traffic on its own. Heavier work runs there too. Vercel's memory and timeout limits are high enough that Interfaze's web scraping, which runs on Puppeteer, works out of the box.

AI Gateway makes model routing reliable at scale

Interfaze pushes large volumes of data cleaning through open source models hosted by third-party providers. A single provider is a weak link. Providers hit rate limits or go down, and when one does, the cleaning stops unless traffic moves somewhere else.

The providers are also not interchangeable. Two of them can claim to host the same open source model and serve it at very different quality.

When a provider fails or throttles, AI Gateway fails requests over to the next provider automatically. It also lets Interfaze choose which provider serves a given model, so the team can run the same workload through each one, see which performs well, and send traffic there.

Workflow SDK runs email sequences over months

Interfaze runs its lifecycle email system on the Workflow SDK, with sends conditioned on product usage. The system tracks which API a customer called, at what volume, and how that compares against their first week. Retries are handled automatically, so one failed step doesn't take down the sequence.

The part Interfaze needed most was durable execution. A workflow can pause a step and pick it back up months later with its state intact, which the team found other systems could not do for long.

Preview deployments carry new model versions to customers

Interfaze runs more than one version of its model at a time, each at its own URL. When an error comes in, the team has to know which version produced the error before they can fix anything. On Vercel every URL is its own deployment with its own logs, so the error is already filed under the version that caused it. There was no separate logging vendor to set up.

Those same preview URLs are how a new model version gets to customers before it ships. The Vercel side of a release builds in about three minutes. Hosting the weights on GPUs is the slow part.

What's next

Interfaze recently released Interfaze 1 Lite, an open-weight version of its model that runs on a single GPU and is served through the same API. Next is a gateway for web search, one API that routes to whichever search provider a developer picks, the way AI Gateway does for models. It launches on the same Vercel backend as everything else.

About Interfaze: Interfaze builds models for deterministic tasks, including OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification. Its customers are engineering teams in legal, healthcare, and finance.

title: HiFlow: Hierarchical Feedback-Driven Optimization for Constrained Long-Form Text Generation
description:
arXiv:2603.04996v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Models face a multi-objective optimization problem in constrained long-text generation, balancing global structure, local coherence, and constraint satisfaction. We propose LoopWeaver, a hierarchical workflow with two sequential offline preference-optimization stages. Constraint-aware planning produces structured plans, feasibility filtering removes invalid plans, and a shared deterministic reward constructs preference pairs for plan-level and generation-level DPO. At inference time, LoopWeaver remains feed-forward: it generates and revises a complete plan, filters the revised plan, and then generates segments conditioned on the current sub-plan and running narrative. We evaluate the method on four LongGenBench-style structured scenarios across multiple backbones. Results show improvements in both constraint accuracy and text quality across all four open-source backbones. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/cgtaa-cmyk/LoopWeaver.

title: AI Agent Memory Explained: Multi-Tier Architecture, Vector Stores & Long-Term State
description:
AI Agent Memory Explained: Multi-Tier Architecture, Vector Stores & Long-Term State

AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of handling complex tasks, interacting with external tools, coordinating with other agents, and making decisions autonomously. However, there is one major limitation developers must solve before deploying intelligent agents in production: memory.

Imagine interacting with an AI assistant that remembers your programming language preferences, understands the context of your previous projects, recalls decisions made during earlier conversations, and continues working without asking you to explain everything again.

Without memory, an AI agent starts almost every interaction with limited context. It may forget previous instructions, repeat completed tasks, lose important information, or make decisions without considering historical events.

This is where AI Agent Memory Architecture becomes important.

Memory allows AI agents to retain information, retrieve relevant knowledge, maintain conversational context, and build persistent state across multiple interactions.

Modern AI memory systems combine several technologies:

  • Short-term conversational memory.
  • Long-term persistent memory.
  • Vector databases and semantic search.
  • Structured databases and key-value stores.
  • Knowledge graphs.
  • Memory retrieval and summarization.
  • Memory expiration and lifecycle management.

In this article, we will explore how AI agent memory works, how multi-tier memory architectures are designed, how vector stores support long-term knowledge retrieval, and how to build reliable memory systems for production AI applications.

If you are exploring AI agents, LLM application development, and modern system architecture, explore more technical guides at DevsCampus.

1. What Is AI Agent Memory?

AI agent memory is the mechanism that allows an AI system to store, retrieve, update, and use information from previous interactions or experiences.

A traditional Large Language Model (LLM) processes a request using the context provided in its current input. Although some models support large context windows, this does not automatically mean they have persistent memory.

For example, consider this conversation:

User:
I am building a data engineering platform using Scala, Apache Spark, and Kafka.

AI Agent:
Understood. I can help you with Spark jobs, Kafka streaming, and Scala development.

Later:

User:
How should I optimize my streaming application?

An AI agent with memory can retrieve the previous information and provide recommendations based on the user's technology stack.

An agent without memory might provide generic recommendations without knowing which technologies the user is using.

AI Agent Memory vs. LLM Context Window

These concepts are related but different.

Feature LLM Context Window AI Agent Memory
Purpose Holds information for current processing Retains useful information over time
Lifetime Usually limited to a request or conversation context Can persist across sessions
Storage Model input context Database, files, vector stores, or application state
Retrieval Directly included in model input Retrieved based on relevance or identifiers
Scalability Limited by model context capacity Can scale independently
Data management Context construction Storage, retrieval, updates, and expiration

The context window determines how much information a model can process at once.

Memory determines what information an agent can retain and retrieve when needed.

A production AI system often uses both.

2. Why Do AI Agents Need Memory?

Without memory, AI agents face several practical problems.

2.1 Loss of Conversational Context

Consider an AI coding assistant.

During one session, a developer explains the application's architecture, programming language, database, and deployment environment.

After restarting the session, the agent may lose access to this information.

The developer must explain the same details again.

Persistent memory solves this problem by storing relevant information outside the LLM context window.

2.2 Repeating Previous Tasks

An AI agent may repeatedly suggest solutions that have already been implemented.

For example:

  • A developer already migrated a service to Java 21.
  • The agent recommends migrating from Java 17.
  • The developer explains that the migration is complete.
  • The agent forgets this information in a later session.

With persistent memory, the agent can retrieve previous decisions and avoid repeating outdated recommendations.

2.3 Personalized Responses

Memory allows agents to adapt their responses based on historical information.

Examples include:

  • Remembering a user's preferred programming language.
  • Understanding previous project requirements.
  • Retaining preferred response formats.
  • Remembering previously selected tools.
  • Tracking progress on long-running tasks.

2.4 Long-Running Autonomous Tasks

Some AI agents perform tasks that take hours, days, or even weeks.

Examples:

  • Research agents.
  • Software development agents.
  • Business automation agents.
  • Monitoring agents.
  • Multi-agent workflow systems.

These systems need persistent state to understand what has already happened and what should happen next.

For a deeper understanding of how multiple AI agents coordinate their tasks, read AI Agent Orchestration Explained: Multi-Agent Systems, Topologies & System Design on DevsCampus.

3. Types of AI Agent Memory

AI agent memory is commonly divided into different categories based on how information is stored and used.

The most important categories are:

  1. Working memory.
  2. Short-term memory.
  3. Episodic memory.
  4. Semantic memory.
  5. Procedural memory.
  6. Long-term memory.

Let's understand each one.

3.1 Working Memory

Working memory contains the information an agent needs to complete its current task.

It is similar to the temporary working area of a computer program.

For example, suppose an agent is debugging a Spark application.

Its working memory might contain:

{
  "task": "Debug Spark streaming application",
  "language": "Scala",
  "framework": "Apache Spark",
  "streaming_source": "Kafka",
  "current_issue": "Consumer lag increasing",
  "current_step": "Analyze partition distribution"
}

This information helps the agent make decisions during the current execution.

Working memory is usually temporary and may be discarded after the task completes.

3.2 Short-Term Memory

Short-term memory stores recent conversational information.

For example:

User: I am using PostgreSQL.
Agent: Which version?
User: PostgreSQL 16.
Agent: What is the issue?
User: Queries are becoming slow.

The agent retains this information so it can understand follow-up questions.

Short-term memory is generally maintained through:

  • Recent conversation history.
  • Message buffers.
  • Context summaries.
  • Session storage.
  • Redis or other temporary storage systems.

Short-term memory is useful when an agent needs to maintain continuity during an active conversation.

3.3 Episodic Memory

Episodic memory stores information about previous experiences and events.

Instead of simply remembering facts, it remembers what happened.

For example:

{
  "event_id": "event-102",
  "event": "Spark job deployment failed",
  "environment": "preprod",
  "cause": "Insufficient executor memory",
  "resolution": "Increased executor memory",
  "timestamp": "2026-11-10T09:30:00Z"
}

Later, when the agent encounters a similar deployment failure, it can retrieve this previous experience.

Episodic memory is particularly useful for:

  • Debugging agents.
  • Autonomous software engineering agents.
  • Incident management agents.
  • Research assistants.
  • Workflow automation systems.

3.4 Semantic Memory

Semantic memory stores general facts, concepts, and knowledge.

Unlike episodic memory, it does not necessarily represent a specific event.

Example:

{
  "technology": "Apache Kafka",
  "concept": "Consumer Group",
  "description": "A group of consumers that coordinate to consume partitions from Kafka topics."
}

Semantic memory helps agents understand relationships between concepts and retrieve useful knowledge.

It can contain:

  • Technical documentation.
  • Business rules.
  • User preferences.
  • Project information.
  • Domain-specific knowledge.

Vector databases are frequently used to support semantic memory retrieval.

3.5 Procedural Memory

Procedural memory stores information about how to perform tasks.

For example, a software engineering agent might remember:

Procedure: Deploy a Spark application

1. Validate the Spark configuration.
2. Check executor resources.
3. Validate the Docker image.
4. Submit the SparkApplication resource.
5. Monitor the application status.
6. Inspect driver and executor logs.

Procedural memory is useful for agents that repeatedly perform structured workflows.

It can be implemented using workflow definitions, stored instructions, reusable tools, or structured procedures.

3.6 Long-Term Memory

Long-term memory stores information that should remain available beyond a single session.

Examples include:

  • User preferences.
  • Project architecture.
  • Previous decisions.
  • Frequently used procedures.
  • Historical incidents.
  • Important business rules.

Long-term memory may use multiple storage technologies depending on the information type.

Information Suitable Storage
Recent conversation Redis
User preferences PostgreSQL
Semantic knowledge Vector database
Historical events Document database
Entity relationships Graph database
Workflow state Relational database

The important point is that long-term memory is not necessarily one database.

It is a combination of storage and retrieval mechanisms.

4. Multi-Tier AI Agent Memory Architecture

A production AI agent should not store every piece of information in one memory system.

Different types of information have different access patterns, retention requirements, and retrieval needs.

This is why modern AI applications often use a multi-tier memory architecture.

A simplified architecture looks like this:

                  USER REQUEST
                       |
                       v
              +------------------+
              |    AI AGENT      |
              |  LLM / Reasoning |
              +------------------+
                       |
                       v
              +------------------+
              |  MEMORY MANAGER  |
              +------------------+
                       |
          +------------+------------+
          |            |            |
          v            v            v
    +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+
    | Working   | | Short-Term| | Long-Term |
    | Memory    | | Memory    | | Memory    |
    +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+
          |            |            |
          v            v            v
    Current Task    Redis       Persistent DB
    State           Session     Vector Store
                                Graph Store
                                     |
                                     v
                              Memory Retrieval
                                     |
                                     v
                              Relevant Context
                                     |
                                     v
                                LLM Response

Let's understand the different tiers.

Tier 1: Working Memory

Purpose: Maintain the state of the current task.

Typical technologies:

  • In-memory objects.
  • Application state.
  • Agent framework state.
  • Temporary execution context.

Example:

{
  "task_id": "task-1001",
  "current_step": "analyze_logs",
  "status": "running",
  "attempt": 2
}

Tier 2: Short-Term Memory

Purpose: Maintain recent conversation history.

Typical technologies:

  • Redis.
  • Session databases.
  • Conversation message stores.

Example Redis key:

agent:session:1001

Stored value:

{
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": "Explain Kafka consumer lag."
    },
    {
      "role": "assistant",
      "content": "Consumer lag measures..."
    }
  ]
}

Redis provides low-latency access to frequently used session information.

Tier 3: Long-Term Memory

Purpose: Retain useful information across sessions.

Typical technologies:

  • PostgreSQL.
  • MongoDB.
  • Vector databases.
  • Knowledge graphs.
  • Object storage.

Example:

{
  "user_id": "user-100",
  "memory_type": "preference",
  "content": "Prefers Scala examples for Spark applications.",
  "importance": 0.95
}

The agent can retrieve this information during future conversations.

Tier 4: Knowledge and Experience Memory

Some architectures introduce another logical tier for larger knowledge collections and historical experiences.

It may contain:

  • Technical documentation.
  • Previous debugging experiences.
  • Business knowledge.
  • Completed workflow histories.
  • Relationships between entities.

This tier is especially useful for enterprise AI systems.

Important: These tiers are logical architectural boundaries, not mandatory separate databases. A system can implement several tiers using the same database technology.

Related Reading: Understanding AI Agent Architecture

Memory is only one component of a complete AI agent architecture. An autonomous agent also needs orchestration, tool execution, decision-making, and state management.

Explore these related DevsCampus guides:

  • AI Agent Orchestration Explained: Multi-Agent Systems, Topologies & System Design – Understand Supervisor-Worker architectures, multi-agent communication, workflow coordination, and shared state management.
  • How AI Agents Use Tools: Complete Architecture & Implementation Guide – Learn how agents interact with external APIs, databases, execution environments, and other tools.

These concepts are closely connected because an orchestrated AI system needs reliable memory to coordinate multiple agents and maintain state throughout complex workflows.

5. How Vector Databases Power AI Agent Memory

One of the most important technologies behind modern AI memory systems is the vector database.

Traditional databases retrieve information using exact conditions.

For example:

SELECT *
FROM memories
WHERE user_id = 'user-100';

However, AI agents frequently need to retrieve information based on meaning rather than exact words.

Consider these two sentences:

  1. "My Spark application is running slowly."
  2. "The distributed processing job has high execution latency."

Although the wording differs, both sentences describe similar concepts.

Traditional keyword searches may not identify their semantic similarity.

Vector search helps solve this problem.

5.1 What Are Embeddings?

An embedding is a numerical representation of text, images, or other data.

An embedding model converts text into a vector containing numerical values.

For example:

Input:
"Apache Spark streaming optimization"

The embedding model produces something like:

[0.21, -0.43, 0.87, 0.12, -0.56, ...]

The actual vector may contain hundreds or thousands of dimensions, depending on the embedding model.

Texts with similar meanings tend to have nearby vector representations.

5.2 How Vector Search Works

The basic workflow is:

        USER CONVERSATION
               |
               v
        MEMORY EXTRACTION
               |
               v
        TEXT EMBEDDING
               |
               v
        VECTOR DATABASE
               |
               v
        SEMANTIC RETRIEVAL
               |
               v
        RELEVANT MEMORIES
               |
               v
        LLM CONTEXT

Let's walk through an example.

Suppose an agent stores the following memory:

User is building a streaming data platform
using Scala, Apache Spark and Kafka.

The system generates an embedding and stores it in a vector database.

Later, the user asks:

How can I reduce processing delays in my application?

The retrieval system converts this question into an embedding.

It searches for similar stored vectors and retrieves relevant memories.

The agent then understands that the user is probably referring to their Spark and Kafka streaming application.

This is called semantic retrieval.

5.3 Similarity Search

Vector databases commonly support similarity metrics such as:

Cosine Similarity

Measures the angle between two vectors.

[
CosineSimilarity(A,B) =
\frac{A \cdot B}{||A|| \times ||B||}
]

Euclidean Distance

Measures the straight-line distance between two vectors.

[
Distance(A,B) =
\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(A_i-B_i)^2}
]

Dot Product

Measures the product of corresponding vector dimensions.

The appropriate metric depends on the embedding model and how its vectors are normalized.

5.4 Popular Vector Database Technologies

Some commonly used technologies include:

Pinecone

Managed vector database designed for similarity search and retrieval applications.

Weaviate

Open-source vector database supporting semantic search and hybrid retrieval.

Milvus

Distributed vector database designed for large-scale vector search.

Qdrant

Vector database providing similarity search, metadata filtering, and efficient retrieval.

Chroma

Developer-friendly vector database commonly used in prototypes and smaller AI applications.

pgvector

PostgreSQL extension that enables vector storage and similarity search inside PostgreSQL.

For applications already using PostgreSQL, pgvector can be a practical starting point because it avoids introducing a separate vector database immediately.

Vector databases are fundamental to semantic memory because they allow AI agents to retrieve information based on meaning rather than exact keyword matches.
