6. Implementing AI Agent Memory Using Python and Vector Stores

Let's understand a simplified implementation using Python, embeddings, and Chroma.

First, install the dependencies:

pip install chromadb sentence-transformers

Create a vector database:

import chromadb
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

client = chromadb.PersistentClient(
    path="./agent_memory"
)

collection = client.get_or_create_collection(
    name="long_term_memory"
)

model = SentenceTransformer(
    "all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
)

Step 1: Store a Memory 

def store_memory(memory_id, text, user_id):

    embedding = model.encode(text).tolist()

    collection.add(
        ids=[memory_id],
        documents=[text],
        embeddings=[embedding],
        metadatas=[
            {
                "user_id": user_id,
                "memory_type": "long_term"
            }
        ]
    )

Store a memory:

store_memory(
    "memory-001",
    "The user develops applications using Scala, Spark and Kafka.",
    "user-100"
)

The system generates an embedding and stores the text alongside its metadata.

Step 2: Retrieve Relevant Memories 

def retrieve_memory(query, user_id):

    query_embedding = model.encode(query).tolist()

    results = collection.query(
        query_embeddings=[query_embedding],
        n_results=5,
        where={
            "user_id": user_id
        }
    )

    return results["documents"]

Example:

memories = retrieve_memory(
    "How can I optimize my streaming application?",
    "user-100"
)

print(memories)

The vector database searches for semantically similar memories belonging to the requested user.

Step 3: Add Retrieved Memory to the LLM Context 

def build_agent_context(user_query, memories):

    memory_context = "\n".join(
        memory
        for group in memories
        for memory in group
    )

    return f"""
    Relevant Previous Memories:

    {memory_context}

    Current User Request:

    {user_query}

    Use relevant memories to provide a contextual response.
    """

Now the application can pass the generated context to an LLM.

This is a simplified example. A production implementation also needs memory deduplication, update operations, access control, expiration policies, retrieval ranking, and error handling.

7. Memory Retrieval Strategies

Storing information is only one part of memory architecture.

The system must also decide which memories should be retrieved for a particular request.

Retrieving everything is expensive and can introduce irrelevant information into the LLM context.

Here are common retrieval strategies.

7.1 Semantic Retrieval

Retrieves memories based on vector similarity.

Example:

Query:
How do I improve Kafka throughput?

Retrieved memory:
The user operates a Kafka-based streaming platform.

This is useful when the wording of the current request differs from the stored information.

7.2 Metadata Filtering

Metadata filtering restricts searches based on attributes.

For example:

{
  "user_id": "user-100",
  "memory_type": "technical_preference",
  "project": "streaming-platform"
}

The system can retrieve only memories belonging to a particular user, project, or category.

This is particularly important in multi-tenant applications.

7.3 Hybrid Search

Hybrid search combines:

  • Keyword-based retrieval.
  • Vector-based semantic retrieval.

Consider a query:

Why did Spark job PIPE-4821 fail?

The exact identifier PIPE-4821 is important.

Vector search alone may not retrieve the exact record reliably.

Keyword search can find the identifier, while semantic search can retrieve related debugging information.

Combining both improves retrieval quality.

7.4 Recency-Based Retrieval

Some information becomes outdated.

For example:

Previous environment:
Java 17

Later:

Current environment:
Java 21

A memory system should consider timestamps and update previous information rather than blindly returning outdated facts.

7.5 Importance-Based Retrieval

Not all memories have equal value.

For example:

Memory Importance
Preferred programming language High
Current project architecture High
Temporary debugging observation Medium
One-time greeting Low

A retrieval system can assign importance scores and use them alongside semantic similarity.

A simplified ranking formula could be:

[
Score =
\alpha S +
\beta R +
\gamma I
]

Where:

  • S = Semantic similarity.
  • R = Recency score.
  • I = Importance score.
  • α, β, γ = Configurable weights.

The weights should be tuned against real retrieval evaluations rather than selected arbitrarily.

8. Memory Consolidation: Turning Conversations into Long-Term Knowledge

Storing every conversation message as a permanent memory is a bad architectural decision.

It creates several problems:

  • Duplicate information.
  • Unnecessary storage growth.
  • Irrelevant retrieval results.
  • Outdated facts.
  • Higher embedding and retrieval costs.

Instead, production AI systems often use a process called memory consolidation.

Memory consolidation converts temporary conversational information into useful persistent knowledge.

Consider this conversation:

User: I am developing a backend service using Scala.

User: The service uses Apache Spark for processing.

User: Kafka is used for event streaming.

User: We deploy workloads on Kubernetes.

Rather than storing four independent memories, the system can consolidate them:

{
  "memory_type": "project_context",
  "content": "The user is developing a Scala backend platform using Apache Spark, Kafka and Kubernetes.",
  "importance": 0.95
}

A typical consolidation workflow looks like this:

         CONVERSATION HISTORY
                  |
                  v
           MEMORY EXTRACTION
                  |
                  v
           INFORMATION FILTER
                  |
                  v
           DUPLICATE DETECTION
                  |
                  v
           MEMORY CONSOLIDATION
                  |
                  v
           IMPORTANCE SCORING
                  |
                  v
           PERSISTENT STORAGE

Memory consolidation can run after each conversation, periodically, or when a particular event occurs.

The system should also preserve the source and timestamp of important memories so that conflicting information can be resolved.

9. Long-Term Memory and Database Architecture

A production AI application often needs multiple database technologies because different memory types have different storage requirements.

Consider this architecture:

                  AI AGENT
                      |
                      v
                MEMORY SERVICE
                      |
        +-------------+-------------+
        |             |             |
        v             v             v
      Redis       PostgreSQL    Vector DB
        |             |             |
        v             v             v
    Session       Structured     Embeddings
    History       Memories       Semantic Data
        |             |             |
        +-------------+-------------+
                      |
                      v
                MEMORY RETRIEVAL
                      |
                      v
                 LLM CONTEXT

Redis: Fast Session Memory

Redis is useful for:

  • Recent conversation history.
  • Active agent state.
  • Temporary task context.
  • Frequently accessed information.
  • Session expiration.

Example:

agent:session:user-100

A TTL can automatically expire session information after a configured period.

PostgreSQL: Structured Memory

PostgreSQL can store:

  • User preferences.
  • Project metadata.
  • Memory categories.
  • Historical decisions.
  • Memory ownership.
  • Timestamps and expiration information.

Example table:

CREATE TABLE agent_memories (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    memory_type VARCHAR(50),
    content TEXT NOT NULL,
    importance FLOAT,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

Vector Database: Semantic Memory

A vector database stores embeddings and associated metadata.

It allows the agent to retrieve information based on semantic similarity.

Graph Database: Relationship Memory

Some AI applications need to understand relationships between entities.

For example:

User
 |
 | works_on
 v
Data Platform
 |
 | uses
 +------> Apache Spark
 |
 +------> Apache Kafka
 |
 +------> Kubernetes

Graph databases can represent these relationships explicitly.

They are particularly useful for knowledge-intensive applications where connections between entities matter.

10. Memory Management Challenges in Production AI Systems

Building a memory-enabled agent is relatively straightforward.

Building a reliable production memory system is much more challenging.

10.1 Memory Explosion

If an agent stores every conversation indefinitely, memory storage grows continuously.

This increases:

  • Storage costs.
  • Embedding generation costs.
  • Retrieval latency.
  • Duplicate information.
  • Context construction overhead.

Solution:

Implement memory lifecycle policies.

Memory Type Retention Strategy
Working memory Until task completion
Session memory Session TTL
Temporary events Configurable expiration
User preferences Until updated or deleted
Important project knowledge Long-term retention
Historical incidents Based on business requirements

10.2 Stale Memories

An agent may retrieve outdated information.

For example, a user previously worked with Java 17 but migrated to Java 21.

If the memory system returns the old information, the agent may generate incorrect recommendations.

Solution:

Use:

  • Timestamps.
  • Versioned memories.
  • Update operations.
  • Expiration policies.
  • Conflict resolution.

10.3 Incorrect Memory Extraction

An LLM may misunderstand a conversation and save an incorrect fact.

For example:

User: We are considering migrating to PostgreSQL.

The system incorrectly stores:

User uses PostgreSQL in production.

These statements have different meanings.

Solution:

Use structured memory extraction with explicit categories such as:

  • Confirmed fact.
  • Planned change.
  • Temporary observation.
  • User preference.
  • Unverified assumption.

Important memories should be validated before being treated as authoritative.

10.4 Multi-Tenant Data Isolation

Enterprise AI platforms may serve thousands of users and organizations.

One user's memory must never be exposed to another user.

For example:

{
  "tenant_id": "tenant-001",
  "user_id": "user-100",
  "memory": "Internal project architecture"
}

Retrieval must enforce tenant and user authorization.

Do not depend only on the LLM to respect these boundaries.

The memory service and underlying database must enforce access control.

10.5 Privacy and Sensitive Information

Long-term memory introduces privacy risks.

An AI agent should not automatically retain every piece of information it encounters.

Production systems should implement:

  • Explicit memory consent where required.
  • Sensitive-data filtering.
  • Data minimization.
  • Encryption at rest and in transit.
  • Access control.
  • Memory deletion.
  • Audit logging.
  • Retention policies.

Memory deletion must cover all relevant representations, including database records, vector embeddings, caches, and derived summaries.

11. Advanced AI Agent Memory Patterns

Beyond basic storage and retrieval, modern AI systems use more advanced patterns.

11.1 Reflection-Based Memory

An agent can analyze its previous actions and identify useful lessons.

Example:

Task:
Deploy a Spark application.

Observation:
Deployment failed because executor memory was insufficient.

Reflection:
The configured executor memory was lower than the workload required.

Learned lesson:
Validate executor memory against workload requirements
before deployment.

The agent stores the lesson and can apply it to future tasks.

11.2 Hierarchical Memory

Instead of storing every detail at the same level, hierarchical memory organizes information into summaries and detailed records.

Example:

Company Knowledge
       |
       v
Engineering Projects
       |
       v
Streaming Platform
       |
       v
Kafka Configuration
       |
       v
Detailed Configuration Records

The agent can retrieve a high-level summary first and fetch detailed information when necessary.

This reduces unnecessary context consumption.

11.3 Shared Memory in Multi-Agent Systems

In multi-agent architectures, multiple agents may need access to shared knowledge.

For example:

             ORCHESTRATOR
                  |
        +---------+---------+
        |         |         |
        v         v         v
     Research   Coding    Testing
      Agent     Agent     Agent
        |         |         |
        +---------+---------+
                  |
                  v
             SHARED MEMORY
                  |
        +---------+---------+
        |         |         |
        v         v         v
      Redis   PostgreSQL  Vector DB

A research agent can store findings that a coding agent later retrieves.

Similarly, a testing agent can store test results that the orchestrator uses to decide the next action.

However, shared memory needs clear ownership, versioning, access control, and conflict-resolution rules.

11.4 Memory-Augmented RAG

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) retrieves relevant external knowledge and provides it to an LLM.

Memory-augmented RAG extends this concept by combining external knowledge with information from previous interactions.

For example:

Current User Query
        |
        v
  Retrieval Engine
        |
        +------------------+
        |                  |
        v                  v
 User Memory         Knowledge Base
        |                  |
        +------------------+
                 |
                 v
          Context Assembly
                 |
                 v
                 LLM
                 |
                 v
             Response

This allows an agent to combine personal context, historical experiences, and external documentation.

Related Architecture: How AI Agents Coordinate and Share Knowledge

In advanced AI systems, memory becomes particularly important when multiple agents collaborate.

For example, a research agent may collect information, a coding agent may implement a solution, and a testing agent may validate the result.

All these agents need access to relevant shared information without losing their individual execution context.

Together, these articles explain how memory, orchestration, and tool execution work together to build autonomous AI applications.

12. AI Agent Memory vs. Traditional RAG

Although memory and RAG are related, they solve different problems.

Feature AI Agent Memory Traditional RAG
Primary purpose Retain information from interactions and experiences Retrieve relevant external knowledge
Data source Conversations, tasks, preferences, events Documents, websites, databases
Persistence Often long-term and continuously updated Usually based on an indexed knowledge collection
Personalization Strong support Requires additional user context
Updates Can change as the agent learns Usually requires document or index updates
Typical use case Personal assistants and autonomous agents Documentation assistants and knowledge search

A production application can use both.

For example, an enterprise coding assistant might retrieve:

  1. The developer's project preferences from agent memory.
  2. Previous debugging experiences from episodic memory.
  3. Current API documentation from a RAG knowledge base.

The LLM combines these sources to produce a contextual response.

Understanding these architectures will help you design AI systems that combine external knowledge with persistent agent memory.

13. Popular Frameworks for Building AI Agent Memory

Several frameworks provide components for building memory-enabled AI applications.

LangChain

LangChain provides tools for building LLM applications, integrations, and agent workflows.

It supports integrations with vector databases and persistent storage systems.

LangGraph

LangGraph supports stateful, multi-step agent workflows.

Its persistence and checkpointing capabilities are useful for maintaining execution state across interactions.

LlamaIndex

LlamaIndex provides data ingestion, indexing, and retrieval capabilities for LLM applications.

It can be used to build knowledge retrieval and memory systems.

Mem0

Mem0 is a memory layer designed for AI applications.

It focuses on extracting, storing, and retrieving useful information from conversations.

Letta

Letta provides an architecture for stateful agents with explicit memory management.

It is useful for exploring agents that manage their own context and persistent state.

These frameworks solve different problems. The right choice depends on whether your application needs workflow persistence, conversational memory, document retrieval, or a dedicated memory-management layer.

14. Production Best Practices for AI Agent Memory

When designing an enterprise-grade AI memory system, consider the following practices.

1. Do not store everything.

Extract only useful, relevant, and appropriate information.

2. Separate memory types.

Keep temporary task state separate from persistent knowledge.

3. Use hybrid retrieval.

Combine semantic search with metadata filtering and keyword search.

4. Implement memory expiration.

Temporary information should not remain indefinitely.

5. Handle conflicting information.

New information should update or supersede old information when appropriate.

6. Maintain tenant isolation.

Enforce access control at the storage and retrieval layers.

7. Track memory provenance.

Store when information was created, where it came from, and whether it has been verified.

8. Evaluate retrieval quality.

Measure whether the system retrieves relevant memories instead of relying only on LLM response quality.

9. Optimize context construction.

Retrieve a limited number of high-quality memories rather than sending entire conversation histories to the model.

10. Monitor memory operations.

Track retrieval latency, storage growth, failed writes, embedding costs, and incorrect retrievals.

15. The Future of AI Agent Memory

AI agent memory is evolving from simple conversation history storage into a more sophisticated system for managing knowledge, experiences, and autonomous workflows.

Several developments are particularly important.

Continuous Learning Through Experience

Agents will increasingly use previous task outcomes to improve future decisions.

Cross-Session and Cross-Agent Memory

Multiple agents will share carefully managed knowledge across workflows and sessions.

Graph-Based Memory

Knowledge graphs will help agents understand complex relationships between users, projects, systems, and events.

Context-Aware Retrieval

Memory retrieval will become more selective by considering user intent, task state, recency, importance, and historical context.

Autonomous Memory Management

Agents will increasingly identify useful memories, summarize experiences, resolve outdated information, and manage their own memory lifecycle under defined policies.

However, persistent memory alone does not make an AI agent intelligent. Reliable memory requires accurate extraction, effective retrieval, controlled updates, and strong security.

Conclusion

AI agent memory is one of the foundational components of modern autonomous AI systems.

It allows agents to maintain conversational context, remember previous experiences, retrieve relevant knowledge, and continue long-running tasks across multiple sessions.

A well-designed memory architecture combines different storage and retrieval mechanisms:

  • Working memory for current tasks.
  • Short-term memory for active conversations.
  • Episodic memory for previous experiences.
  • Semantic memory for facts and knowledge.
  • Procedural memory for reusable workflows.
  • Long-term memory for persistent information.

Vector databases make semantic retrieval possible, while Redis, PostgreSQL, and graph databases provide complementary storage capabilities.

The most important architectural principle is to store the right information, retrieve it at the right time, and maintain it safely throughout its lifecycle.

As AI agents become more autonomous, scalable and reliable memory systems will become increasingly important.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

1. What is memory in an AI agent?

AI agent memory is a mechanism that allows an agent to store, retrieve, and use information from previous interactions, tasks, and experiences.

2. What is the difference between short-term and long-term AI memory?

Short-term memory maintains recent conversational or task context, while long-term memory preserves useful information across multiple sessions.

3. Why do AI agents use vector databases?

Vector databases enable semantic search. They allow agents to retrieve information based on meaning rather than requiring exact keyword matches.

4. Is Redis suitable for AI agent memory?

Yes. Redis is useful for session history, temporary context, active task state, and frequently accessed information. It is not necessarily a replacement for persistent knowledge storage.

5. What is episodic memory in AI?

Episodic memory stores records of previous experiences, including events, actions, outcomes, and timestamps. It helps agents use historical experiences when handling similar tasks.

6. What is semantic memory in AI?

Semantic memory stores facts, concepts, and general knowledge that an AI agent can retrieve when answering questions or performing tasks.

7. Can multiple AI agents share memory?

Yes. Multiple agents can access shared memory services, provided that the architecture includes appropriate access control, data ownership, and consistency mechanisms.

8. What is memory consolidation in AI?

Memory consolidation is the process of converting temporary conversations and experiences into summarized, structured, and useful long-term knowledge.

9. What is the difference between RAG and AI agent memory?

RAG primarily retrieves relevant information from external knowledge sources. AI agent memory retains information about previous interactions, preferences, tasks, and experiences. Both can work together.

10. Which database is best for AI agent memory?

There is no universal best database. Redis works well for short-term state, PostgreSQL for structured persistent memory, and vector databases for semantic retrieval. The best architecture depends on application requirements.

title: Smart2FA: An Offline, Zero-Knowledge 2FA Authenticator Built for Maximum Security and Minimal Friction
description:
A deep dive into Smart2FA (0xid Edition) - an open-source, 100% offline 2FA authenticator with local AES-256 encryption, biometrics, and cross-platform desktop/mobile support.

Security vs. Convenience: The Authentication Dilemma

In modern digital infrastructure, two-factor authentication (2FA) is one of the highest-leverage practices for preventing unauthorized account access. Yet most mainstream authenticator applications introduce unnecessary trade-offs:

  1. Centralized Cloud Sync Risks: Storing unencrypted or vendor-managed tokens in proprietary clouds introduces unnecessary attack surfaces, single points of failure, and vendor lock-in.
  2. Excessive Telemetry & Tracking: Many commercial authenticators harvest analytics, device identifiers, and usage metrics, adding cognitive and privacy overhead.
  3. Platform Lock-In & Friction: Limited export options make migrating between ecosystems unnecessarily difficult, increasing the risk of data loss when changing devices.

To maximize user autonomy, data protection, and operational efficiency, we built Smart2FA (0xid Edition) - an open-source, client-side, zero-knowledge authenticator designed to eliminate telemetry, minimize systemic vulnerability, and deliver maximum utility with an industrial aesthetic.

Core Philosophy: Zero-Knowledge & Local-First Utility

Smart2FA is engineered around three foundational requirements:

  • 100% Offline by Design: No backend services, no analytics, no external network calls.
  • Client-Side Cryptographic Isolation: All secrets remain encrypted at rest and in memory until explicitly authenticated by the user.
  • Portability and Interoperability: Support for standard RFC formats, instant bulk migrations, and frictionless cross-platform access across Web, Desktop (Tauri/Rust), and Mobile (Capacitor).

Capabilities & Architectural Overview

1. Robust Cryptographic Vault Model

Smart2FA never persists your master PIN in plaintext. The storage and decryption flow maximizes resilience against brute-force and local data-dump attacks:

[ User PIN ]
    |
    |-> PBKDF2 (25,000 iters, Salt A, SHA-256) -> PIN Hash (Verification only)
    |
    └-> PBKDF2 (25,000 iters, Salt B, SHA-256) -> AES-256-CBC Key -> Encrypts/Decrypts Vault
  • In-Memory PIN Lifecycle: Decrypted state and working secrets reside strictly in volatile RAM within the Pinia store. Locking the app, navigating away, or refreshing the page immediately purges volatile memory.
  • Biometric Integration (WebAuthn): On supported devices (Touch ID, Face ID, Windows Hello), WebAuthn securely wraps the key, providing frictionless single-touch authentication without compromising cryptographic strength.
  • Automated Inactivity Protection: Configurable auto-lock triggers after idle intervals (30s to 30m) to minimize risk in shared environments.
  • Irreversible Panic Wipe: A high-safety wipe mechanism requiring explicit text confirmation (WIPE) instantly sanitizes all local keys and storage artifacts.

2. RFC 6238 TOTP Engine & Real-Time Ergonomics

  • Broad Protocol Support: Powered by otpauth, supporting SHA-1, SHA-256, and SHA-512 algorithms, 6, 7, or 8-digit codes, and custom time periods (30s / 60s).
  • Visual Expiration Feedback: A real-time countdown progress bar indicates time-to-expire, shifting to an alert state 5 seconds prior to renewal.
  • Instant Copy: One-touch clipboard copying accompanied by concise status notifications.

3. Dual Input, Auto-Categorization & Google Auth Import

  • Integrated QR Scanner: Real-time camera scanner via html5-qrcode with automated otpauth:// URI parsing.
  • Google Authenticator Batch Migration: Scans Google Authenticator's native "Transfer Accounts" export QR code to migrate dozens of tokens in a single operation.
  • Smart Category Detection: Automatically classifies tokens into color-coded categories (Work, Crypto, Finance, Social, Email, Gaming, Other) based on issuer patterns (e.g., GitHub $\rightarrow$ Work, Binance $\rightarrow$ Crypto), with one-tap filtering tabs.

4. Encrypted Portability (.oxid Format)

  • Vaults can be exported as timestamped .oxid files, encrypted with AES-256 derived from the export PIN.
  • These encrypted containers can be safely archived in cold storage or transferred via insecure channels without exposing token secrets.

5. Cross-Platform Desktop & Mobile Support

  • Tauri v2 (Rust Backend): High performance, minimal binary footprint, full system tray integration, and minimize-to-tray capability for unobtrusive background operation.
  • Capacitor Mobile Build: Ready for deployment on Android devices.
  • Responsive Industrial Interface: High-contrast Dark Charcoal (#1A1B1E) and Rust Orange (#E25822) theme with glassmorphism and monospace typography.

Tech Stack

  • Frontend: Vue 3 (Composition API & <script setup>), Pinia 2, Vue Router 4, Tailwind CSS.
  • Desktop Runtime: Tauri v2 (Rust).
  • Mobile Foundation: Capacitor.
  • Security & TOTP Primitives: crypto-js, otpauth, html5-qrcode.

Ideas for Future Development

To continuously improve the security-to-effort ratio, several potential enhancements are under consideration:

  1. Hardware Security Key (FIDO2 / YubiKey) Support: Allowing master vault keys to be backed by a physical hardware token for enhanced physical security.
  2. Encrypted P2P Local Network Sync: Safe, serverless peer-to-peer sync between desktop and mobile devices via local encrypted WebRTC or chunked animated QR codes.
  3. CLI Companion Utility: A headless CLI tool for developers to query TOTP tokens directly from their terminal during SSH or CI/CD operations.
  4. Custom Category Rules & Custom Icons: Allowing users to define regex-based categorization rules and custom issuer icon packs.
  5. Decentralized Encrypted Cloud Storage Backends: Optional integration with WebDAV or user-owned S3 buckets to back up encrypted blobs automatically without vendor intermediaries.

Open Source & Getting Started

Smart2FA is 100% open-source under the MIT license. Check out the repository, star the project, and inspect the codebase:

-->> GitHub Repository: https://github.com/technologiespro/Smart2FA

What capabilities or integrations would provide the highest value for your daily security setup? What features would you like to see added to Smart2FA next?

title: pgvector: Vector Search in PostgreSQL Without a New Database
description:
Every few months the industry discovers a new kind of database. This year it's vector databases — specialized stores for embeddings, the numerical fingerprints that power "semantic search," recommendations, and all the AI features landing in every product you use. The pitch is always the same: spin up this new service, sync your data into it, and pay for another always-on thing.

Before you do that: if you already run PostgreSQL, you probably don't need a new database at all.

pgvector is a Postgres extension that adds vector types, distance operators, and approximate-nearest-neighbor indexes to the database you're already running. I've now used it in production for semantic search over ~200k documents, and this post is everything I wish someone had told me on day one — the setup, the indexes, and the two traps that cost me a weekend.

The problem in one paragraph

Classic search matches words: you type "disk full," you get documents containing "disk full." Semantic search matches meaning: type "out of storage," and it finds the disk-full article too. Embeddings make this work — you send text to a model, it returns a few hundred floating-point numbers representing the meaning, and texts with similar meanings get similar numbers. Storing and querying those numbers at scale is the whole job. Postgres does it fine.

Setup is insultingly easy 

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE documents (
    id        bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    title     text NOT NULL,
    body      text NOT NULL,
    embedding vector(1536)
);

The vector(1536) matches the output width of OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small — the most common embedding model and a fine default. Whatever model you pick, the column width must match its output dimension, or inserts will fail loudly.

Insert and search:

-- insert (embedding generated by your app via the provider's API)
INSERT INTO documents (title, body, embedding)
VALUES ('Disk full', 'When df shows 100%...', '[0.012, -0.034, ...]');

-- find the 5 most similar documents to a query embedding
SELECT title, body, embedding <=> '[0.011, -0.032, ...]' AS distance
FROM documents
ORDER BY embedding <=> '[0.011, -0.032, ...]'
LIMIT 5;

The <=> operator is cosine distance — pgvector ships <-> (L2), <#> (inner product), and <=> (cosine). For normalized embeddings, inner product and cosine rank identically, and cosine is the safe default for text search.

The part everyone skips: indexes

Without an index, every query is a full table scan with a distance computation per row. Fine at 1,000 rows. Ugly at 100,000. Painful at a million.

pgvector gives you two approximate index types. Today, you want HNSW:

CREATE INDEX ON documents
USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);

HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is a graph index — fast to query, great recall, and it doesn't require the data to be present at creation time. The older ivfflat index needs a representative dataset before you build it, or its clusters are garbage; that requirement surprises people exactly once. Just use HNSW.

Two knobs matter at query time:

SET hnsw.ef_search = 40;  -- higher = better recall, slower

Default ef_search is 40, which is a good starting point. If results feel wrong, raise it before you touch anything else. Accuracy problems are almost always recall problems.

Trap #1: the distance threshold nobody agrees on

The query above returns the 5 nearest documents — even if none of them are remotely relevant. Your application needs a cutoff, and here pgvector's docs go silent. There is no universal number because it depends on your embedding model and your data. What worked for me: take 100 queries where you know the right answer, plot the distance of the correct hit, and pick a threshold just past the worst case. Mine landed at 0.30 for that model and dataset. Yours will differ. Measure it.

Trap #2: embeddings generated with different models don't mix

I learned this the expensive way. Early on, I regenerated embeddings with a newer model for some rows and left others alone. Cosine distance between two different embedding spaces is meaningless — your queries will return confident nonsense from the mismatched rows, intermittently, which is the worst kind of bug. Add a column to record which model produced each embedding, and if you ever switch models, re-embed everything in one pass:

ALTER TABLE documents ADD COLUMN embed_model text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'text-embedding-3-small';

Where do embeddings come from?

Any embedding API works — OpenAI, Voyage, Cohere. But if you've been following along with the local LLM setup, here's the part I find genuinely neat: Ollama runs embedding models locally too:

ollama pull nomic-embed-text
curl http://localhost:11434/api/embeddings -d '{"model": "nomic-embed-text", "prompt": "how do I free up disk space"}'

That returns a 768-dimensional vector — so your vector(...) column would be vector(768) for this model — generated on your own hardware, for free, with the text never leaving your network. For a privacy-first stack, local embeddings plus pgvector is a complete semantic search pipeline with zero third parties.

Do you actually need a dedicated vector database?

Honest answer: probably not, at your scale. pgvector comfortably handles millions of vectors at single-digit millisecond query times, and it inherits everything Postgres gives you for free — transactions, point-in-time recovery, the backup strategy you already have, row-level security, and joins with your actual relational data. A dedicated vector store makes sense when you're doing tens of millions of vectors with extreme QPS, or when you need GPU-accelerated indexes. Everything short of that is a second database to run for no reason.

The pattern I keep returning to: Postgres first, specialize only when Postgres measurably fails you. It has not failed me yet.

title: Outgrowing the Curse of Multilinguality: Scaling Strategies for Efficient Language Adaptation
description:
arXiv:2512.10772v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Training high-performing language models which include medium- and lower-resource languages remains a challenge. Massively multilingual models still underperform language-specific adaptations, especially at smaller scales, due to the curse of multilinguality. In this work, we investigate scaling as an efficient strategy for adapting pretrained models to new target languages. Through comprehensive ablations matched for data and training FLOPs, we test whether upscaling from English base models enables more effective and resource-efficient adaptation than standard continued pretraining. We find that upscaling is an efficient strategy for improving target-language performance by relieving capacity constraints, especially for higher-resourced languages. An initial upscaling step in English is beneficial for low-resource languages. However, in higher-resource scenarios it is more compute-efficient to directly scale up on the target language, albeit slightly compromising data efficiency for most languages. For multilingual continued pre-training, we identify directly scaling up using the target data as the optimal setup for both data efficiency and reduced English forgetting.

title: Digital Colonialism & The Architecture of Sovereign Compute: What Early Aviation Teaches Us About the AI Stack
description:
Digital Colonialism & The Architecture of Sovereign Compute: What Early Aviation Teaches Us About the AI Stack

A century ago, in the aftermath of catastrophic geopolitical conflict, nations that wished to maintain genuine sovereignty realized a cold truth: if you do not build your own domestic aviation and industrial machine tools, your national borders are an illusion.

In the 1920s and 1930s, early sovereign pioneers did not just purchase foreign aircraft—they built aircraft manufacturing plants, forged aluminum airframes, and engineered domestic radial engines. They understood that sovereign defense and economic survival break at the supply chain layer.

Today, the battleground of sovereignty has shifted from the sky to the silicon.

The New Architecture of Digital Colonialism

Fast forward to 2026. Across Europe, the Middle East, and Asia, modern technology enterprises proudly announce "national AI initiatives."

Yet if you audit their actual system architecture, an alarming pattern emerges:

  1. The Infrastructure Layer: Rented instances in US hyperscaler availability zones (AWS, Azure, GCP).
  2. The Intelligence Layer: Closed, proprietary black-box APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic) billed per million tokens.
  3. The Data Layer: Enterprise and citizen telemetry routed straight through foreign transit pipes.

When 95% of a nation's enterprise intelligence runs on closed APIs that can be throttled, revoked, or price-hiked by executive decree in Silicon Valley, that nation does not have an "AI industry."

It has a distributed network of digital resellers.

Hardware Is Hard; Renting Is Easy

The commoditization of software was supposed to democratize technology. Instead, the computational intensity of frontier AI has created the most centralized oligopoly in industrial history.

  • True sovereignty is running open weights on bare metal hardware you physically control.
  • True engineering is optimizing local inference kernels (llama.cpp, vLLM) rather than wrapping HTTP endpoints in bloated abstractions.

Renting convenience is tempting. But as history repeatedly demonstrates across every technological revolution—from aerospace to semiconductors—convenience is an installment plan on your autonomy.

Sovereignty does not begin in press releases. It begins in the machine room.

title: How Crowdtesting Helps Businesses Improve Digital Product Quality
description:
The success of a digital product depends not only on its features but also on how effectively it works for real users. Businesses developing websites, mobile applications and software platforms need reliable testing methods to identify problems before launching their products.

Crowdtesting has become a useful approach to software quality assurance because it allows businesses to receive feedback from multiple testers in real-world environments.

What Is Crowdtesting?

Crowdtesting is a testing approach that involves a group of independent testers evaluating a digital product. These testers use different devices, browsers, operating systems and network conditions to identify technical issues and usability problems.

Unlike traditional testing environments, crowdtesting provides insights into how products perform under different real-world conditions.

Benefits of Crowdtesting for Businesses

Crowdtesting offers several advantages:

Access to different devices and operating systems

Identification of unexpected software bugs

Improved website and application usability

Real-world testing conditions

Faster identification of compatibility issues

Feedback from diverse users

Better overall product quality

Why Real-World Testing Matters

Internal testing teams may not have access to every possible device or usage environment. This can make certain problems difficult to identify.

Crowdtesting helps businesses discover issues that may appear only under specific conditions. For example, a mobile application may work correctly on one smartphone but experience performance problems on another.

Real-world feedback helps development teams understand these differences and improve their products.

Crowdtesting for Websites and Mobile Applications

Crowdtesting can be useful for several types of digital products.

Website Testing: Evaluates navigation, forms, responsiveness and browser compatibility.

Mobile App Testing: Checks application functionality across different devices and operating systems.

Usability Testing: Identifies confusing features and difficulties in user interaction.

Functional Testing: Verifies whether important features work as expected.

Compatibility Testing: Checks performance across different technical environments.

Businesses can explore TestLancer to discover testing services and connect with testers and digital professionals for their projects.

How to Build a Better Testing Strategy

A structured testing strategy can help businesses get better results.

Define the objectives of the testing process.

Identify the target audience and supported devices.

Prepare clear testing scenarios.

Collect feedback from multiple testers.

Document bugs and usability problems.

Resolve identified issues.

Conduct another round of testing.

Conclusion

Crowdtesting provides businesses with valuable insights into how their digital products perform in real-world situations. By combining feedback from multiple testers with traditional quality assurance methods, companies can improve reliability, compatibility and user experience.

For businesses looking for website testing, mobile application testing and digital quality assurance solutions, TestLancer is worth exploring.

title: Reformulating KV Cache Eviction Problem for Long-Context LLM Inference
description:
arXiv:2605.07234v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) support long-context inference but suffer from substantial memory and runtime overhead due to Key-Value (KV) Cache growth. Existing KV Cache eviction methods primarily rely on local attention weights, neglecting the influence of value representations, output projection, and inter-head interactions. In this work, we reformulate KV Cache eviction from a conventional head-wise, weight-averaging approach into an output-aware, layer-wise matrix multiplication approximation problem. We introduce LaProx, a novel eviction strategy that explicitly models the multiplicative interaction between attention maps and projected value states to accurately quantify token contributions while accounting for inter-head dependencies. Building on this metric, we propose the first unified eviction strategy that assigns globally comparable importance scores to tokens, enabling model-wide selection instead of local, head-wise decisions. Experimental results across 19 datasets on long-context benchmarks LongBench and Needle-In-A-Haystack demonstrate that our approach maintains model performance with only 5% of the KV cache and consistently outperforms prior works across all configurations. Notably, our method achieves up to 2$\times$ accuracy loss reduction under extreme compression scenarios compared to existing state-of-the-art baselines with minimal overhead. Our code is available at https://github.com/huuthomai/LaProx.

title: How to Choose the Best Open Source Distributed Time Series Database
description:
This article explores what defines the best open source time series database, with a focus on three major projects: Apache IoTDB, TimechoDB, and InfluxDB. We contrast their benefits and help you decide which may be ideal for your application.

Why time-series databases matter

Traditional relational and general-purpose NoSQL databases struggle with workloads that involve high write rates, large numbers of concurrent series (high cardinality), time-window aggregations, and long-term historical retention. 

Time series databases are optimized to the job: they optimize streams of (timestamp, value) pairs, support efficient range queries, down-sampling, and retention policies, and aggressively compress data.

These properties make TSDBs essential when evaluating an open source distributed time series database for industrial telemetry or large-scale metrics pipelines

Apache IoTDB: A Leading Industrial-Grade Open Source TSDB

Apache IoTDB was built from scratch for the Internet of Things (IoT) and industrial telemetry application scenario. It features a cluster architecture (config nodes + data nodes) and offers built-in high-throughput writes, aligned time series, rich query semantics, and close big-data ecosystem integration.

Main features:

  • High compression and cost-efficient storage: IoTDB achieves strong disk compression ratios, reducing storage cost for long-term retention. 
  • Flexible deployment: edge, standalone, and distributed cluster modes are supported.
  • Powerful time-series query language: standard SQL queries support complex time-interval and device-level conditions.
  • Proven in industrial scenarios: widely adopted in energy, transportation, steel, and equipment monitoring industries.

These are the features that make Apache IoTDB one of the strongest choices for organizations seeking for an open source industry time series database that combines scale, performance, and industrial-ready modeling.

TimechoDB: Enterprise-grade Product Build on IoTDB

TimechoDB is the enterprise distribution built on top of the IoTDB open-source community project. The vendor describes TimechoDB as being based on the open‑source foundation and adding enterprise‑level functionalities such as cluster management, tooling, and services.


While not all enterprise features are open source, TimechoDB retains the open-source IoTDB core and is designed specifically for large-scale industrial environments that require: strong reliability, operational tooling, long-term stability, and vendor-backed support.

For businesses with heavy industrial workloads or production SLAs, TimechoDB provides a more complete ecosystem on top of the open-source engine.

InfluxDB: A Popular General-Purpose Open Source Time Series Database

InfluxDB is one of the most widely used open-source time-series databases. Designed for time‑series workloads, InfluxDB features high‑volume ingestion, real‑time analytics, and a mature ecosystem. As is recorded: "The most downloaded, most used, and most trusted open source time series database."

Main Features

  • Supports hundreds of millions of time‑series data points per second, cloud, on‑prem, and edge.
  • Offers SQL‑like query language, retention policies, downsampling, plugin ecosystem (e.g., Telegraf).
  • Huge community and prevalent use cases like monitoring, IoT telemetry, and analytics. Though InfluxDB is not directly comparable when it comes to industrial specialist features to IoTDB (e.g., very high correlation between device hierarchies, industrial directory structure), it is an excellent choice if one wants a general-purpose open-source time series database with very good usability and ecosystem.

How to pick between them

When selecting an open source distributed time series database , consider the following:

  • Ingestion rate & scale: For extremely high-throughput ingestion (millions of points/second) or very large numbers of series, use a system built for that (Apache IoTDB, TimechoDB).
  • Distributed & cluster deployment: Horizontal scaling and cluster mode with auto-failover are significant for an open-source distributed time series database. IoTDB supports auto-failover, cluster mode, and horizontal scaling.
  • Industrial features: If you're in IoT/industry (sensors, devices, edge+cloud), frameworks such as IoTDB bring domain-specific strengths (device tree hierarchies, aligned time-series, edge deployment).
  • Ecosystem & ease-of-use: For normal metrics, dashboards, monitoring, and large community resources, InfluxDB may be the most convenient.
  • Efficiency & hardware cost: If you need extremely high compression and low storage cost, Apache IoTDB or TimechoDB for sure.
  • Enterprise readiness & support: Consider community size, environment maturity, documentation, and enterprise tooling (TimechoDB will add some enterprise features on top of IoTDB).

Conclusion

If you want the best open source time series database, then you need to balance performance, features, and ecosystem. For all typical use-cases (monitoring, IoT backend)–InfluxDB will do perfectly. If you want an open source industry time series database with robust distributed architecture, industrial device modeling, and good compression, then Apache IoTDB is highly sought after. If you want vendor-supported support and enterprise readiness on IoTDB, then TimechoDB is also a good try.

In short, choosing an open source distributed time series database is not a generic decision—matching your workload (ingest volume, cardinality, analytics), deployment architecture (edge vs cloud vs hybrid), and operational needs (tooling, support, community) will guide you to the best solution.

By focusing on tools like IoTDB, TimechoDB, and InfluxDB, you’re positioning yourself to use a genuinely high‑quality open source time‑series platform capable of supporting modern data workloads at scale.

title: Converting Excel Workbooks to TIFF Images in Java: Use Cases, Mechanics, and Trade-offs
description:
Excel workbooks are built for interactive use—formulas, multiple sheets, formatting, and embedded objects all live within a structured grid. TIFF, by contrast, is a flat, raster image format designed for archival stability and consistent rendering across platforms. Converting between the two is less about convenience and more about solving specific problems: preserving the visual appearance of a spreadsheet for legal or regulatory archives, embedding tabular data into document management systems that only accept image formats, or generating fax-ready outputs from financial reports.

This article examines the technical landscape of Excel-to-TIFF conversion in Java, using Spire.XLS for Java as a reference implementation. The focus is on understanding where such conversions fit, what trade-offs are involved, and how the library handles the mechanics.

Why TIFF Remains Relevant for Spreadsheet Archival

TIFF (Tagged Image File Format) dates back to the mid-1980s and was designed for desktop scanning and fax workflows. Its persistence in enterprise environments stems from characteristics that newer formats do not always prioritize: lossless compression through schemes like LZW, support for multiple pages within a single file, and a well-documented, stable specification that archival systems can rely on for decades.

When an Excel file must be retained as evidence—for audit trails, compliance submissions, or legal discovery—a TIFF rendering eliminates concerns about formula recalculation, font substitution, or version incompatibility. The output is what it is: a pixel representation of the worksheet as it appeared at conversion time. This immutability is both the format's strength and its limitation. You gain visual fidelity and long-term readability; you lose searchable text, cell references, and any ability to recompute values.

The trade-off is acceptable in scenarios where the spreadsheet is an endpoint, not a working document. Financial statements submitted to regulatory bodies, invoice archives, and scanned-document workflows that already operate in TIFF are typical candidates.

How Spire.XLS for Java Approaches the Conversion

Spire.XLS for Java provides a saveToTiff method that operates at the worksheet level. The API surface is minimal: load a workbook, retrieve a worksheet by index, and invoke the conversion with an output path. This design treats the conversion as a rendering operation rather than a data transformation.

A basic conversion looks like this:

import com.spire.xls.Workbook;
import com.spire.xls.Worksheet;

Workbook workbook = new Workbook();
workbook.loadFromFile("input.xlsx");
Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);
sheet.saveToTiff("output.tiff");

The method also supports converting a specific cell range rather than the entire worksheet, using an overload that accepts row and column boundaries. This is useful when only a summary table or a defined print area needs to be captured, avoiding the overhead of rendering blank cells or peripheral content.

What the API does not expose, at least in the basic saveToTiff signature, are fine-grained rendering controls. There is no built-in parameter for setting output DPI within the TIFF conversion method itself. The library supports DPI configuration for Excel-to-image conversions through ConverterSetting, but that mechanism applies to image outputs such as PNG, not to the TIFF path directly. For TIFF output, resolution is handled internally, and users seeking precise control over compression type (LZW, JPEG, or uncompressed) or color depth will not find those options in the standard method signature. This is a notable difference from libraries that expose explicit rendering options for TIFF compression and resolution.

Practical Considerations and Limitations

Page Layout and Scaling

Excel worksheets are not inherently paginated in the way that documents are. A worksheet can extend across thousands of rows and dozens of columns, with print areas, page breaks, and scaling settings that determine how the content would appear on paper. When converting to TIFF, the library must decide how to map this unbounded grid onto fixed image dimensions.

The behavior depends on the worksheet's existing page setup. If a print area is defined, saveToTiff generally respects it. If not, the conversion may produce a single very large image or split the content across multiple TIFF pages, depending on internal heuristics. For predictable results, users should configure the worksheet's PageSetup properties—orientation, paper size, fit-to-page scaling—before conversion.

Multi-Sheet Workbooks

A workbook with multiple worksheets requires iteration. saveToTiff operates on a single worksheet, so a complete conversion loop must traverse the worksheet collection and generate one TIFF per sheet. The naming and organization of output files becomes the developer's responsibility. There is no one-call "convert workbook to a single multi-page TIFF" convenience method in the basic API. While TIFF itself supports multi-page documents, the library's worksheet-level method does not aggregate sheets automatically.

Font and Rendering Fidelity

TIFF output is only as accurate as the rendering engine's ability to reproduce the Excel layout. Fonts that are not installed on the server running the conversion will be substituted, potentially altering column widths, row heights, and text wrapping. For organizations with strict branding or document appearance requirements, this is a critical operational detail. The conversion environment must have access to the same font set used when the Excel file was authored.

Compression and File Size

TIFF files are often large, particularly when rendering complex worksheets with dense formatting. The library's internal choice of compression scheme directly affects output size. Without exposed control over LZW versus uncompressed output, developers cannot optimize file size for their storage constraints. For batch archival pipelines handling thousands of workbooks, this lack of granularity may necessitate post-processing or acceptance of larger storage footprints.

Where This Conversion Fits in a Java Application

The most defensible use case for Excel-to-TIFF in Java is as a background archival process. A scheduled job reads spreadsheets from a monitored directory or database, converts each to TIFF, stores the image in a content management system, and optionally records metadata (source filename, conversion timestamp, checksum). The original Excel file may be retained or discarded according to retention policy.

A second scenario is report distribution. When a financial or operational report must be delivered to recipients who should not edit or manipulate the underlying data, a TIFF rendering enforces that boundary. The recipient sees the numbers as rendered; there is no hidden formula to inspect, no cell to modify. This is a control mechanism, not a technical necessity, but it is a legitimate one in regulated industries.

Less compelling is the use of TIFF conversion as a general-purpose export feature for end-user applications. TIFF files are large, not universally previewable in browsers, and poorly suited for on-screen viewing. If the goal is simply to share a non-editable view of a spreadsheet, PDF is almost always the better choice: smaller, searchable, and natively supported by virtually every document viewer. TIFF conversion should be reserved for workflows that specifically require raster images.

Conclusion

Converting Excel to TIFF in Java is a narrow but well-defined operation. Spire.XLS for Java handles the core mechanics—loading a workbook, selecting a worksheet or range, and rendering to a TIFF file—with an API that prioritizes brevity over granular control. The library is suitable for batch archival pipelines where the priority is getting a stable image output without extensive configuration.

The limitations are equally clear: limited exposed control over TIFF compression and resolution, reliance on the host environment's font set for rendering accuracy, and the inherent impedance mismatch between spreadsheet layout and fixed image dimensions. These are not defects in the library so much as characteristics of the conversion domain itself. Understanding them before committing to a TIFF-based workflow is more valuable than any API reference.

title: Virtual models now available on AI Gateway
description:
Virtual models are now available on AI Gateway.

A virtual model is a saved configuration that tells AI Gateway which model and settings to use. Your apps and agents call it with a custom model ID, such as vmc/coding-agent. You can change the model or settings centrally in AI Gateway without redeploying your apps or reconfiguring your agents.

Use virtual models to:

  • Configure coding agents: Set reasoning effort, fast mode, prompt caching, and other options even when your agent doesn’t expose them.

  • Control routing and compliance: Choose providers, configure fallback models, and enforce requirements such as Zero Data Retention.

  • Attribute spend: Attach custom reporting tags to every request that uses the virtual model.

To create a virtual model, open the Virtual Models page and click Create Virtual Model. Enter a slug, choose the underlying model, configure the settings you want requests to use, and save.

Or create one with the Vercel CLI:

To use a virtual model, replace the provider model ID in your AI SDK or compatible API requests with vmc/<slug>, such as vmc/coding-agent.

For coding agents, connect to AI Gateway with vercel ai-gateway setup if needed, then select your virtual model in the agent’s model picker or configuration.

Virtual models work with every model type on AI Gateway. Read the launch post for examples or learn more in the virtual models documentation.
