title: Mastering Advanced Server-Side Caching Patterns in Next.js
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

Next.js ships with a sophisticated, multi-layered caching system that can be a superpower or a footgun. The default behavior—automatic static optimization, fetch caching, and Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR)—gets you 80% of the way there. But when you need fine-grained control over what gets cached, when it gets invalidated, and how it scales across multiple serverless instances, you need to master the advanced patterns the framework exposes.

In this deep-dive, we'll peel back the layers of Next.js caching, then walk through five production-ready patterns—cache-aside, stale-while-revalidate, distributed caching with Redis, per-request memoization with React.cache(), and partial prerendering—complete with runnable code and the pitfalls that bite most teams.

  • 1. Understanding the Next.js Caching Layers
  • 2. The Core APIs: unstable_cache, revalidateTag, revalidatePath
  • 3. Time-Based vs. Tag-Based Revalidation
  • 4. Pattern 1: Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) with unstable_cache
  • 5. Pattern 2: Stale-While-Revalidate (SWR)
  • 6. Pattern 3: Distributed Caching with Redis
  • 7. Pattern 4: Per-Request Memoization with React.cache()
  • 8. Pattern 5: Partial Prerendering (PPR) and Streaming
  • 9. Edge Cases, Pitfalls, and Gotchas
  • 10. Production Best Practices
  • Frequently Asked Questions

1. Understanding the Next.js Caching Layers

Before writing any caching code, you need a mental model of the four distinct caches Next.js maintains. Confusing them is the number-one cause of "why is my data stale?" bugs.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      Next.js Server                      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  1. Router Cache  — client-side, per-session, in-memory  │
│  2. Full Route Cache — static HTML (build-time or ISR)   │
│  3. Data Cache — fetch() + unstable_cache() results      │
│  4. React Cache — memoization per render pass            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  1. Router Cache (client): A client-side in-memory cache that stores the RSC payload of previously visited routes. It's per-session and ephemeral. It's why navigating back to a page feels instant. It has a default staleness of 30 seconds (configurable via staleTimes in next.config.js).
  2. Full Route Cache (FRC): The pre-rendered HTML and RSC payload for statically generated routes. At build time, or on first request if dynamic = 'force-static', Next.js renders the page once and caches the HTML. ISR updates this cache on a timer or via revalidation.
  3. Data Cache: The persistent cache for the results of fetch() requests and unstable_cache() calls. This is the cache you'll interact with most when building custom data layers. It lives on the server (filesystem by default, or a custom handler) and is shared across users.
  4. React Cache (memoization): A per-render-pass memoization that deduplicates identical fetch() or async function calls within the same component tree render. It's wiped after each render completes.

Key insight: The Data Cache and the Full Route Cache are the two server-side caches that matter for advanced patterns. The Router Cache is client-side and often the source of "I updated my DB but the UI is stale" complaints—you must call router.refresh() or revalidatePath() to bust it.

2. The Core APIs: unstable_cache, revalidateTag, revalidatePath

unstable_cache is the workhorse for caching arbitrary async functions. It wraps any function, memoizes its result in the Data Cache, and lets you attach invalidation tags. It's "unstable" because the API may change, but it's widely used in production today.

// lib/cache.ts
import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache';

export const getPosts = unstable_cache(
  async () => {
    const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/posts');
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error('Failed to fetch posts');
    return res.json();
  },
  // Cache key parts (used to build a unique key)
  ['posts'],
  {
    // Revalidate every 1 hour
    revalidate: 3600,
    // Tags for fine-grained invalidation
    tags: ['posts', 'content'],
  }
);

Now you can call getPosts() from any Server Component, Route Handler, or Server Action, and it will be cached in the Data Cache.

To invalidate it, you use revalidateTag or revalidatePath from next/cache:

// app/actions/posts.ts
'use server';

import { revalidateTag, revalidatePath } from 'next/cache';

export async function createPost(data: FormData) {
  // ... persist to DB

  // Bust every cache entry tagged with 'posts'
  revalidateTag('posts');

  // OR bust the entire route path (including FRC)
  revalidatePath('/blog');
}

The difference matters:

  • revalidateTag('posts') invalidates only Data Cache entries that carry the posts tag. It does not re-render any pages immediately.
  • revalidatePath('/blog') invalidates both the Data Cache entries used by that path and the Full Route Cache for that path, triggering a re-render of the page on the next request.

Pro tip: Use revalidateTag for data-layer invalidation, and call revalidatePath only when you need to force a page's static HTML to be regenerated.

3. Time-Based vs. Tag-Based Revalidation

There are two primary strategies for keeping cached data fresh. Choosing the right one is a product decision, not just a technical one.

Strategy Mechanism Use Case Trade-off
Time-based revalidate: 3600 Data that changes slowly and tolerates staleness (e.g., a blog's author list) Simple, but you can't push updates sooner than the interval
Tag-based revalidateTag('posts') Data that changes unpredictably and must be fresh immediately after a mutation (e.g., a user's cart) Requires you to wire up invalidation calls at every mutation point

You can combine them. A common pattern is to set a generous revalidate as a safety net and use tags for instant invalidation on mutations:

export const getProduct = unstable_cache(
  async (id: string) => {
    const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/products/${id}`);
    return res.json();
  },
  ['product', 'id'], // key parts
  {
    revalidate: 86400, // fallback: revalidate daily
    tags: ['products'], // instant invalidation on mutation
  }
);

This gives you the best of both worlds: the cache self-heals after 24 hours even if you forget a revalidateTag, but mutations still propagate immediately.

4. Pattern 1: Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) with unstable_cache

Cache-aside (aka lazy loading) is the simplest advanced pattern: check the cache, and if there's a miss, compute the value, store it, and return it. unstable_cache implements this for you, but you can also build it manually when you need a custom store like Redis.

Here's a manual cache-aside implementation with unstable_cache as the glue:

// lib/user.ts
import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache';
import { Redis } from '@upstash/redis';

const redis = Redis.fromEnv();

async function fetchUserFromDb(id: string) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/users/${id}`);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error('User not found');
  return res.json();
}

export const getUser = unstable_cache(
  async (id: string) => {
    // Manual cache-aside with Redis as L1
    const cached = await redis.get(`user:${id}`);
    if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached);

    const user = await fetchUserFromDb(id);
    await redis.set(`user:${id}`, JSON.stringify(user), { ex: 3600 });
    return user;
  },
  ['user'],
  {
    revalidate: 3600,
    tags: ['users'],
  }
);

What's happening here?

  1. unstable_cache provides a second, Next.js-managed cache layer on top of your Redis. This is useful because it also caches the result in the framework's Data Cache, so you avoid a Redis round-trip on every request.
  2. The manual Redis check acts as a fast L1 cache, letting you control TTL and eviction policies that unstable_cache doesn't expose.
  3. On a cache miss, you fetch from the source of truth, write to Redis, and return.

Caution: Don't double-cache unless you have a reason. Layering unstable_cache on top of Redis means you have two TTLs to manage. If you only need Redis, skip unstable_cache and call fetch directly with next: { revalidate: false }.

5. Pattern 2: Stale-While-Revalidate (SWR)

SWR is a pattern where you serve stale data immediately while revalidating in the background. It's the standard for dashboards and feeds where perceived latency matters more than absolute freshness.

Next.js supports SWR natively through the revalidate option on unstable_cache and fetch. Here's the flow:

  1. First request: cache miss → fetch fresh → store → return.
  2. Second request (before revalidate interval): cache hit → return stale immediately.
  3. Third request (after revalidate interval): cache hit but stale → return stale, and kick off a background revalidation.
  4. Once revalidation completes, the cache is updated; the next request gets fresh data. 
// lib/dashboard.ts
import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache';

export const getDashboardData = unstable_cache(
  async () => {
    const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/dashboard');
    return res.json();
  },
  ['dashboard'],
  {
    // Serve stale for up to 5 minutes, then revalidate in background
    revalidate: 300,
    tags: ['dashboard'],
  }
);

This is the entire SWR implementation—Next.js handles the background revalidation for you. But there's a subtlety: background revalidation only happens when the route is being rendered. If no one visits the page, nothing revalidates. For high-traffic routes this is fine; for low-traffic routes you might want a cron job to warm the cache.

To force a background revalidation from a Server Action without blocking the response, you can fire-and-forget:

'use server';

export async function refreshDashboard() {
  // This triggers revalidation, but doesn't await it in the client
  await revalidateTag('dashboard');
}

Pro tip: For truly low-traffic pages, combine SWR with a scheduled revalidation (e.g., Vercel Cron or a GitHub Action) to keep the cache warm.

6. Pattern 3: Distributed Caching with Redis

When you deploy to serverless (Vercel, Netlify, AWS Lambda), the default filesystem cache is local to each instance and doesn't share across instances. For consistent cache hits, you need a distributed store like Redis or Upstash.

Next.js lets you plug in a custom cache handler via next.config.ts:

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next';
import { Redis } from '@upstash/redis';

const redis = Redis.fromEnv();

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  experimental: {
    // Next 14.1+ supports custom cache handlers
    cacheHandler: './cache-handler.ts',
  },
};

export default nextConfig;

And the handler itself:

// cache-handler.ts
import { Redis } from '@upstash/redis';

const redis = Redis.fromEnv();

export default {
  async get(key: string) {
    const value = await redis.get(key);
    return value ? JSON.parse(value) : null;
  },
  async set(key: string, data: any, ctx: { revalidate?: number }) {
    const ttl = ctx.revalidate ? ctx.revalidate : 3600;
    await redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(data), { ex: ttl });
  },
  async revalidateTag(tag: string) {
    // Upstash doesn't support tag-based deletion natively,
    // so you'd maintain a tag index or use a pattern scan.
    const keys = await redis.keys(`tag:${tag}:*`);
    if (keys.length > 0) await redis.del(...keys);
  },
};

This replaces the default in-memory Data Cache with Redis, giving you shared cache across all serverless instances. The caveat: you're now responsible for implementing revalidateTag and revalidatePath semantics in the handler, which is non-trivial.

A simpler alternative: Use Redis directly in your unstable_cache callback (as shown in Pattern 1) and skip the custom handler. This keeps the framework's cache for what it's good at and uses Redis only where you need explicit control. It's less elegant but far easier to debug.

7. Pattern 4: Per-Request Memoization with React.cache()

React.cache() is the unsung hero of Server Components. It memoizes an async function within a single render pass, deduplicating identical calls. This is perfect for the "N+1" problem where multiple components in the same tree fetch the same data.

// lib/user.ts
import { cache } from 'react';

export const getUser = cache(async (id: string) => {
  const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/users/${id}`);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error('User not found');
  return res.json();
});

Now, if both Header and ProfileCard call getUser(userId) in the same render, the fetch happens once:

// app/dashboard/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react';
import { getUser } from '@/lib/user';
import { Header } from '@/components/header';
import { ProfileCard } from '@/components/profile-card';

export default async function DashboardPage() {
  const user = await getUser('123');

  return (
    <>
      <Header user={user} />
      <ProfileCard user={user} />
    </>
  );
}

Without React.cache(), each component would trigger its own fetch. With it, the framework deduplicates them.

The killer combo: Wrap React.cache() around a unstable_cache call to get both per-request deduplication and cross-request Data Cache persistence:

import { cache } from 'react';
import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache';

const fetchUser = async (id: string) => {
  const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/users/${id}`);
  return res.json();
};

// Persist in Data Cache for 1 hour, with tag-based invalidation
const cachedUser = unstable_cache(fetchUser, ['user'], {
  revalidate: 3600,
  tags: ['users'],
});

// Deduplicate within a single render pass
export const getUser = cache(cachedUser);

This is the pattern I reach for most often in production. It gives you three layers: React memoization (per request), Data Cache (across requests), and tag-based invalidation (on mutation).

8. Pattern 5: Partial Prerendering (PPR) and Streaming

Partial Prerendering (PPR) is the experimental feature that lets you prerender the static parts of a page while streaming the dynamic parts. It's the logical evolution of ISR and is the recommended approach for pages that are mostly static but have a few dynamic islands.

Enable it in next.config.ts:

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  experimental: {
    ppr: 'incremental', // or true
  },
};

Then, mark a route as opting in to PPR:

// app/dashboard/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react';
import { DashboardStats } from './dashboard-stats';

export const experimental_ppr = true;

export default function DashboardPage() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Dashboard</h1>
      {/* This is prerendered at build time */}
      <p>Welcome back, user!</p>

      {/* This is streamed in dynamically */}
      <Suspense fallback={<StatsSkeleton />}>
        <DashboardStats />
      </Suspense>
    </main>
  );
}

With PPR, the shell of the page is static and cached in the Full Route Cache, while the DashboardStats component streams in on demand. This is a massive performance win for pages that are 90% static but have a 10% dynamic section.

The use cache directive (Next.js 15 experimental) is the companion to PPR. It lets you mark a component or function as cacheable, with explicit tags and revalidation, directly in the source:

// app/dashboard/dashboard-stats.tsx
'use cache';

export default async function DashboardStats() {
  const stats = await fetch('https://api.example.com/stats');
  return <StatsView stats={stats} />;
}

This is cleaner than wrapping everything in unstable_cache, and it's the future of server-side caching in Next.js. As of Next 15 it's still experimental, so you may want to stick with unstable_cache for now.

9. Edge Cases, Pitfalls, and Gotchas

Here are the mistakes I see most often in production codebases.

1. Dynamic APIs opt you out of caching.

Calling cookies(), headers(), draftMode(), or reading searchParams in a Server Component forces the route to be dynamically rendered, bypassing the Full Route Cache. It does not bypass the Data Cache, but it does mean your page HTML is generated on every request.

// This page is dynamic — no Full Route Cache
export default async function Page({ searchParams }) {
  const user = await getUser();
  return <div>{user.name}</div>;
}

If you need both dynamic behavior and caching, isolate the dynamic part into a child component wrapped in Suspense.

2. fetch caching changed in Next.js 15.

In Next.js 15, fetch requests are no longer cached by default. You must opt in with next: { revalidate: 60 } or next: { tags: ['posts'] }. If you're upgrading from 14, this is the biggest behavioral change and will silently break your caching assumptions.

const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/posts', {
  next: { revalidate: 60, tags: ['posts'] },
});

3. unstable_cache doesn't know about dynamic values.

If you pass a dynamic argument (like a user ID from cookies()) into unstable_cache, the cache key won't include it unless you add it to the key parts array. This causes cross-user cache pollution.

// BAD — key parts don't include userId
export const getCart = unstable_cache(
  async (userId: string) => fetchCart(userId),
  ['cart'],
  { revalidate: 60 }
);

// GOOD — include userId in the key
export const getCart = unstable_cache(
  async (userId: string) => fetchCart(userId),
  ['cart', 'userId'],
  { revalidate: 60 }
);

4. Nested revalidate values are tricky.

When you use fetch with next: { revalidate: 60 } inside a page that has its own revalidate, the shorter of the two wins for the route's HTML regeneration. This can cause unexpected ISR behavior. Be deliberate about which layer sets the revalidation interval.

5. noStore() is your escape hatch.

If you need to bypass the Data Cache for a specific request (e.g., a live price check), use noStore() from next/cache:

import { noStore } from 'next/cache';

export async function getLivePrice(sku: string) {
  noStore(); // bypass Data Cache for this call
  const res = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/price/${sku}`);
  return res.json();
}

10. Production Best Practices

  1. Prefer tag-based invalidation over time-based for mutable data. If your data changes when a user acts, revalidateTag gives you instant freshness without waiting for a timer. Use time-based revalidation only as a fallback.
  2. Centralize your cache keys. Create a single lib/cache-keys.ts file with constants for key parts and tags to avoid typos and make refactoring safe.
  3. Monitor cache hit rates. Add a counter (e.g., with Sentry or Datadog) to your unstable_cache wrappers to see if your cache is actually being hit. A 0% hit rate means you're paying the cost of caching without the benefit.
  4. Don't cache user-specific data without including the user ID in the key. This is the most common source of security bugs in Next.js apps.
  5. Use React.cache() for deduplication, not for persistence. It's a per-request optimization, not a cross-request cache. Don't try to use it as a global cache.
  6. Test cache invalidation. Write a test that mutates data, calls revalidateTag, and asserts the next request returns fresh data. Cache bugs are silent—they only show up in production.
  7. Start with unstable_cache, graduate to PPR. unstable_cache is stable enough for production today. PPR and use cache are the future, but they're experimental. Adopt them incrementally.

For more on building resilient Next.js applications, check out Tamiz's Insights and the main site for deep-dives on framework internals.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How do I cache data in a Server Component?

Wrap your data-fetching function with unstable_cache from next/cache, specifying key parts and a revalidate interval or tags. Then call that wrapped function from your Server Component. For per-request deduplication, additionally wrap it with React.cache().

Q: What's the difference between revalidateTag and revalidatePath?

revalidateTag invalidates Data Cache entries that carry a specific tag. It doesn't re-render pages. revalidatePath invalidates both the Data Cache entries used by that path and the Full Route Cache for that path, causing the page's static HTML to be regenerated on the next request. Use revalidateTag for data-layer invalidation and revalidatePath when you need the page HTML itself to update.

Q: How do I bypass the cache for a single request?

Call noStore() from next/cache at the top of your data-fetching function, or pass next: { revalidate: 0 } to a fetch call. For unstable_cache, you can't bypass per-call, so you'd need a separate uncached function.

title: Eliminating Sub-Millimeter Drift When Printing Barcode Label Grids from the Browser
description:
Anyone who has built an HTML/CSS sheet-label generator for 30-up Avery 5160 sheets or 4×6 direct-thermal shipping labels eventually hits vertical creep: row 1 aligns inside the die-cut border, while row 10 clips 3 millimeters below the perforation.

1. Why CSS Pixels Drift Across Operating Systems

Browser print engines rasterize or paginate DOM layouts through CSS reference pixels (1in = 96px) before handing the spool to the OS print dialog. Two silent mutations commonly ruin physical pitch accuracy:

  • Fit-to-Page Auto-Scaling: Chrome and Edge shrink printable boxes by 94%–97% whenever unprintable printer hardware margins intersect the CSS @page box.
  • Sub-Pixel Rounding Accumulation: An Avery 5160 cell is 2.625 in × 1.0 in with a horizontal pitch of 2.75 in. Rounding fractional CSS flex/grid tracks over 10 rows accumulates enough vertical error to cross the die-cut line.

2. Computing Directly in PostScript Vector Points (72 pt = 1 inch)

Generating native PDF streams client-side in WebAssembly/JavaScript bypasses DOM layout rounding completely. In the PDF coordinate system (origin at bottom-left), physical measurements convert deterministically:

const INCH_TO_PT = 72;
const MM_TO_PT = 72 / 25.4;

// Avery 5160 exact geometry on US Letter (612 x 792 pt)
const topMarginPt = 0.5 * INCH_TO_PT;     // 36 pt
const leftMarginPt = 0.1875 * INCH_TO_PT; // 13.5 pt
const colPitchPt = 2.75 * INCH_TO_PT;     // 198 pt
const rowPitchPt = 1.0 * INCH_TO_PT;      // 72 pt

3. Crisp Code 128 & EAN-13 Quiet Zones on 203 DPI Thermal Heads

Direct thermal printers (Zebra, Rollo, Dymo) print at 203 DPI (8 dots/mm). Rendering a barcode into a PNG canvas first introduces anti-aliased gray edge pixels that thermal printheads dither, causing handheld laser scanners to reject narrow bars. Emitting each Code 128 module as an unstroked filled PDF vector rectangle guarantees sharp 1-bit bar boundaries at any DPI.

For client-side CSV-to-PDF batch generation with zero cloud uploads, see the CSV and Excel barcode sheet builder on LabelQueue, or query exact template pitches programmatically via npx labelqueue-cli demo.

title: Claude for business: testing three Claude models as SQL agents on a CRM
description:
Claude for business decisions often come down to which model to put behind an agent, and this post shows how to settle that with a small test you can rebuild on your own data: an invented CRM with known traps, ground truth computed two ways, an agent loop with one read-only SQL tool, a scorer with a tolerance, and a cost per right answer instead of a cost per token. By the end you will be able to run the same comparison on your own questions and see what a right answer costs from each model. The trigger was the launch of [Claude Fable 5.2](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2) on 9 November, at $8 / $40 per million input and output tokens, twice [the list price](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing) of Opus 5.5. I had Claude Code build the test, and a GitHub workflow made the API calls. Everything below is from the real files, and every code block is trimmed from them. ![Dark cover dated 9 November 2026, kicker Claude News: Claude Fable 5.2 is here. Sonnet added up the pipeline right every time](https://brinvik.com/claude-news/2026-11-09-claude-fable-pipeline/brinvik-pipeline-cover-en-1920x1080.png) ## The setup in one paragraph Three models (Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5), the same 8 questions from an invented sales director, effort medium\, 2 runs per question per condition, and two conditions: with the export's column documentation and without it. That is 32 runs per model and 96 in all. Every call, every query and every answer is written to a JSONL file. The whole thing cost $9.58 at list price. ## Building a CRM with traps on purpose pack.py\ generates an invented Danish software firm, Saltholm Data ApS, deterministically, so the same seed always gives the same database. It has 150 live deals plus 12 archived copies left over from merged duplicates, amounts in 4 currencies, 9 deals with two CFOs in the contacts table, and 16 live deals that entered proposal more than once. Each of those is there because it makes a naive total wrong. The schema the models see, trimmed to the table that matters most: \sql CREATE TABLE deals (  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,  company\_id INTEGER REFERENCES companies(id),  owner\_id INTEGER REFERENCES users(id),  name TEXT,  pipeline TEXT,         -- 'new\_business' or 'renewal'  stage TEXT,            -- current stage: lead, qualified, proposal, negotiation, closed\_won, closed\_lost  amount REAL,           -- deal value in the deal's own currency  currency TEXT,         -- DKK, EUR, SEK or NOK  close\_date TEXT,       -- expected close date for open deals, actual close date for closed deals  archived INTEGER,      -- 1 = merged into another deal and kept for history only  merged\_into INTEGER    -- the deal this one was merged into, when archived = 1 ); \\ The other tables are deal\_contacts\ (deal, contact, role), deal\_line\_items\, stage\_history\ (deal, stage, entered_at), fx\_rates\ and users\. In the "without documentation" condition, the comments after --\ are stripped, so the model sees bare column names. ## Ground truth, computed twice truth.py\ computes the answer to every question twice: once in plain Python over the generated records, and once in SQL over the SQLite file. The script exits 1 if the two disagree by more than half a krone. For the CFO question, the SQL uses EXISTS\ so a deal with two CFOs counts once: \sql select sum(d.amount\*f.dkk\_per\_unit) from deals d join fx\_rates f on f.currency=d.currency where d.archived=0 and d.stage in ('lead','qualified','proposal','negotiation') and exists (select 1 from deal\_contacts c where c.deal\_id=d.id and c.role='CFO') \\ It also computes the naive answers, so you know what each trap would cost: DKK 12,527,857 instead of DKK 10,983,557 for the open pipeline without currency conversion (14% too big), DKK 11,772,774 with the archived copies counted (7%), and DKK 6,342,447 instead of DKK 5,083,337 when you join to contacts and sum (25%). ![Three horizontal bars on a light ground, one per trap. Each bar runs to a gold line at the true number and carries on in red: CFO rows counted twice gives 25 percent too much, currency not converted 14 percent, merged duplicates counted 7 percent](https://brinvik.com/claude-news/2026-11-09-claude-fable-pipeline/brinvik-pipeline-info-1-faelder-en-1600.jpg) ## The agent loop api\_job.py\ gives each model two tools: run\_sql\, which runs one SELECT against a read-only copy and returns at most 40 rows, and submit\_answer\, which takes the number, the SQL that produced it and a short explanation. The tool descriptions below are translated; the originals are in Danish, as is the question. \python TOOLS = \[    {"name": "run\_sql",     "description": "Run one SELECT against the CRM database (SQLite, read-only). "                    f"Returns at most {MAX\_ROWS} rows.",     "input\_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"sql": {"type": "string"}}, "required": \["sql"\]}},    {"name": "submit\_answer",     "description": "Submit your final answer: the number, the query that gave it and a short explanation.",     "input\_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {         "value": {"type": "number"}, "sql": {"type": "string"}, "forklaring": {"type": "string"}},         "required": \["value", "sql", "forklaring"\]}}, \] \\ The loop is the plain tool-use loop: call the model, run every run\_sql\ it asked for, send the results back, and stop when submit\_answer\ arrives or after 14 turns. Errors are recorded, never hidden. Every one of the 96 runs ended with an answer. The connection opens the database with mode=ro\, so a model that tries an UPDATE gets an error back instead of a changed answer key. ## Scoring with a tolerance score.py\ counts an answer as right when it is within half a percent of the truth: \python right = abs(val - t) / abs(t) <= 0.005 \\ Half a percent absorbs rounding to whole kroner and tiny exchange-rate differences, and nothing else. No trap in this dataset is that small: the smallest, joining the stage history on question 5 so that a deal which entered proposal twice in October counts twice, is about 4%. The scorer also checks every wrong answer against the naive totals, so a miss is labelled with the trap that caused it, or with none. ## Cost per right answer, not per token Cost is input and output tokens times list price, with thinking counted as output. Per run, Fable 5.2 cost 18.0 cents, Opus 5.5 9.3 and Sonnet 5.5 2.7. Divide by right answers instead of runs and you get the number that matters: 2.7 cents per right answer for Sonnet, 9.3 for Opus and 19.9 for Fable, more than seven times Sonnet. Fable also used about twice Sonnet's output tokens on the same questions, and averaged 21 seconds per answer against 7. ![Three columns on a light ground, one per model, with 32 dots each. Fable 5.2 has 29 gold dots and three red rings, Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 have 32 gold dots. Under each: 19.9, 9.3 and 2.7 cents per right answer, with a bar showing the difference](https://brinvik.com/claude-news/2026-11-09-claude-fable-pipeline/brinvik-pipeline-info-2-pris-en-1600.jpg) ## What the results were No model summed a trap in any of the 96 runs. All three left out archived copies every time and converted currency in every run that asked for kroner. Sonnet and Opus matched the answer key 32/32. Fable matched it 29/32. Fable's three misses were all question 5, "the deals that went into proposal in October". It counted only deals whose first entry into proposal was in October (17 deals, DKK 2,797,423) where the key counts every entry in October (22 deals, DKK 3,563,279). None of them was a summing trap: the SQL was correct for the reading it chose. In all 4 of its runs on that question, Fable's explanation named both readings and both numbers. Opus did it in 1 of 4, Sonnet in none. Sonnet's full marks on question 5 came from its reading matching my key. ## Taking the documentation away The counterfactual was the part I was least sure of. With the column notes stripped, Opus and Sonnet answered the same, and Fable got one more right (15/16 against 14/16), so the documentation made no difference you could measure here. Mean queries per answer went up a little: Sonnet 3.9 to 4.1, Opus 4.9 to 5.5, Fable 5.6 to 6.3. The models found archived\, the currency column and the contacts table by querying the data. The caveat is that the names were clear; a column called status\_2\ would be a different test. ## Running it without an API key in the repo The calls run in a GitHub Actions workflow that authenticates with workload identity federation, so no key exists anywhere: the client takes its identity from the workflow's federation settings, and the job only runs on the main branch by manual dispatch. verify.py\ then rebuilds the database from pack.py\, checks that the recorded copy matches it row for row, re-reads every run and writes the facts file every number in the write-up comes from. Doc set and bare set cost $4.72 and $4.86. ## Claude for business in practice: doing this on your own CRM 1. Pick five to ten questions you already know the answer to, and write the true number down before you start. 2. Give each model the schema, one read-only query tool and a submit tool that asks for the number, the SQL and an explanation. 3. Score with a tolerance, and label each miss with the trap it fell into, if any. 4. Divide cost by right answers. 5. Read the explanations, not just the numbers. That is where the ambiguous question showed up. Anthropic's own advice is to start with Opus 5.5 and move up or down as needed. On these eight questions Sonnet was as accurate as Opus at under a third of the price, so I would include Sonnet in your test; that is the advice of this one test, on invented data. The full write-up, with a demo of every run and the SQL each model wrote, is [the article testing Claude Fable 5.2 on a sales pipeline](https://brinvik.com/en/journal/claude-fable-5-2-pricing-sales-pipeline-test?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=2026-11-09-claude-fable-pipeline&utm_content=devto-en). There is a [Danish version of the pipeline test](https://brinvik.com/da/journal/claude-pris-fable-5-2-salgspipeline-test?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=2026-11-09-claude-fable-pipeline&utm_content=devto-da) too. If you want this set up against your own CRM, that is part of my [AI advisory work for sales and RevOps teams](https://brinvik.com/en/services/ai-advisory?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=2026-11-09-claude-fable-pipeline&utm_content=devto-service).

title: スマートグラス元年の前に、「どう見せるか」を設計する
description:
スマートグラス元年の前に、「どう見せるか」を設計する

今朝のXR業界ニュースが面白い。韓国のアイウェア大手Gentle Monsterが、Samsung・Googleと組んだAndroid XRスマートグラスを12月に発売すると発表し、Joaquin Phoenix主演の短編フィルムの予告編も公開した。

ハードウェアのニュースが続くと、つい「デバイスが普及すれば解決する」と考えがちだ。だが、エンジニアとして気になるのはむしろ逆で、スマートグラスが日常の視界に入り込むほど、「目そのものの機能」をどう訓練し、どう可視化するかというソフトウェア側の設計問題が前景化する。弱視（lazy eye / amblyopia）や両眼視機能の調整に課題を抱える成人は少なくない。従来は遮蔽（パッチ）や赤青メガネ、通院訓練が中心で、日常生活に組み込みにくいというUX上の制約があった。

ここで紹介したいのが、Seven Sports が開発した Amblyotube だ。VR上で視覚協調と注意のエクササイズを行うレクリエーション兼教育ソフトウェアで、Meta Quest向けに提供されている。アーキテクチャの面白さは、左右の目に異なる視覚ストリームを同時提示する点にある。YouTubeライクな動画コンテンツをそのまま「視覚のジム」に変換する発想だ。

実装上のポイントを整理すると：

  • 左右どちらの目を対象にするかを選択し、症状の程度に応じたプリセットやLogMAR視力チェックを利用できる
  • 優位眼には調整可能なデジタルブラー、弱視眼にはAI Sharpener（MFBF）が人物を検出して輪郭とハイライトを強調
  • マゼンタのフォーカスキューで両眼の融合（binocular fusion）を促し、立体視の手がかりを訓練

これは臨床の代替ではなく、補助的な視覚トレーニング／支援ツールという位置づけだ。1日30〜40分（最大1時間）、13歳以上が対象。ハードウェアの進化を待つだけではなく、体験の中身を自分で設計できる。そういう選択肢が増えていくことに、少し希望を感じている。

Meta Quest ストア: https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

title: What is actually making your PDF so big? Measure it in 20 lines of Python
description:
"Compress it" is the usual answer to a heavy PDF, but it's a guess. Before you change any export settings, it's worth knowing which objects take the bytes. With PyMuPDF that takes about 20 lines.

A test file that looks like real life

We built a 3 page PDF the way people actually make them:

  • page 1: a title and one 12 megapixel phone photo (4000 x 3000) placed 4 inches wide,
  • page 2: 30 lines of notes in two fonts, embedded in full (Arial and Georgia),
  • page 3: a letter-size page "scanned" in color at 300 DPI (2550 x 3300).

The file came out at 7.87 MB.

The script 

import os
import pymupdf  # pip install pymupdf

def breakdown(path):
    doc = pymupdf.open(path)
    total = os.path.getsize(path)
    images = fonts = 0
    for xref in range(1, doc.xref_length()):
        subtype = doc.xref_get_key(xref, "Subtype")[1]
        if subtype == "/Image":
            images += len(doc.xref_stream_raw(xref))
        for key in ("FontFile", "FontFile2", "FontFile3"):
            kind, value = doc.xref_get_key(xref, key)
            if kind == "xref":
                fonts += len(doc.xref_stream_raw(int(value.split()[0])))
    print(f"{path}: {total/1e6:.2f} MB")
    print(f"  images {images/1e6:.2f} MB ({images*100/total:.1f}%)")
    print(f"  fonts  {fonts/1e6:.2f} MB ({fonts*100/total:.1f}%)")

breakdown("report.pdf")

It walks every object in the cross reference table, adds up the raw (still compressed) stream length of image objects, and follows each font descriptor to its embedded font file. Whatever is left is page content, structure and metadata.

For our file:

report.pdf: 7.87 MB
  images 7.14 MB (90.6%)
  fonts  0.70 MB (8.8%)

The text people read was about 1% of the file. Deleting a page of notes would save a few kilobytes.

Turning bytes into a diagnosis: effective DPI

Image bytes alone don't tell you whether an image is too big. What matters is pixels per inch at the size it's drawn. PyMuPDF gives you both:

doc = pymupdf.open("report.pdf")
for page in doc:
    for info in page.get_image_info(xrefs=True):
        w_in = (info["bbox"][2] - info["bbox"][0]) / 72   # PDF points to inches
        dpi = info["width"] / w_in
        print(page.number + 1, info["width"], "x", info["height"], f"{dpi:.0f} dpi")

The phone photo came out at 1,000 DPI: 4000 pixels squeezed into 4 inches. Screens and office printers can't show more than about 150 to 300, so roughly 90% of those pixels are dead weight. That single image was 74% of the file.

Fonts: full vs subset

Embedded font names tell you if a font is subset. A subset font has a six letter tag in front, like BNJWSA+ArialMT; a full one doesn't. In our file Arial alone was over half a megabyte embedded in full. After a compression pass that subsets fonts, both fonts together dropped from about 696 KB to 29 KB, and the text was still real, selectable text.

What compression did to it

We ran the same file through Ghostscript based compression at three common levels:

Level Result Image resolution
screen 118 KB 72 DPI
ebook 273 KB 150 DPI
printer 1.73 MB higher

The "ebook" level (150 DPI) is the sensible default: 96.5% smaller and still fine on an office printer.

A rule of thumb

  • Images above about 70% of the file: downsample them. That's where nearly all the savings are.
  • Fonts above about 20%: they're embedded in full; subsetting fixes it.
  • Neither, and the file is still big: look for attachments, form fields and incremental saves (old versions of pages kept at the end of the file after each edit).

If you'd rather not run Python, we built the same breakdown into a browser tool: the PDF size analyzer splits a file into images, fonts, content, attachments and metadata, lists each image with its DPI, and reads the file locally without uploading it.

title: GPT-6.1 Terra now available on AI Gateway
description:
GPT-6.1 Terra from OpenAI is now available on AI Gateway.

GPT-6.1 Terra is a fast model for visual reasoning, computer use, and writing, and it improves on the previous Terra model in visual reasoning, factual accuracy, and coding. It suits high-volume work in documents and desktop apps, such as filling out forms, interpreting technical drawings, or entering invoice details into accounting software. OpenAI still recommends its larger GPT-6 models for the most complex coding tasks.

The model accepts text and images and returns text, with a context window of more than 1M tokens. It supports configurable reasoning effort, structured outputs, tool calling, and implicit and explicit prompt caching. For latency-sensitive work, fast mode is available as openai/gpt-6.1-terra-fast.

GPT-6.1 Terra works with the AI SDK, the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API, the Responses API, and coding agents connected to AI Gateway. Use openai/gpt-6.1-terra as the model name:

To use it in Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select openai/gpt-6.1-terra in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try GPT-6.1 Terra in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

You can view all language models available on AI Gateway.

title: Diagnose Vercel CLI setup problems with vercel doctor
description:
Vercel CLI now includes vercel doctor, which checks your setup and shows the command that fixes each problem it finds.

It checks the CLI version and install, your login and current team, the project link, and your project configuration in vercel.json. It also reports active incidents from the Vercel status page.

Each check reports OK, Warning, Failed, or Skipped. When vercel upgrade can't update the installed CLI, the install check shows where the CLI runs from and how to reinstall it.

Doctor runs without a login or a linked project, and it never prompts, logs in, or links a project, so coding agents can run it before guessing at a fix. Add --json to get each check's status and suggested commands as structured output.

Update to the latest CLI version and run vercel doctor to check your setup, or read the doctor command reference.

title: Smart Home i praksis: Når software møder elinstallationer
description:
Smart Home i praksis: Når software møder elinstallationer

Et smart home begynder ofte med noget enkelt.

En intelligent pære. En app, der styrer lyset. Eller en sensor, som registrerer bevægelse i gangen.

Det virker næsten som et almindeligt softwareprojekt. Du vælger enheder, forbinder dem til netværket og opretter automatiseringer.

Men et smart home består af mere end kode og trådløs kommunikation.

Bag den digitale styring findes fysiske installationer, strømforsyninger og elektrisk udstyr. Og netop grænsen mellem software og elinstallation er vigtig at forstå.

Her ser vi på, hvordan de forskellige dele arbejder sammen, og hvornår teknisk gør-det-selv-arbejde bør overlades til en fagperson.

Tre lag i et smart home

En enkel måde at forstå et smart home på er at opdele systemet i tre lag.

Lag Funktion Eksempel
Brugerflade Styring og automatisering App eller smart home-platform
Kommunikation Udveksling af data Wi-Fi, Zigbee eller Thread
Fysisk udstyr Udførelse af handlinger Pærer, sensorer og relæer

Lagene arbejder sammen, men de stiller forskellige krav.

En softwarefejl kan eksempelvis betyde, at en lampe ikke reagerer på en kommando.

En fejl i den elektriske installation kan derimod have betydning for sikkerheden.

Derfor bør fejlfinding begynde med at forstå, hvilket lag problemet hører til.

Eksempel: En lampe med automatisk styring

Forestil dig en lampe, der skal tænde, når en bevægelsessensor registrerer aktivitet.

Systemet kan beskrives sådan:

Bevægelsessensor
       |
       v
Smart Home Controller
       |
       v
Automatiseringsregel
       |
       v
Smart pære
       |
       v
Lys tændes

Selve automatiseringen kan være forholdsvis enkel.

Hvis sensoren registrerer bevægelse, sender systemet en kommando til lampen.

Men der er flere ting at tage højde for:

  • Kan lampen styres med den valgte platform?
  • Er kommunikationen stabil?
  • Hvad sker der, hvis internetforbindelsen forsvinder?
  • Kan lyset stadig betjenes manuelt?
  • Er det elektriske udstyr egnet til installationen?

De sidste spørgsmål handler ikke kun om software.

De handler også om den fysiske løsning.

Smart pære eller intelligent relæ?

Det kan være nyttigt at kende forskellen mellem to almindelige måder at styre belysning på.

Smart pære

En smart pære monteres i et kompatibelt lampeudtag eller en passende fatning.

Den kan typisk styres via en app eller en smart home-platform.

Fordelen er, at løsningen ofte kan tages i brug uden ændringer af den faste elinstallation.

Der kan dog være begrænsninger.

Hvis en almindelig vægafbryder afbryder strømmen til pæren, kan den ikke længere modtage digitale kommandoer.

Intelligent relæ

Et intelligent relæ kan bruges til at styre en elektrisk belastning.

Nogle relæer er beregnet til montering i eller som en del af den faste elinstallation.

Sådanne løsninger stiller krav til korrekt installation, elektrisk beskyttelse og produktets anvendelse.

Et relæ er ikke automatisk et gør-det-selv-produkt, bare fordi det kan konfigureres fra en app.

Hvis monteringen kræver ændring af den faste elinstallation, skal opgaven udføres af en virksomhed med den nødvendige autorisation.

Hvad sker der, når netværket svigter?

Et smart home bør ikke kun vurderes på, hvor godt det fungerer under normale forhold.

Det er også vigtigt at undersøge, hvad der sker, når noget ikke virker.

Forestil dig følgende situationer:

  1. Routeren genstarter.
  2. En sensor mister forbindelsen.
  3. Smart home-controlleren bliver utilgængelig.
  4. En cloudbaseret tjeneste stopper midlertidigt.
  5. En automatisering bliver aktiveret på det forkerte tidspunkt.

Disse situationer behøver ikke være farlige, men de kan påvirke systemets funktion.

Ved valg af udstyr bør man derfor undersøge, om centrale funktioner virker lokalt, og hvordan systemet opfører sig ved forbindelsesfejl.

Man bør ikke være afhængig af en enkelt app for at kunne bruge nødvendig belysning eller andre vigtige funktioner i hjemmet.

Dokumentation gør fejlfinding lettere

Mange smart home-projekter begynder med få enheder.

Efter et stykke tid kan systemet bestå af sensorer, controllere, pærer, smart plugs og flere forskellige kommunikationsprotokoller.

Så bliver dokumentation nyttig.

En enkel oversigt kan indeholde:

Oplysning Hvorfor den er nyttig
Enhedens navn Gør enheden lettere at identificere
Placering Viser, hvor udstyret er monteret
Kommunikationstype Hjælper ved netværksfejl
Platform Viser, hvilken controller der styrer enheden
Automatisering Forklarer, hvad enheden skal gøre
Afhængigheder Viser, hvilke andre enheder der skal fungere

Det er også en god idé at notere ændringer i systemet.

Hvis en automatisering holder op med at fungere, kan dokumentationen gøre det lettere at finde årsagen.

Men softwaredokumentation erstatter ikke den dokumentation, som kan være nødvendig for elektrisk installationsarbejde.

Hvornår kræver et smart home en elektriker?

Der er stor forskel på at konfigurere en app og at ændre den faste elinstallation.

Du kan normalt selv konfigurere smart home-software og tilslutte egnede produkter med almindelig stikprop.

Men nye faste installationer og mange ændringer af eksisterende elinstallationer kræver en autoriseret elinstallatørvirksomhed.

Det kan eksempelvis være relevant ved:

  • Etablering af nye faste stikkontakter.
  • Installation af fast tilsluttede styringsenheder.
  • Ændringer i den faste kabelføring.
  • Installationer, der kræver arbejde i eltavlen.
  • Udvidelser af eksisterende faste installationer.

Der findes særlige undtagelser for enkelte simple elopgaver. Den konkrete opgave skal derfor altid vurderes efter gældende danske regler.

Det er en god idé at planlægge den fysiske installation og softwarestyringen som to forskellige dele af projektet.

På den måde bliver det lettere at afklare både funktion, kompatibilitet og sikkerhed.

Et eksempel på bedre projektplanlægning

Forestil dig, at du vil automatisere belysningen i et hjemmekontor.

Før du køber udstyr, kan du arbejde med denne rækkefølge:

Trin 1: Beskriv behovet

Skal lyset tænde automatisk, dæmpes efter tidspunktet eller styres fra telefonen?

Trin 2: Undersøg eksisterende installationer

Kan løsningen fungere med eksisterende stikkontakter, lampeudtag og kompatible produkter?

Trin 3: Vælg kommunikation

Skal systemet bruge Wi-Fi eller en anden protokol? Undersøg enhedernes kompatibilitet og behovet for en hub.

Trin 4: Afklar eventuelt installationsarbejde

Hvis der er behov for ændringer i den faste elinstallation, skal en autoriseret elinstallatørvirksomhed inddrages.

Trin 5: Test funktionerne

Kontrollér, at automatiseringer fungerer som forventet, og at brugerne kan betjene udstyret på en praktisk måde.

Trin 6: Dokumentér opsætningen

Notér de vigtigste enheder, deres placering og de regler, der styrer dem.

Denne fremgangsmåde gør det lettere at undgå unødvendige indkøb og tekniske overraskelser.

Elektriske installationer og tekniske løsninger i Næstved

For boligejere og mindre virksomheder kan smart home-teknologi være relevant ved renovering, ændringer i belysning og nye tekniske behov.

Sydsjællands El ApS er en autoriseret elinstallatørvirksomhed med base på Lov Enghavevej 10 i Næstved.

Virksomheden arbejder blandt andet med elinstallationer, renovering og data- og netværksinstallationer for private og erhverv.

Hvis du planlægger ændringer, der berører den faste elinstallation, kan du læse mere om elektrikerhjælp i Næstved hos Sydsjællands El ApS.

Det er vigtigt at afklare den konkrete opgave med virksomheden, før du vælger produkter eller planlægger installationsarbejde.

Den bedste automatisering er også praktisk uden appen

Et smart home skal gøre hverdagen lettere.

Det kræver ikke nødvendigvis mange sensorer eller avancerede regler.

Ofte giver enkle funktioner mest værdi, når de er stabile, nemme at forstå og passer til brugernes behov.

Software kan styre, hvornår noget skal ske.

Men det er stadig den fysiske installation, der skal understøtte løsningen på en sikker og pålidelig måde.

Når de to dele planlægges sammen, får du et bedre grundlag for at bygge et smart home, der fungerer i praksis.

title: Vercel CI is now in beta
description:
You can now run CI for your Turborepo with one line of configuration.

In Vercel's internal repositories, our wait time from git push to "CI passed" is 2-6x shorter, dramatically improving our CI's ability to keep up with our coding agents.

To get started, prompt your agent in your repo:

Each task marked with a ci tag runs on every push. Vercel CI automatically takes care of:

  • Task caching with Vercel Remote Cache

  • Installing dependencies once per run

  • Caching dependencies across code updates
